This is the strongest academic warrant this chapter found for a shared, place- or sector-level evidence base rather than every venue proving its own impact.

Toby Lowe's "paradox of outcomes" — "the more we measure, the less we understand" — argues that "a focus on outcome information distorts both the priorities and practice of organizations who deliver such support, resulting in poorer results for those most in need"[abstract or summary only]; his later field paper quotes a practitioner, "Everybody manipulates the outcomes it just wouldn't be honest", and proposes that the purpose of performance management in complex systems should be "to increase the adaptive capacity of the complex system under its purview" — building people's capacity to judge, rather than holding them to targets. And Malin Arvidson and colleagues on social return on investment: "The most common reason for charities to undertake an SROI is to attract funding" within "a competitive search for resources"; "Those carrying out SROI can therefore use their discretion to decide which cost to use"; the ratio serves "as a tool to close a credibility gap between the third sector and funders" while lending "unintentional support to a current dominant business-case perspective." Route one, seen from the grantee's side.

What turns a grant

Arts Council England's own equality analysis of its 2023–26 investment programme describes a two-stage process: applicants are scored on "quality of the applicant's contribution to, and evidence of ability to demonstrate progress against, the Arts Council's Outcomes and Investment Principles", and then a "final balanced portfolio" is built considering "range of artforms and disciplines", "geographical spread" and diverse-led representation. The decision is made twice; a case can score well and lose to a portfolio constraint. That is a decision structure, not an evidence structure, and a dashboard cannot address it except by showing the geography. Panels also reward the known — the pattern sociologists call the Matthew effect, after the gospel line about those who have being given more. A study of fifty years of Flemish arts-grant decisions found "those who are already successful are more likely to receive state support than their less well-known colleagues"[abstract or summary only], and a systematic review of grant criteria across twelve studies found peers assessing "the applicant's reputation, past performance, academic background, skills, and personality" among their criteria. On how foundation officers weigh relationships against reports, this chapter found no robust UK study; "relationships beat reports" is well supported by practitioner survey and thinly by peer review, and is marked as such.

What this section settles

Belief four — monetise it and it will be funded — is half of a picture. The funder's ladders start with a convincing account and admit lived experience; the investor's grammar asks what matters to the people experiencing the outcome; the Treasury's ladder prefers pounds and then grades them by causal design. Funders require more than they use and increasingly want a conversation. And the job of proving impact — as opposed to outputs and outcomes — belongs, on the best argument available, to whoever can see the whole system. For a sector that is many small organisations, that is the case for a shared evidence base, and a dashboard is one of the forms a shared evidence base can take.

8 · The advocate and the coalition

An advocate or trade body reads a dashboard for ammunition, and there is no point pretending otherwise. Sabatier's framework, in section 4, says that technical information is used "primarily in an 'advocacy' fashion" and that coalitions "learn on their own terms". The question for this book is not whether that is regrettable but what it means for a display that several coalitions will read.

Three things from the sources. First, a coalition's shared evidence changes secondary beliefs — how much, how, who delivers — far more readily than anyone's core; a dashboard that sets out to convert an opponent will fail, and one that sets out to settle the secondary questions across coalitions can succeed. Second, the forum matters as much as the data: cross-coalition learning happens where analysts from both sides accept the same figures, which means the figures must be checkable by the other side's analysts, not only persuasive to one's own. Chapter 1's rule that a dashboard is also a data release is, here, a condition of being believed by people who do not already agree. Third, the government reader's trust runs through people: in an Institute for Government roundtable, "Civil servants often rely on personal relationships with academics. These can be helpful in establishing the trust needed to communicate freely", "Ultimately, ministers set the tone for the standard of evidence expected in submissions – and who is trusted and brought into decision making", and, on evidence as an institutional responsibility, "Everyone owns this issue, and so no one does." The Parliament study's finding that charities understand "the timing and the scheduling and what is going to be helpful" is the same point: the advocates who succeed have a relationship and a calendar.

There is an ethical line in this section, and the sources draw it from both sides. The Centre for Cultural Value asks for "positive and actionable change over empty justification and advocacy". Parkhurst's issue bias says the choice of what to count is itself a political act. The UK Statistics Authority's letter about £350 million is the regulator telling an advocate that a true-ish number used for a purpose it cannot bear is "a clear misuse of official statistics". And the headline-to-caveat decay of section 6 is the mechanism by which an honest report becomes a dishonest slide. The distinction this book carries is between numbers for understanding and numbers for advocacy: the first are produced with their caveats and released with their data; the second are selected from the first for a room. A sector's dashboard can only be the first kind, because it will be read by the people the second kind is used against. That is a Nightlife Culture position, consistent with the Code of Practice Chapter 1 adopted, and it has a cost: the dashboard will sometimes show a number the sector would rather it did not. Chapter 10 takes up when that cost falls on a community rather than on an argument.

On how British trade bodies' shared evidence is actually received by government, this chapter found no dedicated study and says so rather than stretching Cairney.

9 · The scene as reader

The last row of the table is the one every other row talks about. The people who make the night — artists, DJs, promoters, crews, venue staff — are the subject of most of the data a nightlife dashboard would hold, and they are also readers of it, with a decision of their own: whether to take part, whether to trust it, whether they can see themselves in it. The brief says a dashboard fails "if they do not recognise their place within the front-end interface." This section asks what the evidence says about lived experience as evidence, and whether recognition is a legitimate test.

Admitted, then re-filed

Lived experience is now named as evidence in principle by nearly every reader in this chapter. The National Lottery Community Fund lists "people with lived experience" among its experts. The investor's first dimension asks "how important the outcome is to the people and communities experiencing it". Parliament's committees, a fellowship study found, show "a growing role of lived experience, an emphasis on diversity of political views and witnesses' representativeness" — and an unresolved lack of "clarity regarding the purpose of 'lived experience'". The theoretical case for treating it as evidence is Jennifer Smith-Merry's: validity in evidence-based policy "is frequently conceptualised in terms of rigour deriving from scientific studies which adhere to highly structured processes", while knowledge from lived experience "is characterised by its tacit nature, unstructure and difficulty in transferring from one actor to another"; her proposal is that "validity should be similarly contextualised, with validity coming not from the rules of policy but from the context in which knowledge is enacted."[abstract or summary only]

What happens in practice is the finding. Clementine Hill O'Connor and Hayley Bennett studied three Scottish Government cases — a small base, read here through the authors' published summary — and found a People's Panel's reflections treated as "qualitative data to supplement official evidence", Social Security Experience Panels "instrumentalised as user-testing and data collection", and an advisory board framed as engagement: participation "shaped by governance-led processes that channel participation into institutional priorities", valued as "authentic knowledge" and then reshaped through "institutional norms". Lived experience is admitted at the door and re-filed, inside, as a supplement — a footnote to the statistics it was meant to stand beside. A dashboard that collects a scene's testimony and places it in a panel labelled "voices" beside the numbers has done the same thing. The scholarly caution runs the other way too: Ian McIntosh and Sharon Wright warn of "assumed authenticity" and "risks of essentialising" — the fact that someone was there does not make what they say representative, and a dashboard that treats one voice as the scene is making the opposite error.[abstract or summary only]

Participation, control and voice

The participatory-evaluation tradition distinguishes two reasons to involve the people a programme is about. In Bradley Cousins and Elizabeth Whitmore's framing, practical participatory evaluation is "a practical approach to broadening decision making and problem solving through systematic inquiry", and transformative participatory evaluation is about "reallocating power in the production of knowledge and promoting social change"; they differ in "control, level, and range of participation." David Fetterman's empowerment evaluation is "the use of evaluation concepts, techniques, and findings to foster improvement and self-determination", with "Community ownership" and "Community knowledge" among its principles. Both are read here through a reference summary rather than the originals. The slogan that travels with this literature, "Nothing About Us Without Us", came into English-language disability activism, James Charlton records, from South Africa in 1993, where two leaders of Disabled People South Africa "had heard [it] used by someone from Eastern Europe"; its "power derives from its location of the source of many types of (disability) oppression and its simultaneous opposition to such oppression in the context of control and voice." Control and voice — not consultation. A dashboard that consults a scene and then decides what to show has met the letter and missed the point.

When does community-produced data become evidence that an official reader will accept? A study of citizen-generated air-quality data by Sachit Mahajan and colleagues is the most concrete answer found: "citizen-generated data is often questioned and challenged by scientists and policymakers"; "data requirements of CS [citizen science] projects don't always match the requirements of policymakers due to very specific project goals"; and success requires that "all stakeholders co-develop the research agendas, the data quality standards, and clearly outline how the data would feed into the decision-making process." The standards and the route to decision are agreed first. That is the same sequence Chapter 1 found for boundary objects — the common ground before the screen — arriving from a different literature.

Is recognition a test?

The brief's failure condition — the scene does not recognise its place — has a methodological name. In qualitative research it is member checking: taking the account back to the people it is about and asking whether they recognise it. Yvonna Lincoln and Egon Guba called it "the most crucial technique for establishing credibility", giving participants "the opportunity to correct errors" — a line this chapter has only through a secondary source. Linda Birt and colleagues then asked whether it is "a tool to enhance trustworthiness or merely a nod to validation", and found it is often the latter: a line in a methods section, a yes/no sign-off; their alternative, synthesised member checking, gives participants "the opportunity to engage with, and add to, interview and interpreted data" — a dialogue that can change the account, not a confirmation of it.[abstract or summary only] Birt and colleagues propose synthesised member checking as a method and as a critique of the nod; in their own study, returning to the data "proved unnecessary", though the check added data and a new concept, so the dialogue that changes the account rests on this chapter's reading, not on Birt's demonstration.

So the answer the sources support is precise. Recognition is a legitimate test of credibility — whether the account is trustworthy to the people it describes — and not of accuracy — whether the numbers are right, which is tested by the methods of Chapters 4 to 7. And it is a test only when the recognising can change the thing recognised. A scene shown a finished dashboard and asked "do you see yourself?" is being offered a nod. A scene whose answer alters what the next release shows is being offered member checking. The brief's failure condition is therefore a design sequence, not a design feature: the check happens before the release, and the route from "no" to a change is part of the dashboard.

10 · What holds true regardless

The candidate canonical truths this chapter contributes, each with its kind and firmness. Later chapters test them; the closing chapter confirms or demotes them.

  1. There is no reader in general. Each reader makes a different decision, is trained or required to accept different evidence, and keeps a different clock; the same display is graded by all of them at once, and the first screen is always in somebody's grammar. Reading of the whole chapter. Fixed (sequence); the design consequence — name each reader, decision, evidence rule and clock, and choose openly whose grammar comes first — is the rule that carries it.
  2. To the official reader a dashboard is monitoring, not evaluation, and on the evidence ladders in common use it stands alone on the first or second rung. It can show that a metric moved; it cannot by itself show that the intervention moved it; the climb needs a comparison it can host but not supply. Standard (Magenta Book 2026; Maryland SMS; Nesta; EEF). Fixed (requirement).
  3. The benefit-cost ratio is not the decision; the Treasury's own order is pounds, then numbers, then words; and who benefits is now a required question. Standard (Green Book 2026; Green Book Review 2025). Fixed (requirement).
  4. Wellbeing becomes pounds by one official route, and that route is graded by causal design. A marginal change in a place's average life satisfaction is the rung marked "less confidence". Standard (Wellbeing Guidance 2021). Fixed (requirement).
  5. What readers say moves them is access, timeliness, relevance and relationship, not rigour — and the field knows this mostly from self-report. Evidence (Oliver et al.; 145 studies). Fixed (statement of the record).
  6. At local level, local beats rigorous, and an elected member's evidence is their ward. Evidence (Kneale; Kelly; Woodall). Fixed (requirement).
  7. Readers triage by the credibility of the source and do not sort research by method. Evidence (Kenny et al., n = 157). Fixed (requirement).
  8. Charts persuade the undecided through the information they carry, not by looking scientific; in one study they did worse than a table with readers already opposed. Evidence (Pandey; Dragicevic & Jansen[abstract or summary only]; Markant[abstract or summary only]). The first clause Fixed (statement of the record); the reversal Adaptable — a hypothesis to test, not yet a rule.
  9. Numbers move belief; stories move intention; both weakly. The identifiable victim is not safe; what survives is that people do not scale with magnitude and do respond to a fraction of a group they can picture. Evidence (Zebregs; Lee & Feeley[abstract or summary only]; Maier et al.; Jenni & Loewenstein). Fixed (statement of the record).
  10. Rankings act on the ranked, not the reader. Evidence (Espeland & Sauder; Marshall[abstract or summary only]; Cochrane 2018). Fixed (requirement).
  11. The persuasive lever in a map is the denominator; the map itself did not reliably teach. Evidence (Engel et al.; Thorpe et al. — two large US studies of static maps). Fixed (statement of the record); as a rule, Adaptable until tested on interactive maps.
  12. Quantified uncertainty is cheap and vague uncertainty expensive, at scale; authors omit it anyway, for reasons their own model calls editorial. Evidence (Kerr et al., n = 10,519; Hullman). Fixed (requirement) — strengthens Chapter 1's truth 8.
  13. A display's effect on behaviour is real: modest for the individual reader, large in aggregate, and never the whole decision. Two per cent; five to seven points; d = 0.09 — and the clearest field result credits clear statistics at the time of choice, not the format. Evidence (Allcott; Hastings & Weinstein; van der Linden et al.). Fixed (statement of the record).
  14. A place indicator built from secondary data is a description of a place and not evidence of an intervention — the concept is fuzzy, the data are proxies at the wrong geography, the indicator rewards the already-successful — so the construct is defined before the proxy is chosen. Reading (Markusen; Jackson et al.), with ArtPlace's abandonment as corroboration. Fixed (requirement); the construct before the proxy, Fixed (sequence).
  15. Every valuation headline carries caveats that the next release drops; the same survey can value the same good thirty-fold apart by method; the dashboard is the last place in the chain the caveats can still be shown. Reading (Fields in Trust; Sport England; Fujiwara). Fixed (requirement).
  16. Property value is the contested indicator: success to the investor, displacement to the resident. Reading (Markusen; What Works Growth). Fixed (requirement).
  17. Funders require more evidence than they use; their ladders start with a convincing account; the conversation is the reporting event. Evidence (NPC 2012, 2013; CEP) and Practice (TNLCF; Esmée; Nesta). Fixed (statement of the record).
  18. Impact is measured at the level that can see the system; single organisations measure outputs and outcomes. Reading of Ebrahim & Rangan. Adaptable — a strong default for a sector of small organisations.
  19. Coalitions learn on their own terms; evidence moves secondary beliefs; cross-coalition agreement needs figures the other side's analysts can check. Reading (Sabatier via Cairney). Fixed (requirement); Chapter 1's data-release rule is its condition.
  20. Lived experience is admitted in principle and re-filed as a supplement in practice; its standing is earned when standards and the route to decision are agreed first. Evidence (Hill O'Connor & Bennett — three cases; Mahajan et al.) and Reading (Smith-Merry[abstract or summary only]). Fixed (requirement); the agreeing first, Fixed (sequence).
  21. Recognition is a test of credibility, not accuracy, and only when it is a dialogue that can change the account. Reading (Lincoln & Guba, secondary; Birt et al.[abstract or summary only], a method and a critique rather than a demonstration). Fixed (sequence).

11 · Where the choice is yours

Which reader comes first. The table in section 1 has eight rows and a first screen has one. Whose grammar does the dashboard speak natively, with the others reached through layers and translations? The chapter's own sources say this cannot be dodged: the choice of what to count is made in somebody's grammar (Parkhurst), and the other readers read through it (Sabatier; Kahan). The evidence says the official reader's grammar (monitoring, social value, the ladder) is the one that will be used to discount the others, and the scene's is the one that will be used to judge whether the thing is real. That is a trade, and it is a Nightlife Culture decision; what is Fixed is that it is made and shown, not hidden under a claim of neutrality. Adaptable in the choice; Fixed in declaring it.

Monetise, quantify or describe. The Treasury's order permits all three. Route one wins rooms and loses credibility among people who check; route two wins the methods appendix and loses the press release. Doing both and labelling which is which is this chapter's default. Adaptable; the labelling is Fixed.

How much to frame for the hostile reader. One study says the table; another says the numerate hostile reader will read it their way regardless. Whether a dashboard offers a plain-table view as a first-class citizen, and for whom, is a design choice with a thin evidential basis that the prototype can thicken. Adaptable.

Where lived experience sits. In a panel beside the numbers (the re-filing), woven through the account as its frame (the harder design), or as the route by which the account can be changed (member checking as a feature). Adaptable in form; the dialogue that can change the account is Fixed.

Which number to show the investor. Property value, footfall and business births move the inward-investment reader and read as displacement to the resident. Whether to show them, and with what framing and company, is a choice to be made openly. Adaptable; showing the choice is Fixed.

Whether to keep the problem documented between windows. Kingdon's "special problem well-documented" implies a dashboard that is maintained when nobody is asking, which is a cost. Whether that is the dashboard's job or a report's is the choice. Adaptable.

12 · What this means for a nightlife dashboard

An illustration, not a specification.

The Vibe Map's brief names three groups who will test it — policymakers and politicians; advocates and trade bodies; funders and investors — with the people who make the night as co-developers. Read through this chapter, those are not three audiences but at least seven graders, and the first thing the illustration does is refuse to collapse them — while admitting that the first screen will be in one grader's grammar, and that choosing which is the studio's decision to make in the open.

The officer will read any panel showing a measure moving over time as monitoring, and will be right. The honest form of a nightlife dashboard, to that reader, is a well-documented account of what happens in a place's night time culture — the Magenta Book's "How are our success metrics changing over time?" — that links, where an evaluation exists, to the evaluation, and never implies a counterfactual it does not have. That is not a weakness to be designed around; it is the only claim the official grammar lets a dashboard make, and made cleanly it is already more than most sectors offer. Where the sector wants to say we caused this, the dashboard is the place to host the comparison, not to assert it.

The councillor will look for the ward. A map that cannot show the member's own patch at the scale they recognise will be discounted in favour of what the ward told them last Thursday, and the evidence says that is a rational thing for a councillor to do. The place reader will look for the seventeen indicators they already have and find none of them; the dashboard's job with that reader is translation — not into their currency, which the wellbeing valuations show is a route with a price, but into their habit, as Gehl did: counts of people, as ordinary as traffic counts, at the geography they plan at. The developer will look for anything that moves gross development value or costs them money, and the dashboard must decide, openly, whether it is willing to show property value and in what company.

The funder will look for the account first — Nesta's Level 1, the narrative that opens the place-based framework — and will know perfectly well that the numbers behind it are Level 2. A sector of small organisations cannot each prove impact; the chapter's best argument says the place can. A nightlife dashboard is, in Ebrahim and Rangan's terms, a candidate for the shared evidence base that measures at the level that can see the system — which is the strongest reason it should exist and the strongest constraint on what it claims.

The advocate will take numbers from it into rooms; the dashboard must therefore release them with their caveats and their data, so that the other coalition's analyst can check them and the UK Statistics Authority never has reason to write a letter. And the scene will ask whether it recognises itself, which is the one test on this list that cannot be passed after the fact: the recognising has to happen before release, and the route from "that's not us" to a changed next release has to be part of the thing. The brief's months of convening are, in this chapter's terms as in Chapter 1's, the method.

Three warnings travel with the illustration. The handsome chart may read as advocacy to exactly the reader the sector most needs to move; a plain-table view is a persuasion strategy with one study behind it, and the Vibe Map's first readers are the place to find out whether it holds. A "voices" panel is the re-filing of lived experience the Scottish cases describe, and the brief's recognition test asks for more. And the single killer number — the night time economy is worth £X — moves the thing it states a lot and the policy a little, and arrives in the council chamber with its caveats already gone; the dashboard that produced it is the last place they could have been kept.

The rules

Kind and tier as in Chapter 0. The Treasury's manuals are quoted in their current editions, the Green Book of 5 February 2026 and the Magenta Book of May 2026; the editions most practitioners still have on their shelves are withdrawn.

Rule Why Kind Tier Source
Name each reader, the decision they make, the evidence they are obliged to accept and the clock they keep, before design; declare whose grammar the first screen speaks Readers grade by contradictory rules; the first screen is always in somebody's grammar; a display built for a reader in general is graded by none Reading Fixed (sequence) Section 1; Oliver 2014; Kelly 2017; Parkhurst 2017
Label every panel as monitoring or as evaluation; never imply a counterfactual the display does not have The official reader's grammar makes the distinction and discounts the breach Standard Fixed (requirement) Magenta Book 2026
State where a claim stands on the evidence ladder when it will be read by a funder or a What Works body A before-and-after is Maryland Level 1; data showing change is Nesta Level 2; the reader will score it so Standard Fixed (requirement) WWC Growth SMS; Nesta 2013
Follow the Treasury's order — monetise, quantify, describe — and label which is which; never present a benefit-cost ratio as the decision The order is mandatory guidance; the ratio is not the decision Standard Fixed (requirement) Green Book 2026; Green Book Review 2025
Any wellbeing value carries its design grade and its range (£10,000–£16,000 per WELLBY) The Treasury grades wellbeing evidence by causal design Standard Fixed (requirement) Wellbeing Guidance 2021
Show "who benefits" — distribution across groups and places — as a panel, not a footnote Distributional analysis is now a required question Standard Fixed (requirement) Green Book 2026 ch. 7
Show the reader's own geography — the ward, the patch — at the scale they plan at Local beats rigorous; the member's evidence is their ward Evidence Fixed (requirement) Kneale 2017; Kelly 2017
Make the source checkable before making the chart persuasive Readers triage by source credibility first and do not sort by method Evidence Fixed (requirement) Kenny et al. 2017; IfG 2020
Design release to the reader's calendar; keep the problem documented between windows Timing is the most prominent barrier and a strategy, not a circumstance Evidence + Reading Adaptable Oliver 2014; Cairney & Kwiatkowski 2017; Kingdon via Mintrom & True
Offer a plain-table view as a first-class route for the reader already opposed In one study, tables out-persuaded charts among the hostile in all three topics; the authors call the result uncertain Evidence Adaptable Pandey et al. 2014
Never add a chart for its air of science; add it for the information it carries The trivial-graph effect did not replicate; and the design system's own rule that strong design must never make weak evidence look stronger Evidence[abstract or summary only] + Nightlife Culture Fixed (requirement) Dragicevic & Jansen 2018[abstract or summary only]; Style Guide v1.5
Name the denominator on every map and comparison, and show the alternative Count versus rate moved perception by nine points; the fraction of a group is the persuasive unit Evidence Fixed (requirement) Engel et al. 2022; Jenni & Loewenstein 1997
Treat a league table as acting on the ranked; never present one as a reader's decision aid without intervals Public performance data barely moves consumer choice and reorganises the ranked Evidence Fixed (requirement) Cochrane 2018; Marshall et al. 2000[abstract or summary only]; Espeland & Sauder 2007; Ch 1
Show uncertainty as a numeric range; never as a verbal hedge; never omit it to protect the signal Numeric ranges cost almost nothing at n = 10,519; omission is an editorial choice Evidence Fixed (requirement) Kerr et al. 2023; Hullman 2020
Never let a place indicator be read as evidence of an intervention; mark descriptions as descriptions Fuzzy concept, proxy data, rewards the already-successful Reading Fixed (requirement) Markusen 2013; ArtPlace 2014
Define the construct before choosing the proxy Or the proxy defines it Reading Fixed (sequence) Jackson et al. 2006
Carry every valuation's caveats on the face of the display The next release will drop them; this is the last place they survive Reading Fixed (requirement) Fields in Trust 2018; Sport England 2020/2025
Decide openly whose reading a property-value or footfall figure serves, and show the choice Success to the investor; displacement to the resident Reading Fixed (requirement) Markusen 2013; WWC Growth 2014
Claim outputs and outcomes for organisations; claim impact only at the level that can see the system Impact belongs to funders, coalitions and places Reading Adaptable Ebrahim & Rangan 2014
Release numbers with their data and caveats so an opposing coalition's analyst can check them Cross-coalition learning needs shared, checkable figures Reading + Standard Fixed (requirement) Sabatier via Cairney; Code of Practice (Ch 1)
Agree data standards and the route to decision with the scene before collecting Community data earns standing when both are co-agreed first Evidence Fixed (sequence) Mahajan et al. 2022
Do not place lived experience in a panel beside the numbers as a supplement That is the re-filing three Scottish cases describe Evidence (three cases) + Reading Fixed (requirement); where lived experience sits, and in what form: Adaptable Hill O'Connor & Bennett 2026
Recognition is checked before release, as a dialogue that can change the next release Member checking is a credibility test only when it can alter the account Reading Fixed (sequence) Lincoln & Guba (secondary); Birt et al. 2016[abstract or summary only] (a method and a critique; the dialogue is this chapter's reading)
Numbers for understanding, not numbers for advocacy: produce with caveats, release with data A sector's dashboard is read by the people advocacy numbers are used against Nightlife Culture Fixed (requirement) Section 8; UKSA 2017
Which reader comes first (declared); monetise/quantify/describe; the plain-table view; where lived experience sits; which numbers the investor sees; documenting between windows Open choices with named trade-offs — Adaptable Section 11
Register, imagery, metaphor Free, within the design system — Decorative —

What proves a break works

If you must break a Fixed rule above — imply an effect without a comparison, show a monetised headline without its caveats, present a ranking as advice, show property value without saying whose reading it serves — the test is the same: find the reader who grades by the opposite rule and show them. Give the impact claim to a What Works analyst and ask what level it is. Give the £-headline to the person who wrote the report it came from and ask if they recognise their caveats. Give the property-value panel to a resident of the street and ask what it means to them. Give the "voices" panel to the people quoted in it and ask whether they could change it. If the break survives that, log it in the deviation entry Chapter 16 describes (what rule, why, for whom, what proved it). If it does not, it was a reader you forgot.

What this chapter could not settle

  • Whether one display can be legible to all readers is unproven; the chapter's own sources say the first screen is always in somebody's grammar. The rule therefore requires that the choice of grammar be made and declared.
  • No reader was interviewed for a chapter about readers, and two rows of the table have no study behind them. Section 1 says so; the table is the first thing to validate.
  • Hastings & Weinstein is routinely cited as evidence that re-sorting into a ranking changes decisions; the authors say the format added little. The chapter quotes their own conclusion and moves the finding from "rankings" to "timing".

Checklist

  • Each reader is named with their decision, their evidence rule and their clock; whose grammar the first screen speaks is written down
  • Every panel is labelled monitoring or evaluation; no implied counterfactual
  • Evidence-ladder level is stated where a funder or What Works body will read it
  • Monetised, quantified and described benefits are labelled as such; no benefit-cost ratio presented as the decision
  • Wellbeing values carry their design grade and range
  • Distribution — who benefits, by group and place — is a panel
  • The reader's own geography is reachable at the scale they plan at
  • Source, method and data are checkable before any chart is persuasive
  • Release timing follows the readers' calendars; the problem is documented between windows
  • A plain-table view exists for the reader already opposed
  • Every map and comparison names its denominator and shows the alternative
  • No league table presented as a decision aid without intervals
  • Uncertainty shown as a numeric range; never omitted to protect the signal
  • Place indicators marked as description, never as attribution
  • Constructs defined before proxies chosen
  • Valuation caveats on the face
  • Property-value and footfall figures carry a stated reading
  • Impact claimed only at the level that can see the system
  • Data standards and the route to decision agreed with the scene before collection
  • No lived-experience "supplement" panel; recognition checked before release as a dialogue that can change it

03The canonical truths of showing data

Seven rules that survived testing, and the record beneath them.

Dashboard Design · Part 0: Foundations

In this chapter

Reading this chapter. This is one chapter of Dashboard Design, Nightlife Culture's research book on how evidence becomes a display a reader can trust, read and act on. The studio ("the house" in some chapters) is Nightlife Culture, a creative policy studio; the brief is its founder Carly Heath's commission for the book, and her eight ways a dashboard fails, the failure register, run through it. The Vibe Map, the studio's prototype for showing a place's nightlife culture, appears only as an illustration, never as a specification. "Version 1" is the book's archived first draft, whose positions this version re-tests against the sources. Every rule carries a kind (where it comes from: Standard, Evidence, Reading, Practice or Nightlife Culture) and a tier (how firm it is: Fixed, Adaptable or Decorative); Chapter 0 explains both, and the three senses of Fixed: a requirement that can be checked, a sequence whose order is the hard line, and a statement of the record. A dagger (†) marks a source read at the authors' abstract or summary only; "secondary" a quotation reached through a named reproduction; "(read once)" a quotation returned on a single reading and not confirmed by a second. Chapter 0 holds the glossary of the words the chapters share; each chapter lists its own coinages before its sources.

The question

Of everything the field says about how to show data, what has actually been tested, what survived, and which of the survivors are hard lines?

The 60-second version

The field that shows data runs on rules, and most of them were never tested. This chapter went looking for the ones that were. The short list that survives is shorter than the textbooks and more useful.

So the canonical truths are these: choose the comparison, not the chart; put the message in words at the top and labels at the mark; never let colour carry meaning alone; start bars at zero and say so when a line does not; show uncertainty as something countable; assume a glance, a phone and a sceptic; and treat every default as advice you are giving.

The eye reads position most accurately, then length, then angle, and area and colour worst — a 1984 finding replicated three times since. But its authors called the bottom half "partly conjectural"; pie charts turn out not to be read by angle at all; and the gaps between chart types are smaller than the gaps between people. The hierarchy settles which form to use for a precise comparison and nothing about memory, understanding or trust. The eye pulls a statistic from a whole chart in a glance and makes one comparison at a time, slowly; everything in design that works, works by choosing the comparison for the reader.

Words carry the message. People look at the title first and longest, remember it when they say they do not, and let it decide what the chart "showed" — even when it contradicts the picture. Readers want more text on a chart than designers give them, and the trend belongs in the title. Nobody has run the obvious experiment on legends against direct labels; the practice stands on a meta-analysis from instructional design and on how often the eye goes back to the key. In the only large eye-tracking study of real dashboards, the small words beside each tile drew more attention than the big words above everything, and a plain number was the most-looked-at object on the screen.

The first impression forms in fifty milliseconds and is about appeal, not understanding; what drives it is simplicity and looking like what you claim to be. Ornament that does not touch the data mark is more memorable and not less accurate; the study that started the argument rested on ten people; and a later experiment found that removing clutter makes a chart look professional while adding a message headline and one highlight is what gets the point remembered. A truncated bar axis exaggerates even when it is labelled and even after people have been taught about it. On a log scale, four readers in ten answered a basic question correctly; on a linear scale, eight in ten. The famous "85% ignore interactives" is one newsroom's click rate on one button; on real public pages, the median use of an optional control is zero, and mobile readers touch less and leave sooner. A default view shifts choices toward it (d = 0.68 across 58 datasets), partly because it is read as the designer's recommendation, and it anchors where people look. "Overview first" is a reminder its author wrote to himself, cited 52 times and validated never; people like overviews reliably and are helped by them unreliably. Animation is enjoyed, slower and less accurate for analysis, and helps in exactly one place — the transition between two states of the same chart.

Uncertainty can be shown in forms people read correctly, and the forms differ: error bars create a region of false certainty; countable dots and animated draws do better; a hard boundary is read as a category; the people who draw error bars misread them themselves. "Likely" means anything until a number sits beside it. A fifth of adults in England struggle with multi-step arithmetic; in Germany and the United States a third of the public has low graph literacy and low numeracy together; and the UK's statistics regulator could find no survey that measures the public's ability to read charts and tables. Of the accessibility standards, five success criteria are the hard lines that bite on charts; plain language is not one of them; and a non-public body is bound by the Equality Act's anticipatory duty with WCAG 2.2 AA as the yardstick.

1 · What showing data is

A chart is a translation. A number becomes a length, a position, an angle, an area, a shade; a reader's eye turns it back into a judgement — this is bigger than that, this went up, this is an outlier — without passing through the number at all. Everything useful that has been learned about showing data is about where that round trip is accurate, where it is fast, and where it quietly fails.

The best current map of that territory is a 2021 review by Steven Franconeri, Lace Padilla, Priti Shah, Jeffrey Zacks and Jessica Hullman, written for a general readership in Psychological Science in the Public Interest. Its abstract is a fair summary of this whole chapter: "Effectively designed data visualizations allow viewers to use their powerful visual systems to understand patterns in data across science, education, health, and public policy. But ineffectively designed visualizations can cause confusion, misunderstanding, or even distrust—especially among viewers with low graphical literacy. … We describe how the visual system can quickly extract broad statistics from a display, whereas poorly designed displays can lead to misperceptions and illusions. Extracting global statistics is fast, but comparing between subsets of values is slow. Effective graphics avoid taxing working memory, guide attention, and respect familiar conventions."

The review organises the evidence under three headings, and this chapter leans on them throughout, though it runs by topic. A display can be perceptually accurate: the eye recovers the right magnitudes. It can be perceptually efficient: the eye finds the right comparison quickly. And it can be understandable: the reader has the schema to read it and the working memory to hold it. Each is a different kind of failure, and a chart can pass one and fail the others. A bar chart with a truncated axis is perceptually efficient and misleading; a rainbow map is attention-grabbing and inaccurate; a parallel-coordinates plot is accurate and, to most of the public, unreadable.

Why bother with a picture at all? Because of what the eye does in parallel. "Visualizations allow powerful processing of an entire two-dimensional rectangle of information at once, in stark contrast to the limitation of reading handfuls of symbolic numbers per second." The review's first figure is Anscombe's old demonstration: "Four sets of 11 numbers have identical statistics but dramatically different patterns, as revealed by the scatterplots below each column." That is the case for charts. The rest of the chapter is about how often the case is undermined by the way they are drawn.

2 · Why people believe what they believe

The folklore of showing data is unusually confident, and most of it has a named source. Each belief is stated fairly here and tested in the sections that follow.

Belief one: there is a hierarchy of encodings, and it decides the chart

Most data-visualisation courses teach a ranking: position is read best, then length, then angle, then area, then colour. From it follow the rules — bar charts good, pie charts suspect, 3D forbidden, choropleths dangerous. The Decision Book, the studio's own rulebook, opens its chart chapter this way: "Almost every chart rule you have ever been given is downstream of one finding." The belief is that the ranking is a law and the rules are its corollaries.

Belief two: less ink is better

Edward Tufte's doctrine — maximise the share of ink that carries data; strip "chartjunk" — is the most influential aesthetic in the field and the house style of the statistics offices. The belief is that ornament costs accuracy and that a clean chart is an honest one.

Belief three: a picture speaks for itself

Charts are made by people who think in charts, and the belief follows that the picture carries the message and the words are furniture: a title to say what the data is, axis labels, a legend. A corollary is "label at the mark, not in a legend", a rule nearly everyone in the field repeats.

Belief four: you have fifty milliseconds

Designers are told that users judge a page in a twentieth of a second and that eyes read a screen in an F-shape, so the top-left corner is where the message must go. The belief is that the first glance decides comprehension.

Belief five: overview first, and let them explore

Ben Shneiderman's mantra — "Overview first, zoom and filter, then details-on-demand" — is the most-cited design rule in interactive visualisation, and the belief that follows is that an interactive display should open on everything and let the reader drill in, and that interactivity is itself a good.

Belief six: never truncate; always start at zero

A rule inherited from statistics offices and style guides, applied to every chart alike, and believed to be about honesty.

Belief seven: uncertainty confuses people, and animation shows change

Two beliefs about what to leave out and what to add. The first says that readers cannot cope with ranges and that a clean point estimate is kinder. The second says that if something changes over time, the natural way to show it is to make it move.

Each belief has a true core. The sections below say how much.

3 · What the eye can read

The hierarchy, and what it actually says

In 1984 William Cleveland and Robert McGill, statisticians at Bell Labs, set out to give graphics "a scientific foundation" by studying "graphical perception—the visual decoding of information encoded on graphs". They proposed what they were careful to call a hypothesis: "In this section we hypothesize an ordering of the 10 elementary perceptual tasks on the basis of the accuracy with which people can extract quantitative information by using them." From most to least accurate: position along a common scale; positions along non-aligned scales; length, direction and angle; area; volume and curvature; shading and colour saturation. The principle that followed: "A graphical form that involves elementary perceptual tasks that lead to more accurate judgments than another graphical form (with the same quantitative information) will result in better organization and increase the chances of a correct perception of patterns and behavior."

Then they tested it — the top of it. In one experiment 51 usable volunteers judged what percentage one marked value was of another on five kinds of bar chart; in another, 51 compared pie charts with bar charts. The results were clear: "average errors for length judgments are 40%-250% larger than those for position judgments"; position judgements were more accurate than angle judgements by a factor of 1.96; "Seventy-eight percent of the large errors occurred for the length judgments." From this they recommended "radical surgery on these popular graphs": replace pie charts with dot charts, divided bars with grouped dots, shaded maps with framed rectangles. And they said what the theory was not: it "does not provide a complete prescription for how to make a graph", should be applied "with judgment", and if accuracy alone were the goal, "We agree with Ehrenberg (1975) that if this were the only goal, tables would be better."

A year later, restating the work in Science, they were plainer still about the bottom of the ladder: "The ordering should be thought of as a tentative working hypothesis, based on current information, that can be expected to evolve." "Aspects of the ordering are partly conjectural in that we have no controlled experimentation to support them." The famous diagram is half experiment and half hypothesis, and its authors said so.

The top held. In 2010 Jeffrey Heer and Michael Bostock reran the experiments on 186 people recruited online, and the results preserved "the rough shape and ranking of judgment types by accuracy"; "The ranking of types by accuracy is consistent between the two experiments." They extended it to area — rectangles and circles were about equally bad, and, "Somewhat surprisingly, comparisons of rectangles with aspect ratio 1 exhibited the worst performance" — and added two practical numbers: gridlines at least eight pixels apart, and little benefit from chart heights beyond 80 pixels on a 0–100 scale. In 2014 Justin Talbot, Vidya Setlur and Anushka Anand took bar charts apart to find out why the types differed: separating two bars added about 0.70 percentage points of error; bars that did not share a baseline, as in a stacked chart, added 1.16; and comparisons within divided bars carried an absolute error of 7.38 percentage points, for which the authors offered "One possible explanation … that subjects are influenced by the part-to-whole comparison." Their conclusion: "even for simple visualizations, such as bar charts, we still do not have a complete understanding of what impacts chart perception."

Two later findings change how the hierarchy should be used. Robert Kosara and Drew Skau showed in three studies that pie charts are not read by angle. Distort a pie so that its angles change but its areas do not, and people read it as well as ever; isolate the angle alone and they do worst of all: "angle cannot be the only way we read a pie or donut chart"; "Area emerges as the most likely cue used to read pie charts." Donuts were not worse than pies. The rule "pies are bad because angle is low on the hierarchy" is a true conclusion with a false reason. And in 2022 Russell Davis and colleagues reran Cleveland and McGill with 109 people and 130,800 judgements, modelling each person separately. The population ranking survived, but "some people show patterns of accuracy that credibly deviate from the canonical rankings": the canonical order held for about a fifth of participants, "around 20-25% of people consistently perform better with another chart type" than bars, and the "expected differences in performance across pie, bubble, and stacked-bar charts (1-1.5pp) is smaller than the expected differences between people (1.5-3pp)." The authors argue against treating the ranking as a design rule.

So here is what the hierarchy settles, stated plainly. For a reader estimating the ratio between two values, position on a common scale beats length, which beats angle; that is replicated and real, and the effect is a few percentage points of error. The hierarchy does not settle anything about what is remembered, understood, trusted or liked; it was never tested below its third rank; it does not say how pies are read; and the gaps between the lower chart types are smaller than the gaps between readers. The Decision Book's first rule — "Use the highest encoding on the perceptual ranking that carries the comparison" — survives as a default for precise comparison. Its gloss that 3D is "banned because volume is fifth" and pies constrained "because angle and area sit two and three ranks down" rests on the conjectural half, and section 8 returns to both.

What is seen before you look

Some visual differences are found without searching. Christopher Healey and James Enns, reviewing the perception literature for visualisation, give the working definition: "Typically, tasks that can be performed on large multi-element displays in less than 200-250 milliseconds (msec) are considered preattentive." Hue, intensity, orientation, size, curvature, motion and flicker all pop out; a red dot among blue ones is found at once however many blue ones there are. The limit is as useful as the list: "When a target is defined by the joint presence of two or more visual properties, it often cannot be found preattentively." A red circle among red squares and blue circles has to be searched for. Anne Treisman's 1980 theory, from which this descends, put it as: attention "must be directed serially to each stimulus in a display whenever conjunctions of more than one separable feature are needed", while single features can be "detected in parallel with no attention limits."

Two design consequences follow and both are evidence, not taste. "Feature hierarchies suggest that the most important data attributes should be displayed with the most salient visual features, to avoid situations where secondary data values mask the information the viewer wants to see." And the features interfere asymmetrically: "random variations in shape have no effect on a viewer's ability to see colour patterns" but colour variation masks shape — which is why a chart that uses colour for decoration makes its shapes harder to read.

Grouping is the other thing the eye does unasked. A century of Gestalt research, reviewed by Johan Wagemans and colleagues, lists the principles — "proximity, similarity, common fate, good continuation, closure, symmetry, parallelism" and newer ones such as "common region" ("elements that lie within the same bounded area") and "element connectedness" ("distinct elements that share a common border"). Franconeri's review makes the bridge to charts in one sentence: "The same classic grouping cues studied in the perception literature can control which values are selected and compared", through "connecting lines, position proximity, and similarity in either color or shape". A dashboard's tiles, borders and gaps are grouping instructions whether or not anyone wrote them deliberately.

Statistics are fast; comparisons are slow

This is the review's central mechanism and the one most worth a first-time reader's attention. "Faster than an eyeblink, we can pull statistics from data encoded as positions, one-dimensional lengths, two-dimensional areas, angles, or intensities" — the average, the spread, the outlier, the trend of a whole field of marks, at once. But "Comparisons include local comparisons between elements, groups of elements, or global trends", and "Each of those verbal sentences describes a single visual comparison that must be extracted serially, as part of a sequence"; "comparisons are already highly capacity limited". A reader can see that a scatterplot slopes upward instantly, and must then work, one pair at a time, to see which two points to compare.

Everything in chart design that works, works by choosing that comparison for the reader. "A visualization designed to guide viewers to make the 'right' visual comparisons can lead those viewers to make meaningful insights." "Visualization designers will often deliberately control visual salience to bring the viewer's eye straight to the critical comparison." "One technique is to add salient color highlighting a single group of items to ensure that viewers process that comparison first." Section 7 reports the experiment that measured this.

Three illusions travel with the mechanism and are worth knowing by name; all three are from the review. The line-graph illusion: two curves of identical shape, one shifted upward, look as if they converge where they steepen — "it is difficult to see that the vertical distance between the two lines is the same across their entire horizontal span", so a chart of two series invites a false reading of their difference; the remedy Cleveland and McGill proposed in 1984, in the same paper as the hierarchy, is to plot the difference itself. Which channel is read: a pictogram scaled by height to a 1:2 ratio is read by area, "leading to something closer to a 1:4 ratio". And categorical perception of colour: the visual system "systematically bins continuous wavelengths into one of several perceptual categories, exaggerating metric differences", which is the mechanism behind section 4.

Working memory and the schema

The third heading is about what the reader brings. Reading a legend is a working-memory task: "Interpreting the graphs … requires individuals to map the symbols and colors in the graphs to their referents in the legends below. This task is highly demanding of limited working memory resources." The review cites one study in which "people answered questions about data both faster and more accurately when the data were directly labeled in graphs compared with when there was a legend", and its advice is unqualified: "instead of legends, use direct labels whenever possible". Section 5 says how thin that single study makes the evidence, and why the rule stands anyway.

Reading any chart at all requires a schema: "a knowledge structure that includes default expectations, rules, and associations." "Reading a bar graph requires a schema that allows the viewer to do what you do when viewing a bar graph: to focus instantly on the positions of the bar tops, because they signal the numbers depicted by the bars." Conventions are part of the schema — "Larger values tend to be mapped to higher vertical positions" — and "When these mappings are violated, viewers can become confused." The sentence in the review that a public-facing designer should pin up is this one, which rests on a Pew survey rather than an experiment: "Even relatively common visualizations such as scatterplots are misunderstood by 37% of adults in the United States." Expert communities "have developed idiosyncratic visualizations that serve important data-analysis or -communication purposes, but they require learning new graph schemas." Section 11 returns to what the public can read; the point here is that familiarity is a perceptual resource, not a failure of ambition.

4 · Colour

Colour is the channel designers reach for first and the eye reads worst, and the evidence sorts into three things: what colour can carry, what it cannot, and the one rule about it that is a hard line.

Three kinds of scheme

Cynthia Brewer's ColorBrewer, built for maps and used everywhere since, distinguishes three jobs. Sequential schemes are for "ordered data that progress from low to high. Lightness steps dominate the look of these schemes, with light colors for low data values to dark colors for high data values." Diverging schemes "put equal emphasis on mid-range critical values and extremes at both ends of the data range", with a light middle and dark, contrasting-hue ends. Qualitative schemes "do not imply magnitude differences between legend classes, and hues are used to create the primary visual differences between classes." This is design logic rather than experiment, but it encodes what the perception work below shows: the eye reads lightness as order and hue as category, and a scheme that uses hue for order asks the reader to learn an arbitrary sequence.

The rainbow

The rainbow colour map — blue through green and yellow to red — is the standard case. Kenneth Moreland's summary of the objections: "The rainbow colors do not follow any natural perceived ordering. Although the order of the hues can be learned, there is no innate sense of higher or lower." "The perceptual changes in the rainbow colors are not uniform. The colors appear to change much faster in the yellow region than the green region." And "It is sensitive to deficiencies in vision". Franconeri's review supplies the mechanism — the seven bands of a rainbow "are not present in the rainbow itself"; the eye bins a continuous scale into categories and "These additional hues create new color-category boundaries that can dramatically exaggerate the differences". Yang Liu and Jeffrey Heer tested nine colour maps on about 166 people making distance judgements and found that the rainbow "performs the worst among all colormaps considered", that the modern lightness-ordered maps (viridis and its family) did best, and that "a combination of perceptual color space and color naming measures more accurately predict user performance than either alone."

The complication, which a careful chapter has to state: Khairi Reda and colleagues, testing 381 people on continuous maps, found that "rainbow schemes afforded the highest accuracy in quantity estimation irrespective of spatial complexity", while "divergent colormaps significantly outperformed other schemes in tasks requiring the perception of high-frequency patterns." More hues help a reader name a value at a point because colour names are a lookup aid; lightness-ordered maps help a reader see a pattern. The rule against the rainbow is a rule about pattern maps and about order; it is not a universal.

Who cannot see it, and how many colours there are

Jennifer Birch's review of population surveys gives the prevalence of red–green colour deficiency: "about 8% in men and about 0.4% in women" of European descent, and "between 4% and 6.5% in men of Chinese and Japanese ethnicity".[abstract or summary only] Franconeri's review gives a global all-population figure of about 4%; the two are different denominators, not a disagreement, and this book uses Birch's. The design consequence is the one sentence everyone agrees on: "The simplest way to make visualizations accessible to viewers with color blindness is to avoid using hue as the only encoding channel or allow viewers to change the color palette."

How many categories can colour carry? The only experimental number found is Healey's from 1996: "seven isoluminant colours is the maximum we can display at one time" for rapid, accurate search, when colour distance, linear separation and colour category are all controlled. The practitioner limits are tighter — the UK Government Analysis Function recommends "a limit of four categories as best practice for basic data visualisations"; the Office for National Statistics says "Always use five colours or fewer" and "Never use more than nine" — and the Decision Book's "four series, maximum" descends from them. Those are Practice and voluntary Standard, not Evidence, and they are sensible precisely because real palettes are not Healey's controlled seven. Two further findings refine them. Danielle Szafir showed on 461 people that "perceived color difference varies inversely with size": the smaller the mark, the bigger the colour difference it needs to be told apart, and lines and elongated marks are easier to tell apart than points of the same thickness — so a small legend dot or a scatter point needs bigger colour steps than a bar. And Sharon Lin and colleagues found that colours which mean something to the reader — blue for oceans, green for parks — let people answer questions about 10% faster than a default palette, a small effect with a large constituency.

The hard line

One rule about colour is a Standard, and it is worth quoting in full. WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 1.4.1, Use of Color, Level A: "Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element." Level A is the floor of conformance. A chart whose series are told apart by colour alone, with a legend, fails it — not as a matter of taste but as a measurable breach. Two companion criteria at Level AA set the contrast floors: 1.4.3 requires text at "a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1" (3:1 for large text), and 1.4.11, Non-text Contrast, requires "Parts of graphics required to understand the content" to have "a contrast ratio of at least 3:1 against adjacent color(s)". The W3C's own explanatory text for 1.4.11 is the only place WCAG speaks about charts by name: for a line graph, "The lines should have 3:1 contrast against their background, but as there is little overlap with other lines they do not need to contrast with each other or the graduated lines." A careful reader will notice what that means: 1.4.11 does not require two data series to contrast with each other. The requirement that they be distinguishable comes from 1.4.1 — not by colour alone — which direct labelling satisfies and a legend does not. That is the logical root of the Decision Book's rule that "direct labelling is the mechanism by which the chart is compliant at all", and section 12 says who is bound by it.

One more word on maps, since belief one listed choropleths among the dangerous forms. A choropleth encodes a value in colour — the bottom of the hierarchy — and is a poor way to read one region's figure; it is the right form when the finding is a pattern across space, provided the colour scale is ordered by lightness and the values are also available as a table. Chapter 2 found that the choice between a map of counts and a map of rates moved readers' perception by nine points; that, not the colour, is the choropleth's most persuasive decision.

5 · Words

People read the title first, longest, and instead

Michelle Borkin and colleagues tracked the eyes of 33 people looking at 393 visualisations and then asked them to describe what they had seen. "People spend the most amount of time looking at the text in a visualization, and more specifically, the title." Titles were fixated 59% of the time when present, 76% when at the top; the elements fixated longest during recognition were titles, followed by recognisable objects; the elements people kept returning to were "the legend, table header row … and title." When asked afterwards what a visualisation had shown, "46% of the time the participants described the contents, or rewording, of the title." Visualisations whose message was stated in words as well as pictures — what the authors call message redundancy — were described better (a quality score of 1.99 against 1.59), and 57% of the best-described charts had it. Their conclusion: "Titles and text are key elements in a visualization and help recall the message."

Laura Matzen and colleagues at Sandia reanalysed the same eye data and ran their own study, dividing each image into regions of interest ("ROIs"). In the memory task, "When the Title ROI was present in a visualization, it was one of the first three visited in 87.8% of the scan paths", and "59.9% … of the participants' fixations fell into ROIs containing text relative to 30.0% … in the data". In free viewing the data took over — "Fixations to the Data ROI surpassed looks to the Title beginning ~1500 ms after trial onset" — but text still drew about 40% of all looks. The first second and a half goes to the words.

For dashboards specifically there is one large study, by Yiming Yang and colleagues, the only one of its kind this chapter found. Sixty people viewed 36 dashboards each, from a pool of 1,216 real ones, for 45 seconds each. Text objects ("TOs") "account for 42.96% of the overall attention intensity whereas VOs [visual objects — charts] constitute 52.02%" — but text is small and charts are large, and by the study's measure of how much of each object's area drew attention, "The average saliency coverage for TOs is 47.21% much higher than 14.37% for VOs". Text draws attention far out of proportion to the space it takes. "Number gains the highest saliency coverage, serving as the primary focal point" — a plain figure is the most-looked-at object class on a dashboard. "Subtitles show significantly higher saliency coverage than titles" — the small label under each tile outdraws the heading above everything. And attention "is concentrated in the upper left corner", starting at "title and filter". The study is free viewing without a task and its sample is aged 18 to 32, and those are real limits; it is still the best picture anyone has of where eyes go on the thing this book is about.

The title decides what the chart showed

Ha-Kyung Kong, Zhicheng Liu and Karrie Karahalios asked what a title does to a reading. In a nationally representative US sample, they put the same chart under titles slanted one way or the other. "The analysis of the perceived main messages revealed that 65% of the answers (N=136) reflected the material covered in the titles"; "the slant of visualization titles resulted in a significant difference in the perceived main message", with "viewers deriving opposing messages from the same visualization." The readers did not notice: "Similar ratios of participants answered that the information was neutral whether they saw an attitude-consistent (80%), attitude-inconsistent (80%), or attitude-irrelevant (89%) visualization." And they did not think they had read the title — "33% of the participants (N=34) stated that they did not remember any of the titles" — while writing its content down as the chart's message. The authors "highlight the danger of subtle statistics frames and viewers' unwarranted conviction of the neutrality of visualizations."

Their follow-up pushed the title further from the picture. Even when the title contradicted the chart, "the majority of the people (72-87%) in all conditions reported that the information was neutral"; "People's recall of the visualization's message more frequently aligned with the titles than the visualization". And the trust ordering is the finding to keep: "data was perceived as the most credible, followed by the visualization, then the title." Readers trust the title least and remember it most. A study by Dae Hyun Kim, Vidya Setlur and Maneesh Agrawala with 2,168 people adds the limit: a caption redirects a reader to a feature the chart already makes visually prominent, and when the caption "describes a low-prominence chart feature, readers rely on the chart and report a higher-prominence feature as the takeaway." Words win when they agree with what the picture makes salient; title and chart must point at the same thing.

How much text, and where

The first controlled study of how much text readers want on a chart is Chase Stokes and colleagues' in 2023. 302 people ranked line charts carrying from no text to a full paragraph with no chart at all. "We find that heavily annotated charts were not penalized. In fact, participants preferred the charts with the largest number of textual annotations over charts with fewer annotations or text alone." The sparsest charts ranked lowest — "participants least preferred the no-text variant … and the title-only variant" — so a title alone is not enough. "a sizable minority — 42, or 14% of participants — ranked the all-text option as their first choice". And placement follows meaning: a statement of the overall trend was "most likely to be matched by participant takeaways when … positioned as the title", while statistics and context worked better placed at the data points. Their guidelines, which transfer directly to a dashboard tile: annotate with several text elements rather than minimally; put the trend in the title; put the numbers and the context next to the marks; and consider a text-only alternative.

The ONS's practice is consistent with this and often cited for it. Since 2019 its chart titles "sum up the main message shown in the chart in 10 words or less", with a subtitle for the data, geography and period; its service manual now says "The chart title should describe the main trend you want the chart to show to the user" and allows "15 words or fewer". The blog post that announced the change claimed "compelling evidence" without naming a study, and its only number was about reading, not titles: bulletins "take 9.5 times longer to read than people are spend on the page" [sic]. It is a well-documented Practice, backed by the Evidence above, not Evidence itself.

Label at the mark — the rule nobody tested

"Label at the mark; legends are a last resort" is a Fixed rule in the Decision Book and a commonplace in every style guide. This chapter searched for the experiment behind it and did not find one. There is no controlled study in the visualisation literature that pits direct labels against a legend on an ordinary chart and measures accuracy, speed or recall. What exists is indirect and, taken together, strong. Lynn Huestegge and Andrea Philipp tracked eyes across graphs with legends: readers made "more frequent" transitions between data and legend when the legend's order did not match the lines ("4.37" against "3.63"), and matching the two "reduced the time needed to understand graphs". Borkin and Matzen both found the legend among the most re-fixated elements — a lookup table the eye keeps returning to. Franconeri's review cites one study where direct labels were faster and more accurate. And the real evidential root is a meta-analysis from educational psychology: Paul Ginns pooled 50 studies of spatial contiguity — placing words next to the thing they explain rather than in a separate key or caption — and found an effect of d = 0.72 across 37 comparisons, larger for complex material. None of that is a legend-versus-label experiment on a chart. The rule stands because the mechanism is understood (the round trip costs working memory), the analogous evidence is large, and the accessibility logic of section 4 requires it. The kind is Practice backed by analogous Evidence, and the book should say so rather than cite a study that does not exist.

6 · The glance

Fifty milliseconds, and what it measures

Gitte Lindgaard and colleagues showed people screenshots of web pages for 500 milliseconds, and then for 50, and asked how appealing they were. The ratings were stable: "visual appeal can be assessed within 50 ms, suggesting that web designers have about 50 ms to make a good first impression." The samples were 22, 31 and 40 students, and the measure was a rating from ugly to beautiful. Alexandre Tuch and colleagues then found what drives it. Across 141 people and 120 real sites, two factors predicted the snap judgement: visual complexity and prototypicality, defined as "the amount to which an object is representative of a class of objects". Both were detectable at 17 milliseconds; by 50, prototypicality was as strong as simplicity; "Overall, websites with low VC and high PT were perceived as highly appealing." Their implication: "Designs that contradict what users typically expect of a website may trigger a suboptimal first impression and impair users' expectations."

The caveat that must travel with every repetition of "fifty milliseconds" is that the thing measured was appeal. Nothing in these studies shows that any information was read. What the first glance decides is whether the reader is disposed to continue, and the two things that dispose them are simplicity and looking like what you claim to be. For a dashboard that means the first glance rewards convention — a point the chartjunk literature never makes and section 7 complicates.

The real cost of a glance

Tanja Blascheck and colleagues measured how long a two-value comparison takes on a tiny screen. Bars needed about a quarter of a second to be read reliably (245–285 ms), donuts slightly less (159–216 ms), and radial bar charts — the decorative wrapped form — about six times longer (1,548–1,772 ms). "Bar and donut charts should be the preferred encodings when quick comparisons are necessary." A dashboard built from slow-glance forms spends its first impression losing, and the penalty for the ornamental form is not a few per cent but a multiple.

Where eyes go, and the F that is not a rule

The Nielsen Norman Group's F-shaped pattern is repeated as a layout law and is nothing of the kind. Its own 2017 restatement says "People scan in an F-shape when all of these 3 elements are present", the first being "A page or a section of a page includes text that has little or no formatting for the web", the others a goal of efficiency and low commitment — and that "the F-shaped scanning pattern is bad for users and businesses: it means that users may skip important content". It was measured on text-heavy pages, not dashboards, and it describes a failure of formatting, not a target to design to. The nearest evidence for dashboards is the upper-left bias and title-first start in the dashboard eye-tracking study above, which is consistent with reading order rather than with any letter. Jakob Nielsen's other famous number — that users read "at most 28% of the words" on a page, "20% is more likely" — is a regression of dwell time on word count against an assumed reading speed; nobody measured which words were read.

7 · Ornament and memory

The doctrine and the study that started the argument

Tufte's doctrine, in the standard reproduction: "A large share of ink on a graphic should present data-information, the ink changing as the data change." Ornament that does not — "chartjunk" — is to be erased. The doctrine is Practice; it was asserted, not tested, and for twenty years it was the field's taste.

In 2010 Scott Bateman and colleagues tested it with Nigel Holmes's heavily illustrated charts against plain redrawings. With 20 students, immediate description accuracy did not differ; after two to three weeks, the ten people in the long-term group recalled the subject and categories of the illustrated charts better. The paper concluded, cautiously, that "Our results question some of the premises of the minimalist approach to chart design". It was over-read for a decade. The long-term condition had ten people; one of its four significant results is significant only one-tailed; the charts were single-series and the embellishment extreme. Stephen Few's critique — "The plain charts used in this study were in fact plain ugly" — was intemperate, and the sample was small. The study is the trigger of a debate, not a settled result.

What memorability is and is not

Borkin's 2013 study, the largest of its kind, had 261 people play a memory game with 2,070 visualisations shown for one second each. Memorability was a stable property — people agreed on which images they had seen before — and it was driven by the things Tufte dislikes: pictograms (1.93 against 1.14), more colours, a low data-ink ratio ("bad" 1.81 against "good" 1.23), and unusual forms; "common graphs are less memorable than unique visualization types." Bar and line charts, the dashboard's staples, are the least memorable images. The authors said in the same paper what this does not mean: "Clearly, a more memorable visualization is not necessarily a more comprehensible one"; the study "examined the memorability of visualizations as if they were images and not memorability based on engagement and comprehension". Their 2015 follow-up closed some of the gap: visualisations memorable at a glance did convey their message, and "Pictograms do not hinder the memory or understanding of a visualization."

Three studies then drew the useful line. Steve Haroz, Kosara and Franconeri tested pictographs across five experiments: "superfluous images can distract. But we find no user costs – and some intriguing benefits – when pictographs are used to represent the data." Pictures that are the data are free or helpful; "including an unnecessary background image in a visualization appears to be distracting." Skau, Harrison and Kosara tested the "styles" business tools offer — rounded, triangular, capped bars — on about 94 people and found that "For nearly all tested chart embellishments, even small changes like rounding the top of a bar, led to higher error rate" for relative judgements. Ornament that touches the data mark costs accuracy.
