And Rita Borgo and colleagues found embellishment helped memory and slowed visual search.[abstract or summary only] People also simply prefer the ornamented version: Ohad Inbar and colleagues showed 87 students Tufte's own minimal redrawing of a bar chart beside the original, and "People did not like Tufte's minimalist design of bar-graphs; they seem to prefer 'chartjunk' instead."[abstract or summary only]

The experiment the debate needed

Kiran Ajani and colleagues — a perception laboratory working with the practitioner Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic — separated the two things that "clean up this chart" bundles together. Declutter: remove backgrounds, borders, gridlines, extra labels, colour variety; focus: add "a clear headline that describes the relevant data pattern", highlight one subset in a distinct colour, and connect it to a short annotation. Twenty-four people — students and community members at one university — redrew and recalled the charts and rated them. Decluttering made charts look more "professional" (up 1.11 points) and that was most of what it did; "we found weaker but generally positive evidence for the benefits of the declutter guideline". Focusing raised aesthetics and clarity ratings and changed what people took away: "Participants were 2.5-3x more likely to recall a focus-relevant conclusion for focused designs relative to the non-focused designs". And "neither decluttering alone nor the addition of focusing showed strong evidence for improving trustworthiness of a graph". The sample is small, the tasks are memory tasks, and the result has not been replicated; it is reported here as the best single test of the question, not as a settled size. What Tufte got right is that clutter competes with data for attention. What he missed is that the thing that makes a chart communicate is not the ink you remove but the message you add — a headline, one highlight, one sentence — and that clean reads as professional, not as honest.

8 · Axes, scales, and the forms the style guides argue about

Truncating the bar

The rule "start bars at zero" is believed to be about honesty, and the experiments show it is about something stranger. Michael Correll, Enrico Bertini and Franconeri truncated bar and line charts by 0, 25 and 50% and asked people how severe the depicted difference was. "Increased y-axis truncation results in increased perceived severity" (p < 0.0001), equally for bars and lines. Then they tried the remedies the style guides offer — a broken-axis marker, a gradient fade at the base: "There was no significant difference between perceived severity among visualization designs" (the test was borderline, p = 0.05, with no pairwise difference). People could read the numbers correctly and still felt the difference as larger: "Surprisingly, the accurate estimation of values does not seem to counteract the visual magnification of difference." Their conclusion: "Merely indicating that truncation has occurred, even in a prominent and unambiguous way, may not be sufficient to 'de-bias' viewers of truncated charts." Brenda Yang and colleagues found the same across five studies: the effect "persisted after viewers were taught about the effects of y-axis truncation", and "83.5% of participants across these 5 studies showing a truncation effect."[abstract or summary only] A 2024 study by Long and Kay adds that objective task accuracy for comparing bar lengths is often unaffected — it is the impression of effect size that inflates. People read the right numbers and feel the wrong size. Correll's authors "reject the unequivocal dichotomy of 'honest' and 'dishonest' charts" and put the responsibility where it belongs: designers should "consider the scale of the meaningful effect sizes and variation they intend to communicate, regardless of the visual encoding." "There is no obvious way for designers to relinquish the responsibility of considering effect size in their charts."

So the Decision Book's Fixed rule — "Never break the numerical axis on a bar chart" — holds, and the Analysis Function's 2023 checklist already gives the better reason: "Even if a break in the axis is clearly signposted, the relative size of bars is still displayed very strongly on bar charts." The experiments confirm it. Its Adaptable rule that a line chart's axis "may be broken where necessary, and labelled" needs the same caveat: the label does not neutralise the impression; the designer is choosing an effect size and must know it.

The forms with less evidence than their reputations

Dual axes. The prohibition on two series sharing a chart with two y-axes is universal in UK government guidance ("they can be easily misinterpreted") and rests, as far as this chapter could find, on no controlled study at all. The experiment usually cited — Petra Isenberg and colleagues, 2011 — is about dual-scale charts, one series shown at two resolutions, and found the superimposed design "very confusing"; it is not about two series. The only recent paper is a defence by Richard Brath and colleagues from financial-services practice, noting dual axes in "19% of 944 timeseries charts". The absence of evidence is itself a finding: the rule is Practice, plausible, and untested.

3D. The study everyone cites for banning 3D bars, by Jeffrey Zacks, Barbara Tversky and colleagues, found the depth cues cost about half a percentage point of accuracy and that "the effect of the bar height manipulation on accuracy was about one order of magnitude larger than the effect of adding depth cues." Their words: "warnings about accuracy decrements due to 3D shading may be overstated, whereas distortions due to neighboring elements should be of more concern." 3D is still a bad idea — it adds nothing, obscures, and fails accessibility — but the Decision Book's reason ("moves the encoding to rank 5") is the conjectural half of the hierarchy again.

Pies. Read by area, not angle (section 3); donuts no worse than pies; the Analysis Function's "five categories or fewer" with "a dominant category" is sound Practice for a form whose real weakness is comparing slices that are nearly equal.

Stacked bars. The one form the evidence does condemn for a specific task: comparing segments that do not share a baseline forces a length judgement and carries the largest error Talbot measured (Cleveland & McGill; Talbot's divided-bar result). Fine for totals and for the bottom segment; wrong for comparing the middle.

Scales that change the reader's mind

Log scales. Alessandro Romano and colleagues showed about 2,000 Americans COVID deaths on a log or a linear scale. On the log scale "Only 40.66% of them could respond correctly to a basic question about the graph (whether there were more deaths in one week or another), contrasted to 83.79% of respondents on the linear scale"; the log group also predicted more deaths and worried less; the authors recommend that public communicators "should always describe the evolution of the pandemic using a graph on a linear scale, at least as a default option."[abstract or summary only] A log scale is a specialist's tool; on the one question tested, it halved the share of the public who could read it.

Cumulative against daily. Nicholas Reinholtz and colleagues, in a preregistered study of 596 people, showed the same twenty days of pandemic data as new cases per day or as a running total. When daily cases were falling, people shown the falling flow judged current risk lower (4.72) than people shown the ever-rising stock (6.58; d = 0.74); when daily cases were rising there was no difference. "The choice of how to present pandemic data can lead people to different conclusions about risk". A cumulative curve always goes up; it is a persuasive choice whether or not it was meant as one, and Chapter 2's finding that the denominator is the persuasive unit has a sibling here in the choice of stock or flow.

Tables, numbers and precision

Tables against graphs. Iris Vessey's cognitive-fit theory, the standard warrant, says that tables suit "symbolic" tasks — looking up a value, reading a point — and graphs suit "spatial" ones — trends, comparisons, shape — and that performance improves when the representation fits the task. The companion experiment with 128 students supports it; for reading individual points "accuracy was higher and reaction time faster with tables than with line graphs", for comparing differences "Performance was better with graphs than with tables".[abstract or summary only] Cleveland and McGill said the same in 1984. A dashboard that shows a value the reader wants to know as a chart has chosen the wrong form.

The big number. The "KPI tile" — one large figure with a label — is the most common object on a business dashboard and this chapter could find no controlled study of whether it is read accurately, trusted or misread against a chart or a table cell. The only direct evidence is that it is looked at: in Yang's dashboard study, "Number gains the highest saliency coverage". Cognitive fit predicts it is right for a point-value question. Its evidential basis is Practice, and the gap is logged.

Rounding. Andrew Ehrenberg's 1977 "Rudiments of Numeracy" gave the rules every statistician learned — round to two effective digits, order rows by size, put figures to be compared in columns, give averages — and, as far as this chapter can find, they were "asserted without experimental results" and never tested with readers. The nearest empirical echo is incidental: in Talbot's bar-chart experiment people answered in "multiples of 10, followed by multiples of 5" and gave 50% "nearly 5 times as often as expected" — readers round to about two digits whether or not the chart does. Tim Cole, a medical statistician, summarises the modern consensus: "the general principle is to use two or three significant digits for effect sizes, and one or two significant digits for measures of variability".

Precision as a signal. Three consumer studies, each read at abstract or press-summary level only, agree that precise numbers are read as confident and trustworthy — "precision is used as a confidence signal"; estimates "expressed in finer granularity" are judged "more precise" and held with "more confidence" — until the reader doubts the communicator's good faith, at which point the effect disappears. This is the mechanism behind the Decision Book's "Never round to imply precision you do not have": spurious precision works on readers, which is exactly why it is a trust hazard when the data cannot bear it.

Frequencies against percentages. Gerd Gigerenzer and Ulrich Hoffrage showed that people reason about chance far better when it is stated as natural frequencies — "9 in 100" rather than "9%" — than as probabilities; Michelle McDowell and Perke Jacobs's 2017 meta-analysis of 226 estimates puts correct Bayesian reasoning at 24% with frequencies against 4% with probabilities, which is both a large improvement and a reminder that three quarters still fail. Section 11 takes this up with risk.

9 · Interaction, defaults and animation

How many readers touch anything

The most-quoted statistic about interactive graphics is that 85% of readers ignore them. Its origin is a footnote. Gregor Aisch, then at the New York Times, wrote in 2017: "The number comes from me measuring the percent of readers who clicked on a prominent button in a couple of graphics we published in 2015. I mentioned the number in a conference talk, from where it ended up in another talk, then on Medium and finally on FastCo.Design. However, the 85% of readers didn't ignore the graphic, they just didn't click the button." His own rule from it: "you should not hide important content behind interactions. If some information is crucial, don't make the user click or hover to see it"; and "not everything is crucial and 15% of readers aren't nobody." His editor Archie Tse's three rules, from a 2016 talk whose slides contain no percentage at all: "1. If you make the reader click or do anything other than scroll, something spectacular has to happen. 2. If you make a tooltip or rollover, assume no one will ever see it. If content is important for readers to see, don't hide it. 3. When deciding whether to make something interactive, remember that getting it to work on all platforms is expensive." The reason given: "readers weren't getting to all of the content"; "Readers just want to scroll."

The best public measurement replaces the anecdote. Matthew Conlen, Alex Kale and Heer instrumented three live interactive articles read by tens of thousands of people. A central one-tap control was used by 85%; a text hover by 54%; and for the optional controls, "The median number of times a reader hovered over an artwork was 4, the median number of interactions with the algorithm details button and with the slider was zero." About three quarters of readers reached the end of two of the articles, under half of the third. On mobile, "Only 10% of mobile readers triggered one of the example audio clips"; median time on a page was 20–41 seconds against 78–116 on desktop; "Mobile readers utilized fewer of the available interactive features than their desktop counterparts, but still largely followed the presented narratives." Their line for designers: "If details were only revealed after a click, readers may never see it." Two further findings complete the picture. Jeremy Boy and colleagues found that readers of charts embedded in text do not know they are interactive unless told, and only one of three visual cues designed to signal it worked.[abstract or summary only] And left to explore freely, crowd participants in Mi Feng's experiments visited about a quarter of twenty available charts and 8% of 255. People finish; they do not fiddle; and on a phone, where hover does not exist, they do less of both.

The default is advice

Chapter 1 cited, from version 1 of this book, the finding that a default is read as a recommendation. Re-verified for this chapter: Jon Jachimowicz and colleagues' meta-analysis of 58 datasets from 55 studies, 73,675 people in all, found a default effect of d = 0.68 (95% confidence interval 0.53–0.83), an opt-out default raising uptake "by an absolute average of 27.24%", and — citing McKenzie and colleagues — that "Individuals commonly perceive defaults as conveying an endorsement by the choice architect": "the more decision-makers believe that the default reflects a trusted recommendation, the more effective the default is likely to be." The domain is policy and consumer choice, not dashboards; the mechanism transfers. Hullman and Diakopoulos named the design-side consequence: "Default views provide an initial point of interpretation anchored to the default visual configuration", and "Choosing a default view, for example, may be unavoidable, but the choice of a single default view for all users is not a given."

The anchoring is measurable. Isaac Cho and colleagues trained 81 people on a multi-view analytics tool starting from either the map or the calendar; the view they started in dominated the first fifth of their session and shaped their estimates, and a high or low number shown first anchored their final answers (52.7 against 21.1 for the same question). Across five studies and 726 people, André Calero Valdez and colleagues found that the chart you saw a moment ago shifts how you judge the next one — a small, reliable priming effect. And Cindy Xiong, Lisa van Weelden and Franconeri documented the designer's blind spot: people told what to see in a chart rated that pattern as more salient and assumed naive viewers would see it too — "The inability to separate one's own knowledge and expertise from that of their audience can make visual data communication more difficult and less clear than presenters realize." The person who chose the default cannot see the chart as a newcomer does.

"Overview first" audited

Shneiderman's mantra is printed ten times in his 1996 paper, followed by: "Each line represents one project in which I found myself rediscovering this principle and therefore wrote it down as a reminder. It proved to be only a starting point". Nine years later Brock Craft and Paul Cairns audited the literature citing it: "At the time of this writing, there are at least 52 citations of the 1996 paper", sorted into implementations, methods, evaluations and taxonomies, and "although numerous authors cite the Mantra, there are no reasonably obvious studies that have validated Shneiderman's recommendations." Kasper Hornbæk and Morten Hertzum then reviewed 60 papers on overviews: "In 16 of the experimental papers an overview is compared with a baseline interface, for a total of 23 such comparisons." "A near unanimous preference for overviews over the baseline interfaces is found" where people were asked; "tasks are solved faster with overviews in half of the comparisons that measure task completion time … but slower in four comparisons"; "only two of 17 comparisons find that overviews are more accurate than baseline interfaces"; "We see a disappointing effect of support for overviewing with overviews". The counter-mantra, Frank van Ham and Adam Perer's "search, show context, expand on demand", argues that "there are many situations where such an overview is not relevant or practical for users, as analyzing the global structure may not be related to the main task" — from case studies, with no controlled test. People like overviews reliably and are helped by them unreliably; a reader who arrives with a place in mind is not an overview reader.

Animation

Barbara Tversky, Julie Morrison and Mireille Bétrancourt reviewed twenty years of studies and found that where animation seemed to beat static graphics, "scrutiny reveals lack of equivalence between animated and static graphics in content or procedures"; "Students in the animated graphic conditions did not outperform those in the equivalent text or static graphic conditions." Animations fail the apprehension principle — "often too complex or too fast to be accurately perceived" — and "many continuous events are conceived of as sequences of discrete steps." Franconeri's review gives the capacity limit: "Our capacity for tracking the motion of objects that move in arbitrary directions is highly limited, to as few as one or two objects at a time."

George Robertson and colleagues tested the Gapminder style directly — animated bubbles against static traces against small multiples — with 36 people for analysis and presentation. "Results indicate that trend animation can be challenging to use even for presentations; while it is the fastest technique for presentation and participants find it enjoyable and exciting, it does lead to many participant errors. Animation is the least effective form for analysis; both static depictions of trends are significantly faster than animation, and the small multiples display is more accurate." Accuracy "averaging 65%" overall; enjoyment 4.3 for animation against 3.7. Their recommendation: "examining their data with a small multiples view, but then presenting it with animation." Brehmer and colleagues replicated the time result on phones with 96 people: small multiples were consistently faster. Waqas Javed and colleagues' comparison of overlaid lines against small multiples found overlay best for local tasks and split charts best for dispersed ones, and that more series meant more errors for everyone.

Animation reliably helps in one place. Heer and Robertson tested animated transitions between states of the same chart — a bar chart becoming a pie, a scatterplot filtering — and animation beat static cuts in every condition for tracking which mark became which, and for estimating how a value changed; staged animation beat direct. "Animation improved graphical perception at both syntactic (object tracking) and semantic (change estimation) levels of analysis", by preserving "object constancy for changing objects". Motion that carries data is a working-memory tax; motion that preserves identity across a change is a working-memory aid.

On scrolling stories, Sean McKenna and colleagues' study of 240 people found that visuals and animated transitions raised self-reported engagement, that choosing to step or to scroll made no measurable difference, and that comprehension was flat across all conditions. "Engagement" was a questionnaire score. The newsroom's "readers just want to scroll" is a true report of behaviour and not yet evidence that scrolling teaches. More generally, belief five's second half — that interactivity is itself a good — has no support in this literature: Boy and colleagues found a narrative lead-in did not make people explore more, McKenna found comprehension unchanged by any flow, and no study found here shows that a reader who interacts understands more than one who does not.

10 · Uncertainty

Chapter 1 established that uncertainty shown as a number does not cost trust, and Chapter 2 that vague hedging does. This chapter asks the design question: in what form do people read uncertainty correctly?

The taxonomy and the known misreadings

Lace Padilla, Matthew Kay and Jessica Hullman's review sorts the options into graphical annotations of a distribution (means, intervals, moments), encodings of probability to a visual channel (colour, position, transparency), hybrids, and frequency-based formats, of which the review reports that "Other work proposes that showing distributional information in a frequency format (e.g., 1 out of 10 rather than 10%) more naturally matches how people think about uncertainty". It names the errors. Deterministic construal: "When individuals attempt to substitute visual uncertainty information for deterministic information." Boundary or containment: "Ranges that are represented by boundaries lead people to believe that data inside and outside the boundary are categorically different." Within-the-bar bias: a point inside a bar is believed to belong to the population and an equidistant point just outside it not to. Its verdict on intervals is firm — "visualizations of intervals have widely documented issues … such as provoking viewers to incorrectly think of distributional data as categorical" — and its recommendation plural: "If a designer needs to show an interval, we also recommend displaying information that is more representative, such as a scatterplot, violin plot, gradient plot, ensemble plot, quantile dotplot, or HOP" — a HOP being a hypothetical outcome plot, an animation of individual draws, described below. "There is no one-size-fits-all uncertainty visualization approach".

The experiments

Correll and Michael Gleicher's "Error Bars Considered Harmful": "A bar in a bar chart creates a region of false certainty" — "values visually within the bar are perceived as likelier data points than values outside of the bar" — and bar-with-whisker charts led people to "predict outcomes that were significantly larger than with other encodings" with "unjustified" confidence; gradient and violin plots aligned lay judgements with the statistics. Hullman, Paul Resnick and Eytan Adar's hypothetical outcome plots — "animates a finite set of individual draws" — on 288 people: "With HOPs, people made much more accurate judgments about plots of two and three quantities", with no advantage for questions about one. Kay and colleagues' quantile dotplots for bus arrival times on about 540 people: twenty countable dots "reduce the variance of probabilistic estimates by ~1.15 times compared to density plots and facilitate more confident estimation"; a hundred dots did no better than a smooth curve, "consistent with people estimating area instead of counting dots". The gain is modest; the lesson is precise — a countable frequency beats an uncountable shape.

Jake Hofman, Daniel Goldstein and Hullman's finding is the one most relevant to a dashboard that puts a confidence interval round an average. Across 1,743 and 1,830 people, showing the uncertainty in the estimate (a 95% confidence interval) rather than the spread of outcomes (a prediction interval) made readers overestimate a treatment's effect on individuals: "participants who saw 95% CIs thought that they would win 86% of the time … whereas those who were shown 95% PIs reported an average probability of superiority of 67%", against a true value of 57%; they would pay "80 Ice Dollars compared to 50" for the same small advantage. "Because scientists often use CIs and publish small effects, many scientific results are likely exaggerated in the minds of some readers." A tight error bar round a mean tells the reader the mean is well known; the reader hears that everyone gets the mean.

Boundaries are read as categories and as shapes. Padilla, Ian Ruginski and Sarah Creem-Regehr found that viewers of the hurricane "cone of uncertainty" believed the storm itself grew — they read "the growing diameter of the cone boundaries" as size — and that places inside the cone were judged categorically differently from places just outside; spaghetti-line ensembles fixed that and created a new error, with viewers over-weighting any town a drawn line happened to cross. "decisions about visualization methods should be informed by the viewer's task." On maps generally, Alan MacEachren and colleagues found that fuzziness, lightness and positional jitter were read as "uncertain" almost without instruction and that hue, shape and orientation were not — though their participants were GIS professionals, and the two cartographic reviews of lay readers conclude only that showing uncertainty usually changes decisions, rarely slows people, and "is context dependent and still thoroughly up for debate".

And the experts cannot do it either. Sarah Belia and colleagues asked 473 published researchers in psychology, neuroscience and medicine to read error bars: "Only 22% of respondents set the means so the p value was between .025 and .10"; "31.5% … used the incorrect rule that error bars just touch when means are just statistically significantly different". "We conclude that very many researchers … have fundamental and severe misconceptions about how CIs and SE bars can justifiably be used." If the people who draw error bars misread them, the public will.

Words for uncertainty

"Likely" is not a number. David Budescu and colleagues, across "25 samples in 24 countries and 17 languages", found that "Laypeople interpret IPCC statements as conveying probabilities closer to 50% than intended by the IPCC authors", and that "An alternative presentation format supplementing the verbal terms with numerical ranges increases the correspondence". Bonnie Wintle and colleagues, with 924 members of the public, measured the fix: agreement with the intended band was 32% for the word alone and 66% when the number sat in brackets beside it; a separate glossary did not help — "Correspondence … is substantially improved only when numerical guidelines are bracketed in text." The negative words were the loosest ("Very Unlikely", "Unlikely"). A dashboard that labels confidence with words puts the number next to the word, every time; even then a third of readers miss the band, so the word is never the only carrier.

David Spiegelhalter's review of risk communication closes the section with rules that transfer whole: "Use absolute risks"; "express chance as a proportion, a frequency, or a percentage—it is crucial to be clear about the reference class"; "provide percentages or frequencies both with and without the outcome"; "Keep the denominator fixed when making comparisons"; "Be explicit about the time interval"; "Consider a good summary table as a visualization"; "Use multiple formats, because no single representation suits all members of an audience"; and "Have the humility to admit uncertainty."

The counterbalance from Chapter 2

Markant and colleagues' 2023 study is the one finding in this section that pulls against the rest, and it is reported with the authors' own caution. Among 331 people shown correlations with or without uncertainty (a bare line; animated draws; a static ensemble), "the effect of global attitude was more pronounced in visualization conditions with uncertainty representations … compared to visualizations with only the scatterplot and correlation line"; for readers with strong prior attitudes, "visual uncertainty representations may amplify this effect" of discounting contrary data. Their reading: a motivated reader "attend[s] to the uncertainty representation … because they are motivated to find support for their existing belief", using the spread of plausible lines as material for doubt. Their caveat: "alternative models achieved comparable performance" and the result "warrants further investigation to evaluate its robustness." Shown uncertainty is not neutral; for the reader who already disagrees, honesty may be read as weakness. That does not license hiding it — Chapters 1 and 2 are clear about what hiding costs — but it means the form matters for the sceptic as much as for the novice.

11 · Risk formats, and what the public can read

Risk

The health-communication literature has done the experiments a civic dashboard needs. Gigerenzer and colleagues' review: with conditional probabilities, 21% of 160 gynaecologists could say what a positive mammogram meant; with natural frequencies, 87%. A relative risk reduction of "25%" was heard as hundreds of lives per thousand when the absolute figure was about one. Elie Akl and colleagues' Cochrane review of 35 studies confirms the pattern: a relative risk reduction "was perceived to be larger and more persuasive" than the same absolute figure, with "little or no difference in understanding" and no difference between professionals and the public. Stefania Pighin and colleagues' seven experiments add the denominator trap: "A 1-in-X format (e.g., 1 in 200) is subjectively perceived as bigger and more alarming than an N-in-XN format (e.g., 5 in 1000)", and the effect "disappears with an icon array visual aid."[abstract or summary only] Rocio Garcia-Retamero and Edward Cokely's systematic review of 36 studies and 27,885 people in 60 countries found that "Eighty-eight percent of the studies showed that static visual aids tend to be beneficial", that icon arrays "can effectively reduce or eliminate denominator neglect, especially in people with low numeracy and/or high graph literacy" — and, from Yasmina Okan's work, that they help the graph-literate most and the graph-illiterate least.[abstract or summary only] A visual aid is not a universal fix. Their design heuristics transfer almost line for line: one message per visual; depict both the affected individuals and the whole population at risk; keep denominators the same size when comparing; "Use absolute rather than relative risks"; "Use frequencies rather than decimals, fractions, or percentages"; validate the visual aid with the audience before using it. Angela Fagerlin's ten steps add the ones about order and quantity: the order in which risks and benefits are presented changes perception; less information may be more effective; and the time interval over which a risk occurs should be stated again and again.

Literacy

Who is the reader? Mirta Galesic and Garcia-Retamero's graph-literacy scale, run on nationally representative samples in Germany (495) and the United States (492): people got "approximately 9 of 13 items" right, and "Approximately one third of the population in both countries had both low graph literacy and low numeracy skills."[abstract or summary only] Katy Börner and colleagues asked 273 science-museum visitors — a more educated and interested public than average — to name twenty visualisations: charts were recognised most, network layouts least; "very few correctly identified the specific visual (technical label: 14%)"; "less than 50% of respondents gave answers that would be considered at least partially accurate"; and when asked how to read them, most "pointed to superficial features such as color, lines, or text". The study measured naming, not reading. Sukwon Lee and colleagues' visualisation-literacy test gives adult internet workers about half of 53 items right, with stacked area charts and treemaps the hardest.

For England, the official numeracy figure is the OECD's 2023 adult skills survey (PIAAC): 21% of adults at Level 1 or below, people who "struggle to complete mathematical tasks with distracting information or carry out multi-step mathematical processes" — better than the OECD average of 25%, and improving since 2012. The famous "half of UK adults have the numeracy of a primary-school leaver" is a different measurement with a different threshold: the 2011 Skills for Life survey found "49.1% were Entry level 3 or below" (the attainment expected at ages 9–11). Both are true; they should not be presented as the same scale. And the Office for Statistics Regulation's own review of statistical literacy is the one a dashboard builder should sit with: it found numeracy surveys, and "No evidence was found that aimed to capture the multidimensional nature of statistical literacy"; it calls for "more up-to-date, large-scale surveys". Nothing it found measured the public's ability to read a chart or a table. The Vibe Map could.

12 · The accessibility standards, classified

The brief asked that the W3C documents be sorted into hard lines and interpretable guidance. Chapter 13 is the accessibility chapter; this section does the sorting, because the one rule this chapter owns (colour never alone) sits inside it, and because a first-time reader needs to know which of these documents can be broken and which cannot.

WCAG 2.2 — W3C Recommendation, 12 December 2024 — is the hard line. Its success criteria have conformance levels; Level AA means "the web page satisfies all the Level A and Level AA success criteria"; the W3C itself says "It is not recommended that Level AAA conformance be required as a general policy for entire sites". The criteria that bite on charts, in their normative words:

  • 1.1.1 Non-text Content (A). "All non-text content that is presented to the user has a text alternative that serves the equivalent purpose". A chart is non-text content; "equivalent purpose" is the operative phrase, and a one-line alt is not equivalent for a chart carrying data.
  • 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (A). "Information, structure, and relationships conveyed through presentation can be programmatically determined or are available in text." The table behind a chart needs real header cells; a dashboard's grouping of tiles must be structural, not only visual.
  • 1.4.1 Use of Color (A). Quoted in section 4. A legend that distinguishes series only by colour fails it.
  • 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum) (AA) and 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast (AA). 4.5:1 for text; 3:1 for "Parts of graphics required to understand the content". The only WCAG text that names charts is 1.4.11's explanatory page.
  • 1.4.10 Reflow (AA). Content must work "at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels" without two-dimensional scrolling — except "Images required for understanding (such as maps and diagrams)" and "data tables". A map is exempt; a dashboard as a whole is not.
  • 2.1.1 Keyboard (A). "All functionality of the content is operable through a keyboard interface". A hover-only tooltip delivers information no keyboard user can reach.
  • 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum) (AA). Pointer targets "at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels", with an exception the W3C illustrates with map pins: "It is essential to show the pins at the correct map location, therefore the Essential exception applies."
  • 3.1.5 Reading Level is AAA: text above lower-secondary reading level needs a simpler version or supplement. Because it is AAA, plain language is not a WCAG hard line; it is guidance, and in this studio a voluntary standard adopted from the design system and the Decision Book.

WAI-ARIA 1.2 is a normative specification of roles and properties, not a conformance target for content. It has no chart role — none exists in ARIA — and the 2015 proposal for chart roles was never standardised. The Graphics Module adds graphics-document, which "authors should use … for structured graphics such as charts, maps, diagrams". Practically: an SVG chart without role="img" (or graphics-document) and an accessible name is invisible to a screen reader.

The WAI tutorial on Complex Images is guidance — educational material, not a standard — but it is the W3C's own reading of how 1.1.1 applies to charts: "A two-part text alternative is required. The first part is the short description to identify the image … The second part is the long description – a textual representation of the essential information conveyed by the image", which for charts should cover "scales, values, relationships and trends". The Decision Book's rule that alt text "states the finding, not the chart type" is this guidance made house rule.

COGA — Making Content Usable for People with Cognitive and Learning Disabilities — is a Working Group Note and says so: "The objectives and patterns presented here provide supplemental guidance beyond the requirements of WCAG"; "Following this guidance is not required for conformance to WCAG." Its patterns that speak to a numbers-heavy screen — "Provide Alternatives for Numerical Concepts"; "Do Not Rely on Users Calculations or Memorizing Information"; "Use Clear Words"; "Provide Summary of Long Documents and Media" — are the closest thing the W3C has to cognitive-accessibility rules for dashboards, and they are interpretable. There is no WAI document on charts or data visualisation; a community group formed to write one closed in 2023 with no deliverables.

Who is bound. The Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations 2018 require public bodies to meet the accessibility requirement — WCAG 2.2 AA, in the government's current guidance — and publish a statement; the Regulations exempt "non-governmental organisations, unless they provide services that—(i) are essential to the public; or (ii) specifically address the needs of, or are meant for, persons with disabilities", which the GOV.UK guidance renders as charities being exempt "unless they are mostly financed by public funding, provide services that are essential to the public or aimed at disabled people". Nightlife Culture is not a public body, so the Regulations do not reach it directly. The Equality Act 2010 does: section 20's duty to make reasonable adjustments, which for information includes ensuring "the information is provided in an accessible format", is, in the Act's explanatory notes, "an anticipatory duty which means service providers … must anticipate the needs of disabled people and make appropriate reasonable adjustments." WCAG 2.2 AA is the standard a court or the Equality and Human Rights Commission would take as the measure of reasonable. So: WCAG 2.2 AA is a hard line for public bodies by regulation and the de facto yardstick for everyone else; the Analysis Function's and ONS's chart rules — no legends, label at the end of the line, bars start at zero, four lines at most, data download with every chart, titles that state the message — are voluntary Standards the studio has, in effect, already adopted through the Decision Book. Chapter 13 takes it from here.

13 · What holds true regardless

The brief asked for "the short list that survives". Here it is in two parts: the canonical truths — seven, each a rule a dashboard can be held to — and, beneath them, the findings of record that justify them, which are true statements about the evidence rather than rules in their own right. Later chapters test both; the closing chapter confirms or demotes.

The seven

  1. Choose the comparison, not the chart. The eye pulls statistics from a whole display at once and makes comparisons one at a time, slowly; every design that works chooses the comparison for the reader — by grouping, by one highlight, by words. Evidence (Franconeri et al. 2021; Ajani et al. 2022, small). Fixed.
  2. Words carry the message: the trend in the title, the numbers beside the marks, and title and picture pointing at the same thing. The title is looked at first and longest, decides what the chart "showed", is remembered when the reader says it is not, and is believed over a picture it contradicts. Evidence (Borkin et al.; Matzen et al.; Kong et al. 2018, 2019 — nationally representative; Stokes et al., n = 302; Kim et al., n = 2,168). Fixed.
  3. Colour is never the only carrier of meaning, and labels sit at the mark. The first is a Level A success criterion; the second is how a chart meets it, and rests on a working-memory mechanism and analogous evidence rather than a direct test. Standard (WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1) and Practice backed by analogous Evidence (Ginns; Huestegge & Philipp). Fixed.
  4. Bars start at zero, and a broken line axis is a chosen effect size, declared. No label or lesson undoes the exaggeration. Evidence (Correll et al.; Yang et al.[abstract or summary only]; Long & Kay) and Standard (Analysis Function). Fixed.
  5. Uncertainty is shown as something countable or continuous, never as a hard boundary; outcome spread where individuals are the subject; and a word for probability carries its number. Evidence (Correll & Gleicher; Hullman et al.; Kay et al.; Hofman et al., n > 3,500; Padilla et al.; Belia et al.; Budescu et al.; Wintle et al.). Fixed.
  6. Nothing crucial lives behind a click, a hover or a tooltip; the display is read on a phone, in a glance, by someone at PIAAC Level 1. Evidence from adjacent domains (Conlen et al. — interactive articles; PIAAC; Galesic & Garcia-Retamero[abstract or summary only]) and Standard (WCAG 2.1.1). Fixed (requirement).
  7. Every default is advice the designer is giving, and it anchors; it is chosen, written down and shown as chosen. Evidence from an adjacent domain (Jachimowicz et al., policy defaults) and in visualisation (Cho et al.; Valdez et al.; Hullman & Diakopoulos). Adaptable (house default).

The record beneath them

These are what the evidence says; they are not rules, and several come from small or adjacent-domain studies, which is noted.

  • For a precise ratio comparison, position beats length beats angle; the bottom of the hierarchy was never tested by its authors; pies are read by area; and the gaps between lower chart types are smaller than the gaps between people. (Cleveland & McGill; Heer & Bostock; Talbot et al.; Kosara & Skau; Davis et al.) As a design rule the hierarchy is a default for precise comparison, Adaptable otherwise.
  • Lightness carries order and hue carries category; the rainbow exaggerates by binning on pattern maps and helps when reading a single value; about 8% of men of European descent have a red–green deficiency; seven is the experimental ceiling for searchable colours and small marks need bigger differences. (Liu & Heer; Reda et al.; Franconeri; Birch[abstract or summary only]; Healey 1996; Szafir.)
  • The first glance judges appeal, not meaning, on simplicity and prototypicality — from website screenshots and small student samples. (Lindgaard et al.; Tuch et al.) A radial bar takes six times longer to read than a bar — from 36 people on a smartwatch. (Blascheck et al.)
  • Ornament that is the data is free; ornament that touches the mark costs accuracy; ornament behind the data costs time; clutter removed reads as professional, and a headline with one highlight is what is remembered — the last from 24 people, unreplicated. (Haroz et al.; Skau et al.; Borgo et al.[abstract or summary only]; Ajani et al.) The data-ink doctrine itself is Practice.
  • A log scale halved correct reading of one question; a cumulative curve raised perceived risk when daily cases fell; a relative risk persuades without informing; "1 in 200" alarms more than "5 in 1,000"; frequencies are reasoned about better than percentages, and three quarters still fail. (Romano et al.[abstract or summary only]; Reinholtz et al.; Akl et al.; Pighin et al.[abstract or summary only]; Gigerenzer & Hoffrage; McDowell & Jacobs.) Linear, daily, absolute, fixed-denominator are the public defaults.
  • Two or three significant figures; precision is read as confidence. (Ehrenberg — Practice; Cole; three consumer studies[abstract or summary only].)
  • Most readers touch nothing optional; mobile readers touch less and leave sooner — from interactive articles, not dashboards. (Conlen et al.; Aisch; Tse.)
  • "Overview first" is a reminder, not a tested law; people prefer overviews reliably and are helped unreliably. (Shneiderman; Craft & Cairns; Hornbæk & Hertzum.)
  • Animation that carries data taxes memory and is less accurate for analysis; animation that preserves identity across a change helps; small multiples for analysis. (Tversky et al.; Robertson et al., n = 36; Heer & Robertson, n = 24; Brehmer et al., n = 96.)
  • Shown uncertainty may harden a reader who already disagrees — one study, with the authors' own caveat. (Markant et al.)
  • Five WCAG success criteria are the hard lines on charts — 1.1.1, 1.3.1, 1.4.1, 1.4.11, 2.1.1 — with 1.4.3, 1.4.10 and 2.5.8 beside them; plain language (3.1.5) is AAA and so guidance; a non-public body is bound through the Equality Act's anticipatory duty with WCAG 2.2 AA as the yardstick. (Standard.)

14 · Where the choice is yours

Which chart, for most purposes. Below a precise ratio comparison, the hierarchy does not decide; convention, the reader's schema, and the comparison you want made do. A donut is not worse than a pie; a treemap is defensible for part-of-whole with labels; a radial bar is six times slower to read. Adaptable.

How many colours. Seven is the experimental ceiling for search; four or five is the house limit of the UK statistics bodies; small marks need bigger steps. Where to set the Vibe Map's limit is a design-system decision informed by section 4. Adaptable.

How much text. The evidence says more than designers give and the trend in the title; how much more, and in what voice, is the studio's. Adaptable.

Convention or novelty at first glance. Prototypicality rewards resemblance to the thing claimed. Whether the Vibe Map claims to be a dashboard, a map, a flyer or something else — and so what it should resemble in fifty milliseconds — is the creative decision this book never makes. Adaptable; the studio's.

Which uncertainty form. Dotplots, HOPs, gradients, violins, ensembles each read differently and each has a failure mode; the choice depends on the question (one quantity or two; a value or a comparison) and the reader (novice or sceptic). Adaptable; the prohibition on bare intervals and hard boundaries is Fixed.

Breaking a line axis. Permitted, and a chosen effect size; declare it. Adaptable.

Overview or search first; animation or small multiples; scroll or step. The reader's arriving question, the task, and the device decide; none is a law. Adaptable.

Rounding. Two or three significant figures; which, by column, is a judgement. Adaptable within the Fixed ceiling of the data's own precision.

15 · What this means for a nightlife dashboard

An illustration, not a specification.

The brief's own failure register says a dashboard fails if "a viewer reads it and asks 'what am I looking at'", if it is "a fancy spreadsheet with some charts that tell you lots of big numbers, but not what actually happens", and if "people don't trust it". Read through this chapter, those three failures have mechanisms.

"What am I looking at" is a schema failure. The public can name a bar chart and cannot name a treemap; scatterplots are misunderstood by more than a third of American adults; the forms expert communities invent require a schema that most of the public — the dancefloor included — does not have. A nightlife dashboard that wants to be read by a promoter and a committee at once builds, at the level of the chart, from forms both already know, and spends its invention — the brief asks for nightlife data to be as exciting as a club flyer — in layout, hierarchy, words and register, where the Decision Book already says a dashboard's creativity should live. The evidence on the first glance says the same thing from the other side: appeal in fifty milliseconds comes from simplicity and from looking like what you claim to be. What the Vibe Map claims to be is the studio's decision; this chapter only says that whatever it claims, it should look like that at once.

"Big numbers, but not what actually happens" is a comparison failure. A big number is the most-looked-at object on a dashboard and this chapter found no evidence that it is understood. The eye pulls a statistic in a glance and makes a comparison slowly; a tile that shows a count and no comparison has given the reader the fast thing and withheld the slow one. The fix is in words and in one highlight: a title that states the trend, a number beside its context, a single comparison chosen for the reader — the design that, in the one small experiment that tested it, was what people remembered. And the numbers themselves: two or three figures, a frequency not a percentage, a fixed denominator, the time interval stated.

"People don't trust it" has, in this chapter, three design mechanisms. A truncated axis, a cumulative curve, a log scale or a relative risk each move the reader without the reader noticing, and a sceptical reader who later notices does not forgive it; the defaults are linear, daily, absolute, from zero. A bare interval or a tight error bar round an average overstates what is known about individuals; the uncertainty is shown as something countable, with the number beside any word. And for the reader who arrives already against the night time economy, Chapter 2's plain table and this chapter's Markant finding point the same way: the form of the uncertainty display is itself something to test with sceptics, because the handsome spread of possibilities can be read as doubt.

Three warnings travel with the illustration. Every default on the first screen — place, measure, period, sort — will be read as the studio's advice and will anchor where the reader looks; there is no neutral default, only a declared one. Most readers will touch nothing, and on a phone, where hover does not exist, they will touch less; the finding lives on the surface or it does not live. And colour is never the only carrier of meaning: for the Vibe Map that is not a style preference but a Level A success criterion, met by labelling at the mark before a series colour is chosen.

The rules

Kind and tier as in Chapter 0.

Rule Why Kind Tier Source
Name the comparison the reader is to make before choosing a form; design the display to make that comparison first Statistics are fast, comparisons slow and serial; design works by choosing the comparison Evidence Fixed Franconeri et al. 2021; Ajani et al. 2022 (n = 24)
For a precise ratio comparison, use position on a common scale, then length; do not ask for a precise reading from area or colour Replicated top of the hierarchy Evidence Fixed for precise comparison; Adaptable as a general form rule Cleveland & McGill 1984; Heer & Bostock 2010
Never let colour be the only means of distinguishing or conveying anything Level A success criterion; 8% of men Standard Fixed WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.1; Birch 2012[abstract or summary only]
Text at 4.5:1; parts of graphics needed to understand the content at 3:1 against adjacent colours Level AA Standard Fixed WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3, 1.4.11
Lightness for order, hue for category; no rainbow for ordered data on a pattern map Lightness is read as order; the rainbow bins and exaggerates Evidence Fixed (pattern maps); Adaptable where the task is reading a value Liu & Heer 2018; Franconeri 2021; Reda et al. 2018
Limit categorical colours — seven is the experimental ceiling for search, four or five the house limit; give small marks bigger colour steps Search degrades beyond seven; small marks need bigger differences than large ones Evidence + Standard (voluntary) Adaptable within the ceiling Healey 1996; Szafir 2018; Analysis Function; ONS
Put the message in the title, in words; put statistics and context beside the marks; never title-only, never no-text Title first, longest, remembered, decisive; readers prefer the most-annotated chart; placement follows meaning Evidence Fixed Borkin et al. 2016; Kong et al. 2018; Stokes et al. 2023
Title and chart point at the same salient thing A caption cannot redirect to a faint feature; a contradicting title is believed and unnoticed Evidence Fixed Kim, Setlur & Agrawala 2021; Kong et al. 2019
Label at the mark; legends only where labels cannot fit, and then ordered to match the data Working-memory round trip; spatial contiguity d = 0.72; the compliance route for 1.4.1 Practice + analogous Evidence + Standard Fixed (evidential status stated) Huestegge & Philipp 2011; Ginns 2006; WCAG 1.4.1
Build first screens from fast-glance forms; avoid radial bars for comparison Six-fold glance penalty for the decorative form — from 36 people on a smartwatch Evidence (small; adjacent device) Adaptable (strong default) Blascheck et al. 2019
Design the first glance for simplicity and for looking like what the display claims to be Appeal forms in 50 ms on complexity and prototypicality — websites, small student samples Evidence (adjacent domain) Adaptable (what it claims to be is the studio's) Lindgaard et al. 2006; Tuch et al. 2012
Pictograms that are the data are permitted; nothing decorative behind the data; no styled bars (rounded, capped, triangular) Free or helpful; distracting; inaccurate, respectively Evidence Fixed Haroz et al. 2015; Skau et al. 2015
Declutter for professionalism; add a headline, one highlight and one sentence for recall 2.5–3× recall of the intended conclusion in one study of 24; consistent with the title and text evidence; trust unmoved by either Evidence (small, unreplicated) + the title evidence Adaptable (strong default); the headline itself is Fixed under the words rule Ajani et al. 2022; Borkin et al. 2016; Stokes et al. 2023
Bar axes start at zero; a broken line axis is declared and the effect size it implies is chosen deliberately Truncation exaggerates even when labelled and taught Evidence Fixed Correll et al. 2020; Yang et al. 2021[abstract or summary only]; Long & Kay 2024
Do not compare non-baseline segments of a stacked bar; use grouped or dot charts Length judgement plus part-of-whole bias Evidence Fixed Cleveland & McGill; Talbot et al. 2014
Public defaults: linear scale, daily flow with the cumulative available, absolute risk with a fixed denominator and a stated interval Log halved correct reading of one question; cumulative raises perceived risk; relative risk persuades without informing; 1-in-X alarms (health domain) Evidence (part adjacent domain) Fixed (requirement) · alternatives offered beside the default: Adaptable Romano et al. 2020[abstract or summary only]; Reinholtz et al. 2021; Akl et al. 2011; Pighin et al. 2011[abstract or summary only]
Show a value the reader wants to know as a number or a table, not a chart; show a trend or comparison as a chart Cognitive fit Evidence[abstract or summary only] + Reading Adaptable Vessey & Galletta 1991[abstract or summary only]; Cleveland & McGill
Two or three significant figures; never more precision than the data has; frequencies ("9 in 100") where chance is involved Readers round anyway; precision reads as confidence; frequencies are reasoned about better Practice + Evidence Fixed (ceiling); Adaptable (digits) Ehrenberg 1977; Cole 2015; Gigerenzer & Hoffrage 1995; McDowell & Jacobs 2017
Nothing crucial behind a click, a hover or a tooltip; everything crucial reachable by keyboard and on a phone Median use of optional controls is zero (interactive articles, not dashboards); hover does not exist on touch; SC 2.1.1 Evidence (adjacent domain) + Standard Fixed Conlen et al. 2019; Tse 2016; WCAG 2.1.1
Every default — place, measure, period, sort, extent — is chosen, written down and shown as a choice Defaults shift choices (d = 0.68, policy and consumer domains), partly by being read as advice; the opening view anchors the session Evidence (adjacent domain + visualisation) Adaptable (house default) Jachimowicz et al. 2019; Cho et al. 2017; Hullman & Diakopoulos 2011
Treat "overview first" as a satisfaction preference; let the reader's arriving question decide 52 citations, no validations; 2 of 17 comparisons more accurate Evidence Adaptable Craft & Cairns 2005; Hornbæk & Hertzum 2011
Small multiples for analysis; animation only for transitions between states of the same chart, or for presentation with the static version available Animation enjoyed, slower, less accurate; transitions preserve identity Evidence Fixed Robertson et al. 2008; Heer & Robertson 2007; Brehmer et al. 2019
Never a bare interval or a hard boundary for uncertainty; prefer countable dots, gradients, violins or animated draws; show outcome spread, not only estimate uncertainty, where individuals are the subject Within-the-bar bias; containment; CI overstates individual effect (a treatment-effect game, n > 3,500) Evidence (part adjacent domain) Fixed Correll & Gleicher 2014; Padilla et al. 2017; Hofman et al. 2020; Kay et al. 2016
A word for probability carries its number in brackets beside it 32% → 66% agreement; a glossary does not help Evidence Fixed Wintle et al. 2019; Budescu et al. 2014
Test uncertainty displays with sceptical readers before release One study: uncertainty may amplify discounting among the strongly opposed Evidence (one study) Adaptable Markant et al. 2023
Plan for a reader at PIAAC Level 1 and with low graph literacy; test with them A fifth of adults in England; a third with both deficits in Germany and the US Evidence Fixed (requirement) PIAAC 2023; Galesic & Garcia-Retamero 2011[abstract or summary only]
Meet WCAG 2.2 AA as the yardstick of reasonable adjustment; two-part text alternatives for every chart; role="img" or graphics-document on every SVG chart Equality Act anticipatory duty; WAI complex-images guidance; no chart role exists Standard + guidance Fixed Equality Act 2010 s.20; WCAG 2.2; WAI tutorials; WAI-ARIA 1.2
Which chart below the top of the hierarchy; how many colours; how much text; convention or novelty at first glance; which uncertainty form; line-axis breaks; overview or search; animation or multiples; rounding Open choices with named trade-offs — Adaptable Section 14
Register, imagery, metaphor, texture around the chart Free, within the design system and provided nothing that carries meaning lives only there — Decorative Decision Book Ch 7

What proves a break works

If you must break a Fixed rule above — a legend instead of labels, a truncated bar, a rainbow, an error bar, a finding behind a hover — the test is the same: give the display to the reader the rule protects, for the time the rule assumes, and ask them what it says. Print the legend chart in greyscale and give it to someone with protanopia — the commonest red–green deficiency. Give the truncated bar to someone for five seconds and ask how big the difference is, then ask them to read the numbers, and notice that the two answers disagree. Give the error bar to a statistician and ask what it means for one person. Give the hover to someone on a phone. If the reading survives, log the break in the deviation entry Chapter 16 describes. If it does not, the rule was right.

What this chapter could not settle

  • No study of the big-number tile; no study of legends against labels; no UK measurement of chart literacy. Said so; flagged all three for the prototype.
  • The field's most-quoted interaction statistic is an anecdote about one button. Replaced it with Conlen et al.'s measured rates and kept Aisch's own correction.

Checklist

  • The comparison the reader is to make is named, and the display makes it first
  • Precise comparisons use position or length; nothing precise rests on area or colour
  • No meaning carried by colour alone; text 4.5:1; graphical parts 3:1
  • Ordered data in lightness; categories in hue; no rainbow on pattern maps
  • Categorical colours within the house limit; small marks given bigger steps
  • The message is in the title; statistics and context beside the marks; no title-only or text-free chart
  • Title and chart point at the same thing
  • Labels at the mark; any unavoidable legend ordered to match the data
  • First-screen forms are fast-glance; no radial bars for comparison
  • No decoration behind data; no styled bars; pictograms only as data
  • A headline, one highlight and one sentence per chart that must be remembered
  • Bar axes at zero; any broken line axis declared with its effect size considered
  • No comparison of non-baseline stacked segments
  • Linear, daily, absolute, fixed denominator, interval stated — or the departure justified
  • Point values as numbers or tables; trends and comparisons as charts
  • Two or three significant figures; frequencies for chance; no precision beyond the data
  • Nothing crucial behind click, hover or tooltip; keyboard and phone reachable
  • Every default written down and shown as a choice
  • Overview or search chosen from the arriving question, not the mantra
  • Small multiples for analysis; animation only for same-chart transitions or presentation
  • No bare intervals or hard boundaries; outcome spread shown where individuals are the subject
  • Every probability word has its number beside it
  • Uncertainty displays tested with sceptical readers
  • Tested with readers at PIAAC Level 1 and low graph literacy
  • WCAG 2.2 AA met; two-part text alternative per chart; SVG charts carry a role and a name

Words this chapter uses

Two statistical conventions, since this chapter reports experiments.

  • d is the difference between two groups measured in standard deviations, where 0.2 is conventionally small, 0.5 medium and 0.8 large.
  • n is how many people took part. Where a finding comes from a few dozen students in one laboratory, the chapter says so; where it comes from thousands of people across countries, it says that too, and the difference matters more than the headline.

04From data to evidence

A number is undefined until its unit, period and base are stated. Nothing is never one thing.

Dashboard Design · Part 1: The analytical foundation

Reading this chapter. This is one chapter of Dashboard Design, Nightlife Culture's research book on how evidence becomes a display a reader can trust, read and act on. The studio ("the house" in some chapters) is Nightlife Culture, a creative policy studio; the brief is its founder Carly Heath's commission for the book, and her eight ways a dashboard fails, the failure register, run through it. The Vibe Map, the studio's prototype for showing a place's nightlife culture, appears only as an illustration, never as a specification. "Version 1" is the book's archived first draft, whose positions this version re-tests against the sources. Every rule carries a kind (where it comes from: Standard, Evidence, Reading, Practice or Nightlife Culture) and a tier (how firm it is: Fixed, Adaptable or Decorative); Chapter 0 explains both, and the three senses of Fixed: a requirement that can be checked, a sequence whose order is the hard line, and a statement of the record. A dagger (†) marks a source read at the authors' abstract or summary only; "secondary" a quotation reached through a named reproduction; "(read once)" a quotation returned on a single reading and not confirmed by a second. Chapter 0 holds the glossary of the words the chapters share; each chapter lists its own coinages before its sources.

The question

What has to be true of a number before it can be shown as evidence — and what does a dashboard owe its reader about where the number came from, what it counts, what it leaves out, and what it may be compared with?

The 60-second version

A dashboard shows numbers. A number is not evidence until five things about it are settled, and most dashboards settle none of them on the face of the display.

First, its grain: what one row of the data is — a person, a venue, a night, a ticket — and what one unit of time is. These are choices, made before any analysis, and the author of the canonical paper on tidy data admits that defining them in general is "surprisingly difficult". European law defines eight different things a "business" can be. The UK counts a hospital bed as occupied if someone is in it at midnight, and a US study found the count at midnight sits well below the late-morning peak. A "day", a "month" and a "night" are measurement rules, and the rule changes the count.

Second, its denominator: a count against what. A rate exists so that places of different sizes can be compared; the choice of base is the least visible and most consequential decision in a display, and the smallest places sit at both ends of any ranking by arithmetic alone.

Third, its provenance. The UK's Code of Practice, European law, the Treasury's guide to analytical assurance and three machine standards converge on the same minimum: who is responsible, what source, what method, what period it describes (separately from when it was published and when it last changed), what status it has, what quality it claims, and what has been withheld. Official usage defines "reliability" as how little a number moves when it is revised; a UK quarterly growth figure typically moves half a percentage point over three years, and the regulator calls that normal.

Fourth, its nothings. The studio names six kinds — zero, free, unavailable, unknown, not collected, suppressed. The official world already distinguishes most of them, splits one of them in two, and has no code at all for "free", which it treats as a price of zero on a real quantity. The UK and European statistical offices both ban the letters "NA" because nobody can tell whether they mean not applicable or not available. The inventor of the relational database wrote in 1986 that zero is "far too valuable" to stand for missing; the database standard kept one null anyway, and the one-line idiom that turns "no rows" into a displayed 0 is in every warehouse. The only official rule for drawing a gap on a chart says: do not join the points either side, "even if the line is dotted or dashed. Joining points implies we know something about the data."

Fifth, its comparability. A comparison is valid "to the extent that differences between statistics can be attributed to differences between the true values" — which means everything else must be held equal or declared: definition, period, geography and boundary vintage, method, disclosure treatment, breaks, revisions, the comparator group and how it was chosen, precision, and what was done with outliers. Finance arrived at the same list independently: a like-for-like figure is a defined figure, and if you change the definition you restate the comparators.

Behind these sit three facts about data itself. A total is a statement about its largest contributors — the long tail of cultural markets is mostly ones and zeros, and in an artificial music market, letting people see what others chose increased both inequality and unpredictability. Size does not cure selection: in the one case where it has been measured, a self-selected dataset covering one in a hundred people was worth a random sample of four hundred, because what matters is the tiny correlation between being recorded and the value recorded. And an outlier is a question before it is a decision: the standard definition is a point that arouses "suspicions that it was generated by a different mechanism", the rule behind every box plot flags an "outlier" in a third of perfectly ordinary samples, two-fifths of papers that claim no exclusions have numbers that do not match, and the good-end outlier — the small place doing unexpectedly well — is a hypothesis about mechanism that has the same undeclared-threshold problem as the bad end.

So the canonical truths are these: a number is undefined until its unit, its period and its base are stated; nothing is never one thing; every figure carries its provenance and the record outlives the number; a comparison declares what it holds equal; a total speaks for the biggest; size does not cure selection; and an outlier is investigated, declared, and shown with and without.

1 · What evidence asks of a number

Chapters 1 to 3 treated a dashboard as an argument addressed to a reader. An argument rests on evidence, and evidence is a stronger word than data. Data is what the system recorded. Evidence is data that has been made fit to bear a conclusion, with the fitness shown. The distance between the two is the subject of this chapter, and it is where the second and sixth items on Carly's failure register — the fancy spreadsheet that tells you big numbers but not what happens, and the display that breaks or is not reliable — mostly come from.

The sharpest single statement of the standard is the UK statistics regulator's. In its 2023 perspective on quality, the Office for Statistics Regulation defines quality as statistics that "fit their intended uses, are based on appropriate data and methods, and are not materially misleading", and then gives the test: "Publishing data and statistics that materially mislead is unacceptable. If the statistics do not bear the weight of the decisions made using them, producers should immediately review whether they should continue to publish them." A number on a dashboard is being asked to bear the weight of a decision; the question is whether it can, and whether the reader can tell.

The regulator also reports what readers say they need in order to tell: "Some users have told us during our designation review that they would like prominent, succinct quality information, which helps them decide whether the statistics are suitable for their own use." Something prominent and short enough to be read at the point of use, by a reader whose use the producer did not anticipate. It should be said at once that this is users' testimony to a regulator; no study was found for this chapter that measures whether provenance shown on the face of a display changes what a reader decides, and section 5 returns to that gap.

The Treasury's guide to analytical assurance — The AQuA Book, first published in 2015 and replaced by a new edition on 30 July 2025 — supplies a distinction this chapter uses throughout. In the 2015 wording, which the 2025 edition keeps in substance: "verification activities ask whether the analysis has been conducted correctly; validation activities ask whether the correct analysis has been performed". A number can be computed flawlessly from the wrong data, at the wrong grain, against the wrong base, for a purpose it was never assured for. The book exists because of a case of exactly that: the 2012 InterCity West Coast rail franchise competition, which collapsed when, in the National Audit Office's words, there were "significant errors in the tool the Department used to calculate how big a loan it would require bidders to have", and — the sentence that matters here — "The model had been designed to inform internal discussions and received no extra quality assurance once the Department decided to use it to calculate the loan, a key commercial decision". The arithmetic was the smaller fault; the larger was a number re-used for a decision heavier than the one it had been built to bear. "Fit for purpose" means fit for this purpose, and purposes drift.

The 2025 AQuA Book names four roles in any piece of analysis, and they are worth carrying into dashboard work because a dashboard rarely assigns them. The commissioner "requests the analysis and sets out their requirements" and "accepts the analysis and assurance as fit for purpose". The analyst "designs the approach, including the assurance" and "carries out their own assurance". The assurer "must be independent from the analysts" and "reviews the assurance completed by the analyst". The approver "scrutinises the work of the analyst and assurer" and confirms that it "has been appropriately assured". Assurance, it says, "should be proportionate to the potential effect it will have and the size and complexity of the analysis". The Macpherson review of 2013, which led to the first edition, recommended that "There should be a single Senior Responsible Owner for each model ("Model SRO") through its lifecycle" and that quality assurance cover "inputs, methodology and outputs". A public dashboard is an analytical model with a user interface. Somebody owns it; the reader should be able to find out who.

The academic literature on data quality arrived at the same breadth from the consumer's side. In 1996 Richard Wang and Diane Strong defined data quality "as data that are fit for use by data consumers" — borrowing the phrase from the quality engineer Joseph Juran — and, from a first survey of 137 people that produced 179 candidate attributes and a second of 355 usable returns that rated 118 of them, found that consumers judge it on twenty dimensions in four groups, not on accuracy alone. The group they call intrinsic contains accuracy, but also objectivity, believability and reputation. That finding is the bridge back to Chapter 1: a correct number from a source the reader does not believe is, to that reader, low-quality data. Provenance is part of what the number's quality consists of, by the consumer's own account.

Three vocabularies for quality are used below and should be told apart. The European Statistical System's, written into Regulation (EC) No 223/2009 and adopted by the UK, is for statistics: relevance, accuracy, timeliness, punctuality, accessibility and clarity, comparability, coherence. The UK Government Data Quality Framework of 2020 is for datasets and uses the six dimensions of the Data Management Association: completeness, uniqueness, consistency, timeliness, validity, accuracy. The Code of Practice for Statistics is for producers and asks about their conduct. A dashboard needs all three, because it is a dataset, shown as statistics, by a producer.

2 · Why people believe what they believe

The beliefs this chapter tests are less often stated than Chapter 3's, because they are rarely noticed as beliefs. Each is given fairly here and met in the sections that follow.

Belief one: a count is a fact

"There were 412 events last month." The number of events feels like a thing that was simply counted. But "event", "last month" and the implied base (412 of what, in how big a place) are each a choice, and the count changes with every one of them. Section 3 is about the first two; section 4 about the third.

Belief two: more data is better data

If a feed covers millions of transactions, it must be more trustworthy than a survey of a few hundred people. The intuition is strong, the vocabulary of "big data" encourages it, and it is wrong in a precise and quantifiable way. Section 9.

Belief three: a blank is nothing, and nothing is small

An empty cell, a flat line at zero, a missing row: the instinct is that absence is harmless, or that it is the same as zero, or that it affects only the cell it sits in. Section 6 shows that statistics, databases and surveys each had to invent a vocabulary to stop that instinct doing damage.

Belief four: the average describes the typical

A mean, a total, a per-capita figure: these feel like descriptions of a population. In a skewed distribution — which is what every cultural market is — they describe its largest members. Section 8.

Belief five: the long tail is a law

"Twenty per cent of the venues produce eighty per cent of the revenue" is said as if it were a law of nature, often with the name Pareto attached. The man who popularised the principle later apologised for its name, and the empirical shape of a cultural market's tail is more extreme and less lawful than the slogan. Section 8.

Belief six: an outlier is an error

When a value is far from the others, the practised reflex is to trim it. The statistical literature's standard definition says an outlier is a point suspected of having been "generated by a different mechanism" — which is a reason to investigate, not to delete — and the field's own audits find that deletion is frequent, silent, and shaped by what the analyst wanted to find. Section 10.

Belief seven: two numbers with the same name can be compared

Two "footfall" figures, two "visitor spend" estimates, two years of the same series: if they share a name, they are comparable. European law defines comparability as the extent to which differences in the numbers reflect differences in reality rather than differences in method, and gives three axes along which that must be shown. Section 7.

Belief eight: "reliable" means accurate

In ordinary speech it does. In official statistics it means something narrower and more useful — how little a number changes when it is revised — and the difference matters for any display that overwrites yesterday's figure with today's. Section 5.

3 · Grain — the unit of observation, and the unit of time

What a row is

Hadley Wickham's 2014 paper "Tidy Data", the standard statement of how analytical data should be shaped for analysis, gives three rules: "In tidy data: 1. Each variable forms a column. 2. Each observation forms a row. 3. Each type of observational unit forms a table." The second rule is the one this section is about. An observation "contains all values measured on the same unit (like a person, or a day, or a race) across attributes". The row of the table is the grain, and what the row is — a person, or a day, or a race — is decided before anything is counted.

Wickham is candid about how slippery that decision is. "For a given dataset, it's usually easy to figure out what are observations and what are variables, but it is surprisingly difficult to precisely define variables and observations in general." If the author of the canonical paper finds the definition hard in general, a dashboard that never states its grain is asking its readers to guess at something its builders may not have settled.

Official statistics has made the distinctions explicit because it had to. Eurostat's glossary separates three things a dashboard usually treats as one. The reporting unit is "the entity from which the recommended data items are collected" — who sent the data. The observation unit is "the entity on which information is received and statistics are compiled in the process of collecting statistical data" — what the data is about. The statistical unit is "the entity for which the required statistics are compiled", which "may be an observation unit … or an analytical unit, which statisticians create by splitting or combining observation units with the help of estimations or imputations". A ticketing platform reports; a venue is observed; a "scene" may be an analytical unit nobody reported and nobody observed, assembled from the other two. Each is a legitimate grain. Confusing them is where a count stops being a fact.

How many things can a "business" be? Council Regulation (EEC) No 696/93, which still governs the statistical units of the European production system, defines eight in its annex. The enterprise is "The smallest combination of legal units that is an organizational unit producing goods or services, which benefits from a certain degree of autonomy in decision-making". The local unit is "An enterprise or part thereof (e.g. a workshop, factory, warehouse, office, mine or depot) situated in a geographically identified place". The enterprise group is "An association of enterprises bound together by legal and/or financial links". Between them sit the institutional unit, the kind-of-activity unit, the unit of homogeneous production, the local kind-of-activity unit and the local unit of homogeneous production.
