The best-known case study is Lazer, Kennedy, King and Vespignani's 2014 article in Science on Google Flu Trends, which at one point was "predicting more than double the proportion of doctor visits for influenza-like illness" that the CDC's surveillance showed. The article's body text was read in two independent teaching reproductions (secondary; the publisher page was not reachable), and three sentences carry the lesson. "'Big data hubris' is the often implicit assumption that big data are a substitute for, rather than a supplement to, traditional data collection and analysis." "Algorithm dynamics are the changes made by engineers to improve the commercial service and by consumers in using that service" — the search engine kept changing, and so did the people using it, so the mapping from searches to flu drifted. And: "The core challenge is that most big data that have received popular attention are not the output of instruments designed to produce valid and reliable data amenable for scientific analysis." A platform's data is a by-product of the platform's purpose, and the platform owes its data nothing.

The ten characteristics

Matthew Salganik's 2018 textbook Bit by Bit gives the checklist, and each line is quoted from its own summary sentence. Three characteristics are, in his words, "generally helpful for research": big ("Large datasets are a means to an end; they are not an end in themselves"), always-on ("Always-on big data enables the study of unexpected events and real-time measurement"), and nonreactive ("Measurement in big data sources is much less likely to change behavior"). Seven are "generally problematic for research": incomplete ("No matter how big your big data, it probably doesn't have the information you want" — typically missing "demographic information about participants, behavior on other platforms, and data to operationalize theoretical constructs"); inaccessible ("Data held by companies and governments are difficult for researchers to access"); nonrepresentative ("Nonrepresentative data are bad for out-of-sample generalizations, but can be quite useful for within-sample comparisons" — Meng's conclusion in one sentence); drifting ("Population drift, usage drift, and system drift make it hard to use big data sources to study long-term trends"); algorithmically confounded ("Behavior in big data systems is not natural; it is driven by the engineering goals of the systems" — his example is a platform that "encouraged people with few connections … to make more friends until they reached 20 friends", so that a histogram of friend counts showed a bump at 20 that was the product's doing); dirty ("Big data sources can be loaded with junk and spam" — in one study of pager messages on 11 September 2001, "Removing the messages generated by this single automated pager completely eliminates the apparent increase in anger over the course of the day"); and sensitive ("Some of the information that companies and governments have is sensitive"). The pager case is also section 8's point in miniature: one unit dominated an aggregate and became a finding. The ten are a textbook's framework, marked Practice; each is a question to ask of a feed before a number from it is shown.

Two framings from the critical literature sit beside this. Kitchin and McArdle, examining 26 datasets, concluded that the traits that actually distinguish big data from small are "velocity (both frequency of generation, and frequency of handling, recording, and publishing) and exhaustivity" — and exhaustivity, the claim that the data covers "entire populations", is the claim Meng dismantles. boyd and Crawford's 2012 provocations (author draft — wording may differ from the published version) include the one that matters most here: "Big data and whole data are also not the same. Without taking into account the sample of a dataset, the size of the dataset is meaningless." And: "Twitter does not represent 'all people', and it is an error to assume 'people' and 'Twitter users' are synonymous: they are a very particular sub-set." The sentence holds with any platform's name in it.

Administrative data

Administrative data — in the words of Administrative Data Research UK, "information created when people use public services, such as schools, the NHS, the courts or the benefits system" — sits between survey and trace. It is often near-complete for the population that touches the service and, as ADR UK says, "most of this data was not originally collected for research purposes". The ONS's 2023 working paper on errors in administrative and alternative sources gives the official taxonomy of what goes wrong: measurement errors (validity, reliability, missing data at unit and item level); representation errors (under- and over-coverage; selection); processing errors (data entry, coding and editing, model and imputation, unit errors, linkage, identification). "Unit errors" and "coverage" are this chapter's sections 3 and 4 by other names. Connelly and colleagues' 2016 review puts the researcher's duty plainly: administrative data "is not originally collected for the purpose of research"; "Researchers generally have no input into the design, structure and content"; it is "not documented in order to support data analysis"; so "researchers must put effort into uncovering the data generation processes which have governed how these data have been created", and "Understanding the processes of how and why administrative data are collected will be central to assessing the data's quality". A licensing register, a business-rates list, a grants database: each is an administrative source whose grain, coverage and purpose were set by someone else's operation, and the provenance line a dashboard owes for each is the answer to "why did this organisation record this, and who is not in it".

10 · Outliers — a signal before it is noise

What an outlier is

The standard definition is Douglas Hawkins's, from 1980, reached here as quoted in Charu Aggarwal's textbook and in Osborne and Overbay (the book itself is not open): an outlier is "an observation which deviates so much from the other observations as to arouse suspicions that it was generated by a different mechanism." The operative word is mechanism. The definition does not say an outlier is wrong; it says it is suspicious, and what it is suspected of is having come from somewhere else. That is a reason to find out where, not a reason to delete.

The other canonical definitions agree in form. Grubbs (1969), as quoted in Hodge and Austin's survey: "An outlying observation, or outlier, is one that appears to deviate markedly from other members of the sample in which it occurs." Barnett and Lewis, likewise quoted: "An observation (or subset of observations) which appears to be inconsistent with the remainder of that set of data." The US standards handbook: "An outlier is an observation that appears to deviate markedly from other observations in the sample", with the two sentences that follow: "Outliers may be due to random variation or may indicate something scientifically interesting." "An outlier may indicate bad data." The data-mining survey by Chandola, Banerjee and Kumar reframes the whole subject from the point of view of someone who wants the anomalies: "Anomalies are patterns in data that do not conform to a well defined notion of normal behavior", and their importance "is due to the fact that anomalies in data translate to significant, and often critical, actionable information" — the hacked computer, the tumour, the stolen card, the failing sensor. They distinguish noise, "a phenomenon in data that is not of interest to the analyst, but acts as a hindrance", from anomalies, which are of interest; the same datum can be either, depending on who is looking. And they distinguish three kinds: a point anomaly, unusual against everything; a contextual anomaly, "anomalous in a specific context, but not otherwise" — a temperature normal in July and anomalous in January; and a collective anomaly, a set of related points that is unusual together. For a display of places over time, the contextual kind is the one that matters, and it cannot be found by any rule that ignores the context.

What the tests assume

The common tests carry assumptions that decide their verdicts. Grubbs' test, per the standards handbook, "is used to detect a single outlier in a univariate data set that follows an approximately normal distribution" — one outlier, one variable, a bell curve — and "If the normality assumption for the data being tested is not valid, then a determination that there is an outlier may in fact be due to the non-normality of the data rather than the prescence [sic] of an outlier." Cultural data has the skewed shape of section 8 rather than a bell curve, so a normal-theory test applied to it will find outliers that are merely the tail.

Tukey's fences — the "1.5 times the interquartile range" rule behind every box plot — were a labelling rule for attention. Tukey's own terms, as quoted in a 2025 paper, were "outside" for points between the inner and outer fences and "far out" for points beyond; the handbook's are "mild" and "extreme". The rule's false-flag rate is a property of the rule: Dawson (2011) shows that "at least 30% of samples from a normally-distributed population of any size will be flagged as containing an outlier, while for small samples (N<10) even extreme outliers indicate little", and "for the normal distribution, the incidence of samples with flagged outliers never drops below about 30%, and above sample size 13 starts to rise." An automated alert on box-plot fences would fire on a third of perfectly ordinary datasets. The handbook's advice on what to do with a flagged point is the right one: "Outliers should be investigated carefully. Often they contain valuable information about the process under investigation or the data gathering and recording process. Before considering the possible elimination of these points from the data, one should try to understand why they appeared and whether it is likely similar values will continue to appear."

The rule most used in published research — flag anything more than three standard deviations from the mean — is self-defeating, and Leys and colleagues (2013) say why in three points: "Firstly, it assumes that the distribution is normal (outliers included). Secondly, the mean and standard deviation are strongly impacted by outliers. Thirdly … this method is very unlikely to detect outliers in small samples." The outlier inflates the yardstick used to catch it. Their survey of 127 published articles found most used mean-and-standard-deviation and none the robust alternative they recommend, the median absolute deviation, with the constant 1.4826 "linked to the assumption of normality" and thresholds of 3, 2.5 or 2 after Miller. Their reporting rule is the one this chapter adopts: "The threshold should be justified and the justification should clearly state that other concerns than cherry-picking degrees of freedom guided the selection." Frank Hampel's overview of robust statistics supplies the reason to prefer rank-based summaries throughout: the proportion of a dataset that can be corrupted before a statistic breaks is "for the median … 1/2" and "for the arithmetic mean … 0", and in "scientific routine data, not taken with utmost care", the fraction of gross errors "is typically between 1 percent and 10 percent".

Artefact or finding

The practical triage is Osborne and Overbay's (2004), whose seven causes of outliers run from process to world. Their headings: "Outliers from data errors"; "Outliers from intentional or motivated mis-reporting"; "Outliers from sampling error"; "Outliers from standardization failure"; "Outliers from faulty distributional assumptions"; "Outliers as legitimate cases sampled from the correct population"; and "Outliers as potential focus of inquiry". The first six are artefacts of how the data was made; the seventh is a finding. Their rule for the artefacts: "If outliers of this nature cannot be corrected they should be eliminated as they do not represent valid population data points." Their rule for the rest: "Before discarding outliers, researchers need to consider whether those data contain valuable information that may not necessarily relate to the intended study, but has importance in a more global sense." And, quoting Barnett and Lewis: "Not all outliers are illegitimate contaminants, and not all illegitimate scores show up as outliers". The sequence is fixed: first ask which of the six artefacts it could be, with the provenance of section 5 as the checklist; only if none fits is it a finding; and only if one fits is it removed, with the removal declared.

What the field actually does

Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn's 2011 paper on false positives lists the ordinary flexibilities an analyst has — "Should more data be collected? Should some observations be excluded? Which conditions should be combined and which ones compared?" — and finds that "it is common (and accepted practice) for researchers to explore various analytic alternatives, to search for a combination that yields 'statistical significance,' and to then report only what 'worked.'" Combining four such flexibilities produced a false-positive rate of about 61% at the conventional threshold. Their fifth requirement for authors: "If observations are eliminated, authors must also report what the statistical results are if those observations are included." Bakker and Wicherts (2014) measured how often removal goes unreported, in 2,667 results from 153 psychology articles. The finding is indirect and they say so: "we did find a discrepancy between the reported degrees of freedom of t tests and the reported sample size in 41% of articles that did not report removal of any data values." Two in five papers that claimed no exclusions had numbers that did not add up. They recommend "an outlier handling protocol" set before analysis and note that inconsistent thresholds permit "self-serving justifications". For a dashboard the translation is direct: the rule and threshold are written down before the data arrives, and any figure shown without a point is shown with it too, one tap away.

The good-end outlier

The small place doing unexpectedly well is the outlier the brief most cares about, and it has a method. Positive deviance, defined in a 2004 BMJ paper by Marsh and colleagues (read in part — the full text was not reachable), is "an uncommon practice that confers advantage to the people who practise it compared with the rest of the community"; the approach is "Identifying individuals with better outcome than their peers (positive deviance) and enabling communities to adopt the behaviours that explain the improved outcome". Its origin is child nutrition in Vietnam, where the families of well-nourished poor children were found to be adding greens and tiny shrimps and crabs from the paddies to meals and feeding more often; the movement's own case study reports malnutrition falling 85% in the pilot, a figure that is the movement's and is marked as such.

Bradley and colleagues' 2009 version for healthcare organisations states the logic in four steps that are the right logic for a place-based display: "Identify 'positive deviants,' i.e., organizations that consistently demonstrate exceptionally high performance in the area of interest"; "Study the organizations in-depth using qualitative methods to generate hypotheses about practices that allow organizations to achieve top performance"; "Test hypotheses statistically in larger, representative samples"; "Work in partnership with key stakeholders … to disseminate the evidence". The second step is the one to hold on to: the outlier at the good end is a hypothesis about mechanism, generated by looking closely, and tested afterwards. A dashboard cannot do the second step. It can do the first properly and point at the second.

The method has the same disease as outlier removal, and the systematic review says so. Baxter and colleagues (2016), reviewing positive-deviance studies in healthcare: "many articles provided limited or no detail about what criteria constituted positive deviance"; "the criteria used often appeared arbitrary and cut-off points were not justified"; "comparison groups were rarely included"; and the rule that follows: "The methods and criteria used to identify positive deviants must always be stated regardless of whether they are exceptionally performing individuals, teams or organisations." The good-end and bad-end outlier need the same declaration — the rule, the threshold, the comparison — and the good-end one needs, in addition, the small-denominator caution of section 4, because the smallest units are over-represented at the top of any rate ranking by arithmetic before any mechanism is involved. A display that celebrates its best small performer has, until it has shown the funnel, not yet shown that there is anything to celebrate.

11 · What holds true regardless

Chapter 3 found it useful to separate a short list of canonical rules from the record of findings beneath them, and this chapter does the same. The seven are the rules a reader should be able to recite; the record is what they rest on.

The seven

1 · A number is undefined until its unit, its period and its base are stated. What one row is (person, venue, night, ticket), what span of time it covers (and which instant or window stands for a day), and what it is counted against. Each is a choice made before analysis; each changes the count; the same market can look concentrated at one grain and diversifying at another. Standard (Eurostat units; Regulation 696/93; the reference period) and Evidence (Wickham; the midnight census; Datta et al.[abstract or summary only]). Fixed (requirement).

2 · Nothing is never one thing. A blank must say which kind it is. Zero is a value, used "only when a data point is a true zero", and never as a stand-in for missing; "NA" is banned because it is ambiguous; a blank is tolerable only when there is exactly one reason for it and the reason is stated; otherwise every nothing is labelled. The official vocabularies agree with the studio's six and split "not collected" into not applicable and not asked. Standard (Analysis Function; Eurostat; SDMX; Codd). Fixed (requirement).

3 · Every figure carries its provenance, and the record outlives the number. Who is responsible; what source and why; what method; what period, as a closed interval; when issued and when last changed; what status; what quality, with error and confidence where they exist; what was withheld or altered. A revised number is a number with a history, and the history belongs where the number is. Standard (Code of Practice 3.0; Regulation 223/2009; PROV; DCAT; FAIR). Fixed (requirement).

4 · A comparison declares what it holds equal. It is valid only "to the extent that differences between statistics can be attributed to differences between the true values"; so definition, period, geography and vintage, method, disclosure treatment, breaks, revisions, the comparator group and its method, precision, and outlier handling are each the same or each stated. The comparator must not contain the outcome. Standard (SIMS; European Code; Code 3.0; ESMA; geography policy) and Practice (PHE; DfE). Fixed (requirement).

5 · A total speaks for the biggest. In a skewed distribution a sum or mean is dominated by its largest terms; the median and the share are not. Beside any total, show the shape — a median, a top-share, a Lorenz curve or a concentration index — and treat "80/20" as a question to answer, not a law to assume. The long tail of a cultural market is mostly ones and zeros, and showing people what others chose makes it more concentrated and less predictable. Evidence (Lorenz; NIST; ONS; Rosen; Salganik, Dodds & Watts; Elberse — the last secondary). Fixed (requirement) for the first sentence; the choice of instrument is Adaptable.

6 · Size does not cure selection. A transactional or digital-trace feed is worth, as evidence, its quality times its quantity times the difficulty of the question, and in the one measured case a defect correlation of half of one per cent reduced millions of records to the worth of a few hundred random ones. Report such feeds as within-sample comparisons unless the selection has been measured; read every feed through the ten characteristics; never claim what a head-only feed cannot see. Evidence (Meng; Lazer et al. — secondary; Salganik 2018; boyd & Crawford). Fixed (statement of the record).

7 · An outlier is a question before it is a decision. The standard definition is a point suspected of a different mechanism; the standard rules for flagging one fire on ordinary data and assume a shape cultural data does not have; the field removes outliers silently and in its own favour. So: investigate against the six artefact causes first; write the rule and threshold down in advance; show the figure with and without; and treat the good-end outlier as a hypothesis needing the same declaration plus the small-denominator caution. Evidence (Hawkins via Aggarwal; NIST; Dawson; Leys; Simmons; Bakker & Wicherts; Gelman & Price; Baxter). Fixed (sequence).

The record beneath them

Findings that support the seven and are worth knowing on their own; rules that follow from them are in the table, not repeated here.

  • "Reliable", in official usage, means how little a number moves on revision, not how accurate it is; a UK quarterly growth figure moves about half a percentage point over three years and the regulator calls that "normal and unavoidable". (ONS; OSR.)
  • The regulator's test for a statistic is whether it can "bear the weight of the decisions made using" it, and readers want quality information that is "prominent, succinct". (OSR 2023.)
  • Verification asks whether the analysis "has been conducted correctly"; validation asks "whether the correct analysis has been performed"; the paradigm failure was a model re-used for a decision it was never assured for. (AQuA Book 2015/2025; NAO.)
  • Quality, to the people who use data, includes believability and reputation as intrinsic dimensions: a correct number from a disbelieved source is low-quality data. (Wang & Strong 1996.)
  • A number has three dates — the period it describes, when it was issued, when it last changed — and a dashboard's single stamp usually gives the least informative. (DCAT 3; Eurostat; ALFRED.)
  • The reason a feed's data is missing matters more than how much is missing, and the reason cannot be learned from the data; the remedy is to show what would change if the nothing were something. (Rubin[abstract or summary only]; Sterne; NRC 2010.)
  • Complete-case analysis — drop the incomplete rows and say nothing — was the primary method in 45% of trials in the four top medical journals in 2013. (Bell et al. 2014.)
  • The database standard has "effectively only one null value"; aggregates skip nulls silently; coalesce(sum(x), 0) turns "no rows" into a displayed 0; the relational model's inventor called zero "far too valuable" to mean missing. (SQL-92; PostgreSQL; Codd 1986.)
  • The one official rule found for drawing a gap: do not join the points either side, "even if the line is dotted or dashed". (Analysis Function 2022.)
  • Free is a price of zero on a real quantity, not a nothing; no official scheme has a code for it. (ONS CPI methodology.)
  • A lagged series ends in a not-yet dressed as a low number: 65% complete at two weeks, 95% at eight, in one case. (CDC NCHS.)
  • The 2021 Census perturbed every cell rather than suppressing some, so a published "1" is not literal and totals need not add. (ONS.)
  • Finance's rule for a defined measure — define, reconcile, show comparators, keep the definition, restate if changed — is the statistical rule arrived at independently. (ESMA 2015; Tesco 2026.)
  • The smallest units sit at both ends of a raw-rate ranking; adjusting for it hands the top to the largest; the funnel plot is the display that is biased toward neither. (Gelman & Price; Spiegelhalter[abstract or summary only].)
  • A hospital bed is "occupied" if someone is in it at midnight; the midnight count sits below the late-morning peak; the official night time window runs 6pm to 6am and straddles the calendar day. (KH03; Pierce et al. — secondary; ONS.)
  • Months are unequal containers and official series are adjusted for the number of Fridays and the date of Easter. (Eurostat.)
  • Big data's distinguishing traits are velocity and exhaustivity, and exhaustivity — "entire populations" — is the claim that selection bias defeats. (Kitchin & McArdle.)
  • In one dataset, one automated pager produced an entire apparent trend in public anger; one unit can be an aggregate. (Salganik 2018, citing Back et al.)
  • The "Pareto principle" was misnamed by the man who named it, and its curves belong to Lorenz. (Juran 1975 — secondary.)
  • Positive deviance is a method for the good-end outlier, and its systematic review found its cut-offs "often appeared arbitrary". (Bradley et al.; Baxter et al.)
  • Grubbs' test assumes one outlier and a normal distribution; Tukey's fences flag a third of ordinary samples; mean-and-SD rules let the outlier inflate the yardstick; the median breaks down at half the data, the mean at none. (NIST; Dawson; Leys; Hampel.)

12 · Where the choice is yours

The seven are Fixed. Within them, these are open, and the chapter names the trade-off without making the call.

Which grain to display. Venue, operator, room, event, night, person: each is a legitimate unit, each answers a different reader's question, and the chapter's only rule is that the one shown is named and that the row count under it is stated. The choice between them is the studio's and the readers' of Chapter 2.

Which instant or window stands for a day. The midnight census is a rule, not a law. A display may choose any boundary that suits its subject, provided it says so and never changes it silently.

Which denominator to lead with. Per place, per resident, per venue-night, per ticket, per pound: the reference class is a choice. The rule is that the chosen base is visible and the alternatives reachable, and that a small base carries its interval.

Which concentration instrument. A median beside the mean is the minimum. A top-share is the plainest. A Lorenz curve shows the whole bow and asks the most of the reader. The Gini and the HHI compress it to a number and lose the shape. Which to show depends on the reader and the question; showing none is not an option under truth 5.

Whether "not applicable" is a seventh kind. Every official scheme splits "not collected" into could not exist and nobody asked. The studio's six do not. Whether to add a kind, split the fifth, or treat it as a sub-kind is a decision about the display's vocabulary, and it has consequences for how many states an empty cell can be in.

How to show a nothing. The standards fix that it is labelled and that a line is not joined across it. They do not fix whether the label is a code, a word, a pattern or a sentence; whether a gap is a blank, a hatched region or an annotation; or how a suppressed cell is distinguished from an unavailable one at a glance. That is a design decision governed by Chapter 3's rules on colour and words, and the design system's.

How much provenance on the face. The minimal set is ten lines. Chapter 3 established that what is crucial cannot live only behind a click; it did not establish that all ten lines are crucial at every moment. Which lines are on the face (period, status, and the fact that caveats exist, at minimum) and which are one tap away is a layout decision for Chapter 11, bounded by the Code's "prominently" and the regulator's "succinct".

Suppress or perturb. Two honest ways to protect small cells, each a different kind of nothing in a number's clothing. The ONS chose perturbation for the census; most tables choose suppression; the Decision Book chooses suppression with secondary suppression. The choice depends on what the reader is to do with small counts, and it should be made once and declared.

Which outlier rule, and which threshold. The median absolute deviation is the literature's recommended default and 2.5 a common threshold; other rules are defensible for other shapes. What is fixed is that the rule is written down before the data arrives, the threshold is justified, and the figure is shown with and without.

Which neighbours. CIPFA's, the ONS classification, a bespoke model on published variables, or none: the choice is open and must be shown, and the variables must not include the thing being compared.

13 · What this means for a nightlife dashboard

An illustration, not a specification. The sector knowledge is the studio's; the method is the chapter's. Chapter 1's definition set the case: a public display of the people, activity, value and support systems that sustain a place's nightlife, for named readers who are not in general.

Begin with the row. Before any chart, the display has decided whether a row is a venue, an operator, a room or an event, and the chapter's first truth says the decision is stated where the number is. A count of "venues" under 1,000 capacity is a count of local units, or of enterprises, or of rooms; the European regulation gives eight candidates, and the one chosen changes the 78%. Then the night. An event that starts at ten and ends at three belongs to one date by one rule and to two by another; the official night time window runs from six in the evening to six in the morning and does not match the calendar; the display's rule — and it may be any rule — is written down and never changed without a [b]. Then the base. Events per what: per resident, per venue, per venue-night; the smallest places will top and bottom any per-capita ranking by arithmetic, so the small place's rate carries its interval and sits in a funnel, not a league table.

The feed. A ticketing platform is a recording mechanism with a defect correlation: it sees ticketed events, on that platform, in the proportion that its users are the city's. Read through the ten characteristics it is big, always-on, nonreactive, incomplete (no demographics, nothing off-platform, nothing on the construct "vibe"), inaccessible beyond what the platform grants, nonrepresentative, drifting as the platform's user base and features change, algorithmically confounded by whatever the platform promotes, dirty, and sensitive. That is not an argument against using it. It is the list of lines the display owes the reader before it shows a number from it, and the reason its findings are reported as "on this platform, this year against last" rather than as the city. The free event is on the feed as a zero in the price column and a count in the quantity column, and a revenue share cannot see it; a display that leads with revenue has chosen, by its denominator, not to see the free event, and should say so.

The nothings. A venue with no row this month is one of six things — it had no events, its events were free, its data did not arrive, it did not answer, nobody asked it, or its figure was withheld because it was one of two — and the display, following the UK rule, labels each, because there is more than one reason a cell can be blank. The line of that venue's history is not joined across the month. The provisional figure wears its [p] until it is final. The month that was perturbed or imputed says who did it. And the small cell that was suppressed is marked, not blank, so that the reader can see that a scene exists there even though its number cannot be shown — which is Chapter 1's position carried through: a display built on official sources is blind exactly where a small scene is, and must say so rather than show a blank.

The comparison. Two places on the display are comparable to the extent that the difference is in the places, so each comparison carries the ten-line declaration, with the comparator group named and its method stated — and if the comparator was built from variables that include the measure being compared, it is not a comparator. The shape, then. Beside any total — revenue, attendance, events — the median venue, the top-tenth share, and the Lorenz curve of the thing by the unit, so that a reader can see whether the bow is bent at the top one per cent or the top fifth, and so that the 78%/32% is a point on a curve rather than a slogan.

And then the outlier, which is the brief's hope. The small venue whose numbers are far above its neighbours' is, in order: possibly a data error, a misreport, a sampling fluke, a definitional slip, a tail of a skewed distribution, a legitimate extreme — or the thing the display was built to find. The display cannot tell which; it can show the value with and without, state the rule that flagged it and the threshold, place it in the funnel so that its small base is visible, and point at the question — what is happening there? — that only someone standing in the room can answer. That is where this chapter hands over to Chapters 6 and 9: finding value in the data, and measuring a vibe, both begin with the outlier the chapter has refused to trim.

The rules

Kind and tier as in Chapter 0.

Any figure shown with a point removed is shown with it included, one tap away "Report what the statistical results are if those observations are included" Evidence (adjacent domain) Fixed (requirement) Simmons, Nelson & Simonsohn 2011
Do not run automated outlier alerts on box-plot fences or normal-theory tests for skewed data without stating the false-flag rate ≥30% of normal samples flagged; non-normality read as outliers Evidence Fixed (requirement) Dawson 2011; NIST (Grubbs)
Treat a good-end outlier as a hypothesis about mechanism; state the criteria, threshold and comparison group; show its base Positive deviance's second step; its systematic review Evidence + Practice Fixed (sequence) Bradley et al. 2009; Baxter et al. 2016; Gelman & Price
Contextual anomalies (unusual for this place at this time) need a model of normal that includes the context; a global threshold cannot find them Point, contextual and collective anomalies Evidence (survey) Adaptable Chandola, Banerjee & Kumar 2009
Which grain, which day boundary, which denominator, which concentration instrument, whether a seventh kind of nothing, how a nothing looks, how much provenance on the face, suppress or perturb, which outlier rule, which neighbours Open choices with named trade-offs — Adaptable Section 12
How the labels, codes, gaps and provenance panels are styled Free within the design system and Chapter 3's rules on colour and words — Decorative Design system

What proves a break works

The Fixed rules above are mostly standards, and breaking a standard is different from breaking an experimental finding: the test is not whether a reader misreads but whether the figure can be checked. If you must show a number without its unit, period or base; a blank without its kind; a line joined across a gap; a comparison without its declaration; a total without its shape; a platform figure as the city; or a trimmed series without the untrimmed one — the test is: hand the display to someone who was not in the room, with the decision it is meant to bear, and ask them to reconstruct how the number was made and what would change it. If they can, from what is on the face and one tap away, the break has cost nothing. If they cannot, the number cannot bear the weight, and the standard was right. Log the break in the deviation entry Chapter 16 describes.

What this chapter could not settle

  • The Decision Book's gap rule ("dashed, hatched, or broken") can be read as permitting a dashed join across a missing point, which the standard it cites rejects; the book's rule here is "never join, dotted or dashed".
  • The Decision Book's provenance set omits the responsible party and the issued/modified dates; both are added from the Code, PROV and DCAT, and the book's "illustrative flag" kept.
  • The studio's six kinds of nothing merge not applicable with not asked, which every official scheme separates, and have no place for "included elsewhere" or "not yet available"; the mapping table is the evidence and the seventh-kind decision is flagged rather than made.
  • Neither the Decision Book nor the design system has a rule on the unit of observation or the row count; the rule is made from Wickham, Eurostat and the regulation.
  • No rule in either on the denominator, the reference class, or the funnel for small bases; made from the CDC primer, Hájek and Gelman & Price.
  • No rule in either on reading a platform feed (coverage, selection, the ten characteristics); made from Meng and Salganik.
  • No rule in either on outliers beyond "show the gaps"; the procedure is made from Leys, Simmons, Bakker & Wicherts, Osborne & Overbay.
  • No rule in either on concentration measures beside totals; made from Lorenz, NIST and the ONS, and the 78%/32% currently stands without its curve.
  • "Reliable" is used in the failure register and the design system in the ordinary sense; official usage means revisions. Both senses are stated; the rule is to use one.
  • No evidence was found that provenance on the face changes a reader's decision; the chapter's thesis rests beside a gap. Section 5 says so, the provenance rules are marked Standard (adopted), not Evidence, and a probe is flagged.

Checklist

  • Every figure states what one row is and how many rows
  • Every figure states its reference period as an interval, and separately when it was issued and last changed
  • The rule for assigning boundary-crossing activity to a period is written down; changes carry [b]
  • Dates are ISO 8601 with offset in data; natural in display
  • Every rate names its denominator; alternatives reachable; time-in-observation used where spans differ
  • Small-base rates carry intervals and sit in a funnel, not a rank
  • The provenance set travels with every figure, and the responsible party is named
  • Previous values and descriptions are kept when a figure changes; revisions visible in one place
  • "Reliable" used only in the official sense; [p] and [r] shown
  • Zero only for true zero; no "NA"; no bare symbols
  • Every empty cell labelled with its kind; blanks only under the one-reason rule
  • Not-applicable distinguished from not-asked (or the decision not to logged)
  • Free shown as zero price with a quantity, never as a nothing
  • No line joined across a gap; every gap highlighted and explained
  • Imputed and estimated values flagged with method and author; imputation rates published
  • Suppressed cells marked, never blank; secondary suppression applied; suppression or perturbation declared
  • Where missingness may correlate with the measure, a sensitivity view exists
  • Every comparison carries the ten-line declaration
  • Definition and method changes marked [b], with a back series where possible
  • Area codes with vintage; best-fit lookups declared
  • Defined measures defined, reconciled, held constant, restated if changed
  • Comparator groups named with method; no comparator contains the outcome
  • Median and a concentration measure beside every total or mean of a skewed quantity
  • No 80/20 assumed; the bow measured
  • Popularity rankings declared as such, with the distribution
  • Platform feeds reported within-sample unless selection is measured; coverage stated
  • Every feed audited against the ten characteristics; audit published
  • No claim about the tail from a head-only feed
  • Administrative sources state why recorded and who is absent
  • Outlier rule and threshold written before data arrives and justified (median absolute deviation as the default)
  • Flagged points investigated against the six artefact causes before removal; removals declared
  • With-and-without views for any removed point
  • No fence-based or normal-theory alerts on skewed data without a stated false-flag rate
  • Good-end outliers carry criteria, threshold, comparison group and base

Reading this chapter. This is one chapter of Dashboard Design, Nightlife Culture's research book on how evidence becomes a display a reader can trust, read and act on. The studio ("the house" in some chapters) is Nightlife Culture, a creative policy studio; the brief is its founder Carly Heath's commission for the book, and her eight ways a dashboard fails, the failure register, run through it. The Vibe Map, the studio's prototype for showing a place's nightlife culture, appears only as an illustration, never as a specification. "Version 1" is the book's archived first draft, whose positions this version re-tests against the sources. Every rule carries a kind (where it comes from: Standard, Evidence, Reading, Practice or Nightlife Culture) and a tier (how firm it is: Fixed, Adaptable or Decorative); Chapter 0 explains both, and the three senses of Fixed: a requirement that can be checked, a sequence whose order is the hard line, and a statement of the record. A dagger (†) marks a source read at the authors' abstract or summary only; "secondary" a quotation reached through a named reproduction; "(read once)" a quotation returned on a single reading and not confirmed by a second. Chapter 0 holds the glossary of the words the chapters share; each chapter lists its own coinages before its sources.

The question

When several things are counted and one number is wanted, what is actually being built — and what has to be shown with that number for it to be a measure rather than an opinion with decimal places?

The 60-second version

A composite index is "formed when individual indicators are compiled into a single index on the basis of an underlying model", and the handbook most indices cite says their construction "owes more to the craftsmanship of the modeller than to universally accepted scientific rules". Its own list of what can go wrong is the best argument for showing how one was made.

So the canonical truths: a composite is a model and is shown as one; weights are judgements and are not importance; aggregation is a price list and the prices are declared; a rank carries its interval; a measure that is used changes what it measures, so the audit is designed with the measure; validity is of a reading for a use, including its consequences; and recognition is necessary and is not validity. The recipe goes on the face.

Four things are decided when indicators become an index, and each is a claim. Normalisation puts them on one scale, and the scale chosen quietly sets the exchange rate between them. Weights are "essentially value judgements"; equal weights are the commonest choice and "does not mean 'no weights'". And weights are not importance: in the Times university ranking, an indicator given 20% of the weight explained 21% of the variance in the result while one given 40% explained 81%, and when the parts all move together "the weights are little more than cosmetic". Aggregation decides whether a strength can pay for a weakness: under addition, a place scoring (21, 1, 1, 1) equals a place scoring (6, 6, 6, 6). The Human Development Index moved to a geometric mean in 2010 to stop that; the UK's deprivation index transforms its domains "to reduce 'cancellation effects'"; a prosperity index uses means that "punish weakness" because its parts "are poor substitutes for one another". Any aggregation is a hidden price list: even after its 2010 reform the HDI valued a year of life in Zimbabwe at $0.51 and in the richest countries at about $9,000. Robustness is whether the ranking survives other defensible choices: audited properly, an index "is no longer a magic number", and a rank comes with an interval — in the 2025 Global Innovation Index, 85 of 139 economies had a 90% rank interval narrower than ten places and seven had one wider than twenty.

A measure that is used changes what it measures. Goodhart's "law" was a joke in a subordinate clause; the sentence everyone quotes is Marilyn Strathern's; Campbell's is the one with the evidence. In the English targets regime, a third of ambulance trusts "corrected" response times to fall under eight minutes, and nine NHS trusts adjusted 6,000 waiting-list records — and waiting times really did fall, faster than in Scotland and Wales, and the comparative studies (read at abstract) found less gaming than the stories suggest. Both are true. Three of the four ways a proxy fails need no cheat at all.

Validity is "the degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses", and it is unitary: the number is not valid, a reading of it is, for a use. It includes what the measure does once used. "Recognition" — the people measured seeing themselves in it — is, in the measurement tradition, face validity and credibility: it corrects facts, confirms resonance, and is not evidence that the construct exists; the one study that tested community-chosen indicators against field science found most of them valid and not all of them reliable. The official precedent for measuring a felt quality is four questions the ONS refuses to combine, "because they are all individually important".

The cultural-value literature mostly declines a single score and says why: "instead of 'measuring' it is more appropriate to speak of 'evaluation', of which measurement is but one component". The leading UK quality instrument reports twelve dimensions from three perspectives and is "not a clapometer". The newest official guidance recommends "that composite indices should be accompanied by dashboards … that give information about the development in the underlying components". The one composite in the studio's own sector publishes its parts and not its recipe, so a reader cannot reproduce its headline from its published parts — and three of the five place indices with published methods publish no sensitivity analysis either.

1 · What a measure is

A dashboard that shows a "score" has done something a dashboard that shows a count has not. It has taken several things that were measured and decided, on the reader's behalf, how they combine. Chapter 4 asked what a count must carry to be evidence. This chapter asks the same of a combination, and the answer is longer, because every step from indicators to index is a decision that could have gone another way.

The governing text is the Handbook on Constructing Composite Indicators, published jointly by the OECD and the European Commission's Joint Research Centre in 2008 and still the method most indices cite. Its definition: "A composite indicator is formed when individual indicators are compiled into a single index on the basis of an underlying model." Its candour about what that involves is unusual for a handbook: "Composite indicators are much like mathematical or computational models. As such, their construction owes more to the craftsmanship of the modeller than to universally accepted scientific rules for encoding." And its warning: "composite indicators can send misleading policy messages if they are poorly constructed or misinterpreted. Their 'big picture' results may invite users (especially policy-makers) to draw simplistic analytical or policy conclusions."

The handbook lists what a composite is for and what it risks; six of its nine pros and all six of its cons are reproduced here, because the second list is the chapter's case. Pros: composites "Can summarise complex, multi-dimensional realities with a view to supporting decision-makers"; "Are easier to interpret than a battery of many separate indicators"; "Can assess progress of countries over time"; "Reduce the visible size of a set of indicators without dropping the underlying information base"; "Facilitate communication with general public (i.e. citizens, media, etc.) and promote accountability"; "Help to construct/underpin narratives for lay and literate audiences". Cons: they "May send misleading policy messages if poorly constructed or misinterpreted"; "May invite simplistic policy conclusions"; "May be misused, e.g. to support a desired policy, if the construction process is not transparent and/or lacks sound statistical or conceptual principles"; "The selection of indicators and weights could be the subject of political dispute"; "May disguise serious failings in some dimensions and increase the difficulty of identifying proper remedial action, if the construction process is not transparent"; "May lead to inappropriate policies if dimensions of performance that are difficult to measure are ignored." Three of the six cons end with the same condition — if the construction process is not transparent. The handbook's own remedy for its own list is the recipe on the face.

The cultural-value literature arrives at a different starting point and the chapter should say so before building anything. The Arts and Humanities Research Council's Cultural Value Project, the largest UK inquiry into the question, concluded in 2016 that "When it comes to cultural value, instead of 'measuring' it is more appropriate to speak of 'evaluation', of which measurement is but one component." It set out to "analyse cultural value without assuming that all registers of value are commensurable, or that they can be reduced to one common denominator", and it sought "a framework within which sits a variety of components of value, each of them to be evaluated by appropriate and often different qualitative and quantitative methodologies." That is a position against a single score, from the field's own research council, and any measure of a cultural quality has to answer it. The chapter does not argue that the position is wrong. It argues that whatever form is chosen — index, profile, set — the same disciplines apply to each number in it, and a profile of twelve declared numbers is better than one undeclared one.

2 · Why people believe what they believe

The beliefs about measures are more deeply held than those about charts, because a number that has been computed looks as though it has been found. Each is stated fairly here and met in the sections that follow.

Belief one: a score is more objective than a judgement

If a number came out of a formula, it was not anyone's opinion. Section 3 shows that the handbook describes the formula's every step as a judgement, and section 5 that the formula is a set of exchange rates nobody announced.

Belief two: equal weights are neutral

Giving every indicator the same weight feels like declining to choose. Section 4: "equal weighting does not mean 'no weights'", and a measure with uneven groups of indicators weights the groups unequally without anyone deciding to.

Belief three: the weights say what matters

A published weight of 40% means that indicator drives 40% of the result. Section 4: it may drive 81%, or 21%; nominal weights "are hardly ever found to match" effective ones.

Belief four: adding is just adding

A total of scores is the natural way to combine them. Section 5: addition is the one method that lets any strength fully pay for any weakness, and the field has spent two decades building alternatives for that reason.

Belief five: a target focuses effort on what matters

Publish the measure and people will improve the thing. Section 7: they will improve the measure, which is sometimes the same thing and sometimes not, and the honest evidence is that both happen at once.

Belief six: if the people measured recognise it, it is valid

A measure of a scene that the scene agrees with has passed the test. Section 9: in the measurement tradition that is face validity, which the official standards do not count as validity at all; recognition does something important and it is not that.

Belief seven: decision-makers want one number

The ranking is what gets read. Section 11: the policy bodies that have thought hardest about it recommend a dashboard beside any index, and one of the handbook's own authors describes the spread of composites as "mostly advocacy-driven".

3 · The handbook's own account

Ten steps

The handbook's method has ten steps: theoretical framework; data selection; imputation of missing data; multivariate analysis; normalisation; weighting and aggregation; uncertainty and sensitivity analysis; back to the data; links to other indicators; visualisation. The first step is the one dashboards skip. The theoretical framework "provides the basis for the selection and combination of variables into a meaningful composite indicator": what is the construct, which indicators stand for it, and why these. Without it, the handbook's steps are arithmetic on whatever was to hand, which is the thing Martin Ravallion named: a "mashup index", "defined as a composite index for which existing theory and practice provides little or no guidance to its design", so that "the index has an unusually large number of moving parts, which the producer is essentially free to set."

Normalisation

Indicators measured in different units — pounds, counts, percentages, scores — are put on a common scale before they are combined. The handbook and the JRC's web guide between them name the options and their costs. Ranking "is not affected by outliers and allows the performance of countries to be followed over time in terms of relative positions (rankings)" but loses the distances (handbook). Standardised scores (z-scores) are, in the web guide's words, "the most commonly used because it converts all indicators to a common scale with an average of zero and standard deviation of one", and "an indicator with extreme values will have intrinsically a greater effect on the composite indicator." Min-max scaling stretches each indicator between its lowest and highest observed values, so "the minima and maxima could be unreliable outliers, and have a distortion effect" (web guide). Distance to a reference "measures the relative position of a given indicator vis-à-vis a reference point" (handbook). "The normalisation method should take into account the data properties, as well as the objectives of the composite indicator" (handbook). What the handbook says more quietly, and Giuseppe Munda and Michela Nardo show with a worked table, is that the normalisation also sets the trade-off between dimensions: change the unit or the scaling of one indicator and the implied rate at which it exchanges for another changes with it. Section 5 returns to this.

Weighting

The handbook's paragraph on equal weights is worth giving whole, because it is the single most-ignored paragraph in the literature:

"Most composite indicators rely on equal weighting (EW), i.e. all variables are given the same weight. This essentially implies that all variables are "worth" the same in the composite, but it could also disguise the absence of a statistical or an empirical basis, e.g. when there is insufficient knowledge of causal relationships or a lack of consensus on the alternative. In any case, equal weighting does not mean "no weights", but implicitly implies that the weights are equal. Moreover, if variables are grouped into dimensions and those are further aggregated into the composite, then applying equal weighting to the variables may imply an unequal weighting of the dimension (the dimensions grouping the larger number of variables will have higher weight). This could result in an unbalanced structure in the composite index."

And the sentence that governs every alternative: "Regardless of which method is used, weights are essentially value judgements." The alternatives are weights from the data's own structure (principal components or factor analysis, where, as the web guide puts it, weighting "only intervenes to correct for the overlapping information of two or more correlated indicators, and it is not a measure of importance of the associated indicator"); "benefit of the doubt" weights, where each unit is scored on the weights most favourable to it, which the handbook calls "extremely parsimonious about weighting assumptions" while noting that "with BOD weights are country specific and have a number of estimation problems"; expert allocation, where, in the web guide's words, "experts are given a budget of N points, to be distributed over a number of indicators, paying more for those indicators whose importance they want to stress"; pairwise comparison (the analytic hierarchy process); and conjoint analysis of stated preferences. The 2019 review by Greco and colleagues confirms the practice: "Equal weighting is the most common scheme appearing in the development of composite indicators", for five reasons they list — "simplicity of construction", "a lack of theoretical structure to justify a differential weighting scheme", "no agreement between decision makers", "inadequate statistical and/or empirical knowledge", and "alleged objectivity" — and they add that "equal weights miss the point of differentiating between essential and less important indicators by treating them all equally." The Social Progress Index states the null that most builders leave unspoken: it "equally weights components for constructing a dimension-level score because there is no clear theoretical or empirical reason to weight any of the components more highly than any other." That is a declared judgement, and declaring it is the point.

Sensitivity

"Several judgements have to be made when constructing composite indicators, e.g. on the selection of indicators, data normalisation, weights and aggregation methods, etc." The handbook's seventh step tests them: "Uncertainty analysis focuses on how uncertainty in the input factors propagates through the structure of the composite indicator and affects the composite indicator values. Sensitivity analysis assesses the contribution of the individual source of uncertainty to the output variance." And the output of the test is a less tidy and more defensible number: "The results of the robustness analysis are generally reported as country rankings with their related uncertainty bounds, which are due to the uncertainties at play." The web guide puts the questions a builder must be able to answer: "How do country ranks (or composite indicator scores) compare to the most likely ranks under all scenarios in building the composite indicator?" and "Which countries are the most volatile and why?" — adding that "A plurality of scenarios (all with their implications) should be initially considered, because no scenario for the development of a composite indicator is a priori better than another …". Section 6 shows what this looks like when done.

Presentation

The handbook's tenth step is the thinnest, and this book's Chapter 3 is the reason it can be. "The way composite indicators are presented is not a trivial issue as the visualisation can influence (or help to enhance) interpretability." "Composite indicators are ultimately a communication tool, which can be greatly enhanced by proper visualisation, both static and interactive (online)." Online tools "give full transparency to the data set and allow users to drill down to underlying data." "Graphical representation of composite indicators should provide clear messages, without obscuring individual data points." What the handbook does not say in its visualisation step, and its sensitivity step requires, is that the rank's interval is shown with the rank. Section 12 makes that a rule.

4 · Weights are not importance

The finding

In 2013 Paolo Paruolo, Michaela Saisana and Andrea Saltelli published a paper whose title asked whether ratings and rankings were "voodoo or science". Its abstract states the problem exactly: "Composite indicators aggregate a set of variables using weights which are understood to reflect the variables' importance in the index. In this paper we propose to measure the importance of a given variable within existing composite indicators via Karl Pearson's 'correlation ratio'; we call this measure 'main effect'. Because socioeconomic variables are heteroskedastic and correlated, relative nominal weights are hardly ever found to match relative main effects" (heteroskedastic: their spread differs from one part of the range to another). The main effect of an indicator is "the expected fractional reduction in variance of the composite indicator that would be obtained if that variable could be fixed" — how much of the index's movement that one indicator accounts for, estimated by regressing the index on the indicator alone and asking how much of the index's variation that explains. The nominal weight is the number the builder published. The two are different things, and the paper measures the gap.

The gap is large. In the Times Higher Education world university ranking as it was then constructed, the academic peer review carried a nominal weight of 0.40 and a main effect of 0.81; the teacher–student ratio carried a nominal weight of 0.20 and a main effect of 0.21. An indicator given a fifth of the weight explained a fifth of the result; an indicator given two-fifths explained four-fifths. In the Shanghai ranking, indicators weighted 0.10 and 0.20 turned out to matter almost equally: "For ARWU the main effects Si are more similar to each other than the nominal weights". In the 2009 Human Development Index, "Although the 2009 HDI developers assigned weights varying between 11% and 33%, all four indicators are roughly equally important." The mechanism is correlation: when the parts move together, the weights cannot separate them, and "In cases like this, where the variables are strongly and roughly equally correlated with the overall index, each of them ranks the countries roughly equally, and the weights are little more than cosmetic." The paper's conclusion is a list of what a builder can do: "avoid associating nominal weights with importance, but inform users of the relative importance of the variables or pillars"; "abstain from aggregating pillars when these display important trade offs"; move "from the linear one (which is fully compensatory) to a partially- or fully-non-compensatory alternative"; or "assess different weighting strategies, so as to select the one that leads to a minimum discrepancy statistic between target weights and variables importance." A 2017 paper by Becker and colleagues builds the tools for the last option — measuring importance, isolating each indicator's effect, and "an optimisation procedure … which allows weights to be fitted to agree with pre-specified values of importance" — so that the gap between what a builder meant and what the arithmetic did can be closed rather than discovered, though where parts are strongly correlated the fit may need a negative weight, which is its own warning.

What a developer does when audited

The Joint Research Centre audits other people's indices — "over 100 statistical audits", by its own count, including the Environmental Performance Index, the Global Competitiveness Index and the Corruption Perceptions Index. Its audit of the 2025 Global Innovation Index, the fifteenth consecutive year, shows the vocabulary that results. The developers have stated since 2012 that their weights "were to be used as scaling coefficients and not importance coefficients, with the aim of arriving at sub-pillar and pillar scores that were balanced in their underlying components" — a developer disowning, in its own report, the reading of weights that section 2's third belief assumes. The audit explains why: "the ratio of two nominal weights gives the rate of substitutability between two indicators, and hence can be used to reveal the relative importance of individual indicators. This importance can then be compared with ex-post measures of a variable's importance, such as the non-linear Pearson correlation ratio." A weight is a price, and the audit checks whether the price did what the builder meant.

What this means for a display

A dashboard that shows a composite and lists its weights has told the reader something that is true about the recipe and false about the dish. The weights are what the builder decided; the importances are what the arithmetic did; and the handbook's equal-weights paragraph says even the first can be an illusion when the groups are uneven. The rule that follows is in section 12: show the nominal weights as what they are, and show the effective importances beside them.

5 · Aggregation is a price list

Compensability

The handbook's passage on aggregation is the chapter's centre and is given at length. "In both linear and geometric aggregations, weights express trade-offs between indicators. A deficit in one dimension can thus be offset (compensated) by a surplus in another. This implies an inconsistency between how weights are conceived (usually measuring the importance of the associated variable) and the actual meaning when geometric or linear aggregations are used. In a linear aggregation, the compensability is constant, while with geometric aggregations compensability is lower for the composite indicators with low values." And: "To ensure that weights remain a measure of importance, other aggregation methods should be used, in particular methods that do not allow compensability. Moreover, if different goals are equally legitimate and important, a non-compensatory logic might be necessary." Munda and Nardo, whose work the handbook cites, define the term: "Compensability refers to the existence of trade-offs, i.e. the possibility of offsetting a disadvantage on some variables by a sufficiently large advantage on another variable." Under addition, "the substitution rates equal the weights of the variables up to a multiplicative coefficient", and "The use of non-compensatory aggregation rules to construct composite indicators is compulsory for reasons of theoretical consistency when weights with the meaning of importance coefficients are used."

The handbook's toolbox gives the illustration that version 1 of this book (the studio's earlier draft of this book, now archived) carried and this chapter has now read at the Joint Research Centre's own reproduction: "if an hypothetical composite indicator was formed by inequality, environmental degradation, GDP per capita and unemployment, two countries, one with values (21,1,1,1) and the other with (6,6,6,6) would have equal composite indicator value (=6) under an additive aggregation. Obviously the two countries would represent very different social conditions that would not be reflected in the composite. Geometric aggregation (i.e. the product of weighted indicators) is a less compensatory approach. In our simple example the first country would have a much lower composite indicator value (=2.14) than the second country (=6.00) under the geometric aggregation." A place with one spectacular strength and three collapses equals a place that is merely sound on everything, if you add. That is not a flaw in addition. It is what addition means, and a builder who adds has claimed it.

The price list can be computed from any additive recipe, and it is worth seeing how, because the normalisation is in it. Suppose two parts, each scaled by min-max to 0–1 and given equal weight: one is a count of events per month, observed between 0 and 200; the other is years in operation, observed between 0 and 40. A rise of one year adds 1/40 to the second part's scaled value; a rise of one event per month adds 1/200 to the first; with equal weights, one year of operation therefore exchanges for five events per month, and the index is indifferent between them. Halve the weight on years, and one year buys two and a half events; widen the observed range of events to 400, and one year buys ten. Nobody chose any of those prices; the ranges and the weights set them together. That is the rate the card must state, in the parts' own units, for every pair of parts that can trade.

The hidden price list

Martin Ravallion's two 2010 papers make the exchange rate visible by computing it. Any index that combines income with life expectancy "implicitly puts a monetary valuation on an extra year of life, where that valuation is defined by the tradeoff between longevity and income, i.e., the extra income needed to compensate for a year less of life expectancy, keeping the HDI constant". Under the old additive index the implied value was, by his account, a roughly constant share of each country's income. He computed it for the reformed 2010 index — the geometric-mean version described below — and found the reform had moved the price rather than removed it: "The HDI's value of longevity in the poorest country, Zimbabwe, is a remarkably low $0.51 per year, representing less than 0.3% of that country's (very low) mean income in 2008. Thus the 2010 HDI implies that if Zimbabwe takes a policy action that increases national income by a mere $0.52 or more per person per year at the cost of reducing average life expectancy by one year, then the country will have promoted its 'human development.' … The value tends to rise with income and reaches about $9,000 per year in the richest countries". His general lesson: "An important lesson for future composite indices is the need for transparency about the implicit tradeoffs, especially in more complicated indices." And on the mashup family as a whole: "We need to know the tradeoffs … built into a composite index if it is to be properly assessed and used." The United Nations' own researchers replied that "it is inappropriate to label the trade-offs implicit in the HDI as 'values,'" and that the ratio "merely says that the HDI puts very low weight on increases in income in rich countries, compared to the very high value on health improvements" — a live dispute about whether an implied substitution rate is a value judgement or an artefact, which this chapter records without settling. What is not in dispute is that the rate exists, can be computed, and was not on the face.

What builders have done about it

The Human Development Index changed its arithmetic in 2010 to end perfect substitutability — and, as Ravallion's figures show, an index that allows imperfect substitution still carries a price list; it is a different one. The report's own words: "A key change was to shift to a geometric mean (which measures the typical value of a set of numbers): thus in 2010 the HDI is the geometric mean of the three dimension indices. Poor performance in any dimension is now directly reflected in the HDI, and there is no longer perfect substitutability across dimensions." The technical note: the new formula "embodies imperfect substitutability across all HDI dimensions. It thus addresses one of the most serious criticisms of the linear aggregation formula, which allowed for perfect substitution across dimensions. Some substitutability is inherent in the definition of any index that increases with the values of its components."

Two UK and international place indices show the same instinct worked out further. The Legatum Prosperity Index combines its three domains with a power mean whose exponent is chosen to encode non-substitutability: "the domains (Development, Freedom, and Society) are poor substitutes for one another as they are all distinct and indispensable components of prosperity"; "When p is less than one, a decrease in one dimension is not fully compensated for by an equal and opposite increase in another, and the lower the value of p the more the overall p-mean decreases, i.e. lower values of p punish weakness more than higher values of p"; "We have elected to set p equal to –1 when calculating the p-mean of the domains". The exponent rises as the parts become better substitutes — minus one at the top, zero (the geometric mean) in the middle, one (plain addition) at the bottom. Whatever one thinks of the index, the aggregation is a stated judgement about which parts may pay for which. The English Indices of Deprivation reach the same end by a different route: domain scores are ranked and then exponentially transformed, a method that "was explicitly designed to reduce 'cancellation effects'", so that "the Indices are specifically constructed to identify deprivation and not affluence" — a one-tailed instrument by design. That is a decision a cultural measure would also have to make, and the arithmetic follows from it. An instrument built to find shortfall should let a bad part dominate (a low exponent; a transformation that stretches the deprived end); one built to find what thrives should let a good part show through; one built for both needs a symmetric rule and a reader who can see the shape. The same parts, under the three designs, rank places differently, and none of the three is neutral.

The survey evidence on how often any of this is done is discouraging. Böhringer and Jochem reviewed eleven sustainability indices in policy use and concluded that "these indices fail to fulfill fundamental scientific requirements making them rather useless if not misleading with respect to policy advice", because the normalisation, weighting and aggregation steps did not meet the conditions under which the arithmetic means anything.

6 · The robustness of a rank

What an audit does

Saisana, Saltelli and Tarantola's 2005 paper in the Royal Statistical Society's journal is where the method of auditing a composite was set out, on the United Nations' Technology Achievement Index. "The construction of composite indicators involves stages where judgement has to be made: the selection of sub-indicators, choice of model, weighting indicators and treatment of missing values etc." The audit varies every one of those judgements at once, many thousands of times, and reports what happens to each country's rank. For the index in question most ranks were stable — "For most countries, the original TAI value is very close to the MCTAI median value of the distribution" — but one was not: "There is, however, one country, the Netherlands, that is strongly favoured in the original TAI … its performance falls at the ninth position, behind Singapore, the UK and Australia." The paper's own summary of the result: "The index is no longer a magic number corresponding to a crisp normalization, weighting scheme and weight assignment, but reflects uncertainty and ambiguity in a more transparent and defensible fashion." And its purpose: the method "could provide information on whether the countries' rankings measure anything meaningful and could reduce the possibility that composite indicators may send misleading or non-robust policy messages."

Twenty years on, this is routine for the indices that submit to it. The 2025 Global Innovation Index audit ran "5,000 runs" varying "the treatment of missing data, the aggregation formula and weights applied to the pillar level", and reported: "For 85 of the 139 economies the width of the 90% GII rank confidence interval is less than 10 positions in rank"; "Seven economies … have 90 percent confidence interval widths of more than 20 positions"; "73 percent of the economies are found to shift fewer than three positions with respect to the median rank". And the reading instruction: readers should "consider an economy's ranking … not only at face value, but also within the 90 percent confidence intervals." The United Nations' own uncertainty analysis of the Human Development Index found "the shifts in ranking are relatively minor and seem not to compromise the robustness of the HDI" while identifying that "the weights applied to income and education are the main drivers of uncertainty". A rank without an interval is a point estimate presented as a fact.

Scores, ranks and digits

Three habits follow. First, a rank is a coarser object than a score, and the English deprivation index uses ranks on purpose: domains are standardised "by ranking the Lower-layer Super Output Areas from least deprived … to most deprived … separately for each of the seven domains" (the small statistical areas of about 1,500 people the index is built on), and sensitivity testing found that alternative weightings "did not have a large impact on the final Index of Multiple Deprivation ranks." Second, a score's digits are a claim about precision, and the official guidance is now, in all but name, the two-significant-digits rule Chapter 3 took from Ehrenberg: the ONS style guide says "You should round the numbers for comparison to two effective digits", that the level of rounding "should be effective, and chosen according to the intended use", and "Always use the lowest level possible for the intended user." The Analysis Function adds the cost: "Rounding does reduce precision. This usually means that the reported totals no longer equal the sum of the component parts." A composite reported to two decimal places on a ten-point scale has claimed a resolution of one part in a thousand from inputs that were ranks, sliders and expert guesses. Third, the Analysis Function's worked example of how to say a range — "between 220 and 250 people were killed … with a central estimate of 230 deaths" — is the sentence form for a rank with its interval: between eighth and nineteenth, most likely twelfth.

7 · When the measure becomes the target

Who said what

Chapter 1 recorded that the most reliable thing a published measure does is change the behaviour it measures. This chapter went to the sources of the two "laws" that are quoted for it, and the record is worth setting straight because the canon is misquoted almost everywhere.

Charles Goodhart's sentence of 1975 was an aside, inside a subordinate clause, in a paper on British monetary policy, and he named it after himself in jest. As Chrystal and Mizen report it, the text reads: "Ignoring Goodhart's law, that any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes". Three independent reproductions agree on the words. The sentence everyone now quotes — "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" — is not Goodhart's. It is the anthropologist Marilyn Strathern's, in a 1997 article on audit in British universities, where she follows it with the application: "The more a 2.1 examination performance becomes an expectation, the poorer it becomes as a discriminator of individual performances." She does not attribute it to Goodhart; she writes that "Hoskin describes this as 'Goodhart's law', after the latter's observation on instruments for monetary control which lead to other devices for monetary flexibility having to be invented." So: Goodhart stated a regularity about monetary indicators; Keith Hoskin, in 1996, generalised it under Goodhart's name; Strathern, in 1997, supplied the sentence. Strathern's own thesis is the one this chapter needs: "audit does more than monitor — it has a life of its own that jeopardizes the life it audits."

Donald Campbell's law has the evidence attached. From his 1976 paper, read at source: "The more any quantitative social indicator is used for social decision-making, the more subject it will be to corruption pressures and the more apt it will be to distort and corrupt the social processes it is intended to monitor." He illustrates with crime statistics — a well-publicised crackdown "had as its main effect the corruption of crime-rate indicators" — and with schooling: "achievement tests may well be valuable indicators of general school achievement under conditions of normal teaching aimed at general competence. But when test scores become the goal of the teaching process, they both lose their value as indicators of educational status and distort the educational process in undesirable ways." His remedy, offered with a doubt attached: "Many commentators, including myself (1969b), assume that the use of multiple indicators, all recognized as imperfect, will alleviate the problem, although Ridgeway (1956) doubts this."
