Steven Kerr's 1975 paper on "the folly of rewarding A, while hoping for B" gives the organisational mechanism — organisms "seek information concerning what activities are rewarded, and then seek to do (or at least pretend to do) those things, often to the virtual exclusion of activities not rewarded" — and names the cause that bears on dashboards most: "Fascination with an 'Objective' Criterion". "Nonetheless, many individuals seek to establish simple, quantifiable standards against which to measure and reward performance. Such efforts may be successful in highly predictable areas within an organization, but are likely to cause goal displacement when applied anywhere else."

The taxonomy, and the evidence

The best-evidenced study of what targets do is Gwyn Bevan and Christopher Hood's 2006 paper on the English public services under what they call "targets and terror". They define gaming as "reactive subversion such as 'hitting the target and missing the point' or reducing performance where targets do not apply", and they name three kinds. "Ratchet effects refer to the tendency for central controllers to base next year's targets on last year's performance" — so that a manager who expects to be in post next year has "a perverse incentive not to exceed targets even if they could easily do so". "Threshold effects refer to the effects of targets on the distribution of performance" — a uniform target gives those above it an incentive "to allow their performance to deteriorate to the standard". And "Attempts to achieve targets at the cost of significant but unmeasured aspects of performance result in output distortions." Underneath all three is what they call synecdoche — "taking a part to stand for a whole" — the assumption "that the part on which performance is measured can adequately represent performance on the whole".

The evidence is specific. "A study by the Commission for Health Improvement (2003c) found evidence that in a third of ambulance trusts, response times had been 'corrected' to be reported to be less than eight minutes", and the distribution showed "a curious 'spike' at 8 minutes – with the strong implication that times between 8 and 9 minutes have been reclassified to be less than 8 minutes." Hospitals held patients "in queues of ambulances outside A&E Departments until the hospital in question was confident that that patient could be seen within four hours". "The National Audit Office (2001) reported evidence that nine NHS trusts had 'inappropriately' adjusted their waiting lists … affecting nearly 6000 patient records." The parliamentary committee that reviewed the regime in 2003 found that "Some ambulance trusts were massaging their response times", that at one eye hospital waiting-time targets "have been achieved at the expense of cancellation and delay of follow-up appointments", and — the figure about the measurers rather than the measured — that "in over 80% of such 'first time' validations" the National Audit Office "found that the organisation had materially misstated their achievements or had failed to disclose potentially material weaknesses with their data." In schooling, Daniel Koretz defines score inflation as "a gain in scores that substantially overstates the improvement in learning it implies", documents the "sawtooth" pattern when a new test is introduced, and reports that "Typically, gains on high-stakes tests have been 3 to 5 times as large as gains on other tests (such as the National Assessment of Educational Progress) with low (or lower) stakes." His conclusion: "score gains achieved under high-stakes conditions should not be accepted at face value."

The symmetry

And yet the measured things improved, and the book must say so with the same force. Bevan and Hood record it themselves: "In 2002, 23 per cent of patients spent over four hours in A&E departments, but in the three months from April to June 2004 only 5.3 per cent stayed that long"; by March 2003, "when virtually no patient in England was reported as waiting more than 12 months for an elective admission, the equivalent figures for Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland were 10, 16 and 22 per cent." Their verdict: "Although there were indeed dramatic improvements in reported performance, we do not know the extent to which these were genuine or offset by gaming that resulted in reductions in performance that was not captured by targets." The economists who tested it found less gaming than the public-administration scholars feared, and all of what follows was read at the authors' abstracts. Kelman and Friedman, using data from all 155 English hospital trusts (abstract [abstract or summary only]): "we find dramatic wait-time performance improvements between 2003 and 2006 and no evidence for any of the dysfunctional effects that have been hypothesized in connection with this target." Propper and colleagues, comparing England with Scotland (abstract [abstract or summary only]): "targets met their goals of reducing waiting times without diverting activity from other less well monitored aspects of health care and without decreasing patient health on exit from hospital." Besley, Bevan and Burchardi, comparing England with Wales (abstract [abstract or summary only]): the policy "did indeed reduce waiting times in England as compared with Wales. However, there is some evidence there was in England, initially, some shuffling of prospective patients to meet specific targets". And the cleanest natural experiment runs the other way: when Wales abolished school league tables in 2001 and England kept them, Burgess, Wilson and Worth found (abstract [abstract or summary only]) "significant and robust evidence that this reform markedly reduced school effectiveness in Wales relative to England." Bevan and Hamblin add the twist that cuts both ways: of the four UK nations, "only in England was this target integral to a ranking system of 'star rating', which inflicted reputational damage on services that failed to hit targets, and only in England has this target been met." The mechanism that produced the gaming produced the delivery.

The summary across the literature is this: every rigorous comparison found the targeted thing really improved; every audit found the numbers were also massaged at the margin; and nobody can say how much of the improvement was real, because nobody built the independent check that would say — Hood's own diagnosis being that "the slow and half-hearted approach to developing independent verification of performance data might itself be interpreted as a form of gaming by the central managers." The centre, by not verifying, was gaming too.

Without a cheat

A 2018 taxonomy by Manheim and Garrabrant is useful because three of its four ways a proxy fails need nobody to behave badly. Regressional: "When selecting for a proxy measure, you select not only for the true goal, but also for the difference between the proxy and the goal." Extremal: "Worlds in which the proxy takes an extreme value may be very different from the ordinary worlds in which the relationship between the proxy and the goal was observed." Causal: "When the causal path between the proxy and the goal is indirect, intervening can change the relationship between the measure and proxy." Only the fourth, adversarial, needs an agent who "react[s] in different ways to create Goodhart-like effects". A dashboard that ranks places by a proxy will see the first three happen on their own — the top of the ranking will be the places where the proxy and the goal diverge most, and acting on the proxy will loosen its link to the goal — before anyone has gamed anything.

Reactivity, and the cultural sector

Wendy Espeland and Michael Sauder's 2007 paper gives the general word: reactivity, "the idea that people change their behavior in reaction to being evaluated, observed, or measured", through two mechanisms, "self-fulfilling prophecy and commensuration" (the book is in Chapter 2). Jerry Muller's name for the policy pathology is "metric fixation", "the seemingly irresistible pressure to measure performance, to publicize it, and to reward it, often in the face of evidence that this just doesn't work very well" — with the proviso, in his own words, that "The problem is not measurement, but excessive measurement and inappropriate measurement".

The cultural sector has written its own version. Eleonora Belfiore and Oliver Bennett, reviewing the social-impact literature: "research on both value and impacts has usually been underpinned by an advocacy agenda, even when the research agenda has been disguised as one of dispassionate enquiry"; "considerably more time and resources have been spent on looking for 'proof' of impacts than on actually trying to understand them"; and the risk of "yet another round of policy-based evidence-making". John Holden, in 2004, quoting a Cabinet Office strategy paper: "those things that [are] easy to measure tend to become objectives, and those that [are not, are] downplayed or ignored"; and in his own words in 2006: "Money thus flows into measurement, and only those things that can be measured get measured." The Centre for Cultural Value's 2021 evaluation principles ask the sector to "prioritise learning over monitoring and foreground understanding over judgement", and their authors' launch essay observes that "Lots of effort goes into producing low-value monitoring and reporting, but too little time is dedicated to the kind of deep reflection and learning required to develop critical understanding and enrich creative practice." Every one of these is Campbell's law in the sector's own voice, and every one bears on a public measure of a cultural quality: once it exists and is read, the scene will be measured by it and may begin to arrange itself toward it. Chapter 10 owns the ethics; this chapter's rule is that the audit — the independent check on whether the measured thing moved — is designed with the measure and not after it.

8 · Validity — what a measure must show

The unified view

The measurement tradition that has thought longest about whether a number means what it claims is psychometrics, and its vocabulary transfers whole. The founding statement is Cronbach and Meehl's 1955 paper: "Construct validation is involved whenever a test is to be interpreted as a measure of some attribute or quality which is not 'operationally defined.'" A construct "is some postulated attribute of people, assumed to be reflected in test performance", and it is given meaning by the web of expected relationships it sits in — "to 'make clear what something is' means to set forth the laws in which it occurs" — so that "A necessary condition for a construct to be scientifically admissible is that it occur in a nomological net, at least some of whose laws involve observables." The line to build a measure on: "Unless the network makes contact with observations, and exhibits explicit, public steps of inference, construct validation cannot be claimed". The same demand this chapter makes of a composite — that the steps from parts to number be explicit and public — was made of psychological constructs in 1955.

Samuel Messick's 1995 statement is the one modern standards rest on. "Validity is an overall evaluative judgment of the degree to which empirical evidence and theoretical rationales support the adequacy and appropriateness of interpretations and actions based on test scores or other modes of assessment". "Validity is not a property of the test or assessment as such, but rather of the meaning of the test scores." He names six aspects of construct validity — "content, substantive, structural, generalizability, external, and consequential" — and two ways a measure fails: construct underrepresentation, where "the assessment is too narrow and fails to include important dimensions or facets", and construct-irrelevant variance, where "the assessment is too broad, containing excess reliable variance associated with other" things. The consequential aspect is the one that matters for a public display: it "appraises the value implications of score interpretation as a basis for action as well as the actual and potential consequences of test use, especially in regard to sources of invalidity related to issues of bias, fairness, and distributive justice".

The 2014 Standards for Educational and Psychological Testing — the joint statement of the American Educational Research Association, the American Psychological Association and the National Council on Measurement in Education — define the term as "the degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses of tests", and insist: "It is the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses that are evaluated, not the test itself." "Validity is a unitary concept. It is the degree to which all the accumulated evidence supports the intended interpretation of test scores for the proposed use." They name five sources of evidence: test content ("the themes, wording, and format of the items, tasks, or questions"); response processes ("the fit between the construct and the detailed nature of the performance or response actually engaged in by test takers" — the official home of cognitive testing, of asking whether respondents understood the question as meant); internal structure ("the degree to which the relationships among test items and test components conform to the construct"); relations to other variables, where "Relationships between test scores and other measures intended to assess the same or similar constructs provide convergent evidence … whereas relationships between test scores and measures purportedly of different constructs provide discriminant evidence"; and consequences of testing. On consequences they draw a line a policy dashboard should know: "Although information about the consequences of testing may influence decisions about test use, such consequences do not, in and of themselves, detract from the validity of intended interpretations" — a consequence counts against validity only if it can be traced to a flaw in the measure, such as underrepresentation or irrelevant variance. And they do not mention face validity at all.

Denny Borsboom and colleagues' 2004 paper is the realist dissent (secondary): "a test is valid for measuring an attribute if and only if (a) the attribute exists, (b) variations in the attribute causally produce variations in the outcomes of the measurement procedure"; "validity is about ontology; validation is about epistemology." For a measure of a felt quality that is the sharpest question there is: does the thing exist, and does it move the number?

Reliability

Reliability is "the consistency of scores across replications of a testing procedure", and the Standards add that "the need for precision increases as the consequences of decisions and interpretations grow in importance." Chapter 4 found that official statistics means something else by the word (how little a number moves on revision); a measure built from judgements needs both senses and should say which. Where people rate things — venues, nights, qualities — the statistic that must be reported is inter-rater reliability, "the extent to which data collectors (raters) assign the same score to the same variable", and simple percentage agreement "does not take account of the possibility that raters guessed on scores. It thus may overestimate the true agreement"; Cohen's kappa exists to correct that for categories, and the intraclass correlation for continuous ratings. A measure can be perfectly reliable and wrong — "consistent but wrong", in the methods-text phrase — so reliability is where validation starts and not where it ends.

Convergent and discriminant

The practical test for a new indicator is Campbell and Fiske's 1959 discipline (the original was not reachable; the definitions are the Standards' and a methods text's, and the one phrase of theirs — "more than one method must be employed in the … validation process" — is as quoted by Rönkkö and Cho): convergent validity is "the degree to which concepts that should be related theoretically are interrelated in reality", discriminant validity "the degree to which concepts that should not be related theoretically are, in fact, not interrelated in reality". Translated: a measure of a place's cultural life should move with other ways of seeing that life (attendance, longevity, what people say) and should not move with things it is not supposed to measure (population size, rateable value, how many people use the platform the data came from). Chapter 4's warning about platform feeds is a discriminant-validity warning: if the measure correlates with platform coverage, some of it is measuring the platform.

The official precedent

There is an official UK precedent for measuring a felt quality, and it is instructive in every detail. Since April 2011 the ONS has asked four questions on its largest household survey: "Overall, how satisfied are you with your life nowadays, where 0 is 'not at all satisfied' and 10 is 'completely satisfied'?"; "Overall, to what extent do you feel that the things you do in your life are worthwhile …?"; "Overall, how happy did you feel yesterday …?"; and "On a scale where 0 is 'not at all anxious' and 10 is 'completely anxious', overall, how anxious did you feel yesterday?" The questions were designed to cover three kinds of wellbeing — "evaluative, eudemonic, and affective experience" — on the recommendation of Dolan, Layard and Metcalfe, whose paper for the ONS concluded that "there are stable and reliable patterns in SWB, even over the course of many years" and that "The time has certainly come for regular measurement of SWB in the largest standard government surveys". The questions were cognitively tested: "Cognitive testing was undertaken to understand how respondents chose their score on the 11-point scale, and what they considered to be 'high', 'low', and 'average' ratings". And — the decision that bears most on this chapter — "It is not appropriate to combine these questions. This is because they are all individually important and together, they give a balanced approach to well-being." The national statistician measures a felt quality with four tested questions and declines to make them one number.

9 · Validation by recognition

The studio's position, from its own published work and carried into the brief, is that a measure of a scene is valid only if the scene recognises itself in it. This section tests that position against the two traditions that have argued about it — qualitative research's "member check" and the participatory-indicator literature — and arrives at a careful answer: recognition does something essential, and it is not what the word "valid" means.

The member check

Lincoln and Guba's 1985 Naturalistic Inquiry called the member check "the most crucial technique for establishing credibility" (secondary): returning "data, analytic categories, interpretations, and conclusions" to "members of those stakeholding groups from whom the data were originally collected", giving them the "opportunity to correct errors of fact and challenge what are perceived to be wrong interpretations". Three decades of practice have split the field. Birt and colleagues' 2016 commentary, whose title asks whether member checking is "a tool to enhance trustworthiness or merely a nod to validation", finds that "Member checking is often mentioned as one in a list of validation techniques" and that "This simplistic reporting might not acknowledge the value of using the method, nor its juxtaposition with the interpretative stance of qualitative research"; it raises "the changing nature of interpretations of phenomena over time" and the question "Are research data 'owned' by the researcher or does it always 'belong' to the participant?", and proposes a structured, late, synthesised version instead. In the authors' own trial of that version, 28 of 50 documents came back and returning to the data "proved unnecessary". Janice Morse, the method's sharpest critic, writes (with colleagues, in 2002) that "member checks may actually invalidate the work of the researcher and keep the level of analysis inappropriately close to the data", because findings are "synthesized, decontextualized, and abstracted from (and across) individual participants, so there is no reason for individuals to be able to recognize themselves or their particular experiences" — and so "it is actually not a verification strategy". David Thomas's 2017 review (secondary) found, in a later summary's words, "limited evidence demonstrating improvements in research findings, credibility or trustworthiness". A 2024 study that tried it reports the texture: eleven of thirteen participants returned their transcripts, nine unchanged, and the edits were "corrections to grammar and punctuation".

The line through this is clear enough to state as a rule. A member check validates resonance and corrects fact. It does not validate an interpretation across people, and it does not establish that a construct exists. Where the thing measured is a person's own experience, their recognition is strong evidence; where the thing measured is an abstraction across many people — a scene, a vibe, a place's cultural life — no individual is positioned to recognise it, and their failure to do so is not a failure of the measure.

Participatory indicators

The participatory tradition makes stronger claims and has started to test them. Fraser and colleagues, from three case studies: "the process of engaging people to select indicators also provides an opportunity for community empowerment that conventional development approaches have failed to provide"; "The extra accuracy and detail that participatory processes bring to indicator selection make an apparently simply job (choosing performance indicators) very complex"; and the warning that "Multi-stakeholder processes must formally feed into decision-making forums or they risk being viewed as irrelevant". Mark Reed's 2008 review of the evidence separates the claims from the proof: "by involving stakeholders, it is argued that the quality and durability of decisions is likely to be greater"; "However, such claims have rarely been tested, and there is growing disillusionment among environmental managers and conservationists who have failed to see these claims realised"; and the verdict — "Although there is evidence that stakeholder participation can lead to more effective and durable decisions, there is little empirical evidence to support many of the other claims that have been made." A 2016 comparative study of 24 cases by de Vente and colleagues found that "factors associated with process design were more significant" than context, that what mattered was "Legitimate representation of stakeholders; professional facilitation including structured methods for aggregating information and balancing power dynamics among participants; and provision of information and decision-making power to all participants", that "Increased trust and learning were perceived as major outcomes", and — the tension a public body should know — that "processes initiated or facilitated by government bodies led to significantly less trust, information gain, and learning", though their decisions "were more likely to be accepted and implemented."

The one study found that directly tested community-chosen indicators against field science is Reed, Dougill and Baker's 2008 work with pastoralists on land degradation (abstract [abstract or summary only]): "Although most indicators suggested by pastoralists were validated through empirical work, they were not always sufficiently accurate or reliable for objective degradation assessment, showing that knowledge cannot be accepted unquestioningly"; "by combining participatory and ecological approaches, it is possible to derive more accurate and relevant indicators than either approach could achieve alone." Mostly valid, not always reliable, and best combined: that is the evidential status of "validation by recognition" as this chapter can find it.

What recognition is, then

In the psychometric vocabulary, a measure the measured people recognise has face validity: in a standard methods text, you "look at the operationalization and see whether 'on its face' it seems like a good translation of the construct", and this is "probably the weakest way to try to demonstrate construct validity" because "it is essentially a subjective judgment call". The Standards do not list it among the sources of validity evidence. In the qualitative vocabulary the same thing is credibility, and it is the first criterion of trustworthiness. Each tradition is right about its own object. Recognition is necessary for a public measure — Chapter 2 found that a reader who does not see their place in a display does not use it, and Carly's failure register says the same — and it is where facts get corrected and where the response-process evidence (did people understand the question as meant?) is gathered. It is not evidence that the construct exists or that the number tracks it. A measure that the scene recognises and that correlates with platform coverage is a recognised measure of the platform.

Two further voices settle where the authority to choose the parts of a measure lies, which is a different question from whether the measure is valid. Amartya Sen, explaining why he will not fix a list of the capabilities that matter, objects to "insisting on one pre-determined canonical list of capabilities, chosen by theorists without any general social discussion or public reasoning", partly because he cannot see "how the exact lists and weights would be chosen without appropriate specification of the context of their use (which could vary)", and because "To insist on a 'fixed forever' list of capabilities would deny the possibility of progress in social understanding, and also go against the productive role of public discussion". The disability movement's principle, "Nothing About Us Without Us", in its own book's words "expresses the conviction of people with disabilities that they know what is best for them", and the United Nations records that the movement's involvement in drafting the disability convention "has proved to be an excellent example of how the principle of full participation can be put into practice". Who chooses the dimensions and the weights is a matter of legitimacy, and the people measured have the first claim. Whether the resulting number is valid is a matter of evidence, and recognition is one source among five. The studio's position survives this section as two rules instead of one: the scene has the authority over what counts, and the measure still owes the other four kinds of evidence.

10 · How culture and place are measured now

This section reads instruments for their published method only — what they combine, how, and what they disclose — and never for their findings about any place.

The cultural frameworks

The AHRC's position was given in section 1. Three UK instruments show the forms that follow from it. The Department for Culture, Media and Sport's Culture and Heritage Capital programme defines its object, after Throsby, as "An asset which embodies, stores or gives rise to cultural value in addition to whatever economic value it may possess", and aims to "create publicly available statistics and guidance that will allow for improved articulation of the value of the culture and heritage sectors in decision making" through "an approach to aid decisions on public funding that is consistent with Social Cost Benefit Analysis principles published in HM Treasury's Green Book" — with the caveat that "economic methodology should be used alongside other information, both quantitative and qualitative". Its form is not an index of a place but a bank of monetary values per kind of asset, for appraisal: Chapter 2's official reader, answered in the official reader's currency.

Arts Council England's quality metrics — the Impact & Insight Toolkit, descended through Manchester and a Western Australian public-value framework — are the clearest UK example of a profile instrument. The 2016 national test used twelve dimension statements, each rated on a slider by the makers before and after, by invited peers, and by the public: Concept "It was an interesting idea"; Presentation "It was well produced and presented"; Distinctiveness "It was different from things I've experienced before"; Challenge "It was thought-provoking"; Captivation "It was absorbing and held my attention"; Enthusiasm "I would come to something like this again"; Local Impact "It is important that it's happening here"; Relevance "It had something to say about the world in which we live"; Rigour "It was well thought-through and put together"; and, for makers and peers only, Risk, Originality and Excellence. Each evaluation "was then summarised with 5 numbers by respondent/time category (self prior, self post, peer and public) per dimension … using medians and interquartile ranges", and read by triangulation: where "self prior scores … are in close alignment with self post, peer and public responses then the work is delivering against the organisation's creative expectations." No single score is produced, and the designers say why: "The dimension scores for individual organisations, or in aggregate, are not a clapometer, in which a successful piece of work has to be seen to score highly on every single dimension." They warn against the comparison the form invites — "comparing apples, pears and pineapples … should only be done in ways that are appropriate" — and record that "Organisations acknowledged that the use of standardised metrics could create anxiety around particular pieces of work being 'judged' in particular ways." The current framework has grown into six domains, five of outcomes and one of "qualities", with outcomes "measuring a change in the survey respondent" and qualities "measuring their personal opinion about the qualities that the work possessed." The report cited is the delivery team's; the independent academic critiques were not reachable.

UNESCO's Culture|2030 indicators — four dimensions, twenty-two indicators — are a third form. "The Indicators are meant to provide evidence of change over time in the same place, rather than global comparability or ranking between different countries or cities"; the framework "is more aspirational than normative, recognizing opportunities for aspiration and improvement, rather than aiming at measuring achievement or failure against absolute benchmarks." No composite is produced. This is the longitudinal self-profile: a place against its own past, not against other places. John Holden's triad is the vocabulary most of this writing uses — "Publicly funded culture generates three types of value – intrinsic, instrumental and institutional", with intrinsic values those "that relate to the subjective experience of culture intellectually, emotionally and spiritually" — and his 2004 diagnosis of the whole field is still the sharpest: "the identifiable measures and 'ancillary benefits' that flow from culture have become more important than the cultural activity itself: the tail is wagging the dog".

The place indices

For the place composites with public methods, the chapter tabulates what each discloses, because the table is the argument.

Instrument Parts Normalisation Weights Aggregation Sensitivity published User weighting Form
Thriving Places Index (UK local authorities) 48 indicators; 17 subdomains; 5 domains; three headline scores z-scores against the England mean, rescaled to 0–10 with the mean at 5 "In almost all cases, all indicators were given the same weighting" Arithmetic means at each level None found No Three scores and colour bands; no single overall number, and no stated reason
Social Progress Index (countries) 52 indicators in the 2015 report read (more in later editions); 12 components; 3 dimensions 0–100 between estimated worst and best case Factor analysis within components; equal across, "because there is no clear theoretical or empirical reason to weight any of the components more highly than any other" Arithmetic ("the simple average of the three dimensions") None in the report read No Score and rank
Legatum Prosperity Index (countries) 150+ indicators; pillars; 3 domains Distance to frontier, 0.1–1 "generally … uniform weights" Power means, p = −1 at domain level rising to 1, chosen because the domains "are poor substitutes for one another" None stated No Score and rank, with domain and pillar scores
English Indices of Deprivation 2019 (small areas) 39 indicators; 7 domains Ranks, then exponential transformation "to reduce 'cancellation effects'" Income 22.5%, employment 22.5%, health 13.5%, education 13.5%, barriers 9.3%, crime 9.3%, living environment 9.3% — inherited from the 2000 indices, whose weights were "derived from consideration of the academic literature … as well as consideration of the levels of robustness of the indicators" Weighted sum of transformed ranks Yes: three weighting approaches tested; small effect on ranks No Rank and deciles; one-tailed by design
OECD Better Life Index (countries) 11 topics 0–1 per measure Set by the user, 0–5 per topic (the OECD's own methodology page was unreadable; confirmed at secondary level and from OECD meta-text) Arithmetic over the user's weights — Yes A composite only the reader makes; no official ranking
ONS Measures of National Well-being (UK) 60 measures; 10 domains — — None Per-measure significance of change — A dashboard: each measure assessed for "positive change, negative change or stayed the same", with confidence intervals; no overall score and no readable statement of why

Three things the table shows. The two instruments with the most thought-through arithmetic — the deprivation index and Legatum — both reach for something other than addition, for the same reason: to stop good parts hiding bad ones. The two UK instruments that chose not to produce one number — the ONS's, from a public body, and the Thriving Places Index, from a charity — enact the choice and do not explain it; three of the five (Thriving Places, Social Progress, Legatum) publish no sensitivity analysis, and so fail this chapter's robustness rule as plainly as any sector instrument; the explicit arguments live in the international literature of section 11. And only one instrument in the table hands the weights to the reader.

The sector's own composite, as method

One composite index exists in the studio's sector, and version 1 of this book named it. This chapter reads its public methodology only for what it discloses, reports nothing about any city, and applies to it exactly the test it has applied to the five instruments above.

Creative Footprint's methodology page states: "We measure a city's Creative Footprint using 15 criteria in three categories: Space, Content, and Conditions." It says who scores — "Some information is objective (ex. size, events per month etc.), but others is more subjective (ex. strength of creative output, overall concept etc.), therefore we employ the services of local experts to accurately assess each and every venue" — and an early overview says the data "is run through an algorithm in order to generate a tangible score out of 10". A 2024 edition's methodology section says interviewees "respond to specific statements using a psychometric response scale called the Likert scale", lists fifteen indicators that differ in name and content from the website's and from the early overview's, and says the data "are also integrated with CFP's proprietary algorithms to calculate the CFP score." Not disclosed anywhere read: the per-criterion scale, the normalisation, the weights, the aggregation, any sensitivity analysis, or a changelog for the indicator set across editions. The one test a reader can run from the published numbers is to ask whether the headline can be reproduced from the parts. The 2024 report prints three category scores of 8.58, 5.90 and 5.41 and a headline of 6.10. The simple means do not give 6.10 — arithmetic 6.63, geometric 6.49, harmonic 6.37 — but several recipes this chapter has described would: a weighted arithmetic mean with about 15% of the weight on the highest category; a power mean with an exponent near −4, of the family Legatum uses to "punish weakness"; or equal weights across the fifteen criteria rather than the three categories, which, by the handbook's own paragraph on uneven groups, would not be recoverable from three category means at all. The headline is consistent with any of these and the published method does not say which. That is the finding, and it is a finding about disclosure, not arithmetic: a reader cannot reproduce the number, and so cannot tell what one part is worth in terms of another, which is what the price-list rule exists to show. On that rule the instrument fails; on the sensitivity rule it fails alongside three of the five instruments in the table; on the parts-list rule it passes. The chapter says nothing about whether its judgements of any place are right, because nothing published allows anyone outside to say.

11 · The form question

Whether to build a composite at all is a choice the literature has argued for the better part of two decades, and the studio's own framework keeps open — version 1 recorded that the result "may be an index, a diagnostic, a framework, a value ledger, a modular evidence toolkit or a hybrid — or a decision that a scored index is not useful". This section gives the forms and the arguments; the choice is the studio's.

The forms this chapter has found exemplars for are five; the studio's "value ledger" and "diagnostic" would be variants of the second and third. A composite: one number per place, with a rank. A scoreboard or dashboard: the component indicators side by side, with no combination. A profile: the components drawn as a shape — a radar, a doughnut, a row of sliders — so the reader sees the pattern. A user-weighted composite: the components with sliders for the weights, so the reader builds the number. A longitudinal self-profile: each place against its own past, with no cross-place comparison at all. Each has a published exemplar in section 10.

The Stiglitz–Sen–Fitoussi Commission of 2009, convened by the French government to rethink the measurement of economic performance and social progress, gave the policy-level answer. On sustainability its eleventh recommendation reads: "Sustainability assessment requires a well-identified dashboard of indicators. The distinctive feature of the components of this dashboard should be that they are interpretable as variations of some underlying 'stocks'." Its analogy: "when driving a car, a meter that added up in one single number the current speed of the vehicle and the remaining level of gasoline would not be of any help to the driver. Both pieces of information are critical and need to be displayed in distinct, clearly visible areas of the dashboard." On quality of life it was plural — "no single measure can summarize something as complex as the well-being of the members of society, our system of measurement must encompass a range of different measures" — and it handed the combining to the reader: "Statistical offices should provide the information needed to aggregate across quality-of-life dimensions, allowing the construction of different indexes", while admitting that "there are strong demands to develop a single summary measure." On the composite health indices then in use: "they all inevitably rest on ethical judgements that are controversial, and on weights for various medical conditions whose legitimacy is not always clear."

The newest official statement is the UN Economic Commission for Europe's 2025 guidelines on measuring well-being, whose chapter on composite indicators defines the alternative with unusual precision: "In a dashboard, the entire set of indicators is presented in such a way that the reader can (and indeed must) deduce developments and comparative levels of well-being from the visualization or database." "A dashboard provides the set of component series but places the onus on the user to consider the overall outcome and trade-offs between the components." "Different stakeholders and other users have different needs. Some users and some purposes are better served by the dashboard model, while other users and purposes benefit more from a composite indicator." It names compensability as the assumption to watch — "In a composite time series that combines two indicators (A and B), the implicit assumption is that an increase in A can be offset by a decrease in B" — and it recommends: "composite indices should be accompanied by dashboards (or other visualizations or dashboards) that give information about the development in the underlying components." And on the absence of objective weights: it "does not necessarily lead to rejection … as long as the entire process is transparent."

The dissenting voice on the composite's purpose is Andrea Saltelli's — one of the handbook's authors — whose 2007 commentary (abstract [abstract or summary only]) describes "the mostly advocacy-driven spread of these measures in recent years" and asks "to what extent composite indicators, capable of aggregating multi-dimensional processes into simplified, stylised concepts, are up to the task of underpinning the development of data-based narratives for political advocacy." Ravallion's conclusion is blunter: "A composite index is not essential for many of the purposes of evidence-based development policy-making", against "the 'dashboard' alternative of monitoring the components separately." No empirical study was found of whether decision-makers use or trust a composite more than a dashboard; the belief that they do is, on this chapter's evidence, Practice.

What the chapter can say about the choice is this. A composite answers one question — which is better overall? — and only that one, and only under its price list. A dashboard answers many questions and asks the reader to do the combining, which Chapter 3 found most readers will not do unaided. A profile shows the shape and invites the reader to see imbalance, which is exactly what addition hides. A user-weighted composite is the handbook's transparency carried to its end: the reader is the builder, and the exchange rates are theirs. A longitudinal self-profile avoids the ranking that Chapter 1 found acts on the ranked, at the cost of the comparison Chapter 2 found some readers need. The one thing every official body agrees on is that whichever is chosen, the components travel with it — which is the subject of the next section.

12 · The recipe on the face

Version 1 of this book stated one Fixed rule for whatever form the studio chooses: the recipe on the face. This chapter has found that rule stated, independently and in different words, by the handbook ("if the construction process is not transparent" is the condition on three of its six cons), by Cronbach and Meehl for psychological constructs ("explicit, public steps of inference"), by Paruolo and colleagues ("inform users of the relative importance of the variables"), by Ravallion ("transparency about the implicit tradeoffs"), by the UNECE ("accompanied by dashboards … that give information about the development in the underlying components"), and by the Code of Practice for Statistics (Chapter 4's practices on methods and quality). The rule is a Nightlife Culture rule with Standard behind it. What follows is what "the recipe" contains, assembled from the sources, and what "on the face" means.

The recipe has nine lines.

  1. The construct, in a sentence, and the theoretical framework that connects it to the parts — the handbook's first step; Cronbach and Meehl's net.
  2. The parts: each indicator, with Chapter 4's provenance set for each (unit, period, base, source, status).
  3. The normalisation, and the fact that it sets exchange rates (Munda and Nardo).
  4. The nominal weights and who set them — statistics, experts, the public, the reader, or nobody ("equal weighting does not mean 'no weights'") — and the effective importances beside them (Paruolo; Becker).
  5. The aggregation rule and the price list it implies: for an additive index, the rate at which each part exchanges for each other, in the parts' own units — the refusal test version 1 posed and this chapter keeps as a Nightlife Culture rule: how many new venues does the measure say compensate for the loss of one forty-year-old institution? If the display cannot answer, the measure is not ready. (The test is a values test, not a method test: method says the rate exists and must be shown; whether a given rate is acceptable is the studio's judgement, and the test makes the studio state it.)
  6. The rank with its interval, from a published sensitivity analysis over the defensible alternatives (Saisana; the JRC audits), and the score at no more digits than the inputs support (two effective digits; the ONS).
  7. The validity evidence under the five headings — content, response process, internal structure, relations to other variables (convergent and discriminant, including against platform coverage), consequences — with reliability stated, including inter-rater reliability wherever a judgement was scored.
  8. The recognition record: who was asked whether they see themselves in it, what they corrected, and who chose the parts (Sen's public reasoning; the member-check literature's limits).
  9. The audit design: how it will be known whether the measured thing moved and not only the measure — the independent check Hood found missing — and what the builder will do when the measure starts to be gamed (Campbell's "multiple indicators, all recognized as imperfect").

"On the face" is bounded by Chapter 3 and Chapter 4 together. Nine lines cannot all sit beside every number, and Chapter 4 proposed the resolution: the fact that a number is composed, and that its recipe exists, is visible on the face; the recipe is one tap away, and it is a document, not a tooltip. The adjacent domain of machine learning has built three such documents and they are the right models, marked Practice. Datasheets for datasets: "every dataset be accompanied with a datasheet that documents its motivation, composition, collection process, recommended uses, and so on", with the insistence that "the process of creating a datasheet is not intended to be automated … our objective of encouraging dataset creators to carefully reflect on the process". Model cards: "short documents accompanying trained machine learning models that provide benchmarked evaluation in a variety of conditions, such as across different cultural, demographic, or phenotypic groups", with sections for intended use, factors, metrics, evaluation data, ethical considerations and "Caveats and Recommendations", and the rule that "Quantitative analyses should be disaggregated". The dataset nutrition label: "a distilled yet comprehensive overview of dataset 'ingredients'", which "creates an expectation of explanation, which will drive better data collection practices." A card — the recipe in nine lines, in a standard form, one tap from the score — is the dashboard's version of all three; its design is Chapter 11's and the design system's. The datasheet authors' insistence that the document not be automated applies to it: a builder who cannot fill it in has learned something about the measure.

Finally, the studio's own rule that no composite cultural-value score exists without an adopted method. This chapter can now say what "adopted" must mean, as a Nightlife Culture rule with the handbook behind it: the ten steps walked and written down; the weights and aggregation chosen as judgements and declared as such; the sensitivity analysis run; the validity evidence gathered under the five headings; the recognition recorded; and the card published. A score published before that is a mashup, in Ravallion's precise sense: a number whose producer "is essentially free to set" its moving parts.

13 · What holds true regardless

The seven

1 · A composite is a model, and is shown as one. It is "formed … on the basis of an underlying model" whose construction "owes more to the craftsmanship of the modeller than to universally accepted scientific rules"; three of its six documented risks are conditional on transparency. The construct and the framework come first, or the result is a mashup. Standard (the OECD/JRC handbook) and Evidence (Ravallion). Fixed (statement of the record).

2 · Weights are judgements, and they are not importance. "Weights are essentially value judgements"; equal weights "does not mean 'no weights'" and weight uneven groups unequally; nominal weights "are hardly ever found to match" effective ones, and can be "little more than cosmetic". Show both. Standard + Evidence (Paruolo et al.; Becker et al.; the JRC audits). Fixed (statement of the record).

3 · Aggregation is a price list, and the prices are declared. Addition lets any strength pay for any weakness — (21,1,1,1) equals (6,6,6,6) — and sets an exchange rate between the parts that can be computed and usually is not ($0.51 against $9,000). The rule is chosen as a judgement about which parts may compensate which, stated in the parts' own units, and answerable to the refusal test. Standard + Evidence (handbook; Munda & Nardo; Ravallion; HDR 2010; Legatum; IoD 2019) + Nightlife Culture (the refusal test). Fixed (statement of the record).

4 · A rank carries its interval, and a score no more digits than its inputs support. A composite audited over its defensible alternatives "is no longer a magic number"; ranks are reported with confidence intervals and read "not only at face value"; two effective digits unless the inputs justify more. Evidence (Saisana et al.; the JRC audits) + Standard (ONS; Analysis Function). Fixed (statement of the record).

5 · A measure that is used changes what it measures, so the audit is designed with the measure. Campbell's law, with the evidence that both things happen at once: the measured thing improves and the numbers are massaged, and three of the four ways a proxy fails need no cheat. The independent check on whether the thing moved is part of the measure's design, not a later repair. Evidence (Campbell; Bevan & Hood; Koretz; Kelman & Friedman; Propper; Burgess; Manheim & Garrabrant). Fixed (statement of the record).

6 · Validity is of a reading for a use, including its consequences — and recognition is necessary and is not validity. "It is the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses that are evaluated, not the test itself"; five sources of evidence; reliability first and not last; a consequence counts against validity when it traces to a flaw in the measure. The people measured have the first claim on what counts, and their recognition corrects fact and confirms resonance; it is face validity and credibility, and the measure owes the other four kinds. Standard (AERA/APA/NCME 2014) + Evidence (Messick; Cronbach & Meehl; Reed 2008; Reed, Dougill & Baker 2008[abstract or summary only]; Thomas 2017 — reconstructed; Morse et al. 2002) + Nightlife Culture (the scene's authority over what counts). Fixed (statement of the record).

7 · The recipe goes on the face. Nine lines, in a standard card, one tap from any composed number; the fact of composition visible beside it; no composite cultural-value score without the adopted method the card records. Nightlife Culture with Standard behind it (handbook; UNECE 2025; Code of Practice) and Practice for the form (datasheets; model cards; nutrition labels). Fixed (statement of the record).

The record beneath them

  • The field's governing text is candid: composites "May disguise serious failings in some dimensions" and "May be misused … to support a desired policy" where construction is not transparent. (OECD/JRC 2008.)
  • Normalisation sets the exchange rate as surely as weights do; z-scores let extreme values dominate; min-max lets outliers set the range. (Handbook; Munda & Nardo.)
  • Equal weights are the commonest scheme, for five reasons including "alleged objectivity". (Greco et al. 2019.)
  • In the Times university ranking as audited, 20% of weight explained 21% of variance and 40% explained 81%; in the Shanghai ranking, 10% and 20% weights mattered almost equally; the 2009 HDI's four parts were "roughly equally important" whatever their weights. (Paruolo et al. 2013.)
  • A developer under annual audit now calls its weights "scaling coefficients and not importance coefficients". (GII 2025 audit.)
  • The 2010 HDI switched to the geometric mean so that "Poor performance in any dimension is now directly reflected"; the UN's own researchers dispute whether the implied exchange rates are "values". (HDR 2010; Klugman et al.)
  • The English deprivation index is "specifically constructed to identify deprivation and not affluence" — a one-tailed instrument; a cultural measure must decide which tail it is for. (IoD 2019.)
  • Eleven sustainability indices in policy use were judged "rather useless if not misleading" on their arithmetic. (Böhringer & Jochem 2007.)
  • In the 2025 Global Innovation Index, 73% of economies shift fewer than three rank places across 5,000 alternative constructions; seven shift more than twenty. (JRC audit.)
  • Goodhart's sentence was a subordinate clause; Strathern's is the aphorism; Hoskin made the bridge; Campbell's is the law with evidence. (Chrystal & Mizen — secondary; Strathern 1997; Campbell 1976.)
  • A third of ambulance trusts "corrected" times to under eight minutes; nine trusts adjusted 6,000 waiting-list records; in "over 80%" of first-time validations the NAO found achievements misstated or data weaknesses undisclosed. (Bevan & Hood; PASC 2003.)
  • Waiting times fell faster in England than in Scotland and Wales; school effectiveness fell in Wales after league tables were abolished; the target was met only where it carried reputational sanction. (Propper et al.[abstract or summary only]; Burgess et al.[abstract or summary only]; Bevan & Hamblin[abstract or summary only].)
  • High-stakes test gains run "3 to 5 times" the gains on low-stakes audit tests. (Koretz 2005.)
  • Messick's two failures — construct underrepresentation and construct-irrelevant variance — are a diagnostic language for any indicator. (Messick 1995.)
  • The Standards do not mention face validity; "response processes" is the official home of cognitive testing. (AERA/APA/NCME 2014.)
  • The ONS measures a felt quality with four cognitively tested questions and refuses to combine them. (ONS.)
  • Member checks correct fact and confirm resonance; the evidence that they improve findings is thin; their critics say they "keep the level of analysis inappropriately close to the data". (Birt et al.; Thomas — reconstructed; Morse et al. 2002.)
  • Participation's proven effects are acceptance, durability and learning; the one direct test found community indicators mostly valid, "not always sufficiently accurate or reliable", and best combined with field measurement. (Reed 2008; de Vente et al. 2016; Reed, Dougill & Baker 2008.)
  • The ACE quality metrics report twelve dimensions from three perspectives as medians and interquartile ranges and are "not a clapometer". (Knell & Whitaker 2016.)
  • UNESCO's indicators measure "change over time in the same place, rather than … ranking". (Culture|2030.)
  • The one sector composite publishes its parts and not its recipe; its headline is consistent with several recipes and the published method does not say which. (Creative Footprint methodology; 2024 report — method only.)
  • No empirical study was found of whether decision-makers use composites more than dashboards; one of the handbook's authors describes their spread as "mostly advocacy-driven". (Saltelli 2007[abstract or summary only], a commentary.)

14 · Where the choice is yours

Which form. Composite, dashboard, profile, user-weighted, longitudinal self-profile, or a hybrid — the UNECE's "side-by-side". The chapter gives what each does; the studio's framework keeps the choice open and this chapter does not close it.

Which construct, and which parts. The theoretical framework is the studio's and the scene's. The chapter's rule is only that it is written first and that each part carries Chapter 4's provenance.

Who sets the weights. Statistics, experts, the public through a deliberative process, the reader through sliders, or equal weights as a declared null. Each is defensible; each is declared; none is neutral.

Which aggregation, and which tail. Additive with its price list shown; geometric; a power mean with a stated exponent; non-compensatory; or none. And whether the instrument is built to find what thrives, what struggles, or both.

How much of the card on the face. The fact of composition and the existence of the card, at minimum; which of the nine lines sit beside the number is Chapter 11's layout decision.

How recognition is gathered. Member checks of fact; a synthesised late check of interpretation; a deliberative choice of parts; or all three — and how its results are recorded on the card.

How the audit is run. Which independent measure stands beside the composite to show whether the thing moved; how often; by whom.

Whether the sector composite's method audit sits here or in Chapter 15.

15 · What this means for a nightlife dashboard

An illustration, not a specification, and not a decision about the measure's form. The sector knowledge is the studio's; the method is the chapter's.

Suppose, for the illustration only, that several things about a place's night have been counted at Chapter 4's standard — venues at a stated grain, events in a stated period, attendance against a stated base, a felt quality asked in tested questions — and that someone wants one number. The chapter's first demand is a sentence: what is the construct, and why these parts? If the sentence cannot be written, the number is a mashup and should not be built. If it can, the handbook's steps follow and each is a judgement. The normalisation decides whether a city with one enormous venue is an outlier or the scale; z-scores would let it dominate, ranks would not. The weights are set by someone — and one candidate, on the studio's own position and Sen's argument, is the scene, through a process the chapter has found earns trust when it is well facilitated and loses it when a public body runs it alone. Whoever sets them, the display shows the nominal weights and the effective importances beside them, because the parts of a cultural ecology move together and the weights may be cosmetic.

Then the aggregation, which is where the studio's values become arithmetic. Under addition, a place with one dominant strength and three collapses can equal a place that is sound on everything — (21,1,1,1) and (6,6,6,6) — and the display has claimed they are the same. Version 1's refusal test stands as the studio's values test: the card must say how many new venues the measure thinks compensate for the loss of one forty-year-old institution, in venues, and if the answer is a number the studio would not defend in public, the aggregation does not express the studio's judgement and should change until it does. The deprivation index's one-tailed design poses a question the studio has not yet had to answer: is the measure built to find where nightlife culture thrives, where it is at risk, or both — because the arithmetic differs.

Then the rank, if there is one. It carries its interval from a sensitivity analysis over the other defensible choices, and the display says between eighth and nineteenth, most likely twelfth rather than twelfth, at two effective digits. Then the validity evidence, gathered under the five headings before anything is published: content (do the parts cover the construct, or is a register of value missing — Messick's underrepresentation?); response process (did people understand the felt-quality questions as meant — the ONS's cognitive testing?); internal structure (do the parts hang together as the framework says?); relations to other variables (does the measure move with longevity, return visits, what people say — and not with population size or ticketing-platform coverage?); consequences (what will the scene do once the measure exists?). Then the recognition record, which does two things and not a third: it corrects the facts a scene knows and the display got wrong, and it confirms that the picture resonates; it does not establish the construct, and the card says so.

And then the audit, designed now. Chapter 1 and this chapter agree that the most reliable thing the measure will do is change the scene. The card names the independent check — the measure that is not on the dashboard, against which the dashboard's movement will be tested — and names what the studio will do when the first venue arranges itself toward the score. That is where this chapter hands over: to Chapter 6, which asks how value is found in data before any score is built, and to Chapter 10, which owns what the measure may do to the people in it.

The rules

Kind and tier as in Chapter 0. "Adjacent domain" marks evidence or standards from education, health, development economics, environmental management or machine learning rather than cultural display.

Rule Why Kind Tier Source
Write the construct and the theoretical framework before choosing parts; a composite without one is not built The handbook's first step; a "mashup index" is one whose producer "is essentially free to set" its parts Standard + Evidence Fixed (sequence) OECD/JRC 2008; Ravallion 2012
Every part of a composite carries Chapter 4's provenance set A composite inherits every defect of its parts and hides them Standard Fixed (requirement) Chapter 4; Code of Practice 3.0
State the normalisation and note that it sets exchange rates; prefer the method that matches the data's shape and the measure's purpose Z-scores let extremes dominate; min-max lets outliers set the range; the trade-off changes with the unit Standard + Evidence Fixed (requirement) · which normalisation: Adaptable Handbook §1.5; Munda & Nardo 2005
Declare who set the weights and how; treat equal weights as a declared judgement, never a default; check for the uneven-group trap "Weights are essentially value judgements"; "equal weighting does not mean 'no weights'" Standard Fixed (requirement) · who sets the weights: Adaptable Handbook §1.6; Greco et al. 2019; SPI methodology
Show the effective importance of each part beside its nominal weight Nominal weights "are hardly ever found to match" main effects; 20% can explain 21% and 40% can explain 81% Evidence Fixed (requirement) Paruolo, Saisana & Saltelli 2013; Becker et al. 2017
Choose the aggregation as a judgement about which parts may compensate which, and say so Addition is fully compensatory; (21,1,1,1) = (6,6,6,6); the HDI changed its arithmetic, and Legatum and the IoD chose theirs, to stop good parts hiding bad ones Standard + Evidence Fixed (requirement) · which aggregation: Adaptable Handbook §1.6 and toolbox (via JRC web reproduction); HDR 2010; Legatum; IoD 2019
Publish the price list of any additive or partly compensatory index — the rate at which each part exchanges for each other, in the parts' own units — and answer the refusal test The exchange rate exists whether or not it is shown ($0.51 against $9,000); "how many new venues compensate for one forty-year-old institution?" Evidence + Nightlife Culture Fixed (requirement) Ravallion 2010/2012; version 1 Ch 6
Decide and declare whether the instrument is one-tailed (built to find shortfall, or thriving) or two-tailed The IoD 2019 is "specifically constructed to identify deprivation and not affluence"; the arithmetic differs Standard (adjacent domain) + Reading Fixed (requirement) · which tail: Adaptable IoD 2019 Technical Report
Run an uncertainty and sensitivity analysis over the defensible alternatives and publish the rank with its interval "No longer a magic number"; ranks read "not only at face value, but also within the 90 percent confidence intervals" Evidence + Practice (JRC audit) Fixed (requirement) Saisana, Saltelli & Tarantola 2005; JRC GII 2025 audit
Report composite scores to two effective digits unless the inputs justify more; never imply a resolution the inputs lack Official rounding guidance; decimal places are a claim Standard Fixed (requirement) ONS style guide; Analysis Function tables guidance; Ehrenberg (Ch 3)
Say a rank as a range with a most-likely value The official form for an uncertain figure Standard Fixed (requirement) Analysis Function 2018
Design the independent audit with the measure: name the check that is not on the dashboard, its frequency and owner, and the response to gaming Measures change what they measure; the improvements were real and remain unverifiable because no independent check was built Evidence (adjacent domain) Fixed (sequence) Campbell 1976; Bevan & Hood 2006; Hood 2006; PASC 2003
Expect ratchet, threshold and output-distortion effects and the three non-adversarial failures of a proxy; monitor the distribution near any threshold The eight-minute "spike"; regressional, extremal and causal failure need no cheat Evidence (adjacent domain) Fixed (sequence) Bevan & Hood 2006; Manheim & Garrabrant 2018
Use "multiple indicators, all recognized as imperfect" and never a single target with sanctions attached Campbell's remedy, with his own doubt; the target was met only where it carried sanction, and gamed there Evidence (adjacent domain) Adaptable (house default) Campbell 1976; Bevan & Hamblin 2009[abstract or summary only]
Validate a reading for a use, under the five sources of evidence; state reliability first, including inter-rater reliability for any judged score "It is the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses that are evaluated, not the test itself" Standard (adjacent domain — psychometrics) Fixed (requirement) AERA/APA/NCME 2014; Messick 1995; McHugh 2012
Test discriminant validity against size and against platform coverage A measure that moves with the platform measures the platform Standard + Reading Fixed (requirement) Standards 2014; Chapter 4
Count a consequence against validity when it traces to construct underrepresentation or irrelevant variance; otherwise record it as a consequence The Standards' boundary; Messick's two failures Standard (adjacent domain) Fixed (requirement) Standards 2014 p. 20; Messick 1995
Cognitively test any felt-quality question before use; present felt qualities as a small panel unless a combination is separately validated The ONS's four questions; "It is not appropriate to combine these questions" Standard Fixed (sequence) · method of testing; combining into one score: Adaptable ONS QMI and user guide; Dolan, Layard & Metcalfe 2011
Gather recognition from the people measured, record what it corrected, and mark it on the card as face validity and credibility — not as evidence of the construct Member checks correct fact and confirm resonance; evidence that they improve findings is thin; the Standards do not count face validity Evidence (adjacent domain) + Nightlife Culture Fixed (sequence) Lincoln & Guba — secondary; Birt et al. 2016; Thomas 2017 — secondary; Morse et al. 2002; Reed 2008
Give the people measured the first claim on which parts count and how they are weighted, through a facilitated process with real decision power The studio's own position, with Sen's argument from public reasoning; the evidence on process design is from environmental management and says how, not whether Nightlife Culture + Reading; Evidence (adjacent domain) for the how Adaptable (house default) Sen 2005; de Vente et al. 2016; Charlton 1998
Combine community-chosen indicators with field measurement; accept neither unquestioningly Mostly valid, "not always sufficiently accurate or reliable" Evidence (adjacent domain; one study) Adaptable Reed, Dougill & Baker 2008[abstract or summary only]
Whatever the form, the components travel with it: a composite is accompanied by its dashboard UNECE 2025 recommendation; Stiglitz–Sen–Fitoussi; Paruolo's second option (do not aggregate pillars with important trade-offs) Standard Fixed (requirement) UNECE 2025 §4.25; SSF 2009 Rec. 9 and 11
Publish the recipe as a standard card, one tap from any composed number, with the fact of composition visible beside the number Three of the handbook's six cons are conditional on transparency; "explicit, public steps of inference" Nightlife Culture + Standard; Practice for the form Fixed (requirement) · how much of the card on the face: Adaptable Version 1 Ch 6; Handbook; Cronbach & Meehl 1955; Gebru et al.; Mitchell et al.; Holland et al.
No composite cultural-value score without an adopted method: the ten steps written, judgements declared, sensitivity run, validity evidence gathered, recognition recorded, card published A score before that is a mashup Nightlife Culture (with Standard behind it) Fixed (sequence) · the form of each step: Adaptable Version 1; Handbook; Ravallion
Treat the belief that decision-makers prefer a composite as Practice until evidence is found No study found either way; the one commentary read calls the spread "mostly advocacy-driven" Reading Adaptable Saltelli 2007[abstract or summary only]
Which form; which construct and parts; who weights; which aggregation and tail; how much of the card on the face; how recognition is gathered; how the audit runs Open choices with named trade-offs — Adaptable Section 14
How the card, the sliders, the profile shape and the interval are styled Free within the design system and Chapter 3's rules — Decorative Design system

What proves a break works

The Fixed rules above are mostly about what is declared, and the test for breaking one is the same as Chapter 4's: hand the composed number and whatever accompanies it to someone who was not in the room, and ask them to reconstruct how it was made, what would change it, and what one part is worth in terms of another. If they can — from the face and one tap — the break has cost nothing. If they cannot say what the weights did, what a strength paid for, or how far the rank could move, the number cannot bear the weight, and the rule was right. For the audit rule the test is harder and later: a year on, can anyone say whether the measured thing moved, from a source that is not the measure? Log the break in the deviation entry Chapter 16 describes.

What this chapter could not settle

  • The Decision Book has no rules on composites, weights, aggregation, sensitivity or what accompanies a score; the rules table above, built from the handbook, the audits and the standards, is the candidate chapter.
  • The studio's "validation by recognition" was a single rule; the measurement literature splits it into legitimacy (who chooses what counts) and validity (five sources), and does not count recognition as the latter. This chapter keeps the studio's authority claim and separates it from the validity claim, marking recognition as face validity and credibility.
  • No house position on whether the measure is one-tailed (shortfall) or two-tailed (thriving); raised here from the deprivation index's design and left open.
  • No evidence found that decision-makers prefer composites to dashboards, though the belief underwrites most index projects; marked Practice.
  • The handbook's own visualisation step says nothing about showing uncertainty, while its sensitivity step requires rank intervals; the rule here is made from the sensitivity step and the JRC audit's reading instruction.

Checklist

  • The construct is written in a sentence and the framework connects it to every part
  • Every part carries its unit, period, base, source and status
  • The normalisation is named and its exchange-rate effect noted
  • Who set the weights, and how, is declared; equal weights declared as a judgement; uneven groups checked
  • Effective importances shown beside nominal weights
  • The aggregation rule is chosen and declared as a compensability judgement
  • The price list is published in the parts' own units; the refusal test answered
  • One-tailed or two-tailed, declared
  • Sensitivity analysis run; every rank shown with its interval; most-likely value stated
  • Scores at two effective digits unless justified
  • The independent audit is designed, owned and scheduled before publication
  • Ratchet, threshold and distortion effects anticipated; distributions near thresholds watched
  • Multiple imperfect indicators; no single sanctioned target
  • Validity evidence gathered under all five sources; reliability stated, inter-rater where judged
  • Discriminant validity tested against size and platform coverage
  • Consequences traced and classified
  • Felt-quality questions cognitively tested; presented as a panel unless combination is validated
  • Recognition gathered, recorded, and marked as what it is
  • The people measured chose the parts, or the card says who did
  • Community indicators combined with field measurement
  • The components accompany any composite
  • The card exists, is standard, is one tap away, and the fact of composition is on the face
  • No score published before the method is adopted

Words this chapter uses

  • A construct is the thing you want to measure and cannot see directly — deprivation, innovation, human development, the quality of a night out.
  • An indicator is something you can count that stands for part of it.
  • A composite indicator, or index, is what you get when several indicators are combined into one number. Most of this chapter is about the distance between the first and the third, and about what has to travel with the third for a reader to see that distance.

06Finding value in the data

Behaviour is evidence of value and every record names who is in it. A dashboard speaks from the first rung and says so.

Dashboard Design · Part 1: The analytical foundation

Reading this chapter. This is one chapter of Dashboard Design, Nightlife Culture's research book on how evidence becomes a display a reader can trust, read and act on. The studio ("the house" in some chapters) is Nightlife Culture, a creative policy studio; the brief is its founder Carly Heath's commission for the book, and her eight ways a dashboard fails, the failure register, run through it. The Vibe Map, the studio's prototype for showing a place's nightlife culture, appears only as an illustration, never as a specification. "Version 1" is the book's archived first draft, whose positions this version re-tests against the sources. Every rule carries a kind (where it comes from: Standard, Evidence, Reading, Practice or Nightlife Culture) and a tier (how firm it is: Fixed, Adaptable or Decorative); Chapter 0 explains both, and the three senses of Fixed: a requirement that can be checked, a sequence whose order is the hard line, and a statement of the record. A dagger (†) marks a source read at the authors' abstract or summary only; "secondary" a quotation reached through a named reproduction; "(read once)" a quotation returned on a single reading and not confirmed by a second. Chapter 0 holds the glossary of the words the chapters share; each chapter lists its own coinages before its sources.

The question

Before anything is scored, how does one ask of a body of data "how is value created here, and for whom?" — and which of the methods that answer that question can be trusted, at what grain, with how many cases, and against what standard of proof?

The 60-second version

A dashboard that scores a place has already decided what value is. This chapter is about the step before: looking at what the data shows of how value is made, who makes it, who receives it, and who takes it — and knowing how far each way of looking can be trusted.

What people do shows what their answers do not. The travel-cost method, the oldest revealed-preference technique, rests on the assumption that the cost of getting somewhere is the price of a visit — and on the assumptions, stated in the UK and US governments' own guidance, that the trip had one purpose, that time has a price, that substitutes were considered, and that only people who came are counted. Movement data has the same shape: the national statistics office's "footfall" is now phone data from one network's 24 million devices, with residents and workers subtracted, and its card-spend indicator comes from customers who "tend to be younger and more metropolitan than the average UK consumer". Whether people come back is a survival question, and a visitor who has not yet returned is censored, not lost.

Diversity has three properties — variety, balance and disparity — and every index weights them differently; a programme can be more diverse by one count and less by another, and what is offered is not what is attended. Access can be scored (walk time, frequency, reliability) and the scorer should say what it leaves out. Welcome has an eight-question instrument, validated for neighbourhoods and to be re-tested for a scene. The national yardstick for "the public" counts reading as arts engagement, and 91% of adults engage; the body that built the sector's audience segmentation went into liquidation four weeks before this chapter was researched.

Longevity is a cohort statistic with a two-year revision lag — business deaths "are not final until the third year" because of reactivations — and survival in the register is continuity of a reference number, not of a venue. Resilience is three concepts (bounce back, absorb, adapt) under one word. Early-warning systems forecast with a 24-month window, and the test of three of them against the Asian crisis concluded "the predictive power of even the best of them may be limited" (both papers at abstract only [abstract or summary only]). The hollow success has a name in the state's own history: legibility, the "abridged maps" that "did not successfully represent the actual activity of the society they depicted", whose forestry example looked like success for a full generation; and a name in medicine: the surrogate endpoint, "expected to predict that clinical benefit" and graded "validated" or merely "reasonably likely".

Value created and extracted is a distinction two centuries old — "Corn is not high because a rent is paid, but a rent is paid because corn is high" — and the UK's appraisal guides give the arithmetic: gross effects, less deadweight, displacement, leakage and substitution, plus multipliers; distributional weights "alongside unweighted estimates"; and a social-return guide that forbids the thing dashboards most want to do with its number: "it is not appropriate to compare the social return ratios alone." The word displacement means two things — activity moved from elsewhere, which the appraisal guides deduct, and people moved out, which is the extraction that matters most to a scene — and the second is measurable only as proxies that "cannot be relied upon to distinguish between involuntary displacement, voluntary outmigration or incumbent socio-economic uplift".

"Because of us" lives on a ladder with three rungs — seeing, doing, imagining — and "Interventional questions cannot be answered from purely observational information". A dashboard lives on the first rung, where the verbs are alongside, after and where.
