Two further things are not tests but the record that lets the tests be run: the date and view in which the pattern was noticed (so that the holdout is one), and the model's assumptions written down with what it is importantly wrong about (Chapter 4's assumptions log). Who counts as competent is the open question. Chapter 5 found, through Sen, that the scene has first claim on what its own measure means, and this chapter takes the position — a Nightlife Culture position, argued from that and from KDD's placing of "the customer's viewpoint" at step one — that the people a pattern describes are among those judged competent to say whether it is true. The seven truths this chapter states have themselves passed only the second test, by the agreement of the few people who have read them; the first awaits the prototype. Which of the scene's people count as "those judged competent" for the Vibe Map's patterns is a question for the three user groups, not for this chapter.

10 · Anomaly as signal

Chapter 4 ended with the outlier as a question rather than an error, and promised that this chapter would take up the discipline that asks the question well. That discipline is statistical process control, built in factories in the 1920s and now the standard method by which the NHS reads its own performance figures; its close relative is public-health surveillance, which watches counts of disease for the week that is not like the others. Both have solved a problem that dashboards in the cultural sector have not yet posed: how to tell a change from noise, and how often one will be wrong.

Two points tell you nothing

The NHS's Making Data Count guide, written to break the habit of reading performance figures as pairs, states the habit and the fault in two sentences. "Many of us will have relied on comparing two points – perhaps performance this month and last, or this year and last." "But the problem with looking at two points of data is that it tells you nothing about trends and how much the data varies naturally." The red-amber-green rating that so many dashboards wear is built on exactly two points — this figure against a target — and the guide says what it costs: "'Green' can provide false assurance and mask deteriorating performance." The failure register for this book says a dashboard fails if it looks the same every month; the NHS's finding is the mirror of that — a dashboard that looks different every month, because two points always differ, is teaching its readers to chase variation that means nothing. "All too often, we overreact to variation which is normal – we waste lots of time investigating a 'deterioration' which SPC tells us is normal; wild goose chases."

The method's first distinction is between two kinds of variation. "This is an example of what is called 'common cause' variation; variation that is outside your control." Common cause is the process being itself: the ordinary month-to-month wobble of a system that has not changed. Special cause is a signal: "Remember that if you find your dataset fits one or more of these rules, then something unusual has happened – generally referred to as special cause variation." The two call for different actions, in the guide's first-pass reading: to reduce common-cause variation you change the process; to reduce special-cause variation you find the special cause. A dashboard that cannot tell its reader which kind of variation they are looking at cannot tell them whether to act.

The chart, and who sets its limits

The tool is a time series with three lines: the mean, and an upper and lower process limit. The guide's point about the limits is the one that distinguishes this method from every target line a dashboard has ever drawn: "You don't set the limits – these are defined by the variability of data for the measure you are plotting." And: "You can expect approximately 99% of data points to fall within the process limits." The limits are a property of the data's own history, not of anyone's ambition for it. The NHS guide does not use the phrase "three sigma"; the NIST handbook does — the limits are usually set at three standard deviations, and "From normal tables we glean that the 3σ in one direction is 0.00135, or in both directions 0.0027", which is where the 99% comes from.

The rules that turn a chart into an alarm are few, and one of them is a choice. A single point outside the limits is a signal. A run of points all above or all below the mean is a signal, and here the guide refuses to fix the number: "Most people use between seven and nine points. You should decide the number based on how frequently you want to ask questions of your system or process", with the floor that "a run of fewer than six points is insufficient as this can occur randomly". A trend is a signal: "A run of six or more values showing continuous increase or decrease is a sign that something unusual is happening in the system." Two of three consecutive points in the outer third near a limit is a signal. The run-length rule being a policy — seven to nine, you decide, by how often you want to be asked a question — matters in itself. The sensitivity of an alert is a design choice with a cost on each side, and the guide puts the choice where it belongs, with the people who will answer the alarm.

How often a correct alarm is wrong

The cost has a number. The NIST handbook defines the average run length: "The ARL tells us, for a given situation, how long on the average we will plot successive control charts points before we detect a point beyond the control limits." For a stable process with limits set correctly at three sigma, "p = 0.0027 and the ARL is approximately 371." A chart that is working exactly as intended, on a process in which nothing has changed, will raise a false alarm from that one rule about once every 371 points; the run and trend rules add their own. A dashboard with a hundred such charts, each updated monthly, will raise a false alarm at least every four months or so from somewhere on the screen with nothing wrong anywhere — and the 371 assumes a long, roughly normal series, which a district's monthly count of a handful of closures is not, so for small counts the rate must be worked out for the count's own distribution. The two questions the handbook poses are the two a dashboard's alert feature must answer in its own documentation: how often there will be false alarms when nothing has changed, and how quickly a real shift will be caught. They pull against each other. Tightening the limits catches shifts sooner and alarms more often; loosening them does the reverse. There is no setting at which both are zero, and a feature described as "alerts you when something changes" without those two numbers has not been designed.

Surveillance, and what "could have" means

The medical version of the method watches a cumulative count against what was expected, and its best-known application is the paper by Spiegelhalter, Grigg, Kinsman and Treasure in 2003 that asked whether sequential monitoring could have caught the Bristol paediatric cardiac surgery deaths and the murders of Harold Shipman earlier than the institutions did. Its abstract — the only part reachable; the page states no full-text access — reports: "Using reasonable boundaries, the procedure could have indicated an 'alarm' in Bristol after publication of the 1991 Cardiac Surgical Register, and in 1985 or 1997 for Harold Shipman depending on the data source and the comparator." [abstract or summary only] Its conclusion: "The risk-adjusted sequential probability test is simple to implement, can be applied in a variety of contexts, and might have been useful to detect specific instances of past divergent performance." The hedges carry the lesson: "could have"; "depending on the data source and the comparator"; "might have been useful". The authors who built the strongest case for statistical surveillance in British medicine stated its result conditionally on the choice of comparator and the choice of boundary, which is to say on the two things Chapter 4 called the comparability declaration and this section calls the alert policy. A dashboard that watches a count for divergence should state both as plainly.

The anomaly in context

Public-health surveillance adds one more idea the cultural sector needs: the expected value is seasonal, and an anomaly is a departure from the same week in previous years, not from last week. The Farrington method, as implemented in the standard statistical package and described in the paper that documents it — the 1996 original is behind a wall — fits its expectation to "w timepoints centred around the timepoint located 1, 2, …, b years before t₀, amounting to a total b · (2w+1) reference values", and alarms when the current count exceeds the upper bound of what that history predicts; the simpler EARS method uses "the 7 timepoints before the assessed timepoint t₀" as its baseline. The reason for reaching back a year rather than a week, in the implementers' words: "data from the less recent past often encompass relevant information about e.g., seasonality and time trend, that one should take into account when estimating the expected count and the associated threshold." The paper is open and the method is standard.

This is Chapter 4's contextual anomaly with a working procedure attached. A January figure is anomalous against Januaries, not against December; a Friday against Fridays. Chapter 4 also noted the good end of the search — positive deviance, the place that is doing better than its conditions predict — and the methods here are symmetrical: a point below the lower limit is as much a signal as one above, and a count persistently under what its history predicts is a question too. No methods paper on positive deviance at small n was reached; the mechanism for judging an apparent small-n outlier is in the next section, and it applies at both ends.

What anomaly detection gives the reader of a dashboard, then, is a sentence beside any highlighted change: this is outside the range this measure has shown for itself, judged against the same season in previous years, by a rule that will be wrong roughly this often. That sentence is the difference between a signal and a colour.

11 · The small place

Everything in this chapter arrives, in the end, at a ward, a street, a scene of a dozen venues, a community of a few hundred regulars. The brief's failure register says the dashboard fails if people "do not recognise their place within the front-end interface", and that place is small. Small numbers have their own statistics: the small place's number is more variable than the large place's, by an exact amount, and the best estimate of it is partly borrowed from elsewhere.

The most dangerous equation

Howard Wainer called it that: the formula for the standard deviation of a sample mean, which shrinks as the square root of the sample size, so that small groups vary more. He named it "the equation that provides us with the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of the mean; what might be called De Moivre's equation", and what makes it dangerous is that it is among the "equations that allow us to understand things clearly, but whose absence leaves us dangerously ignorant." His case is the movement for small schools; by 2001 the foundation that led it "had given grants to education projects totaling approximately $1.7 billion", much of it to that movement, on the evidence that small schools were over-represented among the best performers. They were. "The small schools movement seems to have arrived at one of its recommendations through the examination of only one tail of the performance distribution." Look at the other tail: "Small schools are overrepresented at both tails, exactly as expected, since smaller schools will show greater variation in performance and empirically will show up wherever we look." His verdict: "Expending more than a billion dollars on a theory based on ignorance of De Moivre's equation suggests just how dangerous that ignorance can be."

The reading for a dashboard is immediate and Chapter 5 anticipated it. Any ranking of places by a rate — venues per thousand, spend per head, closures as a share of stock — will have its smallest places at both ends, because their rates swing most. The top of the league table holds the small place that happened to swing up. Chapter 5's one-tailed question returns here as arithmetic: a search for the best will find the small and the lucky, and a search for the worst will find the small and the unlucky, and in neither case has the search found anything about smallness or about quality.

What "small" means, and how many places have no data at all

Eurostat's guideline on small-area estimation defines its subject without any reference to geography: "Small areas/domains denote areas/domains in which the sample size is not large enough for a direct design-based estimation of sufficient precision. Further information from outside the area/domain are required for a reliable estimation." Small is a property of the sample relative to the precision needed. A large borough is a small area for a rare outcome; a single street is a large area for one that is common and well recorded. The question is never "how big is the place" but "how many cases does the measure have here, against how precise it must be to be useful".

How often the answer is "none" is stated by the Office for National Statistics for its own small-area income figures. The survey behind them, "the overall sample of approximately 25,000 responses in England and Wales, is not designed to give accurate income results below regional International Territorial Level (ITL1) level." And: "As approximately 40% of MSOAs in England and Wales will contain no FRS responses, and for some MSOAs the number of survey responses may be too small therefore, it is not possible to create MSOA-level estimates directly from the surveys, and a statistical model is created to estimate mean incomes dependent on available (administrative and census) information about each MSOA." Two in five of England and Wales's middle-layer areas — there are 7,264 of them, each of several thousand households — have nobody in the national income survey at all. For those areas there is no direct number to show, noisy or otherwise. There is a modelled one, or nothing.

Borrowing strength

The modelled one is built by what the statistics office calls, in its own plain phrase, "borrowing strength" between areas: the relationship between the thing wanted and things that are known for every area is estimated from all the data there is, and then applied to the area that has little or none. The Eurostat guideline names the general method: "Indirect estimators denote all estimators which also use information from outside the area of interest. In this context, one strives to borrow strength from additional information outside the area of interest." The standard model, Fay and Herriot's from 1979, produces a figure that the guideline describes as "a weighted average of the direct estimator … and the regression-synthetic estimator" — part what this area's own data says, part what areas like it say.

The United States Census Bureau states the weight in one sentence that a reader can follow with no algebra. For its county poverty estimates, "Final estimates are weighted averages of direct ACS estimates, where they exist, and the model predictions", and "The two weights for each county add to 1.0, and we compute the weight on the model prediction as the sampling variance divided by the total variance (sampling plus lack-of-fit) of the direct estimate." The noisier the area's own figure, the more of the final number comes from the model. "These weights are commonly referred to as 'shrinkage weights' and the final estimates as 'shrinkage' or 'Empirical Bayes' estimates." The word is exact: the small place's own figure is shrunk toward what the model expects of places like it.

The oldest demonstration of why this is right rather than merely convenient is Efron and Morris's, and it uses baseball. Their 1975 paper — the technical version; the 1977 magazine article that made it famous was unreachable beyond its standfirst — took "The batting averages of 18 major league players through their first 45 official at bats of the 1970 season" and set the task "to predict each player's batting average over the remainder of the season using only the data of Column (1) of Table 1." The estimator they used was James and Stein's, which in 1961 was shown to have "uniformly lower mean squared error than the sample mean", and it works by "shrinking all Xi toward X̄" — each player's early average pulled toward the average of all of them. They deliberately included one great hitter, Clemente, "to test the method with at least one extreme parameter, a situation expected to be less favorable to Stein's estimator." The result: "The efficiency of Stein's rule is 3.50 (=17.56/5.01) in this example" — efficiency being the ratio of squared-error losses, so the raw averages' error was three and a half times that of the shrunk ones. The magazine's standfirst puts the paradox in a sentence: "The best guess about the future is usually obtained by computing the average of past events", and "Stein's paradox defines circumstances in which there are estimators better than the arithmetic average". Forty-five at-bats is a small place. Its own average is the worst available guess about its future.

What shrinkage does to the exceptional place

Gelman's short account of the same method, in its modern multilevel form, has the example this chapter has been looking for. His application was radon in American counties, where the aim was "to identify the locations in which residents are at high risk". "Compared with the two classical estimates (no pooling and complete pooling), the inferences from the multilevel models are more reasonable. At one extreme, the complete-pooling method gives identical estimates for all counties, which is particularly inappropriate for this application, whose goal is to identify the locations in which residents are at high risk of radon. At the other extreme, the no-pooling model overfits the data; for example, it gave an implausibly high estimate of the average radon levels in Lac Qui Parle County, in which only two observations were available." Two observations, and the county's raw figure was implausibly high. The multilevel estimate, "shrinking toward the complete-pooling estimate", put it nearer what counties like it show, which is what two observations warrant.

Chapter 4 saw the cost of this through Gelman and Price's work on disease maps, and this chapter states it as a method rather than a worry. Shrinkage pulls every small place toward the average of places like it. The place that is exceptional for a real reason — the one street in the county with a scene — is pulled too, and the model cannot tell a true exception from a lucky swing until it has more data. The display that fits is therefore both numbers: the direct figure with its interval, and the shrunk figure with its weight, so that the reader can see how much was borrowed and from whom. A dashboard that shows only the shrunk figure has hidden the small place's own voice behind its neighbours'; one that shows only the direct figure has shown Lac Qui Parle County's radon level on the strength of two houses. Whether the scene's own people can see their place in a shrunk figure — whether they recognise it, in the failure register's sense — is a thing to test and no literature can answer.

When the number is a count, not a sample

A reader will object at this point that a street's nine venues were counted, not sampled, and ask what interval a complete count can have. The objection is right about the count and wrong about what the dashboard does with it. Nine is nine. But almost everything a dashboard says about those nine is a rate or a comparison — closures as a share of stock, attendance per venue, this year against last — and a rate from nine behaves like a sample from an underlying propensity: one closure moves it by eleven points, and the question the reader is asking is whether the street is becoming a place where venues close, not whether one did. The variability is in time rather than in sampling, and the interval that belongs on the figure is the one section 10 draws from the measure's own history. Survey-based figures for the street — who comes, how they feel — are samples in the ordinary sense and carry the ordinary interval. The two should be labelled differently, and neither should be shown bare.

Intervals that cannot measure change

The modelled small-area figure comes with an interval, and the statistics office attaches a warning to it that bears directly on the thing every dashboard wants to show: the trend arrow. "Confidence intervals describe only the uncertainty from sampling, they do not account for all possible errors and should not be used to measure change." The interval around a modelled figure for a place says how uncertain that figure is; it does not license the comparison of this year's modelled figure with last year's, because the model's own error — the lack of fit, the borrowed relationships — moves between years in ways the interval does not capture. A small-area dashboard that puts an arrow beside a modelled figure has made a claim the producer of the figure says the figure cannot support. Chapter 4's rule that the reference period is declared meets its limit here: for the small place, the period comparison may not be available at all.

Two reasons for an asterisk

When the number is too small, official producers do not show it, and they withhold it for two different reasons that a dashboard should never merge. The first is confidentiality. NHS England's rule for hospital statistics: "Sub-national counts between 1 and 7 (inclusive) will be displayed as ''", "All other counts will be rounded to the nearest 5", and where either the numerator or the denominator of a rate is between 1 and 7, "no percentage or rate is calculated, and a '' will be displayed", "to reduce the risk of identifying individuals from the outputs." The Government Analysis Function's rules for survey tables: "Tables must have at least 2 units contributing to any non-zero cell"; "When the intruder may have response knowledge, cells with three or more units are not considered a disclosure risk"; and the statutory floor for business returns, from the Statistics of Trade Act 1947, that no report "shall disclose the number of returns received...if that number is less than five". The rules' own warning is the small place's: "The disclosure risk in any published table will increase as the sampled population decreases."

The second reason is precision. The ONS publishes estimates from its Opinions and Lifestyle Survey "together with confidence intervals for questions with sample base sizes greater than 10 cases". Its earnings survey grades every cell by its coefficient of variation — "the ratio of the standard error (se) of an estimate to the estimate itself, expressed as a percentage" — and colours the table by it: "estimates with cvs less than or equal to 5% are published with no colour fill", those "between 10% and 20% are published with a dark green background", and "cells for which estimates have been suppressed on quality or disclosure grounds are also filled in dark green." That last clause is the muddle the chapter is warning against, in an official table: the same green means both "imprecise" and "withheld".

The two reasons call for two different things on a screen. A cell suppressed for confidentiality says there is a number and you may not have it, because a person could be identified; it should never be shown, and its suppression should not itself reveal the count. A cell suppressed for precision says there is a number and it is not worth having; it could be shown with its interval, and the designer has chosen not to. A scene of a dozen venues will meet both rules at once — its counts are identifying and its rates are imprecise — and the design must say which rule has fired, because the reader who sees an asterisk and assumes secrecy when the truth is noise, or noise when the truth is that they could be named, has been misled by a symbol. In a scene, moreover, the count at which a figure identifies someone is higher than the national rules assume, because the rules imagine an intruder without local knowledge: a count of three venues in a named district is already suppressed under the rules above, but a count of eight is a list of names to anyone who lives there, and the question is not "is a named venue confidential" — it is public — but what else about it the figure reveals.

When to show a number, an interval, or nothing

The section can now state its procedure, and it is a procedure, with its parameters open. Begin with the reason the number might be withheld: if a person or a venue could be identified, it is withheld, and the threshold is set by the scene's own knowability rather than by a national rule. If not, show the direct figure with its interval whenever there is a direct figure, and the width of the interval is the warning; show the shrunk figure beside it when one exists, with the weight that says how much was borrowed; and show no trend arrow on a modelled figure. If there is no direct figure — the two-in-five case of the income estimates — show the modelled figure marked as modelled, with the covariates it was built from named, or show that the place is unobserved, which is itself a finding Chapter 4 would want recorded. Rank nothing by a rate across places of different sizes without the interval, because the ranking will be a ranking of size. The base-size rule — ten, thirty, the statutory five — is a choice section 13 leaves open; the procedure is not.

12 · What holds true regardless

Seven truths this chapter will defend, each carrying what Chapter 0 calls its kind and the record beneath them.

One. Behaviour is evidence of value, and every behavioural record names who is in it. Where people go, how far they travel, how often they return and whether they come back are evidence of what they value that their answers cannot give, and the travel-cost method has treated distance as a price since the 1940s. But each behavioural record is a record of the people who are in it: the network's subscribers, the card's customers, the ticketing platform's buyers, the people whose precarious housing left no trace. Section 3's methods and section 7's displacement literature agree. Kind: Evidence.

Two. Diversity, access and welcome are measurable, and each measure declares its weighting. Diversity is variety, balance and disparity, and every index trades them against each other; access can be scored and the score should name its blind spot; welcome has an instrument validated for neighbourhoods and to be re-tested for a scene. None is a single number that falls out of the data, and the weighting that made it is part of the figure. Kind: Evidence; the "declares" is a Standard the measurement literature itself sets.

Three. Longevity is a cohort figure with a lag, resilience names its sense, and a proxy for value is graded and watched. "Survived" is defined for a cohort born in a year and active in any part of the next, in a register whose deaths are not final for two years; a closures figure is late and will be revised. "Resilient" means bounce back, absorb, or adapt, and a measure of it says which. Every indicator of a place's value is a surrogate for the thing itself, graded validated, reasonably likely, or neither, and kept beside a measure that is not the proxy — because the hollow success is the proxy that goes on scoring after the thing has gone. Kind: Standard for the definition; Evidence for the lag; Standard (adjacent domain) for the grading; Reading for the requirement to name the sense and to keep the second measure, held as Fixed (sequence).

Four. Value has a creator and a receiver, and the gross-to-net arithmetic is shown. A price can rise because value was made or because a position let someone capture it; the two cannot be told apart from the price alone. Every activity figure is gross until deadweight, displacement, leakage and substitution are shown deducted or shown not deducted; who receives the value is a separate question with an official method whose rule is weighted beside unweighted. Kind: Standard for the arithmetic and the two columns; Evidence for rent; the demand that the deductions be shown on the face of a dashboard, rather than in an appraisal, is a Reading held as Fixed (requirement).

Five. A dashboard speaks from the first rung of the ladder, and says so. The data on the screen is observational; it answers what is, and its verbs are alongside, after and where. "Because" needs something from outside — a counterfactual, or a theory of change whose alternatives have been tested — and a dashboard that claims a cause says what that something was and what rung the claim reaches. "Contributed to" is the second-rung verb a tested theory of change earns, with the story and its challenges shown; without them it is "caused" in a softer voice. Kind: Evidence (Pearl; Hill; Magenta Book; Mayne); the labelling rule is a Standard the evaluation guidance implies.

Six. A pattern becomes a finding only outside the data that produced it, and a change becomes a signal only against the measure's own history. Every view of a dashboard is a path through a garden of forking paths, and a pattern seen at the end of one is a multiple-comparisons result even when nobody fished. It becomes a finding by two tests — it held in data that was not looked at, and those judged competent agreed — with the date it was noticed and the model's known wrongness on record so that the tests can be run. A change on a chart becomes a signal only when it falls outside the range the measure has shown for itself, judged against the same season in earlier years, by a rule whose false-alarm rate is stated. Kind: Evidence; the inclusion of the described among the competent is a Nightlife Culture position argued from Chapter 5's Sen and KDD's first step.

Seven. A small number is shown with its interval, its reason, and what was borrowed to make it. Small places vary more and populate both tails of any ranking; a sound estimate for one borrows strength from places like it and is pulled toward them; an interval around a modelled figure cannot measure change; and a figure is withheld for confidentiality or for precision, which are different reasons and are said. Kind: Evidence for the arithmetic; Standard for the suppression rules; the "say which reason" is a Reading held as Fixed (requirement).

The record beneath them

Chapter 4 asked for a provenance set beneath every number and Chapter 5 for a recipe card beneath every measure. This chapter asks for a claim record beneath every statement of value — the lines that let a reader see what kind of claim they are looking at. Ten lines, as a floor.

  1. What was observed — the behaviour, count or price, in Chapter 4's terms: unit, period, base.
  2. Who is in the record — the population the source observes, and who it cannot see.
  3. Gross or net — and if net, which of deadweight, displacement, leakage, substitution and multipliers were applied, from what source, bespoke or borrowed.
  4. Created or captured — whether the figure is a product or a price, and if a price, whose position it rewards.
  5. For whom — the distributional reading, weighted beside unweighted, with the weight and its source.
  6. The rung — observational; interventional with a named comparison; counterfactual by argument only — and the verb that matches it.
  7. The alternatives considered — the other explanations, in Hill's sense, and what was found against each.
  8. Noticed on — the date and view in which the pattern was first seen, and whether it has yet been tested outside them.
  9. The model's known wrongness — what the baseline, forecast, score or shrinkage cannot see, and the date it was last validated and on what.
  10. The small-number treatment — direct or modelled; the interval; the shrinkage weight; and, if withheld, whether for confidentiality or precision.

Most of these lines will say "not done" for most figures on most dashboards. That is the point of the record. A "not done" that is visible is a boundary; a "not done" that is hidden is an overclaim.

A filled record, for an imagined figure, so that the shape is clear. The figure: card spend in the district rose 18% in the twelve months to March, against 6% city-wide. (1) Observed: card spend, monthly, March-to-March, in pounds, base the previous twelve months. (2) Who is in the record: customers of one bank, "younger and more metropolitan than the average UK consumer"; cash and other banks unseen. (3) Gross; no deduction for deadweight, displacement from neighbouring districts, or leakage to businesses outside it. (4) A product — spend — though part of it is the price of the same goods having risen. (5) For whom: not done; no distributional reading. (6) Rung one: the rise happened alongside the scene's growth; no comparison group beyond the city average, which differs from the district in more than its nights. (7) Alternatives: the new station opened in the same year; the bank's customer base grew; not tested. (8) Noticed on 12 April in the district-filter view; not yet tested against the following year or against districts with a new station and no scene. (9) No model. (10) Direct figure, not modelled; base large enough that no interval is shown; not withheld. Six of the ten lines say "not done" or "not tested", and the figure is still worth showing — with those six lines beside it.

13 · Where the choice is yours

The truths above fix the questions. These are the answers the chapter leaves open, because the evidence does not settle them or because they belong to the people who will live with the display.

Which error you would rather make. Family-wise control means almost nothing lights up and almost everything that does is real; false-discovery control means more lights up and a stated share is noise. The choice depends on what a false alarm costs the reader and what a missed signal costs the scene. Neither literature says which; the NHS guide says to decide the run-length "based on how frequently you want to ask questions", and that is the right frame.

How often an alert may be wrong. The average run length is a parameter. 371 is what three-sigma limits give; tighter limits catch sooner and cry more often. Set it with the people who will answer the alarm, and print it.

Which sense of resilience. Bounce back, absorb, or adapt. The third is the hardest to measure and the first the easiest; which one a reader needs is the reader's question. The chapter does not choose.

Whether to weight at all. The Green Book's 1.3 is for appraisal of public spending. A dashboard that is not an appraisal may show the distribution without weighting it, or weight by some other value its readers hold. What it may not do is weight silently.

What counts as a return, and how long to wait. Retention as survival needs a definition of the event and a censoring rule; a visitor who has not come back in a month is not lost, and one who has not come back in three years probably is. The window is a judgement about the scene's rhythm.

How long a pattern waits before it is promoted. One more month of data, a year, a season — the holdout's size is a choice between acting on something that may be noise and waiting through something that may be real. Hill's close applies: incomplete evidence does not confer a freedom to postpone, and it does not confer a freedom to overclaim either.

The base-size floor, and who sets it. Ten, as the ONS uses for one survey; five, as statute sets for business returns; or the scene's own knowability, which for a named district may need to be far higher than any national rule. The procedure in section 11 is fixed; its number is not.

Who the competent are. The validation standard the UK guidance implies is the agreement of those judged competent. For a measure of a scene, this chapter has argued that the scene is among them. Which of its people, in what forum, with what power to say no, is not a question this book can answer from a desk.

14 · An illustration from nightlife — method only

A district of a city has a reputation. People say its nights are something; the council hears both that it is the city's asset and that it is a nuisance; a landowner has begun to assemble sites. Somebody asks the dashboard: how is value created here, and for whom? What follows is the method's walk through that question, and nothing about the answer, which belongs to the Vibe Map and to the people of the district.

The walk begins with behaviour. Who comes, from where, how far, how often, and whether they return — and before any of those figures is read, whose behaviour the record holds. If it is phone data, it holds one network's subscribers with residents and workers subtracted, so the district's own people are the ones removed from the count of the district. If it is card spend, it holds the customers of one bank who are younger and more metropolitan than the country. If it is tickets, it holds the people who buy tickets. The first line of the claim record is written before the first number is shown.

Next, the offer and the welcome. The district's programme can be counted for variety, balance and disparity, and the count will depend on the categories chosen, so the categories are shown; what is attended is counted separately from what is offered; and if anyone wants to know whether people feel they belong there, an eight-question instrument exists and a footfall figure is not it.

Then time. How many of the venues that were open five years ago are open now is a cohort question, answered from a register in which a closure is not final for two years and "the same venue" means the same reference number. The figure is shown with its cohort and its revision status. If the district has survived a shock — a pandemic, a licensing change, a development — the word resilient is used in one of its three senses and the sense is named.

Then the money. Spend in the district has risen; so have rents. The spend figure is gross and is labelled gross, with a line saying that deadweight, displacement, leakage and substitution have not been estimated, or have been, with a borrowed percentage from a named study. The rent figure is placed beside it with Ricardo's question on the face: is this a product or a price, and if the district has become more desirable, who made it so and who is receiving the rent? The dashboard asks; it does not answer. The distributional reading, if one is attempted, shows the weighted figure beside the unweighted one and says where the weight came from. If someone has produced a social return ratio for the district, it is shown with its story and never in a league table, because the method's own guide says so.

Then the claim. The council's officer wants to say that the district's economy grew because of its nights. The dashboard shows what it can from the first rung — the sequence, the gradient across comparable districts, the consistency across years — and labels the sentence "contributed to" only if a theory of change exists and its alternatives (the new transport link, the housing, the city-wide trend) have been named and tested; otherwise the verb is "alongside", and the alternatives are listed as untested. If a ticketing dataset shows that a share of out-of-town visits began with a ticket bought days before the journey, the fact is stated first and the claim that the event anchored the visit is marked as a contribution claim, with the deadweight share — how many would have come anyway — estimated from a question asked and marked as stated preference, or marked as not yet known.

Then the pattern. An analyst notices that spend in the district rose in the three months after a licensing change. The notice is dated and the view recorded; the comparison is one of some thousands the dashboard offers; it will be tested against the next year's same months and against districts where no change happened, and until then it is a hypothesis with a date on it.

Then the alarm. The district's closure count has gone up this month. The chart shows the count against its own history, seasonally — this month against the same month in past years — with limits the data set and a rule whose false-alarm rate has been chosen and printed; the point is inside the limits or it is not, and if it is not, the question is asked rather than the conclusion drawn.

Then the small place. Within the district is one street with a scene of its own — nine venues, a few hundred regulars. Every rate for it will swing. Its rates are shown with their intervals, from the street's own history; if any figure is modelled, it is marked modelled and the borrowed figure is shown beside the direct one with the weight; it is not ranked against larger places without that interval; no arrow is drawn on a modelled figure; and if a count would let the regulars tell which venue it describes, the count is withheld and the reason given is confidentiality rather than noise. Whether those regulars recognise their street in what remains is a question the Vibe Map asks them.

What the dashboard has not done, at the end of the walk, is say whether the district is valuable. It has shown what the data can say about how the value is made and by whom, who is counted in the making, who receives it, what has been deducted and what has not, which claims reach which rung, which patterns are findings and which are dated hypotheses, and which numbers are too small to be anything but a question. The judgement is the reader's. The method's job was to make it an informed one.

The rules

Kind and tier as in Chapter 0. "Adjacent domain" marks evidence or standards from environmental economics, ecology, epidemiology, clinical trials, industrial quality control, public-health surveillance, machine learning or official statistics rather than cultural display.

Rule Why Kind Tier Source
Before any behavioural figure is read, name the population the record observes and who it cannot see Revealed-preference methods "only measure use-value"; footfall is one network's 24m devices with residents and workers excluded; card data skews "younger and more metropolitan" Standard + Evidence Fixed Fujiwara & Campbell 2011; ONS RTI methodology 2026; ONS 2016; Wesolowski et al. 2012
Treat distance as a price only with the method's assumptions stated: single purpose, a declared value of time, substitutes considered "If a trip has more than one purpose, it almost certainly violates the travel cost model's central assumption"; time valued at "one-third to the full wage", neither bound firm Standard (adjacent domain) Fixed (stated); Adaptable (values) US EPA 2010; Fujiwara & Campbell 2011; Poor & Smith 2004[abstract or summary only]
Define a catchment by a self-containment threshold on observed flows, and state the threshold TTWAs: 75% both ways, 66.7% for large areas — the catchment is a rule, not a radius Standard Fixed (requirement) ONS TTWA 2015
Measure return as survival with censoring; a visitor who has not yet returned is censored, not lost Simple rates "ignore the duration spent"; censoring "(a) a patient has not (yet) experienced the relevant outcome" Evidence (adjacent domain) + Reading Fixed (requirement) Clark et al. 2003
Report diversity as variety, balance and disparity, and declare which the index weights; count supplied and consumed diversity separately "Each is a necessary but insufficient property"; "diversity increases when variety is the sole consideration, whereas taking balance or disparity into account leads to the opposite conclusion" Evidence Fixed Stirling 2007; Benhamou & Peltier 2007[abstract or summary only] ; Jost 2006[abstract or summary only]
Any access score names what it leaves out PTAL "does not take into account the destinations you can travel to from each location or the ease of interchange" Standard + Practice Adaptable (house default) TfL 2015
Measure welcome with an instrument validated for belonging, re-tested in the scene's own wording, rather than with a proxy Four elements; eight items; confirmed by factor analysis on n = 293 residents of neighbourhoods Evidence (adjacent domain — community psychology) Fixed (instrument); Adaptable (wording) McMillan & Chavis 1986; Peterson, Speer & McMillan 2008
When comparing an audience with "the public", state the national yardstick's definition and reference period 91% engage in 12 months when reading counts; response rate 25% Standard Fixed DCMS Participation Survey 2023–24
State survival as a cohort figure with its definition, and mark closures provisional for two years "A business is deemed to have survived if it was born in year t … and it is active … in any part of t plus 1"; deaths "not final until the third year" Standard Fixed ONS Business Demography 2025; QMI
Name the sense of "resilience" before measuring it: bounce back, absorb, or adapt Three interpretations in one word; the authors favour the third Reading (Evidence for the taxonomy) Fixed (sequence) · the measure of resilience: Adaptable Martin & Sunley 2013/2015; Walker et al. 2004
Any early-warning indicator states its window, its threshold, and its out-of-sample record 24-month window; "the predictive power of even the best of them may be limited" Evidence (adjacent domain) Fixed (requirement) Kaminsky, Lizondo & Reinhart 1998[abstract or summary only]; Berg & Pattillo 1999[abstract or summary only]
Grade every proxy for value as validated, reasonably likely, or neither, on the card A surrogate "is expected to predict that clinical benefit"; "In practice, this requirement frequently fails" Standard (adjacent domain) + Reading Adaptable (house default) FDA 2018; Fleming & DeMets 1996
Keep a measure that is not the proxy beside the proxy, and watch for them parting The forest "grew excellently in the first generation" Evidence + Reading Fixed (sequence) Scott 1998; Plochmann via Scott
Label every activity figure gross until the deductions are shown; name which of deadweight, displacement, leakage and substitution were applied and from where "Additionality is the extent to which something happens as a result of an intervention that would not have occurred in the absence of the intervention"; "significant care needs to be taken in using default or ready reckoner values" Standard Fixed HCA Additionality Guide 2014 (withdrawn 2022)
Ask of any price-based indicator whether it measures a product or a rent "a rent is paid because corn is high" Evidence (classical economics) + Reading Adaptable (house default) Ricardo 1817; Mazzucato 2018 (blurb, secondary)
Show distributional figures weighted beside unweighted, with the weight and its source "Practitioners must present weighted estimates alongside unweighted estimates" Standard Fixed HM Treasury Green Book 2026 ch. 7
Never place a social-return ratio in a league table; show it with its story "it is not appropriate to compare the social return ratios alone" Standard (the method's own) Fixed SROI Guide 2012; Social Value International
Keep economic displacement (a deduction) and residential displacement (people moved out) apart; show who left, and call it displacement only with the comparison the literature requires and the three readings named Proxies "cannot be relied upon to distinguish between involuntary displacement, voluntary outmigration or incumbent socio-economic uplift" Standard + Evidence Fixed HCA 2014; Easton et al. 2020
Label every claim of cause with the rung its evidence reaches; from observational data alone the verbs are "alongside", "after" and "where"; "contributed to" only with a theory of change whose alternatives have been tested "Interventional questions cannot be answered from purely observational information"; "Ruling out of alternative causes in order to claim impact" Evidence + Standard Fixed Pearl 2018; Magenta Book 2026; Mayne 2008
Where the question behind a chart is causal, state the question and the rung rather than letting "associated with" stand in for an answer The euphemism hides the question (reconstructed abstract) Reading Adaptable (house default) Hernán 2018[abstract or summary only]
Where a causal reading is wanted, show Hill's viewpoints the data can show — gradient, consistency, sequence — and the alternatives considered "is there any other way of explaining the set of facts before us" Evidence (adjacent domain) Fixed (requirement) Hill 1965
A theory-of-change claim names its alternative explanations and the evidence against each "Ruling out of alternative causes in order to claim impact"; a story "stronger and more credible", never "foolproof" Standard Fixed Magenta Book 2026; Mayne 2008
"Leading" is shown only when a lead has been measured against a named reference series; until then two series are two series "it is only Granger causality"; a CLI is built by turning-point comparison Evidence + Standard Fixed Granger (Scholarpedia); OECD CLI
The studio's claim ladder puts the observed fact on top, the anchor claim beneath it marked as contribution, a deadweight line marked as stated preference, and counter-flows Version 1's form, amended by Pearl, Hill and the Additionality Guide Nightlife Culture (tested) Adaptable (house default) Version 1 Ch 6; this chapter §8
Treat every dashboard view as exploratory; a pattern is a hypothesis with a date until tested outside the data that produced it "the same data cannot be used to generate and test a hypothesis"; holdouts "wear out" Evidence (adjacent domain) Fixed COS; Goodfellow et al. 2016; Google MLCC
Judge the surprise of a found comparison against the number of comparisons the view allowed "multiple comparisons can be a problem, even when there is no 'fishing expedition'" Evidence Fixed Gelman & Loken 2013/2014
Choose family-wise or false-discovery control for any highlighting rule, and say which The two error rates; neither makes every highlight real Standard (adjacent domain) Fixed (declared); Adaptable (which) Benjamini & Hochberg 1995
No "significant" badge standing alone as the reason for a highlight or a decision; an error-controlled highlighting rule is not a badge "decisions should not be based only on whether a p-value passes a specific threshold"; "the glitter of the t table" Standard (professional) Fixed ASA 2016; Hill 1965
Treat two trending series as one comparison; do not report their correlation as a finding "sequential years are not independent of each other" Evidence (Yule by citation; Vigen as plain statement) Fixed Vigen; Yule 1926 (metadata)
Any model on the display states what it is importantly wrong about, which culture it was built in, and the date and population of its last validation "the scientist must be alert to what is importantly wrong"; "population distributions are nonstationary" Evidence Fixed (requirement) Box 1976; Breiman 2001; Hand 2006
A pattern becomes a canonical truth by two tests, out-of-sample and the agreement of the competent; the described are among the competent "Validation literally means to make valid, through the agreement of those judged competent"; KDD step one is "from the customer's viewpoint" Evidence + Standard for the two tests; Nightlife Culture for who is competent Fixed (requirement) · the described among the competent (house default): Adaptable Glover 2014; AQuA Book 2025; Fayyad et al. 1996; Chapter 5 (Sen)
Never read two points as a trend; show a measure against its own history with limits the data set "tells you nothing about trends and how much the data varies naturally"; "You don't set the limits" Practice (NHS guidance) + Evidence (adjacent domain) Fixed NHS Making Data Count 2019; NIST/SEMATECH
Distinguish common-cause from special-cause variation on the face, and say which action each calls for "wild goose chases" Practice (NHS guidance) Adaptable (house default) NHS Making Data Count 2019
Every alert states its false-alarm rate and its detection delay, worked out for the measure's own distribution and agreed with the people who answer it ARL ≈ 371 for one rule of a correct 3σ chart on a long stable series; run-length "between seven and nine … you should decide" Standard (adjacent domain) + Practice Fixed (stated); Adaptable (values) NIST/SEMATECH; NHS 2019
Judge an anomaly against the same season in previous years, not the previous period "data from the less recent past often encompass relevant information about e.g., seasonality" Evidence (adjacent domain) Fixed (requirement) Salmon, Schumacher & Höhle 2016
Surveillance claims state their comparator and their boundary "could have indicated an 'alarm' … depending on the data source and the comparator" Evidence (adjacent domain) Fixed Spiegelhalter et al. 2003[abstract or summary only]
Never rank places of different sizes by a raw rate; show the interval or do not rank "Small schools are overrepresented at both tails, exactly as expected" Evidence Fixed Wainer 2007/2009
Define "small" by precision needed, not by geography "the sample size is not large enough for a direct design-based estimation of sufficient precision" Standard Fixed Eurostat 2019
Show the direct figure with its interval and the shrunk figure with its weight, side by side; mark modelled figures modelled with their covariates named; label a complete count's interval as drawn from its history, a sample's from its sampling Weight on the model = sampling variance ÷ total variance; two observations gave "an implausibly high estimate" Standard + Evidence Fixed SAIPE; Gelman 2006; Efron & Morris 1975; Eurostat 2019
No trend arrow on a modelled small-area figure Its intervals "should not be used to measure change" Standard Fixed ONS income QMI 2025
Say whether a withheld figure is withheld for confidentiality or for precision, and never let the same mark mean both NHS 1–7 as "*"; Analysis Function 2/3/5; OPN base > 10; ASHE's dark green means both Standard + Reading Fixed (requirement) NHS England 2023; Analysis Function 2026; ONS OPN 2025; ONS ASHE 2018
Set the identifying threshold by the scene's knowability, above the national rule where local knowledge would name the units The national rules assume an intruder without local knowledge Nightlife Culture + Standard behind it Fixed (sequence) This chapter; Decision Book Ch 8/15
Record the ten-line claim record beneath every statement of value; "not done" is written, not hidden A visible boundary is a boundary; a hidden one is an overclaim Nightlife Culture (with Standard behind each line) Fixed (sequence) · the lines' content: Adaptable This chapter §12

What proves a break works

Most of the Fixed rules here are about what is declared beside a figure, and the test for breaking one is Chapter 4's and Chapter 5's: give the figure and what accompanies it to someone who was not in the room, and ask them four questions — who is in this record, is this gross or net, what rung does the "because" reach, and could this number be noise? If they can answer all four from the face and one tap, the break has cost nothing. If any answer is "I can't tell", the rule was carrying weight. For the alert rules the test is later and arithmetical: after a year, count the alarms that were answered and found to be nothing, and compare the count with the false-alarm rate the feature declared. For the small-number rules the test is adversarial: try, as someone who knows the scene, to name the venues behind a withheld count; if you can, the threshold was the national rule's and not the scene's. Log the break in the deviation entry Chapter 16 describes.

What this chapter could not settle

  • Two UK method texts were replaced in 2026 at their old addresses (Magenta Book May 2026; Green Book February 2026); the chapter quotes the 2026 editions and says so.
  • The Decision Book has no rules on gross against net, distributional weights, causal rungs, leading indicators, multiple comparisons, alert policy, shrinkage, or the precision reason for withholding; the rules table above is the candidate for a Decision Book chapter on claims about value.
  • Official suppression rules hide small numbers for two reasons (confidentiality; precision) and one official table colours both the same; the chapter separates them, with the rule that the mark says which.
  • The national rules' identifying thresholds (2, 3, 5, 7) assume an intruder without local knowledge, and a scene's regulars can name three venues; the rule is that the scene's knowability sets the threshold.
  • No method was found for commercial displacement (venues, promoters); the household literature is all there is, and for a scene this is the form that matters.
  • The AQuA Book 2025 has no statement about validating a model against outturn; its validation is user-needs-based, so the chapter builds the two-test standard (out-of-sample plus agreement of the competent) from the holdout literature and Glover.
  • The Audience Agency entered liquidation on 10 September 2026 and the sector's audience yardstick has no custodian; any dashboard built on Audience Spectrum needs a fallback.

Checklist

  • Every behavioural source names its observed population and who it cannot see
  • Distance-as-price assumptions stated; the value of time declared
  • Catchments defined by a stated self-containment rule
  • Return measured as survival with censoring; the window declared
  • Diversity reported as three properties; the index's weighting named; supplied and consumed counted separately
  • Access scores name their blind spot
  • Welcome measured by a validated instrument, with the wording change recorded
  • The national yardstick's definition and period stated beside any "public" comparison
  • Survival given as a cohort figure; closures marked provisional for two years
  • "Resilience" named in one of its three senses
  • Early-warning indicators carry window, threshold and out-of-sample record
  • Every proxy graded validated / reasonably likely / neither; a non-proxy measure kept beside it
  • Activity figures labelled gross or net; the deductions and their sources named
  • Price-based indicators asked the rent question
  • Distributional figures weighted beside unweighted, weight and source shown
  • No social-return ratio in a league table
  • Economic and residential displacement kept apart; leavers shown; "displacement" used only with the comparison and the three readings
  • Every "because" labelled by rung; "alongside / after / where" from observational data; "contributed to" only with a tested theory of change
  • No "associated with" standing in for a causal question
  • Hill's viewpoints shown where the data can show them; alternatives named
  • "Leading" shown only with a measured lead against a named reference series
  • The claim ladder: fact on top, anchor claim beneath as contribution, deadweight line marked as stated preference, counter-flows
  • Every found pattern dated and marked untested until tested outside its data
  • Every found comparison judged against the number of comparisons the view allowed
  • Highlighting rule's error control chosen and declared
  • No "significant" badges
  • Trending series not reported as correlated findings
  • Every model states its known wrongness, its culture, and its last validation
  • Canonical truths carry both tests; the described among the competent
  • No two-point trends; limits set by the data's own history
  • Common and special cause distinguished on the face
  • Every alert states its false-alarm rate and detection delay, agreed with those who answer it
  • Anomalies judged against the same season in previous years
  • Surveillance claims state their comparator and their boundary
  • "Small" defined by the precision needed, not by geography
  • No ranking by raw rate across sizes
  • Direct and shrunk figures side by side; modelled figures marked, covariates named
  • No trend arrows on modelled small-area figures
  • Withheld figures say which reason; the scene's knowability sets the threshold
  • The claim record exists beneath every statement of value

07Comparison, time and intervention

A comparison declares what it holds equal and who chose the comparators. After is not because.

Dashboard Design · Part 1: The analytical foundation

Reading this chapter. This is one chapter of Dashboard Design, Nightlife Culture's research book on how evidence becomes a display a reader can trust, read and act on. The studio ("the house" in some chapters) is Nightlife Culture, a creative policy studio; the brief is its founder Carly Heath's commission for the book, and her eight ways a dashboard fails, the failure register, run through it. The Vibe Map, the studio's prototype for showing a place's nightlife culture, appears only as an illustration, never as a specification. "Version 1" is the book's archived first draft, whose positions this version re-tests against the sources. Every rule carries a kind (where it comes from: Standard, Evidence, Reading, Practice or Nightlife Culture) and a tier (how firm it is: Fixed, Adaptable or Decorative); Chapter 0 explains both, and the three senses of Fixed: a requirement that can be checked, a sequence whose order is the hard line, and a statement of the record. A dagger (†) marks a source read at the authors' abstract or summary only; "secondary" a quotation reached through a named reproduction; "(read once)" a quotation returned on a single reading and not confirmed by a second. Chapter 0 holds the glossary of the words the chapters share; each chapter lists its own coinages before its sources.

The question

When a dashboard sets one thing beside another — this place beside that one, this month beside last, the year before a change beside the year after, what is beside what might be — what does each comparison show, what does it hide, and what may be said from it?

The 60-second version

Every comparison is a claim that two things are alike in everything but the thing compared. Chapter 4 asked for that claim to be declared; this chapter is about the four comparisons a dashboard makes — and a fifth discipline, reading the borrowed indices of a market — and what each one's declaration must contain.

Place against place. A ranking is a measure that changes what it measures — rankings "do not simply reflect an underlying social hierarchy but in fact play a crucial role in creating this hierarchy" — and a noisy one: in the standard analysis "about two thirds of all possible comparisons do not allow separation", and a clinic's rank can move substantially between years "even though their live birth rate did not change significantly". The World Bank's own review of its Doing Business index recommended "Remove the aggregate index and country rankings", and a UK publisher of a standardised mortality ratio tells users "It is inappropriate to rank trusts according to their SHMI." The alternative has a name and a shape: the funnel plot, which "avoid[s] spurious ranking of institutions into 'league tables'" [abstract or summary only] by plotting each place against its own precision. Comparing like with like needs standardisation — a ratio of observed to expected — and peers chosen by a published method, because in the one field where self-chosen comparators have been measured, executive pay, "peer groups are constructed in a manner that biases compensation upward". [abstract or summary only]

This period against last. A series has a trend, a season and a remainder, and every "underlying trend" line is a smoothing someone chose. Seasonal adjustment is a model whose factors "are estimates based on present and past experience", revised when "just one additional observation" arrives; a series under three years "cannot be seasonally adjusted"; and comparing this month with the same month last year "does not completely remove all seasonal effects" and is slow at turning points. A year-on-year rate can move because of what happened twelve months ago. Regression to the mean "can make natural variation in repeated data look like real change" and "should always be considered as a possible cause of an observed change". [abstract or summary only] An index is change relative to a reference date the producer calls "arbitrary", and the textbook rules of thumb for how many observations make a trend readable "are misleading and unsubstantiated in theory or practice".

Before against after. The one-group before-and-after comparison was introduced in 1963 "as a 'bad example'", with eight named rivals to the explanation that the intervention did it. The designs that do better each add a comparison: a pre-trend projected forward (interrupted time series); a comparison group whose trend is assumed parallel — an assumption that "cannot be tested because it involves a non-existent counterfactual that cannot be observed" — whose pooled estimate misleads when places adopt at different times and effects change over time; a weighted blend of other places (synthetic control), which "preclude[s] extrapolation" and makes "explicit the contribution of each comparison unit"; a cut-off; a match on what was recorded. Each has stated requirements and a rung on a published ladder on which plain before/after is the bottom and the floor for counting as evidence is a comparison group; the stronger ones have a placebo test. Each rung has its verb: after for a before/after; departed from its trend for an interrupted series; contributed to for a comparison-group design with a tested theory of change; caused only for the designs that earn it. Spillovers and displacement are the ripples, and "Seeing evidence of growth in the zone itself … tells us very little if that activity is simply displaced from elsewhere". A small effect in a noisy series from few places cannot be seen at all.

What is against what might be. The UK's appraisal rules say how such a claim is stated: adjust for optimism bias — "the demonstrated systematic tendency for practitioners to be over-optimistic" — by the organisation's own record of forecast against outturn; give "a central estimate and a range"; calculate the switching value at which the conclusion flips; run scenarios, and (the cross-government uncertainty toolkit adds) an even number of them. The best-known uncertainty display in British official life, the Bank of England's fan chart, was built "without suggesting a degree of precision that would be spurious"; the Office for Budget Responsibility's version carries a note that its width "does not take into account the current level of uncertainty"; and the Bank's was recommended for removal in April 2024 as having "outlived their usefulness" and had gone from its reports by April 2026, replaced by named scenarios. Communicating a numerical range costs little trust; vague words cost more, and people hear "very likely" as very different numbers even with the key in front of them. "Projections are not forecasts." Nowcasting predicts the present, not the future, and its best-known failure overshot by more than double. "Leading" is a word earned by a past record of turning points, hedged "Historically" and "generally".

So the canonical truths: a comparison declares what it holds equal, and who chose the comparators; a rank is a noisy summary and position is shown within a distribution with its interval; like is compared with like by standardisation and by peers chosen by a published method; change is read against the series' own season and history, with the adjustment named as a model; after is not because, and the counterfactual earns the verb on a graded ladder; a claim about the future is a range with its assumptions, its track record and its switching value; and a market movement is an index whose base, adjustment and coverage are declared. Beneath every comparison sits a comparison record, and the line a dashboard cannot fill is written as "not done", visibly.

1 · What a comparison is

A number on its own says almost nothing; Chapter 4 showed that it is undefined until its unit, period and base are stated. A comparison is where a dashboard begins to say something — more than, less than, up, down, better, worse, because — and every one of those words rests on a claim the reader does not usually see: that the two things set side by side are alike in everything except the thing being compared. Chapter 4 called the statement of that claim the comparability declaration and gave it ten lines. This chapter is about the four comparisons a dashboard makes and what each one's declaration must contain to be true.

The four are these. Place against place: this district beside that one, this venue beside its peers, this city in a table of cities. This period against last: this month against the month before, or the same month a year ago, or the trend. Before against after: the years before a change — a licence, a fund, a festival, a road — beside the years after it, which is the comparison that most wants to say "because". And what is against what might be: the projection, the scenario, the "if this policy then that benefit", which compares a measured present with an imagined future. Each has a literature, and the literatures agree on one thing before they disagree on anything: the comparison is only as good as the thing held equal, and the thing held equal is almost never equal.

A fifth kind runs through all four — reading market movement, the indices and prices and counts that dashboards borrow from the economy's own instruments — and section 10 treats it as a discipline of its own, because an index carries a base and an adjustment that are the comparison's hidden terms.

The chapter does not decide which comparisons the Vibe Map should make. It sets out what each one may claim and what it must declare, so that when the studio and its designers choose, they choose with the method in view.

2 · Why people believe what they believe

Eight beliefs sit under most comparisons on most dashboards. Each has a reason to exist and a literature that tests it; the sections that follow give the evidence, and this section only names the beliefs so that the reader can see which ones they hold.

Belief one: a ranking is information

A list of places from best to worst looks like the most informative display there is: every place has a position, and the positions can be read at a glance. The literature on rankings finds two things against this. The ranked change to fit the rank, so that the ranking becomes partly a measure of itself; and at small differences a rank is mostly noise, so that most of the positions in the list cannot be told apart. Section 3.

Belief two: the top of the table is the best

If a ranking is information, its top is where the best place is. Chapter 6 found the first problem: small places sit at both tails because their rates swing most. This chapter finds the second: in a relative ranking a place can improve and fall, if others improved faster, and a place can rise while nothing about it changed, if the method changed. Section 3.

Belief three: like is being compared with like

Two districts, two numbers, one is higher. The comparison assumes the districts are alike in whatever drives the number apart from the thing being compared — age, size, wealth, the mix of what is there. The public-health literature has a method for this, standardisation, and a rule that goes with it: a figure standardised against a national expectation is compared with the expectation, not with another standardised figure. The official methods for choosing similar areas are published, and the one commercial model most used in local government says similarity "can be a subjective process". Section 4.

Belief four: last month is the baseline

This month against last is the simplest comparison a dashboard can make, and Chapter 6's finding was that it "tells you nothing about trends and how much the data varies naturally". This chapter adds the seasonal problem: last month may be a different season, this month against the same month last year carries last year's weather and holidays, and the adjusted series that fixes both is a model that is revised when new data arrive. Section 6.

Belief five: the trend line is the truth under the noise

A smoothed line looks like the real thing with the mess removed. It is one smoothing among several, its smoothness is a parameter someone set, it is least reliable at its most recent point, and the two official traditions disagree about whether to read turning points from it. Section 6.

Belief six: after means because

The change happened; the number moved; the change did it. The 1963 text that founded the study of quasi-experiments called this design a "bad example" and listed eight other things that could have moved the number. The designs that do better all add a comparison, and each comparison carries an assumption that cannot be tested from the data alone. Section 7 and 8.

Belief seven: a forecast is a number

"Spend will rise 12%." The official forecasters who are held to account for their numbers publish them as ranges and distributions, evaluate them against outturn every year, and in one case have abandoned their most famous uncertainty display for named scenarios. Section 9.

Belief eight: an index measures the thing it is named for

A footfall index, a price index, a leading indicator. Each is change relative to a base period someone chose, adjusted or not by a method someone chose, built from the coverage Chapter 4 warned about, and "leading" is a description of a past record. Section 10.

3 · What a ranking does

The ranked change to fit the rank

The sociological account of rankings begins with a word borrowed from methodology. Espeland and Sauder's 2007 study of law-school rankings defined reactivity as "the idea that people change their behavior in reaction to being evaluated, observed, or measured", and proposed "a framework for investigating the consequences, both intended and unintended, of public measures". Their article "first identifies two mechanisms, self‐fulfilling prophecy and commensuration, that induce reactivity". [abstract or summary only] (The dagger marks a source read at the authors' abstract or summary only, not its full text.) The body of that article was not reached; their later book, of which the first chapter is open, states the finding plainly. In the case of law-school rankings, "reactivity" refers to the fact that "the measures do not simply reflect an underlying social hierarchy but in fact play a crucial role in creating this hierarchy". "Because people are reflective and reflexive, they tend to react to being measured in unanticipated ways." "People scrutinize rankings, worry over them, invest in them, and act differently because of them, and these behaviors change the institutions that rankings evaluate." And the reason rankings in particular do this: "One reason that rankings generate such extensive change is that they override the strategies organizations normally use to manage external pressures." Commensuration, the second mechanism, is defined in Espeland and Stevens's earlier review as "the comparison of different entities according to a common metric" [abstract or summary only] — which is what any single score across places does.

Sauder and Espeland's 2009 paper, reached at its abstract, describes the mechanism from the inside: "Members' tendency to internalize these pressures, to become self-disciplining, is also salient", and "Internalization is fostered by the anxiety that rankings produce, by their allure for the administrators who try to manipulate them, and by the resistance they provoke." [abstract or summary only] Chapter 5 found, through Campbell and through Bevan and Hood, that a measure used for decisions changes what it measures. A ranking is the strongest case, because it adds position to measurement, and position is zero-sum.

A rank can fall while the place improves

The arithmetic of a relative rank is stated most plainly by the publisher of the English Indices of Deprivation, in its guidance on comparing editions. "The IMD2019 is a relative measure of deprivation. This means it can tell you if one area is more deprived than another but not by how much." "For example, a small area with a rank of 1,000 is not half as deprived as a place with a rank of 500." And on change over time: "it would not necessarily be correct to state that the level of deprivation in the area has increased on some absolute scale … as it may be the case that all areas had improved, but that this area had improved more slowly than other areas and so had been 'overtaken' by those areas." A rank is a position in a field that moves. The reader who sees a place fall three positions does not know whether the place got worse.

The field's largest recent case is the World Bank's Doing Business index, discontinued on 16 September 2021 after "data irregularities on Doing Business 2018 and 2020 were reported internally in June 2020". The external panel that reviewed it (the External Panel Review, or EPR) — six economists, chaired by Mauricio Cárdenas — made eleven recommendations, of which the one this chapter needs is a heading: "Remove the aggregate index and country rankings". Their reasons: "Doing Business covers a diverse array of indicators that often have little meaning when aggregated with arbitrary weights" (Chapter 5's finding, in an audit), and "Publishing the indicators to enable further analysis elevates the level of global policy dialog; aggregating them and ranking countries lowers it, and invites the type of external interference and conflicts of interest witnessed in recent years". Summarising two earlier reviews of the index, from 2008 and 2013, the panel also records the arithmetic of a rank among bunched scores: "Small changes in actual regulation can produce large swings in rankings, given bunching of scores in the middle of the distribution." A 2018 blog by two authors, one of them a later panel member, had shown a country's rank moving "all due to methodological tinkering and almost no underlying changes in Chile's actual laws or policies". The successor, Business Ready, "does not present an aggregate score by economy"; its FAQ never uses the word "rank"; and it presents economies "into five groups of equal size (quintiles), from highest to lowest performers" within each pillar. The league table went; the ordering, in equal-sized bands, stayed. A display can drop the number and keep the hierarchy, and a quintile band is a rank with fewer rows. The distinction this chapter will draw in section 5 is between bands of that kind — an ordering cut into equal shares — and categories set by statistical separation from an expectation ("higher", "lower", "similar"; "alert", "alarm"), which say how far a place is from what would be expected of it and nothing about its position among the others.

A rank is a noisy summary

The statistical case was made to the Royal Statistical Society in 1996, by Goldstein and Spiegelhalter, in a paper on league tables of schools and hospitals whose typescript is open. Its argument is for intervals: "although such ranks are particularly sensitive to sampling variability, there has been no straightforward way to place interval estimates around those ranks". When intervals are placed, the result in their worked example of 325 schools is that "about two thirds of all possible comparisons do not allow separation".
