Calibration asks whether the things you called 70% likely happened about 70% of the time; sharpness asks whether you said anything — a band wide enough to be always right is perfectly calibrated and useless. The Brier score puts a number on a probability forecast's error: "The Brier score is the squared error of a probabilistic forecast", with a worked example from the forecasting tournament's own guide — a 70% forecast of an event that happened scores (1 − 0.7)² + (0 − 0.3)² = 0.18 [read once]. The verification literature's caution: the score is "Sensitive to climatological frequency of the event: the more rare an event, the easier it is to get a good BS without having any real skill." A dashboard that makes projections can keep the score the forecasters keep — and the OBR's annual evaluation shows what keeping it looks like.

Scenarios are not forecasts

The Government Office for Science draws the line the Bank of England moved toward. "Futures thinking contrasts with forecasting, and forecasting models." "Most forecasting models look at historical trends and, with various degrees of sophistication, attempt to project them forward", and their reliability "starts to break down over the longer term". "Scenarios are compelling stories about a range of different possible futures." "Scenarios are not predictions; they are neither good nor bad, wrong nor right." "No single future scenario will come true, but it is likely that parts of different futures will." The cross-government uncertainty toolkit adds three display rules in official words: "Presenting a single figure is best avoided as it can give a misleading impression of precision"; "Front load the important caveats and explain why they matter"; and "Try to include an even number of scenarios, to avoid having a middle option that may be misinterpreted as the 'most likely' scenario." The ONS's standing caveat on its projections is the label: "Projections are not forecasts and will differ from actual future outcomes to a greater or lesser extent." "These are based on assumptions of future levels of births, deaths, and migration." And the Code of Practice for Statistics makes the rule statutory for producers: they "must prominently explain the quality of the statistics, including strengths and limitations, and communicate the uncertainty in estimates", "by using qualifying words, numbers or graphics"; and, in its standards for public bodies, "Do not use statistics, data or wider analysis in a misleading way. This includes not cherry-picking figures, taking figures out of context or placing undue certainty on them."

A projection on a dashboard, then, has a known form. It is labelled a projection and not a forecast; its assumptions are stated first; it is a central estimate with a range, or an even number of scenarios with what they do not cover; its switching value is given; the body's own record of projection against outturn is kept and shown; the words for likelihood carry their numbers in the sentence; and it is adjusted, in advance, for the demonstrated tendency of the people who made it to be optimistic.

10 · Reading market movement

A dashboard that shows how a district's economy is moving borrows the economy's own instruments — indices, counts, prices, search interest, transactions — and each carries terms that the comparison depends on. This section collects the disciplines for reading them.

Nowcasting predicts the present

Search and transaction data arrive before official statistics, and the method that uses them has a modest founding claim. Choi and Varian: "We are not claiming that Google Trends data can help in predicting the future. Rather we are claiming that Google Trends may help in predicting the present." "Predicting the present, in the sense described above, is a form of 'contemporaneous forecasting' or 'nowcasting'". Their result: simple seasonal models with search terms "tend to outperform models that exclude these predictors by 5% to 20%", and "It is well-known that it is difficult to identify 'turning points' in economic series" [read once]. The best-known failure is Google Flu Trends, which — in Lazer and colleagues' account, itself reporting Nature — "was predicting more than double the proportion of doctor visits for influenza-like illness (ILI) than the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)", "despite the fact that GFT was built to predict CDC reports"; the authors' phrases for why ("big data hubris"; "algorithm dynamics") are not quoted here. The ONS's own fast-indicator programme states its boundary in its own words: the indicators "allow early identification of large economic changes" at "a level of timeliness and granularity not currently possible with official economic statistics", but "we are not attempting to forecast or predict gross domestic product (GDP) or other headline economic statistics here", "none should be used to predict GDP on their own", and "they should be considered early warning indicators providing timely insight into real activities in the economy, and their potential impact on headline GDP should be carefully interpreted." Chapter 6's footfall and card-spend caveats are the same producer saying the same thing of the same kind of data. A fast series on a dashboard is an early sighting of the present, with Chapter 4's coverage caveat, and never a forecast.

"Leading" is a past record

Chapter 6 found that "leading" is measured, not declared, and the producer of the oldest leading index says how. The Conference Board's indexes "are summary statistics for the U.S. economy"; "Historically, the cyclical turning points in the leading index have occurred before those in aggregate economic activity", those of the coincident index "at about the same time", and those of the lagging index "generally … after". A series earns a place by conformity — "the series must conform well to the business cycle" — and consistent timing — "the series must exhibit a consistent timing pattern over time as a leading, coincident or lagging indicator" — and by smoothness and currency. Its own handbook warns against reading it the way dashboards read everything: "if economists took every one- or two-month decline in the index seriously, they would be forecasting a recession several times each year"; "never rely on individual data series or simple rules". And it admits that the published record flatters: although the present version of the leading index has a good historical record, "the index that actually existed at those points in time rarely provided adequate signals of the impending downturns" — a signed article within the handbook, so its author's words — and "peaks (or even troughs, for that matter) cannot always be recognized until months after they occur, especially during periods when the data are subject to significant revision" [read once]. "Historically" and "generally" are the hedges in the definition itself. A series shown as leading a district's economy either has a measured record of turning points against a named reference series, or carries the word as a label.

Indices, concentration and churn

Section 6 gave the index rules — change relative to an arbitrary base, points that are not percentages, cash that is not volume — and they apply doubly to borrowed indices, whose base, adjustment and coverage the dashboard did not set. Two further measures appear on dashboards of a local economy. Concentration: the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index "is defined as the sum of the squares of the market shares; it is small when there are many small firms and grows larger as the market becomes more concentrated, reaching 10,000 in a market with a single firm." The thresholds are American — "Markets with an HHI greater than 1,800 are highly concentrated, and a change of more than 100 points is a significant increase" — and the UK's competition authority applies none: "The CMA does not apply any thresholds to market share, number of remaining competitors or on any other measure to determine whether a loss of competition is substantial", while naming the index among possible measures. A "highly concentrated" label on a UK display has borrowed a foreign threshold, and should say so. Churn: no official UK definition was found; the ONS business demography bulletin uses births ("New business registrations … are referred to as business births"), deaths ("Businesses that have ceased to trade (identified through de-registration of the administrative units)"), and the rates of each "as a proportion of the active businesses", with Chapter 6's caveat that the latest two years are provisional. A churn figure is a construction from those, and its recipe is Chapter 5's.

Two biases in a rising line

Survivorship bias, in Wikipedia's wording, marked as secondary: "a statistical error that results from concentrating on entities that passed a selection process while overlooking those that did not", which "often causes study results to skew higher because only companies that were successful enough to survive until the end of the period are included". A dashboard of venues' average attendance over five years, computed over the venues that still exist, has excluded every venue that closed, and the line rises for that reason among others. And the base effect of section 6, which for a market series read year-on-year is the commonest reason a rate moves when nothing has: last year's spike becomes this year's fall.

What reading market movement gives the chapter is a short list of terms every borrowed series must carry on the face: its base period and whether it has been rebased; whether it is adjusted, and by whom; whether it is cash or real; whose transactions or searches it counts; whether it is a nowcast of the present or a projection of the future; whether "leading" has a measured record; which firms or venues are still in it; and what happened in the base month. Each is a line in the comparison record that section 11 sets out.

11 · What holds true regardless

Seven truths this chapter will defend, each carrying what Chapter 0 calls its kind, and the record beneath them.

One. A comparison is a claim about what is held equal, and the holding is declared — including who chose the comparators. Place against place, period against period, before against after, present against possible: each asserts that two things are alike in all but the thing compared. Chapter 4 asked for the declaration; this chapter adds that the comparators' selection is part of it, because a comparison set chosen by the compared is a different claim from one chosen by a published method. Kind: Standard (the official peer methods; the Code of Practice); the "who chose" line is a Nightlife Culture position, Fixed (sequence).

Two. A rank is a noisy summary that changes what it ranks; position is shown within a distribution, with its interval, and most pairs cannot be separated. The ranked change to fit the rank; a rank can fall while the place improves; in the standard worked example two-thirds of pairwise comparisons cannot be told apart; small units sit at both ends; ranks of a few large units can survive their intervals and ranks of many small places do not; a successor index that dropped the rank kept the bands. The display that shows the finding without the ordering is the funnel, or the distribution with the place marked and its interval drawn, with categories of separation and not of position. Kind: Evidence (Espeland & Sauder; Goldstein & Spiegelhalter; Marshall & Spiegelhalter; Mogstad et al.; the EPR) + Standard (SHMI; RSS); the extension of the ban to every measure on a dashboard of small places is a Reading, Fixed (requirement).

Three. Like is compared with like by standardisation and by peers chosen by a published method; an observed-to-expected ratio is compared with the expectation, not ranked. Standardisation produces an expected figure for each place given what drives the number; the ratio to it answers "how does this place compare with what would be expected", and two such ratios are not, in general, comparable with each other. Peers come from a fixed number, a stated distance and a stated assumption, with a label for how like each is; self-chosen peers are shown beside them and kept as data. Kind: Standard (APHO; ONS; DfE); Evidence (adjacent domain) for self-selection; Nightlife Culture for showing the chosen beside the published.

Four. Change over time is read against the series' own season and history, and the adjustment is named as a model that is revised. A trend line is a smoothing someone chose; a seasonally adjusted figure is an estimate revised when the next month arrives, impossible under three years, and able to manufacture a season; the same month last year is slow at turning points and carries the base month; the latest smoothed point is the least reliable; an index is change from an arbitrary base and its points are not percentages; a money series is cash until deflated; regression to the mean is the first explanation for a change in a place selected for being extreme; and no number of observations makes a trend readable except the one the series' own noise allows. Kind: Standard (ONS; Eurostat; Census Bureau; ABS; the Code of Practice) + Evidence (regression to the mean) + Practice (the forecasting textbook).

Five. After is not because; the counterfactual earns the verb, and its credibility is graded on a published ladder. The one-group before-and-after is a "bad example" with eight named rivals. Each design that does better adds a comparison with an assumption that cannot be tested from the data: a pre-trend projected (interrupted series), a parallel trend (difference-in-differences), a weighted blend (synthetic control), a cut-off, a match. Each has stated requirements, a size below which it shows nothing, and a rung on a ladder on which plain before/after is the bottom and the floor for counting is a comparison group; each rung has its verb, from after through departed from its trend and contributed to to caused. Spillover and displacement are the assumption every design shares and the ripple a place most needs to see. Kind: Evidence (Campbell & Stanley; Bernal; Abadie; Goodman-Bacon; Roth) + Standard (Magenta Book 2026; the SMS; EEF) + Practice (Nesta); the verbs are a Nightlife Culture reading of the ladders.

Six. A claim about the future is a range with its assumptions, its track record and its switching value; scenarios are not forecasts, and the words for likelihood carry their numbers. Optimism bias is adjusted for in advance, by the maker's own record of projection against outturn; the central estimate has a range and the conclusion a switching value; scenarios come in an even number with what they do not cover; a projection is labelled one; the record of projection against outturn is kept and shown; and a numerical range costs little stated trust where a vague word costs more and is heard differently by every reader. Kind: Standard (Green Book 2026; Code of Practice 3.0; the Futures Toolkit; the Uncertainty Toolkit) + Evidence (van der Bles; Wintle; the OBR's record; Bernanke's review).

Seven. A market movement is an index whose base, adjustment, coverage and survivors are declared, and "leading" is a past record. A borrowed series carries terms the dashboard did not set; a nowcast predicts the present and not the future; a leading indicator is defined by a history of turning points, hedged "Historically" and "generally", that looked worse in real time than in the published record; a concentration threshold on a UK display is borrowed from abroad; and a rising average over survivors has excluded the fallen. Kind: Standard (ONS; BLS; the Conference Board; the CMA) + Evidence (Choi & Varian; Lazer et al.) ; Reading for the survivorship line.

The record beneath them

Chapter 4 asked for a provenance set beneath every number, Chapter 5 for a recipe card beneath every measure, and Chapter 6 for a claim record beneath every statement of value. This chapter asks for a comparison record beneath every comparison — the lines that let a reader see what was held equal and by whom. Ten lines, as a floor; the first is Chapter 4's declaration and the rest are this chapter's.

  1. What is held equal — Chapter 4's ten-line comparability declaration for the indicator: same definition, unit, period, base, source, coverage, revision status; and, for a borrowed series, cash or real, who is still in it, and any breaks or vintages.
  2. The comparators, who chose them, and why this place — the places or periods compared; the published method, its distance and its fixed number; or "chosen by the place", labelled; and whether the place was selected for the comparison because its figure was extreme.
  3. The standardisation — what the figure has been adjusted for (size, age, mix), against what expectation; or "crude", stated.
  4. The order on the display — whether the display sorts the places, by what, and whether the sort is a reading aid or the finding.
  5. The interval — the uncertainty on each place's figure, and whether the places can be separated; the funnel's limits, if a funnel.
  6. The season and the smoothing — raw, seasonally adjusted (by what method, revised when, series length) or trend-cycle (what window); and whether the latest point is an end-point estimate.
  7. The base month, and the record — for any year-on-year figure, what happened twelve months earlier; for any series called "leading", its measured record of turning points against a named reference series.
  8. The design, and its assumption — for any before/after: none (Design 2, with the eight rivals listed), interrupted series (impact model chosen when), difference-in-differences (comparison group; pre-trend check; adoption timing), synthetic control (weights; placebos run), cut-off, match; and the rung on the ladder.
  9. The ripple — spillover and displacement considered; the neighbour used as a control, and whether it was reached.
  10. The future's terms — for any projection: the label; the assumptions; the central estimate and range; the switching value; the number of scenarios; the optimism-bias adjustment and its source; the record of past projections against outturn.

A filled record, for an imagined comparison, so that the shape is clear. The comparison: District A's venue closures per hundred venues were 9 last year; the city average was 5. (1) Closures and venue stock from the same register, same twelve months, same definition of "active"; the register's deaths are provisional for two years. (2) The city's twenty-three districts; the comparison is with all of them, not with chosen peers; the nearest-neighbour set by the ONS method would be five named districts, not yet used. (3) Crude — not standardised for venue size, age of stock or type; a district of late-licensed venues is compared with one of cafés. (4) The display sorts districts by rate; the sort is the finding as shown, which is the thing this chapter forbids; the funnel is not yet drawn. (5) District A has thirty-four venues; three closures; the exact binomial interval on 9 per hundred runs from about 2 to about 24, and overlaps the city average. (6) Raw annual count; no season; the series is two years long and cannot be adjusted. (7) Not applicable to an annual rate; the previous year's rate was 3, and the district was chosen for attention because this year's was the highest. (8) No design; no claim of cause is made; if one were, it would be Design 2 with history (a rent review), instrumentation (the register's revision) and regression to the mean (chosen because extreme) among its rivals. (9) Two of the three closures reopened under new names in the neighbouring district; displacement, not loss, is a live reading. (10) No projection. Seven of the ten lines change what the number means, and the comparison as first shown — a sorted bar chart with District A at the top — would have been read as a finding about District A.

12 · Where the choice is yours

The truths fix the questions. These are the answers the chapter leaves open, because the evidence does not settle them or because they belong to the people who will live with the display.

Which peer method, and how many peers. Twenty by Euclidean distance on standardised variables, as the ONS does; ten by weighted distance with closeness labels, as the DfE does; or the studio's own set of variables, documented to the same standard. The literature settles that the method is published and fixed, not which it is. The variables are a judgement about what makes two scenes alike, and that judgement is the studio's and the scene's.

Whether, and against what, to standardise. Standardisation needs the drivers measured; for a scene the drivers (size, mix, hours, tenure) are partly the thing being compared. The choice between a crude rate with a wide caveat and a standardised ratio against a declared expectation is a choice about which misreading is worse.

How the display orders. A funnel sorted by size; a distribution with the place marked; a peer set in closeness order; an unsorted small multiple. All satisfy the rule; which one a first-time reader reads correctly is a thing to test, and the partial-order "incomparable" state most of all.

The smoothing window, and whether to show the latest smoothed point. The textbook says the window is the user's; Eurostat says the end-point should be withheld or warned. Either, declared.

Which growth rate to lead with. Month-on-month on the adjusted series when there is one; year-on-year with the base month shown when there is not; three-month on three-month as the ONS's own compromise. Each answers a different question; what is fixed is that the display says which and shows both ends of a year-on-year figure; which leads is the choice.

Which design, when a cause is wanted. The ladder orders them; the place's circumstances — one treated place or several, adoption at once or staggered, a cut-off or none, a long pre-period or a short one — choose among them. The Magenta Book's own feasibility table is the decision aid.

How much to adjust for optimism, and how many scenarios. The generic uplifts for costs and durations until the studio has a record, a declared judgement for benefits; the record thereafter. The cross-government toolkit says an even number of scenarios and the Bank of England shows a baseline with two; this chapter takes the toolkit's rule as the default and says so; which futures matter to the reader is the judgement.

Whether to show a projection at all. A dashboard of evidence may decide that the future is the reader's to imagine from the past the dashboard shows, and that any line drawn forward is a claim it would rather not make. That is a legitimate answer to section 9, and it is the studio's.

13 · An illustration from nightlife — method only

The same district as Chapter 6's: a reputation, a council hearing both asset and nuisance, a landowner assembling sites. This time the questions are comparative. Is this district doing better or worse than others? Is it getting better or worse? Did the licensing change two years ago do anything? What happens if the council does the thing it is considering? What follows is the method's walk through those four questions, and nothing about the answers.

Better or worse than others. The dashboard does not rank the city's districts on anything. For each rate it shows every district against its size — a funnel or an equivalent — with limits the data set and this district marked; or it shows the distribution with this district's position and its interval, and says whether the district can be separated from the average. The peers it compares against come from the published method, in a number that fits a field of this size, each with a label for how near; if the district's own people would choose different peers, those are shown beside, marked as chosen, and the choice is kept. Where the measure is a rate that depends on what kind of venues the district has, the dashboard either standardises against a declared expectation and compares the district with the expectation, or shows the crude rate with the reason it is crude. Where each of two districts exceeds the other on different measures, the display says they cannot be ordered. Identity measures — what the district sounds like, when its week peaks, who comes — are never on an ordered axis.

Better or worse than it was. The district's series are shown raw, with the season visible, until they are long enough to adjust — the official floor is three years — and are adjusted only if they are seasonal, by a named method, with the note that the adjusted history may change when the next month arrives. The trend line, when drawn, names its window and does not reach the last point, or reaches it with a warning. Year-on-year figures show both ends: this month, and what happened in the same month last year. Index series name their base and are read in per cent, not points; money series say cash or real. When a measure has moved for the better in a district that was chosen for attention because it had moved for the worse, regression to the mean is named beside it as the first explanation. No line is called a trend until the series' own noise allows it, and the dashboard says how long that is.

Whether the licensing change did anything. The before-and-after series across the change is shown with its eight rivals listed beside it — what else happened in the district that year, what was already changing, whether the register changed how it counted, whether the district was chosen because it was extreme — and no verb stronger than "after". If the studio wants more, the display is an interrupted series: the pre-trend drawn forward as the expectation, the shape of the expected effect recorded before the after-data were looked at, the co-interventions named, and a control series — a district with no change, or an outcome the change should not have touched — beside it. If several districts changed their licensing at different dates, the effect is shown by adoption group, never as one pooled number. If the studio wants the strongest claim a single district can carry, it builds the synthetic district — a named blend of other districts, weights on the face — checks that the blend tracked this district for years before the change, runs the placebos in time and in space, and shows the gap against the gaps the method finds where nothing happened. In every case the display says where it sits on the ladder, whether the neighbouring districts were reached by the change, and whether the effect is large enough, in a series this noisy, to be seen at all.

What happens if the council acts. If the dashboard shows a projection, it is labelled a projection; its assumptions come before its numbers; it is a central estimate with a range, or an even number of scenarios with a line saying what they do not cover; the value at which the conclusion flips is stated; the words "likely" and "unlikely" carry their numbers in the sentence; and the figure has been adjusted, in advance, for the known tendency of projections to be optimistic — by a declared adjustment, because the studio has no record yet, and with a note that the record starts now. If the dashboard shows no projection, it says why: that it shows what has happened and leaves what might to the reader.

What the dashboard has not done, at the end of the walk, is say whether the district is better than its neighbours, improving, helped by the licensing change, or wise to do what the council proposes. It has shown each comparison with what it held equal, who chose the comparators, what the interval is, which season and smoothing were applied, which design and which assumption, which ripples were considered, and what the future's terms are. The judgement is the reader's. The method's job was to make the comparison one the reader could trust.

The rules

Kind and tier as in Chapter 0. "Adjacent domain" marks evidence or standards from public health, education, economics, central banking, climate science, intelligence analysis or official statistics rather than cultural display.

Rule Why Kind Tier Source
Every comparison carries the comparison record: what is held equal, who chose the comparators, the standardisation, the order, the interval, the season, the base month, the design, the ripple, the future's terms; a line that cannot be filled says "not done" A comparison is a claim that two things are alike in all but one respect; the claim is shown or it is assumed Standard behind each line; Nightlife Culture for the record as a whole Fixed (sequence) · the lines' content: Adaptable This chapter §11; Chapter 4
No league table of places on any measure, and no bands of position (quintiles and the like); position is shown within a distribution with its interval, in categories of statistical separation from an expectation if categories are needed Rankings "play a crucial role in creating this hierarchy"; "about two thirds of all possible comparisons do not allow separation"; "Remove the aggregate index and country rankings"; ranks of many small units do not survive their intervals, where ranks of a few large ones can Evidence + Standard; the extension to every measure on a dashboard of small places is a Reading Fixed (requirement) Espeland & Sauder[abstract or summary only]; Goldstein & Spiegelhalter 1996; Marshall & Spiegelhalter 1998; Mogstad et al.[abstract or summary only]; EPR 2021; SHMI; RSS 2005 (supports the interval, not the prohibition, which stands on the house's grounds and the EPR)
Where a single place's rank must be stated (a reader asks "where do we stand?"), it is given as a range, and a small unit's rank on a rate is not stated at all "ranks are extremely unreliable statistical summaries … particularly for smaller institutions"; about one city in five has a rank interval of ±3 or more under modelling choices alone Evidence Fixed Marshall & Spiegelhalter; JRC C3 2017/2019; Chapter 5; Chapter 6
Compare places on a funnel or against a declared expectation, never by sorted value alone; where a display is sorted, the sort is a reading aid and the finding is position against limits "avoid spurious ranking of institutions into 'league tables'"; "Always rank bars by value" is a readability rule Evidence + Standard (adjacent domain); Practice Fixed (the principle); Adaptable (the form) Spiegelhalter 2005[abstract or summary only]; APHO 2007; PHE 2017; Analysis Function 2022
State and handle over-dispersion before reading points outside a funnel "could lead to a large number of institutions being inappropriately classified as 'abnormal'" Evidence (adjacent domain) Fixed (requirement) Spiegelhalter 2005b[abstract or summary only]; APHO 2007
Standardise for the drivers of a rate before comparing places, or state that the rate is crude and why Equal crude rates in populations of different structure mean unequal performance Standard (adjacent domain) Fixed (declared); Adaptable (whether) APHO 2008; ONS mortality guide
An observed-to-expected ratio is compared with the expectation, and with other ratios only under the two conditions the method names; it is not ranked "should only be directly compared to each other if the age structures … are similar to the standard, or if the ratio of their age-specific … rates to that of the standard is consistent across the age groups"; "It is inappropriate to rank trusts according to their SHMI" Standard (adjacent domain) Fixed APHO 2008; NHS England SHMI
Peers are chosen by a published method with a stated distance, a fixed number appropriate to the field, and a stated assumption, applied to every place alike before any comparison; each carries a label for how like it is ONS 20 by Euclidean distance; DfE 10 with closeness bands; "It was assumed that local authorities with similar characteristics would perform or progress at a similar rate" Standard + Practice (CIPFA) Fixed (requirement) ONS 2025/2026; DfE 2025; CIPFA
Self-chosen comparators are shown beside the published set, labelled as chosen, and the choice is kept as data; they never define the comparison alone "peer groups are constructed in a manner that biases compensation upward, particularly in firms outside the … S&P 500"; "Preliminary evidence suggests that increased disclosure has reduced the biases" Evidence (adjacent domain, abstract)[abstract or summary only] + Nightlife Culture Adaptable (house default) Faulkender & Yang 2010; Bizjak et al. 2011[abstract or summary only]; version 1 Ch 5
Where each of two places exceeds the other on different measures, say they cannot be ordered "The evidence of conflicts is smashed out by aggregation methods to obtain a single quantity, which allows a ranking" Evidence + Reading Adaptable (house default) Carlsen & Bruggemann 2022; Fattore 2016[abstract or summary only]
Identity measures — those the studio designates nominal, and says so — are never on an ordered axis; condition measures are compared through the gate, which now includes interval, standardisation and order Version 1's split, extended and its examples corrected by this chapter Nightlife Culture (tested) Fixed (requirement) Version 1 Ch 5
Name every trend line's method and window; show no end-point of a trend-cycle without a warning "The smoothness of the trend-cycle can also be controlled by the user"; "the most recent values should not be shown because of the end-point problem" Practice (textbook) + Standard Fixed FPP3 §3; Eurostat 2015 §7.2
Mark seasonally adjusted figures as estimates subject to revision, name the method, and adjust no series under three years "seasonal factors are estimates based on present and past experience"; "just one additional observation results in revisions … for several years"; "Very short series (less than 3 years) cannot be seasonally adjusted" Standard Fixed US Census Bureau; Eurostat 2015 §4.1, §6.1; ONS
Do not seasonally adjust a series that is not seasonal "will often introduce an artificial seasonal element" Standard (adjacent domain) Fixed ABS 2023; Eurostat 2015
A year-on-year figure shows both ends; a period-on-period figure uses the adjusted series; the display says which growth rate it leads with and why "does not completely remove all seasonal effects"; the base effect; "Monthly growth should therefore be used with caution and alongside other measures" Standard Fixed (both ends; say which); Adaptable (which leads) ABS; Eurostat §7.2; ECB 2007; ONS retail bulletin
Percentage points are not per cent; index points are not per cent; cash is not volume; an index names its base "A fall of 1% would result in a value of 9.9%"; "index value changes are affected by the level of the index in relation to its base period"; "value data are deflated to produce … volume measures" Standard Fixed ONS style guide; BLS; ONS RSI QMI; HMT deflators guide
Before any change in a place selected for being extreme is read, regression to the mean is named as the first explanation "should always be considered as a possible cause of an observed change"; "Even if subjects are not treated the mean … will go down" Evidence (adjacent domain) Fixed Barnett et al. 2005[abstract or summary only]; Bland & Altman 1994
Every series carries its breaks and its revision status; a consistent back series is provided or its absence stated "Explain the nature and extent of the change, and provide a consistent back series where possible" Standard Fixed Code of Practice 3.0 §7.5, §3.9; ONS revisions policy
Describe a change by direction, absolute size and relative size; call a change within random variation indicative, not definitive; never caveat with "care must be taken" alone The Analysis Function's own rules Standard Fixed Analysis Function 2018
Do not use "significant" of a change unless making a point about statistical significance ONS style Standard Fixed ONS style guide; Chapter 6
No fixed number of observations is claimed as enough for a trend; the series' length and noise are stated and what they support "These are misleading and unsubstantiated in theory or practice" Practice (textbook) Adaptable (house default) FPP3 §13.7; Hyndman & Kostenko 2007
A before-and-after display lists its eight rivals and uses no verb stronger than "after"; an interrupted series with its impact model declared may say "departed from its trend" Design 2 is "a 'bad example'"; history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, regression, selection, mortality, interaction Evidence; the verbs are a Nightlife Culture reading Fixed Campbell & Stanley 1963; Bernal et al. 2017
An interrupted-series claim records its impact model before the after-data are examined, lists co-interventions, handles season and autocorrelation, and carries a control where one exists "the essential, yet often omitted, step of proposing the impact model a priori"; "cannot exclude confounding due to co-interventions" Evidence (adjacent domain) Fixed (sequence) · form of the impact model and controls: Adaptable Bernal et al. 2017; Lopez Bernal et al. 2018; Magenta Annex A
A difference-in-differences claim names its comparison group, shows its pre-trend check as a check and not a proof, and reports effects by adoption group when adoption is staggered "cannot be tested because it involves a non-existent counterfactual"; "'Passing' these tests does not mean that parallel trends is true"; already-treated units "can serve as controls" Evidence Fixed (requirement) Cunningham; Huntington-Klein; Roth 2022; Goodman-Bacon 2021; Callaway & Sant'Anna
A synthetic-control claim shows its weights, its pre-period fit, and its placebos in time and in space, and checks the six contextual requirements and the pre-period "preclude extrapolation"; "make explicit the contribution of each comparison unit"; "small effects will be indistinguishable from other shocks" Evidence Fixed (requirement) Abadie, Diamond & Hainmueller 2010, 2015; Abadie 2021
A cut-off claim speaks for those near the cut-off, and a matched claim for what was recorded "local average treatment effect"; "only as good as the characteristics used for matching" Standard + Evidence Fixed Magenta Annex A; Lee & Lemieux 2010; DIME
Every intervention claim states whether spillover and displacement were considered, and whether the comparison place was reached by the ripple "Assuming that such spillover effects do not exist is a strong restriction"; "tells us very little if that activity is simply displaced from elsewhere" Standard + Evidence Fixed Magenta Book 2026 §2.3.2; Abadie 2021; What Works Growth
Before an effect is called absent, the minimum detectable effect for the series and the number of places is stated, by a power calculation whose inputs are declared "the effect size below which we may not be able to distinguish that the effect is different from zero, even if it is"; "Sample sizes are too small" Practice (J-PAL; DIME) + Standard (EEF; Magenta Book) Fixed (requirement) J-PAL; DIME; EEF 2019; Magenta Book 2026
Every intervention claim states its rung on the What Works scale, with any other ladder's differing placement beside it, and the verb that rung earns; plain before/after and place-against-place are the bottom "We define SMS 3 methods to be the minimum standard"; "No comparator" scores zero; "it will not evidence direct causality" Standard (SMS; EEF) + Practice (Nesta) Fixed What Works Growth SMS; EEF 2019; Nesta 2013
A projection is labelled a projection, states its assumptions first, gives a central estimate with a range, states its switching value, and has been adjusted for optimism bias by the maker's own record or the generic uplift "Projections are not forecasts"; "Practitioners must account for optimism bias"; "A switching value is the value that a key variable would need to change to such that an option stops representing value for money" Standard Fixed ONS NPP 2025; Green Book 2026; HMT optimism-bias guidance
Scenarios say what they do not cover, and a single future figure is not shown; the default is an even number of scenarios, taken from the cross-government toolkit over the Bank's baseline-plus-two "Try to include an even number of scenarios"; "Presenting a single figure is best avoided"; "neither all-encompassing nor do they reflect the full distribution of risks" Standard + Practice Fixed (requirement: no single figure; say what is omitted) · the number of scenarios (even by default): Adaptable (house default) Uncertainty Toolkit; Bank of England 2026; Futures Toolkit
Keep and show the record of projections against outturn "examines how our forecasts compare to subsequent outturn data"; the Green Book's own-record adjustment Standard + Practice Fixed (requirement) OBR FER; Green Book 2026
Words for likelihood carry their numbers in the sentence; no verbal likelihood term stands without one "substantially improved only when numerical guidelines are bracketed in text"; "only a small decrease in trust … mostly for verbal uncertainty communication" Evidence Fixed Wintle et al. 2019; van der Bles et al. 2020; IPCC 2010
A fast or nowcast series is labelled an early sighting of the present, never a forecast "predicting the present"; "none should be used to predict GDP on their own" Evidence + Standard Fixed Choi & Varian; ONS Data Science Campus; Lazer et al.
"Leading" is used only of a series with a measured record of turning points against a named reference series — the Conference Board's tests of conformity and consistent timing, or an equivalent stated one — and the record's real-time weakness is noted "Historically, the cyclical turning points in the leading index have occurred before"; "rarely provided adequate signals" in real time Standard + Evidence Fixed (requirement) · which test, if stated: Adaptable Conference Board; Chapter 6
A borrowed concentration threshold names its jurisdiction; a churn figure publishes its recipe; an average over survivors says who left HHI thresholds are American and the CMA applies none; no official churn; survivorship Standard + Reading Adaptable (house default) DOJ/FTC 2023; CMA 2026; ONS business demography

What proves a break works

The test for breaking a comparison rule is the same as the earlier chapters': give the comparison and what accompanies it to someone who was not in the room and ask four questions — what is being held equal, who chose the comparators, could these two be told apart, and what else could have moved the line? If the answers come from the face and one tap, the break has cost nothing. For the ranking rule the test is adversarial: crop the display as a hostile reader would, and see whether what survives is a league table; if it is, the rule was carrying weight. For the projection rules the test is later and arithmetical: a year on, compare the projection with the outturn and see whether the range held and whether the switching value was crossed. Log the break in the deviation entry Chapter 16 describes.

What this chapter could not settle

  • The comparison literature's founding article (Espeland & Sauder 2007) and the funnel plot's founding paper (Spiegelhalter 2005) were read at abstract only; the chapter used the authors' open book chapter and the official technical briefings that implement the funnel, and marks the canon [abstract or summary only].
  • The Analysis Function's chart standard ("Always rank bars by value") and the statistical guidance ("inappropriate to rank") pull against each other with no reconciliation in either; reconciled here through the funnel: order as a reading aid, position against limits as the finding.
  • The two official traditions disagree on reading turning points (textbook: from the trend-cycle; Eurostat: withhold the end-point); both are shown, with the rule that the end-point carries a warning.
  • No official rule on percentage change from a small base, on minimum series length (ONS), or on pre-specifying comparator groups in the public sector; the chapter says so and uses the nearest official wording.
  • The Decision Book has no rules on rankings, standardisation, peers, seasonal adjustment, regression to the mean, the designs, spillovers, power, the ladders, or projections; this chapter's rules table is the candidate chapter on comparison.
  • Lee & Lemieux dispute the "only at the threshold" limitation that the Magenta Annex states as fact; both are shown.

Checklist

  • The comparison record exists beneath every comparison; unfilled lines say "not done"
  • No league table and no bands of position; position shown within a distribution with its interval, in categories of separation if any
  • Any stated rank is a range; small units not ranked on rates
  • Funnel or declared expectation; any sort is a reading aid
  • Over-dispersion stated and handled
  • Standardised, or crude with the reason
  • Observed-to-expected ratios compared with the expectation, not with each other
  • Peers by a published method: distance, fixed number, assumption, closeness label
  • Self-chosen peers shown beside, labelled, and kept as data
  • Incomparable places said to be incomparable
  • Identity never ordered; conditions through the extended gate
  • Trend lines name method and window; no bare end-point
  • Adjusted figures marked as revisable estimates; method named; nothing under three years adjusted
  • Non-seasonal series not adjusted
  • Year-on-year shows both ends; period-on-period on the adjusted series; the display says which rate leads
  • Points, per cent, cash and volume kept apart; index base named
  • Regression to the mean named first for any extreme-selected change
  • Breaks and revision status on every series; back series or its absence stated
  • Change described by direction, absolute and relative size; "indicative" within random variation; no empty caveats
  • "Significant" used only statistically
  • Series length and noise stated; no magic number
  • Before/after lists the eight rivals; verb no stronger than "after"
  • Interrupted series: impact model recorded first; co-interventions; season and autocorrelation; control; verb "departed from its trend"
  • Difference-in-differences: comparison group named; pre-trend check as a check; by adoption group when staggered
  • Synthetic control: weights, pre-period fit, placebos in time and space, six requirements
  • Cut-off and matched claims scoped to what they can speak for
  • Spillover and displacement considered; contaminated controls named
  • Minimum detectable effect stated before any "no effect"
  • Rung on the What Works scale stated, with any differing placement, and the verb it earns
  • Projections labelled, assumptions first, central and range, switching value, optimism adjustment and its source
  • Even number of scenarios with what they omit; no single future figure
  • Record of projection against outturn kept and shown
  • Likelihood words carry numbers in the sentence; no likelihood term without one
  • Nowcasts labelled as the present
  • "Leading" only with a measured record against a named reference series; real-time weakness noted
  • Borrowed thresholds name their jurisdiction; churn recipes published; survivors' averages say who left

08Automation without admin

Freshness is a declared lifetime; a dashboard is a service; the phone sets the budget; a map is a licence, a supply and a vintage.

Dashboard Design · Part 1: The analytical foundation

Reading this chapter. This is one chapter of Dashboard Design, Nightlife Culture's research book on how evidence becomes a display a reader can trust, read and act on. The studio ("the house" in some chapters) is Nightlife Culture, a creative policy studio; the brief is its founder Carly Heath's commission for the book, and her eight ways a dashboard fails, the failure register, run through it. The Vibe Map, the studio's prototype for showing a place's nightlife culture, appears only as an illustration, never as a specification. "Version 1" is the book's archived first draft, whose positions this version re-tests against the sources. Every rule carries a kind (where it comes from: Standard, Evidence, Reading, Practice or Nightlife Culture) and a tier (how firm it is: Fixed, Adaptable or Decorative); Chapter 0 explains both, and the three senses of Fixed: a requirement that can be checked, a sequence whose order is the hard line, and a statement of the record. A dagger (†) marks a source read at the authors' abstract or summary only; "secondary" a quotation reached through a named reproduction; "(read once)" a quotation returned on a single reading and not confirmed by a second. Chapter 0 holds the glossary of the words the chapters share; each chapter lists its own coinages before its sources.

The question

What does it take for a dashboard to stay alive — refreshed, reliable, fast on a phone, its maps drawn — without a person tending it every day; what are the technological boundaries of that, what does each cost, and where does it break?

The 60-second version

A dashboard that was true on the day it launched is a different thing a year later, and the difference is operations. This chapter is about what "living" commits a publisher to, what each dependency promises and does not, what breaks when nobody is watching, and what the phone and the map cost.

So the canonical truths: freshness is a declared lifetime, stated as three dates and a frequency; a dashboard is a service with a bus factor, and "no admin" moves the person's job to reading the ticket; a dependency's terms, limits and notice are part of the design, and open licences give the right to reuse, not continued supply; availability is bounded by all the critical dependencies together, and the baked architecture moves them from view time to build time; a scheduled job fails silently by default, so an independent watch checks the effect and the ticket goes to a role; the phone sets the byte budget and the page shows its figures before any script runs; a map is a licence, a tile supply and a vintage, and has a non-map twin. Beneath the dashboard sits a service record, and its retirement is planned on the day it launches.

Freshness is a declared lifetime. The web's own protocol defines it that way — "A 'fresh' response is one whose age has not yet exceeded its freshness lifetime" — and the catalogue standards separate three dates (issued, modified, the period covered) and a stated frequency, with the admission that an absent modification date "MAY indicate that the resource has never changed after its initial publication, or that the date of last modification is not known, or that the resource is continuously updated". A published figure's date is not the date its value became final: national accounts "are usually open to revisions for the period back to 1997". The base rate of decay is measured — "A quarter of all webpages that existed at one point between 2013 and 2023 are no longer accessible, as of October 2023"; one in five government pages has a broken link; "one out of five" scholarly articles suffers reference rot — and the UK's own guidance for dashboards says "Always make it clear which dates or period your dashboard is relevant to", and that a dashboard "is a digital service", "not an appropriate project for a single person or for temporary staff".

A dependency is a promise someone else made. The open licence that most public data carries says "The Information Provider does not guarantee the continued supply of the Information." The UK's standard for government interfaces asks publishers to "try to give users 6 months notice" — for live interfaces, and most public ones call themselves beta. The platform interfaces a place dashboard would most want are the least stable thing it could depend on: one narrowed its interface three times in sixteen months, the first "Effective today", and its policy forbids "creating new or derived listenership metrics, benchmarking … usage statistics"; another reserves the right to block "applications that make a large number of calls to the API that are not primarily in response to direct user actions", which is what a scheduled refresh makes; a third is "non-commercial use only" with limits "continually changed". A map's free tiles come with "no SLA or guarantee" and the words "Our tile servers are not" free.

The chain breaks at its weakest link, silently. "A service cannot be more available than the intersection of all its critical dependencies"; a stated 99.9% is 8.76 hours a year dark. A scheduled job on the free scheduler attached to the commonest code host "may be dropped" under load, is, "In a public repository", "automatically disabled when no repository activity has occurred in 60 days", and sends its failure notices "to the user who last modified the cron syntax". The reliability engineers' remedies are plain: monitor the effect of the job rather than the job; treat a page that loads with wrong content as an error; on failure keep the last good copy — "Stale data is almost always better than incorrect data" — and never empty the page because a refresh failed. The architecture that most nearly means "no admin" bundles a read-only copy of the data with the site and rebuilds on a schedule; its author draws its boundary at content that changes "at most a few times a day".

The phone is the binding constraint, and the map is the heaviest thing on it. The median mobile page is 2.3 MB and more than half of sites fail the web's own speed thresholds on phones; a budget built for the device a typical user owns allows "650KiB of JavaScript" for a five-second load, and the vector map library alone is about 287 KB, by a third-party measurement, before a single tile arrives. The UK public sector's answer is that services "should be functional using only HTML", because "1.1% of people aren't getting JavaScript enhancements (1 in 93)", four-fifths of them involuntarily. A fifth of online adults are smartphone-only; in social grade DE households, three in ten. A map is a licence, a tile supply and a vintage: the full-resolution boundary file for the UK's local authorities is about 128 MB and the 200-metre generalisation under 2 MB; a map needs a non-map twin, and buttons to pan and zoom.

1 · What "living" means

Version 1 of this book opened its chapter on freshness with a case: a city observatory whose front page was maintained and whose datasets were not — update labels reading "almost 7 years ago", one dataset in roughly twenty-four current, and that one maintained by somebody else. The brief's failure register says a dashboard fails "if it breaks or isn't reliable" and "if people don't trust it", and the observatory failed both without a single error page: every chart drew, every number was wrong by years. This chapter is about the distance between a dashboard that works and a dashboard that is alive, and about what closing that distance costs.

"Alive" has a precise meaning in the web's own plumbing and a looser one in the catalogue standards, and the chapter will use both. In the protocol that carries every page, HTTP, freshness is a lifetime that a publisher declares: "A 'fresh' response is one whose age has not yet exceeded its freshness lifetime. Conversely, a 'stale' response is one where it has." The lifetime is "the length of time between its generation by the origin server and its expiration time". A response is not fresh because it is recent; it is fresh because its publisher said how long it would stay so, and that time has not run out. Chapter 4 asked every figure to carry its revision status; this chapter asks it to carry its lifetime — when it was made, when it was last revised, and how long its maker says it may be trusted before it must be looked at again.

The rest of the chapter is in four movements. Sections 3 and 4 are about freshness and the records that describe it. Sections 5 and 6 are about dependencies — the interfaces a dashboard draws on, what they promise, and how they have behaved. Sections 7 and 8 are about reliability — what breaks, how it is noticed, and the architectures that need the least tending. Sections 9 and 10 are about the phone and the map, which are the two places where a dashboard's weight becomes its reader's cost.

2 · Why people believe what they believe

Belief one: a dashboard is finished when it launches

The launch is the visible event; the operations are not. The UK government's own guidance for analysts who build dashboards begins from the opposite premise — a dashboard "is a digital service" that must be "continually" managed — and estimates the resource as larger than people plan for. Section 3.

Belief two: "last updated" tells you how fresh the data is

The stamp on the page is usually the date the page was built, not the date the data was collected, not the date its value became final, and not a promise of when it will next move. The catalogue standards separate those and the national statistics offices revise figures for years. Section 4.

Belief three: an API is a tap

If an interface exists today it will exist next year, at the same address, returning the same fields, at the same rate. The streaming and social platforms' interfaces have each been narrowed, re-priced or closed within the last five years; the ticketing platforms publish too little to know; and the terms of all of them permit narrowing without notice. Sections 5 and 6.

Belief four: free data means free supply

The open licence that covers most UK public data is generous in what it permits and explicit that it promises nothing about continuing to exist. The free map tiles are free data on servers that are not. Sections 5, 6 and 10.

Belief five: if it is up, it is working

Uptime measures whether the page loads. A page that loads and shows last quarter's figures as this quarter's is, in the reliability engineers' own definition, an error — "an HTTP 200 success response, but coupled with the wrong content" — and no uptime check will see it. Section 7.

Belief six: automation removes the person

A scheduled job replaces the daily task; it does not replace the person who notices that the job stopped. Every scheduler documented here fails silently in at least one way, and every reliability text ends at the same place: someone reads the ticket. Sections 7 and 8.

Belief seven: it works on my phone

The phone a typical user carries is "15-25% as fast" as the developer's — the developer's is four to six times faster — and it is on a slower network. The budget for a page is set by the device at the seventy-fifth percentile, not the first. Section 9.

Belief eight: a map is a chart with a background

A map is a dependency on a tile supplier with a licence and a policy, a boundary file with a vintage and a size, and a rendering library heavier than everything else on the page. Section 10.

3 · What a living dashboard commits to

The official account

In February 2026 the Government Analysis Function published guidance on building and managing dashboards, and it is the nearest thing the UK has to an official statement of what a dashboard commits its publisher to. Its premise: "A dashboard is a digital service, which means you must have the skills and resource to continually manage" — among other things — "the flow of data going into the dashboard" and the "relevance of the dashboard over time". Its warning: "Dashboards often require more resource than initially identified due to their complexity." "They are not an appropriate project for a single person or for temporary staff." Its conditions for building one at all include that "data updates are frequent and can be automated, with users likely to revisit the dashboard". Its rules for the face: "Always make it clear which dates or period your dashboard is relevant to", and "When updating the data in your dashboard, add a change note explaining the change and when it happened." And its rules for the end: "Retire your dashboard if it is not being maintained or user feedback indicates that it is no longer useful, relevant or providing value for money"; "Add a banner on all pages of the service to let users know the dashboard will be retired and no longer updated. Do this at least six months before retirement"; and archive by "keeping data and metadata available, with a clear note that it is no longer updated and the dates or period the data is associated with", with the code kept "in a public GitHub repository marked as archived".

Three things in that guidance organise this chapter. The dashboard is a service, with the continuing resource a service needs — and a small studio is close to "a single person". The face states its period and logs its changes — the dated stamp version 1 asked for, now official. And the retirement is planned, announced six months ahead, and ends in an archive that says what it was — which is the anti-observatory move version 1 called "honest amputation", with an official procedure attached.

The GOV.UK publishing guidance has the same shape for a page. "When you update content on an already published page, you may need to write a change note"; change notes are "sometimes published on the page, along with the time and date" and "emailed to anyone who subscribed to the page"; and "Do not say the page has been updated without saying what has changed." Withdrawal is a state, not a deletion: "the page will remain on GOV.UK, but it'll have a banner saying that the content has been withdrawn", with the standard notice — "This publication was withdrawn on 24 February 2022" — at the top. The ONS's release calendar labels each release "Published", "Upcoming" or "Cancelled", and its time-series pages carry "Release date", "Next release" and "View previous versions". A living publication, in UK official practice, tells its reader three times: what period it describes, when it last changed and why, and when it will change next.

Timeliness is not punctuality

The official statistical vocabulary makes a distinction that dashboards conflate. Eurostat's glossary: timeliness is "the lapse of time between the end of a reference period (or a reference date) and the dissemination of the data"; punctuality is "the possible time lag existing between the actual delivery date of the data and the target date when the data should have been delivered". The first is how far behind the world the figure is; the second is whether the publisher kept its promise about when the figure would arrive. A dashboard can be punctual and stale — refreshed every night from a source that is a year behind — or timely and unpunctual. The UK Code of Practice for Statistics uses the words without defining them, and asks producers to "Pre-announce the release of statistics with the time and date in a 12-month release calendar", to "Release on a timely basis, meeting the needs of users as far as possible and as soon as the statistics are ready", to "Give advance notice of material changes to the content of releases, such as the removal of data tables or variables", and to "Ensure that statistics continue to be publicly available, such as through web or data archiving". The stamp on a dashboard, if it is to mean what the official vocabulary means, carries both: the period the data describes, and the date the data was due — which is what a declared frequency, counted from the last publication, gives.

What a living series commits to

Chapters 6 and 7 found that a living series is not a snapshot repeated. A closures count is provisional for two years because of reactivations; a seasonally adjusted series cannot exist under three years and its history changes when the next month arrives; a modelled small-area figure's interval "should not be used to measure change". A dashboard that commits to a living series commits to all of that: to showing provisional figures as provisional, to revising its own history and saying so, to not adjusting what is too young to adjust, and to a release discipline — the data.gov.uk publisher guidance puts it in one line: "Do not create new datasets for data you publish regularly, for example monthly spend data. Instead, create a single dataset and add new data to it." And: "In the interests of transparency, you should not delete datasets". The W3C's best practices for data on the web ask the same of a publisher — "Version information makes a revision of a dataset uniquely identifiable"; "Assign URIs to individual versions of datasets as well as to the overall series" — and the W3C's own implementation report records that, of the catalogue systems it surveyed in 2016, "Concerning BP27 none of the data catalog solutions implement it", BP27 being Preserve identifiers: "In general, when a dataset is not available then just a 404 error message is returned." The practice's title is "Preserve identifiers"; its body was beyond the reach of this research, and the report says that nobody surveyed had built it.

4 · Three dates and a frequency

The catalogue vocabulary

The metadata standard that public data catalogues use, DCAT, separates what a dashboard's single stamp runs together. The release date is "Date of formal issuance (e.g., publication) of the resource", set "using the first known date of issuance". The modification date is the "Most recent date on which the resource was changed, updated or modified", and "The value of this property indicates a change to the actual resource, not a change to the catalog record." The period a dataset covers is a third thing, and the UK's profile defines it separately: "The date period that the dataset applies to." And then the frequency — in the UK profile "The frequency at which dataset is published", expressed as a repeating duration (annual, weekly) "or irregular"; in the European profile "The frequency at which the Dataset is updated"; in the Dublin Core vocabulary it derives from, "The frequency with which items are added to a collection". Three profiles, three meanings of "frequency": published, updated, added to. A dashboard that promises its reader a cadence should say which.

The standard's own usage note for the modification date is the chapter's warning about any "last updated" stamp. "An absent value MAY indicate that the resource has never changed after its initial publication, or that the date of last modification is not known, or that the resource is continuously updated." A missing date means one of three opposite things, and a reader cannot tell which. The American profile adds a fourth twist — "If there is a need to reflect that the dataset is continually updated, ISO 8601 formatting can account for this with repeating intervals" — so that its modification field may hold a repeating interval instead of a date, and "last updated" can carry a promise rather than a fact. For a dashboard, the stamp is three stamps or it misleads: the period the figure describes; the date the figure was last changed; and the cadence at which it is promised to change — with the word "promised" doing work, because section 7 is about the ways the promise fails.

The Data Quality Vocabulary, a W3C note, borrows two definitions that make freshness relative to a use rather than a clock. From an international standard, as the note reproduces it: currentness is "The degree to which data has attributes that are of the right age in a specific context of use." From the research literature: "Timeliness measures how up-to-date data is relative to a specific task". A footfall figure a week old is fresh for a quarterly report and stale for a live display; the same figure, two freshness judgements. Chapter 5 found that validity is of a reading for a use; freshness is too.

Last updated is not last revised

The national statistics offices make the point that a published figure's date is not the date its value became final. The ONS's revisions policy for the national accounts: "A revision is a scheduled change to any published Office for National Statistics (ONS) output." "In early estimates of GDP, there is also inherent levels of uncertainty because of the trade-off between timeliness and accuracy." "Blue Book releases are usually open to revisions for the period back to 1997 (the earliest point for which data are available)." A figure for 1998 can still move. The Federal Reserve's archive of vintages states what that means for a reader who wants to know what was known when: it "allows you to retrieve each economic data release (vintage) that was available on a specific date in history." Chapter 7 called a vintage a snapshot; a dashboard that shows a series without saying which vintage it is showing has hidden the fact that the series it showed last quarter was a different series.

The consequence for the stamp is a fourth part, or a note beside the second: the date a figure was last revised, as distinct from the date the page last refreshed. The statistics office separates two kinds of change: "A revision is a scheduled change to any published Office for National Statistics (ONS) output"; "A correction is an unplanned revision to any published ONS output because of the identification of an error." A dashboard that carries a figure carries which of the two last touched it. Chapter 6's closures count is the simplest case — "not final until the third year" — and a dashboard that refreshes it nightly and stamps it "updated today" has told the truth about the page and not about the number.

How fast things rot

The base rate against which a dashboard's dependencies should be judged is measured, and it is high. The Pew Research Center, in May 2024: "A quarter of all webpages that existed at one point between 2013 and 2023 are no longer accessible"; "38% of webpages that existed in 2013 are not available today" against "8% of pages that existed in 2023"; "21% of all the government webpages we examined contained at least one broken link"; and "54% of Wikipedia pages contain at least one link in their 'References' section that points to a page that no longer exists". The Harvard study of one newspaper's links, in its authors' own account for the Columbia Journalism Review: of 2,283,445 external links in 553,693 articles, "Of these deep links, 25 percent of all links were completely inaccessible", with the rot rising by age — "6 percent of links from 2018 had rotted, as compared to 43 percent of links from 2008 and 72 percent of links from 1998" — and "Fifty-three percent of all articles that contained deep links had at least one rotted link." Klein and colleagues, across 3.5 million scholarly articles: "We find one out of five STM articles suffering from reference rot, meaning it is impossible to revisit the web context that surrounds them some time after their publication." An older study found that a determined searcher could recover most lost addresses — "A single second searcher was able to locate 80 percent of the URLs reported as lost" — which is the distinction between the address rotting and the content being gone; a dashboard's automated fetch does not search.

Whether datasets rot at the same rate is not measured — no study of withdrawal from a UK portal was reachable, and the web-page figures above are the nearest evidence — but the instruments that once measured open-data freshness have themselves rotted. The Open Data Barometer's last edition found that "74% of the data we analysed is up-to-date, which is promising, but means that one quarter of all data surveyed has very limited value"; its page was last modified in 2018. The Global Open Data Index scored datasets on "Is the data up-to-date?" and now carries the notice "This is an archived project from the Open Knowledge Foundation and it is no longer active". The UK's own catalogue is mid-rename — "Since 2010, the data.gov.uk website, now known as the National Data Library" — and no measured study of its datasets' staleness was reachable. The one official form that retirement takes in the UK is the withdrawal banner, which keeps the address and says the date; a third-party archive now keeps a daily copy of the American federal catalogue. A dashboard built on links to other people's data is built on a base rate of a quarter gone in a decade, and the design question is not whether a source will go but what the dashboard does on the day it does.

5 · What an interface promises

The UK's own standard for interfaces

An API — the published way one piece of software asks another for data — is a promise with terms, and the UK government has written down what it thinks the terms should be. Its API standards ask publishers to version carefully — "When you make new versions of your API, try not to make changes that will stop older versions of your API working properly"; "When you retire an old version you must tell users it is no longer supported and give them time to move on to the new version" — and to limit callers: "You should also implement rate limiting or throttling policies – making sure that users don't overuse your resources"; "Anonymous endpoints should also be rate limited to prevent excessive or malicious use." The one number in UK guidance is in the companion page on running a live interface: "You should try to give users 6 months notice if your API is 'live'." Beta interfaces are exempt — "You do not need to give as much notice if your API is in alpha or beta where your users are expecting breaking changes" — and, as section 6 finds, most public interfaces a place dashboard would use call themselves beta.

The guidance on service levels gives the provider's reason why a stated limit is the real limit, which a dashboard builder should read as a user: "When applying rate limiting or throttling, you should not let your users go over the limits you set even if you have spare capacity." "This is because if you need to take the spare capacity away in future and the user has developed their application with the higher rates in mind, their application could break". An interface that answered faster yesterday has made no promise. The same page gives the reason "uptime" hides the shape of failure: "your API could drop 1 in 20 connections or it could be unreachable for 2 hours a day" — the same percentage, a different experience.

What the protocol guarantees, and what it does not

The only standardised signal that a caller has asked too often is a status code. "The 429 status code indicates that the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time ('rate limiting')." The response "SHOULD include details explaining the condition, and MAY include a Retry-After header indicating how long to wait before making a new request" — may, not must. And the standard declines to say how the counting works: "Note that this specification does not define how the origin server identifies the user, nor how it counts requests." The header that would let a server advertise its quota in advance has been an Internet-Draft since before this book began; as of May 2026 it is at its eleventh revision with its intended status listed as "(None)". In practice every platform invents its own header, and a dashboard that calls several must learn several dialects. The protocol's own answer to the problem of asking too often is caching, which section 8 returns to; for now the rule is the one the national statistics office states for its own interface: "Your tooling should respect the Retry-After header and pause your requests for the specified duration", and "If this is not respected our algorithms may impose a block to our services for up to 1 hour."

What the open licence promises

Most UK public data is published under the Open Government Licence, and a dashboard builder should read its last line first. The licence is generous: it grants "a worldwide, royalty-free, perpetual, non-exclusive licence to use the Information"; the licensee may "copy, publish, distribute and transmit the Information", "adapt the Information", and "exploit the Information commercially and non-commercially for example, by combining it with other Information, or by including it in your own product or application", in return for acknowledging the source — "Contains public sector information licensed under the Open Government Licence v3.0" — and not implying endorsement. It excludes "personal data in the Information" and "third party rights the Information Provider is not authorised to license". And it warrants nothing: "The Information is licensed 'as is' and the Information Provider and/or Licensor excludes all representations, warranties, obligations and liabilities in relation to the Information to the maximum extent permitted by law." "The Information Provider and/or Licensor are not liable for any errors or omissions in the Information". "The Information Provider does not guarantee the continued supply of the Information."

That last sentence is the licence's answer to belief four. It gives a perpetual right to reuse what has been received, and no right to keep receiving it. Transport for London's own licence, based on an earlier version of the same text, repeats it — "TfL does not guarantee the continued supply of the Information" — and adds "TfL may at any time revise this Licence without notice." The UK's open data is open the way a tap is open: the water that has run is yours, and the tap may be turned off.

6 · The interfaces a place dashboard would use

Section 5 read the standards and the licence. This section reads the interfaces themselves — the ones a dashboard about a place in the UK would most plausibly call — and reads them as technology only: what each states as its limit, what its terms permit, what it labels itself, and what it says will happen when it changes. No listing, event, track or venue was taken from any of them; the chapter is interested in the pipe and not the water. Every page below was read on 6 October 2026, and most of them carry no date of their own, which is itself a finding: a limit read today from an undated page is a limit as of today.

The public interfaces, read as a table of limits

Start with what each public interface says about how often it may be called, because this is the number a scheduled job must be built around and the number that is hardest to find afterwards.

Interface Stated limit Key required Labels itself Says of its own future
Transport for London Unified API 500 requests a minute with a free account; "Anonymous access to our API is limited to 50 requests a minute" For the higher rate — "TfL does not guarantee the continued supply of the Information"; accounts idle a year are "automatically disabled and deleted"
Companies House public data API "You can make up to 600 requests within a five-minute period" Yes — "We reserve the right to ban without notice applications that regularly exceed or attempt to bypass the rate limits"
Office for National Statistics API "120 requests per 10 seconds"; "200 requests per 1 minute"; "15 requests per 10 seconds" for high-demand site assets "no API keys are required" "currently in Beta" "there may occasionally be breaking changes"; a block "for up to 1 hour"; retirement signalled by headers and then 404
Nomis "a 25000 cell limit on the number of data values downloaded" without a key Optional; removes the cell limit — —
data.gov.uk directory API "You do not need an API key to use the API and there are no rate limits" No — The site is "now known as the National Data Library"
Police API (data.police.uk) "15 requests per second with a burst of 30" No — Data "Frequency: Monthly"
Ordnance Survey APIs "600 transactions per minute" for live projects; "50 transactions per minute" in development mode Yes — Zoomstack basemap "updated every six months"
Food Standards Agency ratings API None stated; a version header is mandatory No — "at least one previous depreciated version" kept
Environment Agency flood-monitoring API None stated; asks for "a single call every 15 mins" No "beta" "do not offer a guarantee of service level"
