Of those smartphone-only users, "49% of these users said they struggled to complete forms on a smartphone compared to doing so on a laptop or PC, while 35% agreed that it was difficult to compare products or services" — though "around three quarters of adults who use a smartphone only to go online reported never feeling disadvantaged by it (74%)". And "6% of adults continuing to not have access to the internet at home in 2024".

The arithmetic a builder should carry from this section is short. One online adult in five has no screen but the phone; in social grade DE households, three in ten. Their phone is, on Russell's model, a seventh to a quarter as fast as the builder's. The budget for them is his: about 1.3 MiB in all if half of it is script, or 2.5 MiB if almost none is, for a five-second load — and the page should show its numbers before any script has run, because about one visit in a hundred, on the one public measurement, never runs it. Chapter 2 said who the readers were; this section says what they are holding. A dashboard that fails on their device has, in the failure register's words, failed because "people don't use it", and they did not use it because it did not open.

10 · The map

Section 9 ended at a budget. A map spends it faster than anything else a dashboard can contain, and it brings with it three dependencies that no chart has: a tile supplier with a policy, a boundary file with a vintage, and a rendering library heavier than the rest of the page. This section reads each, and ends with what the map must have beside it. It says nothing about what the map should look like, which is a design decision and not this book's.

Two kinds of tile

A web map is drawn from tiles — square pieces of the world at each zoom level, fetched as the reader pans — and there are two kinds. The older kind is a picture: a raster tile is an image rendered on a server and sent finished, and the phone only has to display it. The newer kind is data: "A Vector tile is the vector data equivalent of raster image tiles for web mapping" — "a space-efficient encoding format for tiled geographic vector data" in which the roads, buildings and names arrive as geometry and the phone draws them. The specification is Mapbox's, open — "the use of this spec in products and code is entirely free: there are no royalties, restrictions, or requirements" — and the vendor's own account of the trade is the one most builders meet: "Tiles are styled at runtime, allowing for many map styles on global data." "Vector tiles are small, enabling global high-resolution maps, faster map loads, and efficient caching." And, read as probable rather than confirmed: "Rendering vector tiles in the browser or device requires more processing power compared to displaying pre-rendered raster images."

That last sentence is the trade, and it should be read beside the two vendors' claims that vector maps load faster, which are claims about bytes on the network and not about work on the device; section 9 says which way the device half cuts for the phone most readers hold. Vector tiles move the styling and the drawing from the server to the device; raster tiles move them to the server. A vector map can be restyled to the studio's palette, rotated, labelled in the house face — everything a styled map offers — at the price of a rendering library and a working graphics processor on the reader's side. The Ordnance Survey offers both: a vector service that is "a customisable basemap" that "Loads maps quicker than traditional raster-mapping services", and a raster service of "pre-rendered raster tiles". The choice between them is a performance decision disguised as a styling one.

Four ways to get tiles, and what each promises

Whoever draws the tiles, someone has to serve them, and the research found four models of supply, each with its own promise and its own way of ending.

Donated and unguaranteed. The OpenStreetMap Foundation's tile servers are the free default in thousands of tutorials, and the Foundation's policy — rewritten since it was first read for this book, in softer and more operational language — separates the data from the servers in its first lines: "OpenStreetMap (OSM) data is free for everyone to use. Our tile servers are not: they are funded by donations and sponsorship, and capacity is limited." Then: "Availability is best-effort: there is no SLA or guarantee." "We may block access, without notice, if your usage degrades the service." The client must "Honour server caching headers (Cache-Control, Expires, Etag). If your cache cannot read them, cache each tile for at least 7 days", must send "a clear, unique User-Agent string that names your app", and must not bulk download — "any pre-emptive fetching of tiles other than those a user is actively viewing" — or use the tiles offline: "Offline use is not permitted on tile.openstreetmap.org." This is belief four exactly. The map data is free; the map service is a gift with conditions, and the Foundation says plainly that a project which cannot meet them should "use an alternative OSM-derived service … or run your own".

The national mapping agency. The Ordnance Survey's Data Hub serves tiles behind a key, with the rate limits section 6 tabled — 600 transactions a minute live, 50 in development, 429 beyond — and with a branding condition: "Our logo should be positioned in the embedded map window across all your digital applications", and the copyright statement, terms and error-reporting link likewise. Its free allowances could not be read, and the chapter does not print them from memory. What it does offer, and what matters most for section 8's architecture, is a basemap that can be downloaded whole: OS Open Zoomstack is "an open vector basemap showing coverage of Great Britain from a national level, right down to street detail", "updated every six months in June and December", available "in just one single file" and "Free to use for everyone". Neither page reached names the Open Government Licence, so the licence basis is recorded as unverified. A basemap in one file on a six-month cadence is a basemap that can be baked.

Metered and commercial. Mapbox and MapTiler sell tiles by the unit, and section 8 did the arithmetic for the first: free to 50,000 map loads a month, then $5 per thousand, a load being each time the library "initializes on a webpage", with, in the company's glossary, "The maximum session length for a map load is 12 hours." MapTiler's free plan allows "100k/month" requests and "5k/month" sessions, is "Suitable for testing, PoC, prototyping, personal, or non-commercial use", puts the "MapTiler logo on the map", and — the same clause as the free static host — "On a FREE plan service will pause until the next month without an upgrade to paid plans." Its paid tier is "$30/month" for "500k/month" requests. A metered supplier promises current tiles and someone else's operations in exchange for a bill that rises with the dashboard's success and a map that stops when the free month runs out.

A file you host yourself. Protomaps' PMTiles, from section 8: "a single-file archive format for pyramids of tiled data", hosted "on a storage platform like S3", read by range requests so that no tile server exists. The project's own basemap is "available as a single PMTiles archive, distributed as an Open Database License Produced Work (OpenStreetMap attribution required)"; "A full planet file is roughly 120 gigabytes, including zoom levels from 0 to 15", and "Each additional zoom level roughly doubles the size of the file" — so a studio extracts the city it needs, which is a small fraction of that, and the file sits on a static host inside the limits section 8 listed, or on object storage if it is over 25 MiB. The promise here is the inverse of the others: no supplier can rate-limit, re-price or close it, because there is no supplier at read time; in exchange the studio owns the vintage — "PMTiles is a read-only format" — and must rebuild the file to move it. The project's own "read-only" is confirmed at source; even the download is only best-effort: "Please note that URLs may change and hotlinking to these downloads are discouraged."

Four supplies; four endings. The donated servers may block without notice; the agency's key has a rate and a logo; the metered service has a bill and a pause; the file has a date. The service record, in section 11, has a line for which one the map uses and what it has agreed to.

The boundary file: the size is the decision

A place dashboard draws boundaries — wards, districts, output areas — and the boundary file is the one piece of a map whose weight is entirely in the builder's hands, because the national statistics office publishes each boundary at several resolutions and the choice of suffix is the performance decision.

The office's own page lists four: "(BFC) Full resolution - clipped to the coastline (Mean High Water mark)"; "(BFE) Full resolution - extent of the realm"; "(BGC) Generalised (20m) - clipped to the coastline"; "(BUC) Ultra Generalised (500m) - clipped to the coastline" — "designed to be used in different contexts (such as analysis or visualisation)". The portal publishes a fifth that the explainer omits: "(BSC) Super Generalised (200m) - clipped to the coastline (Mean High Water mark)." The portal's size fields for the December 2024 local authority districts — indicative only, since what the field measures is undocumented — give the full-resolution file at about 128 MB and the 200-metre file at about 1.7 MB in the same record type: roughly seventy-five to one, by the chapter's division. Against section 9's budget of 1.3 to 2.5 MiB for everything, the full-resolution national file is a hundred times the whole page, and even the 200-metre national file is more than the page can afford. The answer is not the national file at all: a map of one district needs only its own boundaries, cut from the generalised product, and the figure drawn on top of them is the same whichever resolution carries it.

Two further facts about boundary files belong in the service record. They are dated products — the record is "as at December 2024" — and the geography underneath them moves: "Electoral ward and electoral division boundary changes are usually enacted on the first Thursday in May each year, to coincide with the local government elections in the UK", and the census geographies were redrawn in 2021 "by merging or splitting 2011 LSOAs to ensure that population and household thresholds were met". A dashboard pins a boundary vintage the way it pins a data vintage, and says which, because a figure for a ward that no longer has that shape is a figure for a place that no longer exists. And they carry a licence with two owners: "Source: Office for National Statistics licensed under the Open Government Licence v.3.0" and "Contains OS data © Crown copyright and database right [year]" — the boundaries "Contains both Ordnance Survey and ONS Intellectual Property Rights."

When the published generalisation is not enough, the builder simplifies, and should know what the tools do to small places. Mapshaper, the usual instrument, "supports Douglas-Peucker simplification and two kinds of Visvalingam simplification": the first "Guarantees that simplified lines stay within a fixed distance of the original" but "tends to introduce visible spikes at high simplification"; the second "Iteratively removes the point that forms the triangle of smallest area with its two neighbors", and its weighted form is the default "because it produces generalizations that look good enough for most web maps, even if they fall short of true cartographic quality." The warning is one sentence: "At high simplification, small polygons can disappear entirely". The smallest areas are the first to vanish, and in a city the smallest areas are usually the densest. Shared borders survive simplification together "but only if their vertices are perfectly aligned to begin with", which is why the topology-preserving format exists: TopoJSON "encodes topology", stitching geometries "from shared line segments called arcs", and is "substantially more compact than GeoJSON, frequently offering a reduction of 80% or more even without simplification."

The library

Before a single tile arrives, the map has to be drawn by code the phone downloads, and here the raster-versus-vector trade becomes a number. Leaflet, the standard raster-map library, describes itself as "Weighing just about 42 KB of JS" gzipped. MapLibre GL JS, the open vector renderer — "an open-source fork of mapbox-gl-js, before their switch to a non-OSS license in December 2020", "licensed under the 3-Clause BSD license", drawing by "GPU-accelerated vector tile rendering" — is reported by a third-party measurement at about 287 KB gzipped for a recent version (the version number could not be matched to the project's own releases). The vector renderer alone is about seven times the raster library, and about 43 per cent of Russell's entire JavaScript budget for his seventy-fifth-percentile phone, by the chapter's arithmetic, before any tile, boundary or figure has been fetched. A vector map on a phone is a decision to spend over two-fifths of the script budget on the ability to restyle.

What nobody has measured

The research looked for a measurement of what a map view costs a phone in bytes — a typical city basemap at a typical zoom, tiles and all — and found none. The suppliers bill by load, session or request, not by byte; the OpenStreetMap wiki's aggregate — "during August 2026 the tile.openstreetmap.org CDN served approximately 1.7 PB per month (outbound) and 135 billion requests per month" — divides to about 12.6 KB per request by the chapter's arithmetic, an average over every response and not a per-view figure; the tile encoder's 500 KB ceiling per tile is a limit and not a measurement. This is a gap in the published record, and it is a gap the prototype can fill with its own numbers in an afternoon: open the page on the baseline device, on the baseline network, and count. Until then, the plain statement is that nobody official knows what a map costs the median reader, and the library figure above says the answer starts high.

The twin

A map is also the one element of a dashboard that the accessibility standards use as their worked example, twice. The success criterion on dragging: "All functionality that uses a dragging movement for operation can be achieved by a single pointer without dragging, unless dragging is essential or the functionality is determined by the user agent and not modified by the author"; the example, "A map allows users to drag the view of the map around, and the map has up/down/left/right buttons to move the view as well." The criterion on gestures: "All functionality that uses multipoint or path-based gestures for operation can be operated with a single pointer without a path-based gesture, unless a multipoint or path-based gesture is essential"; the example, "A website includes a map view that supports the pinch/spread gesture to zoom into the map content. As a single-pointer alternative, the map also includes plus/minus buttons to zoom in and out." Pan and zoom buttons are, in effect, the cited way to conform. The web accessibility tutorials class maps among the complex images — "maps showing locations or other information such as weather systems" — for which "a two-part text alternative is required", the second part being "a textual representation of the essential information conveyed by the image". And the cross-government guidance on colour names the specific difficulty: "Maps provide a particular challenge for accessibility as colours are not presented in an order. This can make it difficult to match colours against a legend when there are insufficient contrast ratios between sequential colours." Its instruction for maps: "make sure the data is available in another format such as a downloadable data table". Its palette tops out at five sequential blues — "Where 5 sequential colours are required, the full set of blue colours shown in the palette table can be used" — because "The more categories you use in a sequential colour palette, the less accessible the colours become".

The map, then, needs a twin: a table of the same figures, by the same places, reachable without the map and before the script. The twin is not an accessibility afterthought. It is the version of the page that the one visit in ninety-three receives, that the slowest quarter of phones receives first, that a screen reader receives, and that survives the day the tile supplier blocks without notice. A dashboard whose map has no twin has made its most expensive element its only one.

11 · What holds true regardless

Seven truths, in the chapter's own words, each with its grounds; then the record that sits beneath them. They are stated for any dashboard that intends to be read next year; the nightlife case in section 13 is one application.

1 · Freshness is a declared lifetime, not a stamp. A dashboard states, for each series, the period the data describes, the date it was published, the date it was last revised and the frequency at which it is expected to move; "last updated" alone names none of these. An absent date, by the catalogue standard's own admission, means one of three things and a reader cannot tell which. The page's own freshness lifetime — the age at which what it shows is to be treated as stale — is written down and compared against the data's date on the page itself, in words a reader can read. (Sections 3, 4, 7; DCAT 3; RFC 9111 §4.2; the Analysis Function's dashboards guidance; the SRE workbook's freshness objectives.)

2 · A dashboard is a service, and "no admin" moves the job, it does not remove it. The UK's own guidance calls a dashboard a digital service that is continually managed and "not an appropriate project for a single person". Automation replaces the refresh; it does not replace the person who reads the ticket, re-points a job when an interface moves and decides what happens when a source closes. That person is a named role with a successor, and the signals they receive are sorted into alerts, tickets and logs so that attention is spent once. (Sections 3, 7, 8; the Analysis Function; the SRE book on monitoring and toil; Eghbal; Avelino et al.)

3 · A dependency's terms, limits and notice are part of the design, and an open licence gives reuse, not supply. Every interface a dashboard calls is a service run by someone else, on terms that may be revised without notice, with a stated limit that is the real limit and a history of closing that is the best guide to its future. The Open Government Licence permits everything and promises nothing about continuing to exist; the platform terms forbid, clause by clause, the things a dashboard does. The dashboard records, for each dependency, which kind it is — supply or terms — and what notice it has been promised: twelve months by contract with exceptions, six as an aspiration, or none. (Sections 5, 6; GDS; RFC 6585; the OGL; the platform terms and histories.)

4 · Availability is bounded by the weakest thing the page needs at the moment of reading, so the work is done before the reader arrives. A page that fetches live from ten dependencies has given itself days a year of showing nothing. Fetched the night before and baked, the page depends on its host alone, the night's job can fail without the reader seeing it, and the last good copy is kept and shown with its age — which is what the protocol already does when allowed and what the cloud provider's own anti-pattern list requires. A series that fails floods one compartment, not the page. (Sections 7, 8; Treynor et al.; RFC 9111, RFC 5861; Fowler; AWS REL05-BP01; Willison.)

5 · Scheduled jobs fail quietly, so the effect is watched, not the job, and the ticket goes to a role. The oldest scheduler, on a reading of its manuals, has no notion of failure to report; the free one documents that it delays, drops, disables after sixty quiet days and notifies one person. The watch is therefore independent of the scheduler, checks that the data's date advanced, and raises a ticket to an address the studio reads. Refresh jobs are built to be run twice safely, and to be skipped rather than doubled. (Section 7; the cron manuals; GitHub's documentation; the SRE book on cron; heartbeat monitoring practice.)

6 · The phone sets the budget, and the page shows its figures before any script has run. The phone to design for is a seventh to a quarter as fast as the builder's, on a network of a few megabits; one online adult in five, and three in ten in social grade DE households, has no other screen; about one visit in a hundred, on the one public measurement, arrives without the script, four-fifths of them involuntarily. The budget is Russell's — about 1.3 MiB with half of it script, or 2.5 MiB with almost none — measured at the seventy-fifth percentile, and the figures are in the HTML. (Section 9; Russell; the Web Almanac; GDS; Herlihy 2013; Ofcom.)

7 · A map is a licence, a tile supply and a vintage, and it has a non-map twin. A map brings a supplier with one of four endings, a boundary file whose resolution is chosen and whose date is pinned, and a rendering library that can take over two-fifths of the script budget before a tile arrives. The same figures, by the same places, are reachable as a table without the map and before the script; pan and zoom have buttons; the colour ramp is short. (Section 10; the OSMF policies; OS; Mapbox and MapTiler; Protomaps; the ONS boundary products; WCAG 2.5.1 and 2.5.7; the Analysis Function on colour.)

Beneath the dashboard: the service record

The truths are kept by a record, as Chapters 4 to 7 each produced one — the provenance set, the recipe card, the claim record and the comparison record — and Chapter 16 gathers these five, with the records of later chapters, into one record of the dashboard. The service record is written before the dashboard launches, by the person who will keep it, and it answers ten questions. Each line is short; the point is that each is answered, and that the last — what is not promised — is answered too, because section 7 showed that a year of silent reliability makes a promise whether or not one was written.

Line What it states
1 · Freshness promise For each series: period described, published, last revised, declared frequency; the page's own freshness lifetime, in days, and where it is shown
2 · Dependencies Each interface, file and host the page needs — at build time and at read time, marked which — with its stated limit, its terms (supply or terms), the notice it has promised, and the date its page was read
3 · Refresh mechanism What runs, where, on what schedule, off the hour; what it fetches and what it commits; that it can be run twice safely
4 · Watch and alarm What checks that the data's date advanced, independent of the job; where the ticket goes — a role, not a person — and who is second
5 · Availability target and degraded mode The objective in the data's terms ("the oldest figure is never more than N days behind, 11 months in 12"); what the page shows when a fetch fails, series by series; when the degraded mode was last exercised
6 · Budget and baseline device The byte budget; the device and network it was tested on; what the page shows before any script runs
7 · Map supply, licence and vintage Which of the four supplies; what has been agreed to (cache, attribution, logo, offline, non-commercial); the boundary product and its date; the renderer and its weight; where the twin is
8 · Retirement plan and archive How a series ends when its source closes: the notice given, what is archived, where the last state stays reachable; how the whole page ends
9 · Owner and successor Whose job the ticket is; who takes it when they leave; where this record lives
10 · Not done What the record declines to promise, and why

A filled example, invented for the method. 1. Series A: monthly, period = calendar month, published ~6 weeks after period end, revised for 3 months; page lifetime 50 days; shown beside the figure. 2. Build time: statistics API (beta; 200/min; no notice stated; read 6 Oct 2026), boundary file BSC Dec 2024 (OGL + OS copyright). Read time: static host only (25 MiB/asset; no availability commitment established). 3. Scheduled job, 03:17 UTC daily, commits fetched files to the repository; idempotent. 4. Heartbeat monitor pinged after the data's date is confirmed to have advanced; ticket to data@ (role); second: named. 5. Newest figure published ≤ 50 days ago, 11 months in 12; on fetch failure each series keeps its last good copy and shows its age in words; degraded mode last exercised: date. 6. 900 KB total, 60 KB script; Galaxy A51-class device on 7 Mbps; all figures and the table render without script. 7. Self-hosted PMTiles extract, OSM attribution; district boundaries cut from BSC, December 2024; MapLibre 287 KB gz — flagged against a 60 KB script line; raster fallback under test; twin table reachable from the face. 8. On source closure: notice on the face for 6 months, series archived with last state at a fixed address, then removed from the face. 9. Owner: role; successor: role; record at /service. 10. Not promised: any live figure; any uptime percentage for the host; any platform-derived series.

The example is a shape and not a plan; the prototype's record will have different lines in it, and some of them will say "not yet".

12 · Where the choice is yours

The truths bind; these do not. Each is a decision the evidence informs and does not make, and Chapter 0 asks that they be recorded as choices so that nobody mistakes a studio preference for a finding.

Live or baked, panel by panel. The chapter's architecture is nightly, and Willison's own boundary — "at most a few times a day" — covers every public data source in section 6's table but the real-time flood feed. A studio may still want one live element: a count that moves while the reader watches. That element accepts the chain arithmetic of section 7, with its own dependency line in the record, and the rest of the page does not depend on it. How much liveness is worth that cost is the studio's to weigh.

Vector or raster. Section 10 priced the vector renderer at over two-fifths of the script budget and the raster library at a seventh of that. The vector map can be restyled to the house; the raster map cannot. Whether the recognisable face is worth the budget — and whether a raster fallback for the slowest quarter of phones is an acceptable version of it — is a creative decision and this book does not make it. It does require that the twin exist either way.

Which of the four tile supplies. Donated, agency, metered or self-hosted; each has an ending and a cost, and the right one depends on the studio's traffic, money and tolerance for owning a vintage. The record states which was chosen and what was agreed to.

Which objective, and how large a budget. "Eleven months in twelve" is the chapter's example. A studio may promise more and spend more attention, or less and say so. The reliability engineers' advice is to set it no higher than readers can tell, and to write it down before the year in which it is silently exceeded trains readers to expect the excess.

The notice the studio gives when it retires a series. The UK's aspiration is six months for a live interface; the contractual best case is twelve with exceptions; most of the studio's own suppliers promise none. What the studio promises its own readers is its choice, and the chapter's only requirement is that it be written in line 8 before the first series needs it.

Whether to call the platforms at all. Section 6 reported the terms. The decision is the prototype's and Chapter 10's, and it is listed here so that it is not mistaken for something this chapter settled.

Who reads the ticket. A role, the chapter says; but which role, with what second, at what hours, is an organisational choice the studio makes about itself.

13 · A nightlife illustration — method only

What follows shows how the method would be applied to a dashboard about where people go at night; it draws no conclusions about any place, names no venue and proposes no design. It is the service record's ten questions asked of a hypothetical page.

Suppose a studio proposes a page about a district — some monthly series by small area, a map because the design system asks for one, and one panel fed from a platform. Before any of it is built, the record is opened.

Line 1. Each monthly series is traced to its publisher's calendar: the period it describes, the lag to publication, how long it is revised. The platform panel is a different animal — daily or hourly, from a platform — and gets its own line with its own lifetime. The page's freshness lifetime is set from the slowest monthly series' frequency, counted from its publication date, plus a margin; and the four parts that will appear beside each figure — period, published, last revised, how often — are drafted now, in whatever words the designers choose.

Line 2. The build-time dependencies are listed with their pages open: the statistics interface with its beta label and 200 a minute; the geocoder with its four requests a minute for scheduled scripts; the boundary file with its date and two owners. The read-time dependencies are the host and, if the map is live-tiled, the tile supplier — and here the studio sees that it has a choice to make about line 7 before line 2 is complete. The platform panel's dependency is a platform whose terms forbid caching beyond "reasonable periods", reserve the right to block calls "not primarily in response to direct user actions", and may change "at any time". That is a dependency on terms, not supply, and it is written down as such; whether it is acceptable is the prototype's question, and the record leaves the line open rather than answering it.

Line 3. A scheduled job, at seventeen minutes past three, that fetches each monthly series, commits what it finds, and is safe to run twice. The job is in a public repository, so the studio writes beside it: may be disabled after sixty days without activity, and whether the job's own commits count is unconfirmed; the watch in line 4 is what catches this either way.

Line 4. An independent heartbeat, pinged after the job has confirmed that at least one series' date advanced, raising a ticket to a shared address, with a named second. The studio notes that the scheduler's own notifications go to whoever last edited the schedule, and routes them to the same address.

Line 5. "The newest monthly figure on the page was published no more than fifty days ago, eleven months in twelve." When a fetch fails, each series shows its last good figure with its age in words; the platform panel, if its platform refuses, shows the last successful fetch and its time — for as long as the terms recorded in line 2 allow it to be kept — and never nothing. The degraded mode is exercised on launch day by breaking the job on purpose, and the date is written down.

Line 6. The page is opened, before launch, on a four-year-old mid-range phone on a throttled connection. The budget is written down. The figures and the table are in the HTML and appear before the map's script has been fetched.

Line 7. The map's supply is chosen with its ending in view, and the boundaries are the district's own, cut from a generalised product, dated, with their two-owner attribution. The renderer's weight is measured against the budget; if it is most of the script allowance, the studio decides — a creative decision, recorded as one — whether the restyled face is worth it or whether a raster version serves the slowest quarter. The twin table exists at launch, not later.

Line 8. The studio writes, before anything has closed, what happens when a monthly source retires or the platform withdraws: the notice shown on the face, the archive address at which the series' last state remains, and the day the tile comes off. It writes the same for the page as a whole.

Line 9. A role, a second, and the address of this record.

Line 10. Not promised: a live count of anything; an uptime figure for the free host; any series derived from a platform whose terms forbid deriving it.

The record is published beside the page. Nothing in it says what the district is like, and nothing in it is a design; where it names a form — a table, a set of words beside a figure — the form is the designers' to choose. It is the method of keeping the promise the page's first screen makes the moment it appears: that what it shows is current, and that someone is keeping it so.

The rules

Kind and tier as in Chapter 0. "Standard" here includes protocol specifications, licences and published platform terms, which bind in the way a standard does. "Adjacent domain" here means reliability engineering, web standards and performance research rather than cultural display. Every limit, price and term in this table is as read on 6 October 2026 and carries that date.

Rule Why Kind Tier Source
Every dashboard that intends to be read next year carries, published beside it, the service record: freshness promise, dependencies, refresh, watch and alarm, availability and degraded mode, budget and device, map supply, retirement, owner, not-done A dashboard is "a digital service" to be "continually" managed; the promise its first screen makes has to be kept by something Standard + Nightlife Culture for the record as a whole Fixed (sequence); what each line says: Adaptable Analysis Function 2026; this chapter §11
Each series states the period it describes, the date published, the date last revised and its declared frequency; "last updated" alone is never shown "Always make it clear which dates or period"; the catalogue standards separate the dates and the frequency; a date without a frequency does not say whether the figure is late; an absent date means one of three things Standard (the period); Nightlife Culture (the four parts) Fixed (requirement) (period); Adaptable (house default) (four parts) Analysis Function 2026; DCAT 3; DCAT-AP 3; DCMI; ONS revisions policy
The page's freshness lifetime is declared in days, compared against the data's date on the page itself, and shown in words a reader can read "A 'stale' response is one where" its age has exceeded its lifetime; "The oldest data is no older than Y" is a checkable sentence Standard + Practice (adjacent domain) Fixed (requirement) RFC 9111 §4.2; SRE workbook
A change to the data carries a change note saying what changed and when; the page is never marked updated without saying what "Do not say the page has been updated without saying what has changed" Standard Fixed GOV.UK change notes; Analysis Function 2026
Revisions and corrections are distinguished and dated; a figure open to revision says until when "A revision is a scheduled change"; "A correction is an unplanned revision … because of the identification of an error" Standard Fixed ONS revisions policy; Code of Practice 3.0 §3.9
Every dependency is recorded with its stated limit, its terms, the notice it has promised, and the date its page was read; it is marked as needed at build time or at read time, and as a dependency on supply or on terms The open licence "does not guarantee the continued supply"; the platform terms address storing, deriving, combining and scheduled calling clause by clause Standard Fixed (requirement) OGL v3.0; the platform terms §6
The stated rate limit is the real limit; the refresh job never relies on capacity beyond it, respects Retry-After, keeps a clock per interface, and backs off with jitter "you should not let your users go over the limits you set even if you have spare capacity"; "Always use randomized exponential backoff" Standard + Practice Fixed GDS service levels; RFC 6585; ONS bots; SRE ch. 22
A beta-labelled or no-service-level interface is treated as able to change without notice, whatever its publisher "there may occasionally be breaking changes"; beta "where your users are expecting breaking changes" need not be given the six months Standard Adaptable (house default) ONS developer hub; GDS live API guidance
Response headers announcing deprecation and sunset are read by the refresh job and raise a ticket The statistics office signals retirement by Deprecation, Sunset and Link headers, then 404; a client reading only the body cannot see it coming Standard + Practice Adaptable (which interfaces signal); Fixed (that the job reads them) ONS retirement guide
Platform interfaces are used only within their written terms; a series derived from a platform whose terms forbid deriving it is not built III.13: "Do not analyze … creating new or derived listenership metrics"; "non-commercial use only" Standard Fixed Spotify Developer Policy; Skiddle; Last.fm; Ticketmaster
Whether to call a platform at all is a recorded decision made with its terms open, not a default A dependency on terms is theirs to withdraw Nightlife Culture Adaptable This chapter §6, §12
Fetch at build time, not at read time; the reader's page depends on its host alone, and every other dependency is the night's job's "A service cannot be more available than the intersection of all its critical dependencies"; ten at 99.9% is 3.65 days a year Practice (adjacent domain) + chapter's arithmetic Adaptable (house default); Adaptable for a declared live element Treynor et al. 2017; SRE availability table; Willison 2021
On a failed fetch the last good copy is kept and shown with its age; the page is never blanked "Invalidating or emptying local state as a result of a failed refresh" is a named anti-pattern; stale-if-error; "Stale data is almost always better than incorrect data" Standard + Practice Fixed AWS REL05-BP01; RFC 5861; SRE workbook
Each series is its own compartment; a closed source empties one panel and not the page "if one element fails, the others continue to function"; "Integration points are the number-one killer of systems" Practice (adjacent domain) Fixed (requirement) Azure bulkhead; Nygard; Fowler
The degraded mode is exercised before launch and on a schedule, and the date recorded "the code path you never use is the code path that (often) doesn't work" Practice (adjacent domain) Fixed (sequence); the schedule of later exercises: Adaptable SRE ch. 22
The availability objective is set in the data's terms, written before launch, and not higher than readers can tell "100% is the wrong reliability target"; "Users build on the reality of what you offer, rather than what you say you'll supply" Practice (adjacent domain) Adaptable (house default); Adaptable in value SRE ch. 1, 3, 4
A page that loads with the wrong or stale content is counted as an error, so the watch checks the data's date and not the status code Errors include "an HTTP 200 success response, but coupled with the wrong content" Practice (adjacent domain) Fixed SRE ch. 6
The watch is independent of the job and the scheduler, pinged by the job after the effect is confirmed, recorded as a dependency in its own right, and its ticket goes to a role with a named second Schedules are delayed, "may be dropped", are disabled after 60 quiet days and notify "the user who last modified the cron syntax"; "monitoring of the effect of cron jobs" Standard (platform) + Practice Fixed (requirement) GitHub docs; SRE ch. 24; Healthchecks.io
Signals are sorted into alerts, tickets and logs; a failed refresh is a ticket; the one alert is the page lying about its date "Every page should be actionable" (a page being a pager alert); "humans should be notified only when they need to take action" Practice (adjacent domain) Fixed SRE ch. 1, 6
The refresh job is idempotent and, in doubt, skipped rather than doubled; scheduled off the hour "we favor skipping launches rather than risking double launches"; "High load times include the start of every hour" Practice + Standard (platform) Fixed (requirement) SRE ch. 24; SRE workbook; GitHub docs
Every fetch is committed to a version history so that any figure's vintage is recoverable by date "records changes to that resource over time in the commit history"; a living series owes its archive Practice Fixed (requirement) Willison 2020; Chapter 4
The free tier's limits are recorded in the service record as design constraints with a date, and no availability is assumed of it 25 MiB per asset; 1 GB per site; paused at the credit cap; no commitment could be established Standard (platform) Fixed (requirement) Cloudflare; GitHub Pages; Netlify
The cost of a live element is computed with the studio's own expected numbers before it is chosen Billing is per initialisation; "A map load is counted every time Mapbox GL JS initializes" Standard (price list) Adaptable Mapbox pricing; this chapter's arithmetic
The page is budgeted for the seventy-fifth-percentile phone and network, not the builder's, and tested on one "15-25% as fast as those carried by programmers and their bosses"; "a good threshold to measure is the 75th percentile" Practice (a reasoned model) + Evidence (the Almanac's medians) Fixed (sequence) Russell 2024; web.dev; Web Almanac
Figures and the table are in the HTML and shown before any script runs; the page is not a single-page application "Government services should be functional using only HTML" (a standard for government services, adopted here); "1.1% of people aren't getting JavaScript enhancements (1 in 93)", four-fifths involuntarily Standard (adopted) + Evidence (one measurement) Fixed (requirement) GOV.UK Service Manual; Herlihy 2013
Total weight is held within Russell's five-second budget for the baseline phone — about 1.3 MiB with half script, 2.5 MiB with almost none — and the vector renderer is counted against the script line before it is chosen "650KiB of JavaScript" or "100KiB of JavaScript" at five seconds; the renderer is about 287 KB gzipped Practice (a reasoned model) Adaptable (house default); Adaptable in figure Russell 2024; Bundlephobia (secondary)
The "53% abandon" figure is not used without its date, source and wording, and preferably not at all Vendor research, 2016, n=3.7K opt-in sites, "likely to be abandoned" Reading Fixed Google 2016
The map's tile supply is one of four named kinds, recorded with what was agreed to: cache, attribution, logo, offline, non-commercial, pause "Our tile servers are not [free]"; "no SLA or guarantee"; "service will pause"; "Offline use is not permitted" Standard (policy) Fixed (requirement) OSMF; OS; MapTiler; Mapbox; Protomaps
Boundary files are the generalised product appropriate to the scale, cut to the area shown, with their date and two-owner attribution; a boundary vintage is pinned and stated BFC about 128 MB against BSC about 1.7 MB in the same record; "as at December 2024"; "Contains both Ordnance Survey and ONS Intellectual Property Rights" Standard Fixed ONS digital boundaries; Open Geography Portal; Decision Book DTA-05/06
Simplification is checked for vanished small polygons before publication "At high simplification, small polygons can disappear entirely" Practice Fixed (requirement) Mapshaper
Every map has a non-map twin — the same figures by the same places as a table — reachable before the script; pan and zoom have buttons; the sequential ramp is short "make sure the data is available in another format such as a downloadable data table"; WCAG 2.5.1 and 2.5.7 examples; five blues Standard Fixed Analysis Function colours; WCAG 2.2; WAI complex images
The notice the studio gives when retiring a series, and the archive address, are written before the first series needs them; a retired series stays reachable "Do this at least six months before retirement"; "keeping data and metadata available, with a clear note that it is no longer updated"; "This publication was withdrawn on" Standard Fixed (sequence); period and content: Adaptable Analysis Function 2026; GOV.UK withdrawal; Code of Practice 3.0 §10.7
The owner of the ticket is a role with a successor, and the record says where it lives "not an appropriate project for a single person"; 65% of projects at truck factor ≤ 2 Standard + Evidence [abstract or summary only] Adaptable (house default) Analysis Function 2026; Avelino et al. 2016 [abstract or summary only]
The record's last line states what the dashboard does not promise "Users build on the reality of what you offer, rather than what you say you'll supply" Practice (adjacent domain) Fixed (requirement) SRE ch. 4

What proves a break works

The test for whether a departure from one of this chapter's rules has cost anything is the same shape as the earlier chapters', with a different clock: take one of the page's sources away, or stop its refresh, and open it on the baseline phone a week later. If a reader who was not in the room can tell, from the face alone, how old each figure is, which series is missing and why, and that someone knows — the break has cost nothing. If the page is blank, or shows a date that is the page's rather than the data's, or shows last month's figures as this month's with no sign, the break has failed, however well the page loaded.

For a departure that adds a live element, the test is the chain arithmetic done with real numbers and written in the record. For a vector map, it is the renderer's weight counted against the script budget on the baseline device, with the twin table present. For a platform dependency, it is the clause that permits what the dashboard does, quoted in the record beside the series. For a studio of one, it is the name of the second.

What this chapter could not settle

  • Eventbrite's developer site, the OS plans page and the ONS geography portal could not be read; the search-endpoint removal and the OS free allowances could not be verified. Recorded as unverified; no figure printed from memory; the failure used as evidence in section 9.
  • No open primary source for the "60–80% of lifecycle cost is maintenance" figure; GAO measures spending, not lifecycle. The chapter asserts only that operating costs more than making, on GAO and practitioner authority.
  • No measured evidence that stale dashboards cost trust; no measured study of UK open-data staleness; no measured bytes-per-view for a map. Said so three times; each is a test for the prototype or for users.
  • No design system reached (GOV.UK, Carbon, PatternFly) says a dashboard should show its last refresh. The rule is grounded in the catalogue standards, the protocol and one product's practice; precedent marked thin.
  • The Decision Book treats empty and error states as Decorative (DSH-21); this chapter holds that the degraded state is Fixed and only its look Decorative. Logged as a conflict, not resolved.
  • The Decision Book has no rules on freshness display, dependencies and terms, refresh, watch and alarm, availability objective, budget and device, progressive enhancement, tile supply, or retirement. This chapter's rules table stands in; logged as a candidate chapter.
  • The design system has no map component, no freshness component, no degraded-tile state, no byte budget. Logged; design decisions not made.

Checklist

  • The service record exists, is dated, and is published beside the page
  • Each series shows period described, date published, date last revised, declared frequency
  • The page's freshness lifetime is declared in days and compared against the data's date on the face, in words
  • Change notes say what changed and when; revisions and corrections distinguished
  • Every dependency listed with limit, terms, notice promised, date read; marked supply or terms; marked build-time or read-time
  • Beta and no-service-level interfaces treated as able to change without notice
  • The refresh job respects Retry-After, keeps a clock per interface, backs off with jitter, reads Deprecation/Sunset headers
  • No series derived from a platform whose terms forbid it; any platform call a recorded decision
  • Fetch at build time; the reader's page depends on the host alone, or any live element is declared with its own line
  • On fetch failure: last good copy kept and shown with its age; never blanked
  • Each series in its own compartment
  • Degraded mode exercised before launch; date recorded; scheduled re-test
  • Availability objective in the data's terms, written before launch
  • The watch checks that the data's date advanced, independent of the job, pinged after the effect, recorded as a dependency; ticket to a role; second named
  • Scheduler's own notifications (sent to the last editor of the schedule) known and forwarded to the role
  • Job idempotent; skip over double; scheduled off the hour; the 60-day disabling known and covered by the watch
  • Every fetch committed to a version history
  • Free-tier limits recorded with date; no availability assumed
  • Cost of any live element computed with the studio's numbers
  • Budgeted and tested on a seventy-fifth-percentile phone and network
  • Figures and table in the HTML, shown before script; not a single-page application
  • Total weight within the five-second budget for the baseline phone; renderer counted against the script line
  • "53%" not used without date, source and wording
  • Tile supply named; what was agreed to recorded
  • Boundary product generalised to scale and cut to the area; vintage pinned and stated; two-owner attribution
  • Simplification checked for vanished small polygons
  • Non-map twin exists at launch; pan and zoom buttons; short sequential ramp
  • Retirement notice period and archive address written; retired series stay reachable
  • Owner is a role; successor named; record's address known
  • The "not done" line is filled

Words this chapter uses

  • A tile is one square of a map, served separately so that only the squares in view are fetched; a dashboard's panels are called panels here, never tiles.
  • A heartbeat is a signal a scheduled job sends to say it ran, and the service that listens for it. Chapter 1 and the glossary also use the word for the visible age of a dashboard's data; this chapter means the job's signal.
  • A page, in the reliability engineers' vocabulary quoted in section 7, is an alert sent to a person's pager, not a web page.
  • Sizes in KB and MB are decimal; KiB and MiB, used by one source, are binary (1 KiB = 1,024 bytes) and are quoted as written.

Three of this chapter's founding texts could not be read in full — RFC 9110's Retry-After and conditional-request sections, the Data on the Web Best Practices on freshness and preservation (BP21, BP22, BP27, BP28), and DCAT 3's frequency definition — and the sibling and profile texts that stood in for them are named below. Grouped by section. Each entry says the kind of source and how it was read. "At source" means the link was opened on 6 October 2026 and a second reading confirmed the quotation; "spot-checked" means it was re-opened the same day; "verified" means it was independently re-traced. "(read once)" marks a sentence seen on a single pass, so marked in the body. "Secondary" means the text reached the chapter through a named reproduction. "Unreached" means the source was sought and could not be opened; nothing is quoted from it. Pages that carry no date of their own are so noted; every limit, price and term is as of 6 October 2026.

09Measuring a vibe

A vibe is three constructs, never one number; a felt measure is a distribution with its sample; who was asked is part of the measure.

Dashboard Design · Part 2: The felt layer

In this chapter

  • The 60-second version

Reading this chapter. This is one chapter of Dashboard Design, Nightlife Culture's research book on how evidence becomes a display a reader can trust, read and act on. The studio ("the house" in some chapters) is Nightlife Culture, a creative policy studio; the brief is its founder Carly Heath's commission for the book, and her eight ways a dashboard fails, the failure register, run through it. The Vibe Map, the studio's prototype for showing a place's nightlife culture, appears only as an illustration, never as a specification. "Version 1" is the book's archived first draft, whose positions this version re-tests against the sources. Every rule carries a kind (where it comes from: Standard, Evidence, Reading, Practice or Nightlife Culture) and a tier (how firm it is: Fixed, Adaptable or Decorative); Chapter 0 explains both, and the three senses of Fixed: a requirement that can be checked, a sequence whose order is the hard line, and a statement of the record. A dagger (†) marks a source read at the authors' abstract or summary only; "secondary" a quotation reached through a named reproduction; "(read once)" a quotation returned on a single reading and not confirmed by a second. Chapter 0 holds the glossary of the words the chapters share; each chapter lists its own coinages before its sources.

The question

How might one measure a vibe — a felt quality of a place: its atmosphere, its welcome, its liveliness, the sense that something is happening here — in a way that is evidence and not decoration; by which families of method; what does each need and what can each claim; and how is any such measure validated, above all by whether the people who make the place recognise themselves in it? The book does not answer this for any place. It sets out the methods, their requirements and their failure modes, so that the prototype can choose among them knowing what each costs and what each can say.

The 60-second version

"Vibe" is not one construct. The literatures that have tried to measure a felt quality of place split it three ways, and the three have different methods and different validation histories. As something perceived, it has an international standard: the soundscape series defines its object as the "acoustic environment as perceived or experienced and/or understood by a person or people, in context" (secondary), asks people in situ to rate eight attributes — "Pleasant, Chaotic, Vibrant, Uneventful, Calm, Annoying, Eventful, and Monotonous" — and whose analysts argue for reporting the spread of answers rather than a median; "vibrant" is not a primary dimension but a derived diagonal between pleasant and eventful, and the one study of how people use the scales found "a general non-equidistant interpretation of the scales, particularly on the vibrant-monotonous direction". As something made — by lighting, sound, welcome, staging — it has a qualitative protocol whose author calls it "extremely difficult to be analytically precise". As something in excess of both, its theorists offer no number, and the one dancefloor ethnography reached warns that felt togetherness "may hide exclusions and injustices".

So the canonical truths: a vibe is named as a construct and a register before it is measured, and the three registers are never collapsed into one number; a felt measure is a distribution of people's answers, reported with its spread and its sample, never a point alone; who was asked, who answered and who was missing are part of the measure; participation is evidence of what participants placed, not of the place, until selection is accounted for, and it becomes co-production only when what it changed is shown; co-presence is not a tie and a trace is not a feeling — each is read for what it records, and a derived signal is validated against the people before it stands for them; a new felt measure is validated from five sources of evidence, and recognition by the people described supplies two of them and not the other three; when the felt and the counted disagree the disagreement is reported, not resolved by preferring the number. Beneath any felt measure sits a measure record, and the measure's first validation is a conversation with the people it describes.

Four families of method could evidence any of the three, and each has a known failure. Participatory methods — maps people mark, self-placed distributions, stories of change — are strongest on legitimacy and weakest on who turns up: in internet mapping "Mapping effort was highest in sampling groups whose livelihoods were closely related to the purpose of the study"; the most-significant-change method's own manual lists understanding "the average experience of participants" among the things it does less efficiently than other methods; a visible self-placement narrows as people see each other's — "even mild social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect" — and an open vote records the organising capacity of whoever arrives ("Boaty McBoatface topped the list with over 124,000 votes"). Relational measures — who is there with whom — rest on a duality the founders named, and on a distinction they also named: co-presence is not a tie. The strongest test found, across six datasets from five settings with both kinds of data, concluded that co-presence "is not easily usable to build in a reliable and systematic fashion surrogate contact data" for simulating contagion. Traces of behaviour explain a great deal of variance in a proxy its authors did not validate — "as much as 77% of the variability of district activity is explained by simple structural and static features", where activity is phone connections and "has been assumed to be a good proxy for city's vitality" — and the people in the trace are not the people in the place. Signals read as feelings — text sentiment, images, sound, song features — track surveys weakly or inconsistently unless fitted to them (dictionary methods "yielded inconsistent county-level well-being measurements"; the founders of the hedonometer wrote "we quantify only how people appear to others"), and the authoritative review of faces found "no unique mapping between a configuration of facial movements and instances of an emotion category" — a finding the EU has since written into law as the reason for a prohibition.

The method closest to asking the person at the moment is experience sampling by location, and the US National Academies say momentary methods "are often regarded as the gold standard for capturing experiential states" while recommending they stay "experimental" in official surveys. The official precedent for building a felt measure properly is the national wellbeing programme: four questions on a 0–10 scale after "an extensive programme of question testing" [read once], reported as bands as well as means because "relying only on average ratings might mask important differences in how people rate their well-being", not published "if the sample size they are based on is fewer than 50", within a framework developed from "over 34,000 responses" to a public question about what matters.

Validation of a new felt measure is argued, not declared: "Validity refers to the degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses of tests", from five named sources of evidence, and "Face validity is at best a very weak kind of evidence". So "the scene recognises itself" is necessary and not sufficient: it is content and response-process evidence from the people described, plus legitimacy about who chose what counts, and it still owes the other three. When the felt and the counted disagree, that is a reportable result — "Discordance occurs if the qualitative and quantitative findings are inconsistent, incongruous, contradict, conflict, or disagree with each other" — and the method pre-commits to reporting it.

1 · What the word is asked to carry

The brief asks: "Instead of measuring 'feeling of safety', why are we not instead measuring the vibe that night time communities create?" Before a method can be chosen, the chapter has to say what the word is being asked to carry, because the literatures that have tried to measure something like it do not agree on what it is, and their disagreement is the first finding.

Three senses, from three literatures

Version 1 of this book split the vibe into three registers and held that they are never collapsed. The split is re-tested here against the sources rather than assumed, and it holds, with one correction: the perceived register's word "vibrant" turns out to be a derived quantity, not a measured one (section 3).

The first sense is atmosphere as something made. Gernot Böhme's founding paper could not be opened; what the one reachable study of his method quotes from it is "aesthetic work", which Böhme describes as "'making' atmospheres through work on an object" (secondary, via Michels). Michels, taking this into an empirical programme, writes that "Aesthetic work can be described as a process through which material components are selected and shaped" — in a venue, to take the chapter's own examples, the set, the lights, the sound, the door, the welcome. In this sense a vibe is produced by identifiable people doing skilled work, and the work is observable.

The second sense is atmosphere as something perceived. The International Organization for Standardization's soundscape series defines its object as the "acoustic environment as perceived or experienced and/or understood by a person or people, in context" — the wording is reached here through a protocol paper that quotes it, since ISO's own text is closed (secondary) — and the definition's weight falls on perceived and in context: the thing measured is not the sound but people's experience of it where they stand. Section 3 shows that this is the one sense with an instrument, a standard and a validation history, and that one of its eight attributes is "Vibrant".

The third sense is atmosphere as something in excess of both. Ben Anderson's 2009 paper was also closed; what Michels quotes of it is that atmospheres "emanate from the assembling of the human bodies, discursive bodies, non-human bodies, and all the other bodies that make up everyday situations" and are "always in the process of emerging and transforming" (secondary). This is the sense in which a room has a feeling that no one person made and no one rating captures. Its theorists do not offer a measure, and the chapter does not invent one for them.

Two further literatures use the word's neighbours and are read for their methods. Urban studies has vitality, from Jane Jacobs's four conditions — "(1) mixed use, (2) small blocks, (3) aged buildings, and (4) a sufficient concentration of buildings" (secondary, via Sung et al.; the book itself was unreached) — operationalised in Seoul as pedestrian activity, in Barcelona as a map of the conditions, and in six Italian cities as mobile-phone connections; section 8 reads the Italian study. Marketing has atmospherics, from Philip Kotler's 1973 coinage (reached only in tertiary form and not quoted), Mary Jo Bitner's "servicescape" framework for "exploring the impact of physical surroundings on the behaviors of" customers and employees (†), and a line of scales for stadiums, festivals and destinations. Destination-image research made, thirty years ago, a point this chapter will return to: the components of a place's image are "attribute-based images, holistic impressions, and functional, psychological, unique and common characteristics" (†), and "a combination of structured and unstructured methodologies" is needed to reach them — the holistic and the unique parts do not come through rating scales alone.

The construct before the proxy

Chapter 5's first instruction was to define the construct before the proxy, and this chapter's sources show what happens when the order is reversed. Thomas Frank's 2012 essay on the planning word "vibrant" found that "no one seems to be exactly sure what vibrancy is", and quotes the funder consortium that had made "Vibrancy Indicators" its measure of success saying, on its own website, "While we are not able to measure vibrancy directly" — and continuing, in Frank's quotation, that "we believe that the measures we are assembling, taken together, will provide useful insights into the nature and location of especially vibrant places within cities" (Frank quoting ArtPlace; Markusen quotes the same sentence with a different last word, and the funder's page was not sought). Ann Markusen, the same year, named the problem: "A fuzzy concept is one that means different things to different people, but flourishes precisely because of its imprecision", and "In any particular place, changes in the proposed indicators will not be attributable to the creative placemaking intervention alone" [read once]. A word that flourishes because it is imprecise is a word that any indicator can be attached to and none can be held to.

The soundscape researchers' vocabulary is the chapter's corrective. Francesco Aletta and colleagues distinguish descriptors — "measures of how people perceive the acoustic environment" — from indicators, "measures used to predict the value of a soundscape descriptor", and from indices, "single value scales derived from either descriptors or indicators that allow for comparison across soundscapes" (the first two at source; the third secondary, via Mitchell et al.). Read across the four families below, the distinction does most of the work: the participatory and experience-sampling methods produce descriptors — people's own reports; traces, signals and amenity counts produce indicators at best — things that may predict a descriptor, and that have to be shown to before they stand for one; and anything that collapses either into one number is an index, with Chapter 5's price list attached. A vibe, measured, is a descriptor. Everything else stands for it on evidence or does not stand for it.

Why not "feeling of safety"

The brief's contrast case is worth one paragraph of method, because it is not only a different construct. The official measure of feeling safe — the crime survey's question about walking alone after dark — could not be reached in its current wording (the questionnaires could not be read; the chapter does not print it from memory). What could be reached is the official statistics office's own caution that "individuals' perceptions of crime on a national level do not typically match well to reality", and the criminological record of testing the question inside the official survey. Farrall and colleagues' 1997 methodological study "raised the possibility that the fear of crime has been significantly misrepresented", concluding that "our understanding of the fear of crime is a product of the way it has been researched rather than the way it is" (†). Gray, Jackson and Farrall, running new frequency-and-intensity questions beside the old ones in the 2003–4 survey, found that "few people experience specific events of worry on a frequent basis", that the old questions "magnify the everyday experience of fear", and that worry about crime "is often best seen as a diffuse anxiety about risk rather than any pattern of everyday concerns over personal safety" (†). The office's own note records that the feeling-safe questions "are not included on the year ending 2017 and year ending 2018 questionnaires". So the contrast case is a warning rather than a foil: a single felt item, asked for decades, was shown, by new questions run beside it in the official survey, to "magnify" what it reported. A vibe question asked without the same tests would be in no better position, whatever its intention.

2 · Why people believe what they believe

Belief one: a vibe cannot be measured, so it is decoration

The register in which it cannot be counted is one of three. The perceived register has an international standard, an eight-item questionnaire and a protocol that collects "a minimum of 100 responses" per location. What cannot be done is to measure the three as one. Section 1 and 3.

Belief two: a vibe can be measured, so give it a score

The standard's own analysts argue against collapsing a place to a median and for reporting the "percent of people likely to perceive" it one way or another; the national wellbeing measure reports bands because averages "might mask important differences". A felt measure is a distribution or it is misleading. Section 3 and 11.

Belief three: ask the people and you have the answer

Ask which people. In participatory mapping, effort is highest among those whose livelihoods depend on the result; people mark near home; the recruitment route that raises response lowers data quality; and "those who choose to participate are frequently quite unrepresentative of any larger public". Section 5.

Belief four: if they came together, they are connected

Co-presence is "(by definition) much denser than" contact, and surrogate networks built from it are "only partially able to identify the most central nodes". Who is in the room together is first a fact about the pool. Section 7.

Belief five: the data already knows — count the phones, the check-ins, the posts

A trace is evidence of what it records. The best-known vitality model explains 77 per cent of a proxy its authors call "assumed"; geotagged posts are "approximately 1%" of posts and skew by income, age, urbanity and ethnicity; perceived and objectively measured neighbourhood variables "exhibited low agreement". Section 5 and 8.

Belief six: sentiment analysis measures feeling

Its founders say it measures "how people appear to others". Dictionary methods were "inconsistent" at county scale; the models that worked were trained on the survey they were meant to replace; the face is "neither reliably expressed through nor perceived from a common set of facial movements". Section 9.

Belief seven: recognition is validation

"Face validity is at best a very weak kind of evidence." Recognition by the people described is necessary — it is response-process and content evidence, and it is legitimacy — and it supplies two of the five sources of validity evidence, not the other three. Section 12.

Belief eight: when the number and the feeling disagree, the number is right

Mixed-methods doctrine names the disagreement discordance, treats it as a result, and lists "challenging the validity of the constructs" among the responses. Section 13.

3 · The perceived register: the one with an instrument

Of the three senses, one has been turned into a standard, and the chapter reads it closely because it is the nearest thing that exists to a tested way of asking people how a place feels.

The standard and its lineage

ISO 12913-1:2014 "provides a definition and a conceptual framework of soundscape" and "explains factors relevant for measurement and reporting in soundscape studies". Part 2 (2018) "specifies requirements and supporting information on data collection and reporting"; its methods, as the protocol paper describes them, are "soundwalks combined with questionnaires (Methods A and B) and narrative interviews (Method C)" (secondary), and its questionnaire asks respondents to rate the present sound environment on eight attributes — "Pleasant, Chaotic, Vibrant, Uneventful, Calm, Annoying, Eventful, and Monotonous" — on a "5-point Likert scale" from strongly disagree to strongly agree. Part 3, on data analysis, was withdrawn on 8 May 2025 and replaced by a 2025 second edition; anything citing the 2019 analysis standard as current is out of date, and the chapter could read neither edition's text.

The eight attributes are not arbitrary. They come from a 2010 listening experiment in which "One hundred listeners measured 50 excerpts of binaural recordings of urban outdoor soundscapes on 116 attribute scales", yielding "three components: Pleasantness, eventfulness, and familiarity, explaining 50, 18 and 6% of the total variance, respectively" (†) — the listeners being "100 students" in Sweden, a later paper notes. Three components, of which the third was dropped downstream; the two that remain are placed at right angles, and the eight attributes sit around them at forty-five-degree intervals. That geometry descends from James Russell's 1980 circumplex of affect — "affective concepts fall in a circle in the following order": pleasure, excitement, arousal, distress, displeasure, depression, sleepiness, relaxation — built on "36" and "34" undergraduates and "343 male and female students" at one Canadian university, which Russell himself said "accounts for a substantial proportion, but not all, of the variance in self-reported affective states"; and from his 1981 study with Ward and Pratt of "105 commonly used adjectives descriptive of the affective quality of molar physical environments", rated by "323 subjects", which found two bipolar factors of "pleasing and arousing quality" (†). "Vibrant", in other words, is the great-grandchild of "exciting": the pleasant-and-aroused corner of a circle drawn around student ratings in 1980.

What the measure does with the answers

The analysis standard (2019 edition; formulae reached through the authors' software tutorial, secondary) turns the eight ratings into two coordinates. Pleasantness is the sum of (pleasant − annoying), of cos 45° × (calm − chaotic) and of cos 45° × (vibrant − monotonous), scaled to lie between −1 and 1; eventfulness is (eventful − uneventful) plus cos 45° × (chaotic − calm) plus cos 45° × (vibrant − monotonous), scaled the same way. Two things follow that a builder should see before borrowing the word. First, "vibrant" has no coordinate of its own: the vibrant–monotonous difference loads positively on both axes, so vibrant is, by construction, the diagonal where pleasant meets eventful. A place can land on the vibrant diagonal by the arithmetic even where few respondents endorsed the "Vibrant" item itself. Second, the arithmetic assumes that respondents treat the five points of each scale as equally spaced and the eight attributes as evenly placed around the circle — and the one study that tested this, on "984 soundscape assessments across 11 urban locations in London", found that "it is still unclear whether the metrics of the scales are consistently interpreted during a typical assessment task" and that "The overall results show a general non-equidistant interpretation of the scales, particularly on the vibrant-monotonous direction". The weakest axis of the standard instrument is exactly the one the brief's word sits on.

The protocol's authors have made the argument that matters most for a dashboard. Against describing a location by a single average, they compute the coordinates "for each individual response" — "rather than calculating the median response to each PA in the location, then calculating the circumplex coordinates" (PA is the protocol's abbreviation for a perceptual attribute, one of the eight) — and urge speaking of the "percent of people likely to perceive" a place as pleasant or vibrant. The standard's recommendation, as its analysts report it, is the median; theirs is the distribution. A place does not have a vibe score; it has a spread of people's perceptions, and the spread is the finding.

How it is collected, and by whom

The Soundscape Indices protocol is the fullest worked example of the perceived register in the field. It pairs "a Recording Stage to collect audio-visual recordings" with "a Questionnaire Stage to collect in situ soundscape assessments via a questionnaire method paired with acoustic data collection", and "Typically, a minimum of 100 responses are collected at each location during multiple 2–5-h sessions" — no rationale for the hundred is given — with recordings "taken next to each respondent", building a database of "nearly 4000 participants' responses from 59 locations in 10 cities and provinces across the UK, China, Spain, and Italy". Recruitment is to "Approach participants and ask if they would be willing to take part in a research study": the people asked are the people present, which is a strength (they are the ones experiencing the place) and a selection (section 5 returns to who is present). And "there are questions that cannot be practically addressed in situ". Translation is its own validation programme: the standard "does not provide official translations in languages other than English" (secondary), a dataset of "17,441 samples, including 645 participants, for 27 recordings, in 19 languages" exists to supply them, and the Thai team's warning generalises beyond translation — small expert panels "could lead to translations with psycholinguistic meanings that, in a non-expert setting, deviate or distort from that of the source language" (†). A word that means one thing to the people who chose it may mean another to the people asked.

Other perceived constructs that were tested before they were counted

The soundscape standard is not alone. The environmental psychology of place attachment offers the cleanest case of a felt bond with a place being tested before being counted. Scannell and Gifford's framework — "a three-dimensional, person–process–place organizing framework", whose psychological dimension "includes the affective, cognitive, and behavioral components of attachment" — is offered to "create operational definitions for quantitative studies, guide semi-structured interviews for qualitative studies", with the instruction that "One approach would be to develop a place attachment measurement instrument, and explore the factors that emerge". Williams and Vaske did that. Their twelve-item measure splits into "Place dependence (a functional attachment)" — "the importance of a place in providing features and conditions that support specific goals or desired activities" — and "Place identity (an emotional attachment)" — "the symbolic importance of a place as a repository for emotions and relationships that give meaning and purpose to life" — with example items like "I feel 'X' is a part of me." Across four samples (students rating recreation sites; "Shenandoah National Park (n = 2005)"), "The Cronbach alphas for both place identity (range = 0.84 to 0.94) and place dependence (range = 0.81 to 0.94)" supported the two dimensions (an alpha is the conventional index of how far a scale's items agree with one another, running from 0 to 1), and the analysis "suggested that each attachment dimension can be reliably measured with as few as four questionnaire items". Then the candour that a builder should copy: "A general limitation of previous on-site place attachment studies is the relatively low variance and high scores observed on attachment." Ask people who are already there how attached they are, and most say very. The ceiling is in the sampling, not the place.

The UK's own official felt-place item is simpler and less tested. The Community Life Survey asks "how strongly do you feel you belong to your immediate neighbourhood?", with "By neighbourhood we mean a few minutes walking distance from your home" — and, for satisfaction, "Please think of the area within 15 to 20 minutes' walking distance from your home". The question defines its place for the respondent, at two scales, in walking minutes, which is a discipline worth borrowing. Its 2024/25 headline — "62% of adults felt they belonged 'very strongly' or 'fairly strongly' to their immediate neighbourhood", from "177,749" respondents by "Address-Based Online Surveying (ABOS)" at an individual response rate of "19.86%" — is quoted as a method precedent and not as a finding about anywhere. As far as could be found, the technical report describes no cognitive testing of the belonging item and no mode-effect analysis; an absence claim is weaker than a presence claim, and it is recorded as such.

What the perceived register teaches, then, is this. It can be asked. When it is asked well, the question defines its place, uses a tested set of attributes, pairs the rating with the moment and the conditions, collects a hundred answers at a location, and reports the spread. When it is asked badly, it inherits an untested word, averages a room into a point, and measures the ceiling of whoever was already there.

4 · The made register and the excess register
