The cut-points are grounded two ways: "qualitative testing has shown the mid-point of the scale (5) acts as an important cut-off for respondents for assessing their own well-being, with responses below five seen largely as a negative response", and "policy-makers are particularly interested in people reporting the highest or lowest levels". The purpose, in the quality report, is "a summary measure of well-being through the mean and an indication of inequality through the dispersion of the results". This is section 3's finding — a felt measure is a distribution — adopted as official practice, with the bands chosen by asking respondents where the scale turns negative for them.

The rules for small places

The official rules for publishing a felt measure for a small area are exact, and they are Chapter 6's small-number discipline applied to feeling. "Estimates of personal well-being are not published if the sample size they are based on is fewer than 50, or their numerator is less than 5." Precision is graded by the coefficient of variation: "If the CV is less than or equal to 5%, the estimate is considered to be precise", reasonably precise to 10, acceptable to 20, and "If the CV is greater than 20% or unavailable, the estimate is considered to be unreliable". "Personal well-being questions cannot be answered by proxy." And on comparison: "The most appropriate comparisons are progress over time within the same local authority, or across local authorities that share a similar demographic composition" — Chapter 7's own-history and published-peers rules, in the office's words, for a felt measure. The annual estimates rest on "approximately 90,000 individuals". A felt measure for a district, a street or a scene has to say how many answered, and if it is under fifty it is not published.

Built with the public, and revised by asking again

The programme began by asking. The national debate on what matters "generated over 34,000 responses, which were used to develop the national well-being framework that the ONS has been reporting on ever since." A 2022–23 review drew "A total of 118 responses" online "and an additional two" by email, with "focus groups to collect feedback from socio-demographic groups more likely to report low well-being", after which "22 new measures were added, one was replaced, and six existing measures were removed"; the office's user guide adds that "We also commissioned targeted qualitative research with under-represented groups" and that the framework grew "from 44 to 60 measures". The precedent is complete: a felt measure built by asking the public what matters; tested cognitively for how people choose a score; placed and administered with known context and mode effects; reported as bands as well as means for a stated reason; suppressed below fifty; compared within its own history or against declared peers; and revised by asking again, with the groups the first round under-heard deliberately sought. The local translation exists too: a six-month scoping project with "26 different organisations, including nine city councils, seven county or district councils, the three devolved governments" produced "26 indicators of individual wellbeing and its determinants" as the ideal set and "23 indicators" currently available. Nothing in the precedent is beyond a studio in principle. All of it is work, and the chapter's next section says which parts of the work are the validation.

12 · Validating a felt measure

The brief's own answer to validation is recognition: whether the people who make a scene recognise themselves in the measure. Chapter 5 found that this splits into legitimacy and validity. This section says, from the measurement standards, what validity is, what recognition supplies of it, and what else is owed.

What validity is

The governing standard — now open to read — puts it in one sentence: "Validity refers to the degree to which evidence and theory support the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses of tests." Three consequences follow in the next lines. "It is the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses that are evaluated, not the test itself" — a vibe question is not valid or invalid; a reading of its answers for a purpose is. "Validity is a unitary concept": "It is the degree to which all the accumulated evidence supports the intended interpretation of test scores for the proposed use", and the five named kinds of evidence — "Evidence Based on Test Content"; "Evidence Based on Response Processes"; "Evidence Based on Internal Structure"; "Evidence Based on Relations to Other Variables"; "Evidence for Validity and Consequences of Testing" — "may illuminate different aspects of validity, but they do not represent distinct types of validity". And the root text underneath, Cronbach and Meehl in 1955: "Construct validation is involved whenever a test is to be interpreted as a measure of some attribute or quality which is not 'operationally defined'", and "Construct validity must be investigated whenever no criterion or universe of content is accepted as entirely adequate to define the quality to be measured". A vibe has no criterion and no accepted universe of content. Its measure is validated the hard way or not at all.

What building one involves

The scale-development primers agree on the steps and the numbers. The current edition of the standard textbook lists nine: "Determine Clearly What It Is You Want to Measure"; "Generate an Item Pool"; "Determine the Format for Measurement"; "Have Initial Item Pool Reviewed by Experts"; "Cognitive Interviewing"; "Consider Inclusion of Validation Items"; "Administer Items to a Development Sample"; "Evaluate the Items"; "Optimize Scale Length" — cognitive interviewing promoted, in the latest edition, to a step of its own. The open primer gives "three phases that span nine steps" — domain and items; content validity; pre-testing; administration and sample size; item reduction; factor extraction; dimensionality; reliability; validity — with its conventions: "an ideal ratio of respondents to items is 10:1"; samples of "100 = poor, 200 = fair, 300 = good, 500 = very good"; "A reliability of 0.90 is the minimum recommended threshold" though "a reliability coefficient of 0.70 has often been accepted as satisfactory"; pre-testing by "A range of 5–15 interviews in two to three rounds, or until saturation". Cognitive interviewing is, in Beatty and Willis's definition (†), "the administration of draft survey questions while collecting additional verbal information about the survey responses, which is used to evaluate the quality of the response or to help determine whether the question is generating the information that its author intends" — the method that produces response-process evidence, by think-aloud and verbal probing. Test–retest reliability two weeks apart has been measured in one small sample at "r=0.59" for single-item life satisfaction and "0.64" for a diary-based net-affect measure, "probably sufficiently high to support much of the research" where "group means are compared" (†); the open textbook's rule of thumb is that "a test-retest correlation of +.80 or greater is considered to indicate good reliability".

One design decision the atmosphere literature forces is whether the measure is reflective or formative: whether the items are symptoms of a single underlying quality (and so should correlate, and be averaged) or ingredients that together build it (and need not correlate, and are summed into an index). The methods literature complains that "few studies use formative indicator measurement models, even though they should" (†), that measurement guidance "is replete with advice regarding the development and validation of multi-item scales based on reflective measures" while "the issue of index construction using formative measures has received little attention" (†), and that misspecification biases the results. A made-register measure, if one is attempted — lighting, sound, welcome, programme — is formative: the parts build the atmosphere and need not agree. A perceived-register measure whose items are meant to reflect one quality — pleasant and annoying reversed, say — is reflective: the ratings are supposed to hang together. The two are validated differently, and Chapter 5's recipe card (the document that states how a composite is made) should say which the measure is.

What recognition is, in these terms

"The scene recognises itself" is, in the testing Standards' vocabulary, two kinds of evidence and one kind of legitimacy. It is content evidence — the people described agree that the items cover what matters — and response-process evidence — they understood the question as its author intended, which cognitive interviewing tests directly. And it is legitimacy, in Chapter 5's sense: they, not the studio, chose what counts. It is not, on its own, internal-structure evidence, relations-to-other-variables evidence or consequences evidence, and the textbook position on what it is worth alone is blunt: "Face validity is at best a very weak kind of evidence that a measurement method is measuring what it is supposed to", because "it is based on people's intuitions about human behaviour, which are frequently wrong"; the Standards' five sources do not include it by name. The chapter's own extension, marked as such, is that when the people described judge the items and explain their readings, the result is content and response-process evidence and not face validity alone. The one paper that defends face validity defends it as a measurable property — "face validity is a characteristic of tests that can be validly and reliably measured" (reconstructed) — which is the right reading for this chapter: recognition can be measured properly, by asking the described whether the items fit and how they read them, and the result is evidence of two kinds and a claim to legitimacy. It is necessary; it is not sufficient; and it should be gathered as evidence rather than announced as approval.

The qualitative tradition's version is member checking, and its own literature is careful about it. "Member checking, also known as participant or respondent validation, is a technique for exploring the credibility of results"; "Data or results are returned to participants to check for accuracy and resonance with their experiences"; it "is often mentioned as one in a list of validation techniques", and "This simplistic reporting might not acknowledge the value of using the method, nor its juxtaposition with the interpretative stance of qualitative research" (†). The foundational text, as a methods guide reports it, held it "the most crucial technique for establishing credibility" (secondary; check against Lincoln and Guba before quoting as theirs); the same guide's criticisms are that it "relies on the assumption that there is a fixed truth of reality that can be accounted for by a researcher and confirmed by a respondent", and that "Members may tell stories during an interview that they later regret or see differently". "little has been published about the effects the member checking process may have on participants" (†) — the check acts on the checked. In the authors' own synthesised member check, returning to the data "proved unnecessary", though the check added data and a new concept; the paper is a method and a critique, not a demonstration that the dialogue changes the account. Tracy's eight criteria for qualitative quality name resonance and credibility among "(a) worthy topic, (b) rich rigor, (c) sincerity, (d) credibility, (e) resonance, (f) significant contribution, (g) ethics, and (h) meaningful coherence" (†). Recognition, done as member checking, is a procedure with a literature, not a vote.

What else is owed

The other three sources are the ones a studio is least likely to gather and most likely to be asked for by Chapter 2's sceptical reader (the reader who asks what the evidence supports). Internal structure: do the items hang together as the construct says they should (reflective), or build what they are said to build (formative)? Relations to other variables: does the felt measure move with what it should (a known-groups test: places the scene itself calls different should score differently; a convergent test: another method's reading of the same places) and not with what it should not? Section 5's finding that perceived and measured place are "related but distinct constructs" is a reason to expect modest convergence and to say so, not a reason to skip the test. Consequences: what the measure does once published — Chapter 5's Goodhart section (a published measure changes what it measures) and section 6's extraction finding — gathered as evidence after launch. The measure record in section 14 carries the five across its lines — content in lines 3 and 10, response process in line 7, internal structure in line 8, relations in line 9, consequences in line 12 — and the truthful early state of most of them is "not yet".

13 · When the felt and the counted disagree

A dashboard that carries a felt layer beside counted ones will find them disagreeing, and the doctrine for what to do then exists. Mixed-methods research names the assessment "fit": "The fit of integration describes the extent the qualitative and quantitative findings cohere", and "The assessment of fit of integration leads to three possible outcomes." "Confirmation occurs when the findings from both types of data confirm the results of the other", and "As the two data sources provide similar conclusions, the results have greater credibility". "Expansion occurs when the findings from the two sources of data diverge and expand insights" by addressing different aspects of one phenomenon. "Discordance occurs if the qualitative and quantitative findings are inconsistent, incongruous, contradict, conflict, or disagree with each other." And what to do about the third: "Options for reporting the findings include looking for potential sources of bias, and examining methodological assumptions and procedures"; "Investigators may handle discordant results in different ways such as gathering additional data, re-analyzing existing databases to resolve differences, seeking explanations from theory, or challenging the validity of the constructs." The last option is the one a dashboard is most tempted to skip: the disagreement may mean the counted measure is not measuring what the felt one is.

A second framework uses four cells rather than three. The triangulation protocol produces "a 'convergence coding matrix' to display findings emerging from each component of a study on the same page", with "consideration of where there is agreement, partial agreement, silence, or dissonance between findings from different components"; "This technique for triangulation is the only one to include silence—where a theme or finding arises from one data set and not another", and "Silence might be expected because of the strengths of different methods to examine different aspects of a phenomenon." Silence is the cell Chapter 4's six kinds of nothing (not collected, unknown, zero, free, unavailable, suppressed) did not have: not a missing value but a finding one method can see and another cannot. A room that the counted layer records as nothing and the felt layer shows as the centre of a scene is not an anomaly in the data. It is a silence in one method, and the matrix has a cell for it.

Version 1 built a rule on this — when the felt and the counted disagree, that is a finding, shown on one screen — and illustrated it with a case from the studio's own research. The chapter keeps the rule and drops the case, because the case is a finding about a place and this book does not make those. What it keeps as method is the shape: the economically marginal and culturally load-bearing room is the discordant cell, and a dashboard pre-commits, before it is built, to reporting that cell rather than resolving it by preferring the number. Chapter 7's verbs apply to the disagreement too: the layers disagree; the dashboard does not say which is wrong until someone has looked for the bias, re-examined the assumptions, or challenged the construct. How large a disagreement counts is a question of the felt measure's interval at its sample size — Chapter 6's small-number rules — which is why the matrix has a cell for partial agreement and why a felt result at the floor is shown with its interval.

14 · What holds true regardless

Seven truths, each with its grounds; then the record beneath them. They are stated for any felt measure of a place; the nightlife case in section 16 is one application.

1 · A vibe is named as a construct and a register before it is measured, and the three registers are never collapsed into one number. Made, perceived and excess have different instruments, units and validation histories; a "vibe score" that blends them is an index with Chapter 5's price list attached and no literature behind it. The measure says which register it is in and whether it is reflective or formative. (Sections 1, 3, 4, 12; ISO 12913; Michels; Russell; Jarvis et al.; Chapter 5.)

2 · A felt measure is a distribution of people's answers, reported with its spread and its sample, never a point. The standard's analysts compute coordinates per respondent and speak of the percentage likely to perceive; the national measure reports bands because "relying only on average ratings might mask important differences"; the mid-point cut comes from asking respondents where the scale turns and the top band from stated policy interest. A place does not have a vibe score; it has a spread of perceptions, and the spread is the finding. (Sections 3, 11; Mitchell, Aletta & Kang; ONS.)

3 · Who was asked, who answered and who was missing are part of the measure. Effort is highest among those with most at stake; people mark near home; one per cent contribute most; those who choose to participate are "frequently quite unrepresentative"; a strong togetherness score is compatible with exclusion. The measure states its sample, its recruitment and its known gaps on the face, and is not published below the official floor; a room under the floor is shown as present and unmeasured, never as absent. (Sections 4, 5, 11; Brown 2017; Haklay; Fung; Bethlehem; Garcia-Mispireta; ONS QMI.)

4 · Participation is evidence of what participants placed, not of the place, until selection is accounted for; and it becomes co-production only when what it changed is shown. A heat map is a picture of who marked; a visible self-placement measures the room's convergence; consultation without consequence is "a sham"; "what this changed" is a duty in the official consultation principles and, where a problem was answered by action, a predictor of taking part again (11.6 against 18.2 per cent, observational). (Sections 5, 6; Arnstein; Fung; Cabinet Office 2018; Sjoberg et al.; Boyle & Harris; Lorenz et al.)

5 · Co-presence is not a tie and a trace is not a feeling; each is read for what it records, and a derived signal is validated against the people before it stands for them. Co-presence networks are denser than contact and misplace the central; a co-occurrence count is tested against opportunity before it is an edge; a trace describes the platform's users and is "incomplete" of the construct; text sentiment measures "how people appear to others" and tracks surveys only when trained on them; faces have "no unique mapping"; perceived and measured place are "related but distinct constructs". (Sections 7, 8, 9; Génois & Barrat; Neal et al.; McPherson et al.; Salganik; Dodds et al.; Jaidka et al.; Barrett et al.; Orstad et al.)

6 · A new felt measure is validated from five sources of evidence for a stated use, and recognition by the people described supplies two of them and not all. Validity belongs to an interpretation for a use; it is argued from content, response process, internal structure, relations to other variables and consequences; recognition supplies the first two and legitimacy, is "at best a very weak kind of evidence" alone, and is gathered as member checking with its own cautions. The measure is built by the steps the precedents used — items, expert review, cognitive interviewing, a development sample, reliability, and the known effects of context, order and mode. (Sections 11, 12; AERA/APA/NCME 2014; Cronbach & Meehl; DeVellis & Thorpe; Boateng et al.; Birt et al.; ONS; OECD.)

7 · When the felt and the counted disagree, the disagreement is reported, not resolved by preferring the number. Discordance is one of three outcomes of integration and has a procedure — look for bias, re-examine assumptions, challenge the constructs; the triangulation protocol's four cells — agreement, partial agreement, silence, dissonance — add silence, where one method sees what another cannot. The dashboard pre-commits to the cell before it is built. (Section 13; Fetters, Curry & Creswell; O'Cathain, Murphy & Nicholl.)

Beneath the measure: the measure record

Chapters 4 to 8 each left a record beneath a dashboard's numbers — the provenance set, the recipe card, the claim record, the comparison record, the service record — and Chapter 16 makes them sections of one record. A felt measure needs its own, because none of the five says who was asked how they felt and how the asking was tested. The measure record has twelve lines; it is opened before the first person is asked and filled as the work proceeds.

Line What it states
1 · Construct and register What the measure is of, in words; which register (made / perceived / excess); reflective or formative; what it is not
2 · Items and format The questions as asked, their scale and anchors, the language(s), and where the words came from (standard, adapted, the scene's own)
3 · Who chose what counts How the items were arrived at and with whom; what was proposed and dropped
4 · Who was asked, how, when, where Recruitment route; in situ or later; mode; moment; the place as defined to the respondent
5 · Who answered and who did not n per place and period; response rate where known; the known gaps; the share contributed by the most active
6 · The spread The distribution and its bands; the cut-points and how they were chosen; the official floor applied
7 · Response-process evidence Cognitive interviews: how many, in what rounds, what changed
8 · Internal structure and reliability Do the items hang together (reflective) or build as intended (formative); reliability and test–retest where known
9 · Relations to other variables Known-groups and convergent tests run; what the measure moved with and did not; the trace or signal indicators checked against it
10 · Recognition Member checking: who was shown what, when, what they said, what changed; the legitimacy claim stated
11 · Discordance Where this measure disagrees with the counted layers; the matrix cell; what was done about it
12 · What this changed What the measure has been used for; what the people in it were told; the consequences evidence gathered since launch

A filled example, invented for the method. 1. Perceived register; welcome in a room, as felt by people present; reflective (four items expected to agree); not a measure of safety, quality or value. 2. Three items adapted from a standard's attribute pairs plus one in the scene's own words from workshop 2; 0–10 with labelled ends; English and one other language, back-translated and tested. 3. Items proposed by the studio, reduced and reworded in two workshops; two proposed items dropped as unanswerable in situ. 4. Approached in the room, late in the evening, by a recruiter from the scene; phone-based; the place defined as the room and the night. 5. 112 answers across three nights; approach-to-answer ratio recorded; under-25s and people who left before midnight under-represented; each respondent answered once, so no contributor dominates. 6. Bands set at the mid-point and the top two points after cognitive interviews; distribution shown; floor of 50 met. 7. Nine cognitive interviews in two rounds; one item reworded; one dropped. 8. The four items correlate as expected; test–retest not yet done — not yet. 9. Known-groups: two rooms the scene itself calls different scored differently; convergent test against a counted layer — not yet; no trace indicator validated. 10. Results shown back at a third workshop; two readings challenged and recorded; items retained by participants' choice. 11. One room discordant with the counted layer — reported in its cell, not resolved. 12. Cited once in a submission; the people who answered told, at the room, in a notice — what else it changed: not yet.

The example is a shape and not a plan; its words, its scale and its rooms are placeholders. Several of its lines say "not yet", and a record whose lines say so is a record a sceptical reader can trust more than one that does not.

15 · Where the choice is yours

Which register to measure first, and whether to measure the third at all. The perceived register has a standard measure; the made register has the protocol and the makers; the excess register has testimony and a warning about who is missing. A studio may begin with any, and may decide that the third is shown as testimony and never scored. The chapter requires only that the choice be named in line 1.

Standard words or the scene's own. The soundscape attributes are tested, translated and comparable, and their weakest axis is the one the brief's word sits on; the scene's own words are legitimate, recognisable and untested. The precedent for a hybrid is destination-image research: structured items beside open questions. Which words, in what mix, is a decision about the scene's voice and the studio's, and this book does not make it.

Private or public self-placement. A private mark is a measure; a public one is a conversation. The prototype may want both, in that order, and the design of the room is the designers'.

How much of the co-produced layer is community-held and not published. The house framework asked the question; Chapter 10 treats consent at scene level. The measure record's line 5 and line 12 are where the decision is recorded, whichever way it goes.

Whether to show a trace or signal indicator at all before it has been validated against a descriptor. Sections 8 and 9 say what each can claim; the studio may show one as an indicator, unvalidated here with Chapter 4's provenance, or wait. The chapter requires the label, not the choice.

The bands. The national measure's cut-points were set by asking respondents where the scale turns. The studio's bands may be the same, or the scene's own, and either is defensible once line 6 says how they were chosen.

Who does the member checking, and how often. A procedure with a literature; its frequency, its form and its facilitation are the studio's to decide with the scene.

16 · A nightlife illustration — method only

What follows shows how the method would be applied to a felt layer in a dashboard about where people go at night; it draws no conclusion about any place, names no venue, chooses no words and proposes no design. It is the measure record's twelve questions asked of a hypothetical layer.

A studio wants a panel that shows how rooms feel to the people in them. Before any question is written, the record is opened.

Line 1. The studio names the register, and decides — this is one of section 15's choices, made here only to illustrate — that the panel is about the perceived register, that the made register is shown separately with its makers named, and that testimony is shown as testimony. It writes what the panel is not.

Lines 2 and 3. The studio has a tested attribute set to hand and the scene's own vocabulary. It decides, with the people who will be asked, which words to use and in what mix, and records what was proposed and dropped. It notes that the standard attribute closest to its word is a derived diagonal, and that the one study of how people use the scales found that axis the least evenly read.

Line 4. The studio decides whether to ask in the room, now, or later, elsewhere, and knows these are two different measures (experienced; evaluative). It defines the place to the respondent — the room and the night, in whatever words the designers choose — as the official belonging question defines a neighbourhood in walking minutes. It chooses a mode and knows the mode moves the answers.

Line 5. The studio records who approached whom, how many answered, and who it did not reach, and expects the ceiling that Williams and Vaske found among people already at the place. It expects participation to be uneven. It applies the floor: a room with fewer than fifty answers is not shown.

Line 6. The studio reports the spread, not the mean; it sets its bands by asking respondents where the scale turns, or adopts the national cut-points and says so.

Line 7. Before launch, the studio runs cognitive interviews — a handful, in two rounds — and rewords or drops what people misread.

Lines 8 and 9. The studio checks that the items agree with each other as a reflective measure should, and runs the one test it can afford before launch: two rooms the scene itself calls different should score differently. It writes "not yet" against test–retest and against convergence with any counted layer, and it does not show a trace or song-feature indicator as the room's feeling until one has been checked against this record.

Line 10. The studio shows the results back to the people who gave them, before publication, as a procedure and not a vote; records what they challenged; and treats their recognition as content and response-process evidence and a claim to legitimacy — necessary, and not the whole of validity.

Line 11. Where a room's felt result disagrees with the counted layers, the panel shows the disagreement in its cell and the studio looks for bias, re-examines assumptions and asks whether the counted measure is measuring what the felt one is.

Line 12. The studio writes, before the first answer, how the people who answer will be told what their answers changed, and keeps that line current.

The record is published beside the panel. Nothing in it says how any room feels, and nothing in it is a design. It is the method by which a felt layer earns the word evidence — and the first thing it says to the people it describes is what it asked, whom, and what it did with the answer.

The rules

Kind and tier as in Chapter 0. "Adjacent domain" here means soundscape acoustics, environmental psychology, survey methodology, network science, computational social science and official statistics rather than cultural display.

Rule Why Kind Tier Source
Every felt measure carries the measure record: construct and register, items, who chose, who was asked, who answered, the spread, the five sources of validity evidence, recognition, discordance, what this changed A measure is validated by accumulated evidence for a use; without the record nothing accumulates Standard + Nightlife Culture for the record as a whole Fixed (sequence) AERA/APA/NCME 2014; this chapter §14
The construct is named in words, and its register (made / perceived / excess), before any item is written; the three registers are never collapsed into one number "define the construct before the proxy"; a "fuzzy concept … flourishes precisely because of its imprecision"; no literature proposes a blended score Evidence + Reading Fixed (sequence) Chapter 5; Markusen 2012; §1, §4
A measure says whether it is reflective or formative and is validated accordingly "few studies use formative indicator measurement models, even though they should"; the two are misspecified for each other Evidence (adjacent domain) [abstract or summary only] Fixed (requirement) Jarvis et al. 2003 [abstract or summary only]; Diamantopoulos & Winklhofer 2001 [abstract or summary only]
A felt result is reported as a distribution with bands, never as a point alone; coordinates or scores are computed per respondent, not from the room's median "relying only on average ratings might mask important differences"; "percent of people likely to perceive" Standard + Practice (adjacent domain) Fixed (requirement) ONS FAQ; Mitchell, Aletta & Kang
Bands' cut-points are chosen by a stated method — the respondents' own turning point, or an adopted official set — and the method is on the record "the mid-point of the scale (5) acts as an important cut-off for respondents" Standard Fixed (requirement); the cut-point values Adaptable ONS FAQ 35
A borrowed attribute word is checked for how it is read before it is used; "vibrant" in particular is a derived diagonal and the least evenly read axis of the standard instrument "a general non-equidistant interpretation of the scales, particularly on the vibrant-monotonous direction" Evidence (adjacent domain) Fixed (sequence) Lionello et al. 2021; ISO/TS 12913-3 formulae (secondary)
The place is defined to the respondent in the question, at a stated scale "By neighbourhood we mean a few minutes walking distance from your home" Standard Fixed (requirement) Community Life Survey questionnaire
In situ and retrospective answers are different measures (experienced; evaluative) and are not pooled or compared as one Experienced wellbeing "is concerned with people's emotional states"; evaluative "refers to judgments" Standard (adjacent domain) Fixed (requirement) National Research Council 2013; ONS4
Every felt measure states its recruitment route, response, known gaps and the share contributed by its most active contributors "Mapping effort was highest in sampling groups whose livelihoods were closely related to the purpose"; "90-9-1"; "those who choose to participate are frequently quite unrepresentative" Evidence [abstract or summary only] + Practice Fixed (requirement) Brown 2017 [abstract or summary only]; Haklay 2016 [abstract or summary only]; Nielsen 2006; Fung 2006
The ceiling is named: a felt measure taken only among those present is a measure of those who chose to be there "relatively low variance and high scores observed on attachment" Evidence (adjacent domain) Adaptable (house default) Williams & Vaske 2003
No felt estimate is published below the official floor (fewer than 50 answers or a numerator under 5), and its precision band is stated "not published if the sample size they are based on is fewer than 50"; CV bands Standard Fixed (requirement) ONS QMI
A felt measure for a place is compared with its own history or with declared peers, and Chapter 7's rule against ranking applies "progress over time within the same local authority, or across local authorities that share a similar demographic composition" Standard Fixed (requirement) ONS QMI; Chapter 7
Self-placement used as a measure is private before it is public, is one item among several, and its visible form is labelled a conversation, not a measure "even mild social influence can undermine the wisdom of crowd effect"; a single item of a non-concrete construct; the living histogram's artefact Evidence (adjacent domain) [abstract or summary only] Adaptable (house default) Lorenz et al. 2011 [abstract or summary only]; Diamantopoulos et al. 2012; Schilling et al. 2002
An open, repeatable vote is never presented as a measure of the place "Boaty McBoatface topped the list with over 124,000 votes"; "this is an Internet poll" Evidence (case) Fixed (requirement) BIS/NERC 2016; TIME 2009
Where representativeness is claimed, recruitment is by sample first; where it is not, the claim is bounded to the participants "Randomly selecting participants from among the general population is the best guarantee of descriptive representativeness"; "We make no claim that the maps produced represent a coherent and fixed" community Evidence + Practice Adaptable (house default) Fung 2006; Deliberative Democracy Lab; Reed et al. 2025
A story-of-change method is used for the significant, not the average, and is not relied on as the accountability case its own manual lists "understand the average experience of participants" and accountability reporting among the things other methods do more efficiently Practice Fixed (requirement) Davies & Dart 2005
"What this changed" is a line on every felt measure: how many answered, what they said, how it informed the decision, within a stated time, told to the people who answered "Explain the responses that have been received from consultees and how these have informed the policy"; a problem answered by action "associated with a 57 percent increase" in reporting again (11.6 against 18.2 per cent; reports, not people; observational; action, not telling) Standard + Evidence [abstract or summary only] Fixed (requirement) Cabinet Office 2018; Sjoberg et al. 2017 [abstract or summary only]; Arnstein 1969
Report-back is tailored to those who answered, not generic "the tailored newsletter, or sending no newsletter at all, were equally effective … and significantly better than the general newsletter" Evidence [abstract or summary only] Adaptable Cleary & Balmer 2015 [abstract or summary only]; Fumagalli et al. 2010 [abstract or summary only]
"Co-produced" is used only where the people who gave the data share in what is done with it; otherwise "participatory" "Co-design and other forms of asking the advice of users … can lack any continuing involvement in delivery" Practice Adaptable (house default) Boyle & Harris 2009; Chambers 2007
Co-presence is shown as who was there together; it is called a tie only after the co-occurrence count has been tested against opportunity, and centrality computed from co-presence is not shown as a measure of anyone's importance "not easily usable to build in a reliable and systematic fashion surrogate contact data"; "whether an observed number of co-occurrences … is significant"; baseline v inbreeding homophily Evidence (adjacent domain) Fixed (requirement) Génois & Barrat 2018; Neal et al. 2021; McPherson et al. 2001
A two-mode network states its boundary — which events and people are in it — because omitting contexts inflates clustering "network boundary specification and fixed choice designs can dramatically alter estimates of network-level statistics" Evidence (adjacent domain) [abstract or summary only] Fixed (requirement) Kossinets 2006 [abstract or summary only]
Return is shown as return; stated intention to return is not a measure of it, and return alone is not attachment "no statistically significant correlation exists between intention and actual repeat visitation rates"; loyalty is attitude and patronage Evidence [abstract or summary only] Fixed (requirement) McKercher & Tse 2012 [abstract or summary only]; Dick & Basu 1994 [abstract or summary only]
An amenity or premises count is labelled an indicator coded by outsiders, never a descriptor "Can what are in the end organizational directories really get at … the experiential meaning of place?"; "availability does not necessarily mean access" Evidence + Reading Fixed (requirement) Silver, Clark & Navarro 2010; Rhubart et al. 2022
A trace is labelled for the population it records and used within-sample; its skew is stated "Nonrepresentative data are bad for out-of-sample generalizations, but can be quite useful for within-sample comparisons"; "24.4 times the number of Foursquare users per capita" Evidence + Practice Fixed (requirement) Salganik; Hecht & Stephens 2014; Malik et al. 2015; Chapter 4
A trace or signal is shown as an indicator of a vibe only after it has been validated against a descriptor in the place and population concerned; until then it is labelled an unvalidated indicator 77% of an "assumed" proxy; dictionaries "inconsistent"; a signal that flipped sign; "related but distinct constructs" Evidence Fixed (requirement) De Nadai et al. 2016; Jaidka et al. 2020 (reconstructed); Brown & Coyne 2018; Orstad et al. 2017 [abstract or summary only]
Text sentiment is labelled as "how people appear to others", with its platform's reach and the tools' known error by speaker stated "we quantify only how people appear to others"; parser recall "64.0%" against "80.4%" Evidence Fixed (requirement) Dodds et al. 2011; Blodgett et al. 2016
No inference of feeling from faces is built, and none from gait or voice without the evidence the face lacks "no unique mapping between a configuration of facial movements and instances of an emotion category"; the field's own ethics sheet on "utterance, facial expression, gait, etc."; Article 5(1)(f) for biometric inference at work and in education Evidence + Practice + Standard (law) Adaptable (house default) Barrett et al. 2019; Mohammad 2022; Regulation (EU) 2024/1689
Crowdsourced perception of images is labelled as the judgement of the raters, with who they were "76.0% identified themselves as male"; predicts "human judgments of pairwise image comparisons" Evidence Fixed (requirement) Salesses et al. 2013; Dubey et al. 2016
A sound measure uses what is heard and by whom before how loud; a song-feature proxy is labelled defined-not-derived and supply-withdrawn the review's report of Axelsson et al.: "perceived sound sources are more important as indicators … than sound levels"; valence defined, derivation unpublished; endpoint withdrawn Nov 2024 Evidence + Standard (platform) Fixed (requirement) Aletta, Kang & Axelsson 2016; Spotify reference; Chapter 8
Experience sampling, where used, is within-person, its sample described, and its respondents' burden counted as a cost "using only the within-individual variation"; "all Apple iOS users"; "difficult to scale up" Evidence [abstract or summary only] + Standard Fixed (requirement) MacKerron & Mourato 2013 [abstract or summary only]; Seresinhe et al. 2019; NRC 2013
A new felt item is cognitively tested before it is asked, placed with known context effects, and administered in a stated mode "Cognitive testing was undertaken to understand how respondents chose their score"; "strongly affected by question structure and context"; mode effects Standard Fixed (sequence) ONS user guidance; OECD 2013
Validity is claimed for an interpretation and a use, argued from the five sources; the record says which have evidence and which say "not yet" "It is the interpretations of test scores for proposed uses that are evaluated, not the test itself" Standard Fixed (requirement) AERA/APA/NCME 2014
Recognition is gathered as member checking — who was shown what, what they said, what changed — and recorded as content and response-process evidence plus legitimacy; it is never presented as validation complete "Face validity is at best a very weak kind of evidence"; member checking "often mentioned as one in a list" (Birt et al. is a method and a critique; in their own check returning to the data "proved unnecessary"; the rule stands on Price et al. and the Standards) Evidence + Reading Fixed (sequence) Price et al. 2015; Birt et al. 2016 [abstract or summary only]; Chapter 5
Reliability is reported where measured and marked "not yet" where not; a 0.70 floor is named as the common minimum and 0.90 as the recommended one "a reliability coefficient of 0.70 has often been accepted as satisfactory"; "0.90 is the minimum recommended threshold" Practice (primer) Adaptable Boateng et al. 2018
Felt and counted layers are integrated by a declared protocol with four cells — agreement, partial agreement, silence, dissonance — and discordance is reported, not resolved by preferring the number "Discordance occurs if …"; "the only one to include silence" Standard (method) Fixed (requirement) Fetters, Curry & Creswell 2013; O'Cathain, Murphy & Nicholl 2010
The discordant cell is pre-committed before the dashboard is built Pre-registration of the integration; version 1's rule Practice + Nightlife Culture Adaptable (house default) Version 1 Ch 4; this chapter §13
The measure's effect on the measured is gathered as consequences evidence after launch, including the extraction question Consequences are a source of validity evidence; "the mix and balance of extraction and empowerment" Standard + Nightlife Culture Fixed (requirement) AERA/APA/NCME 2014; Chambers 2007; house framework (confidential)

What proves a break works

The test for a departure from one of this chapter's rules is a conversation: show the felt result, with its record, to someone who gave an answer and to someone who was not asked, and listen for three things. Does the person who answered recognise the question they were asked and see what their answer changed? Does the person who was not asked see, from the face, that they were not — who was, how many, and what that means for the number? And can either of them tell, from the face alone, that the number is a spread and not a verdict? If all three, the break has cost nothing — this is a test of whether the face is legible, not a test of the measure's validity, which the record carries. If the person who answered does not recognise the question, the content and response-process evidence has failed; if the person not asked cannot see the gap, the selection has been hidden; if either reads the number as a verdict on the place, the register or the spread has been collapsed.

For a trace or signal shown as an indicator, the test is the convergent one: the number beside the descriptor it is supposed to predict, in the same place, with the correlation stated. For a public self-placement, it is the private version run first and compared. For a departure from the floor, it is the interval shown and the reason given.

What this chapter could not settle

  • The founding texts of the made and excess registers (Böhme; Anderson), the place-attachment review (Lewicka), the standard's own texts (ISO 12913) and the strongest sentiment test (Jaidka 2020) were all closed; the chapter used what reachable sources quote of them, marked secondary, with abstracts marked [abstract or summary only] and one abstract reconstructed from an index, and nothing printed from memory. Its two theoretical registers are cited at one remove.
  • No empirical study of dot-voting bias; no ticketing-records network study with validation; no measured "you said, we did" effect; no study comparing crowdsourced place scores with residents' own ratings. The chapter said so, used the nearest evidence, and flagged each for the prototype.

Checklist

  • The measure record exists, is dated, and is published beside the panel
  • Construct named in words; register named; reflective or formative stated; "what it is not" stated
  • Items as asked, scale, anchors, language(s) and their origin recorded
  • Who chose what counts recorded, with what was dropped
  • Borrowed attribute words checked for how they are read; "vibrant" treated as a derived diagonal
  • The place defined to the respondent in the question
  • In situ and retrospective answers kept as different measures
  • Recruitment route, response, known gaps and most-active share stated on the face
  • The ceiling of asking-those-present named
  • Result reported as a distribution with bands; cut-point method stated
  • Floor applied (50 / 5); precision band stated
  • Compared with own history or declared peers; never ranked
  • Self-placement private before public; one item among several; the public form labelled a conversation
  • No open repeatable vote shown as a measure
  • Representativeness claimed only with sample-first recruitment; otherwise bounded
  • Story-of-change methods used for the significant, not the average or the accountability case
  • "What this changed" line filled: how many, what they said, how it informed, by when, told to whom (tailored where possible)
  • "Co-produced" used only where the people share in what is done; otherwise "participatory"
  • Co-presence shown as "who was there together"; no tie claim without the null test; no centrality from co-presence as importance; network boundary stated
  • Return shown as return; intention not used as return; return not called attachment
  • Amenity counts labelled indicators coded by outsiders
  • Traces labelled by population, used within-sample, skew stated
  • No trace or signal shown as an indicator of a vibe until validated against a descriptor here; otherwise "unvalidated indicator"
  • Text sentiment labelled "how people appear to others" with reach and speaker error
  • No facial, gait or voice emotion inference
  • Image perception labelled as the raters' judgement, with who they were
  • Sound measured by what is heard and by whom; song features labelled defined-not-derived and withdrawn
  • Experience sampling within-person; sample and burden stated
  • New items cognitively tested; placement and mode recorded
  • Validity claimed for a use; five sources listed with evidence or "not yet"
  • Recognition gathered as member checking and recorded as two kinds of evidence plus legitimacy
  • Reliability reported or "not yet"
  • Integration protocol declared; four cells; discordance reported; the discordant cell pre-committed
  • Consequences evidence gathered after launch; extraction question asked

Words this chapter uses

  • A construct is the thing one is trying to measure, named in words before any number is attached.
  • A measure is the question, scale or procedure that produces the answers, and its result is the distribution of those answers; an item is one question in it; "instrument" is used only as a synonym for a measure in the psychometric sense, never for the dashboard.
  • A register is one of three senses in which the word "vibe" is used — as something made, something perceived, something in excess of both — and section 1 says where the three come from; the brief's failure register, a different sense, is the list of ways a dashboard fails.
  • Following the soundscape researchers, a descriptor is a measure of how people perceive a place, an indicator is a measure used to predict a descriptor, and an index is a single value derived from either.
  • Validity belongs to an interpretation of a number for a use, never to the number itself; reliability is whether the same measure gives the same answer twice.
  • Participatory means that the people of a place contribute the measurement, and section 5 calls that family participatory for that reason; co-produced is reserved, following the definition in section 6, for the case where they also share in what is done with it.
  • Co-presence is two people being in the same place at the same time; a tie is a relationship between them; section 7 is about why the first is not the second.
  • A trace is a record of behaviour left for some other purpose and read for this one.

Williams & Vaske 2003 — what "tested before it was counted" looks like for a felt bond with a place, including the ceiling.

10Safety, ethics and consent

Anonymity is a property of data in its environment; the house does not publish on consent; a community is consulted, governs and agrees.

Dashboard Design · Part 2: The felt layer

Reading this chapter. This is one chapter of Dashboard Design, Nightlife Culture's research book on how evidence becomes a display a reader can trust, read and act on. The studio ("the house" in some chapters) is Nightlife Culture, a creative policy studio; the brief is its founder Carly Heath's commission for the book, and her eight ways a dashboard fails, the failure register, run through it. The Vibe Map, the studio's prototype for showing a place's nightlife culture, appears only as an illustration, never as a specification. "Version 1" is the book's archived first draft, whose positions this version re-tests against the sources. Every rule carries a kind (where it comes from: Standard, Evidence, Reading, Practice or Nightlife Culture) and a tier (how firm it is: Fixed, Adaptable or Decorative); Chapter 0 explains both, and the three senses of Fixed: a requirement that can be checked, a sequence whose order is the hard line, and a statement of the record. A dagger (†) marks a source read at the authors' abstract or summary only; "secondary" a quotation reached through a named reproduction; "(read once)" a quotation returned on a single reading and not confirmed by a second. Chapter 0 holds the glossary of the words the chapters share; each chapter lists its own coinages before its sources.

The question

How does a public dashboard tell the story of the communities in its data without exposing or exploiting them — what do the disclosure methods do and cost; what does UK law require of a private platform; what do consent, withdrawal and voice mean when the unit is a community and not a person; what is the harm a map or a figure can do to a place; how are hostile contributors met; what do the justice frames add — and where are the lines that are not crossed? The book does not decide this for any scene. It sets out the methods, the law as it stood on the date it was read, the precedents for holding what is known, and the harms that have been measured, so that the prototype can draw its lines knowing what each costs and whom each protects.

The 60-second version

The brief's phrase has two verbs. Exposing is a problem of disclosure, and its methods are old and well measured; exploiting is a problem of consent, benefit and voice, and the law has an answer for persons and none for communities. A dashboard sits exactly where the two meet, because what it publishes is aggregate — which the law treats as outside data protection once it is "aggregate data that is not personal data" — and what it is about is a community, which data-protection law does not address and which equality law and fairness reach only in part.

So the canonical truths. Anonymity is a property of the data in its environment, and a public release is the environment in which control is lost; the test is an intruder who knows the community, and the community's knowability sets the disclosure floor above any national rule. Aggregation protects persons and not groups; identity, attribute and group disclosure are three different things with three different remedies. A filter is a table builder, and an interactive view is protected as a query system — stricter than a static table, with fixed classifications, consistency across views, either a limit on overlapping views with a log or a consistent cell key, and a friendly intruder's walk before release. A lawful basis is chosen before collection, and the house does not use consent for what it will publish, because once a figure is published withdrawal cannot reach it; withdrawal is graded, with the irreversible part named and told beforehand. A community cannot consent and is never asked to; it is consulted, it governs and it agrees — three things with three entries in the record — and the models for holding are cited for their questions and never borrowed for their authority. "Known but not shown" is a declared status for a category, with a reason, a resolution, a decider and a review date, never a marker on a unit; the small room is shown as present in a coarser count, never as empty. The harm a dashboard can do runs through representation — labelling a place, making a community findable, turning a figure into a price — so it is assessed before launch as harm to persons, groups and places, with those affected consulted; and proportion is not exemption. Beneath any dashboard that shows people sits a safeguards record, and its first entry is written before the first row is collected.

On disclosure, four things hold. Whether data is anonymous "is not a property of the data" but of the data in its environment, and a public release is the environment in which "you lose control of the data"; the regulator's test is a motivated intruder who "is reasonably competent", has "access to appropriate resources" and may be moved by "curiosity (eg a local person's desire to find out who has been involved in an incident shown on a crime map)", and "Identifiability risk can arise where one person or group knows a great deal about another person" — which is Chapter 6's reasoning that a community's own regulars could name the venues behind a count of three. Aggregation protects a person only as far as the aggregate does: a table whose cells are all large can still tell an intruder what everyone in a cell has in common ("so Alice concludes that Bob has cancer"), and the strongest formal guarantee, differential privacy, promises only that "It is the conclusions reached in the study that affect the smoker, not his presence or absence in the data set" — it does not protect the group. A filter is a table builder: the Office for National Statistics says of online tools that "any disclosure control applied to online data will have to be stricter than is applied to outputs which the provider is able to assess individually for risk", suggests "A minimum cell count equal to five", registration, a log "audited for potentially suspicious activity" and, "If possible", "a limit on the number of similar tables which can be requested, this is to avoid disclosure by differencing"; the census's own table builder caps the variables, perturbs the same cell the same way in every table, and "will not provide details of which rule or rules have caused the areas to fail". And the price of protection lands on the small: suppression "disproportionately impact[s] small population groups and small areas", and the US census's formal method "systematically undercounts the population in mixed-race and mixed-partisan precincts" while "it does not prevent accurate predictions of an individual's race and ethnicity".

On the law, as read on 6 October 2026 and reported, not advised: the research provisions the brief expected under Article 89 and section 19 were omitted on 5 February 2026 and now sit in Chapter 8A of the UK GDPR, which excludes processing "likely to cause substantial damage or substantial distress" and processing "for the purposes of measures or decisions with respect to a particular data subject", and admits research "whether carried out as a commercial or non-commercial activity". The regulator says of research that "If you would not be able to fully action a withdrawal of consent … then you should not use consent as your lawful basis", and that "There is no exemption to this for scientific research"; a published figure cannot be un-published, and the house takes that sentence as its reason not to publish on consent; the legitimate-interests route carries a three-part test and "extra responsibility"; a DPIA is required for "Combining, comparing or matching personal data obtained from multiple sources", and — "when combined with any other criterion" from the European list — for "the novel application of existing technologies" and for tracking "geolocation or behaviour"; and the statute says that "Where appropriate, the controller shall seek the views of data subjects or their representatives". Inference of a special-category characteristic is special-category processing on the regulator's intention test "regardless of how confident you are that the inference is correct", while what onlookers "could (rightly or wrongly) infer" is a fairness question. A free, non-commercial site is inside the Equality Act — services "to the public or a section of the public (for payment or not)" — and inside the Online Safety Act if users can post what other users see, with no size exemption: "The Act covers services of all sizes … through to services run by micro businesses".

On consent at scene level, the research-ethics literature is consistent on one point: "In no case should a collective community agreement or the consent of a community leader or other authority substitute for an individual's informed consent", and "Community consultation should not be mistaken for community consent". A community can be consulted and can govern; it cannot consent for its members, and "disease-based communities and many social groups typically lack a political structure, which makes community consent inappropriate". The models for a community holding its own data — the CARE principles, OCAP, Māori data sovereignty — offer "a normative foundation" that their authors extend to "minority groups, distinctive communities, or other collectives", but rest their authority, as the scholars of the movement put it, on "inherent rights to self-determination as sovereign entities", and the owner of OCAP says its principles are "specifically First Nations—not Indigenous"; a scene borrows the questions and the structure, never the authority. Withdrawal does not reach the archive — "it would not be possible to remove data from research that had already taken place", "You cannot remove sensitive data from other users' clones of your repository" — so practice is a declared cut-off, graded withdrawal with the irreversible part named, and a tombstone that keeps the identifier and states the reason.

On harm, the regulator's own harm lists are framed on individuals and name no harm to a place; the statistical system's do: geospatial data "has the potential to unfairly disadvantage or blight a geographic area or community", "harm can also include things like stigmatisation", and "potential risk should not necessarily be used as a rationale for avoiding local or small area data altogether". The historic lending maps "led to reduced home ownership rates, house values, and rents and increased racial segregation in later decades"; fine-grained venue data "is a leading indicator for housing price changes"; a crime-map publisher "may be powerless to prevent secondary uses of the data recorded on it once it has gone into the public domain"; and an app that hid one field still let an adversary locate a user "up to the victim's building". "Known but not shown" has clean precedents — sensitive species "Shown at grid-cell level (400 km2 accuracy)", a list "agreed by the UK's statutory bodies and relevant experts" so that partners "do not have to make their own assessments", a presumption of openness with a named harm and a public-interest test — and the platforms and the list state what is held, for the category, and why.

1 · Two verbs, and the unit between them

The brief asks "how do we tell THAT story, without exposing or exploiting those communities in the data?" The sentence contains two verbs and one noun, and the chapter is organised around the fact that they belong to different literatures.

Exposing is the vocabulary of statistical disclosure control, a discipline older than the web, whose question is whether a published figure lets someone learn something about a person that they were not meant to learn. Its methods — floors, suppression, rounding, swapping, perturbation, and in the last two decades the formal guarantee called differential privacy — are well described, and their costs are measured. Sections 3 to 7 set them out in plain terms, with the costs, and section 7 adds the one thing a dashboard changes: a filter is a table builder, and a table builder is a different object from a table.

Exploiting is the vocabulary of research ethics and of the justice frames, whose question is who benefits, who decided, and whether the people in the data would recognise and accept what was done with it. Its methods — consent, consultation, governance, withdrawal — were built for persons taking part in studies, and the chapter's second finding is that they do not transfer cleanly to a community that did not take part in anything but was described. Sections 11 to 14 set out what the literature says a community can and cannot give, what the models for a community holding its own data actually claim, what withdrawal can and cannot reach, and what the precedents are for knowing something and not showing it.

Between the two verbs sits the noun, and the noun is the problem. UK law protects persons: personal data is "any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person", and the statute's new definition of statistical purposes requires that "the information that results from the processing is aggregate data that is not personal data" — so a dashboard that publishes only aggregates is, on the regulator's own test, aiming at a status the law does not regulate. The ethics literature protects participants: people who gave something and can take it back. A dashboard about a scene is about neither. It is about a community of people most of whom gave nothing, were asked nothing, and will appear in it as a count, a share, a shape on a map or an absence; the harm it can do to them is a harm to a group or to a place, which the regulator's own harm lists do not name and the statistical system's do. The chapter's third job, in sections 15 to 17, is to say what that harm is, where it has been measured, and which of the frames gives it a name.

The brief's failure register supplies the test. A dashboard "fails if people don't trust it"; it fails, for nightlife, "if they do not recognise their place within the front-end interface"; and "it fails if it's an aggregation of 'the biggest'". The first is this chapter's subject. The second and third pull against it, because the surest way to protect the small is to not show them, and the brief says that is a failure too. Section 14 is where the chapter finds, in other fields, the form that resolves the pull: a layer that is known, held and declared — present on the face, not shown in detail, with its reason stated — which is neither exposure nor erasure.

2 · Why people believe what they believe

Eight beliefs sit under most conversations about privacy and dashboards. Each has a reason to exist; each is wrong in a way the evidence can state.

Belief one: aggregates are anonymous

The intuition is that a count of forty is about nobody. It is true that a count is not a row; it is false that a count discloses nothing. A count of one in a cell is a person; a count of forty in a cell all of whom share a characteristic discloses that characteristic about every one of them to anyone who knows they are in the cell; and two counts that differ by one, in overlapping tables, disclose the one. The Office for National Statistics' own policy states the first — "A cell with a count of one is a potential disclosure risk as it allows for possible immediate identification" — and the discipline's founding critique states the second: k-anonymity "can create groups that leak information due to lack of diversity in the sensitive attribute". The belief persists because it is true for most cells most of the time, and disclosure control exists for the rest.

Belief two: anonymised once, anonymous forever

The intuition is that anonymisation is a state the data reaches and keeps. The practitioners' framework the UK uses says the opposite in its first pages: "whether data are or are not anonymised is not a property of the data, but determined by the relationship between the data and the context(s) in which they are held", and "Functional anonymisation does not assume that anonymisation can be zero-risk or irreversible". The regulator agrees: "Information may 'move' along the spectrum of identifiability to the point that data protection law starts to apply to it, or stops applying to it", and "You should periodically review the decisions you take when anonymising personal data and the assessments that underpin them". What changes is the environment — what else is published, who is motivated, what tools exist — and the regulator's own worked example is an authority answering yearly information requests for a programme's statistics, safe for three years and refused in the fourth because "the number of participants in the programme had decreased compared to previous years", "a high-profile event involving the participants increased the likelihood that there were people motivated to re-identify them", and more was by then in the public domain. The belief persists because anonymisation feels like an operation performed on a file, and the file does not change.

Belief three: it is already public

The intuition is that information people posted, or that is on an open map or a listings site, carries no obligation. The regulator's statement is flat: "Organisations must have a lawful reason for collecting and using people's data, even when it is publicly available", and on the duty to tell people, "There is no automatic exception from the right to be informed just because the personal data is in the public domain". The scholarship states the distinction the law assumes: "There is a considerable difference between being in public (i.e. sitting in a park) and being public (i.e. actively courting attention)", and "Data may be public (or semi-public) but this does not simplistically equate with full permission being given for all uses". The sharpest version is that "Publicly available data can be put to a wide range of secondary uses, including being combined with other data sets, that can pose serious risks to individuals and communities". The belief persists because the cost of collecting public data is near zero and the act of collecting it is invisible to the people collected.

Belief four: consent fixes it

The intuition is that if people agree, the rest follows. Three things cut against it. In law, consent is only one of seven bases, and the regulator says it "won't always be the most appropriate or easiest", is unsuitable "if there is a clear imbalance of power", and — of research — should not be used where withdrawal cannot be honoured: "If you would not be able to fully action a withdrawal of consent … then you should not use consent as your lawful basis". In ethics, consent is a person's act, and "In no case should a collective community agreement or the consent of a community leader or other authority substitute for an individual's informed consent". And in practice, a published aggregate cannot be withdrawn from the people who have read it, so consent to be published is consent to something that cannot be undone — the situation the regulator's research sentence describes. The belief persists because consent is the one word in this field everyone has heard, and because it moves the responsibility to the person who gave it.

Belief five: small numbers — just hide them

The intuition is that suppressing cells under a floor is costless. It is not. Suppression has to be secondary as well as primary — "In order to ensure that the value cannot be discovered by differencing from the row or column total, additional cells will have to be suppressed" — so one small cell takes others with it; it falls on the people who are few — "suppression rules disproportionately impact small population groups and small areas"; and the alternative, perturbation, protects by making every small count doubtful rather than absent, which the UK census chose and declared: "Where there is a cell count of one in a published output, there is a high chance that it could be a swapped record, a perturbed count or an imputed record". Hiding is one choice among several, each with a cost that lands somewhere, and the brief's "aggregation of 'the biggest'" is the name for where the cost of hiding lands.

Belief six: differential privacy solves it

The intuition is that there is now a mathematical guarantee and the problem is closed. The guarantee is real and narrow. Its authors describe it as "a promise, made by a data holder, or curator, to a data subject" that "You will not be affected, adversely or otherwise, by allowing your data to be used in any study or analysis", and in the same pages say what it does not promise: "A medical database may teach us that smoking causes cancer, affecting an insurance company's view of a smoker's long-term medical costs … It is the conclusions reached in the study that affect the smoker, not his presence or absence in the data set". It protects participation, not groups; its guarantee deteriorates with group size — "Any (ε, 0)-differentially private mechanism M is (kε, 0)-differentially private for groups of size k", and, in the authors' footnote, "As the group gets larger, the privacy guarantee deteriorates, and this is what we want"; and it has a price, measured in the one national deployment: the US census system "systematically undercounts the population in mixed-race and mixed-partisan precincts", and the Bureau itself tells users to "aggregate small populations and geographies to improve accuracy". The belief persists because the word privacy in the name promises more than the definition does.

Belief seven: the community can consent — ask its leaders

The intuition is that a scene has representatives, and their yes is the scene's yes. The ethics literature has considered this for forty years in medicine and public health and declines it: "For community consent to be valid, there must be a legitimate political system in place, with representatives properly empowered to make such decisions on behalf of the community", and most social groups "typically lack a political structure". The models that do assert collective authority over data — the CARE principles, OCAP, Māori data sovereignty — rest, in the words of the scholarly collection behind them, on "inherent rights to self-determination as sovereign entities predating European settlers", which is not a claim a place-based cultural community can make. Gatekeepers "may also have other interests and may hold preconceived, conventional, and biased ideas". A community can be consulted and can govern a layer it holds; it cannot give the consent the law means on behalf of people who were not asked. The belief persists because asking leaders is easier than asking everyone, and because it is sometimes what the leaders want.

Belief eight: if it harms no individual, it harms nobody

The intuition is the law's own: harm attaches to persons. The regulator's DPIA guidance lists harms to individuals — "inability to exercise rights", "discrimination", "re-identification of pseudonymised data" — and its 2022 taxonomy adds a societal tier, but neither names harm to a place or a community by stigma. The statistical system's ethics guidance does: "The use of geospatial data also has the potential to unfairly disadvantage or blight a geographic area or community", and "harm can also include things like stigmatisation". The historic case is a set of maps that identified nobody and "led to reduced home ownership rates, house values, and rents and increased racial segregation in later decades". The scholarship has a name for the object the law lacks — group privacy, "a third interest to balance alongside individual privacy and social, commercial and epistemic benefits" — and a reason it is needed: data technologies "formulate types, not tokens". The belief persists because the remedies all run through individuals, and a harm with no claimant is easy to leave uncounted.

3 · What exposing means: identity, attribute and group

Disclosure control begins by distinguishing what can be learned. Three things can be, and they need three different protections.

Identity: who someone is

The founding case is simple enough to retell. In the mid-1990s a US state released hospital records with names removed but with date of birth, sex and postal code kept. A researcher bought the voter roll for the city — "For twenty dollars I purchased the voter registration list for Cambridge Massachusetts" — and found the governor: "six people had his particular birth date; only three of them were men; and, he was the only one in his 5-digit ZIP code". From this came k-anonymity: "A release provides k-anonymity protection if the information for each person contained in the release cannot be distinguished from at least k-1 individuals whose information also appears in the release". The attributes an intruder can match on — date of birth, sex, postcode — are quasi-identifiers, and the method coarsens them (a year for a date, a district for a postcode) until every combination appears at least k times.

The number most often quoted with it should be handled as what it is. The claim that "87% (216 million of 248 million) of the population in the United States had reported characteristics that likely made them unique" on postcode, sex and date of birth comes from a working paper, not a reviewed article, and its author says it rests on "experiments I conducted using 1990 U.S. Census summary data" — an estimate of likely uniqueness from summary tables, not a count of people found. It is still the most repeated number in the field. The method itself names its limits in its first paper: it "also examines re-identification attacks that can be realized on releases that adhere to k-anonymity unless accompanying policies are respected" — among them releasing a second table of the same rows, cut differently.

Attribute: something about someone already placed

The second thing an intruder can learn is not who, but what. If a table has been coarsened until every combination of quasi-identifiers appears five times, but all five people in one combination share the same sensitive value, then anyone who knows a person is in that combination learns the value. The paper that showed this put it in two sentences: "First, an attacker can discover the values of sensitive attributes when there is little diversity in those sensitive attributes", and "Second, attackers often have background knowledge, and we show that k-anonymity does not guarantee privacy against attackers using background knowledge". Its examples are a neighbour — "so Alice concludes that Bob has cancer" — and a known fact about a nationality — "Therefore Alice concludes with near certainty that Umeko has a viral infection". The remedy it proposed, ℓ-diversity, requires each group to contain "at least ℓ 'well-represented' values for the sensitive attribute"; and the paper after that showed ℓ-diversity "is neither necessary nor sufficient to prevent attribute disclosure", because a group can be diverse and still skewed ("When the overall distribution is skewed, satisfying ℓ-diversity does not prevent attribute disclosure") or diverse in values that mean the same thing ("semantically similar"), and proposed t-closeness, under which the distribution of the sensitive value in each group must stay within a distance t of its distribution in the whole table. Its authors add the price in their own words: "requiring that P and Q to be close would also limit the amount of useful information that is released", and the limit: "t-closeness protects against attribute disclosure, but does not deal with identity disclosure".

The ladder from k to ℓ to t is worth knowing for one reason: each rung fixes the previous attack by removing more information, and none of them addresses a group that is uniform on the sensitive value because that is what the group is, nor an intruder who asks many questions. Those two gaps are where the next two sections go.

Group: something about everyone in a cell

The third thing an intruder can learn is not about a person at all. A table that identifies nobody and whose every cell is large can still say that a district is poor, that a venue's regulars are mostly of one ethnicity, that a scene's members are young, or that an area is where a kind of activity happens. The regulator's position is that this is not a disclosure of personal data unless it attaches to a person: "You must have a degree of certainty that information is about one person and not another. The mere possibility of making an educated guess about a person's identity does not present a data protection risk. Even if a guess based on anonymous information is correct, this does not mean that a disclosure of personal data has happened."
