12 · Tests and review The two-readers test result; the walk (Chapter 10) for this view; the glance and small-screen checks; the review date

A filled example, invented for the method. 1. "Fewer late rooms this quarter than any since 2023." Nine words; written for the three readers alike; after a postcode is entered, a district line generated from a template, checked, labelled "sentence generated from the data; checked by hand". 2. Message-then-input: the regional sentence and one small chart first, then the postcode box; the chart's example district rotates weekly and the page says so, so that the choice reads as the endorsement it is. 3. On the face: period and stamp; the unit ("rooms open after 1 a.m."); provenance tier chip; claim rung chip ("counted, not estimated"); comparison method in a word ("against its own history"); the disclosure floor's kind on any withheld cell; one step away: each record; on request: the method page. 4. Two districts under the disclosure floor, marked "withheld: too few to show"; one scene's rooms held at category level, shown as a district count with the held status and its reason. 5. Postcode entry (personalisation; decision cost low); period toggle from a fixed list (filter; treated as a table builder; floor per view); peer choice from the declared set (comparison; default peers named as the endorsement); "read this as a sentence" link from every chart (linking); share (state). Nothing is only behind a control. 6. Tooltips redundant to the labels at the mark, dismissible, hoverable, persistent, keyboard-reachable; map pinch has plus/minus; drag-to-pan has arrows; dense venue dots under 24 px with the table as the equivalent route. 7. Phone first: one sentence, one chart, the box; the map one tap down with its table above it; no hover content anywhere load-bearing. 8. ?area=…&period=…&peers=… in that order; data version 2026.3; spec version 11.2; degraded state "last good copy, aged 9 days" shown with its stamp. 9. Snapshot taken at each release, named by date, linked previous/next/live; citation generated with retrieval date, snapshot date, data version; a cropped share carries the stamp, the floor note and the snapshot date. 10. Title eight words; annotations' content repeated in the text beneath; generated label present. 11. Rate per 10,000 residents; five quantile bands fixed across periods; small districts drawn with an inset; no red for low; districts without a figure marked as held, withheld or unmeasured, never blank. 12. Three-phones test run with one reader from each group — each gave the sentence, found the figure and named a step; two-readers test run — the account-only and views-only readers described the same quarter; the walk run by a regular — two low-confidence claims, one banded; review in six months.

The example is a shape and not a plan; its sentence, its districts and its parameters are placeholders.

11 · Where the choice is yours

Which of the six landing patterns, and which exemplar. The evidence names none as best. The chapter requires that the choice be made, written in line 2, and that the exemplar be understood as an endorsement.

How long the sentence is. The house rule is five words where possible and ten at most; the official limits are fifteen words and sixty characters. Which the Vibe Map uses, and whether a generated sentence is held to the poster rule, is the studio's.

Whether to generate sentences per place at all. The method exists and its maker says what it costs. A studio may write ten sentences by hand and generate none; the chapter requires only that any generated sentence be checked and labelled.

How much furniture before the sentence. A stamp, a unit, a floor note and a status chip are each defensible on the face; together they are a paragraph. That the records' kinds appear on the face as text is Fixed; which kinds, in what order, and how far below the sentence, is the studio's, with the design system's evidence that hidden things the majority need are a defect and the reading evidence that long text is skipped.

Which interactions to build. The purchase list is a procedure, not a list of requirements. A dashboard may ship with a postcode box and a share button and nothing else.

Whether to hover at all. A tooltip that repeats the mark's label, keyboard-reachable, harms nobody; a studio may also decide that the label at the mark is enough.

How states are frozen. At every release, on request, or on share; as a static page, a data file or a rendered image. The standards say what a snapshot must do; the studio decides when and how.

The map's form. Choropleth with an inset, hex tiles, a cartogram, dots, or no map on the first screen. The evidence prices each; the choice is a design decision within Chapter 8's budget.

The breaks. Quantiles have the experiment; natural breaks have the design system; either is defensible once declared and held constant across views of the same measure — a change of measure or of population is a new legend, declared as one.

Scrollytelling and the editorial layer. Free, above the dashboard, carrying its states and their snapshots.

What the dashboard measures about itself, and whether it publishes it. Under Chapter 10's rule; the chapter's view is that publishing it would be the first public evidence of its kind.

12 · A nightlife illustration — method only

A studio has a sentence for a region and wants a first screen. The chapter's method, as a sequence, with no finding about any place.

It writes line 1 before anything is drawn: the sentence, within the house's word limit, for the reader the view is for, and decides whether a district's version of it will be written by hand or generated and checked. It chooses the landing pattern and writes why; if the first thing a reader sees is one district as an exemplar, it writes that the district was chosen and that the choice will be read as a recommendation.

It lays the face out for a phone: the sentence, one figure or one small chart that the sentence rests on, the period and the stamp beside it, the unit, and the input. It marks beside the figure the kinds — counted or estimated; against its own history; who was asked and how many, for a felt figure — as text chips, and makes each chip open its record. It writes the "how this argues" page for the reader who will check, and does not mistake it for a reason the others will.

For every control it writes the purchase and the cost, and checks that a reader who touches nothing still gets the sentence and the figure. It keeps the tooltip, if there is one, as a repetition of what is at the mark, dismissible, hoverable, persistent, reachable by keyboard; it gives the map plus and minus and arrows; it puts the venue table under the venue dots because the dots are too small to be targets.

It decides the address: the parameters in a fixed order, so one state has one address. It decides the snapshot: at each release, a dated copy of the data and the text, linked to the one before and the one after and to the live view, and a citation generated from it. It writes what a cropped share carries.

For the map it uses a rate, chooses its breaks and holds them across every period and every peer set, gives the small districts size — an inset, say — keeps red away from low values, and writes the sentence that says what the darkest shape means. It draws the withheld districts as withheld and the held rooms as a district count under a held status, and never as empty.

Then it gives the first screen to one reader of each of the three user groups, on their own phones, and asks each what the dashboard says, which figure it rests on, and what they would do next. If the answers are the sentence, the figure and a step, the first screen works. If they are "what am I looking at", or the sentence without its figure, it starts again at line 1.

The rules

Kind and tier as in Chapter 0. Standard (design system) is a public design system's published guidance, backed by stated research only where it says so; Standard (W3C) is a WCAG 2.2 success criterion at the level named; Standard (community) a community-endorsed declaration or recommendation; Standard (method) a published grammar or method; Standard (regulator) and (law) as in Chapter 10. "Adjacent domain" here means news graphics, business dashboards, health risk communication, scholarly publishing and cartography rather than cultural display.

Rule Why Kind Tier Source
Every view carries a face sheet: the sentence, the pattern and first state, what of each record sits on the face, the nothings, the interactions and their costs, hover and pointer routes, the small-screen form, the state and its address, the snapshot and citation, words, map and colour, tests and review The field describes dashboards and does not evaluate them; the surface must account for itself Nightlife Culture + Practice Adaptable (house default) This chapter §10; Sarikaya et al.; Bach et al.
The first screen's sentence is written before the screen is designed; it answers the named reader's question and works with no interaction Titles are visited first by two-thirds of readers in the one study; a title is remembered over its chart; most readers touch nothing optional Evidence + Standard (design system) Fixed (requirement) Sultanum & Setlur 2026; Kong, Liu & Karahalios 2019; ONS interactive charts; Chapters 1, 3
A dashboard is justified before it is built: a named reader, data updated often enough to revisit, a need for combination, and the resource to maintain it; otherwise charts with specific insights "Only use a dashboard if you have clear justification"; "put the burden of interpreting and understanding data onto the user" Standard (design system) Fixed (sequence) ONS dashboards; Analysis Function 2026
The most important information comes first on every page, section and chart; chart titles state the trend; headings and titles within the official lengths, and within the house's shorter one where it applies Inverted pyramid; "around 28% of content"; "15 words or fewer"; "fewer than 60 characters"; "65 characters or less" Standard (design system) + Nightlife Culture Fixed (requirement); the house limit Adaptable (house default) ONS content; GOV.UK content; Chapter 1
The landing pattern is chosen from the six, named in writing, and the exemplar (if any) is declared an endorsement No study compares the patterns; the first-shown view anchors Reading + Evidence Adaptable (house default) Version 1 audit; Cho et al. (Chapter 3)
Nothing is asked of the reader before something is given: no configuration, registration or weighting before the sentence and a figure; a skippable guess offered after the sentence is not a toll "shows the main message without needing any interaction"; a start point gives "just enough information" first; configuration-first taken up by one or two in a hundred Standard (design system) + Evidence (case) Fixed (requirement) ONS; GOV.UK start page; OECD BLI figures
A search or place input sits beside content that already says something, never instead of it Search adopted by two-thirds to four-fifths when offered beside a display; "deeply personal"; no evidence for a blank screen Evidence (adjacent domain) Adaptable (house default) Feng et al. 2018
The small screen is designed first; what is removed for it is recorded as not the message; no hover content is load-bearing "Over half" (ONS) to "Two-thirds" (Analysis Function) arrive on a phone or tablet; "80% … do not scroll past the first quarter"; phone versions "remove content" and "removed the interactivity completely" Standard (design system) + Evidence Fixed (requirement) ONS; Analysis Function; Hoffswell, Li & Liu 2020; Kim, Moritz & Hullman 2021
On a phone, linear layouts and small multiples are the defaults over radial forms and animation 2.8–5.4 s against 3.3–6.9 s; small multiples "consistently completed tasks in less time" Evidence (adjacent domain) Adaptable Brehmer et al. 2019, 2020
The authored account and exploration are both reachable from the first screen; neither is a toll on the other "The reader is not forced to interact in order to learn"; the taxonomy's commonest structure may open on a default view; the null (secondary) Practice + Evidence + Reading Adaptable (house default) Victor 2011; Segel & Heer 2010; Boy et al. 2015 (secondary)
Every written line links to the view that shows it, and every view to its line Linking "significantly increased user engagement" Evidence (adjacent domain) [abstract or summary only] Fixed (requirement) Zhi, Ottley & Metoyer 2019 [abstract or summary only]
Text on the face is not treated as clutter: the title carries the trend, statistics and context sit by the point, and whatever an annotation carries is also in the text, because annotations may vanish on a phone "heavily annotated charts were not penalized"; "Perceptual content … should be positioned in the title"; "Annotations may not display on mobile devices" Evidence + Standard (design system) Fixed (requirement) Stokes et al. 2023; Ajani et al.; ONS annotations
A title never says what the chart does not show; where they would disagree, the chart is redrawn or the title rewritten Readers recall the title's message and call the result neutral; the chart wins when the caption names a weak feature Evidence Fixed (requirement) Kong, Liu & Karahalios 2018, 2019; Kim, Setlur & Agrawala 2021
Generated sentences are built by rule from checked data, their topics ranked per place, checked by a person, labelled as generated, written in the house's voice, and aware of every series break they speak across "not a labour-saving tool"; "all data are checked before publishing"; readability d = 2.8 against; the stock-split error Practice (official) + Evidence Fixed (requirement) ONS 2023; Graefe 2016; Graefe & Bohlken 2020
The "how this argues" page states the display's rhetorical positions — defaults, orderings, denominators, what is held — and is linked from every view; it is written for the reader who checks Four editorial layers; "provenance rhetoric"; "Disclosing some of these decisions is a way to establish trust"; metadata changed thoroughness, not accuracy Evidence + Reading + Practice Adaptable (house default) Hullman & Diakopoulos 2011; Dörk et al. 2013; Burns et al.
Every interaction names its purchase from the table and its costs from the seven, or is cut; the static reading works before it is added "does not improve participants' accuracy … can significantly detract"; a required interaction cut completion and correct choice; seven costs Evidence + Practice Fixed (requirement) Mosca, Ottley & Chang 2021; Zikmund-Fisher et al. 2011 [abstract or summary only]; Lam 2008 [abstract or summary only]; Decision Book Ch 7
Guided tours and onboarding are not relied on to fix a first screen; a familiar form and a sentence are No correctness difference with or without onboarding; readers skim the guide; "only useful once" Evidence Adaptable (house default) Stoiber et al. 2022; Sultanum & Setlur 2024
Nothing the majority of readers need is one step away; nothing one step away is hidden behind a control readers think will take them off the page; detail on request is two levels at most, with an obvious route "some users avoid clicking the link"; "Do not use the details component to hide information that the majority of your users will need"; "beyond 2 disclosure levels typically have low usability" Standard (design system) + Practice Fixed (requirement) GOV.UK details, accordion, tabs; Nielsen 2006
Content on hover meets the three conditions (dismissible, hoverable, persistent) and is also reachable by keyboard focus; nothing is only on hover, because touch has no hover SC 1.4.13 and its reasons; "not normally available on touchscreens"; "people using a touchscreen device may not use a physical keyboard" Standard (W3C, AA) + Practice Fixed (requirement) WCAG 2.2 1.4.13, 2.5.7; NN/g 2019; Decision Book Ch 15
Every control works by keyboard and by a single pointer without a path or a drag; maps have buttons for zoom and pan SC 2.1.1 (A), 2.5.1 (A), 2.5.7 (AA) Standard (W3C) Fixed (requirement) WCAG 2.2
Targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or have an equivalent control that is; dense data marks that must be smaller get an equivalent route — the table twin SC 2.5.8 and its "interactive data visualization where targets are necessarily dense" exception, with "equivalent functionality through alternative means" Standard (W3C, AA) Fixed (requirement) WCAG 2.2 2.5.8; Chapter 8
A tooltip, where used, repeats what is at the mark or in the table, is spoken and keyboard-reachable, and is never the only place a value lives The ONS's components; the ONS's exemption; no public design system has a tooltip component Standard (design system) Fixed (requirement) ONS chart components; ONS interactive charts
Every reachable state has one canonical address that encodes the selection in a fixed order "a URL that links to the current state"; "different parameter settings result in different URLs, and yet provide exactly the same visualization view"; 2,000 characters Evidence + Practice Fixed (requirement) Heer, Viégas & Wattenberg 2007; Shiny docs
Every state can be frozen as a dated, unchanging snapshot of its data and text — at each release at least, and on request or on share — findable from the live view and linking previous, next and live; the citation is generated and carries the address with its selection, the snapshot date, the data version and the retrieval date Links rot; content drifts; "Interactive content usually cannot be archived"; "timeslice, version and/or granular portion"; R1–R14; OWID's archived citations Standard (community) + Evidence + Practice Fixed (requirement) FORCE11 2014; RDA WGDC 2015; Jones et al. 2016; The National Archives; Our World in Data 2025
Data are versioned and timestamped; a correction is announced at the top of the affected view with when and why; a retired view keeps its address under a dated banner; statistics are never silently replaced ONS versions and corrections policy; "Correction of errors are reported at the top of the affected release"; "withdraw the content - this keeps the content on the site" Standard (regulator; design system) Fixed (requirement) ONS revisions policy; GOV.UK publisher guidance
A cropped or shared copy carries the stamp, the floor note, the unit and the snapshot date The share is the state's afterlife; the data dump is the commonest use Nightlife Culture + Evidence Fixed (requirement) Version 1 crop test; Tory et al. 2021
Every view declares the data version, the specification version and the selection it was built from, and a degraded state is a state with an aged data version "independent from the other components"; "unit := (data, transforms, mark-type, encodings)"; "re-evaluated as selections change" Standard (method) + Reading Fixed (requirement) Wickham 2010; Satyanarayan et al. 2017; Chapter 8
The records' kinds sit on the face as statuses in text that open the record; a source line is followable, not only present Metadata read as "more thorough" without accuracy; a source line "suggests that there may be no need for the user to check"; beauty trusted via inferred competence Evidence + Reading Fixed (requirement) Burns et al.; Kennedy et al. 2016; Lin & Thornton [abstract or summary only]; Chapter 4
A cell not shown is marked, explained by kind, and never blank; nothing is imputed into a withheld cell; a series is never joined across a gap; the maker expects, and does not design away, the lower confidence a shown gap produces against a dropped one Dropping the gap was the most biased and the most confident; an explained empty cell beat a blurred one for confidence and raised risk-taking; "Do not join the points" Evidence + Standard Fixed (requirement) Sarma et al. 2022; Andreasson & Riveiro 2014 [abstract or summary only]; Analysis Function; Chapters 4, 10
A felt distribution and a funnel carry their reading in their title and their band and n in words beside the shape The public has no schema for either; a distribution is a slow glance Reading Adaptable (house default) Chapters 3, 7, 9
A choropleth shows rates, never counts; its breaks are declared and, "when possible", held constant across every view of the same measure; its legend is matched "standardised rates, not absolute values"; "matched legends across series … increased map-comparison accuracy by approximately 28 percent" Standard (design system) + Evidence [abstract or summary only] Fixed (requirement) ONS choropleth maps; Brewer & Pickle 2002 [abstract or summary only]
Breaks by quantile unless a declared reason; five bands Quantiles best in the one controlled test; the design system's default is natural breaks Evidence [abstract or summary only] + Standard (design system) Adaptable Brewer & Pickle 2002 [abstract or summary only]; ONS
Small areas are given size — an inset, a tile form or a second view — and the map's sentence says what the darkest shape means "small areas were missed by approximately 30–40% of map users"; 93 per cent chose the darker map without a legend and about half with one; the remedy is the chapter's, since the study endorses none Evidence + Reading Adaptable (house default) Schiewe 2019
Cartograms are used knowingly: contiguous over rectangular, and never as the only map, since a choropleth with circles beat them in the one head-to-head "Rectangular cartograms are a clear outlier"; "choropleth/graduated circles are more effective" (secondary) Evidence + secondary Adaptable Nusrat, Alam & Kobourov 2018; Nusrat & Kobourov 2016
The stigma check runs on every map before publication: no red or dark for low; large empty areas do not dominate; missing is not zero; the held category is coarsened Chapter 10's rules; dark-is-more measured Standard (regulator) + Evidence Fixed (requirement) UKSA (Chapter 10); Schiewe 2019
Two tests are run on every first screen. The two-readers test: one reader given the authored account alone and one the views alone, each asked what the place is like. The three-phones test: a reader of each user group asked, on their own phone, what the dashboard says, which figure it rests on and what they would do next The field's test gap; the design systems' "test with users" Nightlife Culture + Standard (design system) Fixed (requirement) Version 1 Ch 10; DSH-12
The dashboard measures its own use as how, not who; publishes it aggregate and dated; and reads "those who interacted did better" with the confound named "not about who uses it"; publishers "unwilling to share internal metrics"; "an artifact of participant engagement, or an effect of interacting" Standard (law) + Evidence + Nightlife Culture Fixed (requirement) Chapter 10; Hohman et al. 2020; Mosca et al. 2021
A dashboard has a retirement plan: a banner six months ahead, the state preserved, data and metadata kept and marked, code archived in public The lifecycle's fifth stage; every stated cause of a retirement read was supply-side Standard (design system) + Evidence (cases) Fixed (sequence) Analysis Function 2026; Chapter 8
Scrollytelling and other editorial forms sit above the dashboard, carry its states and snapshots, and are priced as unevaluated for comprehension Recall equal to video and worse than text per second; scroller v stepper no difference; "it doesn't hide content" Evidence + Practice Adaptable Schneiders 2020; McKenna et al. 2017; The Pudding 2017

What proves a break works

The test for a departure from one of this chapter's rules is two conversations and a phone. First, give the first screen to one reader of each of the three user groups the studio tests with (Chapter 2), on their own phone, and ask three things: what the dashboard says, which figure it rests on, and what they would do next. If each gives the sentence, points to the figure and names a next step, the first screen works whatever pattern it took — the second and third questions are there because the title evidence says a reader will repeat a sentence whether or not the view supports it; if any answers "what am I looking at", or repeats the sentence and cannot find its figure, the schema, the sentence or the device has failed and the break has cost the reader. Second, give one reader the authored account alone — the sentence and the written lines, with the charts covered — and one the views alone with their titles but without the written account, and ask both what the place is like. If they agree, the two layers are one dashboard and the sequencing break has cost nothing; if they diverge, the authored account says something the views do not show, and the "how this argues" page is where to look for the crack.

For a break in the interaction rules, the test is the Bayesian study's: show the static reading working without the control, then watch one real reader meet the control cold, and if they do not use it, remember that most will not and the surface they saw was the product. For a break in the hover rule, the test is a touchscreen and a keyboard, in that order. For a break in the citation rule, the test is a year: cite the state, change the data, and see whether the citation still finds what was cited. For a break in the map rules, the test is the 260-person study's: ask a reader to point to the smallest area and the largest value, without the legend, and count.

What this chapter could not settle

  • The storytelling null — version 1's load-bearing evidence for "the story is never a gate" — could not be re-read at source, and its two figures are not in the reachable abstract; the chapter carries the direction as secondary through three papers that cite it, withdraws the figures, and rests the house shape on three mechanisms that were read.
  • No empirical dashboard literature evaluates dashboards: the surveys describe, the catalogue says it ranks nothing, the official guidance is practice; the chapter is built from perception evidence (Chapter 3), single-mechanism experiments and design-system practice, each marked.
  • No study compares the six landing patterns; no study of empty states or map-first landing; no measured tooltip discovery; no reach figures newer than 2019; no dot-density or hex evaluations; no "red = bad" map study; the chapter says so, uses single-pattern evidence, and leaves the tests to the prototype.
  • The national web archive cannot hold interactive content, and the one public model that took citation seriously changed its practice in 2025; the snapshot is made a layer of the citation rule.
  • The design system's default map breaks (Jenks) sit against the one controlled experiment (quantiles); both are reported, and quantiles are the Adaptable default with a declared reason either way.
  • The trust evidence says a source line is read as a reason not to check, and metadata changes perceived thoroughness, not accuracy; "followable, not only present" is the rule, and the furniture is kept and made to open the record.

Checklist

  • Face sheet exists for every view; line 1 written before the view was drawn
  • The first screen's sentence answers the named reader's question with no interaction
  • Dashboard justified: reader, cadence, combination, resource — or charts with specific insights instead
  • Most important thing first on every page, section and chart; titles within limits; chart titles state the trend
  • Landing pattern named in writing; exemplar declared an endorsement
  • Nothing asked before something given; any input sits beside content
  • Small screen designed first; removals recorded; no load-bearing hover
  • Authored account and exploration both reachable from the first screen; every line links to its view and back
  • Text on the face carries trend in the title, statistics and context by the point; annotation content repeated in text
  • No title says what its chart does not show
  • Generated sentences: by rule, topics ranked per place, checked, labelled, in the house voice, series-break aware
  • "How this argues" page written and linked from every view
  • Every interaction has its purchase and costs on the sheet; static reading works first; cut list recorded
  • No onboarding relied on; familiar forms and sentences instead
  • Nothing the majority need is one step away; at most two levels of detail on request; route obvious
  • Hover content: dismissible, hoverable, persistent, keyboard-reachable; nothing only on hover
  • Every control by keyboard and single pointer; maps have zoom and pan buttons
  • Targets ≥ 24 CSS px or an equivalent control; dense marks have the table twin
  • Tooltips repeat the mark or table; spoken; never the only place a value lives
  • One canonical address per state; parameters in fixed order
  • Snapshots: at each release at least, and on request or share; dated, unchanging, previous/next/live links; generated citation with address and selection, snapshot date, data version, retrieval date
  • Data versioned and timestamped; corrections announced with when and why; retired views keep their address under a banner
  • Cropped shares carry stamp, floor note, unit, snapshot date
  • Each view declares data version, spec version, selection; degraded states shown as aged data
  • Records' kinds on the face as text statuses that open the record; source lines followable
  • Cells not shown marked by kind, never blank; no line joined across a gap
  • Felt distributions and funnels titled with their reading; band and n in words
  • Maps: rates; breaks declared and held across views; matched legends; small-area form; stigma check; table twin
  • Two-readers test run; three-user-group phone test run
  • Own use measured as how, not who; published aggregate; the interaction confound named
  • Retirement plan written

Words this chapter uses

  • The sentence is a view's headline message — what it says, to whom — written within the house's word limit; the title is the sentence as it sits above a chart.
  • The first screen is what a reader sees on arrival before doing anything; its configured state is the default view, in Chapter 3's sense; a landing pattern is one of the six shapes a first screen takes, named in section 3.
  • A view is a panel in one state; a state is the set of values of every selection that makes a view; a query is the request for a state; an address is the URL that encodes one; a snapshot is a dated, unchanging copy of the data and text behind a view; a version is a numbered edition of a dataset.
  • The face of a panel is its visible surface, and the chapter distinguishes three distances from it — on the face (seen without acting, including by scrolling the page the panel is on), one step away (opened from the face by one action and shown beside it), and on request (a separate page reached by a link, such as the method page); Nielsen's phrase "progressive disclosure" appears only inside quotation marks, because Chapter 10 reserved "disclosure" for the statistical sense.
  • The authored account is what the maker wrote — the sentence, the lines beside the charts, any text generated by rule — and exploration is what the reader does to make states; the word "story" appears only in quotations and in the names of the genres that use it.
  • An interaction is anything a reader does that changes what is shown, and a control is the thing they do it with; hover is a pointer resting without a click; a tooltip is content shown on hover or on keyboard focus; touch is a pointer that cannot hover.
  • An interaction's purchase is what it buys, version 1's word, kept; its costs are Lam's seven, named in section 6.
  • Generated text is sentences produced by rule from data, which the ONS calls "semi-automated".
  • An empty state is an input-first screen before input, and is never called a nothing; the three nothings are Chapter 10's.
  • A small screen is a phone; "mobile" appears in quotations and figures.
  • Rhetoric is Hullman and Diakopoulos's sense — how a display argues — and the house's "how this argues" page is its statement of its own.

12Recognising your place

A figure about a place is a figure about a unit; identity is never ranked; the two columns side by side; discovery is matching; a crop carries its provenance.

Dashboard Design · Part 3: The reading experience

In this chapter

  • The question
  • The 60-second version
  • 1 · What "recognising your place" means
  • 2 · What people believe about recognition, and what the evidence says
  • 3 · Finding your geography: the unit
  • 4 · Finding yourself: personal relevance
  • 5 · The two columns: counted beside missed
  • 6 · Identity is never ranked; conditions are compared with a gate
  • 7 · Discovery as matching, not ranking
  • 8 · The crop: what a cut-out carries
  • 9 · Harm through representation, at the scale of a place
  • 10 · The failures, decomposed
  • 11 · What holds true regardless
  • 12 · Where the choice is yours
  • 13 · A nightlife illustration — method only
  • The rules
  • What proves a break works
  • What this chapter could not settle
  • Checklist
  • Words this chapter uses
  • Sources

Reading this chapter. This is one chapter of Dashboard Design, Nightlife Culture's research book on how evidence becomes a display a reader can trust, read and act on. The studio ("the house" in some chapters) is Nightlife Culture, a creative policy studio; the brief is its founder Carly Heath's commission for the book, and her eight ways a dashboard fails, the failure register, run through it. The Vibe Map, the studio's prototype for showing a place's nightlife culture, appears only as an illustration, never as a specification. "Version 1" is the book's archived first draft, whose positions this version re-tests against the sources. Every rule carries a kind (where it comes from: Standard, Evidence, Reading, Practice or Nightlife Culture) and a tier (how firm it is: Fixed, Adaptable or Decorative); Chapter 0 explains both, and the three senses of Fixed: a requirement that can be checked, a sequence whose order is the hard line, and a statement of the record. A dagger (†) marks a source read at the authors' abstract or summary only; "secondary" a quotation reached through a named reproduction; "(read once)" a quotation returned on a single reading and not confirmed by a second. Chapter 0 holds the glossary of the words the chapters share; each chapter lists its own coinages before its sources.

The question

What makes a person, or a scene, recognise its place in a public data display — and what must the display do so that what is counted and what is missed sit together without the counted winning; so that what a place is is never ranked while what it has is compared, with the gate on the face; so that the unit shown is the one the scene lives at, and the display says which unit that is and what it hides; so that finding a place that suits you is matching and not ranking, with the why shown; and so that whatever is cut out of a view and carried away still says what it is?

The 60-second version

The brief's fourth failure — "for nightlife, it fails if they do not recognise their place within the front-end interface" — is several failures. Section 1 splits the word into four senses and section 10 into five tests; the headline findings fall under five heads, and each has its own evidence and its own remedy.

The first is the unit. People do not live in output areas. The largest measurement of residents' own neighbourhoods that this chapter could reach — 7,498 households in ten American cities, asked to draw "the area around where you live" on a street map — found a median drawn area of 0.35 square miles against the programme's own target areas of 2.23. The United Kingdom's smallest census units, the output areas, "were designed to have similar population sizes and be as socially homogenous as possible", and the official releases that call them "neighbourhoods" do so by definition, not by anyone's recognition. Change the unit and the finding changes: in a test on the whole of the 2001 English census, moving between output area, ward and district changed the correlation between a pair of variables in "about 60 per cent of cases", and the author's verdict — "Most of the time, not very – but there are occasions when it can make a great deal of difference. Unfortunately it remains difficult to predict these occasions" — is the fairest sentence in the literature. So the unit is a declared choice with a known cost, stated on the face with what it hides, and a page about a place offers more than one.

The second is whether the reader is in it. The one interview study reached of lay readers choosing between charts, some of them maps, found that "People often determined the quality of a graph containing geographical information based on how easy or difficult it was to find their home state", and that "The most recurring theme in our analysis were decisions framed or driven by personal experience" — 42 interviews, one topic, a self-reported ranking, and the authors' own request that it be replicated. The official body that wrote 331 local stories found that readers "really valued being able to read all about the place they call home", and that within days "every individual area's page had been read". No controlled experiment was found. The display acts on the interviews and flags the gap — and notes that the places those readers found were states, counties and local authorities, units with names; section 3 shows that the small-area units have neither names nor edges people hold, so the rule is that the reader's place is found by a name.

The third is the two columns, and here version 1 loses the reason for its best-known rule. Version 1 said the counted column must never be shown first because "repeating the opposing frame strengthens it". The corrections literature now says, in the words of its own 2020 handbook, that "exhaustive experimental attempts to induce a backfire effect through familiarity alone have come up empty"; a 2020 review concludes that "backfire effects are not a robust empirical phenomenon"; and the competitive-framing experiments that bear on it found that "framing effects depend more heavily on the qualities of frames than on their frequency of dissemination". Value-first survives — as a house stance, with the order itself resting on one ground, that the first thing shown is read as an endorsement (Chapter 11), and the missed column's presence and equal standing resting on two more: a bar chart of a gap "may encourage deficit thinking" and hiding variability "tends to increase stereotyping while emphasizing variability reduces it"; and leading with a prevalence figure "had no significant effect on issue salience" in a series of experiments with 12,448 respondents — opening on a count buys nothing, which is not the same as saying it harms. What else survives: numeric uncertainty costs little or no trust (a review of 48 experiments found "only positive or null effects" [abstract or summary only]), so the missed column's intervals are not a weakness to hide; dropping a gap is the most biased way to show it (Chapter 11), and the Analysis Function's table shorthand already has a symbol for every kind of nothing; two unlike measures never share an axis ("In general, we do not recommend using dual axis charts because they can be easily misinterpreted"), with the measured cost that side-by-side charts have "almost never outperformed" other layouts for precise comparison. And "equal visual dignity" — version 1's rule that the missed column is never the sketchy one — remains untested: the one experiment on sketchy rendering found it cost accuracy and raised engagement, and said nothing about belief.

The fourth is the ranking, and it has three parts. Identity is never ranked, and that is a stance, not a measurement fact: Velleman and Wilkinson showed in 1993 that "Scale type, as defined by Stevens, is not an attribute of the data, but rather depends upon the questions we intend to ask of the data", so a profile is nominal because the house has decided what question its profile answers. The display forms follow: the radar chart was "the least effective and least liked" in the one head-to-head on composite indicators that was reached (†), a filled radar's ranking by area reverses when its axes are reordered (†), and the United Kingdom's own area classifications were named by a published rule — "words and phrases that might be construed as pejorative were not used", and descriptors present each cluster "as consequences of factors that have happened to areas rather than the consequences of human agency" — a rule for naming without blame, whose output still includes "Hard-Pressed Living" — because a label for a condition cannot be neutral, which is why the house's labels name identity and conditions are shown as numbers. Conditions are compared with a gate, and the gate is a standard with official cousins: the European code's Principle 14, the Code of Practice 3.0's practice 6.6 ("comparable across and within geographies at regional, national and local levels, where possible"), and the ONS's own local statistics service, which keeps non-coherent data "as separate indicators to try to avoid inappropriate comparisons" and turns a comparison into three words by a published rule — "higher", "lower" or "similar" at one median absolute deviation. Discovery is matching, and the recommender literature draws the line exactly: explanations raise acceptance (the founding study's "86%" is 86 per cent of 97 people asked about the interface they had just used, and the same study found "no statistically significant difference" in decisions); neighbour-style "people like you" explanations caused users "to overestimate the actual-rating by 0.74 on average" while content cues "were found to be significantly more effective at enabling accurate assessments"; personalising the explanation was "detrimental to effectiveness, though it may improve user satisfaction" (†); and sorting by popularity is itself the treatment — in a 14,341-person experiment, "Increasing the strength of social influence increased both inequality and unpredictability of success". "An aggregation of the biggest" has a name in that literature: exposure, "largely determined by position in the ranking", where a relevance gap of 0.03 can become 30 per cent less exposure.

And the fifth is the crop. Of 9,958 coded posts carrying visualisations about the pandemic, of every stance, "only 12%" broke a design guideline and "the majority (55.3%)" of the charts were screenshots of existing charts; among the sceptics' charts alone, more than two-fifths were screenshots of data-exploration dashboards. The United Kingdom's official guidance puts a chart's title and source in the page text and not in the image, for accessibility, and says in terms that "This does mean the image of the chart can be taken out of context if it is copied and pasted elsewhere". So the crop test is a provenance rule before it is a layout rule: what a cut-out must carry, inside its frame, is title, unit, source, base, address and snapshot date, and for a comparison its gate and its wording — the missing-context half of what goes wrong, not the misreasoning half, which no caption cures. The one study that designed against cherry-picking found that "Juxtaposed approaches are croppable and thus not tamper-evident", that a superimposed guardrail worked best, and that 38 per cent of readers did not notice it; the lesson the chapter takes from it is tamper-evidence, and it applies it to the two columns too: each column's frame carries the bridging sentence, so a cropped counted panel still says what sat beside it.

Beneath each place's page the chapter leaves a ninth record, the ten-line recognition record: unit; residents' unit; scale; identity fields; labels; gates; peers; sentences; review; errors. The pass tests are version 1's, sharpened by Chapters 9 and 11: a reader from the scene says what is there and what is missing from their own knowledge of the place; a reader from a place whose counted column is thin opens its page and does not read "you lost".

1 · What "recognising your place" means

The brief's sentence is short and the thing it names is not one thing. When a person opens a page about a place and says "that's not us", they may mean four different things, and a dashboard that fixes one will still fail the other three.

Sense one: the geography. The reader looks for where they live, work or play and cannot find it, because the display's unit is not the one they hold. The evidence on how people hold a place is a method literature — sketch maps, drawn boundaries, vague regions — and section 3 reads it. Chapter 3 settled the perceptual half: a reader recognises what they already have a schema for. This chapter settles the spatial half: the schema is a place with a name and fuzzy edges, and the statistical unit is neither.

Sense two: the self. The reader finds the place and does not find themselves or their people in what is said about it. The evidence here is thin and interview-based, and section 4 gives it at its true strength.

Sense three: the account. The people the page describes do not agree that it describes them. Chapter 9 placed this: recognition by the described is member checking, which supplies two of the five sources of validity evidence and legitimacy, and never the whole. This chapter asks for the procedure's form when the members are a scene and not a sample, and finds that the literature on returning findings to a community is a literature of procedures and principles with almost no evaluation behind them — and one researcher's own account of harm done.

Sense four: the standing. The reader finds the place, finds themselves, agrees with the account, and still reads the page as a verdict: ranked, labelled, compared to their cost. This is the sense the deck's two columns are about, and the sense that recognition as a political category names — Taylor's "Nonrecognition or misrecognition can inflict harm" (as the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy quotes him; secondary), and Fraser's two hazards, that a politics of recognition may "displace" a politics of redistribution and may "reify" the identities it recognises. The chapter takes those two hazards as a frame for its own structure and draws no authority from the philosophy: a display of identity that stands in for a comparison of conditions is displacement on a screen; a profile that freezes a place into a type is reification on a screen.

The house already has a test that spans the four. Its own slide reads: "Does it paint a recognisable picture? Ask hyperlocal scenes whether they recognise their activity, relationships and identity. Record who is missing and what contributors change." (Nightlife Culture; Style Guide v1.5, slides.) That is sense three made a procedure, with sense two's "who is missing" and Chapter 9's "what this changed" inside it. The chapter's job is to give each sense its evidence, and to say what the display owes to each.

2 · What people believe about recognition, and what the evidence says

Eight beliefs, each common in the trade, each tested below.

"People don't engage with statistics about their area because statistics are abstract." The one interview study reached of lay readers choosing among charts found something else: readers judged a chart with a map in it by whether they could find home. The engagement problem, on that evidence, is the unit and the self, not the statistics. (Section 4.)

"Open on the problem, then answer it." The counted column first, the value column as the reply. Version 1 rejected this for a reason that does not survive; this chapter rejects it for three that do. (Section 5.)

"Never repeat the opposing frame." Version 1's rule, the Decision Book's ARG-12, and Lakoff's. The corrections literature has since looked hard for the mechanism and not found it. (Section 5.)

"Hard data looks truer, so the softer column should be dressed up." The first half has a measured cousin — precision is read as confidence — and the second half was barred by version 1 on the Style Guide's evidence standard and is now barred by the evidence: quantified uncertainty costs little or no trust, so the missed column's intervals are not a liability. (Section 5.)

"You can't rank identity because it's nominal." True as a stance; false as a fact about data. Stevens's typology does not fix the scale type of anything; the question asked does. The house decides the question. (Section 6.)

"The ward is the neighbourhood." No UK statistical unit was designed around what residents recognise. Output areas were built for size and homogeneity; wards vary "from fewer than 100 residents to more than 30,000"; and the deprivation indices call super output areas "neighbourhoods" by stipulation. (Section 3.)

"A recommendation is just a ranking with a nicer face." The recommender literature separates them by a measurable line: an ordering made for one reader from their own weights, with the why shown as content, is a match; an ordering published as the maker's, or driven by popularity, is a rank and behaves like one — it concentrates exposure and it changes what it ranks. (Section 7.)

"A chart carries its caption." The measured population of charts in circulation is mostly screenshots, and official guidance keeps the title and source outside the image on purpose. The caption does not travel; the image does. (Section 8.)

3 · Finding your geography: the unit

How people hold a place

The founding method is Kevin Lynch's, from The Image of the City (1960): residents asked to sketch their city from memory and to describe routes, from which Lynch drew his five elements — paths, edges, districts, nodes and landmarks. The book could not be reached at source; the instruction his interviewers gave, as a secondary page quotes it, was to draw "just as if you were making a rapid description of the city to a stranger, covering all the main features" and "We don't expect an accurate drawing- just a rough sketch" (secondary; Wikipedia quoting Lynch). The method's later literature is more useful to this chapter than the founding text would have been, because it says what a sketch map can be trusted for. Wang and Schwering (2015), with 21 participants drawing 45 maps of areas they knew, found that "sketch maps are incomplete, distorted, and schematized" and yet carry "a set of seven sketch aspects that constitute invariant spatial information", among them the topology of streets, their orientation, the cyclic order of things around a point, the topology of blocks and the orientation of landmarks — each reproduced in well over nine maps in ten — while distances "were found either lengthened or shortened without discernable patterns". (Evidence; small sample, one city.) A review of the method's analysis found "its analytics ad hoc and piecemeal" (Gieseking 2013 [abstract or summary only]). The reading for a dashboard: what a person holds about a place is which things are there, what is next to what, and in what order along a way — not how far, and not where the line is. A display that asks a reader to recognise a place by its boundary is asking for the thing their map holds least; the two methods below ask people to draw one anyway, and measure how far they agree.

Residents' neighbourhoods against the units

The direct measurement is drawn boundaries. Coulton and colleagues' 2001 pilot found that when residents' maps were used to define neighbourhoods, "the resulting units covered different space and produced different social indicator values than did census-defined units", and that "Residents' agreement about their neighborhoods' boundaries differed among the neighborhoods studied" ([abstract or summary only]; the body, with its sizes and overlaps, was not reachable). The same team's large survey is reachable in a research report: 7,498 households across ten American cities were read the prompt "By neighborhood, I mean the area around where you live and around your house. It may include places you shop, religious or public institutions, or a local business district", and asked to draw it in pencil on a street map with their home marked. Eighty-three per cent drew one. "The median area of the RD maps was 0.35 square miles", ranging from 1.2 square miles in one city to 0.09 in another, against "the typical initiative target area (2.23 square miles)" — roughly a sixth. Where several residents gave the same neighbourhood name, the team built a consensus area from blocks "included by at least 33 percent of the respondents" (Coulton, Chan & Mikelbank 2010; research report, not journal-reviewed). (Evidence; the largest reachable measurement; American.) Two limits for this book. The comparator is a programme's target area, not a census or administrative unit; and every drawn-boundary study reached asks where people live, and a scene's people often do not live where the scene is. What a scene's own unit looks like, drawn by the people who make it rather than the people who sleep there, is unmeasured.

The United Kingdom has no measurement of that size that this chapter could reach. What it has is definitions that leave the unit to the respondent. Understanding Society asks "I feel like I belong to this neighbourhood" with no spatial definition at all; the Community Life Survey (Chapter 9) defines a neighbourhood as "a few minutes walking distance from your home" for belonging and a "wider local area" as "within 15 to 20 minutes' walking distance from your home" for satisfaction — two frames in one questionnaire, each named. The policy literature's standard account is Kearns and Parkinson's three scales, as Lupton summarises them: "the home area, has a psycho-social purpose, fostering attachment and belonging"; "the locality, is the locale for residential activities, and denotes social status and provision"; "the urban district or region provides a wider landscape of social and economic opportunities" (Lupton 2003, secondary). And the plainest sentence in Lupton's paper is borrowed too: "neighbourhood delineation has been defined by the limitations of an available data set" (Lupton quoting Dietz).

A vague place has a method

Where a place has a name and no edge — a city centre, a quarter, a scene's patch — the behavioural method is Montello and colleagues' (2003): 36 pedestrians stopped on the street and asked to "outline the area of the city that you consider to be downtown", then the area they were "100% confident was downtown", then "50% confident", then a core point. Of the 36, 33 drew 50 per cent regions larger than their 100 per cent regions; "The core was located an average of nearly 300 meters from the centroid of the 100% region"; and, the finding that matters for a display, "respondents will be willing to make discrete judgments about area membership" of what the authors call "a vague region". (Evidence; one city; street-intercept sample.) The display form that follows is bands of agreement rather than a line. A crowd-sourced neighbourhood map of Boston did it on an "arbitrary hexagonal grid", tallying for each cell how many respondents' polygons covered it — 300 submissions at the time — "divided that count by the total number of respondents for the neighborhood", and drew the 25, 50 and 75 per cent contours as "a notable minority, a majority, and a strong majority" — among, as the author says, "the self-selected people who responded to the survey" (Bostonography 2012; practice). Passive crowd data can do the same at scale: from 8 million geotagged photographs, Hollenstein and Purves (2010) outlined city cores from the "0.5–2% of tags" that name one, with a measured contributor problem — "42% of the outliers stem from only three contributors" — and the caution that the contributors "should not be considered to be representative of society as a whole". (Evidence; method with stated bias.) A fuzzy-set method publishes the shape as a core and a boundary zone rather than a line (Aadland, Farah & Magee 2016 [abstract or summary only]). The rule these point at is simple: a place with no administrative edge is shown as a core and bands — one person's confidence in Montello's method, the share of people agreeing in Boston's — with the number of people whose agreement it is.

What the official units were built for

None of the United Kingdom's small-area units was designed around what residents recognise, and the ONS says so in its own description. Output areas, the smallest census unit, "were designed to have similar population sizes and be as socially homogenous as possible based on tenure of household and dwelling type (homogeneity was not used as a factor in Scotland)"; "The minimum OA size was 40 resident households and 100 resident people, but the recommended size was rather larger at 125 households"; "Urban/rural mixes were avoided where possible". Lower-layer super output areas "comprise between 400 and 1,200 households and have a usually resident population between 1,000 and 3,000 persons"; middle-layer ones "between 2,000 and 6,000 households" and "between 5,000 and 15,000 persons". They exist because wards "vary greatly in size, from fewer than 100 residents to more than 30,000. This was not ideal for nationwide comparisons, and also meant that some data could not be released for smaller wards due to disclosure issues". Wards themselves: "8,483 electoral wards and electoral divisions, with 6,904 in England", average "about 7,900" people, boundaries changed "on the first Thursday in May each year". Built-up areas are the one unit shaped like a settlement — "a geography based on the physical built environment, using Ordnance Survey topographic data to recognise developed land, such as cities, towns, and villages" — and they pay for it in time: "statistics from 2021 BUAs cannot be directly compared with those from 2011". Postcodes "mostly do not align with other geographic boundaries" and are "subject to continuous change". (Standard (ONS geography); all at source.)

Two official habits follow from this and both matter to a page about a place. The first is stipulation: the English Indices of Deprivation say "LSOAs are also referred to as 'neighbourhoods' throughout this release", and the 2025 edition repeats it — a unit "designed to be of a similar population size" is called a neighbourhood because a release needs a word. (Standard (official statistics).) The second is best-fit: postcodes and small areas are assigned to larger geographies by a method the ONS describes — "postcodes with addresses that straddle a boundary will be assigned to the area where the mean grid reference of all the addresses within that postcode falls" — and the Decision Book already requires that a comparison across boundary vintages carries "an explicit, stated lookup" because "Best-fit lookups carry error that must be declared" (Decision Book, data rules on geography; read directly). Middle-layer super output areas "were not given recognisable names when designed" — the default looks like "Ashfield 004" — and the House of Commons Library has named all 7,264 of them "based on the towns, villages and neighbourhoods that they cover", publishing drafts on a map in 2019 for public correction, with the caveat that "The names aren't intended to supplant any names that might already be used locally and they aren't 'official' names" (practice; version 2.3, 13 February 2026). That project is the nearest thing the country has to a statistical unit made recognisable by the people who live in it, and its method — publish, invite correction, keep a standing errors channel — is one this chapter will borrow in section 9. The ONS has also, since January 2023, let a reader draw their own unit: "simply select an area on a map and get the data directly", built from output areas by "population weighted centroid" — a tool its authors later described as "designed to help people get census data that didn't fit standard geographies" (practice; two posts, 2023 and 2025). The official body no longer insists the reader take its unit.

Change the unit and the finding changes

The modifiable areal unit problem is Chapter 1's (Openshaw's "There are no rules for areal aggregation, no standards, and no international conventions") and Chapter 4 carries the ecological fallacy. This chapter needs the demonstration, because "a borough with a scene beats a borough with a superclub" — version 1's illustrative claim, not a finding — is a MAUP consequence if it is anything, and it should be stated as one. The problem has two parts, in the words Jelinski and Wu quote from Openshaw and Taylor: the scale problem is "the variation in results that may be obtained when the same areal data are combined into sets of increasingly larger areal units of analysis", and the zoning problem is "any variations in results due to alternative units of analysis where n, the number of units, is constant". The famous demonstration is theirs: for the 99 counties of Iowa, "correlations ranging from + 0.979 to - 0.811 could be produced by varying the scale and zoning strategies" (secondary, via Jelinski & Wu 1996; the "−0.99 to +0.99" that circulates could not be verified and is not printed). Fotheringham and Wong's multivariate test concluded that the problem "is shown to be essentially unpredictable in its intensity and effects in multivariate statistical analysis" (†). The United Kingdom's own test is Flowerdew's (2011), on the 2001 census of England across its output areas, wards and districts (165,665, 7,969 and 354 — read once): eighteen variables, "153 correlations at each of the three scales"; "68 of these were negative at all three scales, while 60 were positive at all three", and the rest changed sign somewhere between output area and district (the paper's own breakdown of the remainder does not reconcile with its total, and is not printed); by Fisher's test between scales, "the MAUP does make a difference in about 60 per cent of cases"; and his summary — "How serious is the MAUP? Most of the time, not very – but there are occasions when it can make a great deal of difference." "Unfortunately it remains difficult to predict these occasions" [read once] — with the general warning that "correlations over virtually the whole range from -1 to +1 can be reached by judicious placement of zone boundaries". (Evidence; scale effect only; the national census.)

The reading is not that small units are true and large ones false. It is that any figure about a place is a figure about a unit, that the choice of unit can change the sign of a finding, and that nobody can tell in advance which findings. So the unit is declared, with what it hides, on every place-page; and where the house chooses the scene scale as the landing unit (a choice Chapter 11 left to the studio), the page says so and offers the administrative unit beside it, because the reader's councillor, funder and licensing officer live in the administrative one.

The scene as a unit

Version 1 used "scene" as if it were a place. The sociology of culture uses it as a unit of analysis with a definition, and the definition is the reason the scene scale is hard to draw. Straw (1991): a community "presumes a population group whose composition is relatively stable" rooted "within a geographically specific historical heritage", whereas "A musical scene, in contrast, is that cultural space in which a range of musical practices coexist, interacting with each other within a variety of processes of differentiation, and according to widely varying trajectories of change and cross-fertilization". (Reading of a conceptual text; read for the unit, never for any scene.) A scene, on that definition, is a space of practices, not a space on the ground, and its later theorists split it into local, translocal and virtual (Bennett & Peterson 2004; not reached; named only). The one tradition that turns scenes into a measurable unit of place is the Chicago "scenes" method: a scene is "a cluster of urban amenities", scored by coders on fifteen sub-dimensions from 1 to 5, "where 5 indicates that participation in the activities promoted by an amenity is fundamentally defined by the given sub-dimension", with the score attached to a postal area by multiplying "the number of amenities of a given type in a zip code by that amenity-type's score", summing, and dividing "by the total number of amenities in the zip code" (Silver, Clark & Rothfield, working paper; Silver, Clark & Navarro 2010 [abstract or summary only]). Read only for method, it teaches two things. The unit is built from what is listed — the census of business, the yellow pages — so, as Straw's later essay puts it, scenes "make cultural activity invisible and indecipherable by 'hiding' cultural productivity behind seemingly meaningless (or indistinguishable) forms of social life", and a method built on listings cannot see what is not listed; that is Chapter 4's aggregation finding at the level of the unit. And the method's own authors rank on it: "We can also use these profiles to create rankings and maps of the U.S. in terms of zip codes' scores on individual sub-dimensions". A profile built as identity was ranked by the people who built it. That is the pattern this chapter's section 6 exists to prevent, and it is worth knowing that the method nearest to the house's own ambition did not prevent it.

4 · Finding yourself: personal relevance

The evidence that a reader attends to data about their own place is real, interview-based and small, and the chapter states it at that size.

Peck, Ayuso and El-Etr (2019) ran "42 semi-structured interviews in rural Pennsylvania", asking people to rank ten charts on one topic "Based on how useful they are to you". Their headline: "The most recurring theme in our analysis were decisions framed or driven by personal experience." On geography: "People often determined the quality of a graph containing geographical information based on how easy or difficult it was to find their home state." They counted "more than 20 instances in which participants referenced a relatable component", and one participant said of a map, "It has my own county in it. If this would have been like all the countries of the world or something, I really wouldn't have been interested in it because it just affects me personally." The design implication is the authors': "it may be necessary to not only provide mechanisms that allow people to explore personal dimensions of data, but to make sure those personal dimensions are front-and-center in first encounters with a visualization." And the limits are theirs too: "It is unclear how representative our sample is"; "The findings in this paper should be replicated with controlled studies, different populations, and larger sample sizes." (Evidence; interviews; usefulness self-reported; one topic.) Chapter 11 took the same study's finding on source lines; this is its other half.

The Seeing Data study — "nine focus groups with a total of 46 participants", ages 11 to 70 — found six factors in engagement, of which subject matter is one: "When subject matter spoke to participants' interest, they were engaged", and "Strong emotions may arise when considering a visualization, and these also affect engagement" (Kennedy, Hill, Allen & Kirk 2016). The paper frames relevance as interest in a subject, not as seeing one's own place; the companion paper on the feeling of numbers could not be read beyond its abstract. The nearest experiment is on spatial analogies rather than places: shown a distance or area re-expressed in terms of somewhere they knew, 40 crowd-workers rated the information's helpfulness "1.9 points higher (on a 7 pt scale)" than with no analogy and "0.7 points higher than when they see generic spatial analogy", on the premise that "people struggle to understand these measurements when they cannot relate them to measurements of locations that they are personally familiar with" (Kim, Hullman & Agrawala 2016; self-rated helpfulness, not comprehension). And the one official account is the ONS's, from its 331 Census stories (Chapter 11): "We tested the concept with different users who really valued being able to read all about the place they call home in a journalistic style"; "Within a few days of publication in December 2022, every individual area's page had been read"; "The story was taken up by dozens of local news titles" — with no participant numbers, page views or trust measure given. (Practice.)

What is missing is the controlled study: nothing this chapter could reach has measured whether readers attend to, understand or remember a chart better when it is about their own locality, as against the same chart about somewhere else. Two things about that evidence before the display acts on it. The places those readers found were a state, a county and a local authority — units with names — and section 3 has shown that the small-area units have neither names nor edges people hold; so what the evidence supports is that a reader looks for a named place, and the rule is that the reader's place is found first and found by a name people use, whatever unit the figures are for. And "found home" is the beginning of attention, not the measure of understanding; none of these studies measured comprehension. The prototype can run the test the literature has not.

The political frame belongs here because it names the risk of acting on sense two alone. Fraser's warning is that "questions of recognition are serving less to supplement, complicate and enrich redistributive struggles than to marginalize, eclipse and displace them" — "the problem of displacement" — and that recognition "risks sanctioning violations of human rights and freezing the very antagonisms it purports to mediate" — "the problem of reification" (Fraser 2000; the reachable opening; reported as frame). A page that gives a scene the pleasure of seeing itself and does not set its conditions beside its peers' has displaced; a page that types a scene and keeps the type has reified. The two columns and the identity/conditions split are the display's answer to both, and the next two sections build them.

5 · The two columns: counted beside missed

The deck's slides 7 and 8 set the problem: one column of what systems already count about a place and one of what a scene holds and almost nobody counts. Version 1 gave the display five rules — value first; the counted column never omitted; equal visual dignity; gaps rendered full-size and labelled; no shared scale — and a bridging sentence. This section tests each against evidence version 1 did not have, and the first rule loses its reason and keeps its conclusion.

The framing rule, re-tested

Version 1's first rule rested on a synthesis of framing research carried into the Decision Book as its Chapter 16 and its rule ARG-12: "Never repeat the opposing frame in order to deny it — Repetition reinforces it" (Fixed). The source behind that is Lakoff, in his own words: "In general, negating a frame just activates the frame and makes it stronger", and the advice "not to repeat the language of the other side or negate their framing of the issue" (Lakoff 2016, blog; no study cited on the page). The rule could not be found in the Othering & Belonging Institute's public narrative essays; if the house document attributes it there, the attribution is unconfirmed.

The empirical literature that tests the mechanism is the corrections literature, and it has moved. The Debunking Handbook 2020, written by twenty-two of the field's researchers: "Early evidence was supportive of this idea"; "exhaustive experimental attempts to induce a backfire effect through familiarity alone have come up empty"; "Debunking a myth makes it more familiar but the debunking usually overpowers the increase in familiarity"; and the practical rule, "Repeat the misinformation, only once, directly prior to the correction" — with the residue that remains, "Although backfire effects are uncommon, we know that repetition makes information appear true". Swire-Thompson, DeGutis and Lazer's review (2020): "We suggest that backfire effects are not a robust empirical phenomenon"; the familiarity version "rarely, if ever, occurs when the misinformation is paired with a clear and salient correction"; the origin of the idea was "an unpublished manuscript (Skurnik, Yoon, & Schwarz, 2007)" with "failures to directly replicate"; and the recommendation, "Avoiding the repetition of the original misconception within the correction appears to be unnecessary and could even hinder corrective efforts", while "needless repetitions of the misconceptions should still be avoided". The one published finding in the old direction is Skurnik and colleagues' (2005): "Repeatedly identifying a claim as false helped older adults remember it as false in the short term but paradoxically made them more likely to remember it as true after a 3 day delay" (†) — older adults, after a delay, on memory for truth status. Wood and Porter's "more than 10,100 subjects" and "52 issues" found "no corrections capable of triggering backfire" (†), but that is the worldview backfire, not the familiarity one, and the chapter does not cite it for repetition. (Evidence; the field's own reviews.)

Two cautions before the rule is retired. The corrections literature tests belief in a factual claim; Lakoff's claim is about evoking a frame, which is not the same thing, so the literature weakens the rule's usual justification without testing its mechanism head-on. And the framing literature proper does bear on it: Chong and Druckman's competitive experiments (869 and 1,277 participants) found that "framing effects depend more heavily on the qualities of frames than on their frequency of dissemination", that "competition alters but does not eliminate the influence of framing", and that "in no case did repetition of a weak frame allow it to prevail over a strong opposition frame". (Evidence.) When both frames are on the page, strength decides, not count.

So the rule "never show the counted column first because showing it strengthens it" is withdrawn as an evidence claim, and ARG-12 is logged as a conflict for the Decision Book. Value-first survives as a house stance, and the chapter is careful about what supports what. The order rests on one ground, Chapter 11's: the first thing a page shows is read as an endorsement of it, so the choice of first column is a declaration, and the house's declaration is "lead with abundance" (Nightlife Culture). No evidence reached speaks to the order of two true columns either way. The missed column's presence and equal standing rest on two more. The deficit evidence, which is about what a chart of a gap does to its reader rather than about repetition: Holder and Xiong's four experiments (329, 434, 281 and 266 crowd-workers after exclusions) found that "bar charts may encourage deficit thinking" — "the perception that outcome disparities are caused by groups' personal strengths or deficiencies, rather than external factors" — and that "Hiding variability tends to increase stereotyping while emphasizing variability reduces it" (first experiment d = 0.322); Quinn's three randomised experiments found that a news story about group gaps "led viewers to express more exaggerated stereotypes" (0.30 and 0.38 of a standard deviation), "did not affect viewers' explicit competence-related racial stereotyping, the explanations they gave for achievement inequalities, or their prioritization of ending achievement inequalities", and that "After 2 weeks, the effect on stereotype exaggeration faded" (†). Both concern social groups, not places; the transfer is this book's reading. And the finding that opening on a count buys nothing: in FrameWorks' United Kingdom poverty research, a series of experiments with "a nationally representative sample of 12,448 respondents", "leading with prevalence data had no significant effect on issue salience" — "leading with data is the same as saying nothing at all". (Evidence; practitioner research with experiments.) That is a null on salience: it shows no gain from opening on a count, not a harm.

The case version 1 took from Chapter 1 is also corrected. Chapter 1 cited a community-safety dashboard that "refocused the conversation" from an asset-based to a deficit-based model. That sentence is Sarikaya and colleagues' gloss, and the original report says something more useful: "Community engagement experts often take an asset-based approach to development"; "The asset-based approach is challenging in settings such as the Data Dashboard project"; "Yet the data sets of key relevance to public safety are largely negative"; "We invited the community to suggest place-based assets that we could include on the map"; and "We do not yet know how effective our methods have been in conveying an asset-based approach" (O'Connell et al. 2016). (Practice; a design case with no evaluation.) It is a supply problem — the counted data are negative — with three attempted responses, not a finding about readers. Which is exactly the two columns' problem, named by a team that met it.

The asset tradition and its own cautions

The vocabulary of "assets" and "deficits" comes from community development, and the founding text is reachable in its 1990 form: "most Americans think about lower income urban neighborhoods as problems"; "They are noted for their deficiencies and needs"; "residents come to believe that their well-being depends upon being a client"; against which "every neighborhood has a map of riches, assets, and capacities", and the alternative is "to develop policies and activities based on the capacities, skills, and assets of low-income people and their neighborhoods" — "a map of the same territory as the neighborhood needs map" (McKnight & Kretzmann 1990; practitioner framework). The tradition's own reviews are careful. The Glasgow Centre for Population Health: "Asset based approaches are not a replacement for investing in service improvement or attempting to address the structural causes of health inequalities"; "evidence of the effectiveness of these approaches at present largely comes from case studies and small scale exploratory research"; and "it is also conceivable that the adoption of asset based approaches may increase health inequalities" (2011); "difficulties are inherent in measuring assets"; "One of the initial challenges for asset working is to find and collate data that measure positive health and wellbeing" (2012). The Lowitja Institute's review of deficit discourse — "discourse that represents people or groups in terms of deficiency – absence, lack or failure", which "narrowly situates responsibility for problems with the affected individuals or communities, overlooking the larger socio-economic structures" — insists that "These should not be mistaken for calls to deflate the realities of disadvantage", finds that gap framing "certainly appears to carry (and replicate) an implicit assumption of deficit", quotes an interviewee for whom "These statistics became like a mantra" and "I felt like statistics were defining my cultural identity", and reports "almost a complete lack of evaluation of actual impact on discourse itself" (Fogarty et al. 2018; the report quoting others where marked). (Practitioner reviews; evidence status stated by the reviews themselves.) The house's voice rule already holds the conclusion — "Generous: Recognise capability and knowledge before proposing something new", against "Defining people or places only through failure or need" (Style Guide v1.5) — and the chapter adds what the tradition's own reviewers add: the missed column is shown beside the counted one, never instead of it, and nothing in it deflates what the counted column records.
