WebAIM's tenth screen-reader survey, 1,539 self-selected respondents in 2023–24: primary screen reader JAWS 40.5 per cent, NVDA 37.7, VoiceOver 9.7; "91.3% of respondents report using a screen reader on a mobile device"; to find information on a long page, 71.6 per cent "Navigate through the headings on the page". The WebAIM Million, February 2026: "95.9% of home pages had detected WCAG 2 failures", "an average of 56.1 errors per page", low-contrast text on 83.9 per cent, missing alt text on 53.1, and "96% of all errors detected fall into these six categories" — worse than February 2025 on failures, errors per page and contrast, better on missing alt text (55.5 to 53.1). Populations, with their sources' limits: "16.8 million (25%)" disabled people in the United Kingdom (Family Resources Survey 2023/24); "more than 2 million people are living with sight loss in the UK", "around 340,000" registered blind or partially sighted (House of Commons Library, quoting the NHS); colour vision deficiency "approximately 1 in 12 men (8%) and 1 in 200 women" (a charity, unsourced); dyslexia "Ten percent of the population are believed to be dyslexic" (a charity, "believed"); balance and dizziness problems in "About 15 percent of American adults" (United States; no UK figure found). (Evidence; surveys and official statistics; the charity figures marked.)

Reading, numbers and type

The reading-age claims the trade repeats have thin footing. GOV.UK's content guidance has moved and no longer states a reading age; a county council still cites "a reading age of 9 to match GOV.UK standards"; the NHS manual says "We aim for a reading age of 9 to 11 years old" with no source on the page. What stands: "1 in 6 (18% / 6.6 million people) adults aged 16 to 65 in England have very poor literacy skills" (National Literacy Trust, from the Survey of Adult Skills 2023); the NHS's "more than 6 in 10 adults struggle with health content that includes numbers and statistics", introduced by "Research shows that" with no source named; and GOV.UK's "80% of people preferred sentences written in clear English", which traces, through a 2014 guest post, to a legal-writing survey of "376 responses" (†) — a preference, not a comprehension measure. COGA's "lower secondary education level" for a summary is the W3C's own figure. (Evidence; Standard (design system); provenance of each claim stated.) The house's register is cognitive access by COGA's patterns and the literacy figure, not by a reading age nobody can source.

On type, the measured results are clearer than the guidance. With 48 dyslexic readers and twelve fonts, "Sans serif, monospaced and roman font styles significantly improved the reading performance over serif, proportional and italic fonts", "Arial It. should be avoided since it significantly decreases readability", and "The fonts designed specifically for dyslexia, OpenDys and OpenDys It., did not lead to a better or worse readability" (Rello & Baeza-Yates 2013); extended to 97 readers, "Using fonts that are good for people with dyslexia improves accessibility for a large percentage of the population and are also beneficial for those without dyslexia" (2016). With 170 dyslexic children reading text, and then 102 with and 45 without dyslexia reading word lists, "Words written in Dyslexie font were not read faster or more accurately", and "the Dyslexie font neither benefits nor impedes the reading process of children with and without dyslexia" (Kuster et al. 2018 [abstract or summary only]); a single-subject design found "no improvement in reading rate or accuracy" and "None of the participants reported preferring to read material presented in that font" (Wery & Diliberto 2017 [abstract or summary only]). On size, an eye-tracking study of 104 readers recommends "at least 18-point font size for the text body of websites", replicated on 28 dyslexic readers (Rello, Pielot & Marcos 2016) — above the British Dyslexia Association's "12-14 point or equivalent (e.g. 1-1.2em / 16-19 px)". The BDA's other rules — sans serif, "1.5/150%" line spacing, "Left align text, without justification", "dark coloured text on a light (not white) background", "Avoid green and red/pink" — are unsourced on the page, and its own closing line is the convergence claim: "Adopting these principles for dyslexic readers has the advantage of making all written communication easier on the eye for everyone." (Evidence; charity guidance marked.) The reading for the design system: the body type and its size are an accessibility decision with measured bounds; a "dyslexia font" is not one of them.

Convergence, where it is measured

The claim that an accessible page is a better page for everyone has two experiments behind it, both from one laboratory. "Sixty-one nondisabled participants used one of three Web sites differing in levels of accessibility (high, low, and very low)"; "A high level of Web accessibility led to better performance (i.e., task completion time and task completion rate) than low or very low accessibility", and "improved user ratings (i.e., perceived usability, aesthetics, workload, and trustworthiness)" (Schmutz, Sonderegger & Sauer 2016 [abstract or summary only]). Then "55 participants with visual impairments and 55 without impairments", randomly assigned to sites at three levels of WCAG 2.0 conformance: "Higher conformance to Web accessibility guidelines resulted in increased performance and more positive user ratings (e.g., perceived usability or aesthetics) for both user groups" (2017 [abstract or summary only]). The same group then found, for easy-to-read language on a disability-friendly site, effects on non-disabled users of "increased reading time, decreased text liking and reduced intention to revisit the web site" (2019, secondary). Captions: Ofcom's 2006 review found "about 7.5 million people had used them to watch television, of whom about 6 million did not have a hearing impairment" — "had used", from a sample of 4,365 adults; a 2021 survey found "80% of 18- to 24-year-olds 'use subtitles some or all of the time'", a tenth of them deaf or hard of hearing (Stagetext); a review claims "More than 100 empirical studies document that captioning a video improves comprehension of, attention to, and memory for the video" (Gernsbacher 2015 [abstract or summary only]). Typefaces: Rello's "also beneficial for those without dyslexia". And the public sector's own standard says it as a stance: "Inclusive, accessible services are better for everyone. For example, using simple words helps people who are in a hurry as well as people who have a learning disability" (Service Standard, point 5); "Accessible websites usually work better for everyone" (GOV.UK). (Evidence; two experiments; reviews; a stance.)

The reading, at its measured size: conformance to the guidelines helped non-disabled users in the two experiments that asked, both read in abstract; typefaces and captions converge; easy-to-read language had a measured cost for non-disabled readers in one study and plain English a preference among many; and nothing measures convergence for charts, dashboards or maps. "Accessible as the good version" is therefore a stance the house takes with evidence for pages and a named gap for charts, and the prototype's observed sessions are where the first measurement of that gap can be made.

6 · What official bodies do, and admit

The two rules for a chart's description

The ONS and the Analysis Function, the United Kingdom's two sources of official guidance on statistical publishing, disagree about where a chart's description lives. The ONS: "Use chart alt text to provide a specific description of the type of chart and the main trend that it is showing"; "A chart alt text sentence should be between 100 and 200 characters and always end with a full stop"; "Use the format 'A [chart type] showing that [chart title].'"; and for tools, "For some interactive tools, it may not be possible or useful to provide a title that describes a trend". The Analysis Function: a chart may meet 1.1.1 by a table or "a text description of the message the chart is presenting", and "Which you choose should depend on what you would expect a non-disabled user to get from the chart"; "We advise that it should live in the body text rather than in the alt attribute"; "The text description should never be in both the alt attribute and the body text" "as this causes auditory clutter for screen reader users"; "It should also never be in a caption as screen readers do not always pick up on these"; "There is no specific character limit for the text description of a chart as charts can be complex"; and "It is best practice to provide the data displayed in each chart as an accessible data download." Its chart guidance: "all text related to the chart should be in the body text of the webpage unless it is essential for it to be in the image"; a text description, if used, "should live in the body of the page, directly underneath the chart", and in that case "the image of the chart should be marked as decorative and therefore hidden from screen reader software"; legends that match by colour alone fail 1.4.1; "when writing the chart's alternative text you should incorporate any messages given by annotation". Its format advice: build charts in HTML where the site can and "this is known to meet accessibility standards"; otherwise "we consider it the most accessible option for images of charts" — SVG. (Standard (official statistics); Standard (design system).) The two can be read together: the W3C's two-part rule is the ONS's formula as the short part (which identifies the chart and names its trend) and the Analysis Function's body text as the long part (which gives the figures and the relationships), and the Analysis Function's "never both" is about not giving the long description twice. The short part naming the trend that the long part then gives is the W3C's own pattern ("The short text alternative for the chart indicates that a description follows").

The dashboard sentences

The Analysis Function's dashboards guidance (6 February 2026), under what it means by a dashboard: "Dashboards rarely meet full accessibility requirements." "This means you should: not publish a dashboard without the data being available in another form; consider a statistical bulletin to accompany your dashboard." Its software page: "External dashboards must meet WCAG 2.2 guidelines"; "Open-source languages (such as R, and Python) will give greater control over accessibility"; "Out-of-the-box options (such as Power BI) come with some accessibility features built in, but they can be difficult to customise"; "accessibility features are available but are not always used by analysts in a way that meets the WCAG 2.2 requirements"; "users who are reliant on keyboards or assistive software can find it difficult to interact with these dashboards"; Power BI "has a limited Accessibility Checker which does not cover all possible issues". An answer in its 2022 Q&A: "It is hard to make dynamic charts and dashboards fully accessible." "I have been looking into it but I am yet to find a fully accessible dashboard." The ONS's own page: dashboards "are difficult to make accessible and responsive for different devices"; "always make sure any dashboard design meets accessibility standards". (Standard (official statistics).) Chapter 11 attributed the "rarely" sentence to the ONS; it is the Analysis Function's, and the correction is logged.

What the statements declare

Each accessibility statement of an official dashboard that could be read and states a status says "partially compliant", and where a fallback is named it is the data in another form. The UKHSA data dashboard: "partially compliant with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines version 2.2 AA standard"; "some charts present on the dashboards use colour alone to differentiate between lines on the chart … This fails WCAG 1.4.1"; "we have made no claims of disproportionate burden"; prepared and last reviewed 19 December 2023. The ONS: "partially compliant" with 2.2 AA; "Some of our data visualisations may not load or function correctly for users who have JavaScript disabled", "particularly the case for our more advanced interactive tools such as Explore local statistics, Build a custom area profile and Census maps"; "In all instances, the underlying data are accessible through other formats, such as the accompanying dataset files and the surrounding commentary on the HTML web page"; a disproportionate-burden claim for the 2018–2020 back catalogue of visualisations; a new platform "in 2026". Fingertips: "partially compliant" with 2.1; "Interactive elements within data tables are not keyboard operable"; "Relationship between information in data table cells is not always clear to those using a screen reader"; "Colour is the only method used for conveying information within some tables". Public Health Scotland, prepared 18 May 2026: "The R dashboards currently published on this website have a range of accessibility issues and fail the following WCAG 2.2 success criteria" — "Title of the graph is not communicated to screen reader users as it is an image of text."; "The graph is not announced by screen reader."; "Slider widget is inoperable with screen reader activated."; "Dynamic content is not announced."; "Content overlapping at 400% browser zoom." — some twenty items for its R dashboards and fifteen for its Tableau ones, by the tool's count; and of the Tableau dashboards, "Screen reader users do not have access to tooltip information." Two councils' Power BI — Scottish Borders: "Visitors using screen reader software or a keyboard will not be able to interact with them in the same way"; mapping and zoom "do not have an equivalent for keyboard only or screen reader users"; "Some graphs and charts within PowerBI dashboards rely solely on colour"; and Kingston, "partially compliant": "longer strings of alternative text may be cut off when using a screen reader"; "The frame does not reflow when zoomed in at high levels." (Practice; official statements read for what they declare.) The reading: the public record of what official dashboards cannot do is a list of the criteria this book's accessibility rules rest on — 1.4.1, 1.4.5, 1.1.1, 2.1.1, 4.1.3, 1.4.10, 1.4.12 — and the list is the house's test plan.

Design systems, platforms and the two bad answers

The GOV.UK Design System declares itself "fully compliant" with 2.2 AA and says in its strategy that "Using the GOV.UK Design System in a service does not immediately make that service accessible" and "WCAG does not cover all aspects of accessibility"; "To ensure services are accessible, user research must include disabled people"; its own statement says a visitor can "listen to most of the website using a screen reader (including the most recent versions of JAWS, NVDA, TalkBack and VoiceOver)" and that "The details component does not work well with Dragon and older versions of VoiceOver". The NHS manual: "Do not include text in graphical (raster) formats like PNG, JPEG or GIF"; alt text "ideally under 125 characters", with the caveat that for "a complex chart" the information may go in the alt text or a link. The BBC's infographics guide: alt text "Describes what is in the infographic; a literal interpretation of its form"; the caption "Explains what the infographic says; an editorial summary of its salient points"; "Multi-dimensional data that can be represented as a chart or graph should also be provided as a data table"; "Design it monochrome to begin with, and only add colour where desirable"; and "In most cases, you should avoid creating interactive visualisations". Platforms: Datawrapper, "The elements of all your Datawrapper charts, maps, and tables can be navigated using only the keyboard", an alt-text field and a "Get the data" link; Flourish, "instead of a blanket WCAG AA certification, we focus on enabling and guiding users"; Highcharts, keyboard navigation, "Screen reader users can explore the chart and its data point by point", and a sonification module with Georgia Tech's Sonification Lab; Vega-Lite, an aria flag and "A text description of the mark item for ARIA accessibility (SVG output only)"; Tableau, "You can use Tableau to create dashboards that conform to the Web Content Accessibility guidelines (WCAG 2.2 AA)" — what an author can build; Power BI, "All Power BI visuals support keyboard navigation", "The Alt Text textbox has a limit of 250 characters", "The accessibility features have a few known problems and limitations." Eurostat: "The interactive tools and visualisations on this site do not always have text alternatives"; "Interactive maps are not always accessible to blind users and users who rely on keyboard navigation". (Standard (design system); Practice; vendor documentation.)

The two bad answers have a record. Overlays: "full compliance cannot be achieved with an overlay"; "We will always advocate for the remediation of accessibility issues at the source of the original error" (Overlay Fact Sheet, about a thousand signatories); among 758 practitioners, "A strong majority (67%) of respondents rate these tools as not at all or not very effective. Respondents with disabilities were even less favorable with 72% rating them not at all or not very effective, and only 2.4% rating them as very effective" (WebAIM 2021); and the United States Federal Trade Commission's order of 2025 requiring one vendor "to pay the FTC $1 million" over claims that its widget made sites compliant — a consent order, not a finding; no UK regulator has spoken. Text-only versions: "Text-only versions do not accomplish the goal of accessibility"; "They accommodate users with some disabilities but neglect other types of disabilities"; "Updates may not be reflected on the text-only version, and the information can quickly become outdated and inaccurate" (WebAIM); the staleness claim is practitioner consensus with no audit behind it; a GDS staff comment of 2013, "I'd rather we didn't build a separate 'accessible' site". (Practice; Evidence (survey); the regulator's order reported as fact.)

7 · Chapter 12's departure, tested

Chapter 12 ruled that every chart carries, inside its frame, its title, unit, source, base, address and snapshot date, and for a comparison its gate and its wording — eight items — so that a screenshot says what it is — against the Analysis Function's rule that "titles should be in the body of the page or document, as opposed to within an image", given for accessibility, with the cost admitted: "This does mean an image of a chart can be taken out of context if it is copied and pasted elsewhere." This chapter owes it the test against the criteria.

The criterion is 1.4.5 Images of Text (AA): "If the technologies being used can achieve the visual presentation, text is used to convey information rather than images of text except for the following: Customizable: The image of text can be visually customized to the user's requirements; Essential: A particular presentation of text is essential to the information being conveyed." Its definition of an image of text excludes "text that is part of a picture that contains significant other visual content", and its Understanding page names the case: "Examples of such pictures include graphs, screenshots, and diagrams which visually convey important information through more than just text." Then the sentence that decides it: "Where images of text are used in addition to text to convey the same information, and where both are presented to the user, this success criterion is met." The page's example is a poster whose text is also given beside it. 1.4.11 adds that "Text within a graphic must meet 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)", and the Analysis Function itself says "Chart labels and annotations can be considered essential images of text". 1.4.12 treats canvas text as images of text and does not mention SVG; the Analysis Function considers SVG "the most accessible option for images of charts". The one official failure on record is Public Health Scotland's: "Title of the graph is not communicated to screen reader users as it is an image of text" — a title that existed only in the image. (Standard (W3C); Standard (official statistics); Practice.)

The reading, and it is a reading: on the live page, the chart is SVG or HTML with its title, unit, source and date as real text in the page, which is what the Analysis Function asks and what 1.4.4, 1.4.5 and 1.4.12 are for; the frame that carries them as part of the graphic is text inside an SVG, which is text, or — in the exported image — text inside a picture "that contains significant other visual content", given "in addition to text", with "both … presented to the user". Chapter 12's rule, built that way, meets 1.4.5 by its own Understanding page. What it must not become is Public Health Scotland's failure: a title that lives in the picture and nowhere else. So the rule is restated with its condition: the frame's text — the identifying items, not the long description — is drawn as text in SVG on the page, repeated as HTML text beside the chart (the heading, the source line), and baked into the downloaded image; never the image alone. That repetition is of the title and source, which the Analysis Function itself places in the body; it is not the "never both" case, which concerns the long description. The remaining cost is 1.4.4's — text in a raster export "does not scale as well" — and that is the export's cost, not the page's; the design system's own preference for text outside images stands for the page and is kept. Whether eight items fit a phone-sized frame legibly remains the open question Chapter 12 left.

8 · The routes, and what each carries

Pulling sections 3 and 5 together: a dashboard view reaches a reader who cannot see it, or cannot see it well, or cannot read numbers easily, or cannot use a mouse, by several routes, and the evidence says what each carries and what it drops.

The written account. Chapter 11's sentence on every view and its generated account per place are, in this chapter's terms, the long description the W3C asks for, at the levels blind readers rank highest — the statistics and the trend — in the plain words COGA asks for. It is the one route every assistive technology handles, and it is the route the ONS, the Analysis Function and every official statement fall back on ("the surrounding commentary on the HTML web page"). It carries the meaning, for every reader, which is where interpretation lives; it does not carry the data.

The table twin. It carries the data, is the route screen-reader auditors rated best, is the route the Regulations' map exemption and the Analysis Function's "data being available in another form" point at, and is a native HTML table, which the Authoring Practices Guide prefers to any ARIA grid. It does not carry shape, and for a map it carries the figures and not the geography (0.23 against 0.44). It is paginated and sortable by keyboard; it has real header cells (1.3.1).

The navigable structure. A chart exposed as a tree — overview, groupings, marks — with keyboard movement and the focused node's name and value spoken at each step, built from the chart's specification by tooling that exists. It carries shape and lets a reader explore; the one study found the plain table easier to use than its richest prototype; it is the route to build second and test first. The tree is built on graphics-document and native roles, never on ARIA invented for the purpose: "No ARIA is better than Bad ARIA".

Audio. Overview and trend for a trained listener; unfamiliar to most; not maps; the platform's audio graph where the platform offers one. A labelled extra beside the routes above.

Tactile. The route the most surveyed users named as preferred (50 of 127), and the one a web page cannot give except as a file to emboss. Out of scope for the display; in scope for the data download, which is the file.

The eye, helped. Zoom to 400 per cent without two-dimensional scrolling (1.4.10), with the map and the data table excepted and the furniture around them not; text that reflows, resizes and respaces (1.4.4, 1.4.12), which rules out canvas text; colour never alone and 3:1 on each line and slice that carries meaning unless labels do (1.4.1, 1.4.11); the reduced-motion preference honoured and auto-updates pausable (2.2.2, 2.3.3); focus visible and never under the filter bar (2.4.7, 2.4.11); type at a size the eye-tracking evidence supports, in a face the dyslexia evidence supports, which is an ordinary sans serif and not a special one.

The hand. Everything by keyboard with no trap (2.1.1, 2.1.2); every control by single pointer without a drag (2.5.1, 2.5.7); targets at 24 pixels or the table twin (2.5.8); nothing fires on mouse-down (2.5.2).

The mind. One brief status message per change, never the view read aloud (4.1.3); interpretation in the authored account, on the page for everyone, and not in the chart's description (section 5); a filter that changes content and not context (3.2.2); numbers reinforced with words, each step carrying what the last one knew, uncommon terms explained within a click, a summary at lower-secondary level (COGA).

What no route carries alone is the whole, and that is the point of section 3's first finding: the routes sit on one page, as supplementary content, and the page conforms or it does not.

9 · The failures, read for the disabled reader

People do not use it. Because they cannot: 61.48 per cent less accurate, 210.96 per cent longer; "Many visualizations are entirely indetectable to screen readers"; 73 per cent of screen-reader users did not agree that the data they met was typically accessible. Test: a screen-reader user, using the written route and the table together, says the view's sentence, the figure it rests on and a next step (Chapter 11's three); the pass is all three; the time is recorded against a sighted reader's, and the ratio is the measure the prototype tracks, because the literature's ratio is three to one.

People do not trust it. Because it says nothing about itself: 94 per cent of screen-reader users had concerns about getting accurate pandemic information in time; the government found "many accessibility statements are now out-of-date". Test: the house's statement is dated within the last twelve months, lists each view's routes and failures, and names what it was tested with and by whom; a statement is a necessary condition for trust and not evidence of it, and the chapter claims no more.

It breaks. Because the keyboard route was never walked: focus visibility and keyboard the first and third commonest public failures, found by hand and missed by scanners. Test: the mouse unplugged, every view reached and left.

It looks the same every month. Because the accessible route is a frozen alt text on a changing view. Test: the description says the current figure, and a person has read it against the data since the last change.

The parallel version. Because a second build is a second thing to maintain, which the standard calls a fallback and practice says goes stale. Test: there is one page per layout, and the accessible routes are on it.

10 · What holds true regardless

Seven truths, each with its grounds, then the record. Stated for any public dashboard; the nightlife case in section 12 is one application.

1 · The accessible version is the version: a page conforms whole or not at all, the standard names a separate accessible version a fallback and prefers content "directly accessible", and the written account, the table and the structure are supplementary content on the one page — so the house, going one step past the standard's preference, builds one page per layout and no parallel one. "cannot be achieved if part of a web page is excluded"; "a fallback option for conformance to WCAG"; "the preferred method of conformance is to make all content directly accessible"; "should be deprecated"; "Text-only versions do not accomplish the goal of accessibility". (Section 3; W3C Understanding Conformance; WebAIM; US Department of Justice.)

2 · No rule names a chart, so a chart meets the standard by readings the W3C has written down: a short description that identifies it and a long description that gives its values, relationships and trends with the data in a table where practical; contrast on each line and slice that carries meaning unless labels do; one brief status message when a filter changes a view and never the view itself; auto-updating that can be paused; motion that can be disabled; text that is text — and ARIA offers graphics-document and its generic roles and no chart role, so none is invented. "scales, values, relationships and trends"; "Where possible and practical, the actual data is provided in a table"; "each line in a graph"; "'18 results returned'"; "too 'chatty'"; "a mechanism for the user to pause, stop, or hide it"; "The impact of animation on people with vestibular disorders can be quite severe"; "canvas implementations of text are considered to be images of text"; "Future work will expand on this framework"; "No ARIA is better than Bad ARIA". (Section 3; WCAG 2.2 Understanding pages; Graphics Module; APG.)

3 · The description that stands in for a chart carries the chart — its type, its figures and its trend — in plain words, two to eight sentences, generated from the data by a published rule and read by a person against the figures; interpretation lives in the authored account on the page, for every reader — because blind readers rank the statistics and the trend most useful and were emphatic against an author's interpretation in the description, sighted readers with the chart rank interpretation highly, half of alt texts in the one measured sample omit the extrema and seven in ten the trend, and a reviewer anchored on a machine's draft reviews less. "blind readers rank content and Levels 2 and 3 as most useful"; "emphatic that descriptions should not contain an author's subjective interpretations"; "reference the underlying data instead of visual elements"; "only 50% … extrema or outliers"; "only 31% … major trends or comparisons"; "significantly lower quality alt text when starting from the automatic alt text". (Section 5; Lundgard & Satyanarayan; Jung et al.; Chintalapati, Bragg & Wang; Mack et al.)

4 · A table carries the data and is the type most often rated accessible in the one audit; it does not carry shape or geography, so a map's table twin is joined by a sentence for the shape and, where the house builds one, a text route that answers "where"; the navigable structure carries shape and is built second and tested; audio carries point estimates to a trained listener and an overview by its vendors' account, and is a labelled extra. "tables … the only type … (54%, 7/13)"; "7% (1/15) of maps"; "multi-view was more difficult to use than table"; 0.44 against 0.23 on geographic questions, with lower workload on the table; "reduce performance error by 50%" after twenty minutes; "63% … had never encountered sonification"; "task accuracy did not differ significantly across systems". (Section 5; Fan et al.; Zong et al.; Biggs et al. preprint; Walker & Nees; Sharif et al. 2025; Chundury et al. [abstract or summary only].)

5 · The texts that bear on a private provider are the Equality Act's: a duty owed by a service "to the public or a section of the public (for payment or not)" to "disabled persons generally", which the explanatory notes call anticipatory, whose reasonable steps include "the information is provided in an accessible format"; the Regulations bind public bodies, presume conformity at WCAG Level A and AA "as amended from time to time" (WCAG 2.2 by the government's statement, monitored since October 2024), and do not apply to "third-party content that is neither funded nor developed by, nor under the control of, the public sector body" — content a body did not fund it must declare exempt in its statement, and content it funded is, on the government's reading, its responsibility; no regulator's text read names WCAG and no reported website judgment was found. Reported, not advised. (Section 4; S.I. 2018/952 regs 3, 4, 6–9, 12; Equality Act ss. 6, 20, 21, 29, Sch 2; the 2026 Code; GOV.UK guidance.)

6 · Official bodies admit that dashboards "rarely meet full accessibility requirements", each official dashboard statement read is "partially compliant" with the data in another form as its fallback, and the failures they declare are the criteria above — so the house publishes an accessibility statement in the public sector's model form, as its own procedure, declaring per view what each route carries and what fails, dated, with the technology it was tested with. "I am yet to find a fully accessible dashboard"; "In all instances, the underlying data are accessible through other formats"; "Title of the graph is not communicated to screen reader users as it is an image of text"; "Screen reader users do not have access to tooltip information"; "an explanation of those parts of the content that are not accessible and the reasons why". (Sections 4, 6; Analysis Function; ONS; PHS; Fingertips; UKHSA; reg 8.)

7 · Convergence is measured narrowly and holds where measured — conformance helped non-disabled users in the two experiments that asked (both read in abstract), readable typefaces for dyslexia read better for everyone, most subtitle users hear — and is unmeasured for charts, so "accessible as the good version" is a stance with evidence for pages and a named gap, which observed testing with disabled readers of the real audience is the way to begin measuring. "better performance … than low or very low accessibility" (†); "for both user groups" (†); "also beneficial for those without dyslexia"; "about 6 million did not have a hearing impairment"; "increased reading time, decreased text liking"; "user research must include disabled people". (Section 5; Schmutz, Sonderegger & Sauer [abstract or summary only]; Rello & Baeza-Yates; Ofcom; GOV.UK Design System.)

Beneath the dashboard: the accessibility statement

Chapters 4 to 12 each left a record; whether they are one document is answered in Chapter 16. This chapter's tenth is different in kind from the others and the same in kind as the public sector's: it is published, in the model statement's form, and it is the record. Its lines — the model's own (status; non-accessible content and why; alternatives; contact; preparation and testing) with the house's per-view lines between them:

Line What it records From
1 Status Fully, partially or not compliant with WCAG 2.2 AA, in the model's words, for each layout Reg 8; model statement
2 Per view: description The short description's place and the long description's (body text); that it carries type, figures and trend and not interpretation; how it is generated and who read it against the data Section 5; Analysis Function
3 Per view: table The table twin's location, its headers, pagination, and what it cannot carry (shape; geography) Sections 5, 8
4 Per view: structure Whether a navigable structure exists, on what roles, tested with which screen readers Section 3; APG
5 Per view: audio Whether an audio graph or sonification exists, and that it is an extra Section 5
6 Motion and updates The reduced-motion behaviour; the pause control for auto-updating views Section 3; 2.2.2, 2.3.3
7 Keyboard and focus The walk's result per view: reached, operated, left; focus visible and unobscured 2.1.1, 2.1.2, 2.4.7, 2.4.11
8 Zoom and reflow 400 per cent result per layout; what is excepted (map, table) and what is not (their furniture) 1.4.10, 1.4.4, 1.4.12
9 Non-compliances Each failure by criterion, in the public sector's form, with the route around it Reg 8(4)(a), (b); PHS as model
10 Burden Any claim and its assessment; the house's default is none Reg 7
11 Tested Date, technologies (named screen readers, browsers, platforms), and who tested, including disabled readers of the audience Design System; Chartability
12 Contact The errors channel (Chapter 12) and the request route for information in another format Reg 8(4)(c); reg 13

A filled example. Invented, to show the record's shape; nothing in it is a decision or a finding. Status: partially compliant with WCAG 2.2 AA on desktop and phone layouts, because of the non-compliances listed. Description: each view's sentence and account in the page body, generated from the current state at levels 2 and 3, read by a person before release; no alt attribute duplicates them. Table: beneath each view, native HTML, headers marked, paginated at fifty rows, sortable by keyboard; for the map it carries values by area and not adjacency. Structure: the two-column view exposed as a tree on graphics-document and native roles; tested with NVDA and JAWS on Chrome and VoiceOver on iOS. Audio: none in this release. Motion: transitions off under the reduced-motion preference; the live panel's refresh pausable from its header. Keyboard: all views reached and left; focus visible; the filter bar does not cover a focused mark. Zoom: 400 per cent without two-dimensional scrolling except the map and the table, whose headings and pagination reflow. Non-compliances: the brush on the time view requires a drag and has no single-pointer alternative yet (fails 2.5.7; fix planned). Exceptions claimed: the map's dense pins under 2.5.8's essential exception, with the table as the equivalent route. Burden: no claim. Tested: 2 November, with three screen-reader users from the user groups and one magnifier user, by the studio; Chartability pass by a trained auditor, four hours. Contact: the errors channel; a form for information in another format.

11 · Where the choice is yours

Whether to build a navigable structure, an audio route or a "where" route for the map, and when. Description and table are the chapter's rules; the rest are routes with evidence of their own size, and the order after the first two is the studio's.

Which screen readers, browsers and platforms to test with. The survey's shares (JAWS, NVDA, VoiceOver; nine in ten on mobile) are the evidence; the Design System's list is a precedent.

Which sans serif, and which size between the two measured figures. The chapter's rule is a sans serif at a measured size; the design system's tokens decide which face and where between 16 and 18 pixels the body sits, and record why.

How the reduced-motion page looks. Open, provided nothing crucial moved in the first place.

Whether the frame's provenance text fits a phone. Chapter 12's question, tested in section 7 for the criteria and left for the prototype on legibility.

The reading-level test. The community's phone-read test, COGA's lower-secondary summary, or both.

Whether to seek the adviser's view now. On what the Act's duty asks of the studio, on what "funded" covers under the Regulations, and on whether a published statement of partial compliance has consequences for a body not bound by the Regulations; the chapter reports and does not advise.

12 · A nightlife illustration — method only

Illustrative; fixes nothing about the design; invents no findings.

A place-page from Chapter 12, read four ways.

By keyboard. Tab lands on the page's sentence, then the two columns as landmarks; the status region that will speak when a filter changes is never in the tab order. Into the missed column's profile as a tree: the chart's name, "four groupings", the first grouping, its marks by arrow key, each mark's label and value spoken, and a way out by Tab. The filter bar is below the focused mark, never over it. The map is a landmark too; where its pins must be small the table twin is the next landmark.

By screen reader, without entering a chart. The sentence; the generated account at levels 2 and 3 — the figures and the trend, no interpretation; the table for each view, headers announced; for the map, the sentence for the darkest shape and a short list of which areas sit beside which. When the reader changes the district, one polite message of the kind "District changed; 3 of 20 shown", and the reader goes to the sentence.

By ear, if the house builds it. An audio graph of the time view, labelled as an extra, after the description and the table; the sound of the place, if that is ever on the page, as content and not as the route to a figure.

At 400 per cent on a phone, with motion reduced. One column at a time, poster above door; the table paginates; the map keeps its two dimensions and its heading does not; nothing slides; the live panel says when it will next refresh and can be stopped.

The statement. Linked from the footer; twelve lines per the record; the non-compliances in the public sector's form; the test date and the screen readers named; the errors channel.

The tests. A scanner first, for what it catches. The mouse unplugged, every view reached and left. The phone layout at 400 per cent. A screen-reader user from the user groups completes the three — sentence, figure, next step — by the written route and the table together, and the time is recorded against a sighted reader's. A blind reader is asked what the district's trend is, what the figures are and, on the map, which places sit beside it, and a sighted reader is asked the same from the chart; the answers are compared on those things. Chartability's critical fourteen are walked before release. And the statement is read back against the page by someone who did not write it.

The long description is two to eight plain sentences generated from the current state by a published rule and read by a person against the figures; it is never duplicated in an alt attribute Interviews; audit of alt texts; the anchoring finding; "auditory clutter" Evidence + Standard (official statistics) Fixed (requirement) Jung et al.; Chintalapati et al.; Mack et al.; Analysis Function
The chart's description carries the chart and not the author's interpretation; interpretation lives in the authored account on the page, read by everyone Blind readers emphatic against interpretation in the description; sighted readers rank it highly; both read the account Evidence + Reading Adaptable (house default) Lundgard & Satyanarayan; Chapter 11

A map's twin is joined by a sentence for the shape and the statement says the twin does not carry geography Tables lost to a text map on geographic questions Evidence (one preprint) Fixed (requirement) Biggs et al.; Chapter 11
A navigable structure is built on graphics-document and native roles, never invented ARIA; tested with named screen readers before release "A role is a promise"; "No ARIA is better than Bad ARIA"; ARIA pages carry more errors Standard (W3C) + Evidence Fixed (requirement) APG; Graphics Module; WebAIM Million

Each line, slice or mark that carries meaning has 3:1 contrast unless labels carry the same information 1.4.11's chart cases Standard (W3C) Fixed (requirement) Understanding 1.4.11
Colour is never the only carrier; legends match by more than colour 1.4.1; declared in most of the dashboard statements read Standard (W3C) + Practice Fixed (requirement) Chapter 3; UKHSA; PHS; Analysis Function

Numbers are reinforced with words; each step carries what the last knew; uncommon terms are explained within one click; the "how this argues" page has a lower-secondary summary COGA's patterns, specific where WCAG is silent Standard (W3C), informative Adaptable (house default) COGA; Chapters 7, 9, 11, 12

How the routes look and sound; the reduced-motion page; the structure's narration style Open, within the rules above — Decorative Chapter 14 of this book

What proves a break works

A scan, three walks and a question; each has a pass. The scan: an automated checker on every layout, for contrast and the rest of what it catches; a pass is zero detected failures. The keyboard walk: mouse unplugged, every view reached, every control used, every view left, with focus visible throughout, on the desktop layout and on the phone layout with an external keyboard; a pass is no failure. The zoom walk: the phone layout at 400 per cent, which is the 320-pixel width 1.4.10 names, every view read, no two-dimensional scrolling except inside the map and the table and never for their headings or controls; text respaced to 1.4.12's values with nothing lost; a pass is no failure. The screen-reader read: a screen-reader user who has not seen the page, with one of the two commonest desktop readers or VoiceOver on a phone, says the view's sentence, the figure it rests on and a next step, using the written route and the table together; a pass is all three; the time against a sighted reader's is recorded. The question: a blind reader is asked what the trend is, what the figures are and, on a map, which places sit beside the one named; a sighted reader is asked the same from the chart; a pass is agreement on the trend, the figures and the neighbours — the chapter's evidence says the groups differ on interpretation, which is why interpretation is not asked. The structure, where built, is tested by the screen-reader read with the table covered. A departure from any Fixed rule above is logged with the five results attached, and the statement's line 9 carries it until it is fixed.

What this chapter could not settle

  • No controlled comparison of description, table and structure for the same chart with time and accuracy; the chapter states each route's evidence separately and leaves the order as a procedure.
  • Nothing measures convergence for charts; the chapter states the page-level evidence and the gap.
  • UK prevalence for colour vision deficiency, dyslexia and vestibular disorders has no official source; charity and US figures, marked.
  • Reading-age figures have no source anywhere official; replaced with the literacy survey figure and COGA's level.
  • Official bodies disagree on where a chart's description lives; reconciled as the W3C's two parts; the house picks one.
  • No UK regulator text on overlays; no UK website judgment; the absence is reported.

Checklist

  • One page per layout; routes on it; no parallel version
  • Short description identifies; long description in body text carries statistics and trend; data in a table where practical
  • Descriptions generated from state, two to eight plain sentences, read by a person, not duplicated in alt
  • Native HTML table twin per view; map's twin joined by the shape sentence
  • Structure, where built, on graphics-document and native roles; tested with named screen readers
  • 3:1 on meaningful lines, slices and marks unless labelled; colour never alone
  • Chart text as SVG or HTML; frame text on page, beside chart, and in export
  • Keyboard walk passed; focus visible and unobscured; no trap
  • No mouse-down firing; drags have alternatives; 24 px or the twin
  • Auto-update pausable; motion reducible
  • Reflow at 320 px; only map and table excepted
  • One polite status message per change
  • COGA: words with numbers; steps self-contained; terms explained; summary at lower-secondary level
  • Sans serif at a size between the measured figures, recorded
  • No overlay
  • Statement published, twelve lines, per view, dated, tested-with named
  • Non-compliances declared by criterion with routes
  • Tooling chosen against the rules in week one
  • Scan, three walks and the question, with passes; Chartability criticals per release
  • Disabled readers of the audience in observed testing

Words this chapter uses

  • The table twin is Chapter 8's rule that every map, and Chapter 11's that every dense chart, has the same figures as a table reachable before any script.
  • A navigable structure is a chart exposed to a screen reader as a tree the reader steps through, rather than as one sentence or one flat table.
  • The four-level model is a published account of what a chart description can contain, from the chart's looks (level 1) through its statistics (2) and its trends (3) to its meaning in the world (4); section 5 gives it.
  • The floor is version 1's name for the set of accessibility requirements the house adopted from its design system and its Decision Book — keyboard operation including chart elements, visible focus, 200 and 400 per cent zoom, semantic structure, alt text generated from the current state, user override of colour, contrast and font, and observed testing — which this chapter maps to the criteria.
  • View, layout and route are used as in Chapter 11: a view is one chart or panel with its data, specification and selection; a layout is the page as presented at one screen size; a route is one way a reader reaches a view's content.
  • The Regulations are the Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations 2018, S.I. 2018/952, as amended; the Act is the Equality Act 2010; the anticipatory duty is the name the Act's explanatory notes give to the duty to make reasonable adjustments for "disabled persons generally", in advance of any individual asking.
  • The three user groups are the studio's testing groups, named in its design repository and not here.

14Where evidence meets expression

Expression is tested by what remains when it is removed, and it buys engagement, mood and recognition — not accuracy.

Dashboard Design · Part 4: The boundary and the practice

Reading this chapter. This is one chapter of Dashboard Design, Nightlife Culture's research book on how evidence becomes a display a reader can trust, read and act on. The studio ("the house" in some chapters) is Nightlife Culture, a creative policy studio; the brief is its founder Carly Heath's commission for the book, and her eight ways a dashboard fails, the failure register, run through it. The Vibe Map, the studio's prototype for showing a place's nightlife culture, appears only as an illustration, never as a specification. "Version 1" is the book's archived first draft, whose positions this version re-tests against the sources. Every rule carries a kind (where it comes from: Standard, Evidence, Reading, Practice or Nightlife Culture) and a tier (how firm it is: Fixed, Adaptable or Decorative); Chapter 0 explains both, and the three senses of Fixed: a requirement that can be checked, a sequence whose order is the hard line, and a statement of the record. A dagger (†) marks a source read at the authors' abstract or summary only; "secondary" a quotation reached through a named reproduction; "(read once)" a quotation returned on a single reading and not confirmed by a second. Chapter 0 holds the glossary of the words the chapters share; each chapter lists its own coinages before its sources.

The question

Where is the line between the evidence layer and the expressive layer of a public dashboard — what must stay true under any creative treatment, and how is that tested; what does the measured evidence on embellishment, affect and persuasion license an expressive treatment to claim, and on what conditions; what do the conventions of "objective-looking" display themselves do to a reader, and what follows for a house whose evidence standard is written against strong design; what does the strongest expressive work in the field do when each piece is read for what it breaks of this book's rules, what substitutes, and whether it was ever evaluated; and what does a dashboard about sound owe a reader who cannot hear it?

The 60-second version

The boundary has a formal name, from 1986. Mackinlay's criterion: "A set of facts is expressible in a language if it contains a sentence that (1) encodes all the facts in the set, (2) encodes only the facts in the set." The second clause is the removal test. The classic case of a sentence that says too much is his own: "Most people perceive the lengths of the bars as an encoding of an ordered or quantitative set" [read once], so a bar chart of unordered categories encodes an order that is not there. Expressiveness asks whether the picture says what the data says and nothing else; effectiveness — which Mackinlay calls "conjectural" and, beyond quantitative data, "not been empirically verified" — asks how well a person reads it. The house's three tiers sit inside this: a Fixed rule about a chart is, in the main, an expressiveness rule (or a floor rule from Chapter 13); an Adaptable one is an effectiveness rule; Decorative is what neither criterion can see. Munzner's nested model says where the line falls — inside the encoding level, between the encodings that carry the abstraction (what is counted and compared) and the choices around them that change no fact — and why no amount of care at that level repairs a wrong abstraction above it: "an upstream error inevitably cascades to all downstream levels."

Plain is also a style. Kennedy, Hill, Aiello and Allen name four conventions that "imbue visualisations with a sense of objectivity, transparency and facticity": "a) two-dimensional viewpoints; b) clean layouts; c) geometric shapes and lines; d) the inclusion of data sources" — the last of which "performs the rhetorical, persuasive work of ascribing transparency and trustworthiness to visualisations." Data Feminism says the same more sharply: "The more plain, the more neutral; the more neutral, the more objective; and the more objective, the more true" — "or so this line of reasoning goes." Correll: "The clean lines and structured layouts of traditional visualizations communicate authority and certainty in implicit but measurable ways." The Style Guide's evidence standard — "Strong design must never make weak evidence look stronger than it is" — therefore cuts both ways. A plain chart with a source line at the bottom is making a claim about its own trustworthiness, and the claim has to be true. The conventions paper itself tested no readers: thirteen designer interviews and a semiotic reading of ten pieces; its claim about what readers perceive is an argument, and the chapter says so.

What expression is measured to buy is engagement, mood and recognition — and, from Chapter 3's line, memorability — and not accuracy, and not action beyond a small effect on a hypothetical allocation. Humanising the marks did not move people: across seven experiments of fifty participants each, Boy and colleagues "consistently find that anthropomorphized data graphics and standard charts have very similar effects on empathy and prosocial behavior"; the largest preregistered test since, with 786 participants, put the effect of an information-rich anthropographic on hypothetical allocation at 3.4 points in a hundred, 95% CI [0.021, 6.8] — an interval whose lower bound sits just above zero, and whose standardised form includes it. The ethics paper most cited for humanising data concedes it: person-shaped glyphs have "not been shown to produce any additional empathic response" [read once]. Mood can be carried without a measured reading cost: animated charts built to express five positive feelings scored the same as a baseline animation on three comprehension questions and higher on engagement (197 readers; comprehension differences not significant, which is not equivalence); in a corpus of 976 infographics rated by 490 readers, negative feeling "are mainly caused by poor usability" and small type, so in that corpus feeling and legibility ran together; small palettes carry calm, excitement, seriousness and playfulness through lightness and chroma, while "Trustworthy showed very little structure." Visualisations that readers rate as images rather than as information are found "more aesthetically appealing, enjoyable, and pleasing" and convey less of their trend and message (250 online, 101 in person; correlational). And the desirable-difficulties argument for making charts harder on purpose does not survive the meta-analysis: across 3,135 participants, "there was no effect of perceptual disfluency on recall (d = − 0.01) or transfer (d = 0.03)", while it made people slower and less confident.

Costs the register must price. Dark grounds: 85 older and 84 younger adults read small text better dark-on-light, with "A positive polarity advantage was found for both age groups" (d = 2.17 for the young at threshold); the penalty appears in dark rooms and disappears in daylight-like light; for charts rather than text, which polarity helped was individual and preference did not predict it, so the sound position is "making visualizations available in both contrast polarities." Saying it twice: redundant coding yields "a large benefit for rapidly segmenting objects within a dense display", which grounds carrying a category in two channels and is a different claim from the twin's; and putting a text and a chart side by side did not raise accuracy (55, 56 and 59 correct of 87) and eye-tracking suggested readers "do not integrate information well across the two representation types" [read once] — the twin must be reachable as well as present. Reading in passing: the sign trade's planning average is thirty feet of reading distance per inch of capital height; four to eight words in "approximately four seconds"; "one-tenth of a second per letter"; a 1965 report summarised by a reviewer as "Only 3-4 short, familiar words can be read in a single glance at a sign"; in an unprimed threshold test of 33 fonts, capitals out-read lower case in all 31 fonts that had both. The "seven words" rule the trade repeats has no study behind it on any page that repeats it.

The removal test — mono, silent, still, undressed, then stripped beside dressed — is run by official bodies under other names. The Analysis Function's infographic rule is a plain-text twin: "provide a plain text alternative explaining all the information within the infographic", and a user test — "do they understand the story without explanation?" The ONS's motion rule: "never make an animation the only way to get the information." The W3C's own definition of decoration is a removal test in a sentence: "Text is only purely decorative if the words can be rearranged or substituted without changing their purpose"; and it has a third category the house's tiers lack, the "specific sensory experience", which "words cannot fully capture" [read once] and which must be identified in words rather than ignored. In the regulator's casework read here the line runs through encodings and not ornament: an inflation chart was "misleading" because "the y-axis beginning at 8%", and "This would still be the case had the axis been labelled clearly with a break"; the government's own teaching case is an infographic whose two houses — one "much larger" than the other, perhaps, the guidance suggests, "because it has more writing on it" — were read as the size of the numbers. Tufte, in his own hand, comes nearest to the two-layer position: "design architectures should be spare, straightforward, conventional, and self-effacing; AND the evidence presented should be rich, complex, multivariate, causal."

The gallery holds, and almost none of it was tested. Audited live, the strong work still leads with a written sentence, keeps provenance a scroll away, makes interaction optional and spends its craft on one authored thing; the Doughnut's authors print their own perceptual defect in the caption — "a quadratic scaling of wedge area that may lead some readers to perceive small changes as more significant than they are" — and supply a bar chart; Chalabi says her drawings are registered "pixel-for-pixel" to computed charts, and, in another interview, that "computer-generated images overstate certainty"; the museum records are real (Wind Map and Noise Pollution given by their designers; Dear Data bought with committee funds) and a MoMA label calls the field's subject "an expressive interpretation of reality" [read once]. The evaluated exception survives, qualified: a 2026 peer-reviewed paper with 177 survey responses and 23,346 logged sessions, in which "20% of all analyzed sessions reach the flowchart's final node", stated preference (40 per cent for narration) and logged behaviour (54 per cent of sessions spent mostly exploring) diverge, there is no control, the raw survey is withheld, and the journal's own open-practices reviewer could not open the evaluation materials. The field's main prize has eight criteria — impactful, engaging, clarity, innovative, inclusive, accessible, effective, beautiful — and none of them is accuracy.

A dashboard about sound owes its deaf reader a document. Level A, in the standard's words: for prerecorded audio-only content, "An alternative for time-based media is provided that presents equivalent information"; where audio accompanies video, captions, in the Understanding text, "include non-speech information conveyed through sound, including meaningful sound effects"; and "If any audio on a web page plays automatically for more than 3 seconds, either a mechanism is available to pause or stop the audio, or a mechanism is available to control audio volume independently". Silent is one of the four removals, and for sound that is content the standard makes it a requirement rather than a test.

Beneath the dashboard the chapter leaves an eleventh record: the boundary log, an entry of eleven lines per expressive element naming what it buys, which encoding or claim it touches, what happened under each of the four removals, where its precise twin lives, how it is identified to a reader who cannot see or hear it, and whether it was ever tested with a reader. Shipping is gated by the four removals and the fifth check, run and recorded; the log stays open until readers who saw only the stripped version and readers who saw the dressed one agree on what the data said. And the division the brief asked for is section 11's: the whole register is the studio's, part of it priced by evidence; the evidence layer and the audit's order are not.

1 · What the boundary is, and what the chapter is not

Version 1 made the case, in its Chapter 13, that "the rules don't forbid the art; they name where it lives", and it located the art in two places: the Decorative tier and the register. This chapter takes the same position and tests it, because a position that says where expression lives has to say three further things to be usable. It has to say what the line is made of, so a designer can tell which side a given choice falls on. It has to say what is measured about the choices that fall on the expressive side, so the house can say what a treatment buys without claiming what it cannot. And it has to say how the line is checked, by a procedure that someone other than the designer can run and record.

What the line is made of. Section 3 finds that the field has had a formal statement of it since 1986 — Mackinlay's expressiveness criterion — and a model of where it sits since 2009 — Munzner's nested levels — and that the house's tier test is those two things in plainer words. This converts the house's "Fixed" from a stance into a definition: a Fixed rule is one whose breach makes the picture say something the data does not say, or fail to say something it does.

What is measured on the expressive side. Section 5 reads the affect, persuasion and perception evidence that Chapters 2 and 3 did not reach — humanised marks, affective design, affective colour, display polarity, redundancy, disfluency, physical and glanceable displays, reading at a distance — and finds that expression is measured to buy engagement, mood and recognition (and, from Chapter 3, memorability) and is not measured to buy accuracy or action. That finding is the licence's wording: a treatment may claim what expression is measured to give and may not be allowed to touch what it is not.

How the line is checked. Section 6 formalises the removal test and finds it in official guidance under other names, and section 10 writes the record that makes it auditable.

What the chapter is not. It is not a brief. Nothing here decides the Vibe Map's palette, type, imagery, sound, motion or opening; where the chapter walks through an example in section 12 the example is invented and the walk is the method. It is not a critique of the gallery's works as art; section 7 reads each for what it breaks of this book's rules and what substitutes, which is the only reading this book is entitled to. And it is not an argument that plainness is wrong: section 4 finds that plainness is a rhetoric, and the finding's consequence is that plainness, too, must earn its claim, not that it should be abandoned.

What the failure register asks of this chapter is the two failures that sit on either side of the line. "It fails if a viewer reads it and asks 'what am I looking at'" is the expressive layer eating the evidence layer. "It fails if it's just a fancy spreadsheet with some charts that tell you lots of big numbers, but not what actually happens" is the evidence layer with no expressive layer at all — accurate, and unread. The boundary is drawn so that neither happens, and the chapter's claim is that it can be drawn by rule and checked by procedure, leaving the whole of the expressive side to the people whose job it is.

2 · What people believe about expression and evidence, and what the evidence says

Belief: decoration harms a chart. Chapter 3 settled the embellishment line and this chapter cites it rather than re-running it: the measured verdict is that titles and text carry the message, memorable charts are often also effective, and the costs that are measured are costs of distortion, not of ornament. What this chapter adds is the official version of the same finding: the Analysis Function's list of what to avoid in a chart — "shaded backgrounds", "unnecessary borders", "patterns, textures and shadows", "3D shapes", "thick or dark gridlines" — is a list of things that touch the encoding or the reading, and its infographic guidance never uses the words "pictogram", "icon", "3D" or "decorative" at all; it governs infographics through user need, clutter and a plain-text alternative. Newsrooms and chart publishers forbid "3-D charts at all costs" (ProPublica) and "Stay away from 3-D" (Urban Institute); none of the house-style documents read forbids decoration by name. The regulator's casework is about axes, bar sizes, sources and context. Where decoration is forbidden it is forbidden because it distorts; the EU's public guide says it plainly — "a lot of chart junk is actually harmless: the message of the chart survives the embellishments and decorations" — and separates the harmless from what it calls, after Kosara, "harmfull junk" (spelling as printed), the kind that "actively interferes with the reading" [read once]. (Standard (official statistics); Practice; Reading.)

Belief: a chart that moves people moves them to act. The one line of evidence that tests it directly — charts whose marks look like people, shown to people asked to feel and to give — finds little or nothing. Seven experiments found "very similar effects on empathy and prosocial behavior"; the largest since found at best "a small effect on money allocation" and said that "the large sample sizes required to observe an effect and the noise involved in measuring it make it very difficult to study in more depth" ([abstract or summary only], read once). Section 5 gives the numbers. Chapter 2's persuasion line (Pandey; Liem; Allcott) stands: a chart can shift an attitude, and the shift is measured on the claim, not on the ornament. (Evidence.)

Belief: plain is neutral. It is a style, and the field's reading of it is that it persuades. Section 4. (Evidence of method; Reading.)

Belief: the art end and the dashboard end are opposite ends of one scale, and a public display picks a point between them. Kosara put pragmatic and artistic visualisation "on opposite ends of the sublimity scale" and "thus theoretically impossible to reconcile", then proposed "a third way". The EU guide puts Tufte and Holmes as "two extremes of a continuum" and lets "your own taste and style" choose the point. The house's tiers refuse the scale: a display has an evidence layer with an expressive layer on it, rather than a position between evidence and art, and the test is what remains when the layer is removed. The chapter argues this in section 3 and holds it as a stance in section 10. (Standard (method); Reading.)

Belief: beauty earns a licence. The field's prize has eight criteria and none of them is accuracy; a chart can be impactful, engaging, clear, innovative, inclusive, accessible, effective and beautiful by that rubric and wrong. The regulator's rubric is the reverse: encodings first, and "The misleading presentation of statistics cannot be dismissed as just a matter of opinion." [read once] The Decision Book already names "Beauty as an accessibility exemption" as "The most common failure in award-winning work." Section 7. (Practice; Standard (regulator); Reading.)

Belief: dark is the night, so a dashboard about the night is dark. The register may be; the text has a measured price, and so does the chart. Section 5. (Evidence.)

Belief: harder to read is better remembered. The 2011 paper that proposed "visual difficulties" for charts drew on a psychology effect that a 2018 meta-analysis of 25 empirical articles and 3,135 participants found null on recall and transfer, while it made readers slower and less sure; a 2024 preregistered replication found "null results for disfluency" ([abstract or summary only], read once). (Evidence.)

Belief: seven words. The trade's rule for a sign read in passing is repeated on billboard companies' pages with no study behind it; the nearest research statement is three or four short words per glance, itself a reviewer's summary of a 1965 report, and the planning rule is a letter-height ratio and about four seconds for four to eight words. Version 1's "five words where possible, ten at most" is a house mantra and the chapter re-tiers it in section 5. (Evidence; Practice.)

Belief: the hand-drawn look is a style choice. It is also read as a cue about precision. Sketchiness "is a viable alternative for the visualization of uncertainty in lines and is as intuitive as blur" ([abstract or summary only], read once); the practitioner whose illustrated statistical reporting won a Pulitzer says "computer-generated images overstate certainty" and that "You'll never see decimal places on my illustrations." On that evidence — one abstract and one practitioner — a drawn line is read as rough, and the house's position is that it should then be. (Evidence, [abstract or summary only]; Practice; Reading.)

3 · The vocabulary: what the field says expression is, and how it is judged

Mackinlay: all the facts, and only the facts

The oldest formal statement of the boundary is in a paper about automating chart design. Mackinlay's 1986 Automating the Design of Graphical Presentations of Relational Information (ACM Transactions on Graphics 5(2)) separates two criteria. "Expressiveness criteria determine whether a graphical language can express the desired information." "Effectiveness criteria determine whether a graphical language exploits the capabilities of the output medium and the human visual system." Expressiveness has a precise definition: "A set of facts is expressible in a language if it contains a sentence that (1) encodes all the facts in the set, (2) encodes only the facts in the set." The second clause is the one most designers have never been told. A picture can fail by saying too much as well as by saying too little, and Mackinlay's example is a bar chart of a nominal variable: "The difficulty with this intuition is that the sentence may encode additional incorrect facts", because "Most people perceive the lengths of the bars as an encoding of an ordered or quantitative set" [read once]. (Standard (method).)

Effectiveness is a different kind of question and Mackinlay is careful about its status. "Effectiveness criteria can be based on a number of different factors": "a design can be judged effective when it can be interpreted accurately or quickly, when it has visual impact, or when it can be rendered in a cost-effective manner". The ranking of perceptual tasks that the field has since treated as settled he presents with a caution: "The core of this conjectural theory is an observation, made by Cleveland and McGill" that "people accomplish the perceptual tasks associated with the interpretation of graphical presentations with different degrees of accuracy"; of the quantitative ranking "Cleveland and McGill empirically verified the basic properties", and the extension to ordinal and nominal data "has not been empirically verified." And from the ranking comes a principle the house will recognise: "Principle of Importance Ordering: Encode more important information more effectively." (Standard (method).)

The tier test is, for a chart's encoding, these two criteria in other words. A Fixed rule, in the Decision Book's language, is "uncertainty — there is a right answer": contrast passes or fails, a cell of two is suppressed or breached. Some Fixed rules are floor rules of that kind (Chapter 13) and some are disclosure rules (Chapter 10); the Fixed rules about what a picture says are expressiveness rules, and expressiveness is the same kind of thing: a picture either encodes all and only the facts or it does not, and a breach is an encoding that says something false or leaves something out. An Adaptable rule is "ambiguity — no single correct answer": type scale, grid, density, chart form within a task. Effectiveness is that: a matter of degree, of which perceptual task the reader is asked to do and how well people do it, with a ranking that its own author calls conjectural. And the Decorative tier is what neither criterion sees — everything whose presence or absence changes no fact encoded and no perceptual task required. Version 1's formula, "nothing load-bearing in decoration", is Mackinlay's second clause read from the other side: if removing an element changes what the picture says, the element was encoding a fact, and it was never decoration. (Reading.)

Munzner: where the line sits, and why care below it cannot repair error above

Munzner's A Nested Model for Visualization Design and Validation (IEEE TVCG, 2009) puts four levels inside one another: "characterize the task and data in the vocabulary of the problem domain, abstract into operations and data types, design visual encoding and interaction techniques, and create algorithms to execute techniques efficiently". The model's purpose is to say what can go wrong at each level and how each is checked, and its central sentence is about direction: "an upstream error inevitably cascades to all downstream levels". At the encoding level "the threat is that the chosen design is not effective at communicating the desired abstraction to the person using the system", and "One immediate validation approach is to justify the design with respect to known perceptual and cognitive principles" — but "The immediate validations only offer partial evidence of success" and "none of them are sufficient to demonstrate that the threat to validity at that level has been addressed" [read once]. The sentence the house should keep is this one: "If a poor choice was made in the abstraction stage, then even perfect visual encoding and algorithm design will not create a visualization system that solves the intended problem." [read once] (Standard (method).)

For this chapter the model does two things. It places the boundary: the evidence layer is the abstraction (what is counted, how it is defined, what is compared to what — Chapters 4 to 9 of this book) and the encoding that carries it; the expressive layer is a set of choices made at the encoding level and around it that do not change the abstraction. And it warns that the removal test is an encoding-level check and cannot substitute for the upstream ones: a beautifully stripped chart of the wrong measure is still the wrong measure, and a chart that passes every test in this chapter can still fail Chapter 9's. A compressed statement of the two principles — "expressiveness principle – match channel and data characteristics" and "effectiveness principle – encode most important attributes with highest ranked channels" — was read from her 2015 slides, since the textbook itself was not reachable; the version two course pages attribute to the book, "Visual encoding should express all of, and only, the information in the dataset attributes", is Mackinlay's clause made into a rule for students, and the chapter cites it as secondary. (Standard (method); secondary.)

Kosara: the sublimity scale, and the picture that stands on its own

Kosara's Visualization Criticism — The Missing Link Between Information Visualization and Art (IV 2007) is a position paper, and the most useful thing in it for a boundary chapter is a three-part definition of what counts as a visualisation at all. "It is based on (non-visual) data." "It produces an image." "The result is readable and recognizable." Each has a body, and two of the bodies are rules. Under the second: "the visual must be the primary means of communicating the data. Other media can be part of a visualization, but the visualization must be able to stand on its own." [read once] Under the third: "Visualization images must also be recognizable as such, and not appear to be something else", and "The use of additional elements (or even "eye candy") is certainly possible, but must not take precedence over the communication goals of the visualization". The "stand on its own" sentence [read once] is about the image surviving without the other media that may accompany it, and the eye-candy sentence is about precedence; together they are the nearest published statement from inside the field to the position this chapter holds. (Standard (method).)

The paper's other contribution is a scale that the chapter's stance rejects, and it should be stated accurately before it is rejected. "One aesthetic criterion of particular interest is the sublime", which "can be understood as that which inspires awe, grandeur, and evokes a deep emotional and/or intellectual response". Technical visualisations "are thus designed to remove any sublimity, and instead foster immediate understanding"; "while the classical technical information visualization is entirely anti-sublime, artistic visualizations are primarily sublime". The sublime "subsumes the two criteria of readability and recognizability, since for a work of art to be sublime, it cannot be easily readable (or user friendly)"; "It must present enough of an enigma to keep an audience interested without being easy to solve". Pragmatic visualisation "is what we term the technical application of visualization techniques to analyze data"; "The goal of artistic visualization is usually to communicate a concern, rather than to show data"; "Visual efficiency does not play a role in artistic visualization, quite the contrary". And the two are "on opposite ends of the sublimity scale" and "thus theoretically impossible to reconcile, should not deter us from trying, though"; hence "a third way". He never uses the word continuum. (Standard (method).)

Where the house departs is on the geometry. A scale with two ends invites a public display to pick a point along it, and every point short of the pragmatic end gives up some readability for some enigma. The tiers say instead that a display has an evidence layer, which must be readable in full, and an expressive layer, which may be as sublime as its maker likes provided the first layer survives its removal. On that account the two things Kosara found irreconcilable are not on one axis at all; one sits on top of the other.
