Breaks: Chapter 11's message-before-input rule, on both landings (the ELS lands with a sentence and then an input, which is the rule's shape with no finding in the sentence; the Census landing lands with a choice); the Census page's date is printed bare with no "Published:" label. Substitutes: the sentence before the box; the QMI; the per-chart furniture, which is Chapter 12's cut-out rule in full. Holds once an area is chosen; the landing is the one place the official exemplar breaks a rule this book holds Fixed. Evaluated: Chapter 11 has it. (Practice.)

The BBC's postcode interactives. Not audited: bbc.co.uk, bbc.com and the archived copy could not be read. What could be read is the method as the BBC described it in the Data Journalism Handbook: "Enable a reader to discover information that is personally relevant", "Reveal a story that is remarkable and previously unknown", "Help the reader to better understand a complex issue"; "Readers can find local schools by entering a postcode, and compare them on a range of indicators."; "The ability to easily share a 'personal' fact is something we have begun to incorporate as standard." And the agency that built the 2013 class calculator: "It wasn't just a black box that spat out a result at the end."; "We tested it on people to ensure not only that the algorithm worked, but also that it was fun and easy to use"; "the most shared BBC page ever". The BBC's shared data unit's public code organisation lists "10 of 317 repositories" [read once]. Breaks, substitutes, holds: not determinable. Evaluated: none published found. (Practice; not read.)

Gapminder. The home page's door is a challenge rather than an input: "You are probably wrong about"; "Upgrade your worldview"; "Gapminder is an independent educational non-profit fighting global misconceptions." The Upgrader: "We can predict what you are wrong about."; "We have asked thousands of important fact-questions to lots of people and identified the most common misconceptions." Dollar Street shows content at once with no input — "Dollar Street", "Families", "The World by income per month", "Poor", "Rich" [read once] — describes itself on its landing page as "photos as data to kill country stereotypes", and states its method on an about page: "Imagine the world as a street ordered by income."; "Everyone lives somewhere on the street."; "taking photos of up to 135 objects"; it "tries to measure consumption rather than salary or income". The Ignorance Project's method: "We use surveys to ask representative groups of people simple questions" "about key-aspects of global development"; "The surveys were commissioned to Novus and Ipsos MORI"; "Every question had three alternative choices: A, B or C."; "Chimpanzees picking answers randomly would get one third correct, on average."; the 2019 study "asked a total of 15500 people in 31 different countries" [read once]. Breaks: Chapter 12's identity line — a street "ordered by income" orders households by a condition, which the house holds as a thing never done to a place's people; Dollar Street's about page and landing give different family and country counts. Substitutes: the method pages; the photographs as the unit; a baseline of random guessing in place of a control. Holds as the model of a misconception quiz whose method is public; the ranking is the break the house would not import. Evaluated: Gapminder's own surveys measure audience knowledge, not the display; not peer-reviewed. (Practice.)

The museum records. Read at the record on 6 October 2026 and verified there except where marked, and none says more than it says. MoMA 163892: "Fernanda Bertini Viégas, Martin Wattenberg", "Wind Map", 2012, "Interactive software", "Gift of the designers", "1751.2012"; Department of Architecture and Design; "Not on view" [read once]; shown in six exhibitions from Applied Design (2013) to Pirouette: Turning Points in Design (2025) [read once]; its label: "to create a "living portrait" of the wind landscape over the United States". MoMA 447623: "Noise Pollution (Data visualization for La Lettura)", Federica Fragapane, 2020, "Digital image", "Gift of the designer", "98.2023"; no gallery label, no exhibition on its record. Her two companion records — Land Defenders (97.2023) and Space Junk (96.2023, read once) — share a label attributed to Pirouette [read once] that is an institutional statement of this chapter's subject: "Information design often goes beyond mere description to become an expressive interpretation of reality." (first clause verified; the remainder read once on two records) MoMA 215813: "Giorgia Lupi, Stefanie Posavec", Dear Data, 2015, "8 moleskin sketchbooks" (spelling as printed), "Committee on Architecture and Design Funds", "963.2016.1-8" — bought, where the others were given; the weekly postcards are separate records, for example "Dear Data: Week 1 (What's the Time / A Week of Clocks)", 2014, "Ink and pencil on paper", "962.2016.1a-b". A caution for anyone re-checking: MoMA's collection search returns the same default set whatever the query, so records have to be reached by their number. And Flight Patterns (Koblin) sits in three museums under three dates and two flight counts — MoMA 2005, "Video (color)", "Gift of the designer"; the V&A "2009 (made)" [read once], "205,000" flights on "12 August 2008"; the Art Institute of Chicago 2011, "Animation", "140,000 airplanes" — which is the chapter's smallest finding and one it keeps: a data work is a versioned thing, and a record's date is the version's. What the records establish: custody and provenance rather than evaluation; that institutions file data works as design, as "Interactive software" or "Digital image"; and that an expressive data work can be held by a museum and still be, by the house's test, an evidence layer with a layer on it — Wind Map is a map of wind. What they do not establish: that any of these works was ever tested with a reader, or that custody is a licence. (Practice.)

Mona Chalabi. The Pulitzer record: 2023, "Illustrated Reporting and Commentary", "Mona Chalabi, contributor, The New York Times", for "9 Ways to Imagine Jeff Bezos' Wealth" [read once]; the citation is in section 5. No piece of hers could be read, since her publishers could not be read and her own project page showed filters and no items with the description "Under construction" [read once]; the chapter therefore cannot say whether her pieces carry a source line, and the word "source" appears in none of the three interviews. Breaks: by her own account, the house's precision rule where a number is exact. Substitutes: registration to a computed chart ("pixel-for-pixel"), and a stated purpose ("the real margin of error"). Holds as the clearest practitioner statement found of an expressive register carrying an evidential claim about uncertainty rather than decorating one. Evaluated: none found. (Practice.)

Neil Halloran's The Fallen of World War II. fallen.io redirects to the maker's site. First elements: "Neil Halloran", "English", "The Fallen of World War II", "Interactive", "Best experienced on a computer.", "YouTube", "Interactive Mode" [read once] — a mode choice leads, with no data input. "The film follows a linear narration but pauses at key moments, letting viewers step into the charts and explore the numbers themselves." Sources are in prose below: "Much of the underlying data draws from sources similar to those listed in the" World War II casualties article on Wikipedia; "Post-WWII statistics were sourced from the" Uppsala Conflict Data Program; "Written, directed, coded, and narrated by Neil Halloran". No sentence on estimates, uncertainty or disputed figures was found. Breaks: Chapter 6's uncertainty rule, for counts of this kind; Chapter 4's provenance set, which "sources similar to" does not meet. Substitutes: the linear film as the whole route, with exploration optional. Holds as a demonstration that a narrated linear route can carry a whole argument with the interactive layer entirely optional — the strong-work pattern — and fails the provenance test. Evaluated: no empirical evaluation found; one critical essay exists in search results and was not read. (Practice.)

Raworth's Doughnut. As a display: "The environmental ceiling consists of nine planetary boundaries, as set out by Rockstrom et al"; "The twelve dimensions of the social foundation are derived from internationally agreed minimum social standards"; "Between social and planetary boundaries lies an environmentally safe and socially just space in which humanity can thrive."; it "offers a visual monitor of progress". The method paper is Fanning and Raworth, Nature 646, 47–56 (1 October 2025), with "a revised set of 35 indicators" (21 dimensions; 22 social and 13 ecological indicators; 2000 to 2022, read once); "The grey wedge indicates missing data." [read once]. The strongest critique of the display is the authors' own, in the Figure 1 caption: "Values are proportional to the length of each wedge, which leads to a quadratic scaling of wedge area that may lead some readers to perceive small changes as more significant than they are." and "To address this limitation, we provide Fig. 2 with a bar-chart representation that avoids this quadratic scaling issue." Breaks: Mackinlay's second clause — the wedge's area encodes a fact (a squared one) the data does not say. Substitutes: a printed admission and a bar chart of the same values in the next figure: the precise twin, shipped by the authors in a Nature paper. Holds as the one case in the gallery where the makers ran the fifth check themselves and published the result. Evaluated: no user study found; an external "Deconstructing the Doughnut" exists and could not be read. (Practice; Evidence of method.)

The flowchart — the evaluated exception, verified and qualified. The entry is an interactive, narrated flowchart built from Andrew Boyd's book I Want a Better Catastrophe (flowchart.bettercatastrophe.com; the live site was not read). Version 1 claimed it as the one gallery entry with a published evaluation and released data. The claim mostly checks out. Pomerance, Boyd and Dörk, Navigating and Narrating Interactive Flowcharts, Journal of Visualization and Interaction 1(1), published 10 April 2026, doi 10.54337/jovi.v1i1.8418, CC BY-SA 4.0 [read once]; peer-reviewed, with the reviews public — "Round 1 Reviews", "Round 2 Reviews" and an "Open Practices Review" on the article page. The display: "visitors are greeted with an introductory panel suggesting two viewing options" — "listening to the narration or exploring the chart on their own"; "the case study flowchart contains 330 nodes and the narration spans over 52 minutes of audio". The paper has no sentence on transcript, captions, keyboard or mobile. The evaluation is observational field data with no control: a survey "to which we received 177 responses" from self-selected visitors; logs, "29,112 such logs were collected" "of which we will use 23,346 for further analysis" after "ignoring sessions without any interaction with the flowchart". Findings: "20% of all analyzed sessions reach the flowchart's final node"; "a slight overall preference for narration (40%)" in the survey of self-selected respondents [read once], against logs in which most sessions spent most of their time exploring (54 per cent of sessions, read once) and "the 'balanced' use of both modes is noticeably rarer (7%)"; about 4.6 per cent of sessions reached the full narration time, the median session visited 30 nodes, and about 7 per cent of respondents did not notice the audio (all read once). The authors' limit: "the asynchronous and anonymous nature of these sources also limits the study of engagement". Three qualifications on "released evaluation data": the materials are on OSF, which could not be opened; "The complete submissions to the feedback survey (see subsection 5.1) are not shared publicly, as participants were not asked to consent to their responses being shared with others" [read once]; and the journal's Open Practices Review records that "It looks like the Evaluation Materials component is unreachable and marked as 'currently archiving'." [read once]. Also Gold, Places, Spaces & Environment, Information is Beautiful Awards 2024. Breaks: nothing this book holds, given the mode choice is before content and not before data; the deaf reader is owed a transcript the paper does not mention (section 8). Holds as the standard version 1 set — and the standard is now specified: field logs plus a survey, no control, a self-selected survey whose stated preference differs from what the logs show of all sessions, and open materials that a reviewer must be able to open. Evaluated: yes, with those terms. (Evidence of method; Practice.)

The Information is Beautiful Awards. Status: "The IIB Awards is currently on hiatus and will resume in 2027."; "Submissions are now closed." The judging criteria, eight, in page order: "Is the work impactful?"; "Is the work engaging?"; "Does the work display clarity of analysis, including clear guidance that makes the visual usable?"; "Is the work innovative and creative, celebrating novel formats and design approaches?"; "Is the work inclusive, including using inclusive language, and considering representations of equity appropriately?"; "Is the work accessible, including design decisions to support interaction from all users?"; "Is the work effective, achieving its goals and connecting an audience to the underlying data"; "Is the work beautiful, celebrating aesthetic beauty and design broadly?" There is no criterion on accuracy, sourcing or data integrity; a check for one found none. Process: "each submission was reviewed by at least three people"; "Both the works themselves (links and/or images) and your descriptions will be considered in the judging process." [read once]. The showcase pages carry title, credits, a paragraph and a link, with no method or source field. What it establishes: the field's stated standard for its best work scores eight qualities and not truth, and judges the maker's description alongside the work. The house's audit is the reverse: accuracy first, beauty never as a licence. A "truthful, insightful, beautiful" formula is on neither page checked. (Practice.)

The incumbents, as case law. The Thriving Places Index's old domain now redirects; its dashboard is an embedded Power BI report that is select-first inside the embed — "Select the name of the local authority using the drop-down in the top corner" — with a band statement in words ("< 3.5 = very low compared to the England average" through "> 6.5 = very high compared to the England average"; "The Index scores are between 0 and 10."), a colour statement that does not say which colour means which band ("Colour coding is applied to make it easy to see how your place compares to other Local Authorities."), a "Full methodology (8mb PDF)" that could not be read, no "Last updated" label, and an edition stated only in prose. Breaks: Chapter 11's message-before-input rule; Chapter 12's identity line (places scored and compared on a single scale); Chapter 13's floor (an image-only method; a colour meaning stated nowhere in text). The London Night Time Data Observatory's landing — "Welcome to the Night Time Data Observatory."; "This webpage contains a range of research and data on London at night."; "over 30 data sources" — shows no dated contents; its four theme pages hold 24 entries [read once] with relative stamps ("Updated almost 6 years ago"; most five to seven years; one "Updated 3 months ago"; read once), no page-level date, and a count below the landing's "over 30". Breaks: Chapter 8's service record (no date on the face; containers outliving contents). Neither was researched for content; both have drifted since version 1 read them, and the drift is itself the service-record finding. (Practice.)

A newsroom piece and a vocabulary. ABC News (Australia), What's driving up burger prices? (dated 5 August 2024, read once; Silver, Business Analytics, IIB 2024): leads with a written sentence, then photography and charts, with no input; sources are given once, at the end, under "About the story" — "Big Mac prices were sourced from The Economist's Big Mac Index data."; "(The exact price at individual stores across Australia can vary.)" — and individual charts carry no source line [read once]. Breaks: Chapter 12's cut-out rule. Substitutes: an end note. The FT's Visual Vocabulary is a training artefact, "inspired by the Graphic Continuum by Jon Schwabish and Severino Ribecca", with nine categories — Deviation, Correlation, Ranking, Distribution, Change over Time, Part-to-whole, Magnitude, Spatial, Flow [read once] — and its page makes no claim to have been tested with readers. (Practice.)

What the gallery shows, read together

Across the entries that could be read, the strong-work pattern version 1 found holds under audit, with its edges visible: the pieces that lead with words lead with a sentence (The Pudding; Our World in Data; the ABC; the Census article once an area is chosen), and the three that lead with a mode choice (Dollar Street; Halloran; the flowchart) put content before any data input; the message is carried in words and structure; the craft is spent on one authored thing; the interactive layer is optional everywhere it exists, with a linear or static route beside it (The Pudding's video; Halloran's film; the flowchart's narration; the Census article's text). Provenance sits a scroll away and is almost never on the first screen, which is where this book's rules part from the gallery's practice and where Chapter 12's cut-out rule is justified. Two things the audit adds. The makers who ran the removal test's fifth check on their own work — the Doughnut's authors — published a defect and a twin in the same paper, and nothing in the gallery is stronger evidence of a form holding than that. And, of the entries read, one has a published evaluation — a peer-reviewed field study with no control and with materials a reviewer could not open; one has in-house audience surveys; for one (Our World in Data) no evaluation was searched for; the museum records are custody; the prize scores no accuracy. The house's probes, if they are to meet the evaluated exception's standard, meet a specified one — logs plus survey, open materials, behaviour against self-report — and can add the one thing it lacks, a comparison. (Reading.)

8 · The deaf reader of a dashboard about sound

Chapter 13 read the W3C's criteria for an interactive data display and flagged the deaf reader to this chapter, because a dashboard whose subject is heard as much as seen may carry sound as content — recordings, sonifications, a narrated route — and the floor was written for the eye. The criteria that bite, under four headings, in their normative words and with the Understanding pages' intent text marked as such (WCAG 2.2, read through the Understanding pages, which reproduce the criteria):

1.2.1 Audio-only and Video-only (Prerecorded), Level A. "For prerecorded audio-only and prerecorded video-only media, the following are true, except when the audio or video is a media alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such:" — prerecorded audio-only: "An alternative for time-based media is provided that presents equivalent information for prerecorded audio-only content." The defined term: a "document including correctly sequenced text descriptions of time-based visual and auditory information and providing a means for achieving the outcomes of any time-based interaction"; "audio-only" is "a time-based presentation that contains only audio (no video and no interaction)". Intent: "to make information conveyed by prerecorded audio-only and prerecorded video-only content available to all users", because text "can be rendered through any sensory modality (for example, visual, auditory or tactile) to match the needs of the user." The word "transcript" appears only in the examples; the requirement is the document, and the page states no exemption for music. (Standard (W3C).)

1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded), Level A. "Captions are provided for all prerecorded audio content in synchronized media, except when the media is a media alternative for text and is clearly labeled as such." The intent text: "Captions not only include dialogue, but identify who is speaking and include non-speech information conveyed through sound, including meaningful sound effects."; the definition's note: "Captions convey not only spoken dialogue but also equivalents for non-dialogue audio information, including sound effects, music, laughter, speaker identification and location." [read once] (Standard (W3C).)

1.2.3 Audio Description or Media Alternative (Prerecorded), Level A, and 1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded), Level AA. "An alternative for time-based media or audio description of the prerecorded video content is provided for synchronized media"; at AA, "Audio description is provided for all prerecorded video content in synchronized media." — the blind reader's side of the same content, which Chapter 13's routes already cover. (Standard (W3C).)

1.4.2 Audio Control, Level A. "If any audio on a web page plays automatically for more than 3 seconds, either a mechanism is available to pause or stop the audio, or a mechanism is available to control audio volume independently from the overall system volume level." The note: "Since any content that does not meet this success criterion can interfere with a user's ability to use the whole page, all content on the web page (whether or not it is used to meet other success criteria) must meet this success criterion." [read once] Intent: "Individuals who use screen reading software can find it hard to hear the speech output if there is other audio playing at the same time."; "Therefore, it is important that the user be able to turn off the background sound."; and the W3C's preference, "that the sound be started by an action initiated by the user after they reach the page, rather than requiring that the sound be stopped by an action of the user after they land on the page." [read once] (Standard (W3C).)

Two design systems say the same in fewer words: Material, "Give visual alternatives to sound, and vice versa." [read once]; Carbon, "Find an alternative way to convey information exclusively with sound." and "Transcribe and caption all videos and animations that have meaningful audio." [read once]. (Standard (design system).)

What follows is three rules, one distinction and one observation. Any sound that is content — a recording, a sonified series, a narrated route — has a text document equivalent to it, at Level A, with no exemption for music; any sound that accompanies video is captioned, including non-speech sound; and no sound starts by itself for more than three seconds without a stop. The distinction is the W3C's own, and the author makes it: sound that conveys information is content and owes the document; sound that is "primarily intended to create a specific sensory experience" — the W3C's flute solo — owes "descriptive identification" in words; and a dashboard about a culture's sound will carry mostly the first kind, because its recordings are evidence of something. The observation is that silent, the second of the four removals, is for sound-as-content a requirement before it is a test: the standard asks the house to build the silent version as a document, and the removal test then checks that the dressed version added nothing the document lacks. The flowchart paper, the gallery's evaluated exception, has fifty-two minutes of narration and no sentence on a transcript; the house's probes should not repeat that silence. (Reading.)

Chapter 13 reported that sonification is a route beside a text route and never instead of it, from the blind reader's side. This section adds the deaf reader's: the same rule, for the opposite reason. A sonified series without its document excludes one reader; a sonified series without its chart excludes the other; the series, the chart and the document are three routes to one view, and the view record (Chapter 11) lists all three. (Reading.)

9 · The failures, read for the boundary

The brief's register, each failure read for what this chapter adds.

"It fails if a viewer reads it and asks 'what am I looking at'." This is the expressive layer eating the evidence layer, and the removal test is its diagnosis: if the stripped version is readable and the dressed one is not, the dressing is in the way. Section 5 adds the measured form of the failure: visualisations readers rate as images are found more pleasing and convey less of their message; and one badly read form cost about six times a bar's glance in one study. The focus-group authors said it of their participants in one sentence: "This type of visualization was new to many of our participants who therefore did not like it." [read once]

"It fails if it's just a fancy spreadsheet with some charts that tell you lots of big numbers, but not what actually happens." The other side of the line: an evidence layer with no claim stated and no register at all. Chapter 6 answered it with the claim in the title; this chapter adds that plainness does not make the numbers true and that the ONS's own aims for a chart include "engaging". Version 1's twin to the Style Guide line stands: strong evidence is never made to look weaker by timid design.

"It fails if it looks the same every month." Not this chapter's, except in one respect: an expressive layer is the thing most tempting to change for change's sake, and the Decision Book already names "The bespoke annual encoding" as a failure — "Invent a new form each year and you have made your own work incomparable with itself." The register may change; the encodings do not.

"For nightlife, it fails if they do not recognise their place within the front-end interface." Chapter 12's, and this chapter sharpens one part of it: recognition is social and reflective insight in Pousman's terms, which the expressive layer can serve and the evidence layer cannot by itself, and the FT's pictogram condition is the test for any humanised mark that serves it — whole units only.

"It fails if people don't use it." The affect evidence says what expression is measured to buy — engagement, mood and recognition, and from Chapter 3 memorability — and these are the use failure's levers, within the conditions section 5 sets. It also says what it does not buy, which is action; a display that is used is not thereby acted on.

"It fails if it breaks or isn't reliable." The expressive layer is the least reliable layer on a page: fonts fail to load, images are blocked, scripts are off, audio is muted, motion is disabled by preference. A display whose evidence survives the four removals is one whose evidence survives those failures, which is Chapter 8's service record arriving by another route.

"It fails if people don't trust it." Section 4's finding is the hard one: the plain look makes a trust claim readers may take as a reason not to check, and so does the polished look (Sunlight's sentence), and so does beauty (Chapter 11). None of the three is evidence of trustworthiness; the records beneath the dashboard are, and the conventions of objectivity are a promise about them. Chalabi's practice names the one way the register can carry a trust claim that is true: a drawn mark that says, accurately, that the number is rough.

"It fails if it's an aggregation of 'the biggest'." Not this chapter's. The one thing it adds is that humanising the marks does not answer it; the choice of what is counted and framed does.

10 · What holds true regardless

Seven things this chapter can state for any public dashboard, each with its kind and its grounds.

1. Expression is tested by what remains when it is removed. Sort each element into a layer by the designer's claim; strip the expressive layer — mono, silent, still, undressed — and the evidence layer must still encode all of the data and only the data (a lost fact sends the element back to the evidence layer; an added fact is a breach); then put the stripped and dressed versions side by side and they must say the same thing, judged by readers asked what the data said. For sound that is content, silent is a Level A requirement before it is a test. Fixed (requirement). Grounds: Mackinlay's expressiveness criterion ("encodes all the facts in the set" and "encodes only the facts in the set"); Kosara's "must be able to stand on its own" [read once]; the W3C's definition of decoration ("rearranged or substituted without changing their purpose"); the Analysis Function's plain-text twin and user test; the ONS's "never make an animation the only way to get the information"; WCAG 1.2.1 and 1.4.2; the government's own two-houses infographic (section 6) as the fifth check failed.

2. Expression is measured to buy engagement, mood and recognition — and, from Chapter 3's line, memorability — and is not measured to buy accuracy, and not action beyond a small effect on a hypothetical allocation. A treatment may claim what it is measured to give and may not claim, or be built as if it gave, what it is not. Fixed (requirement) (the house's reading of the state of the evidence, which new evidence can move). Grounds: Boy et al. ("very similar effects on empathy and prosocial behavior"); Morais et al. (3.4 points in a hundred, 95% CI [0.021, 6.8]); Kineticharts (no detected comprehension cost; engagement higher; not equivalence); Lan 2023 ("not at odds", on two studies); Bartram (mood in lightness and chroma; "Trustworthy showed very little structure"); Arunkumar (image-rated displays convey less); Xie et al. (disfluency null on recall; slower; less confident). Counter-grounds the house records: Chapter 2's persuasion line, which is about the claim and the frame.

3. Plainness is a register too, and makes a trust claim that must be true. The conventions of objectivity — two dimensions, clean layout, geometric marks, a source line — do persuasive work, and a source line in particular suggests "there may be no need for the user to check". So the house's evidence standard reads three ways: strong design never makes weak evidence look stronger; timid design never makes strong evidence look weaker; and plain design never stands in for a record. Fixed (requirement). Grounds: Kennedy et al. 2016 (13 interviews; 10 pieces; no readers tested — "there may be no need for the user to check", read once); Data Feminism chapter 3; Correll; the Sunlight Foundation's 2014 sentence; the ten records of Chapters 4 to 13 as the thing the conventions promise.

4. A register that signals imprecision may be worn only where the data is imprecise. A drawn, sketched or approximate mark is an encoding wearing a register, and the register is read as a cue about the number beneath it; where the number is an estimate the form and the data agree; where it is exact the form understates it and its precise twin is one step away. Adaptable. Grounds: Boukhelifa et al. (sketchiness works as an uncertainty cue, [abstract or summary only], read once); Chalabi's stated method ("pixel-for-pixel"; "computer-generated images overstate certainty"; "You'll never see decimal places"); Lupi's "embrace imperfection and approximation" read as a stance about her own data.

5. A dark ground is priced, and the price is paid by the reader's choice. Small text read worse light-on-dark in both age groups tested, and in glance-like reading the penalty appeared in a dark room; for charts, which polarity helps is individual and preference does not predict it. A dark register ships with the light one and the reader chooses. Fixed (requirement) (the choice), Adaptable (the register, which is Decorative until text or a chart sits on it). Grounds: Piepenbrock et al. (85 and 84; d = 2.17 and 0.58); Buchner & Baumgartner (†); Dobres et al. ([abstract or summary only], read once); While & Sarvghad ("making visualizations available in both contrast polarities"); the Analysis Function's "anchor" and its wish for customisation; Chapter 13's floor.

6. The twin is required and is not thereby read. Every expressive form has a precise twin one step away; the form itself states its finding, and any distortion it carries, in words on itself; and no form relies on a twin the reader must go and find to correct an impression the form gives. Fixed (requirement). Grounds: Ottley et al. (text and chart together did not raise accuracy; not integrated, read once); Stokes et al. (text on the chart not penalised, [abstract or summary only], read once); the Decision Book's Chapter 7; the Doughnut's caption and Figure 2 as the rule done by its authors.

7. The field's prize scores no accuracy; the regulator's casework scores encodings, sources and context; the house audits in the regulator's order — accuracy, then the floor, then beauty. Beauty is never a licence, and the strongest expressive work in the field holds by carrying its message in words and structure, spending craft on one authored thing, making interaction optional, and — in the one case where its makers checked — publishing its own defect with a twin. Almost none of it was evaluated. Adaptable (house default). Grounds: the eight IIB criteria, with none on accuracy; OSR's casework and "cannot be dismissed as just a matter of opinion" [read once]; the gallery audit; the flowchart paper's terms.

Three things the chapter will not state as truths. That expression harms comprehension (the one study that measured feeling and comprehension together found no cost; the costs that are measured are of distortion, of forms the eye reads badly, and of displays taken as pictures). That the plain look is wrong (it is the look disabled readers can use; it must be earned rather than dropped). And that any of the above says what the Vibe Map should look like.

Beneath the dashboard: the boundary log

Each earlier chapter left a record beneath the display; this one leaves the eleventh, and it is a log rather than a sheet, because it grows by one line each time an expressive element is added. The boundary log records, for each expressive element, what the removal test found. It is the Decision Book's override log ("Trigger · rule and tier · alternative chosen · evidence") specialised to the line this chapter draws, and it is where version 1's Chapter 13 said a leaked meaning "wants the entry". It has eleven lines per element. The four removals and the fifth check gate shipping; the reader comparison in the last line may follow shipping in a probe, and the entry stays open until it is done.

Line What it holds Why
Element What the expressive element is, where it appears, and the version of the display it was added to A register entry outlives the person who made the choice
Tier claimed Decorative; specific sensory experience; or a named Adaptable choice at the encoding level The tier is the argument's first move (Decision Book Ch 18)
Purchase What it buys, in the affective-intent template — "The viewer will [observe / position / strengthen / connect / behave] [noun]" — limited to what expression is measured to buy An unnamed break is a mistake made confidently; an over-claimed one is a false one
Touches Which view, encoding or claim it sits on or near Blair: palette moves feeling more than data; the register must say what it is next to
Mono What the greyscale render lost or changed Hue is the commonest leak
Silent What muting lost; for sound-as-content, where the text document is WCAG 1.2.1; 1.4.2
Still What disabling motion lost; where the pause control is ONS; WCAG 2.2.2 (Chapter 13)
Undressed What stripping the register lost or changed Mackinlay's second clause
Stripped beside dressed Whether the two versions say the same thing — no added size, order, brightness or cause — and, for a form, its estimated glance cost against a bar The fifth check; the two-houses infographic; Blascheck
Twin and identification Where the precise twin is, how many steps away, and the words that identify the element to a reader who cannot see or hear it Ottley; WCAG's "descriptive identification" for a sensory experience
Tested, and status Whether readers saw the stripped and dressed versions and what each took from the data — figures and trend agreeing is the pass; the sample is the three user groups' readers (Chapter 0 names the groups), as Chapter 13's test; two readers is the shape of the test, not its size — with date, who ran it, and the entry's status (open, closed, re-tiered, removed) and owner The evaluated exception's standard, with the comparison it lacked

A filled example, invented, for method only — brightness is used because it is the simplest scaled channel to walk through, and nothing about the Vibe Map is implied by it. Element: an authored opening image on the landing page, added at version 0.4, in which a field of marks brightens with a count. Tier claimed: specific sensory experience. Purchase: the viewer will connect the count to a feeling of scale. Touches: the headline count beside it. Mono: nothing lost; brightness survives greyscale. Silent: not applicable; no sound. Still: the brightening is a build; with motion disabled the field renders at its final state; nothing lost. Undressed: with the image removed the headline count stands with its unit, base and date. Stripped beside dressed: the two do not say the same thing, because the field's brightness was scaled to fill the frame and reads as "high" whatever the count is — a fact the data does not say. Twin and identification: the headline count is the twin, zero steps away; identification text, "An image of a field of lights, brighter where the count is higher; the count is stated beside it." Tested, and status: not yet; open; the element does not ship until the brightness scale is either fixed to the count's own range or the element is re-tiered as Decorative with a constant brightness, and the reader comparison follows in the probe. The example decides nothing about the Vibe Map; it shows what a line in the register looks like when the fifth check fails and what it takes to close it.

Whether the eleven records beneath the dashboard are one document is the standing question; this one is the first that is a log, and a log may want to live in the design repository rather than on the public page, with its existence declared on the page.

11 · Where the choice is yours

The chapter has drawn a line and said how to check it; everything on the expressive side of the line is the studio's, and the chapter's only contribution there is to say which choices the evidence prices and which it leaves free.

Free, by the evidence. The register as a whole, within the conditions sections 5 and 10 set: the palette beyond the encoding; the display type; illustration; pattern; imagery; pacing; the poster layer; ambient sound that is stoppable; motion that means nothing and can be disabled. Kosara's enigma is available here. So is the whole of the Decorative tier, which the Decision Book says is "larger than most designers use", and which this chapter has not shrunk.

Priced, by the evidence. The genre the display claims (re-tiered Adaptable in the rules table). The dark ground (truth 5). A drawn or approximate register (truth 4). An invented form, at a measured glance cost (one radial form took about six times a bar) and at the cost of readers taking it as an image (section 5). A humanised mark, which may serve recognition and may not be priced as buying empathy or giving, and which must be whole units (section 6). A mood palette placed beside a scale, since colour moved feeling more than the data's trend did (Blair); on the scale itself it is forbidden by the rule that mood is carried only in channels that encode nothing. Headline length for a display read in passing, set by distance and seconds rather than by a word count (section 5).

Not open, by this chapter. The facts the evidence layer must carry and the furniture that carries them: that every encoding says all and only what the data says (which encoding, among effective ones, is an Adaptable choice and the studio's); the title's claim; the unit, base, date, source and gate; the twin; the identification text for a sensory experience; the stop control for sound; the pause control for motion; the records. And the order of the audit: accuracy, then the floor, then beauty.

Open, and the house's to decide with a reason recorded. Whether the boundary log is public or internal. Whether the committee export is a separate deliverable or the stripped state of the same page. Whether the studio adopts the W3C's third category, "specific sensory experience", into its tier vocabulary as a fourth tier or as a sub-kind of Decorative with an identification duty; this chapter uses it, requires the identification the W3C requires, and leaves its place in the house's vocabulary to Chapter 16. Whether a probe is built to test the two-audience claim, which has no measurement anywhere in this book.

12 · A nightlife illustration — method only

The method only. Suppose the studio proposes an expressive element for a view: a form in the culture's visual tradition in which a measured quantity about a place's activity is carried by something other than a conventional mark — a scaled shape, field, texture or line of any kind. The chapter does not say which, and the walk is the same for any of them.

First, the tier. Ask whether removing the element changes any fact the view states. If the quantity is carried only by the form, the form is in the evidence layer and is an Adaptable encoding choice, to be judged by effectiveness — which perceptual task it asks of the reader, and how well people do that task (Mackinlay's ranking, conjectural; Blascheck's glance costs). If the quantity is also carried by a conventional mark and the form repeats it, the form is Decorative or a sensory experience and the removal test governs it.

Second, the purchase, written. "The viewer will [verb] [noun]", from the five verbs, limited to what expression is measured to buy. "The viewer will connect the count to the place" is a claim the evidence allows; "the viewer will feel more and act" is not.

Third, the four removals, run and written into the register. Mono: does the form survive greyscale, or did hue carry its direction? Silent: does it make sound, and if so where is the document? Still: does it build or move, and if so what remains with motion disabled? Undressed: with the register stripped, is the quantity still stated — in a conventional mark, a number, a sentence — with its unit, base, date and gate?

Fourth, the fifth check. Put the stripped view beside the dressed one and ask whether they say the same thing. The commonest failure for a form that carries quantity in size, brightness or density is the one the Doughnut's caption names and the DWP houses show: an area that scales as the square of the value, a brightness normalised to the frame, a texture whose density the eye reads non-linearly — each adds a fact (how much bigger) that the data does not say. The fix is to scale the form to the value, or to do what the Doughnut's authors did: state the distortion in words on the form and ship the bar beside it.

Fifth, the twin and the identification. Where is the precise form, and how many steps away; what words identify the element to a reader who cannot see it, and, if it sounds, to one who cannot hear it.

Sixth, the test, planned. Readers from the three user groups Chapter 0 names, some shown the stripped view and some the dressed, each asked what the data said about the place; compared on the figures and the trend, as Chapter 13's pass test asks, and additionally on recognition, which Chapter 12 asks. The entry stays open until the two groups' answers agree on the figures and the trend; a difference that is small in two readers is not agreement, and the sample is the user groups', as in Chapter 13. What they may differ on — how the view felt, whether it looked like the place — is the purchase, and the register records it as such.

Nothing above names the form, the palette, the type, the sound or the place. It is the procedure by which any of them can be proposed by the people whose decision it is and checked by someone else.

The rules

Rule Why Kind Tier Source
Sort every element into a layer, then run the removal test on every expressive one — mono, silent, still, undressed — and the fifth check: stripped and dressed say the same thing Expressiveness is "all the facts" and "only the facts"; a lost fact is a wrong sort, an added fact is a false fact Standard (method); Reading Fixed (requirement) Mackinlay 1986; Kosara 2007; W3C 1.1.1; AF infographics; ONS animations; AF §10
Record each element in the boundary log, eleven lines, before it ships An unlogged break is indistinguishable from negligence at the next audit Nightlife Culture Fixed (sequence) Decision Book Ch 18; this chapter
Name the purchase in the affective-intent template, limited to what expression is measured to buy Engagement, mood and recognition are measured, and memorability in Chapter 3; empathy, giving and accuracy are not Evidence; Evidence of method Fixed (requirement) Lee-Robbins & Adar 2022; Boy 2017; Morais 2021; Kineticharts; Arunkumar 2023
The precise twin is one step away and the form states its finding, and any distortion, in words on itself A twin beside a form is not thereby read Evidence; Practice Fixed (requirement) Ottley 2019; Decision Book Ch 7; Fanning & Raworth 2025
Humanised marks are whole units and are never priced as buying empathy or action A sliced person encodes a fraction the data does not say; the measured effect on a hypothetical allocation is at best about 3 in 100 Evidence; Practice; Reading Fixed (requirement) FT Visual Vocabulary; Boy 2017; Morais 2021; Correll 2019
A dark register ships with a light one and the reader's choice is honoured Positive polarity advantage in both age groups at small sizes; chart polarity individual; the floor already carries user override Evidence Fixed (requirement) Piepenbrock 2013; Dobres 2017 [abstract or summary only]; While & Sarvghad 2024; AF colours; Chapter 13's floor
A drawn or approximate register is worn only where the data is imprecise, and says so Sketchiness works as an uncertainty cue Evidence [abstract or summary only]; Practice Adaptable Boukhelifa 2012 [abstract or summary only]; Chalabi interviews
Mood is carried only in channels that encode nothing Palette moved feeling more than the data's trend did Evidence Fixed (requirement) Blair 2024; Bartram 2017; Anderson & Robinson 2022 [abstract or summary only]
Any sound that is content has a text document; captions include non-speech sound; nothing autoplays beyond three seconds without a stop Level A Standard (W3C) Fixed (requirement) WCAG 1.2.1; 1.2.2; 1.4.2
A specific sensory experience is identified in words, never ignored The standard's third category Standard (W3C) Fixed (requirement) WCAG 1.1.1
The conventions of objectivity are earned by the records beneath them; a source line points to a reachable source The source line "performs the rhetorical, persuasive work of ascribing transparency" Evidence of method; Reading Fixed (requirement) Kennedy et al. 2016; Chapters 4–7
Never make the evidence layer harder to read on purpose Disfluency: recall d = −0.01; slower; less confident Evidence Fixed (requirement) Xie et al. 2018; Weissgerber 2024 [abstract or summary only]; Hullman 2011 (the proposal)
A headline read in passing has its letter height set from the distance it is read at, and its finding restated in the body text at arm's length The legibility index; three or four words a glance Standard (method); Evidence Fixed (requirement) USSC 2015; Bullough 2017; Garvey 2016
Short headlines; the count is the house's The mantra; the measured numbers are distance, seconds and glance Nightlife Culture Adaptable (house default) Version 1 Ch 13; the sign literature
The display's genre is the house's to choose; the evidence layer passes the removal test in any genre Prototypicality is about speed of judgement; unfamiliar forms cost glances and liking Reading Adaptable Chapter 11; Kennedy focus groups; Blascheck 2019
No form is invented without a glance-cost estimate and a plan to measure it One radial form took about six times a bar's glance, in one study Evidence Adaptable Blascheck 2019
Audit accuracy, then the floor, then beauty; beauty is never a licence The field's prize has no accuracy criterion; the regulator's casework is about encodings, sources and context Practice; Standard (regulator) Adaptable (house default) IIB FAQ; OSR casework; Code 3.0 9.2
Probes meet the evaluated exception's standard and add a comparison Logs plus survey, open materials, behaviour against self-report; no control Evidence of method Adaptable Pomerance, Boyd & Dörk 2026
Everything else in the register — palette beyond the encoding, display type, illustration, pattern, imagery, pacing, the poster layer, stoppable sound, disableable motion Free, under the rules above — Decorative Decision Book Ch 18

What proves a break works

Run the four removals and the fifth check, and write the register entry. If the stripped version states every figure with its unit, base, date and gate, and the dressed version says nothing the stripped one does not, the expressive layer was free and the entry closes. If the stripped version lost a fact, the sort was wrong: the element was encoding it and belongs in the evidence layer, to be judged as an encoding and to meet the floor, and the test runs again. If the dressed version added a fact — a size, an order, a brightness, a cause — the element has failed Mackinlay's second clause, and the fix is to scale it to the data, or to state the distortion in words on the form and ship the twin beside it as the Doughnut's authors did, or to re-tier it as Decorative and remove the scaling. Then the comparison: readers who saw the stripped view and readers who saw the dressed one, asked what the data said; the entry closes when the two groups agree on the figures and the trend and may differ on everything else.

What this chapter could not settle

  • No reader study compares an expressive form with its precise twin on what readers take from the data. Arunkumar 2023 (correlational) as the nearest; the probes run the comparison.
  • The two-audience test has no measurement anywhere in the book. Held as a stance; a probe can measure it.
  • The tier vocabulary lacks the W3C's "specific sensory experience". Used in the register; adoption left to Chapter 16.
  • "Seven words" has no source. Mantra re-tiered Adaptable; measured numbers given.
  • Kineticharts' comprehension count: the paper names four aspects and asks three questions. Reported as three.

Checklist

  • Every element sorted into a layer; every expressive element has a boundary-log entry, eleven lines, before it ships
  • Tier stated: Decorative, specific sensory experience, or a named encoding choice
  • Purchase written as "The viewer will [verb] [noun]", within what expression is measured to buy
  • Mono: greyscale render loses no fact and changes none
  • Silent: muting loses no fact; sound-as-content has its text document; nothing autoplays beyond three seconds without a stop
  • Still: motion disabled loses no fact; pause control present
  • Undressed: the committee export states every figure with unit, base, date and gate
  • Fifth check: stripped and dressed views say the same thing (no added size, order, brightness or cause)
  • Precise twin one step away; the form states its finding in words on itself
  • Humanised marks are whole units; no empathy or action claimed for them
  • Dark register has a light alternative and the reader's choice is honoured
  • Drawn or approximate register used only where the data is imprecise, and the imprecision is stated
  • Mood carried only in channels that encode nothing; a mood palette beside a scale priced in the log
  • Sensory-experience elements identified in words for readers who cannot see or hear them
  • Every source line points to a reachable source and a record beneath it
  • Headline read in passing: letter height set from distance; finding restated in the body
  • Any invented form has a glance-cost estimate and a measurement plan
  • The evidence layer is never made harder to read on purpose
  • Reader comparison planned: stripped against dressed, figures and trend, the user groups' readers
  • Audit order: accuracy, then the floor, then beauty
  • Probe plan meets the evaluated exception's standard and adds a comparison

Words this chapter uses

  • The evidence layer is everything in a display that makes or supports a claim about the world: the data, the encodings that carry it (position, length, colour, area, motion where it means something), the titles, the units, the sources, the dates, the gates on a comparison and the written account.
  • The expressive layer is everything else that a designer adds on purpose: register, palette beyond the encoding, type beyond legibility, illustration, pattern, sound, motion that does not mean anything, pacing, and the form chosen for its feel.
  • The removal test is the procedure this chapter formalises: take the expressive layer away — in version 1's four words, mono, silent, still, undressed — and check that the evidence layer still expresses all of the data and only the data.
  • Expressiveness and effectiveness are Mackinlay's 1986 names for two different questions about a graphic — whether it can say exactly what the data says, and how well a human can read what it says — and the chapter uses them as the formal names of the house's tier test.
  • An anthropographic is a chart whose marks are made to look like the people they count.
  • Affective design is the field's term for designing a display to carry a feeling.
  • Display polarity is whether text is dark on light (positive) or light on dark (negative); contrast polarity is the same thing said of a chart.
  • Redundant encoding is carrying one variable in two visual channels at once.
  • A legibility index is the sign trade's ratio of reading distance to letter height.
  • Register, on its own, means tone and style — the look a display wears; where this book names a log (the failure register, the Decision Book's rule register) it says "log" or "register" with its qualifier, and the record this chapter leaves is called the boundary log to keep the two apart.
  • The precise twin is the Decision Book's rule that any expressive form ships beside the same data in a precise, standard form; the committee export is version 1's name for the same thing at the scale of a whole page.
  • Decorative has two official senses that the chapter keeps apart: ornament, in the plain meaning; and the technical status a design system or the W3C gives to an image that carries no information and may be skipped by assistive technology.
  • A specific sensory experience is the W3C's third category, between information and decoration, for content "that words cannot fully capture" [read once].
  • The gallery is version 1's set of studied exemplars, audited live for this chapter. The evaluated exception is version 1's name for the one gallery entry with a published evaluation.

15Learning from the best

Trust is measured as producers measure theirs, or not claimed; no arrow without a printed rule; every public data project ends, and the plan is written first.

Dashboard Design · Part 4: The boundary and the practice

Reading this chapter. This is one chapter of Dashboard Design, Nightlife Culture's research book on how evidence becomes a display a reader can trust, read and act on. The studio ("the house" in some chapters) is Nightlife Culture, a creative policy studio; the brief is its founder Carly Heath's commission for the book, and her eight ways a dashboard fails, the failure register, run through it. The Vibe Map, the studio's prototype for showing a place's nightlife culture, appears only as an illustration, never as a specification. "Version 1" is the book's archived first draft, whose positions this version re-tests against the sources. Every rule carries a kind (where it comes from: Standard, Evidence, Reading, Practice or Nightlife Culture) and a tier (how firm it is: Fixed, Adaptable or Decorative); Chapter 0 explains both, and the three senses of Fixed: a requirement that can be checked, a sequence whose order is the hard line, and a statement of the record. A dagger (†) marks a source read at the authors' abstract or summary only; "secondary" a quotation reached through a named reproduction; "(read once)" a quotation returned on a single reading and not confirmed by a second. Chapter 0 holds the glossary of the words the chapters share; each chapter lists its own coinages before its sources.

The question

Sector by sector — public health dashboards, finance and risk, economic development and place, the culture and charity sectors' impact practice, and the great public data projects — what did the best public data displays get right about trust, provenance, change over time and reach; how is each of those four properties measured or evidenced where it is measured at all; what did each sector get wrong or leave unsolved; which of their mechanisms are documented well enough, with a printed rule and a stated reason and either evidence or a named cost, to be borrowed by a public dashboard about a place's culture; and does the chapter find enough that Chapters 2 and 5 did not to earn its place as a chapter rather than a reading list?

The 60-second version

Trust is measured for producers, and for how government presents their figures, and almost never for displays. The Public Confidence in Official Statistics survey asks the same questions in waves (2,364 adults in 2023; 3,398 in 2021): "87% of respondents who gave an opinion indicating that they tend to trust it (71%) or trust it a great deal (16%)" — the ONS — while agreement that "the government presents official statistics honestly" "remained relatively low (32%, compared to 35% in 2021)"; the two items have sat between 54 and 60 points apart across four waves. Charities are trusted at 6.5 out of 10 (4,681 respondents, 2026), and the drivers people name are where the money goes (55 per cent) and "a real difference" made (51 per cent). The most-used public dashboard in the UK, by its own team's account, evidences its trust with one blog sentence — "an outstandingly high level of user trust in the dashboard data at 90.3%, up from an already high level in November when 73.4% of users responded that they trusted the data" — from a self-selected on-site survey with no n or wording; the one randomised test found of whether a dashboard changes trust — trust in government, read through the authors' own summary (secondary) — reported that "information disclosure has no direct effects on willingness to trust". A central bank's layered report raised comprehension in two experiments (285 and 2,275 readers) and moved trust only slightly, for one "relatable" wording, in one; "the simplification of language increases public comprehension more than the inclusion of visuals" (†). Showing uncertainty as a range beside a point lowered trust little or not at all — "only a small decrease … mostly for verbal uncertainty communication" across five experiments (n = 5,780), none in the field, and none in the office across two waves of over 3,000 and over 4,000 — while a verbal hedge alone "tends to have little effect" on understanding [read once].

Provenance is where the best projects are most alike, and the pattern is a record per metric plus a dated log. UKHSA gives every metric a page with the same five headings — Summary, Rationale, Definition, Methodology, Caveats [read once] — and a change log, separate from the weekly refresh, whose entries are labelled and paired: "Issue: COVID-19 deaths data", "Resolved: duplicated rows in bulk download files". Fingertips gives every indicator a thirty-two-field record with the numerator and the denominator defined and sourced separately. Johns Hopkins kept two ledgers: its own errors in a machine-readable errata file and its sources' revisions in a dated prose list with the reason. Our World in Data's testing dataset carried, for every observation, "a URL at which the specific observation of the corresponding raw data can be found". The ONS separates a revision ("a scheduled change") from a correction ("an unplanned revision … because of the identification of an error", read once) and labels the second as such. The statistics regulator's 2025 guidance makes a minimum list for any official dashboard — sources, status, strengths and limitations, revisions, update schedule, archive, contact — and a clause the sectors' own documents had not: "come with a plan for maintaining, updating and retiring the dashboard".

Change over time is documented well where the rule for the arrow is printed, and badly where it is not. Fingertips will not draw a trend arrow unless "There must be at least five points in the series", the periods are independent, the trend passes "χ² > 9.5495" (p < 0.2 per cent) and survives dropping any one point — and still says the arrows "do not constitute a rigorous analysis of the time series". Its colour rule: "indicator values should only be given red or green RAG ratings if they are statistically significantly higher or lower than the comparator", with the warning that "one in twenty red or green ratings could be expected even where all the underlying distributions are essentially amber". The OECD's regional tool prints its arrow rule in one sentence (±5 per cent against a fixed start year); Wales prints a significance test where intervals exist and a declared expert judgement where they do not; Scotland's per-indicator rules lived on pages that now redirect. Finance keeps vintages ("Economic data time travel since 2006"), and the reason is on record — re-running a classic test on later data, "the coefficients change dramatically", though for many studies results were "generally robust" [read once]; the ONS prints the size of its own revisions ("The mean absolute revision between the first and final estimates is 0.27 percentage points"); the Bank of England's fan chart has a printed band rule that changed from 10 per cent steps to 30 per cent steps without the picture changing, survived a review that said "They should be eliminated", and was then found, in the Bank's own staff test of 300 members of the public and 75 experts against five other formats, to be "well understood". A cumulative axis "can show only an upward or flat trend", and in two experiments with 2,549 participants it "consistently led to participants believing that they and others were at more risk" (both read once). The deprivation indices say in print what a rank cannot: "a small area with a rank of 1,000 is not half as deprived as a place with a rank of 500", and "Indices releases should not be viewed or construed as a time-series".

Reach is counted in server events and self-reports, and almost never as decisions. "over 300,000 unique users every day, and five million hits a week"; "3·6 billion page views"; "nearly 100 million page views" in a year; Nomis, forty-five years old, publishes no usage figure on any page reached; a case study of the ONS's local statistics service reports "93% of users found it easy to use" with no n; Our World in Data's own audience survey found 17.5 per cent of respondents said they download data when analytics showed "1.6% of sessions have a CSV download" [read once]. The one service assessment of a dashboard team told it to "create a measurement framework that demonstrates how metrics map to key performance indicators (KPIs) and goals". The question that measures use is the one a Scottish government evaluation asked of 41 users of an internal dashboard: whether the data informed "their decisions or conclusions as part of their role" (49 per cent, read once).

Public data projects end or change hands — four of the five read here have since 2021 — and the culture sector's own yardstick had no published plan. Johns Hopkins gave four weeks' notice, a reason located upstream ("U.S. states and counties began to consistently reduce the amount of publicly reported data", read once), and a frozen open repository; the COVID Tracking Project announced its end date five weeks ahead and promised "gap analyses noting where replacement data still doesn't exist"; Our World in Data swapped a dying source for a living one with "The URL of all our charts and the variable names in our dataset will remain the same" and later listed, dataset by dataset, what continues and what stops; UKHSA ran old and new in parallel and published a 1.4 GB archive with a page of its known gaps. The Audience Agency entered liquidation on 10 September 2026; its notice names no successor for Audience Spectrum or Audience Finder, and the former funder's statement rests on "our understanding is that organisations are currently still able to access and download their historic data". The quality-metrics line the culture sector built — whose 2016 evaluation found 63 per cent of organisations agreeing the framework was useful and the resulting data "regularly referenced as 'interesting' rather than 'useful'" — became a funding condition; separately, the funder's mandatory audience-data platform had its survey requirement suspended from 2023 to 2025; and a review of the funder, read through the trade press (secondary), says "The present reporting requirements are not fit for purpose."

What the chapter adds to Chapters 2 and 5. A set of mechanisms with their printed rules, reasons, evidence and costs — the five-heading metric page and the thirty-two-field record; the labelled change log and the two ledgers; the revision-versus-correction distinction and the printed revision size; the vintage archive; the no-arrow-without-a-rule standard and the one-in-twenty warning; the incomplete-tail band with the direction of its bias; the not-a-time-series sentence and the not-half-as-deprived sentence; the refusal to aggregate; the fixed trust question in waves, of those with a view; the question of whether the data informed a decision; the retirement clause and the sunset note. Seven of these the chapter holds true regardless (section 11); the rest are an offer with terms. Beneath the dashboard the chapter leaves a twelfth record, the precedent record: one entry of nine lines per mechanism considered — the mechanism and the record it feeds; the source and its date; the rule as printed; the reason given; the evidence or its absence; the condition or cost; what the house changes; the status; the review date. The pass test is that every borrowed rule the build uses can be traced to an entry, and that no entry rests on "this is what everyone does".

1 · What "learning from the best" means here

This chapter exists because "take inspiration from the best in the world" was said at the start. Chapter 2 settled what turns a reader's decision and what is measured about trust in a display; Chapter 5 settled how a measure is built and audited. So this chapter has a test to pass before it has anything to teach: it must find, sector by sector, things those chapters did not, and it must deliver them as mechanisms with their terms rather than as examples to admire. It found about forty, listed in section 9; about six were already in the book in another form.

What "the best" means here. The chapter did not pick the best by taste. It read the displays the brief named, the ones the sectors' own regulators, reviews and evaluations cite, and the ones whose documentation other displays copy — and it reports each for what its documentation makes transferable, not as a verdict on the project.

The four properties, made measurable. The brief's four words are not the same kind of thing, and the chapter keeps them apart. Trust is reported here only where someone asked people a question about it, with the question's wording, the sample and the base; the chapter distinguishes trust in a producer (the ONS; "charities"; a central bank) from trust in a display, because the first is measured in long series and the second almost never is. Provenance is read as documentation: what a metric's page carries, what a change log records, whether a dataset's past versions can be retrieved. Change over time has two senses that the sectors handle differently — how a display shows that a quantity moved (arrows, colours, trends, fans) and how a display's own figures move after they are first published (revisions, vintages, corrections) — and the chapter reads both. Reach is reported in whatever unit the source counted in, with the unit named, because the units do not convert: a "feature layer request" is a map tile, a "hit" is a server event, a "unique user" is a cookie, a survey percentage is a self-report. Where a source counts decisions informed, the chapter says so, because that is the only unit the failure register cares about.

The borrowing test. A mechanism is borrowable when three things are true of it. Its rule is printed — thresholds, intervals, colours, cadence, wording — so that someone else can apply it and a reader can check that it was applied. Its reason is stated, so that the house can tell whether the reason holds for a place's culture as it held for a pandemic or a bank. And either its evidence is known (someone measured what it did, with a sample and a design) or its cost is named (what it needs — a forecast-error history, five annual points, confidence intervals, a stable indicator set — and what it does when those are absent). A mechanism with no printed rule is a look; one with a rule but no stated reason is a habit; one with a rule and a reason but neither evidence nor a named cost is a bet. The chapter uses the three words in those senses only. The precedent record in section 11 is the form in which the test is run and kept.

What the chapter is not. It is not research into any sector's subject matter: the public health displays are read for their banding rules and not for what they say about health; the deprivation indices for what they say a rank can mean and not for which areas rank where; the charity codes for what they require and not for any charity. It is not research into nightlife, in any form. It is not a verdict on any of these projects as projects; several of them did their work under conditions no studio will face, and the chapter reads them for what their documentation makes transferable. And beyond the seven truths and their procedures, it does not decide what the Vibe Map borrows; section 9 lists what each sector offers with its terms, section 12 says which decisions are the studio's, and the precedent record is where each decision would be written.

What the failure register asks of this chapter is mostly the two failures that sit at either end of a display's life: "It fails if it looks the same every month" and "It fails if it breaks or isn't reliable". The sectors that have run public displays for years — a labour-market statistics service since 1981, a mortality database with a versioned method, a dashboard whose team reported "over 300,000 unique users every day" — have written down how they handle the first (revisions, vintages, arrows with rules) and the second (release calendars, change logs, retirement plans), and that writing is what this chapter went to find. Section 10 reads the whole register.

2 · What people believe about the best, and what the evidence says

Belief: the most-used dashboards have the best evidence that they are trusted. The UK's coronavirus dashboard evidences its trust in one blog sentence, from an on-site survey with no sample size or question wording; the regulator's praise ("one of strongest examples of open data and statistics being used by a huge number of individuals") is praise; the one randomised test found of a dashboard's effect on trust reported no average effect and a split by prior trust. Where trust is measured in series it is measured for producers — the ONS, charities — by a fixed question repeated in waves. Section 3 and section 7. (Evidence; Practice.)

Belief: showing uncertainty makes people trust the number less. Five experiments with 5,780 participants found "only a small decrease in trust in numbers and trustworthiness of the source, and mostly for verbal uncertainty communication"; in a field test in a BBC article, a range beside the point estimate "did not affect participants' trust in the number"; two waves of a UK GDP experiment found that communicating uncertainty "improves the public's understanding of data uncertainty, but does not reduce its trust in the statistical office", and that "The textual uncertainty qualifier given to Group 2 tends to have little effect" [read once]. A verbal qualifier did little for understanding; the range did the work, and the measured cost in trust was small and mostly for the verbal form. Section 4. (Evidence.)

Belief: pictures make the public understand. In the Bank of England's four-arm experiment with 2,275 respondents, the published visual summary improved comprehension by "25% (0.5 points)", half the words did as well as the pictures, and plain "relatable" wording did best at "42% (0.8 points)" — which still left readers at "2.85 out of 5 questions correctly" [read once]. The journal version's abstract: "the simplification of language increases public comprehension more than the inclusion of visuals" (†). Section 4. (Evidence.)

Belief: a rank is harmless if the method is published. The place instruments' own method texts, and two analysts of ranking, say otherwise: "they show that one area is more deprived than another but not by how much"; "The web tool does not include a regional composite well-being index"; "rankings can be too unreliable to be helpful"; "Typical risk matrices can correctly and unambiguously compare only a small fraction (e.g., less than 10%) of randomly selected pairs of hazards" (†). An audited index that publishes rank intervals says that "These confidence intervals also have to be taken into account when comparing economy rank changes from one year to the next". Section 5. (Standard (official statistics); Evidence of method.)

Belief: an index built to track change over time tracks change over time. The deprivation indices, updated "every 3 to 5 years", "cannot be used to identify real change in deprivation over time", and their users asked for exactly that; the Health Index, built so that "comparisons can be made between scores over time", last released in June 2023 and showing "Next release: To be announced" on 6 October 2026, with no status notice found; the levelling-up metrics were announced before some of them existed and are still reported annually by a government that "has moved away from the levelling up programme" because a statute requires it. Section 5. (Standard (official statistics); Practice.)

Belief: the yardstick's owner will always be there. The Audience Agency, custodian of the culture sector's audience segmentation and its audience-data platform, entered liquidation on 10 September 2026 with no successor named in anything that could be read. Section 6. (Practice.)

Belief: usage is reach. The units do not convert, and no source read counts decisions except by asking. Section 1's rule, and section 8. (Reading.)

Belief: a public data project is forever. Four of the projects read have ended or changed source since 2021, and the statistics regulator now asks every official dashboard to "come with a plan for maintaining, updating and retiring the dashboard". Section 7. (Standard (regulator); Practice.)

3 · Public health

Public health built, under pressure and in public, the most complete provenance furniture of any sector read, and left the most exact printed rules for colour and for arrows. It also left the thinnest evidence of its own reach and trust, and three documented retirements.

A dashboard that says what it is not

The UKHSA data dashboard — successor to the coronavirus dashboard, which was retired on 21 December 2023 — carries a page headed "Compliance" that states, pillar by pillar against the Code of Practice for Statistics, what the dashboard meets and what it cannot. "it is not possible for the dashboard to be classed as official statistics", because "different classifications of data are displayed" [read once]; among the things it cannot do is "Pre-announce the release time of data (usually 4pm every Thursday) via the release calendar" [read once] — the official release calendar is for official statistics, which this is not — so it makes the commitment on its own page instead: "so we commit to update the data at 4pm every Thursday"; "On the rare occasions when delays are unavoidable, we announce this on our homepage"; "We announce any unexpected changes to the data we release on the homepage and add an explanation to our What's new or About pages"; "We have carried out over 100 individual user research sessions"; "allowing users to download data from every graph displayed on the dashboard". The Code is open to voluntary application by producers who are not official statisticians, and this is what a voluntary statement looks like: a short public page saying which requirements a mixed-status display meets, a fixed weekly release time, and a named place where surprises are announced. (Practice; Standard (official statistics).)

A page per metric, and a log apart from the refresh

Each metric on the dashboard has a documentation page — the two read carry the same five headings, Summary, Rationale, Definition, Methodology, Caveats (confirmed at source for the cases page) — and a machine name that matches the API. The cases page, for example: "New cases are reported by specimen date - the date the first sample that identified the infection was taken"; "Data for the last 5 days by specimen date are considered incomplete" "as it takes time to get test results and record them on relevant lab systems"; "This figure will underestimate the actual number of COVID-19 infections". The log entry that announced the documentation (21 December 2023) names the template's purpose in four clauses: "definition (what the metric is), rationale (why we're showing the metric), methodology (how the metric is collected and calculated), caveats (additional information that will help users to understand what the metric is showing)" [read once]. What the template lacks is as instructive: no separate "source" or "update frequency" field was visible on the pages read; cadence lives on the compliance page and in the log. (Practice.)

The log — "What's new" — is the chapter's primary change-log specimen. "Here we'll show a timeline of changes that have happened outside of the weekly data refresh"; its entries are labelled (New metric, New Feature, New content, Update, Change to metric, Data issue, Other — read once as a set) and the data issues are opened and closed in public: "Issue: COVID-19 deaths data" — "Due to a data issue, COVID-19 deaths data are only available to 29th December 2023"; "Resolved: duplicated rows in bulk download files", ending "We appreciate the user feedback we received flagging this issue"; "On 11 November 2024, a data processing error led to a pipeline failure and prevented the COVID-19 positivity dataset from being produced." [read once]. Cadence changes are logged as changes to the metric: "Respiratory viruses data to be updated every 2 weeks"; "The severity of the measles outbreak has been downgraded. As a result, we will report measles data monthly rather than every 2 weeks." [read once].
