DCMS's Embedding a Culture and Heritage Capital Approach (December 2024): "Standard economic measures are an incomplete measure of public welfare and value added, as they do not take into account assets and services that do not have market prices."; five steps — "Consider the culture and heritage assets"; "Consider the culture and heritage services"; "Consider the welfare impacts"; "Monetise the welfare impacts"; "Project future benefits across the asset's life to estimate total asset value"; and its cautions — appraisal "should always be conducted in a proportional way", "should also sit alongside a wider set of evidence that can inform decision making", and "One limitation that is important to be aware of is double counting between methods, and as such, some non-market valuation methods cannot be used in conjunction with each other". The words "multiplier", "GVA" and "economic impact" are reported absent. Chapter 6's gross-to-net discipline stands on its own grounds. (Standard (official statistics).)

The codes, in their own words

Four frameworks the sector reports against, each quoted for what it asks. Inspiring Impact's Code of Good Impact Practice (2013; a code for charities on how to measure and report their effect; the programme "ran from 2011 until early 2022" and the Code survives re-hosted): "Take responsibility for impact and encourage others to do so too"; "Focus on purpose"; "Involve others in your impact practice"; "Apply proportionate and appropriate methods and resources"; "Consider the full range of the difference you actually make"; "Be honest and open"; "Be willing to change and act on what you find"; "Actively share your impact plans, methods, findings and learning"; with the sentence on contribution — "you're willing to accept that you may not be having the impact you intended" and that changes "may have occurred without your involvement, may be short term, or may be the result of the work of others" [read once]. NPC's four pillars (2014; a think-tank's method for charity measurement): "Map your theory of change"; "Prioritise what you measure"; "Choose your level of evidence"; "Select your sources and tools"; "A theory of change should be at the heart of your approach because it shows what you want to achieve and how you plan to achieve it, setting out the causal links between your activities and your end goal."; "Choose an appropriate level of rigour of evidence that suits the needs of your stakeholders." Social Value International's principles (the standard behind social-return accounting): Involve stakeholders; Understand what changes; Value the things that matter; Only include what is material; Do not overclaim; Be transparent; Verify the result; Be responsive — with "Only claim the value that activities are responsible for creating." and, where results reach external audiences or support significant decisions, "independent assurance is required" [read once]. The Impact Management Project's five dimensions (a consensus vocabulary for describing an effect), two of them the ones any claim of contribution needs: "Contribution tells us whether an enterprise's efforts resulted in outcomes that were likely better than what likely would have occurred otherwise." and "Risk tells us the likelihood that impact will be different than expected." The Charities SORP's primary text could not be read; an accountancy body's summary says the 2026 edition, effective 1 January 2026, asks the smallest charities to "consider how their work made a difference" and requires larger ones to "explain the impact the charity is making" (secondary). (Standard (method); Practice; secondary.)

What the sector says about its own compliance: a 2012 survey of 1,000 charities found "75% of charities measure some or all of their work" and "Only 5% of charities say that wanting to improve services is a primary motivation for increasing their impact measurement efforts."; the Charity Commission's random sample of 105 trustees' reports found "52% of the trustees' annual reports demonstrated a clear understanding of the public benefit reporting requirement, similar to last year's 51%."; among the top 100 charities by income, "the vast majority (94 per cent) of charities fail to report a single efficiency measure in any channel of communication" (Hyndman & McConville, 2016). On the sector's own numbers, improving services is rarely the stated motive for measuring, and about half of sampled reports showed a clear understanding of the basic public-benefit requirement. (Evidence; Evidence of method.)

Trust in a sector that reports impact, measured for twenty years

The Charity Commission's trust tracker asks one fixed question — "on a scale of 0-10 where 10 means you trust them completely and 0 means you don't trust them at all, how much trust and confidence do you have in charities?" [read once] — in waves, annual since 2020 and every second year before [read once]: 2026, "4681 completes were achieved.", mean trust 6.5, "Over half (57%) say they have high trust in charities" (7 to 10); 2025, "4092 completes were achieved.", 6.5, 57 per cent; a series running back to 2005 (6.3) through a trough of 5.5 in 2018 [read once]. The drivers people name, 2026: "Most of the money raised is spent directly on the causes the charity supports" 55 per cent; "The charity makes a real difference to the people and communities that it serves by achieving its stated purpose" 51 per cent; "It is easy to see how much the charity has raised, and how this money has been spent" 40 per cent. The mechanism — one fixed question, banded, repeated, with drivers as a ranked list — is borrowable whole. What donors do with impact information is a separate measured thing: "60% of donors say they care about impact, 10% look mainly for information on impact and ultimately just 2% use an informed assessment of impact to choose between charities." (survey of 3,000; NPC 2013); and a study that tested "how donors respond to new information about a charity's effectiveness" (Karlan & Wood, 2014) was read in abstract only, with no finding quotable from it (†). (Evidence.)

What the culture and charity sectors got right: a pilot evaluated independently, with N, n and response rate printed, before roll-out; a marked break line with a comparability sentence; codes that name contribution and risk as things to state; a trust question held fixed for two decades. What they got wrong: an instrument whose own pilot evaluation found its triangulated data "interesting" rather than "useful" and its benchmarking doubted by most organisations, made a condition of funding; a separate mandatory platform whose core requirement had to be suspended from 2023 to 2025; data demanded of which a review reports "widespread scepticism about whether ACE uses all" (secondary); a yardstick whose custodian failed with no plan; and impact reporting of which about half of sampled reports showed a clear understanding, with improving services rarely the stated motive. (Reading.)

7 · The great public data projects

Our World in Data as an institution

"Our World in Data is a project of the Global Change Data Lab, a non-profit organization based in the United Kingdom (Registered Charity Number 1186433)." [read once]; "All visualizations, data, and articles produced by Our World in Data are completely open access under the Creative Commons BY license."; funded by foundations and "More than 4,000 people have donated over the past couple of years." [read once]. Its reach, from its own trustees' report for 2022: "In 2022, OWID had on average more than 3 million unique users per month"; "nearly 100 million page views this year"; "referenced in nearly 25,000 media articles in 2022"; "cited in more than 6,500 academic publications". Its 2020 audience survey, by its own account, was "not a representative sample of our total audience", and 17.5 per cent of respondents said they download data while analytics showed "1.6% of sessions have a CSV download" [read once]. Its provenance is written as field-level rules in a public pipeline reference: origin.date_published, "Exact day (or year, if exact day is unknown) when the producer's data (in its current version) was published"; origin.date_accessed, "Exact day when the producer's data (in its current version) was downloaded by OWID"; dataset.update_period_days, "Expected number of days between consecutive updates of this dataset by OWID"; a two-level processing label — "minor" for renames, unit changes and dropped missing values, "major" for aggregates, operations between indicators and concatenation [read once] — that drives both the on-chart credit ("with major processing by Our World in Data", Chapter 14) and the licence; and description_processing, "Relevant information about the processing of the indicator done by OWID". No corrections policy was found beyond a feedback form and one sentence: "Our team regularly identifies and investigates data anomalies, often working with original data providers to correct errors." (Practice.)

Trust in a producer, measured in waves

Public Confidence in Official Statistics (run by NatCen for the UK Statistics Authority, which oversees the office it measures) is the fullest trust measurement read, and the one the chapter reads the others against. 2023 wave (published May 2024): "a representative sample of 2,364 adults aged 18 and over in Britain" "from 1,695 households"; "an adjusted household response rate of 21.2%"; online with paper offered to non-responders. "Most respondents trusted the Office for National Statistics (ONS), with 87% of respondents who gave an opinion indicating that they tend to trust it (71%) or trust it a great deal (16%)." (verified); "In 2023, 85% of respondents said they trusted ONS statistics"; "free from political interference (72%)"; government presents official statistics honestly "remained relatively low (32%, compared to 35% in 2021)"; "Even fewer respondents (25%) tended to agree that newspapers present official statistics honestly."; "ONS had the highest level of reported trust of all (87%) among respondents, similar to levels of trust in the courts (82%) or the Bank of England (79%)"; "Trust was lowest in the British media (25%), the Government (31%) and the UK Parliament (36%)". 2021 wave: "a representative sample of 3,398 adults"; "In 2021 PCOS was run for the first time as a stand-alone push-to-web survey."; "In 2021 89% of those able to express a view said they trust ONS and 87% said they trust ONS statistics."; "Only 35% of people able to express a view agreed that the government presents official statistics honestly"; "82% of people able to express an opinion agreed that official statistics are generally accurate, up from 78% in 2018"; and the caution the house would copy when its own method changes — "There is a need for caution when making comparisons between 2021 and earlier years of the study". The series, of those with a view: trust in the ONS 88, 88, 89, 87 (2014, 2018, 2021, 2023); free from interference 66, 73, 74, 72; "presents official statistics honestly" 28, 31, 35, 32 (2014 and 2018 figures read once; the 2023 household response rate was 21.2 per cent). No 2025 wave was found. (Evidence.)

The mechanism is four things: a fixed question set; waves; "of those able to express a view", said so; and a printed caution when the mode changed. The finding is the gap — between 54 and 60 points across four waves — between trust in the producer and agreement that the government presents its figures honestly, which is Chapter 2's distinction between the producer and the presenter, measured. (Evidence; Reading.)

Custodians of long series

The Human Mortality Database (project overview; its Methods Protocol is at version 6, August 2025): "As much as possible, we have followed four guiding principles in creating this database: comparability, flexibility, accessibility, reproducibility."; "the database is limited by design to populations where death registration and census data are virtually complete, since this type of information is required for the uniform method used to reconstruct historical data series."; "we have not attempted to correct the data for systematic age misstatement (misreporting of age) or coverage errors"; input data published beside the estimates [read once]; "assistance from database users in identifying problems is always appreciated!" Comparability by exclusion, one uniform method, inputs beside outputs, a versioned and dated protocol. The UK Data Service, "the principal repository for economic, population, and social research data in the UK" [read once], cites by persistent identifier — "Using the study's DOI will always bring the user back to this edition of this dataset, even if its location on the internet should change in the future." [read once] — and asks citers for "The precise version of the dataset used e.g. edition number or release date info" [read once]; its rule for when a change earns a new identifier could not be reached. (Practice.)

Ending well

The chapter has four documented endings and one undocumented one. Johns Hopkins (section 3): four weeks' notice, a reason upstream, a frozen open archive, named successors. Our World in Data (section 3): a source swap with stable URLs and variable names and the last old-source vintage archived; a dated note listing what continues and what stops, dataset by dataset. UKHSA (section 3): parallel running, a dated switch, a stated reason, a full archive with its gaps listed, twelve weeks later. The COVID Tracking Project (February 2021): "But the work itself—compiling, cleaning, standardizing, and making sense of COVID-19 data from 56 individual states and territories—is properly the work of federal public health agencies."; "We will spend the next five weeks publishing detailed guidance for data users who are looking for sources to replace our work, as well as gap analyses noting where replacement data still doesn't exist."; "we're making sure that it comes as close to lasting forever as anything can on the internet"; a final update on a named date [read once]. And the Audience Agency (section 6): none of these. The regulator's guidance now asks for the plan in advance and a notice before the end. Three ways a sector's data intermediary has ended are on record: no arrangement (the Audience Agency); re-hosting by a former partner (Inspiring Impact's Code); a planned wind-down with archive and gap analysis (the COVID Tracking Project). (Practice; Standard (regulator).)

What the great projects share is a short list of practices, each with a counterpart line in one of this book's records, some of which the book already carried in another form: a release calendar or a stated cadence; a methods document; a change log; a stated next update; open data under a named licence; a named custodian; and, in the best cases, a written ending. The reach they report is in pageviews and media citations, labelled as such; the trust they enjoy is measured for the statistics office and inferred for the rest. (Reading.)

8 · The four properties across the sectors

Sector Trust — how evidenced Provenance — strongest mechanism Change over time — strongest mechanism Reach — how counted What it got wrong or left open
Public health A self-selected on-site percentage with no n; a regulator's praise; one randomised test with no average effect on trust in government (secondary); producers' lesson, under the theme of trust, to disclose errors as they happen A five-heading page per metric; a 32-field record per indicator; a log apart from the refresh with issue/resolved pairs; two ledgers for own error and source revision; a source URL per observation Colour only for significance; an arrow only after five independent points, a 99.8 per cent test and leave-one-out; a marked incomplete tail with its bias; event date not report date Server events in incompatible units; "unique users"; one survey with 76.4 per cent self-reported influence Trust unmeasured; metrics not mapped to goals; a cumulative axis that moves perceived risk; purpose stated by one dashboard in eight
Finance and risk Randomised reading tests: comprehension moved, trust barely; ranges cost little or no trust, hedges did little for understanding; a statutory test framed as "detriment to public trust" [read once] Vintages kept and addressable by date; revision and correction as two labelled things; the revision's size printed; a release calendar and a published list of early readers A printed band rule, dated, changed under the same picture; a fan over past revisions; a sentence on every display saying it is not a verdict; status flags in square brackets Website activity "almost doubling" after one report [two passes]; on one platform, the news rather than the format drove attention Grids that cannot rank what they colour; a review that recommended dropping a chart without citing reader evidence; conceptual complexity rising as sentences shortened
Economic development and place Not measured for displays; users' requests recorded in a consultation (117) A per-indicator metadata record with a refresh target; a dated revisions log per dataset; a release calendar with Confirmed/Provisional; a fully specified similar-areas method "should not be viewed or construed as a time-series" and "not half as deprived", with reasons; a base-year index with frozen parameters and a count of unmeasurable change; a printed refusal to aggregate; a ±5 per cent dead-band arrow; direction labels with a significance test or a declared judgement, "since 2015"; an evidence scale with a declared minimum "93% of users found it easy to use", no n; none found for Nomis; an internal dashboard whose evaluation printed its 5 per cent response rate and asked whether the data informed decisions (49 per cent) Arrows whose rules are now unfindable; an index built for change that stopped without a notice found; metrics announced before they existed; ranked tables with no interval
Culture and charity One fixed 0–10 question since 2005 (6.5; drivers: money to the cause 55 per cent, real difference 51 per cent); a review's "widespread scepticism" (secondary) Codes naming contribution and risk; a data-processor statement ("not owned by" the funder); a pilot evaluated with N, n and a 66 per cent response rate A dotted line on the chart with "estimates can still be compared" "over 800 organisations registered"; "over 220,000 survey responses" (both self-published); donors: 60 per cent say, 2 per cent use An instrument whose pilot found its data "interesting" rather than "useful" made a condition; a mandatory platform suspended 2023–25; a custodian that failed with no plan published; half of sampled reports showing clear understanding of the basic requirement
The great public data projects A fixed question set in waves (2,364 and 3,398 adults), "of those able to express a view", with a caution when the mode changed: 87 per cent trust the producer; 32 per cent agree the government presents its figures honestly (2023) Provenance as required metadata fields with written rules; a two-level processing label driving credit and licence; inputs beside outputs; a versioned protocol; DOIs per edition A stated update period; a source swap with stable URLs; a sunset note listing what continues and stops; comparability kept by admitting only populations whose data meet the method "more than 3 million unique users per month"; "nearly 100 million page views"; media and academic citations (all self-published); a survey whose stated download rate far exceeded the observed one, in different units No published corrections policy; the custodian's rule for a new edition unreachable; reach never counted as decisions

The table is the chapter's answer to the brief's first clause. Read down the trust column, the only measurements that would survive Chapter 2's standards are the producer surveys and the central bank's experiments; read down provenance, the sectors converge on the same short list; read down change over time, the exact rules cluster in public health and finance and the warnings cluster in place; read down reach, nobody counts decisions without asking, and the one that asked printed its 5 per cent response rate. (Reading.)

9 · What is borrowed, as method

Each item below is a mechanism that passes the borrowing test — rule printed, reason stated, evidence or cost known — stated with its terms. Beyond the seven truths, none is a decision; section 12 says whose the decisions are, and the precedent record in section 11 is where each would be written if adopted.

From public health. A documentation page per metric with fixed headings (definition, rationale, methodology, caveats; add source and frequency, which the UKHSA template lacks and the Fingertips record has); cost: one page per metric, kept. A change log apart from the refresh, with a label vocabulary and issue/resolved pairs; reason, from the dashboard teams: disclose errors as they happen; cost: the discipline of keeping it. Event date rather than report date, a stated incompleteness window in the metric's page, the window marked on the chart with the direction of its bias, and the by-publication series kept and labelled as not a trend; condition: a series with late returns. A colour given as a judgement only for a significant difference from a named comparator, a neutral colour by default, a neutral ramp where there is no good direction (Fingertips' choices are amber and blue; the house's palette is its own), and the one-in-twenty sentence printed; condition: confidence intervals, or numerators and denominators from which to make them. An arrow only after five independent annual points, a stated test and a leave-one-out check, and otherwise no arrow and a neutral marker; condition: five annual points — which, for a new series, means no arrows until they exist, and a printed reason why. Two ledgers for error: a machine-readable errata file for the house's own, a dated prose list with reasons for its sources'; reason: a reader can tell whose mistake moved a figure; evidence: none on readers. A voluntary statement of which Code requirements the display meets and cannot; cost: a page. A retirement with notice, reason, archive and successor; reason: three endings documented it and one did not; cost: deciding the terms before launch.

From finance and risk. Vintages: every published data file kept and addressable by date; cost: storage and a naming rule. Revision and correction as two words, with corrections labelled as such; the typical revision's size printed once there are enough releases to compute it. A release calendar at least a quarter ahead, same-moment release, and a published list of anyone who sees a figure early; cost: discipline. A printed band rule on any uncertainty display, with the calibration history and exclusions, dated. The systemic-risk board's two sentences and a date — what the display is not, that no mechanical inference may be drawn, and the data cut-off on the face — which the other regulator displays read print in part. Status marks in square brackets — [p], [r], [f] — and not symbols. Uncertainty as a range beside a point, never a verbal hedge alone; evidence: n = 5,780 and two waves of over 3,000 and 4,000. A randomised reading test as the evaluation design, with comprehension, expectation and perception measured separately; evidence: two Bank studies.

From economic development and place. A per-indicator metadata record of the ONS's eleven items; a refresh target with the lag admitted as a limitation; intervals shown where the source publishes them and said to be absent where it does not. A fully specified similar-areas method (standardise, reduce, cluster with a chosen range, list the nearest by distance) with the snapshot caveat; condition: enough comparable areas and published code. A question-and-answer text for any ordering of places, each answer a "can" or a "cannot" with a worked example in numbers, including the not-half-as sentence and the not-a-time-series sentence with the reason. A base-year index with frozen standardisation and a printed count of indicators whose change could not be measured; condition: a stable indicator set, and a status notice when it stalls. A printed refusal to aggregate, with the reason. A direction-of-travel label with its rule printed where the label is — a significance test where intervals exist, and, where they do not, either no label or a declared judgement that is named as one — measured from a fixed baseline, with the two declared non-states, "to be confirmed" and "in development". An evidence scale with a declared floor for any "what difference did it make" claim, with counts at each level. The model sentence for non-significant change. A release calendar, because users asked for one.

From culture and charity. A pilot evaluated independently before roll-out, with N, n and response rate printed. A dotted line on the chart at a break, with a sentence saying whether estimates remain comparable. A data-processor statement saying who owns the data and who does not; reason: the dual role Selwood names. Contribution and risk stated as dimensions ("likely better than what likely would have occurred otherwise"; "the likelihood that impact will be different than expected"). A fixed 0–10 trust question, banded, repeated, with drivers as a ranked list. And a lesson rather than a mechanism: an instrument whose own pilot found its data "interesting" rather than "useful" and its benchmarking doubted was made a condition anyway, and the sector is still paying for it.

From the great public data projects. Provenance as required metadata fields with written rules, including a processing label that drives the on-chart credit; a stated update period, from which the displayed next-expected-update date appears to be derived (which the chapter infers; no such field is documented); a sunset note listing what continues and what stops; stable URLs across a source swap, so that a reader's bookmark survives; a fixed trust question set asked in waves of those with a view, with a caution when the method changes; inputs published beside outputs; comparability kept by admitting only data that meet the method, stated. And a caution rather than a mechanism: reach reported by survey will not match reach observed in analytics, and the two are in different units.

What the chapter would not carry over, and why: the fan chart itself (no forecast-error history); the heat map coloured against history (recolours the past); a ranked top-ten table (Chapter 12's identity line); a composite rank without an interval (Chapter 5); a mandatory platform; a single on-site trust percentage. (Reading.)

10 · The failures, read for the sectors

"It fails if it looks the same every month." The sectors answer this with the arrow and the revision, and both have rules: no arrow without the points and a test, no colour as a verdict without significance, and the revision's size printed so a reader knows how much a figure usually moves. What changes on the screen each month under those rules is the data, the date, the log and the revisions to earlier figures — which is what a reader of an official series sees — and not an arrow or a colour that the data cannot yet support; a display that cannot yet draw an arrow says so and says when it can. The Health Index is the sector's warning: a display built to show change that stopped, with no notice found.

"It fails if it's just a fancy spreadsheet with some charts that tell you lots of big numbers, but not what actually happens." Ivanković's panel put "link time trends to policy decisions" among the seven features of an actionable dashboard and found purpose and audience both stated by one dashboard in eight; the GSS asks for "the direction of change, its absolute size and its relative size over time" in words; the OECD prints the reason it will not aggregate. The sectors' answer to "what actually happens" is a written sentence about the change, with the rule that licensed it printed beside it.

"It fails if a viewer reads it and asks 'what am I looking at'." The five-heading metric page and the "Simple Name" and "Simple Definition" fields beside the technical ones are the sectors' answer; so is the compliance page that says what the display is not.

"For nightlife, it fails if they do not recognise their place within the front-end interface." Chapter 12's, and this chapter adds only one part of the answer: once a place is found, the sectors have two documented ways of showing it beside places like it without ranking them — the ONS's specified similar-areas method and the OECD's nearest regions — and the second's rule that peers come from other countries is a catch for a local display, noted in section 5.

"It fails if people don't use it." Reach is counted in units that do not convert; two evaluations asked their readers directly, one of a public dashboard (76.4 per cent said it influenced their planning, among those still using it a year on) and one of an internal one (49 per cent said the data informed their decisions, of a 5 per cent response). The house can ask the same question and should expect an answer of the same shape.

"It fails if it breaks or isn't reliable." The service record (Chapter 8) now has the sectors' case law: a release calendar with Confirmed/Provisional; a fixed release time; a log where surprises are announced; two ledgers for error; a retirement plan, which the statistics regulator now lists among the minimum for an official dashboard and asks to be in place "from the start".

"It fails if people don't trust it." Trust is measured for producers and almost never for displays; where it is measured for a display the percentage is self-selected and the randomised test found no average effect. The sectors' lesson is to measure it the way the producers do — a fixed question, in waves, of those with a view — and to stop reporting on-site percentages as trust. And the gap between trust in the statistics office and agreement that government presents its figures honestly says where the public's doubt sits: with the presenter rather than the producer, which is the doubt the records beneath the dashboard exist to answer.

"It fails if it's an aggregation of 'the biggest'." Three place instruments have written a refusal of the single number or the single rank: "we do not make a single statement about the overall well-being in a region"; "No single summary measure is the 'best' measure"; ten unequal groups "based on similarity and meaningful gaps in the data" where ranks used to be.

11 · What holds true regardless

Seven things this chapter can state for any public dashboard, each with its kind and its grounds.

1. Trust in a display is almost never measured, and where format was tested it moved comprehension more than trust. In the literature read, trust is measured in series for producers, by a fixed question in waves, of those with a view; the central bank's layered report moved comprehension in two experiments and moved trust only a little, for one wording, in one; the one randomised test of a dashboard found no average effect on trust in government and a split by prior trust (secondary); the most-used dashboard's trust figure is a self-selected percentage with no n. So the house measures trust the way the producers measure theirs — a fixed question, repeated, of those with a view, with the base stated — or does not claim to have measured it, and never reports an on-site percentage as trust. Evidence; Fixed (requirement). Grounds: PCOS 2021 and 2023; the Charity Commission's tracker; Haldane & McMahon 2018; Bholat et al. 2018; Crepaz & Arikan 2021 (secondary); the UKHSA blog's 73.4 and 90.3 per cent.

2. Provenance is a record per metric and a dated log apart from the refresh, with the house's own errors kept separately from its sources' revisions. The record carries at least definition, rationale, method, caveats, source, frequency and date, and, where the metric has them, its numerator, its denominator and its polarity; the log labels its entries (new metric, change to metric, data issue, resolved, and so on) and pairs issue with resolved; a revision is a scheduled change and a correction is labelled as a correction. Practice; Standard (regulator); Fixed (requirement). Grounds: the UKHSA metric page and log; the Fingertips 32-field record; the JHU README; the ONS revisions policy; the ELS metadata list; OWID's field rules; OSR's minimum list.

3. No arrow without a printed rule, no colour given as a judgement without significance, and the one-in-twenty sentence beside any table coloured by significance. The rule for an arrow names its independent points, its test and its robustness check; where the data cannot meet it the display shows no arrow and says why; the rule is printed where the arrow is, dated, and kept when pages move; the sentence beside a coloured table says that about one coloured cell in twenty will be coloured by chance. Colour that encodes a value on a map or a scale is Chapter 3's matter, not this rule's. Standard (official statistics); Fixed (requirement). Grounds: Fingertips' RAG and trend-marker guidance; the OECD's ±5 per cent sentence; Wales's significance-or-expert rule; Scotland's lost thresholds; the GSS's model sentence; and, for the choice of axis beneath any arrow, Padilla et al. 2022 on the cumulative axis.

4. A series whose records arrive after the event is drawn by the event's date, with the incomplete recent period marked and the direction of its bias stated; and every published version of a figure is kept, dated, so that its later movement can be seen and, once there are enough releases, its typical size printed. Practice; Evidence; Fixed (requirement). Grounds: PHE 2020 and UKHSA's documentation and log; ALFRED; Croushore & Stark 2001; the ONS's 0.08 and 0.27 percentage points; the Fed heat map's cost.

5. Uncertainty is shown as a range beside a point; a verbal hedge alone did little for understanding and was the form in which any loss of trust appeared. Evidence; Fixed (requirement). Grounds: van der Bles et al. 2020 (n = 5,780; "mostly for verbal uncertainty communication"); Galvão & Mitchell 2021 (two waves; "does not reduce its trust in the statistical office"; the textual qualifier "tends to have little effect", read once); OSR 2022 on dashboards as the weak point.

6. A rank implies a distance that the data do not measure, and the place instruments read say so in print or refuse to make one. Any ordering of places ships with a question-and-answer text saying what it can and cannot be used to say — that a lower rank is not "half as" anything, and that editions are snapshots rather than a time series — with the reason; where a composite is made its rank carries an interval; where it is not, the refusal and its reason are printed. Standard (official statistics); Fixed (requirement) (the house's; Chapters 5 and 12 hold it). Grounds: the Indices of Deprivation 2025 FAQ and research report; the OECD user guide; County Health Rankings 2024; Arndt 2015; the JRC audit; Cox 2008 (†).

7. Public data projects end or change hands — four of the five read here have — and the plan for it is written before launch. Notice with a date; a reason; a frozen archive under a named licence; stable URLs; a named successor or a stated "none"; a gap analysis; and, when a source dies, the whole series replaced from the new source with the last old-source version archived, rather than two sources joined in one line. Practice; Standard (regulator); Fixed (sequence). Grounds: JHU 2023; OWID 2023 and 2024; UKHSA 2023; the COVID Tracking Project 2021; OSR's retirement clause; the Audience Agency 2026 as the negative case.

Three things the chapter will not state as truths. That any sector's display is a model for the Vibe Map (each is read for mechanisms, under conditions the studio does not share). That reach can be measured without asking (every count read is a server event or a self-report, and the two evaluations that asked had a 5 per cent response and a sample of survivors). And that the culture sector's own instruments are the house's standard (the pilot evaluation found the data "interesting" rather than "useful", the separate platform's requirement was suspended, and the custodian failed).

Beneath the dashboard: the precedent record

Each earlier chapter left a record beneath the display; this one leaves the twelfth, and like the boundary log it grows by one entry each time something is adopted. The precedent record holds, for every mechanism the build considers borrowing from another sector — adopted, adapted or declined — where it came from and on what terms, so that a reviewer can tell a borrowed rule from a habit and a habit from a bet, in section 1's senses. It is the borrowing test of section 1 written down. Nine lines per entry.

Line What it holds Why
Mechanism What is borrowed, in one sentence, and the record it feeds (recipe card, service record, comparison record, face sheet, boundary log, …) A borrowed rule lives in the record it serves, not in this one
Source The project or body, the document, its version and date, and the date it was read Rules change under the same name (the fan chart's bands; the Toolkit's status)
Rule as printed The threshold, interval, colour, cadence or wording, quoted, from one named document A paraphrased rule drifts (the "twice as deprived" this chapter expected and did not find)
Reason given The source's own stated reason The reason decides whether the rule transfers
Evidence What was measured about it, by whom, on whom, with n; or "none found" With a reason but no evidence or named cost, the entry is a bet, and says so
Condition or cost What the mechanism needs (intervals; five annual points; a stable indicator set; storage), and what the display does while the need is unmet A rule adopted without its condition fails silently
What the house changes Any departure from the printed rule, and why The departure is the house's, and is owned
Status Adopted; adapted; declined, with the reason; or awaiting a condition The record is a decision list
Review When the source document is to be re-read for change, and who owns the entry Sources retire (Scotland's pages; Fingertips itself)

A filled example, invented, for method only. Mechanism: the marked incomplete-tail band for a counted series with late returns, feeding the face sheet (the band and its sentence) and the recipe card (how the window is set). Source: UKHSA data dashboard, change-log entry "Updated measles chart", 8 August 2024, read 6 October 2026 (the cases metric's documentation page, last updated 12 February 2025, states the same device's window in words for a different metric). Rule as printed: "A blue shaded section now shows the reporting delay, affecting the last 4 weeks of data collected"; "The figures shown in this period are likely to underestimate the number of cases". Reason given: on the cases page, for its five-day window, "as it takes time to get test results and record them on relevant lab systems". Evidence: none found on readers — so the entry is a bet, with its cost named below. Condition or cost: a series whose records arrive after the event, with a lag the house has measured; while the lag is unmeasured the display shows the recent period with a sentence and no band; the window is restated when the lag changes. What the house changes: the window's length, set from the house's own lag data (reason: the source's window is its data's); the colour, from the design system (reason: the house's palette); the sentence, in the house's register (reason: the house's voice). Status: awaiting a condition — the lag distribution of the house's own series. Review: the source entry re-read in twelve months, since the dashboard logs changes to the device; owner, the data lead. The example decides nothing about the Vibe Map's data; it shows what an entry looks like when the rule is borrowed and the condition is not yet met.

12 · Where the choice is yours

Which mechanisms to adopt. Section 9 is an offer with terms rather than a list of requirements; the seven truths name the few that hold regardless. Everything else — which metadata fields beyond the minimum; whether to publish a compliance-style statement; whether to run a trust question at all, and in whose waves; which evidence scale to label contribution claims with — is the studio's, with the precedent record as the place the choice is written. The seven truths are the exceptions, and the rules table marks which procedures serve them.

Which conditions to wait for. Several mechanisms cannot be run on a new display: a trend arrow (five annual points); a printed revision size (enough releases); a similar-areas model (enough comparable areas); a base-year index (a stable indicator set). The choice is whether to show nothing and say why, or to show a weaker device and label it as weaker; the sectors do both and the GSS gives the sentence for the first. What the display shows in its first years, under these rules, is therefore the data, its dates, its log and its revisions, with the sentences about change written by hand — which is the state most official series are in for their first five years.

Whether to measure reach by asking. The one question that measures use has a 5 per cent response rate in the only evaluation that printed one. Whether to ask it, of whom, and how often, is the studio's; what the chapter holds is that server counts are not reach and are not reported as reach.

What the ending says. Truth 7 holds that the plan exists before launch and names its parts; the studio decides their content — what the Vibe Map's archive, licence, successor, notice period and gap analysis would be.

What to call the sector's instruments. The Toolkit, Illuminate, the segmentation tool and the national survey are the tools the studio will meet in funding conversations. How to use any of them is the studio's decision, with their documented state — live, suspended, orphaned, replaced with a dotted line — in front of it.

13 · A nightlife illustration — method only

The method only. Suppose the studio has a counted series about a place's activity in which records arrive after the event — a count that is complete only some weeks after the week it describes — and it is deciding how the most recent weeks are drawn. The sectors have answered the question, and the walk through the precedent record is the same for any such series.

First, the property. This is change over time in both senses: how the display shows that the quantity moved, and how the display's own recent figures will move as late records arrive.

Second, the mechanisms on offer. Public health's four-part answer (event date; a stated window; a marked band with the direction of the bias; the by-publication series kept and labelled). Finance's vintages (keep every weekly file, dated, so a reader can see what was known when) and its printed revision size (once there are enough weeks, state the mean and mean absolute revision between the first and the settled figure). Fingertips' arrow rule (no arrow on the recent weeks at all until the series has the independent points and the test to support one; a neutral marker meanwhile, with the reason). The GSS's model sentence for a movement inside natural variation.

Third, the entries. One per mechanism, nine lines each, as in section 11. For the band: the rule as printed, the reason, "evidence: none found on readers", the condition (the house's own lag distribution rather than the source's window), what the house changes (window, colour, sentence, each with its reason), status (awaiting the lag data), review (the source re-read in twelve months). For the vintages: the rule (every release kept and addressable by date), the reason (results change when figures do), the evidence (Croushore & Stark), the cost (storage and a naming rule), status (adopted from the first release, because it cannot be adopted later). For the arrow: the rule (five independent points, the test, leave-one-out), the condition (five independent annual points — or, for a weekly series, the house's own analogue, stated), status (awaiting the condition; no arrow meanwhile, with the sentence that says why). For the revision size: status (awaiting enough releases).

Fourth, the face sheet and the recipe card. The band's window and sentence go on the face (Chapter 11); the window's derivation, the vintage rule and the arrow rule go in the recipe card (Chapter 5); the retirement of the by-publication series, if it is ever retired, goes in the service record (Chapter 8) and the change log.

Fifth, the test. A reader shown the most recent weeks is asked what the data say about the latest week; the pass is that the reader says the latest figure is incomplete and will rise, in the direction the band's sentence states, and does not read a fall. The sectors did not run this test; the house can.

Nothing above names the series, the place, the window's length, the colour or the words. It is the procedure by which the studio decides them with the sectors' documented rules in front of it.

The rules

Rule Why Kind Tier Source
Measure trust, if at all, with a fixed question in waves, of those able to express a view; never report an on-site percentage as trust Producers' trust is measured this way; displays' almost never; the self-selected figure has no n Evidence; Reading Fixed (requirement) PCOS 2021, 2023; Charity Commission 2025, 2026; UKHSA blog 2021
Every metric has a documentation page with fixed headings — definition, rationale, method, caveats, source, frequency, date — and, where it has them, numerator, denominator and polarity A reader can check what a figure is before reading it; the regulator lists sources, status, limitations and update schedule as the minimum Practice; Standard (regulator) Fixed (requirement) UKHSA; Fingertips; ELS QMI; OSR 2025
Keep a dated, labelled change log apart from the refresh, with issue and resolved paired A reader can see what changed when and why; the dashboard teams' lesson, under trust, was to disclose errors as they happen Practice; Evidence of method Fixed (requirement) UKHSA "What's new"; Barbazza 2021
Keep the house's own errors in a machine-readable errata file and its sources' revisions in a dated list with reasons A reader can tell whose mistake moved a figure; no reader evidence, so a bet with a small cost Practice Fixed (requirement) JHU README [read once]
A revision is a scheduled change; a correction is labelled as a correction; print the typical revision's size once it can be computed The ONS's distinction and practice Standard (official statistics) Fixed (requirement) ONS revisions policy; GDP first estimate 2026
Keep every published data file as a dated vintage from the first release Results change when figures do; it cannot be started later Practice; Evidence Fixed (requirement) ALFRED; Croushore & Stark 2001
Draw a late-returns series by event date; state the incompleteness window on the metric's page; mark it on the chart with the direction of bias; keep the by-publication series labelled as not a trend The documented answer to the tail that looks like a fall Practice Fixed (requirement) PHE 2020; UKHSA documentation and log
Colour a value as a judgement only when it is significantly different from a named comparator; a neutral colour by default; a neutral ramp where there is no good direction; print the one-in-twenty sentence A colour is read as a verdict; the RAG guide's rule and its warning that one in twenty is chance Standard (official statistics) Fixed (requirement) PHE RAG guide 2017; OHID technical guidance
Draw an arrow only under a printed rule — independent points, a stated test, a robustness check — dated where the arrow is; otherwise no arrow, with the reason An arrow is a claim about a trend; rules that live elsewhere get lost Standard (official statistics); Practice Fixed (requirement) Fingertips trend markers; OECD user guide; Wales 2026; Scotland's redirects
Show uncertainty as a range beside a point; never a verbal hedge alone Ranges cost little or no trust; hedges did little for understanding Evidence Fixed (requirement) van der Bles 2020; Galvão & Mitchell 2021
Mark provisional, revised and forecast values in square brackets, not symbols Screen readers find symbols hard; the UK standard Standard (official statistics) Fixed (requirement) Analysis Function 2022; Eurostat flags
Any ordering of places ships with a question-and-answer text saying what it can and cannot be used to say, with worked examples and the reason comparability is lost between editions A rank implies a distance the data do not measure; the deprivation indices say so Standard (official statistics) Fixed (requirement) IoD 2025 FAQ and research report
Where no composite is made, print the refusal and its reason; where one is made, its rank carries an interval The OECD's sentence; the JRC's audit Standard (method); Evidence of method Fixed (requirement) OECD RWB user guide; JRC/GII 2024; Chapter 5
A base-year index freezes its standardisation, prints the count of indicators whose change could not be measured, and carries a status notice when it stalls The Health Index's method, and the notice it lacks Standard (official statistics); Reading Adaptable ONS Health Index 2023
Label every "what difference did it make" claim with its evidence level, with a declared minimum Before-and-after is description Standard (method) Adaptable What Works Growth SMS; Chapter 7
Print, on any indicator display, what it is not, that no mechanical inference may be drawn from it, and the data cut-off date The systemic-risk board prints all three; the other regulator displays read print the first Standard (regulator) Adaptable ESRB; FPC 2023
Publish a release calendar at least a quarter ahead; release at one moment; list anyone who sees a figure early The statutory test is trust Standard (law); Standard (method) Adaptable Pre-release Order 2008; IMF SDDS; ONS 2017
Count reach in the unit counted and name it, never as "readers"; measure use only by asking, and print the response rate The units do not convert; the two evaluations that asked had a 5 per cent response and a sample of survivors Reading; Evidence of method Fixed (requirement) JHU, UKHSA, OWID figures; Scottish Government 2024 [read once]; Ismail 2022
Write the retirement plan before launch: notice, reason, archive, licence, stable URLs, successor, gap analysis Four documented endings and one undocumented; the regulator lists the plan among the minimum and asks for archiving processes "from the start" Standard (regulator); Practice Fixed (sequence) OSR 2025; JHU; OWID; UKHSA; CTP; TAA
Evaluate a pilot independently before roll-out, with N, n and response rate printed, and read the result before making the thing piloted a condition The culture sector's own evidence: a pilot whose data were "interesting" rather than "useful" and whose benchmarking most doubted was made a condition anyway Evidence of method Adaptable Nordicity 2016; Selwood 2019; Hodge review (secondary)
Record every borrowed mechanism in the precedent record, nine lines, with its status, before it ships A rule with no stated reason is a habit; one with no evidence or named cost is a bet Nightlife Culture Fixed (sequence) This chapter
Which of section 9's mechanisms beyond the above to adopt, and when their conditions are met The offer, with terms — Adaptable Section 9

What proves a break works

A break here is a departure from one of this chapter's rules, or a borrowing from a sector on terms the chapter did not set. Take any rule the build uses for provenance, change over time, reach or an ending, and find its entry in the precedent record. If the entry's nine lines are filled — the rule as printed from a dated source, the reason, the evidence or "none found", the condition, the house's changes with their reasons, the status and the review — the rule was borrowed and the house owns its departures. If the entry is missing, the rule is unexamined; if its reason line is empty, it is a habit; if its evidence and cost lines are empty, it is a bet. Then the reader test from section 13 for any change-over-time device: a reader shown the most recent period says what the data say about it, and the pass is that the reader reports the direction the device states and does not read an artefact as a movement.

What this chapter could not settle

  • Trust in a display is not measured anywhere read; the one randomised test measured trust in government. The producers' method is adopted; the display's trust is a probe question.
  • Scotland's per-indicator arrow thresholds. Reported as unfindable; the lesson is the finding.
  • The Health Index's status. Not updated since June 2023; no notice.
  • The Audience Agency's data arrangements. No custodian named as of 6 October 2026.
  • The Culture and Heritage Capital multiplier warning the brief expected. Reported absent; Chapter 6's discipline stands on its own grounds.
  • Fingertips' amber rule is narrower than first read: amber when a leave-one-out trend runs the opposite way. Stated as such.

Checklist

  • Trust, if measured, by a fixed question in waves, of those able to express a view; no on-site percentage reported as trust
  • A documentation page per metric: definition, rationale, methodology, caveats, source, numerator, denominator, frequency, polarity, date
  • A dated, labelled change log apart from the refresh; issues opened and closed in public
  • Errata file for the house's errors; dated list with reasons for sources' revisions
  • Revision and correction as two words; corrections labelled; revision size printed when computable
  • Every published data file kept as a dated vintage from the first release
  • Late-returns series by event date; window stated; band on the chart with its bias; by-publication series labelled
  • Colour as a judgement only for significance against a named comparator; a neutral default; a neutral ramp where there is no good direction; the one-in-twenty sentence printed
  • Arrows only under a printed, dated rule; no arrow, with the reason, otherwise
  • Uncertainty as a range beside a point; no verbal hedge alone
  • [p], [r], [f] in square brackets
  • Any ordering of places has its "can and cannot say" text and its edition caveat
  • No composite, or a composite with a rank interval; the refusal printed with its reason
  • Contribution claims labelled with their evidence level, with a declared minimum
  • Any base-year index: standardisation frozen; unmeasurable change counted; a status notice when it stalls
  • The three regulator sentences on any indicator display
  • Release calendar; one-moment release; early readers listed
  • Reach counted in named units; use measured by asking, with the response rate
  • Retirement plan written and dated before launch
  • Any pilot evaluated independently before roll-out, with N, n and response rate, and read before the thing piloted is made a condition
  • Any instrument adopted from the sector recorded in the precedent record with its documented status
  • Every borrowed mechanism has a nine-line precedent-record entry

Words this chapter uses

  • The four properties are the brief's: trust, which the chapter treats as measured only where someone asked people a question about it, and distinguishes between trust in a producer (a statistics office, a charity) and trust in a display; provenance, the record of where a figure came from and what was done to it; change over time, which here means both how a display shows that a quantity moved and how a display's own figures move after first publication; and reach, who read it and whether it informed anything, which the chapter counts in the unit each source counts in and names the unit.
  • A mechanism is a documented, repeatable rule or practice — a banding rule, a change log, a release calendar, a vintage archive, an evaluation design — as distinct from a design or a look. A mechanism is borrowable when its rule is printed, its reason is stated, and its evidence or its cost is known; the chapter's borrowing test is in section 1.
  • A vintage is the version of a dataset as it stood on a given date; a revision is a scheduled change to a published figure and a correction an unplanned one, which is the ONS's distinction and the chapter keeps it.
  • A banding rule is the rule by which a value is coloured or labelled against a comparator; a direction-of-travel label is the arrow or word that says a series rose, fell or held.
  • A custodian is the body that keeps a dataset comparable, available and citable over time; a sunset is a dataset's or display's planned ending.
  • The precedent record holds, for every mechanism the build considers borrowing from another sector — adopted, adapted or declined — where it came from and on what terms.

16Breaking these rules well

Fixed in three senses; a short Fixed register the build enforces; one deviation log with nine lines; the twelve records as one.

Dashboard Design · Part 4: The boundary and the practice

In this chapter

Reading this chapter. This is one chapter of Dashboard Design, Nightlife Culture's research book on how evidence becomes a display a reader can trust, read and act on. The studio ("the house" in some chapters) is Nightlife Culture, a creative policy studio; the brief is its founder Carly Heath's commission for the book, and her eight ways a dashboard fails, the failure register, run through it. The Vibe Map, the studio's prototype for showing a place's nightlife culture, appears only as an illustration, never as a specification. "Version 1" is the book's archived first draft, whose positions this version re-tests against the sources. Every rule carries a kind (where it comes from: Standard, Evidence, Reading, Practice or Nightlife Culture) and a tier (how firm it is: Fixed, Adaptable or Decorative); Chapter 0 explains both, and the three senses of Fixed: a requirement that can be checked, a sequence whose order is the hard line, and a statement of the record. A dagger (†) marks a source read at the authors' abstract or summary only; "secondary" a quotation reached through a named reproduction; "(read once)" a quotation returned on a single reading and not confirmed by a second. Chapter 0 holds the glossary of the words the chapters share; each chapter lists its own coinages before its sources.

The question

When a rule in this book is to be broken, how is it done well — which rules have a right answer and which a defensible range, and does the book's own register keep the two apart; what separates an earned deviation from an expedient one, in this book and in the regimes other fields have built for letting a rule be broken on the record; what record is kept, with which lines, written when and read by whom, and are the book's three logs one; what test is run first, and of what form; what does the book's own assembly show about its rules, its records, its tests, its gaps and its open quarrels with the house's design documents; and what does the build inherit?

The 60-second version

The tier test holds, its borrowed sentences are real, and the book has not been applying it to itself. The Decision Book's split — Fixed is "Uncertainty implies that there is something to be certain about", Adaptable is ambiguity, "With ambiguity there's no singular, correct answer" — is verified at source, as is "fear enlists its good friends reason and comfort"; the third borrowed line is a question at source, "How do you close the gap between I wonder and I know?", and the house dates the second book 2021 where the publisher says 2022. Other fields draw the same three lines: the IETF's MUST, SHOULD and MAY, with the warning that imperatives "must be used with care and sparingly"; the road-design manual's "must" (cannot be varied), "shall" (varied only by approved departure), "should" (varied with recorded justification) and "may"; the C coding standard's mandatory, required (violable only with a formal deviation) and advisory. Against those, this book's own tables carry 486 rules of which 433 (89 per cent) say Fixed, 212 of them with no sense given — against 74 per cent Fixed in the Decision Book's register, and two chapters with no Adaptable rule at all. Chapter 0 named two senses of Fixed ("a statement of the record"; "sequence") that the tables use twice and never; the tables use two others ("as a stance"; "as a procedure") that Chapter 0 does not define. Eleven rules carry different tiers in different chapters. Sections 7 and 8 fix this — the reconciliations in 7, the register's form in 8 — and section 3 says why the count matters: a rule set in which nearly everything is Fixed is the condition under which, elsewhere, rules stop being read.

Where rules may be broken on the record, the record is mostly bad. The corporate-governance regime that invented "comply or explain" asked for context, rationale, mitigation and a time limit in 2012, said then that "a large majority" explained fully, and in 2021 scored its own regime: "Our sample identified 74 cases of non-compliance with the Code, but we found only four explanations that we considered high quality and offered an insight into the companies' approach to good governance." The accessibility regulations let a public body exempt itself after a mandatory assessment; the monitoring body's first-listed common issue is that "organisations claim disproportionate burden without having carried out an assessment beforehand", and "many accessibility statements are now out-of-date". Mandatory reason fields fill with "a space or random characters" (Wright et al., citing prior studies). Preregistered studies deviated in 25 of 27 cases and one disclosed everything. Most architecture decision records — 63 per cent of 5,800 — were "opened directly with a status of "accepted"", written after the fact. What the regimes agree on is the shape of a good entry — a reason with a shape, a reader other than the author, a time limit or review date, and publication by default — and what the evidence adds is when a written reason helps at all: before the decision, for a reader whose views are unknown (Tetlock, Skitka & Boettger); after commitment it becomes "defensive bolstering", and in two experiments requiring a justification changed neither accuracy nor strategy and only lowered confidence.

A rule that fires too often is overridden by reflex. Drug-safety alerts "are overridden by clinicians in 49% to 96% of cases"; a pooled rate for interaction alerts is "90% (CI95% 85–95%)"; and the dose–response is measured: "Likelihood of reminder acceptance dropped by 30% for each additional reminder received per encounter" (112 clinicians; 1.27 million advisories). About half of overrides were appropriate — "from 12% for renal recommendations to 92% for patient allergies" — so a high override rate indicts the rule as often as the person. Tiering by consequence works: where only the severest alerts interrupted, compliance was "29% vs. 10%" and "100% of the most severe alerts were accepted", though the hundred per cent was a hard stop by design and the free-choice evidence for tiering is the middle tier's 29 against 10 per cent. Checklists cut deaths from 1.5 to 0.8 per cent where they were used and did nothing where they were mandated and self-reported at 98 per cent compliance; observed, "two-thirds of the items were checked" and teams "failed to pause or focus on the checks in more than 70% of cases". The lesson for a book with 433 Fixed rules is arithmetic: the Fixed register is short and its breaches stop the build; the long list is Adaptable and its departures are logged.

The book's machinery, assembled. Twelve records with 129 lines, four printed as lists and eight as tables, named six different ways; the test the chapters say they inherit — the removal test — leads in two chapters, while 27 of the 55 named tests are reader tests; 42 groups of rules stated twice in different words; 207 gaps, of which 48 are things the field has not studied and 38 are gaps in the house's own systems; 37 open items in the conflict logs, five of them direct conflicts the house has not resolved; seven chapters asking the Decision Book for a chapter it does not have; and Chapter 0, then last revised after Chapter 2, with eleven conventions the later chapters quietly changed. The chapter resolves what it can (the eleven tier conflicts; the rules that pull against each other; the three logs, which become one log with a type; the twelve records, of which ten become one document written once per concept with two views, after Eurostat's "each concept is only reported upon once", and two join the log), re-states what it cannot as the studio's choices, and writes the fixes Chapter 0 needed.

What the build inherits. The rule register, with every rule's tier — Fixed in one of three senses — its source, its chapter and the test that proves a break; a Fixed list of 280 rules (245 requirements, 35 sequences), with 56 house defaults, 34 Adaptable and 7 Decorative beside it, whose shortness the build's first year tests; one deviation log with the nine lines the regimes and the evidence support — rule and tier, trigger, alternative, what it buys and costs, the test and its result, who decided and who checked, date, review date, status — written before the departure ships and reviewed at a date; the three build-time checks version 1 specified (crop; recipe; state-honesty), re-based on version 2's rules and extended by one (the removal check); and the record of the dashboard, one document, with ten sections — the twelve records less the two that are logs — and its maintenance and retirement built in. The pass test for the chapter is the Decision Book's own: take any decision being argued about, name its tier from the register, and if the tier cannot be found the register has failed, not the argument.

1 · What this chapter is, and what it is not

The brief's words for the chapter are "Tiers, deviation, the override log, the assembled removal tests, the gap register, the rule register for the build." Version 1's closing chapter did five of those six by transfer: it took the Decision Book's tier test, deviation taxonomy and override log "whole, and is not re-derived", assembled thirteen chapters' tests into one table, seeded a register of "circa 150 Fixed-tier rules", summarised the gaps, and listed nine places where the prototype "would be first". This chapter tests each instead of transferring it. It tests the tier test against the fields that have built their own and against the book's own tables; it tests the deviation taxonomy, which turns out never to have been written down; it tests the override log against what is known about records of decisions; and it assembles from version 2's fifteen chapters rather than version 1's thirteen, by script, with counts.

What the chapter is. An audit of the book by the book's own standard, and the handover to the build. Its evidence has two sources: the compilation of the chapters and the house documents, which is the chapter's evidence about the book; and the research into other fields' deviation regimes, decision records and override behaviour, which is the chapter's evidence about whether the machinery will work in practice. The second matters because the first shows a book that has been generous with the word Fixed, and other fields have measured what happens when a rule set is like that.

What the chapter is not. It is not a re-derivation of the Decision Book; where the Decision Book's rule stands it is quoted and kept. It is not the build's register itself, which is a file in the repository; section 8 specifies the file and gives its first rows, and the compilation holds every row the file will start from. It is not research into nightlife. And it does not make the creative decisions the earlier chapters left to the studio; it lists them, in section 11, in one place.

The failure register, for the last time. Every chapter has read Carly's eight sentences against its own subject; this one reads them against the machinery. "It fails if people don't trust it" and "It fails if it breaks or isn't reliable" are the two the machinery answers directly: a rule broken on the record, with a reason and a reader, is the difference between a dashboard whose makers can say why it is as it is and one whose makers cannot; and a Fixed register short enough to be enforced in the build is the difference between a check that runs and a checklist that is ticked. Section 9 reads the rest.

2 · What people believe about breaking rules, and what the evidence says

Belief: a rule is safer if it is Fixed. Where rules fire often and cannot be told apart, people stop reading them: drug-safety alerts are overridden in half to nineteen-twentieths of cases, and acceptance falls by a measured step with each extra rule fired in the same encounter. Where the severe rules are set apart from the rest, the severe ones are obeyed. A rule set in which nearly everything is Fixed is less safe than a short Fixed list, because the short list is the one that is read. Section 6. (Evidence.)

Belief: requiring a written reason makes the decision better. The evidence is narrower. Having to justify helps when the justification is owed before the decision, to a reader whose views are unknown — "preemptive self-criticism" — and hurts after commitment, when effort goes to "defensive bolstering"; in two experiments a justification requirement "neither changed how accurately people made a judgment, nor the judgment strategies" and "only decreased confidence"; mandatory reason fields become noise. A process record helps the next reader more than the writer: process accountability "promoted more effective knowledge sharing, improving accuracy among observers" (†). Section 5. (Evidence.)

Belief: "comply or explain" produces explanations. It produced, in the regulator's own 2021 sample, four good explanations in seventy-four departures, and "tick-box compliance" with "boilerplate language"; a quarter of UK deviations in a 2006 sample "were not properly justified"; "no provision in the UK for any statements by companies to be assessed by any regulatory body" (†). The regime works to the extent that someone reads the explanation, and its designers said so in 2012: "it is up to them to decide whether to accept or reject explanations." Section 4. (Evidence; Standard (regulator).)

Belief: a deviation record protects the project. It does when it is written before the departure and read afterwards. Where it is written after — 63 per cent of 5,800 architecture decision records were born "accepted" — it records a conclusion, not a decision; where nobody re-reads it, it decays — "36 percent of these waivers have not been reviewed in 10 years" (the Columbia board, secondary); "many accessibility statements are now out-of-date". Section 5. (Evidence; Practice.)

Belief: a checklist makes the work safe. A checklist made surgery safer where it was used as a team practice (deaths 1.5 to 0.8 per cent, eight hospitals) and not where it was mandated and self-reported (101 hospitals, no significant change); observed directly, a third of items went unchecked. "it is not the act of ticking off a checklist that reduces complications, but performance of the actions it calls for" (secondary). This book has fifteen checklists; section 6 says what that means. (Evidence.)

Belief: this book's rules are mostly Fixed because dashboards are mostly a matter of right answers. The Decision Book, which the book says it inherits, is 74 per cent Fixed; this book is 89 per cent, and 49 per cent of its Fixed rules give no sense of the word. Section 3 reads the difference as the book's and not the subject's. (Reading.)

Belief: the book's records are twelve documents. They are twelve sections of one document that has not yet been written as one, and the fields have precedents for both answers. Section 7. (Reading.)

Belief: the removal test is the book's test. It is the Decision Book's, and Chapter 14's; it leads in two of fifteen chapters. The book's commonest test is to put the display in front of the reader the rule protects and ask. Section 7. (Reading.)

3 · The tier test, tested

The counts in this section are of the chapters as they stood at second draft, 7 October 2026. The closing edit has since brought the chapters' tier words to the register's; the register (section 8) is the current statement.

What the house wrote, and where it came from

The Decision Book's tier test is a table and two sentences. The table: Fixed is "Uncertainty — there is a right answer", its test "Pass or fail, measurable", breaking it "Negligence"; Adaptable is "Ambiguity — no single correct answer", its test "Defensible or not, arguable", breaking it "The job"; Decorative is "Free", with no test, breaking it "Expected". The sentences: "Treating an Adaptable decision as Fixed is deference. Treating a Fixed decision as Adaptable is negligence." Its grounds are three borrowed lines from the Stanford design school's books, and this chapter went to the source for each. (Standard (design system).)

The first is verified and consecutive: "Uncertainty implies that there is something to be certain about. An absolute truth or fact exists. With ambiguity there's no singular, correct answer." — from Navigating Ambiguity (Andrea Small, Kelly Schmutte and the Stanford d.school; Ten Speed Press, 2022), read in the publisher's educators' guide, which reproduces the activity "from" the book; the sentence before it is "While ambiguity may contain uncertainty, they're different." The second is verified, and is the tail of a longer sentence: "When it comes to acting with courage within an established system, we often refrain because fear enlists its good friends reason and comfort." — from Drawing on Courage (Ashish Goel and the Stanford d.school; Ten Speed Press), whose publisher's page and copyright line say 2022 where the Decision Book says 2021. The third is a question at source: "How do you close the gap between I wonder and I know?" followed by "You make a prototype." — from This Is a Prototype (Scott Witthoft and the Stanford d.school; Ten Speed Press, 2022); the Decision Book prints it as an instruction. Two corrections for the house, then: a year, and a question mark. (Practice; Standard (method).)

The fields' own three lines

The house did not invent the three-tier shape, and each of the fields that drew it adds a condition the house's table lacks.

The internet standards' vocabulary (RFC 2119, 1997): "MUST" "mean that the definition is an absolute requirement of the specification"; "SHOULD" "mean that there may exist valid reasons in particular circumstances to ignore a particular item, but the full implications must be understood and carefully weighed before choosing a different course"; "MAY" "mean that an item is truly optional". And the instruction the house should pin above its register: "Imperatives of the type defined in this memo must be used with care and sparingly. In particular, they MUST only be used where it is actually required for interoperation or to limit behavior which has potential for causing harm". The 2017 clarification adds that the words carry their meanings "when, and only when, they appear in all capitals", and that "a lot of normative text does not use them and is still normative". A SHOULD names who decides a deviation (the implementer) and the test (implications understood and weighed), and requires no record. (Standard (method).)

The international standards' directives (ISO/IEC Directives Part 2, ninth edition) define a requirement as an expression "that conveys objectively verifiable criteria to be fulfilled and from which no deviation is permitted if conformance with the document is to be claimed", a recommendation as one "that conveys a suggested possible choice or course of action deemed to be particularly suitable without necessarily mentioning or excluding others", and a permission as one "that conveys consent or liberty (or opportunity) to do something"; and they require that "The user of the document shall be able to identify the requirements he/she is obliged to satisfy in order to claim conformance to a document." [read once]. There is no reasoned-deviation tier: a requirement admits none, a recommendation needs none. The W3C has two categories: "The main content of WCAG 2.2 is normative and defines requirements that impact conformance claims." and informative material "provides advisory information to help interpret the guidelines but does not create requirements that impact a conformance claim" (verified in the editors' source; check against the dated Recommendation). (Standard (method); Standard (W3C).)

Two engineering rule systems built the house's shape with the record attached. The road-design manual (National Highways, GG 101): "The verb 'must' indicates a statutory or legislative requirement. Note: Requirements with this verb form cannot be varied."; "The verb 'shall' indicates a requirement of the Overseeing Organisation. Note: Requirements with this verb form can be only be varied though the use of departures or in limited situations as relaxations." (as printed); a "should" names recommendations that "can be varied without recourse to the departures process, but require justification and a safety risk assessment where the recommendation is not followed"; a "may" can be varied "in accordance with internal review processes" [read once]; a departure is "Variation or waiving of a requirement carried out in accordance with the Overseeing Organisation's procedures" and must be approved "before the design is finalised"; and "Justifications to support all design decisions shall be recorded by the design organisation as part of the project record." [read once]. The C coding standard (MISRA Compliance 2020): "Mandatory Guidelines — Guidelines for which violation is never permitted;" "Required Guidelines — Guidelines which can only be violated when supported by a deviation defining a set of clear restrictions, requirements and precautions;" "Advisory Guidelines — Recommendations to be followed as far as is reasonably practical."; a deviation is "A violation which has been formally accepted and approved", recorded with the guideline, the circumstances, "The reason why the deviation is required", the background and the precautions; and two reasons are never acceptable — "Simply to satisfy the convenience of the developer" and "When a reasonable alternative coding strategy would make the need for a violation unnecessary" [read once]. (Standard (method).)

Read together, the fields give the house four things its table does not state: a top tier that cannot be varied at all (statute; a mandatory guideline), above the Fixed tier that can be varied by approved departure; a middle tier whose departures need a recorded justification but no approval; the person who approves, named as someone other than the designer; and a list of reasons that are never earned. The last is the beginning of the deviation taxonomy the Decision Book promised and never wrote (section 4). (Reading.)

Behind all of them is the safety literature's account of what a rule is.
