Hale and Borys's review contrasts "a top-down classical, rational approach in which rules are seen as static, comprehensive limits of freedom of choice, imposed on operators at the sharp end and violations are seen as negative behaviour to be suppressed" with "a bottom-up constructivist view of rules as dynamic, local, situated constructions of operators as experts, where competence is seen to a great extent as the ability to adapt rules to the diversity of reality", and their framework "places the monitoring and adaptation of rules central to its management process" and asks for "regular and explicit dialogue" with the people who follow the rules (†). The house's Fixed tier is the first model and its Adaptable tier is the second; what the review adds is that the second needs a process for keeping its rules alive, which is what the logs are for. (Evidence of method, [abstract or summary only].)

What the book's own tables show

The compilation read every rules table in Chapters 1 to 15 — Chapter 0 has none — and counted. 486 rules. 433 of them (89.1 per cent) carry Fixed in the tier cell: 405 Fixed only, 28 with a Fixed and an Adaptable part. 45 (9.3 per cent) are Adaptable only. 8 (1.6 per cent) are Decorative. The Decision Book's own register, which the book says it inherits, is 258 Fixed of 347 (74.4 per cent), 75 Adaptable (21.6 per cent) and 14 Decorative. By run of chapters: Chapters 1 to 5 have 21 Adaptable rules in 140 (15 per cent); Chapters 6 to 10 have 5 in 193 (2.6 per cent) — Chapters 7 and 10 have none; Chapters 11 to 15 have 19 in 153 (12.4 per cent). Chapter 8 noticed it of itself: "Fixed", "Fixed as a procedure" and "Fixed as a stance" are nearly equal in number, with almost nothing Adaptable. (Reading; the compilation.)

The tier cells use 53 distinct wordings. Of the 433 Fixed rows (a cell can carry two qualifiers, so the senses below sum past 433), 212 say exactly "Fixed" with no sense; 102 say "procedure" ("as a procedure" in Chapters 4 to 13, "(procedure)" in 14 and 15); 90 say "stance"; 2 say "sequence"; none says "statement of the record"; 31 carry another qualifier — "(adopted)", "(declared)", "(unit)", "as defaults", "as disclosure", "as the planning assumption". Chapter 0 named two refinements of Fixed in its legend — "Fixed as a statement of the record" and "Fixed as sequence" — and its own gap row asked that "Chapter 16's rule register should check every Fixed for which sense it carries". The tables used Chapter 0's senses twice and never, and used two senses Chapter 0 does not define, which the chapters defined in four different wordings in their own opening notes: Chapter 5's "a rule the studio adopts and will not reopen on a given display though its source is a reading or a practice"; Chapters 6 to 11's "a rule the studio adopts whose source is a reading or a practice"; Chapter 12's "the house has decided it and the chapter gives the grounds"; Chapters 13 to 15's the same without the last clause. (Reading; the compilation.)

Eleven rules carry different tiers in different chapters. Investigating an outlier before treating it as noise is Adaptable in Chapter 1 and Fixed in Chapter 4. Stating where a causal claim stands on the evidence ladder is Fixed in Chapters 2 and 7 and Adaptable in Chapter 15. Recognition checked with the people described before release is "Adaptable in method; Fixed as sequence" in Chapter 1, "Fixed as sequence" in 2, "Fixed as a stance" in 5 and 9, and "Fixed as a procedure" in 12. The house's headline length is "Fixed; the house limit Fixed as a stance" in Chapter 11 and Adaptable in Chapter 14, which re-tiered it on evidence and said so in its conflict log, while Chapter 11's row stands unmarked. The retirement plan is Fixed as a procedure in three chapters and then listed by Chapter 15 as a question for this one. And some rules pull against each other: Chapters 1 and 2 allow a ranking with intervals and Chapters 7, 10 and 12 forbid a league table of places, with 12 and 15 then regulating the ordering they forbid; Chapters 1, 2 and 15 ask for uncertainty as a numeric range and Chapter 3 says "Never a bare interval"; Chapters 1, 10 and 11 have the dashboard count its own use and Chapter 15 says use is measured "only by asking"; Chapters 4 to 7 put detail "one tap" away and Chapters 11, 13 and 14 "one step". Each is reconciled in section 7. (Reading; the compilation.)

What the count means

Three readings are possible and the chapter takes the third. The first is that dashboards are a subject of right answers, so the book's 89 per cent is the subject's; the Decision Book's 74 per cent, on the same kind of material, says otherwise. The second is that the chapters' "Fixed as a stance" is a third tier in disguise — the house's position, held with reasons, which the Decision Book would call Adaptable with a strong default — and that re-labelling 90 rows would bring the book to about 70 per cent, near the Decision Book; that is part of the answer. The third is that the book has been using Fixed to mean "important", which is the drift Chapter 0's gap row foresaw, and that the cost is the one section 6 measures in other fields: a rule set in which nearly everything carries the strongest word is a rule set in which the word is read as noise. The road-design manual's and the coding standard's top tiers are short; RFC 2119's own instruction is "sparingly"; the clinical evidence is that acceptance falls with every extra rule that fires. (Reading.)

So the register in section 8 does three things to the tiers. It gives Fixed one of three senses, each with its test: Fixed as a requirement — a right answer that can be checked, whose breach is negligence, which the build enforces as a check that fails (contrast; disclosure thresholds; the floor; expressiveness in Chapter 14's sense); Fixed as a sequence — an order of operations that is the hard line while each step's form is open (construct before proxy; recognition before release); and Fixed as a statement of the record — a finding the book is confident of, from which a design rule may or may not follow, and which is not a rule at all but a truth, listed separately. Everything the chapters called "Fixed as a stance" becomes Adaptable (house default) — the house's position, held with its grounds, which a later display may leave with a logged reason — unless the chapter's own grounds show it to be a requirement, in which case it is one. And "Fixed as a procedure" becomes either a requirement (the procedure is the check) or a sequence, by its wording. The result, in the register as built, is a Fixed list of 280 rules, 245 requirements the build can test and 35 sequences, and an Adaptable list of 90, 56 of them house defaults and 34 Adaptable, with 7 Decorative, each with their grounds: 74 per cent Fixed, the Decision Book's own share, because most of the 212 unmarked rows and the 102 procedures proved to be presences, thresholds, lines of a record or prohibitions a build can check, so the first reading above is nearer the truth than the chapter allowed. The Fixed list is the shape the fields recommend; whether 280 is short enough to be read is what truth 2 tests in the build's first year. (Nightlife Culture; Reading.)

The W3C's fourth category, which Chapter 14 found the tiers lack — the "specific sensory experience" that may not be ignored and need not carry data — is not a tier of rule but a tier of element, and belongs in the boundary log's "tier claimed" line, where Chapter 14 put it. The register does not add it as a fourth tier of rule; it notes, under the Decorative tier, that an expressive element is Decorative only if it can be ignored, and otherwise is a sensory experience owing identification. (Reading.)

4 · The kinds of deviation, and the regimes that let a rule be broken on the record

A taxonomy the house named and never wrote

The Decision Book's chapter on breaking rules promises in its subtitle "the taxonomy of deviation" and delivers it as one checklist line, printed twice: "Deviation classified honestly: ignorant, lazy, expedient or earned". No table, definition or paragraph sets the four out, in that file or in any of the fifteen beside it; "expedient" and "earned" appear as a pair in one rule's reason ("Turns an expedient decision into an earned one") and "expedient" once more in the chapter's list of failures — "The undocumented expedient decision. Indistinguishable from negligence at the next audit, including to you." — and "ignorant" and "lazy" appear nowhere else. Version 1 of this book inherited the line as an axiom and added a gloss of its own, "only the record separates expedient from earned", which is close to the Decision Book's reason and is not quite what the fields say. This book's Chapters 0 to 15 never use the four words as a taxonomy. So the first thing this section does is write the definitions the house owes itself, from the regimes that have had to draw the same lines, and the second is to say what separates the third class from the fourth. (Practice; Reading.)

Ignorant. The rule was not known, or could not be found, when the decision was made. The regimes treat this as a failure of the register rather than of the person: the Decision Book's own rule is "Give every rule in the system its tier", with the reason that "An untiered rule cannot be argued about productively"; the road-design manual requires that justifications "shall be recorded by the design organisation as part of the project record" [read once] precisely so that a later designer can find them; and the auditors' finding about records is that they survive but cannot be found — "Most of the data has been preserved … but it is poorly organised and indexed, and is mixed in with ephemera and duplicate copies" (Sir Alex Allan's review of government digital records, 2015). In the preregistration audit, eleven of thirty-eight plans could not be assessed at all because the plan was ambiguous, in several versions, not frozen or too thin — the record failed before any deviation could be judged (this book's reading of the split; the exclusion counts are the paper's). An ignorant deviation is therefore logged against the register, not the designer: the entry says which rule was missed and why it was not findable, and the fix is to the register's index. This book's own count of eleven rules carrying different tiers in different chapters is a list of places where an ignorant deviation was waiting to happen. (Standard (design system); Standard (method); Evidence; Reading.)

Lazy. The rule was known and the departure was taken to save the person effort, with no reason that would survive being written down. Two regimes name this class in so many words. The coding standard: "Deviations must not be permitted: Simply to satisfy the convenience of the developer" [read once]. The accessibility regulations' guidance: "You cannot take things like lack of time or knowledge into account in your assessment - or argue that making things accessible is a disproportionate burden because you've not given it priority."; and the monitoring body, in its report: "Lack of time or knowledge does not constitute a disproportionate burden". What a lazy deviation looks like in a log is also measured: "when mandatory free-text reasons are required, users often enter a space or random characters to move past the screen" (Wright et al. 2019, citing prior studies). A lazy deviation is a breach rather than a departure to be logged, and the entry — if there is one — is a space. (Standard (method); Standard (regulator); Evidence.)

Expedient. The rule was known, the departure was taken for a reason — speed, a deadline, a tool's default, an unmeasured lag — and the reason was real but either a reasonable alternative existed or the departure was not recorded at the time. The coding standard's second forbidden ground names the first half: a deviation is not permitted "When a reasonable alternative coding strategy would make the need for a violation unnecessary" [read once]. The Decision Book names the second: "The undocumented expedient decision. Indistinguishable from negligence at the next audit, including to you." The National Audit Office's investigation of pandemic procurement is the public case: rules were relaxed for speed, and what went missing was the record of why — "we also found specific examples where there is insufficient documentation on key decisions, or how risks such as perceived or actual conflicts of interest have been identified or managed", with the head of the office's sentence that "it remains essential that decisions are properly documented and made transparent if government is to maintain public trust". The government's own architecture-decision standard gives the useful other side: a recorded decision lets a later team understand "whether a particular choice was made for the sake of expediency and can therefore be changed with little impact". An expedient deviation logged at the time, with its reason and the alternative it passed over, is the cheapest kind of decision to reverse; unlogged, it is the Decision Book's negligence. (Standard (method); Standard (design system); Practice; Reading.)

Earned. The rule was known; the departure was taken before it shipped; the reason was specific to the case and not generic; the alternative was named and declined for a reason; what the departure buys was stated and its cost named; a test was run and its result kept; someone other than the author read the entry; and the entry carries a date by which it is re-read. That list is the intersection of what the regimes below ask for. The preregistration literature gives the sharpest criterion for the reason: "One justifiable reason to deviate from a preregistered statistical analysis plan is to increase the validity of the scientific claim – even if doing so comes at the expense of the severity of the test." (Lakens 2024; read once in full, the first clause verified) — a reason that names what is bought and what is paid. The regulator of the comply-or-explain regime gives the reason's shape: "Set the context and background." "Give a convincing rationale for the approach being taken." "Consider any risks and describe any mitigating actions." "Set out when the company intends to comply (timescales)." [read once], with the 2012 paper's demand that explanations "should be specific to the company's position, not generic or off-the-shelf" [read once]. The financial regulator gives the two-limb test for granting a departure: compliance "would be unduly burdensome or would not achieve the purpose for which the rules were made" and the departure "would not adversely affect the advancement of any of the regulator's objectives" (FSMA 2000 s.138A(4), as substituted; verified at legislation.gov.uk, 6 October 2026). The Decision Book's own fourth rule gives the purchase list: "Name what the break buys: attention, retention, comprehension, context, register or fit", because "An unnamed break is a mistake made confidently". (Standard (method); Standard (regulator); Standard (law); Standard (design system); Reading.)

What separates expedient from earned. Not the record alone. Sixty-three per cent of 5,800 architecture decision records were born accepted — "opened directly with a status of "accepted" or equivalent", "thereby bypassing the deliberative context that ADRs are intended to capture" — a record exists for every one of them, written after the fact, and it records a conclusion, not a decision. Four things separate the classes, and the record is the place they are visible: the timing (written before the departure ships, not after — the quality vocabulary keeps a word for each, a deviation permit "prior to its realization" [read once] and a concession for a nonconforming product already made); the specificity of the reason (the regulator's 2021 finding is what a generic reason looks like at scale); the test (a result, not a tick); and the reader (someone other than the author, whose views the author could not predict — section 5 says why that condition matters). Version 1's one-line gloss, "only the record separates expedient from earned", should read: the record, written before, specific, tested and read, is what separates them; a record written after records an expedient decision for what it is, which is better than not recording it and is not the same as earning it. (Evidence; Standard (method); Reading.)

Twelve regimes that let a rule be broken on the record

The chapter read twelve regimes in which a rule may be departed from without the departure being a breach, chosen because each publishes its mechanism and several have measured its use. They are set out briefly, in the regime's own words, with the mechanism in one line each — who decides, who checks, what is written, whether it expires, whether it is published — and then compared.

Comply or explain (UK corporate governance). The 2024 Code: "The Code does not set out a rigid set of rules; instead, it offers flexibility through 'comply or explain' reporting against the Provisions." [read once]; "Explanations should set out the background, provide a clear rationale for the action the company is taking and explain the impact that the action has had."; "Where a departure from a Provision is intended to be limited in time, the explanation should indicate when the company expects to conform to the Provision."; and "Explanations should be a positive opportunity to communicate, not an onerous obligation." The regulator's 2012 paper, which set the template, proposed that an explanation "should set the context and historical background, should give a convincing rationale for the action it was taking, and describe mitigating action to address any additional risk and to maintain conformity with the relevant principle", and "should indicate whether the deviation from the Code's provisions was limited in time and when the company intended to return to conformity" [two passes]; and it placed the reader: "The FRC believes strongly that explanations are directed to shareholders and it is up to them to decide whether to accept or reject explanations." The regulator's news page in 2012 said "a large majority of companies who do not comply with one or more provisions of the Code provide a full explanation of their reasons." Nine years later, the regulator scored a random sample of 100 companies: "Our sample identified 74 cases of non-compliance with the Code, but we found only four explanations that we considered high quality and offered an insight into the companies' approach to good governance."; "The majority of explanations were inadequate, and in one instance, not given at all."; "We found that 'tick-box compliance' continues to be preferred over high quality reporting of good governance practice." [read once] "Such a formulaic approach leads to boilerplate language, and ineffective reporting that lacks substance and information about governance outcomes."; and some companies "that claimed full compliance with the Code, on further investigation had not acknowledged departure from one or more Provisions" [read once]. Earlier academic counts agree: in 2006 statements, "almost 25% of UK deviations, and almost 50% of German deviations were not properly justified" (Seidl, Sanderson & Roberts, working paper; the published article, abstract only, reports "some 715 records of deviation" from 257 companies [abstract or summary only]); across 245 UK companies in 1998–2004, "Almost one in five instances of non-compliances (on average 17%) are not explained" and "the frequency of good explanations is roughly about 20%" (Arcot, Bruno & Faure-Grimaud, discussion paper; read once for the second); and a legal review notes "There is no provision in the UK for any statements by companies to be assessed by any regulatory body." (Keay 2014 [abstract or summary only]). The regulator's 2025 review counts companies in its 100 disclosing any departure falling from 73 in 2022 to 25 in 2025 [three passes] and gives no proportion judged adequate [two passes]; set beside the 2021 finding of undisclosed departures, a falling count of declared deviations is ambiguous. Mechanism: the board decides; shareholders are the checker and mostly do not check; the record is the annual report, with four elements and a time limit; published. (Standard (regulator); Evidence; Evidence [abstract or summary only].)

Disproportionate burden (public-sector accessibility). The regulation: "Regulation 6 does not require a public sector body to comply with the accessibility requirement if doing so would impose a disproportionate burden on the public sector body." [read once]; "A public sector body must perform an assessment of the extent to which compliance with the accessibility requirement imposes a disproportionate burden."; the assessment must weigh "the size, resources and nature of the public sector body" and "the estimated costs and benefits for the public sector body in relation to the estimated benefits for persons with disabilities, taking into account the frequency and duration of use of the specific website or mobile application"; and if the body so determines it "must— (a) explain in its accessibility statement the parts of the accessibility requirement that could not be complied with" (SI 2018/952, reg. 7; verified 6 October 2026; the regulation shows no outstanding effects). Regulation 8 requires the statement and that the body "keep that statement under regular review" [read once]. The guidance adds the review condition — "If your circumstances change, you'll need to review whether something's still a disproportionate burden." — and the model statement's wording for it: "We will make another assessment when the supplier contract is up for renewal, likely to be in [rough timing]." The monitoring body's 2022–24 report, on 1,203 websites and 21 apps: the share "with a disproportionate burden claim at closure" was 17 per cent of simply tested sites, 37 per cent of fully audited sites and 57 per cent of apps; "The understanding of disproportionate burden varies greatly and has often caused confusion and questions. Common issues include:" first, "organisations claim disproportionate burden without having carried out an assessment beforehand"; statements compliant with the model rose from 8 to 65 per cent over monitoring (simplified tests); 55.3 per cent of issues found were fixed during monitoring; and "many accessibility statements are now out-of-date and have not been reviewed in the last 12 months." Mechanism: the body decides after a mandatory assessment; nobody approves in advance; the record is the public statement, with a review condition; monitoring and enforcement come afterwards, and the first listed failure is the claim without the assessment. (Standard (law); Standard (government guidance); Evidence.)

Partial conformance (WCAG). The W3C has no deviation tier; what it has is a statement whose first words are the admission. "Conformance claims are not required. Authors can conform to WCAG 2.2 without making a claim."; where third-party content cannot be controlled, "A 'statement of partial conformance' may be made that the page does not conform, but could conform if certain parts were removed.", and "The form of that statement would be, 'This page does not conform, but would conform to WCAG 2.2 at level X if the following parts from uncontrolled sources were removed.'"; the excluded parts must be identifiable — "they cannot be described as 'all parts that we do not control' unless they are clearly marked as such." — and "No conformance claim can be made if it is not possible to monitor or correct non-conforming content" (verified in the editors' source file; check against the dated Recommendation). The Understanding document: "It is important to recognize that this is a statement of non-conformance". Mechanism: self-declared, in a fixed sentence that says "does not conform" first, with the exclusions identified; no approver; no review date. (Standard (W3C).)

Service assessments (UK government digital services). "'Amber' means that the standard has not yet been met, but the issues are not critical. The service can continue to the next phase of delivery while you work on the amber issues." [read once]; "You need to fix amber issues within a reasonable period of time, usually up to 3 months."; "You must record your progress in a live 'tracking amber evidence' document which will be visible to the assessments team." [read once]; red means "The service will stay in its current phase of delivery."; the panel is independent for larger services ("more than 100,000 transactions per year" or used by "civil servants in more than one organisation") and departmental otherwise; and the outcome is published [read once]. No exemption from the standard exists; only the scope rule. Mechanism: an independent peer panel decides; a failed point blocks the next phase; a non-critical failure is a time-boxed, tracked, visible non-conformance; published. (Standard (government guidance).)

The Code of Practice for Statistics (voluntary application and exemptions). Two mechanisms. For producers outside official statistics, "Where an organisation chooses to adopt and apply TQV for all or some of its statistics or functions, we encourage it to publish a TQV statement."; "It is helpful to your users to be clear if there are aspects of the Code that are not applied"; the regulator adds the organisation to a public register when the statement is published [read once], "will conduct a short annual review to check in with organisations on the Register", and intervenes only on a concern, "on an informal and advisory basis". For official statistics, "Exemptions are rare." "They have mainly been agreed where it is not possible to give contact information for the responsible statistician for security reasons."; the route, shown on the page as Code text with the edition not stated, is that the head of profession "should request an exemption from that practice of the Code from the Director General for Regulation and publish details of the exemption"; and the regulator keeps two public tables, permanent and temporary, the second with a "Duration" column [read once]. Edition 3.0's practices carry the deviation duty for methods in plain words: "Base methods on national or international good practice, scientific principles or professional consensus. … Use recognised standards, classifications and definitions. Explain reasons for deviations from these standards and any related implications for use." (practice 6.7; read once). Mechanism: a named professional head requests; an independent regulator grants; the producer publishes; the list is public and the temporary ones carry a duration; for voluntary adopters, a self-declared statement, a public register and an annual check-in. (Standard (regulator); Standard (official statistics).)

Waivers (financial regulation). The statutory test is quoted above; the regulator's own pages add the procedure: "You will need to explain how: Complying with the rule would be unduly burdensome or not achieve its purpose. Granting a waiver will not adversely affect our 3 objectives" [two passes]; "Most waivers and modifications are granted for a set period and then cease to apply."; "A waiver or modification will not apply retrospectively."; "We publish all approved waivers and permission notices unless we consider it inappropriate or unnecessary."; and the handbook: "A waiver may be given for a specified period of time only, after which time it will cease to apply." (SUP 8.3.6). Mechanism: the rule-subject applies with reasons and evidence; the regulator decides against a two-limb test, with other factors; time-limited by default; never retrospective; published by default. (Standard (law); Standard (regulator).)

Concession and deviation permit (quality management). The vocabulary standard separates permission after the fact from permission before it. A concession is "Permission to use or release a product or service that does not conform to specified requirements", and "is generally limited to the delivery of products and services that have nonconforming characteristics within specified limits and is generally given for a limited quantity of products and services or period of time, and for a specific use."; a deviation permit is "Permission to depart from the originally specified requirements of a product or service prior to its realization" [read once], with the same limits (ISO 9000:2015 definitions, read in a railway agency's terminology collection that reproduces them; the standard itself is not open). The management-system standard's clause on nonconformity could not be read: ISO withdrew the 2015 edition on 16 September 2026 and the 2026 edition is not open; the only wording on which two secondary sources agree is that the organisation shall "retain documented information as evidence of: a) the nature of the nonconformities and any subsequent actions taken; b) the results of any corrective action." (secondary; withdrawn edition). Mechanism: a named authority grants; before or after is a different word; limited in quantity, time and use. (Standard (method); secondary.)

Exception reporting (the family-doctor contract). The best-measured override mechanism found. A clinician may exclude a patient from a quality target for a listed reason; since April 2019 the mechanism is a "Personalised Care Adjustment", for reasons including "Intervention described in the indicator is clinically unsuitable." and "The patient has chosen not to receive the intervention described in the indicator.", and "the decision to apply a PCA should be based on clinical judgement, informed by patient preferences, and underpinned by shared decision-making principles." [read once]. Across 8,229 practices in 2008–09: "The median rate of exception reporting was 2.7% (interquartile range 1.9-3.9%) overall and 0.44% (0.14-1.1%) for informed dissent, but variation in rates was wide between practices and across indicators."; "Common reasons for exception reporting were logistical (40.6% of exceptions), clinical contraindication (18.7%), and patient informed dissent (30.1%)."; the cost was £0.58 per patient; and "our findings raise the possibility of gaming" (Doran et al. 2012; read once for the last). A co-author's later summary: "The overall rate of exception reporting has been relatively low, with an initial median rate of 5.3%, which fell to 4.5% in 2008/2009."; "However, 1% of practices initially excluded more than 15% of their patients."; and "we still do not know whether the ability of doctors to exclude patients from the P4P scheme has been in the interests of patients or not." (P4P: pay for performance) (Roland 2016). A cohort of 2.46 million patients found that "Exempted patients had a higher adjusted risk of death in the following year than non-exempted patients, regardless of whether this exemption was for contraindication (hazard ratio 1.37, 99% CI 1.33 to 1.40) or for informed dissent (1.20, 99% CI 1.17 to 1.24)." (Kontopantelis et al. 2016). The 2024–25 official statistics show adjustment rates from 1.8 per cent (smoking) to 29.9 per cent (COPD) by indicator group. Mechanism: the person at the point of decision decides, against a closed list of reasons; the record is a coded reason; the commissioner may audit; the rates are published nationally; no time limit; and the override's use rose after a missed target and its subjects did worse. (Standard (regulator); Evidence.)

Ministerial directions (public money). "If the minister decides it is nevertheless appropriate to continue with a course that does not meet the Managing Public Money standards, the accounting officer should ask for a formal written direction to proceed." and "Since 2011, there has been a presumption that such directions are published, unless the matter must be kept confidential." (HM Treasury). The route runs to the auditor and the committee: the accounting officer tells the Treasury, which tells the Comptroller and Auditor General, who tells the Public Accounts Committee (Institute for Government, two passes), and 107 are known since 1990 [read once]. Mechanism: the person who must break the rule asks the person who wants it broken for the order in writing; the auditor is told; published by presumption. (Standard (government guidance); Practice.)

Departures and relaxations (road design). The manual's verbs were quoted in section 3; the procedure is that "a departure application shall be submitted in accordance with the procedures required by the relevant Overseeing Organisation and approved: 1) before the design is finalised; and, 2) prior to their incorporation into the works."; "Adoption of a relaxation and its reasoning shall be recorded by the design organisation." [read once]; and for a recommendation not followed, "A justification shall be developed", "Justifications to support all design decisions shall be recorded by the design organisation as part of the project record." and "Any deviation from a recommendation along with the supporting justification shall be available to the Overseeing Organisation as required." [read once]. Mechanism: four tiers; the top cannot be varied; the second only by prior external approval; the third by recorded justification and risk assessment; the fourth freely; the record is part of the project record. (Standard (method).)

Deviations (the C coding standard). A deviation is "A violation which has been formally accepted and approved"; its record holds the guideline violated, "A concise description of the circumstances in which a violation is acceptable", "The reason why the deviation is required", the background, and "A set of requirements to include any risk assessment procedures and precautions which must be observed" (two passes, wording stable); the two forbidden grounds are quoted above; and re-categorisation "may only move a guideline to a stricter category, except that Advisory may be disapplied" [read once]. Mechanism: formal acceptance by someone other than the developer; a record with circumstances, reason, background and precautions; two reasons never accepted; rules may be tightened but not loosened. (Standard (method).)

Waivers nobody re-read (the shuttle). The negative case, secondary because the board's report could not be reached: "Of the 4,222 Criticality 1/1R Items, '3,233 have waivers (and) 36 percent of these waivers have not been reviewed in 10 years.'" (the Columbia Accident Investigation Board, as excerpted on a third-party site; secondary), with the board's recommendation, in a tertiary report, that "an independent group rather than shuttle program managers be given sole authority to grant waivers." [read once]. Mechanism: the body that wanted the waivers granted them, and nobody was paid to re-read them. (Practice; secondary.)

What the twelve share

Set side by side, the regimes agree on more than they differ.

Regime Who decides Who checks What is written Expires or reviewed Published
Comply or explain the board shareholders (in practice rarely) context, rationale, impact, timescale if time-limited, a date yes, annual report
Disproportionate burden the body, after assessment monitoring body, afterwards the parts not met and why; alternatives "under regular review"; re-assess on change yes, the statement
WCAG partial conformance the author none "This page does not conform, but would…", exclusions identified none yes, if a claim is made
Service assessment independent panel the panel, at reassessment the report; a live amber-tracking document amber ≤ about 3 months yes
Code of Practice head of profession; voluntary adopter Director General; annual check-in the exemption's details; the TQV statement Duration column; "review regularly" yes, a register
FCA waiver regulator, on application the regulator the direction, with conditions set period; never retrospective yes, by default
ISO concession / permit a named authority — the permission, its limits and use limited quantity, time, use internal
Exception reporting the clinician the commissioner, by audit a coded reason none rates, nationally
Ministerial direction the minister, in writing auditor; committee the direction — by presumption
DMRB departure Overseeing Organisation, before design is final the Overseeing Organisation the project record — internal
MISRA deviation formal approval the approver guideline; circumstances; reason; background; precautions — internal
Shuttle waiver programme managers nobody, for a decade the waiver none, in practice no

Four things recur, and the chapter takes them as the test of a regime. First, a reason with a shape — context, rationale, risk, time — and the measured finding that without a reader the shape fills with boilerplate. Second, a reader other than the author — a panel, a regulator, an auditor, a Director General — and where that reader is nominal (shareholders; nobody) the record decays. Third, a time limit or a review condition, near-universal: the Code's "when the company expects to conform", the statement's "another assessment when", the waiver's "set period", the concession's "period of time", the exemption's "Duration", the amber's three months; the regimes without one in the text read are the partial-conformance statement, exception reporting — the one whose subjects did worse — and the three engineering records whose review is the project's. Fourth, publication by default, with the one regime whose private waivers were counted being the one that had not re-read a third of them in ten years. What none of the regimes shows, in the evidence read, is a controlled test that publishing or checking changes behaviour; what three show is a direction: statements compliant with the model rose from 8 to 65 per cent under monitoring, the exception median fell from 5.3 to 4.5 per cent under commissioner audit, and declared departures from the governance code fell while undisclosed ones were found. (Reading; Evidence.)

Two things the regimes add that the Decision Book's four lines lack: the who — who decided and who checked, which the government's analysis-quality guidance has in both its logs ("explain who made the decision and who signed it off"; read once) — and the when next — a review date, which the house's template has nowhere. Section 5 builds the entry. (Reading.)

5 · The record

What the house's log asks for, in how many versions

The Decision Book's override log is printed five times and is three different things. The sentence this chapter was briefed on — "Trigger · rule and tier · alternative chosen · evidence. Four lines." — is at one line of the skill file. The rule in the register, BRK-08, is "Log every override: trigger, rule, alternative, evidence" — "rule" without "and tier", "alternative" without "chosen". The checklist, printed in two files, is "Override logged: trigger, rule and tier, alternative, evidence". And the template file, under the words "Four lines per departure", is a table with five columns: Date, then the four. This book inherited the drift: Chapter 0 gives the skill file's four; Chapters 2 to 5, in their break tests, give a different four — "(what rule, why, for whom, what proved it)" — of which "for whom" is in none of the house's printings and "alternative chosen" is in none of the chapters'; Chapters 1, 6 and 7 name the record without fields; Chapters 8 to 11 do not mention logging a break; Chapters 12 and 13 say a break "is logged" without saying where; and Chapters 14 and 15 log to records of their own. It is what Chapter 15 found of every rule system it read, the rule changing under the same name, and the Decision Book's own eleventh rule is the cure: "State every value in the design system once; other mentions point to it", because "A value stated twice has already begun to diverge". The entry below is stated once, in section 10, and this chapter's rules point to it. (Standard (design system); Reading; the compilation.)

What other fields put in the record

Seven records of decisions were read for their fields, and the fields are set out here because the entry in section 10 is their intersection.

The architecture decision record. The founding post names its purpose — "One of the hardest things to track during the life of a project is the motivation behind certain decisions." — and the two bad choices a newcomer otherwise has, to "Blindly accept the decision." or "Blindly change it." [read once]; its form is Title, Context ("the forces at play … These forces are probably in tension, and should be called out as such."), Decision ("stated in full sentences, with active voice"), Status ("proposed" or "accepted"; later "deprecated" or "superseded" "with a reference to its replacement") and Consequences ("All consequences should be listed here, not just the "positive" ones."); "The whole document should be one or two pages long."; "ADRs will be numbered sequentially and monotonically. Numbers will not be reused."; "If a decision is reversed, we will keep the old one around, but mark it as superseded." The immutability the house may have assumed is not in that post — the word is absent — and lives in later guidance: "When the team accepts an ADR, it becomes immutable." and "When the team accepts the new ADR, it supersedes the previous ADR." (AWS). The government's standard adds the location and the reason for it: "Architecture decisions should be stored in version control so there is a record of what was changed, who by, and when."; "If a decision has been superseded by another decision, the old ADR must be clearly marked as 'superseded'." (the GDS Way, reviewed 5 March 2026); and a cross-government framework published on 4 November 2025 fixes the fields as title, date, status, context, decision, consequences, stakeholders consulted and links to supporting documents [two passes]. The measured life of the form: adoption "is still low", "About 50% of all repositories with ADRs contain just one to five ADRs" (Buchgeher et al. 2023 [abstract or summary only]); 63 per cent of 5,800 records born "accepted" (Santana Junior et al. 2026 [abstract or summary only]); and in one controlled comparison, the short founding template beat the longer one on an overall score, 0.8 against 0.7, with 33 students (Nogueira, Silva & Conte 2026; read once for the scores). (Practice; Standard (government guidance); Evidence [abstract or summary only].)

The preregistration deviation. The definition: "any discrepancy between what the authors said they would do in the preregistration and what the authors actually did in the final article." The table proposed for reporting it has columns for the number, the details (type, reason and timing), the original wording, the deviation's description and the reader impact (two passes; headings not checked letter by letter); the reasons offered are a typo or oversight, a data or documentation error, a plan "not possible or inappropriate because of data", new knowledge, a reviewer's suggestion and miscommunication [read once]; and the timing is the field the others lack — "It is important to transparently report the timing of when the deviation was recognized or occurred because data-dependent deviations increase risk of bias." The authors ask that the table sit in the paper and that "researchers should also include the results of the preregistered analyses alongside the deviated analyses". The base rate it answers is the audit's: "Two out of 27 preregistered studies contained no deviations from the preregistration plan."; "One study (4%) reported all the deviations."; "In the remaining 24 of 27 (89%) studies, there was at least one item for which a discrepancy between the preregistration plan and the journal article was not fully disclosed."; and the reason disclosure matters is the reader's default — "Few readers will take the time to meticulously compare the published paper with the preregistered plan. Instead, they will assume that, unless noted otherwise, the preregistered plan was followed" [read once]. The repository's own procedure fixes the before-and-after split: before analysis, an amendment with a mandatory justification ("You will be prompted to enter a justification for the update." "This field must have information entered in order for the update to be submitted."); after, "Start a Transparent Changes document now" and keep the original standing. (Standard (method); Evidence; Practice.)

The analysis-quality logs. The government's own guidance for analysis has two registers with the same spine. "The assumptions log is a register of assumptions … that have been risk assessed and signed off by an appropriate governance group or stakeholder." and its entries "describe each assumption, quantify its effect and reliability, set out when it was made, explain why it was made, explain who made the assumption and who signed it off"; "The decisions log is a register of decisions" whose entries "describe each decision, set out when it was made, explain why it was made, explain who made the decision and who signed it off." [read once]. (Standard (government guidance).)

The appraisal record. The Treasury's appraisal guidance, rewritten in February 2026, uses "must" for the reason: "Practitioners must record the reason for each rating in a brief paragraph, explaining the underlying evidence, assumptions and sources."; "Practitioners should explain transparently what options have been considered as well as the reasons they have or have not been progressed to shortlist appraisal."; and the purpose: "This provides a clear sequence of reasoning for reviewers and decision makers, and supports future evaluation." (Standard (government guidance).)

The changelog. The lightest of the conventions and the only one whose first principle is the reader: "Changelogs are for humans, not machines."; "There should be an entry for every single version."; "The release date of each version is displayed."; "Keep an Unreleased section at the top to track upcoming changes."; "If you do nothing else, list deprecations, removals, and any breaking changes in your changelog."; and the warning this book's records should carry on their face: "A changelog which only mentions some of the changes can be as dangerous as not having a changelog." The versioning convention beside it gives the never-edit rule in full: "Once a versioned package has been released, the contents of that version MUST NOT be modified. Any modifications MUST be released as a new version." and, for when the rule itself is broken, "Even under this circumstance, it is unacceptable to modify versioned releases." (Semantic Versioning 2.0.0). (Practice; Standard (community).)

The datasheet and the model card. The one-document conventions, read for section 7 and for their maintenance sections. The datasheet's questions are grouped by "motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing/cleaning/labeling, uses, distribution, and maintenance" [read once], the last asking "Who will be supporting/hosting/maintaining the dataset?", "Is there an erratum?", "Will older versions of the dataset continue to be supported/hosted/maintained?" and "If so, please describe how its obsolescence will be communicated to dataset consumers."; and the authors insist the document is written, not generated: "We emphasize that the process of creating a datasheet is not intended to be automated." The model card is "short (one to two page)" [read once], carries a date, a version and "Where to send questions or comments about the model", and its authors name its limit: "the usefulness and accuracy of a model card relies on the integrity of the creator(s) of the card itself." The measurement of 32,111 cards: the Training section filled in 74.3 per cent of cards, Limitations in 17.4 per cent, Evaluation in 15.4 per cent, Environmental Impact in 2.0 per cent (Liang et al. 2024). People fill in what they did and leave blank what limits it. (Standard (method); Evidence.)

The code's practices. The Code of Practice's reason duty for a method ("Explain reasons for deviations from these standards and any related implications for use."; read once), its openness practice ("Be open about your decisions and reasons for change.") and its schedule-change practice ("Agree changes to pre-announced release dates or times with the Chief Statistician/Head of Profession for Statistics and announce promptly, explaining the reasons") put the reason and its implication for use in the same sentence — a field the override log lacks and the deviation table has as "reader impact". (Standard (official statistics).)

Three fields appear in nearly every record and in none of the house's four lines: who decided and who signed off; when, with a status that moves; and what the reader should now do differently — the deviation table's reader impact, the code's "implications for use", the datasheet's communication of obsolescence. One field appears in the house's lines and in few of the others: the test and its result, which is the house's strength and is kept. (Reading.)

When a written reason helps, and when it is noise

The belief that requiring a reason improves the decision has been tested, and the result is narrower than the belief. The experimental core is a 1989 paper whose abstract states the model and reports that the experiment supported it: "(a) when people know the views of the audience and are unconstrained by past commitments, they will rely on the low-effort acceptability heuristic and simply shift their views toward those of the prospective audience,"; "(b) when people do not know the views of the audience and are unconstrained by past commitments, they will be motivated to think in relatively flexible, multidimensional ways (preemptive self-criticism),"; "(c) when people are accountable for positions to which they feel committed, they will devote the majority of their mental effort to justifying those positions (defensive bolstering)."; "The experiment yielded results supportive of these 3 predictions." (Tetlock, Skitka & Boettger 1989 [abstract or summary only]; authorship confirmed through Crossref, JPSP 57(4):632–640). The review that made the finding famous could not be read beyond its abstract, which asks "Under what conditions will accountability attenuate, have no effect on, or amplify cognitive biases?" and "Does accountability alter how people think or merely what people say they think?" (Lerner & Tetlock 1999 [abstract or summary only]); the words "unknown views" and "defensive bolstering" are the 1989 paper's and are not placed in the 1999 review's mouth here. A later summary states the condition in a sentence: "Accountability in front of an audience with unknown views generally results in more cognitive effort." (Vieider 2008, secondary). (Evidence [abstract or summary only]; secondary.)

Against it, two experiments found nothing. In 144 and then 110 participants asked to justify their judgements on randomly chosen trials, "Process accountability neither changed how accurately people made a judgment, nor the judgment strategies." and "Justifying the judgment process only decreased confidence in trials involving a justification." (Hoffmann, Gaissmaier & von Helversen 2017). And a forecasting tournament of more than a thousand people over ten months found that accountability for outcomes "boosted forecasting accuracy beyond holding them accountable for process", while "Process accountability promoted more effective knowledge sharing, improving accuracy among observers." (Chang et al. 2017 [abstract or summary only]). The audit evidence is of the same shape: impact assessments "are being used once a policy decision has been taken" and "A predetermined policy agenda can have a far greater influence on government action than the outcome or findings of the impact assessment." (NAO 2007); two years later, "only 20 per cent presented the results of an evaluation of a range of options", "60 per cent of IAs included £0 for either the costs or benefits" and "approximately one fifth provided no justification for this assessment" (NAO 2009), with the mechanism named — "the new requirements have led policy officials to provide only the information specifically requested rather than present an analysis of a range of regulatory proposals." And a reason-giving duty was repealed in England in 2013 because the reasons were being written twice: the requirement on planning authorities "to provide a summary of reasons for approval" was said by the local government planning community to be "both burdensome and unnecessary because it duplicates material documented elsewhere", since officer reports "typically provide far more detail on the logic and reasoning behind a particular decision than a decision notice" (Explanatory Memorandum to SI 2013/1238; the memorandum says "duplicates", not "boilerplate"). (Evidence; Evidence [abstract or summary only]; Practice; Standard (law).)

Read together: a written reason improves the decision when it is owed before the decision, to a reader whose view the writer cannot guess; it improves the next reader's decision in most conditions, which is the architecture-record argument and the forecasting tournament's finding; it does nothing, or lowers confidence, when demanded after the fact as a form; and it should be written once, where the reasoning is done, and pointed to from everywhere else. For a book of 486 rules this says four things about its deviation entry: it is written before the departure ships; it names a reader who is not the author and whose view is not known in advance; it is kept where the work is kept, in the repository beside the build, as the government standard and the Technology Radar entry both say ("stored in version control"; "storing these details in source control, instead of a wiki or website, as then they can provide a record that remains in sync with the code itself"); and it is one entry, not an entry here and a summary there. (Reading.)

How records decay, and who reads them

Nobody has measured the readership of decision records directly; the nearest are the founding post's "six to ten developers" and the mining study's contributor counts, which give no readership. What has been measured is decay. Software engineers "often do not maintain documentation"; "When SEs do update documents, they usually do so several weeks after changes are made to the code."; forty-four per cent of forty-five respondents somewhat agreed and 24 per cent strongly agreed that "Documentation is always outdated relative to the current state of a software system."; and the one condition under which they kept it current is the one this book's records should be built on — "SEs were likely to update documentation continually only when it was attached to the process for completing a change request" (Lethbridge, Singer & Forward 2003). Architects defer the record and "at that point, they've often forgotten many decisions and the rationale behind them" (Harrison, Avgeriou & Zdun 2007). Outward-pointing records rot: "one out of five STM articles suffering from reference rot", and "seven out of ten" of those with web references (Klein et al. 2014) — which bears on every record in this book that cites a URL, including this chapter's. Institutional memory leaves with people: "Several departments, including the Treasury and the Cabinet Office, lose a quarter of their staff each year" (Institute for Government 2019). And a record-keeping rule that depends on each person deciding, as a separate act, what counts as a record is not followed: "Existing systems which require individual users to identify documents that should constitute official records, and then to save them into an EDRMS [an electronic records system] or corporate file plan, have not worked well. The processes have been burdensome and compliance poor." (Allan 2015). (Evidence; Practice.)

The design consequence is the same one Chapter 8 drew for the dashboard's freshness and Chapter 15 drew for its retirement: the record is kept current only where updating it is part of the step that makes the change. For the deviation log that means the entry is written in the same change that ships the departure, and the build refuses the change without it — section 8's check. For the record of the dashboard it means the record's review line carries a date and the build reports the records whose date has passed, as the accessibility statement's "last reviewed" line and the datasheet's maintenance section both intend, and as the monitoring body found many statements had not been. (Reading.)

Does disclosing a deviation cost trust?

No experiment on it was found. The nearest evidence is a preregistered survey of 34 journal editors (of 170 emailed), who rated a disclosed deviation with an explanation as neutral to slightly positive for their view of a manuscript — "M = 3.3, SD = 1.3" on a scale from 1 to 5 — and an undisclosed deviation found in review as strongly negative, "M = 1.3, SD = 0.5" (Willroth & Atherton 2024; the article's own sentence for the second scenario prints "reported" where the scenario is the unreported one, so the numbers are quoted and the sentence is not). The same editors said they checked adherence to the plan "65% of the time, on average". A registered report testing whether the preregistered label raises trust was inconclusive — "we report ambiguous Bayes factors and conclude that we do not have strong evidence towards answering our research questions." (Field et al. 2020) — and is not about deviations. So, on a small sample of gatekeepers' stated attitudes: the penalty attaches to concealment, not to the deviation. That is the only evidence this book has on the question Chapter 15 raised of whether printing a dashboard's departures costs it, and it points the same way as Chapter 15's producers, who disclosed errors as they happened. (Evidence; Reading.)

The entry, derived

From the regimes' agreement (section 4), the records' fields and the evidence on when a reason helps, the deviation entry has these lines, and section 10 states them once as the chapter's record: the rule and its tier, in the register's sense; the trigger — what made the departure necessary, specific to the case; the alternative — what was done instead, and the alternative that was declined; what it buys, from the Decision Book's list, and what it costs; the test — which of the six forms, and its result; who decided and who checked, the second not the first; the date; the review date or the condition on which it lapses; and a status that moves — proposed, accepted, superseded, lapsed — with the old entry kept. Nine lines where the house had four. The four are kept, with the rule placed first so that its tier is read before the reason; the five added are the ones every regime read either has or was found to need. (Reading; Nightlife Culture.)

6 · Overrides in practice: what a rule set that fires too often does to the people under it

The measured rates

In the one field that logs every override, the rates are known. The 2006 review of seventeen papers: "Drug safety alerts are overridden by clinicians in 49% to 96% of cases." — and in the same abstract, the finding that keeps this from being a story about careless people: "Alert overriding may often be justified and adverse drug events due to overridden alerts are not always preventable."; the fault is placed in "error-producing conditions like low specificity, low sensitivity, unclear information content, unnecessary workflow disruptions" (van der Sijs et al. 2006 [abstract or summary only]). A 2020 review of 23 articles: "The range of average override alerts was 46.2%-96.2%." and "An average of 29.4%-100% of the overrides alerts were classified as appropriate" (Poly et al. 2020). A 2024 meta-analysis of fifteen studies, for drug-interaction alerts only: "the overall prevalence of alert override by physicians was 90% (CI95% 85–95%)" (Felisberto et al. 2024). In one system, 157,483 alerts on two million orders: "82 889 (52.6%) of alerts were overridden."; by chart review of 600 overrides, "An average of 53% of overrides were classified as appropriate" ranging "from 12% for renal recommendations to 92% for patient allergies" (Nanji et al. 2014 [abstract or summary only]). The last range is the point: whether an override is right depends on the rule, from one in eight to nine in ten, so a high override rate indicts the rule as often as the person. (Evidence; Evidence [abstract or summary only].)

The dose–response

What drives the rate is measured in one cohort of 112 primary-care clinicians over three and a half years, 1.27 million advisories and 326,203 drug alerts: "Likelihood of reminder acceptance dropped by 30% for each additional reminder received per encounter, and by 10% for each five percentage point increase in proportion of repeated reminders."; "Clinicians became less likely to accept alerts as they received more of them, particularly more repeated alerts."; and, as important for a rule set, "There was no evidence of an effect of workload per se, or of desensitization over time for a newly deployed alert." (Ancker et al. 2017). What cuts acceptance is neither busyness nor habituation but how many rules fire at once and how often the same one repeats. The patient-safety primer states the end state: clinicians "ignore both the bothersome, clinically meaningless alarms and the critical alerts that warn of impending serious patient harm". (Evidence; Practice.)

Tiering by consequence, and hard stops

Two studies measure the remedy the fields' three-tier vocabularies imply. Where interaction alerts were tiered by severity at one centre and not at another, across 71,350 alerts, "Compliance with DDI alerts [drug–drug interaction alerts] was significantly higher at the site with tiered DDI alerts compared to the non-tiered site (29% vs. 10%, p < 0.001)." and "At the tiered site, 100% of the most severe alerts were accepted, vs. only 34% at the non-tiered site" — with the caveat that the tiered site used hard stops for the severest alerts, so the hundred reflects in part that the top tier could not be overridden (Paterno et al. 2009 [abstract or summary only]; the caveat read once). Where most alerts were made non-interruptive and only a minority interrupted, the interrupting ones were accepted 67 per cent of the time (Shah et al. 2006; secondary, no control group). And a systematic review of 32 studies of hard stops — rules that cannot be overridden — found "Seventy-nine percent showed improvement in health outcomes and 88% in process outcomes.", "Hard stops were superior to soft stops in 3 of 4 studies.", and the cost: "Eleven studies reported on unintended consequences including avoidance of hard-stopped workflow, increased alert frequency, and delay to care." (Powers et al. 2018 [abstract or summary only]). A rule that cannot be broken works better than one that can, and people route around it. (Evidence; Evidence [abstract or summary only]; secondary.)

Checklists, used and ticked

The book has fifteen checklists, one per chapter, and the evidence on checklists is the evidence on the difference between a list that is used and a list that is ticked. The eight-hospital study: "The rate of death was 1.5% before the checklist was introduced and declined to 0.8% afterward (P=0.003)." and complications from 11.0 to 7.0 per cent, with the study's own hypothesis sentence saying what the checklist was for — "a 19-item surgical safety checklist designed to improve team communication and consistency of care" (Haynes et al. 2009 [abstract or summary only]). The 101-hospital study of a mandated checklist, 109,341 procedures before and 106,370 after: "Implementation of surgical safety checklists in Ontario, Canada, was not associated with significant reductions in operative mortality or complications." (Urbach et al. 2014 [abstract or summary only]). The accompanying editorial, read only as quoted on a third party's page: "it is not the act of ticking off a checklist that reduces complications, but performance of the actions it calls for"; "In the absence of direct monitoring by observation, true compliance is unknown."; "Compliance was undoubtedly much lower than the reported 98%."; and "If a checklist is required, the person responsible for documentation will ensure that all boxes are ticked." (Leape 2014, secondary; read once for the last). Observed directly in five English hospitals, 565 time-outs and 309 sign-outs: "On average, two-thirds of the items were checked, team members were absent in more than 40% of cases, and they failed to pause or focus on the checks in more than 70% of cases."; "Surgical safety checklist performance was better when surgeons led and when all team members were present and paused." (Russ et al. 2015 [abstract or summary only]). The pooled estimate across seven studies is a risk ratio of 0.59 for any complication and "a strong correlation between a significant decrease in postoperative complications and adherence to aspects of care embedded in the checklist" (Bergs et al. 2014 [abstract or summary only]); the sceptical review of 25 studies notes that "Postoperative mortality rates were not significantly decreased in any studies in developed nations" and that "many of the positive changes … were due to temporal changes, confounding factors and publication bias" (De Jager et al. 2016; the journal attribution unverified). The flight-deck literature had said it first, qualitatively: "a long and detailed checklist is no guarantee of absolute safety. Indeed, it carries the risk that some pilots might choose not to use the checklist or conduct it poorly because of its length." (Degani & Wiener 1990). (Evidence; Evidence [abstract or summary only]; secondary.)

What this means for a book with 433 Fixed rules and fifteen checklists

A rule set in which nearly everything carries the strongest word, and in which the strongest word is enforced by a person reading a list, is the condition under which, in the one field that measures it, between half and nineteen-twentieths of firings are dismissed — nine in ten for interaction alerts — and the dismissal reaches the ones that matter. The remedy the fields use is also measured: fewer rules in the top tier; the top tier set apart and, where the consequence warrants it, not overridable; everything else logged rather than enforced. The remedy the checklist evidence adds is that a list works where it changes what a team does together and is observed to be used, and not where it is a document someone is responsible for ticking.

So the register in section 8 is built in three parts and the book's fifteen checklists become two things. The Fixed register is short — the requirements the build can test, which fail the build; the sequences, which the build checks by the order of records and dates — and is the only list a reviewer is asked to hold. The Adaptable register is long, and it is a list of house defaults with their grounds rather than a checklist — the list a departure is logged against. And the checks are the build's: the fifteen chapters' lists are folded into the register's test column and run by the build or by a named reviewer, with the result written, as Chapter 13's scan and Chapter 12's crop test already are; what is left of each chapter's checklist is the handful of items that are a conversation and not a check, which stay as the chapter's "what proves a break works". Section 8 gives the counts and the form. The evidence read here does not say how many rules a person can hold; the field's own folklore figures were not verifiable at source and are not printed. What it does say is that every extra rule that fires in the same encounter costs a measured share of the attention paid to all of them. (Reading; Nightlife Culture.)

7 · The book's machinery, assembled

Everything in this section is a statement about what the fifteen chapters and Chapter 0 printed at second draft, on 7 October 2026, counted by script and re-checked against the source line, and then what the chapter does about it. The chapters' tables have since been brought to the register's tier words, so the wordings counted here ("as a stance", "as a procedure", the bare "Fixed") are the audit that produced the register, not the tables as they now stand. Where the chapter decides, it says so and gives the grounds; where the decision is the studio's, it says that and moves it to section 11.

The rule register: 486 rows, and what is wrong with them

The counts and the tier distribution are in section 3. Four more findings bear on the register's form.

The same rule is stated twice, forty-two times. The compilation groups 42 sets of rules stated in more than one chapter in different words — the precise twin, the table route, the sentence first, the source line, the dates, the comparison gate, ranks and intervals, identity never ranked, uncertainty as a range, a cell not shown is marked, nothing crucial behind a hover, colour never the only carrier, recognition before release, construct before proxy, the denominator, the unit declared, release the data, defaults declared, monitoring not evaluation, the retirement plan, revisions and status marks, the disclosure floor, outliers, measuring use and trust, the phone first, "not done" written, and the rest. Each group is one rule in the register with the chapters that state it listed as its sources, the strictest consistent wording kept, and the Decision Book's rule BRK-11 (state every value once) applied to the book's own text: stated once, pointed to from the rest. (Reading; the compilation.)

The Kind column outgrew its legend. Five kinds defined in Chapter 0, with Evidence of method added by the chapters; 182 distinct wordings printed; 141 of them used once; 163 of 486 rows (34 per cent) use one of the five words alone; thirty sub-kinds of Standard introduced chapter by chapter; fourteen rows with "—". Chapter 0's rule that a Standard "says whether it binds Nightlife Culture or is adopted voluntarily" is met in eight rows. The register keeps the five kinds, with Evidence of method as a sub-kind of Evidence, keeps the sub-kind of Standard as a second field since the chapters found it useful (regulator; law; method; design system; official statistics; W3C; government guidance; community), and adds a one-letter field for whether a Standard binds the studio or is adopted, which Chapter 0 asked for and nearly every row omits. (Reading; the compilation.)

Seventeen Fixed rules are sourced only to the book. Five rows cite the chapter itself and nothing else, three a section of the same chapter, nine other chapters of this book or version 1; all seventeen are Fixed in some form; four of them are the rules that carry a record (the claim record, the comparison record, the recognition record, the precedent record). A rule sourced only to the house is the house's position, and under section 3's re-basing it is Adaptable (house default) unless its grounds are a requirement; the four record-carrying rules are sequences — the record is written before the thing ships — and are tiered so. (Reading; the compilation.)

Forty-nine Fixed rows rest on a dagger and none carries the flag. Chapter 0's rule is that "A Fixed rule resting on a [abstract or summary only] source is flagged [Further research] until the full text has been read." Forty-nine Fixed-bearing rows have a dagger in their Source or Kind cell; no row carries the flag; Chapters 1 to 7 carry it for the whole table in the table's note, Chapters 8 to 11 do not, and Chapters 12 and 14 have dagger rows and no note. The register gives every such row the flag as a status, and the build lists them. (Reading; the compilation.)

The eleven tier conflicts, reconciled

Each is given the chapters' wordings in the compilation; here is the decision and its ground, under section 3's three senses.

The rule As printed The register's tier, and why
Investigate an outlier before treating it as noise Adaptable (Ch 1); Fixed (Ch 4, twice) Fixed as a sequence: the investigation precedes the treatment; what the investigation is, is Adaptable. Chapter 4's grounds (every official scheme's procedure) are a sequence, and Chapter 1's "Adaptable" was about the method
State where a causal claim stands on the evidence ladder Fixed (Chs 2, 7); Adaptable "with a declared minimum" (Ch 15) Fixed as a requirement that the rung is stated; Adaptable which scale names it, with Chapter 15's declared minimum. The two chapters were tiering different parts
Recognition is checked with the people described before release sequence (Chs 1, 2); stance (Chs 5, 9); procedure (Ch 12) Fixed as a sequence, as Chapter 0's own example says; the method of checking is Adaptable
Construct before proxy, parts or items Fixed (Chs 2, 5); stance (Ch 9) Fixed as a sequence, Chapter 0's other example; the proxy is Adaptable
Uncertainty as a numeric range, never a verbal hedge Fixed (Chs 1, 2); procedure (Ch 15) Fixed as a requirement: a range is present beside any point; the form of the range is Chapter 3's and is Adaptable; see the next table for the "bare interval" rule
"Leading" only with a measured record Fixed (Ch 6); procedure (Ch 7) Fixed as a requirement: the record exists and is cited; the word is otherwise not used
The disclosure floor set by the scene's knowability stance (Ch 6); "procedure; Adaptable in value" (Ch 10) Fixed as a sequence: the floor is set, per view, before the view ships; its value is Adaptable, as Chapter 10 says. The floor's value for a room under both floors is in section 11
The house's headline length Fixed, limit Fixed as a stance (Ch 11); Adaptable (Ch 14) Adaptable (house default), as Chapter 14 re-tiered it on evidence and logged; the distance and seconds beneath it are Fixed as a requirement. Chapter 11's row is marked superseded in the register
The retirement plan procedure, Adaptable in period (Ch 8); procedure (Chs 11, 15) Fixed as a sequence: the plan is written before launch; its period and content are Adaptable. Chapter 15 asked this chapter whether it is Fixed at all; the regulator lists the plan among its minimum, and three chapters already print it so
No league table of places Fixed (Chs 1, 2, 6); stance (Chs 7, 10, 12) See the next table
Cognitive testing of a felt question "Fixed (test); Adaptable (combine)" (Ch 5); procedure (Ch 9) Fixed as a sequence: a felt question is tested before it is fielded; the method of testing is Adaptable

Nine of the eleven resolve to a sequence or a requirement, most with an Adaptable part, which is to say the chapters were tiering different parts of one rule under one word; one resolves to Adaptable (house default); one is the ranking question below. None needed new evidence. The lesson for Chapter 0 is that a rule with a hard order and an open form needs both tiers printed, and the register has two columns for it. (Reading; Nightlife Culture.)

The rules that pull against each other, reconciled

Ranking. Chapters 1 and 2 allow a ranking with intervals; Chapters 7, 10 and 12 forbid a league table of places; Chapters 12 and 15 regulate the ordering the three forbid. The register resolves it as three rules at three tiers. Fixed as a requirement: no screen, export or crop carries an ordered all-places list of places on any measure (Chapters 7, 10, 12; version 1's crop check). Fixed as a requirement: any ordering of anything the dashboard does show — a ranking by rate as a screening instrument, a position within a distribution — carries its interval and the official wording (Chapters 1, 2, 12). Adaptable (house default): whether the dashboard shows position at all, and in what form (Chapter 7's categories of statistical separation). Chapter 15's usage text (15.12) is the requirement's text. The three chapters that forbid and the two that regulate were never in conflict about a league table; they were in conflict about whether a screening ranking with intervals is one, and Chapter 7's own gap row records that its first draft "would have forbidden the chapter's own recommended forms". The register says: it is not, provided the interval and wording travel, and the crop check proves they do. (Reading.)

Uncertainty. "A numeric range, never a verbal hedge" (Chapters 1, 2, 15) and "Never a bare interval" (Chapter 3) are reconciled as Chapter 3 intended and no table said: the range is present, in numbers and in words (requirement); the drawing of it is not a bare error bar where a better form is available (Chapter 3's Adaptable list: countable dots, gradients, violins, draws), and the drawing's form is Adaptable (house default) with Chapter 3's grounds. (Reading.)

Measuring use. Chapters 1, 10 and 11 have the dashboard count its own use; Chapter 15 says reach is measured "only by asking". Both stand, as two rules: the site counts how it is used, never who, in aggregate and dated (Chapters 10, 11; requirement), and that count is never reported as reach or as use by readers, which is measured only by asking, with the response rate printed (Chapter 15; requirement). The conflict was in the word "use", which the first three used for events and the fourth for people. (Reading.)

One tap or one step. Chapters 4 to 7 say "one tap", Chapters 11, 13 and 14 "one step", and Chapter 11 asked whether the legend should carry "on the face / one step away / on request". The register adopts Chapter 11's three positions as its vocabulary — on the face, one step away, on request — maps "one tap" to "one step away", and lists Chapter 11's constraint as the requirement: nothing the majority of readers need is one step away. Chapter 0's glossary takes the three. (Reading.)

Text inside the chart frame. Chapter 12's rule that every chart carries its title, unit, source, base, address and date inside its frame departs from official practice and from the design system's preference for text outside images, and Chapters 12 and 13 made the departure "in addition to page text, never instead". The register keeps it as Adaptable (house default) with the condition Chapter 13 stated for the accessibility criterion, and the departure is this chapter's own first deviation entry in section 10's example, because it is a house rule that departs from a cited standard with a reason and a test (the crop test) and is exactly what the log is for. (Reading.)

The twelve records: one document, written once per concept, in two views

Twelve chapters each left a record and each asked whether the records are one document; the question is flagged [Revisit at end] in every chapter from 7 to 15, in truths, flags and gap rows. The compilation answers the factual part. Twelve documents, 129 lines; four printed as lists and eight as tables; headed seven different ways ("The minimal set"; "The recipe on the face"; "The record beneath them" twice; "Beneath the dashboard" five times; "Beneath the measure / view / page" once each); kept per different units (every figure; every composed number; every statement of value; every comparison; the dashboard; every felt measure; every dashboard that shows people; every view; every place-page; the dashboard with lines per view; every expressive element; every borrowed mechanism); and declared public in four, internal or unstated in six, and open in two. The names drift: the boundary log is called a register in five places of the chapter that named it a log; "recognition record" names a line of the recipe and the whole of Chapter 12's record; "recipe card" is not in the chapter that made it; the count of records wobbles at the face sheet.
