The line names recur little — only "Review" and "Status" repeat exactly — but the concepts recur: a date or period is in the text of all twelve; who was asked or consulted is in eleven; a version or vintage in eight; a test in eight; a status in nine; a review in five; an owner in four; and four of these words mean different things in different records (four different things have a status; "review" is a re-reading date in three records and a review by the scene in one; "held" is held equal in one and the held layer in two). Three chapters say outright that their last line and an earlier record's are "the same field" (the measure record's line 12, the safeguards record's line 14, the face sheet's line 12 — what this changed; tests and review). (Reading; the compilation.)

The fields read for this chapter hold three positions. Many small immutable records, on the ground that "Large documents are never kept up to date." and "Nobody ever reads large documents, either." (Nygard). Two tiers — the critical caveat beside the figure and the rest in one background report: "Information about the quality of statistics should be provided in the commentary of the statistical bulletin and in accompanying Background Quality Reports" (the Analysis Function); "All regular, established bulletins must have a quality and methodology information (QMI) report published alongside them." and "QMI reports do not need to be updated with every edition of your bulletin." (the ONS). And one source, each concept written once, several views: the European statistical system's Single Integrated Metadata Structure (SIMS) was built to create "the framework for 'once for all purposes' reporting, where each concept is only reported upon once" (read once; the key clause verified), from which two reports are drawn — "ESMS files provide non-specialist users with the information needed to correctly interpret the data" and "ESQRS files provide producers and advanced users with detailed information for assessing the quality of the datasets". The machine-learning conventions take the one-document side and build a maintenance section in; the measurement of them shows the section people leave empty is the one about limits. The data archive's practice is to receive many records and bind them "into a bookmarked PDF/a user guide" [read once]. (Practice; Standard (official statistics); Evidence.)

The chapter's answer, with its publication left to the house in section 11: the twelve records are one record of the dashboard — ten sections, with the two logs moved to the deviation log — written once per concept, kept in the repository, and drawn into two views. The reasons. First, the European structure's rule meets the book's own measured problem exactly: a date is written in twelve places under twelve names, a status in nine under four meanings, and the chapters themselves say three of their lines are one field — "each concept is only reported upon once" is the cure for that, and the Decision Book's BRK-11 is the same rule. Second, Nygard's objection is to a large document maintained by hand as prose; a record kept in the repository as structured lines, with the build generating its views and refusing a change that leaves a line stale, is the condition Lethbridge found documentation is kept under — "attached to the process for completing a change request" — and is not what Nygard was describing. Third, the two-view form answers the chapters' own split: four records are declared public, six are internal or unstated, two are open; the public view is the reader's (the recipe on the face, the service record beside the page, the measure record beside the panel, the accessibility statement, the parts of the safeguards record marked published), the producer's view is the whole, and the line-by-line "published or not" that Chapter 10 built into the safeguards record becomes a property of every line. Fourth, the growing lists are not records of the dashboard but logs of decisions about it, and they are separated: the boundary log and the precedent record go to the deviation log, next. (Reading; Nightlife Culture.)

The one record's shape, for the build. Its unit is the dashboard; its sections are the ten records' names, kept, because the chapters' readers will look for them and because each section is kept per the unit its chapter set (per figure; per view; per place-page). Its concepts are written once and referenced: one date convention (issued; last changed; next review), one status vocabulary per thing that has a status (a figure's; a line's publication; a compliance claim's; an entry's), one owner line, one who was asked line, one test and result line, one review line per section with a date, and one what this changed line, which the three chapters asked to be one. Its maintenance is a section, as the datasheet's is, with the questions the datasheet asks — who maintains it, where errors go, whether older versions are kept, how obsolescence will be communicated — answered, and the service record's retirement plan is where the last answer lives. Its "not done" convention is the service record's and the claim record's: a line that cannot be filled says so, and the build counts the unfilled lines, because the one measurement of such documents found the limits section filled one time in six. And the public view's face is the recognition and accessibility statements' first words, not its last: as the W3C's partial-conformance sentence and the accessibility statement's model both begin with what is not met, so the public view begins with status and non-compliances. (Reading; Nightlife Culture.)

What the chapter does not decide: whether the whole producer's view is published (Chapter 14 asked whether a log belongs on the page or in the repository with a declaration on the page; Chapter 10 made publication a line-level property; the regimes read publish by default and the one that did not had the waivers nobody re-read); and what the record is called in the house's vocabulary, since the Decision Book's "provenance set" and this book's twelve names now sit under one roof. Both are in section 11. (Nightlife Culture.)

The three logs: one deviation log, with a type

The Decision Book's override log, Chapter 14's boundary log and Chapter 15's precedent record are three growing lists, and Chapter 15 asked whether they are one. They are one log with three types of entry, and the test is the same one as for the records: the concepts recur under different names. All three have the rule or mechanism; the trigger or purchase; the alternative or departure; the test and result; a status; a date; and an owner or reviewer. The boundary log's eleven lines are the override entry specialised for an expressive element — what it is, what it carries, what it buys, the tier claimed, the four removals and the fifth check, the twin, the status; the precedent record's nine lines are the entry specialised for a borrowed mechanism — the source and its date, the rule as printed, the reason given, the evidence, the condition or cost, what the house changes, the status, the review. Each has lines the others lack, which become the type's own fields; each has the spine, which section 10 writes as nine lines. The log is therefore one file in the repository with the nine-line spine of section 10 and a type — departure, expressive element, borrowed mechanism — that opens the type's lines, and the Decision Book's override log is the departure type. Chapter 14 asked whether the boundary log is "the override log's specialisation"; it is. (Reading; Nightlife Culture.)

Two consequences for the records. The claim record's and comparison record's "not done" rule, the safeguards record's "published or not" and the accessibility statement's non-compliances are states of the record rather than deviations, and stay there. And the deviation log is where Chapter 12's "logged with these two results attached" and Chapter 13's "logged with the five results attached" land, with the test and result line carrying them. (Reading.)

The tests: fifty-five, by form, and what the break test actually is

Fifteen sections, nineteen paragraphs, 55 separate tests named: reader test 27, removal 10, record check 7, recomputation 6, adversarial walk 4, and one battery that fits no single form (Chapter 13's scan, two walks and two readers). By the leading test of each chapter: reader test in eleven, removal in two (Chapters 8 and 14), adversarial walk in one half (Chapter 10), record check in one (Chapter 15), recomputation in none. The chapters from 1 to 7 end their test by sending the break to "the deviation entry Chapter 16 describes"; Chapters 8 to 11 do not say to log anything; and from Chapter 7 the section's job changes, from testing a break of a Fixed rule to testing any departure, and in Chapters 12 and 13 it is the page's release test whether or not anything is broken. Version 1's closing chapter said "almost every test turns out to be a form of removal or of adversarial walking"; version 2's tests, counted, are mostly a form of asking the reader the rule protects what they took from the display, which is what Chapter 1 said and twenty-six later tests repeated. The Decision Book's BRK-07, "Run the removal test for the relevant chapter", names the test two chapters lead with. (Reading; the compilation.)

The register resolves this by tying the form of the test to the sense of the tier, which is what the chapters were doing without saying so. A requirement is proved by the check that can fail: a recomputation (the chain arithmetic; the composite from its parts), a record check (the clause quoted; the nine lines filled), an automated scan, a measured removal (the crop test's pass rate; the four removals). A sequence is proved by a record check of dates and order (the record's first line dated before the thing it governs). An Adaptable rule's departure is proved by a reader test — the reader the rule protects, asked what the display says, compared with what was meant — or an adversarial walk where the rule protects against a hostile reader. So the build runs the requirement checks and the sequence checks, and the deviation log's test line names the reader test or walk for the rest, with its result. Version 1's three build checks and the fourth this chapter adds are in section 8. (Reading; Nightlife Culture.)

The flags to this chapter, answered

Six lines carry [Revisit → Ch 16] and 27 more hand something to this chapter in other words. The face sheet, the recognition record, the accessibility statement, the label rule, the purchase table's cut list and the retirement plan as build artefacts (Chapters 11, 12, 13): they are sections of the one record and lines of the deviation log, and section 8 names the build's checks on them. The crop test, the three walks and Chartability as release gates (Chapters 12, 13): requirement checks in the register, run by the build or a named reviewer before release, with the result in the record's test line. The rules register's accessibility rows (Chapter 13): in the register, by chapter, under the requirement sense, with the automated scan as their check. The boundary log as the override log's specialisation (Chapter 14): yes, above. Whether the tier vocabulary adopts "specific sensory experience" (Chapter 14): as a tier of element in the boundary type's "tier claimed" line, not a tier of rule, section 3. The three-sentence evidence standard (Chapter 14): a candidate addition for the Style Guide, in section 11. The precedent record beside the other logs (Chapter 15): one log, three types. The status marks [p] [r] [f] against the dagger (Chapter 15): below. The twelve records as one document (Chapter 15): above. The regulator's minimum list as a checklist the house can voluntarily meet (Chapter 15): the TQV statement is the public view's model and section 11 lists the choice. The retirement plan as a Fixed rule (Chapter 15): Fixed as a sequence, above. What the regime costs the maker (Chapter 11, [Further research]): not priced in this book either; the datasheet's authors say the cost in a sentence — "creating datasheets for datasets will necessarily impose overhead on dataset creators" [read once] — and the build's first release is where the hours are counted. (Reading.)

Forty-four uses of [Revisit at end] reduce to twelve questions. About half are the records-as-one question, answered. Eight or nine are the floor, the threshold and the small room (Chapters 1, 4, 9, 10), which Chapter 10 narrowed to a precision rule and left to the end: the end's answer is that the register carries two floors as two rules of two senses — the disclosure floor as a sequence (set per view before it ships; value Adaptable) and the precision floor on a felt mean as a requirement with Chapter 9's value as the house default — and that a room under both is shown as present and unmeasured, never absent, as Chapters 9 and 10 both already say; who decides which of "unmeasured" or "held" is shown is the scene's governance under Chapter 10's record, and is in section 11 as the house's. Three mention the 60-second version's length, raised nine times before this chapter; this chapter's own runs to five paragraphs, and the question is in section 11. One asks whether "dashboard" survived fifteen chapters: the word appears 1,271 times across Chapters 1 to 15 — least in Chapters 12, 14 and 9 (15, 26 and 28), which say page, view and panel — and the book's own definition from Chapter 1 held; it survived, and it was joined by the three words for its parts. One asks whether "canonical" survived and which truths were cited later: Chapter 3 answered it for itself by splitting seven truths from the findings of record; the register adds a cited by column for truths and rules, which the compilation did not count. One asks whether one display can be legible to eight graders (Chapter 2) and whether truth 1's design consequence should be demoted: Part 3 found a form that keeps the other grammars reachable one step away rather than on the face (Chapter 11's layers; Chapter 2's plain route), so the consequence is re-based to a sequence — the grammar of the first screen is chosen and declared — which is what Chapter 2's own rewritten rule already says. One asks which of the five forms the book's own evidence favours for the measure (Chapter 5) without deciding: the chapters after 5 added no evidence that one form is read better than another, and the question is in section 11 as it was, the studio's. One asks whether the gross-to-net arithmetic becomes a house standard, and one whether the two tests for a canonical truth do (Chapter 6): the first is a Standard (adopted) in the register with the withdrawn guide as its source and the flag it already carries; the second is adopted as Chapter 0's definition, below. One asks whether the dashboard projects at all (Chapter 7): the studio's, section 11. One asks whether a sonified series' three routes are listed in the view record (Chapter 14): yes, in the face sheet's section of the one record. And one asks whether Chapter 15 folds (the fold question): the studio's, section 11. (Reading.)

The gaps: 207 rows, grouped

Sixteen tables; 207 rows; 48 are evidence or official rules the field does not have (23 "no study"; 25 "no official rule, source or custodian, or official sources disagree"); 32 are sources this book could not reach; 4 are decisions that are the studio's; 38 are gaps in the house's own systems; 85 are the book's own apparatus and corrections. Chapters 4, 8, 10 and 11 carry the most (18 and 19 rows each); Chapters 0 and 1 the fewest (4 and 6). The 48 are the book's research agenda, and version 1 said what it is for: "a research agenda the field itself is missing — the instrument can publish evidence, not just use it." In version 2's words, the Vibe Map is the only place most of the 48 can be settled, and each is already a [Prototype flag] or a [Further research] in its chapter. The 32 are a reading list for a library card: the full texts behind the daggers. The 38 are the Decision Book's and the Style Guide's; section 11 carries the fifteen tensions and twelve candidates among them, and the compilation holds the rest by chapter. The 85 are closed by this chapter's fixes to Chapter 0 or were closed where they arose. The register's gap rows are not re-printed here; the compilation holds them by chapter with their first-column text. Chapter 0's cost column — red, amber, yellow, printed in the chapter against the design system's "never RAG tags" and Chapter 0's own "internal only" — is kept internal in the register and shown in the reader as words. (Reading; the compilation.)

The conflict logs: thirty-seven open items

Fifty-seven rows across the chapters, 37 still open: five direct conflicts, fifteen tensions, twelve candidates, four carried to this chapter and one more that is the studio's. The four carried are answered above (two re-tierings, in the register; the dagger, below; the three logs, one). The twelve candidates are the Decision Book's and the Style Guide's to accept, and section 11 lists them. The fifteen tensions are, with one exception, gaps in the house's systems that a prototype will turn into conflicts if it ships first — a status chip that can say what six chapters need it to say; a filter set as a query system; a felt-distribution component; a held-layer status; a dated snapshot and citation; a map whose breaks hold across filters; a label for a generated sentence; the small screen named as the first version — and each is a row in the house's gap register with an interim rule, which the Decision Book requires of itself ("Attach an interim rule to every known gap"); section 11 lists them by document. The exception is the oldest, from Chapter 2, the guide's joy-first register against the plain view for the reader who arrives opposed, which is a design question and the studio's.

The five direct conflicts, which this chapter resolves where the resolution is a reading and refers where it is a decision:

ARG-12, "Never repeat the opposing frame in order to deny it", Fixed in the Decision Book. Chapter 12 found its reason no longer holds against the corrections literature and proposed re-basing or retiring it; Chapters 14 and 15 carried it as unresolved. This chapter adds only that the Decision Book's own re-categorisation rule — borrowed from the coding standard, which allows a guideline to move only to a stricter category — does not apply, because the house's register is not a safety standard and a rule whose reason is wrong is the Decision Book's "rule wrong" kind of gap, which it closes by amending the chapter. The decision remains the studio's; the register carries ARG-12 as disputed with Chapter 12's rule beside it. (Reading.)

DSH-21, empty and error states classed Decorative, against the degraded state as a Fixed procedure (Chapters 8, 11). Resolved as a reading: the rule needs the split both chapters gave it — that a degraded tile shows the last good copy with its age is Fixed as a requirement; how it looks is Decorative. The Decision Book's tier test itself says meaning may not live in the Decorative layer; the age of a stale number is meaning. Referred to the Decision Book's gap register as "rule wrong". (Reading.)

The withheld cell's "why" (Chapter 10). Version 1 and the Decision Book require a withheld cell to say why; the national office states neither rule nor parameter. Chapter 10 narrowed the house rule to the kind of reason. Resolved as that reading: the cell says the kind (withheld for disclosure; unmeasured below the floor; held by the scene), never the parameter, and the parameter is published as policy in the safeguards section of the record if the house so decides — section 11. (Reading.)

DAT-14, "dashed, hatched, or broken" (Chapter 4). Red in Chapter 4's gap table; resolved as a reading: the standard the Decision Book cites rejects a dashed join across a missing point, and the book's rule "never join, dotted or dashed" stands; referred as "rule wrong". (Reading.)

DTA-19, the provenance set's omissions (Chapters 4, 9). The Decision Book's set omits the responsible party and the issued and modified dates, and has no lines for who was asked, who answered and who was not. Resolved by the one record: the provenance section carries Chapter 4's lines and the measure section Chapter 9's; referred as "rule too weak". (Reading.)

And the one standing request: seven chapters in a row, 5 to 11, each ask the Decision Book for a chapter it does not have — on composites, on claims about value, on comparison, on running a dashboard, on felt data, on safeguards, on the surface — and the same seven are Red gap rows. This book's chapters are the candidates, their rules tables the draft, and the register's chapter column is the map from one book to the other. Whether the Decision Book grows by seven chapters, by one on dashboards, or by a pointer to this book is the house's, section 11. (Reading; Nightlife Culture.)

Chapter 0, revised after Chapter 2 and not again until this chapter

Chapter 0's header read "revised 6 October 2026, after Chapters 1 and 2". Seven later chapters opened a thread asking it to change and it had not. Eleven conventions drifted, and the fix for each is listed here so that Chapter 0's revision is a transcription and not a judgement.

The rules-table note (printed in Chapters 1 to 11, absent from 12 to 15): the register makes it unnecessary; Chapter 0 says the register carries the legend. The gap table's columns (four fields in Chapters 0 to 13; four different ones without a cost in 14 and 15): Chapter 0 adopts the later columns and keeps the cost as a word, since the Decision Book's stored form has both a consequence and a status. The conflict log's parts (three in some chapters, two in others, a status table in the last two): Chapter 0 adopts the status table, which is the only form whose rows this chapter could de-duplicate. The section names (three generations of "what this means for a nightlife dashboard"; two of "what people believe"): Chapter 0 prints the latest. The dagger's definition (four wordings): Chapter 0 prints the widest — an abstract or a secondary account — and the ledger carries which. The flag on Fixed rules resting on a dagger: a status in the register, above. The marks Chapter 0 does not define — "reconstructed", "(read once)", "two passes", "adjacent domain", the sub-kinds of Standard: defined in Chapter 0 from the chapters' own glosses. The tiers' definitions (two generations): Chapter 0 prints section 3's three senses of Fixed, the Adaptable (house default), and Decorative with the sensory-experience note. The flag [Counterbalance → Ch n], used fifteen times to point at the design system, the Decision Book or version 1: Chapter 0 widens the definition to any document the finding pulls against. The "symmetry test (Chapter 0)" credited by four chapters to a chapter that did not then contain the word: Chapter 0 defines it, from Chapter 4's gap row where it was born and Chapter 5's use, as the test a chapter runs on its own brief — whether what it found is what the brief expected, and what it did when it was not. And the severity colours in the chapters: internal in the register, words in the reader, as Chapter 0 already said and did not do. Two more things Chapter 0 adopts from later chapters: Chapter 6's two tests for a canonical truth — out-of-sample, and the agreement of the competent — as its definition, which it currently leaves to the reader; and the three positions on the face, one step away, on request. (Reading; Nightlife Culture.)

The book's own marks, against the floor

Chapter 15 found the Analysis Function advising against the dagger: "We do not recommend using symbols such as '. :', '' or '†' anymore because they can be difficult to see and screen reader software can find them hard to recognise." [read once], with its own convention of bracketed letters — "[p] = provisional", "[r] = revised", "[f] = forecast". This book uses the dagger in prose, where a screen reader will read it as a word or not at all, and never in a data table. The chapter's answer, under Chapter 13's floor, is that the book's marks in the reader are rendered as bracketed words — [abstract], [secondary], [read once], [two passes] — which is what they already are in the ledger, and the dagger remains a typographic convenience of the manuscript, as a footnote mark is. The register carries the marks as words. Chapter 0's legend changes accordingly. (Standard (official statistics); Reading; Nightlife Culture.)*

8 · The build's register

The file

The register is one file in the repository, generated from the chapters' tables as the Decision Book's is generated from its chapters ("Generated from chapters/ by build/build_register.py. Do not edit by hand — edit the chapter."), and the compilation made for this chapter is its first input: every one of the 486 rows with its file line. The build keeps the compilation's row identifiers (chapter.row) as the trace back to the chapter and gives each register rule — one per group after de-duplication — an identifier of its own, DD-nnn. Each register row carries ten fields; all but cited by are decided by this chapter from what the chapters printed.

Rule: one wording, the strictest the source chapters share, with the chapters' variants kept in the compilation and not in the register. Tier: one of five — Fixed (requirement), Fixed (sequence), Adaptable (house default), Adaptable, Decorative — with a second tier column for the open part of a rule whose order is fixed and whose form is not. Kind: one of Chapter 0's five, with the sub-kind of Standard in a second field and a one-letter field for whether a Standard binds the studio or is adopted. Source: the chapters' sources, and the chapters themselves by row. Chapter: the chapters that state the rule, first the one that made it. Test: the form — recomputation, record check, scan, removal, reader test, adversarial walk — and, for a requirement, the check the build runs; for a sequence, the records and dates compared; for an Adaptable rule, the reader the rule protects and the question. Status: current; superseded by; disputed; open in the decision log; and the dagger status, full text not read, which the build lists. Cited by: the chapters and truths that lean on the rule, filled by the build and not by this chapter. Record: which section of the one record the rule writes to, where it writes to one. Statement of the record: for the rows that are truths and not rules, which Chapter 0's third sense names and the tables used for none — listed apart, under the chapters' "What holds true regardless", with the register pointing at them.

The shape after re-basing, in the file as built: of 433 Fixed rows, the 212 unmarked and the 102 procedures sorted into requirements and sequences by their wording, and most proved to be requirements the build can test (contrast; thresholds; the floor; the furniture on the face; the lines of a record; the dates); 51 of the 90 stances became Adaptable (house default), the rest having grounds that show a requirement; the 45 Adaptable and 8 Decorative rows stand. The 42 duplicate groups collapsed into one rule each. The register has 377 rules from the source rows: 280 Fixed, of them 245 requirements, most of them checks, and 35 sequences; 56 Adaptable (house default); 34 Adaptable; 7 Decorative, each with its grounds. The share of Fixed, 74 per cent, is the Decision Book's own. (Nightlife Culture; the compilation.)

The checks

Version 1 specified three build-time checks "in the Decision Book's enforcement spirit (a rule that can be measured is a rule that is run)" and seeded no register to run them against. This chapter re-bases the three on version 2's rules and adds a fourth, and separates checks that fail the build from reports that list.

The crop check (version 1): "no exportable state renders an ordered all-places list". Re-based to the three ranking rules of section 7: every exportable state, screenshot region and share is tested for an ordered list of places on any measure, and for the interval and official wording travelling with any ordering that is shown; Chapter 12's measured crop test — a screenshot of each panel put before someone who has not seen the page, scored for what it is about, unit, source, date, gate and the other column — is the reader half, run per release, and its pass rate is written in the record. Fails the build on the first half; reports the second.

The recipe check (version 1): "every displayed composite recomputes from its displayed parts". Re-based to Chapter 5's rules and Chapter 8's chain arithmetic: every composed number is recomputed from the parts shown on its face and one step away, and every live element's arithmetic is rerun with the current data; the recipe section of the record is where the parts are declared. Fails the build.

The state-honesty check (version 1): "every reachable state carries heartbeat, gaps-with-reasons, and threshold behaviour". Re-based to Chapter 8's freshness statement (the data's date, the refresh, the last good copy with its age in the degraded state), Chapter 4's kinds of nothing (every empty cell marked with its kind, never blank), and Chapter 10's floors (every view's disclosure floor set before the view ships, and a room under both floors shown as present and unmeasured, never absent). Walks every reachable state. Fails the build.

The removal check (this chapter, from Chapter 14): every expressive element has an entry in the deviation log of the expressive type, with its four removals and the fifth check run and their results written, and its precise twin one step away. Fails the build where the entry is missing; reports where a removal failed, because the decision to ship a failed removal is a logged departure, not a build error.

And two reports, not gates: the stale-record report — every section of the record whose review date has passed, and every entry of the deviation log whose review date or lapse condition has passed, listed at each build, after the accessibility statement's "last reviewed" line, the datasheet's maintenance questions and the monitoring body's finding that many statements had not been reviewed in a year; and the register report — the rules whose status is disputed, open in the decision log or full-text-not-read, and the record's lines that say "not done", counted, since the one measurement of such documents found the limits section filled one time in six. The sunset principle behind both is older than any of this: in one jurisdiction legislative instruments are "automatically repealed on set dates … 10 years after the instrument is registered", because "Sunsetting ensures that legislative instruments are kept up-to-date and only remain in force for as long as they are needed." (read once; fragments verified). A register entry nobody has re-read by its date is the shuttle's waiver, not a rule. (Nightlife Culture; Reading; Standard (government guidance).)

The gate on the log

The one check that makes the deviation log a record: no change to the build that departs from a rule tiered Fixed (requirement) or Fixed (sequence) is merged without a deviation entry of the departure type in the same change, with its status proposed and its checker named; the build fails on a departure without an entry, and the entry's status moves to accepted only by the named checker. This is Lethbridge's one condition under which records are kept — "attached to the process for completing a change request" — and the government standard's "stored in version control so there is a record of what was changed, who by, and when". With the entry present, the requirement check the departure breaks is marked as a logged exception by the entry's identifier, so the check still runs on everything else and the exception is visible in the register report. For Adaptable rules, the entry is written when the departure is made and the build does not gate it; the stale-record report lists entries without a review date. (Reading; Nightlife Culture.)

The first rows

Ten rows, to show the form and the re-basing; the compilation holds all 486 source rows. The test column names the form and, for a requirement, the check. The identifiers are illustrative: the built register numbers its rules in its own order, and its notes refer to these ten as "Chapter 16 §8 row n".

DD-008 The headline sentence is five words where possible and ten at most Adaptable (house default) · the distance and seconds beneath it, Fixed (requirement) Nightlife Culture; Evidence 14 (11 superseded) reader test (three phones) current; 11.4 superseded
DD-009 Every chart carries, inside its frame, title, unit, source, base, address and snapshot date, in addition to page text and never instead Adaptable (house default), departing from official practice with a logged reason Reading; Standard (W3C) condition 12, 13 crop test, measured current; deviation entry 1
DD-010 A withheld, unmeasured or held cell says its kind, never its parameter Fixed (requirement) · whether the parameter is published as policy, the studio's Standard (official statistics); Reading 4, 10 state-honesty check current

(Nightlife Culture; the compilation.)

9 · The failures, read for the machinery

Carly's eight sentences, read against a register and a log rather than a display.

"A dashboard fails if it looks the same every month." The machinery's version is a register that looks the same every year: rules nobody re-reads, waivers nobody reviews. The review date on every entry and the stale-record report are the answer, and the regimes' near-universal time limit is the precedent. (Reading.)

"It fails if it's just a fancy spreadsheet with some charts that tell you lots of big numbers, but not what actually happens." The register's equivalent is a log that records conclusions — 63 per cent of records born accepted; a reason field with a space in it — and not decisions. The entry written before, with the alternative declined and the test's result, is what records what actually happened. (Reading.)

"It fails if a viewer reads it and asks 'what am I looking at'." A rule set in which 89 per cent of rules carry the strongest word, in fifty-three wordings, 182 kinds and six names for the documents beneath it, is one a reviewer reads and asks that of. Section 3's three senses, section 7's one record and one log, and Chapter 0's revision are the fix; the Decision Book's test is the pass — name the tier, or the register has failed. (Reading.)

"For nightlife, it fails if they do not recognise their place within the front-end interface." The machinery's reader is the scene's own governance under Chapter 10's record, and the one line that touches recognition in the log is who checked. A deviation that changes how a place is shown is checked by someone from the place, which is what Chapter 12's review line already says. (Reading.)

"It fails if people don't use it." The one field that logs every override found that people stop using rules that fire too often, by a measured 30 per cent per extra rule, and that a short top tier set apart is obeyed. A register with 280 Fixed rules enforced by the build and ninety Adaptable rules logged is the design that is used; fifteen checklists ticked by a person is the one that is not. And a research-ethics scholar's sentence about a different regime is the warning for this one: a formalised structure can "rupture the relationship between following the rules and acting ethically" (Haggerty 2004 [abstract or summary only]). (Evidence; Reading.)

"It fails if it breaks or isn't reliable." A Fixed requirement enforced by a check that fails the build is the only kind of rule that cannot be broken by accident; everything else can, and is logged when it is. Hard stops worked in three of four comparisons and people routed around them, so the hard stops are few and the routes around them are reported. (Evidence; Reading.)

"It fails if people don't trust it." The only evidence this book has on disclosed departures is thirty-four editors' stated attitude: a disclosed deviation with a reason was neutral to slightly positive; a concealed one found later was strongly negative. The log is public by default under the regimes read, and the one that was not had a third of its waivers unread in a decade. A dashboard whose makers can say why it is as it is, with the entry to show, is the one the regimes were built to produce; the regulator's finding that its regime produced four good explanations in seventy-four says that the reader of the entry is what makes it work. (Evidence; Reading.)

"It fails if it's an aggregation of 'the biggest'." The machinery's biggest is the Fixed tier: everything important made Fixed, so that nothing Fixed is read. The register's shortest list is the one that is obeyed. (Reading.)

10 · What holds true regardless

Seven things this chapter can state for any rule system beneath a dashboard, each with its kind and its grounds.

1. A tier is a statement about whether a right answer exists, and the fields that draw the same three lines add a top tier that cannot be varied at all, a named approver who is not the designer for departures from the tier below it, and a list of reasons that are never earned. The house's split is verified at source; the IETF's, ISO's, W3C's, the road manual's and the coding standard's are set beside it; and the instruction that comes with every one of them is to use the strongest word sparingly. Standard (method); Fixed (statement of the record). Grounds: Navigating Ambiguity (verified in the publisher's guide); RFC 2119 §6; ISO/IEC Directives Part 2 [read once]; DMRB GG 101; MISRA Compliance 2020 [two passes].

2. A rule set in which nearly everything carries the strongest word is read as noise, and the cost is measured: acceptance falls by a step with each extra rule that fires, and the severe rules are obeyed only where they are set apart, with the limit that the hundred per cent at the tiered site was a hard stop by design and the free-choice evidence is the middle tier's 29 against 10 per cent. Evidence; Fixed (statement of the record). Further research is owed for the full texts behind the daggers. Grounds: Ancker et al. 2017 (30 per cent per additional reminder; 112 clinicians; 1.27 million advisories); van der Sijs 2006 (49–96 per cent [abstract or summary only]); Felisberto 2024 (90 per cent pooled); Nanji 2014 (53 per cent of overrides appropriate, 12–92 by rule [abstract or summary only]); Paterno 2009 (29 against 10 per cent; 100 per cent of the severest at the tiered site, with hard stops [abstract or summary only]); Powers 2018 (hard stops better in 3 of 4; routed around [abstract or summary only]).

3. A written reason improves a decision when it is owed before the decision to a reader whose view is unknown, improves the next reader's decision in most conditions, and is noise when demanded after the fact as a form. Evidence; Fixed (statement of the record). Further research is owed for the full texts behind the daggers. Grounds: Tetlock, Skitka & Boettger 1989 (†); Hoffmann et al. 2017 (null on accuracy; lowered confidence); Chang et al. 2017 (observers' accuracy [abstract or summary only]); the FRC's 4 of 74; the NAO's 20 and 60 per cent; Wright et al. 2019 ("a space or random characters").

4. A deviation is earned by its timing, its specificity, its test and its reader, and the record is where the four are visible; a record written after the fact records an expedient decision for what it is and does not earn it. The entry has nine lines — rule and tier; trigger; alternative, and the one declined; what it buys and what it costs; test and result; who decided and who checked; date; review date or lapse condition; status, with the old entry kept — stated once, below. Reading; Fixed (sequence) (before the departure ships) and Fixed (requirement) (the lines are filled). Grounds: the twelve regimes of section 4; the eight records of section 5; Santana Junior et al. 2026 (63 per cent born accepted [abstract or summary only]); Claesen et al. 2021 (1 of 27 disclosed all).

5. A record is kept current only where updating it is part of the step that makes the change, and a record nobody is paid to re-read decays; so every entry carries a review date and the build lists the entries whose date has passed. Evidence; Fixed (requirement). Grounds: Lethbridge, Singer & Forward 2003; GDS 2024 ("many accessibility statements are now out-of-date"); the Columbia board's 36 per cent (secondary); Klein et al. 2014 (reference rot); the near-universal time limit of section 4.

6. Many records that write the same concept under different names are one record written once per concept and drawn into views, and the view the public sees begins with what is not met. Standard (official statistics); Reading; Fixed (requirement) (each concept once) with the publication of the producer's view the house's. Grounds: Eurostat's SIMS ("each concept is only reported upon once"); the ONS and Analysis Function's two tiers; Nygard against the hand-maintained large document; the compilation's matrix (a date in twelve records under twelve names; three lines the chapters call one field); WCAG's partial-conformance sentence and the accessibility statement's model.

7. A checklist works where it changes what a team does together and its use is observed, and not where it is a document someone is responsible for ticking; a book's rules are therefore enforced by the build where they can be checked and logged where they cannot, and the list a person holds is short. Evidence; Fixed (statement of the record). Further research is owed for the full texts behind the daggers. Grounds: Haynes 2009 (1.5 to 0.8 per cent, eight hospitals [abstract or summary only]); Urbach 2014 (101 hospitals, no significant change [abstract or summary only]); Leape 2014 (98 per cent reported; secondary); Russ 2015 (two-thirds of items; 70 per cent no pause [abstract or summary only]); Bergs 2014 (effect tracks adherence [abstract or summary only]); Degani & Wiener 1990.

Three things the chapter will not state as truths. That disclosing a dashboard's departures costs it nothing (thirty-four editors' stated attitude is the only evidence, and it is about concealment). That a register of 280 Fixed rules is short enough (the fields' folklore figures for how many rules a person can hold were not verifiable at source; the build's first year is where the count is tested). And that the one record will be read (nobody has measured the readership of such records; what is measured is that they are not kept, and the one record is designed for the condition under which they are).

Beneath the dashboard: the rule register and the deviation entry

The twelve records of Chapters 4 to 15 are, after section 7, one record of the dashboard with ten sections, the boundary log and the precedent record having gone to the deviation log; this chapter leaves nothing beneath the dashboard and two things beside it, in the repository: the rule register, whose fields section 8 gives and whose rows the compilation holds, and the deviation log, whose entry is given once here. The log has three types — departure, expressive element, borrowed mechanism — and the second and third open the lines Chapters 14 and 15 specified; the nine lines below are the spine every type carries.

Line What it holds Why
Rule and tier The register's identifier, the rule's wording, and its tier in the register's sense A departure from a requirement, a sequence and a default are three different things
Trigger What made the departure necessary, specific to this case — the data, the reader, the device, the deadline Four of seventy-four explanations were judged high quality by their own regulator; "lack of time or knowledge" is not a reason
Alternative What was done instead, and the alternative that was considered and declined, with why A departure with "a reasonable alternative" available is expedient by the coding standard's rule
Buys and costs What the break buys, from the house's list — attention, retention, comprehension, context, register or fit — and what it costs, named "An unnamed break is a mistake made confidently"; a purchase without a price is a bet
Test and result The form — recomputation, record check, scan, removal, reader test, adversarial walk — and what it showed, as a result and not a tick "it is not the act of ticking off a checklist … but performance of the actions it calls for"
Who decided, who checked Two names; the second not the first, and where the departure changes how a place is shown, someone from the place The regimes that work have a reader; the waivers nobody re-read were granted by those who wanted them
Date When the entry was written, before the departure ships; and, for an entry written after, that it was A record born "accepted" records a conclusion; the quality vocabulary keeps two words for before and after
Review The date by which the entry is re-read, or the condition on which it lapses, and who owns it Near-universal in the regimes read; absent in the house's four lines; the build lists the overdue
Status Proposed; accepted; superseded by; lapsed — with the old entry kept and never edited "If a decision is reversed, we will keep the old one around, but mark it as superseded."

A filled example, invented, for method only. Rule and tier: the official practice, and the design system's preference, for text outside images (Analysis Function; Style Guide) — the source rule that DD-009 departs from, held in the register as Adaptable (house default) for the house, since the practice does not bind it. Trigger: the crop test; panels shared as screenshots from the page lose their title, unit, source and date, and the place-page is the one most likely to be shared as an image. Alternative: every chart carries title, unit, source, base, address and snapshot date inside its frame, in addition to the page text and never instead; declined — page text only with a share control that attaches provenance to the image, because the share control is bypassed by a screenshot. Buys and costs: context (provenance travels with the crop); costs density on a phone and a second copy of six items on every panel. Test and result: the measured crop test, Chapter 12's form — screenshots of each panel put before readers who had not seen the page, scored for subject, unit, source, date, gate and the other column — run on the first build; result, invented for the example, 18 of 20 readers named the source and date from the crop alone, 11 of 20 the gate; the gate line is to be redrawn. Who decided, who checked: the design lead; the accessibility reviewer, against the W3C criterion Chapter 13 stated the condition for. Date: written before the panel shipped, 6 October 2026. Review: at the first release's crop test, and when the design system's in-frame provenance block exists; owner, the design lead. Status: proposed when written; accepted on the result above, with the gate line's redraw as a new entry. The example decides nothing about the Vibe Map's panels; it shows what the entry looks like when a house rule departs from a cited practice with a reason, a cost and a result.

[Revisit at end] is answered here, for the last time: the twelve records are one record; the three logs are one log; and whether the producer's view is published is the house's, in section 11.

11 · Where the choice is yours

Every decision the fifteen chapters left to the studio, in one place, grouped by what it decides. Each stays where its chapter put it; this is the index.

The book's own form. Whether to trim the template's restatement in the chapters (asked at Chapter 12). Whether the 60-second version keeps its form or becomes sixty seconds (raised ten times; this chapter's runs to five paragraphs). Whether Chapter 15 stands or folds into Chapters 2 and 5 (the brief's note; the count is about forty mechanisms, about six already in the book). Whether the sector composite's method audit sits in Chapter 5 or Chapter 15. Whether a library pass for the unreached full texts behind the daggers is scheduled — 32 unreachable sources in the gap tables, and 49 Fixed rows resting on one. Whether a figure is added to the chapters, which no chapter has.

The measure. The form question — composite, dashboard, profile, user-weighted, longitudinal self-profile — which the chapters after 5 added no evidence to; whether the measure is one-tailed, two-tailed or built to find what thrives; whether the gross-to-net arithmetic is adopted from a withdrawn guide; which register of a vibe is measured first and whether the excess register is ever scored; standard attribute words or the scene's own; the bands; who does the member checking; whether any trace or signal indicator is shown before validation.

The data. Whether "not applicable" becomes a seventh kind of nothing; which grain is displayed, with the administrative unit beside it; whether readers may draw their own unit; the disclosure floor's value per view and whether suppression, banding or perturbation is declared per layer; whether the parameter of a withheld cell is published as policy; the held layer's resolution and who governs it; the withdrawal tiers and the cut-off; whether the public may contribute at all; whether the DPIA is published; the lawful basis as reported, and whether counsel is asked; whether any platform interface is called with the terms open, and whether a free public page is "commercial" under them; and who decides, for a room under both floors, between "unmeasured" and "held" — the scene's governance under Chapter 10's record is the chapters' answer, and the house's name for the layer is open.

The surface. Which landing pattern and which exemplar; the headline sentence's length (Adaptable (house default) in the register; the official limits beside it); whether a sentence is generated per place; which interactions from the purchase list, and whether to hover at all; when states are frozen; the map's form and breaks; one sentence or three for the three user groups; how the vague place is drawn; how the two columns are composed; which identity fields in what order, and what question the profile answers; whether the house labels places or types; the peer method; how much of the discovery layer exists; the review's form and the errors channel; whether the Vibe Map projects at all; whether to publish the dashboard's own reach figures; vector or raster for the face; which tile supply; the availability objective.

Expression. Whether the committee export is a separate deliverable or the stripped state of the page; whether a probe is built for the two-audience claim; the club-flyer question itself, which Chapter 14 set out and stopped at.

Access. Whether the adviser's view is sought now on what the Act's duty asks of the studio, what "funded" covers, and whether a published statement of partial compliance has consequences for a body not bound; which routes for the map and in what order; which screen readers, browsers and platforms are tested with; which sans serif and which body size between 16 and 18 pixels; how the reduced-motion page looks.

The records and the log. Whether the producer's view of the one record is published, in whole, in part by line as the safeguards record does, or declared on the page and kept in the repository (the regimes publish by default); what the one record is called in the house's vocabulary, now that the Decision Book's "provenance set" and twelve names sit under one roof; whether the deviation log is public (Chapter 14 asked it of the boundary log); whether the house publishes a statement in the regulator's voluntary form and asks to be listed; whether a trust question is run at all, and in whose waves; whether reach is measured by asking, of whom and how often; the retirement plan's contents; which of Chapter 15's mechanisms are adopted beyond the seven truths; the identifier scheme of the register, provisionally DD-nnn.

The house's two documents. ARG-12 — re-base or retire, with Chapter 12's reasons; the register carries it as disputed. The four other direct conflicts, resolved here as readings and referred: DSH-21 split; the withheld cell's kind not parameter; DAT-14 never joined; DTA-19's missing lines. The fifteen tensions, each a gap in the house's systems with an interim rule owed: the status chip that can say what six chapters need (the kind of nothing; a robustness mark; the kind of claim; the comparison's terms; "indicator, unvalidated here"; held distinct from withheld); the filter set as a query system; a form for position against limits; a raster or static map fallback and a twin-table component; a freshness statement component and a running-foot date slot; a felt-distribution component; the provenance lines for who was asked; one identifying threshold per view; the held layer as a status with a decider, resolution, reason and review date; a dated snapshot and generated citation; map breaks held across filters; a label for generated text; the small screen named as the first version; the body size against the 18-point finding; and the joy-first register against the plain view for the reader who arrives opposed, which is the one that is a design question. The twelve candidates (eleven rows) logged by Chapters 14 and 15: the three-sentence evidence standard; the tier test's note on sensory experience; the boundary type of the log; "alongside" amended to "one step away, finding in words on the form"; the polarity choice for dark grounds; the human figure as a mark, priced; the retirement plan and vintages from the first release; the ELS field list as the recipe's minimum; the usage text beside any ordering; colour only for significance with the one-in-twenty sentence and bracketed status marks; the two measurement rules for trust and use. And whether the Decision Book grows by the seven chapters Chapters 5 to 11 asked for — composites; claims about value; comparison; running a dashboard; felt data; safeguards; the surface — plus the candidate sections from Chapters 12 and 13 (the place-page; the statement), by one chapter on dashboards, or by a pointer to this book.

12 · A nightlife illustration — method only

An illustration of the method, not a decision about the Vibe Map. Suppose a page about a scene carries, under its sentence, a small chart of a counted series with late returns — the kind Chapter 15 borrowed the incomplete-tail band for — and the designer wants to animate the band's edge as the data fill in, because the page is dull and the band is the one thing on it that tells the reader the truth about the data. The register is consulted first, as the Decision Book says: motion is Chapter 14's; the rule there is that an expressive element may not carry data it does not have and must survive the four removals, and its tier in the register is a requirement for the removals and Adaptable (house default) for the form. The tier found, the argument is over before it starts: the animation is a logged expressive element, not a breach, provided the removals pass. The designer writes the entry of the expressive type before the element ships — what it is (a moving edge on the band); what it carries (nothing the still band does not); what it buys, from the list (attention; register); the tier claimed (Decorative, if it can be ignored, or sensory experience, if it cannot, in which case it is identified in text); the four removals — mono, silent, still, undressed — and the fifth check, the still band saying what the moving one says; the twin, one step away; who decided and who, from the scene, checked; the date; the review; the status, proposed. The build's removal check finds the entry and runs the removals; the still removal passes because the band is drawn before it moves; the reduced-motion page shows the still band by rule. The entry's status moves to accepted when the named checker has read it. Six months on, the stale-record report lists the entry because its review date was the first release's crop test and the test was run; the designer re-reads it, finds the band's edge is now read by one tester as the series ending, and writes a new entry that supersedes the first, keeping it. That is what the machinery does when a rule in this book is broken well. (Nightlife Culture; method only.)

What proves a break works

The test for a departure from one of this chapter's rules is the Decision Book's own, with one line added. Take any decision currently being argued about in a project and name its tier from the register. If it is a requirement, the argument is over and the build's check decides; if it is a sequence, the record's dates decide; if it is Adaptable, the argument is a design conversation to be had properly and its outcome is an entry; if it is Decorative, there was never anything to argue about. If the tier cannot be found, the register has failed, not the argument — and that is a gap in the register, logged in four fields with an interim rule, and closed only when a rule exists that would have caught it. Then find the entry: a departure from this chapter's own rules — a Fixed register that grew long; an entry written after; a record edited rather than superseded; a review date left blank — is proved to work the way every other one is, by the entry that says so, read by someone who did not write it, with a date on which it is read again. If no such entry exists, it was not a break; it was the undocumented expedient decision, and the Decision Book has already said what that is indistinguishable from.

What this chapter could not settle

  • The Decision Book's deviation taxonomy is a checklist line with no definitions; defined here from the regimes' forbidden grounds.
  • The override log is printed five times in three forms, and the chapters added a fourth; the nine-line entry stated once in section 10.
  • The tier test's second borrowed book is dated 2021; the third sentence is a question at source; corrected in the register's source rows.
  • 49 Fixed rows rest on a dagger with no flag; a status in the register.
  • 17 Fixed rules are sourced only to the book; Adaptable (house default), or a sequence for the record-carriers.
  • The Kind column has 182 wordings; five kinds, a sub-kind field, a binds/adopted letter.
  • No experiment on whether a disclosed deviation costs a reader's trust; thirty-four editors' stated attitude, reported as that.
  • No study isolating the effect of a mandatory logged reason on an override rate; Wright 2019 and Powers 2018 reported for what they measure.
  • No measurement of who reads decision records; decay reported instead.
  • The regime's cost to the maker is unpriced; counted in the first release.
  • The field's folklore figures for how many rules a person can hold were not verifiable; not printed.

Checklist

  • The tier found in the register before the argument, in one of its five wordings
  • The departure classified — ignorant (fix the register), lazy (a breach), expedient (logged, cheap to reverse) or earned (nine lines)
  • Neither forbidden reason: not convenience; no reasonable alternative untaken
  • The entry written before the change ships, in the same change, type named
  • A checker named who is not the author; from the place, where the place is what changes
  • The test's form matched to the tier's sense, and its result written, not ticked
  • A review date or lapse condition on the entry, and on every record section touched
  • Nothing accepted edited; superseded and kept
  • The stale-record and register reports read at this build
  • If the register had no rule: the gap logged with an interim rule, and closed only by a rule that would have caught it

Words this chapter uses

  • The tier test is the Decision Book's first move on any disagreement: decide whether a rule is Fixed, Adaptable or Decorative before arguing about it. Deference is the Decision Book's name for treating an Adaptable decision as if it were Fixed; negligence for treating a Fixed one as if it were Adaptable.
  • A deviation is a departure from a rule; the Decision Book names four kinds — "ignorant, lazy, expedient or earned" — in one checklist line and nowhere defines them, and section 4 does.
  • The override log is the Decision Book's four-line record of a deliberate departure — "Trigger · rule and tier · alternative chosen · evidence"; the boundary log (Chapter 14) and the precedent record (Chapter 15) are this book's two further logs, and section 7 asks whether the three are one.
  • The compilation is kept as a working file beside this chapter (02-research-notes/ch16-assembly.md) and its counts are the chapter's evidence about itself.
  • Comply or explain is the corporate-governance regime in which a company may depart from a code if it explains; disproportionate burden is the accessibility regulations' name for a self-assessed exemption; a waiver is a regulator's permission to depart from a rule; a concession and a deviation permit are the quality-management vocabulary for permission after and before the fact; exception reporting is the family-doctor contract's mechanism for excluding a patient from a target.
  • An architecture decision record is software's one-file-per-decision convention; a preregistration deviation is a departure from a study's registered plan; a changelog is a dated list of a product's notable changes; a datasheet and a model card are machine learning's one-document conventions.
  • Alert fatigue is the clinical finding that rules which fire too often are overridden by reflex.
  • Version 1 is this book's archived first draft; its Chapter 14 is this chapter's predecessor.

BThe decision log

Every open choice in one place, with the book's steer and the moment the build will raise it

14 October 2026. The one place an open choice lives. The book is finished; its chapters state positions and leave trade-offs open for the build. This log gathers every open choice the book carries, gives each the book's steer, and names the moment the build will raise it. When that moment comes, look at the steer, use it or change it, and move on. Nothing here waits on anyone before then.

In this appendix

  • At a glance
  • A · Before the first screen is designed
  • B · The data
  • C · The measure
  • D · Claims about value, comparison and time
  • E · Running it
  • F · Safeguards and consent
  • G · The first screen and the surface
  • H · Access
  • I · Expression
  • J · The records, the log and the house's documents
  • K · The book's own form
  • Not in this log, and why
  • Register queries

How it works

  • Each entry: the question, what rides on it, the options, the book's steer and why, what it touches, its status.
  • Ordered by when the build will raise them: what the first screen raises comes first. None holds anything up; each is a question to answer when it comes up, with the book's steer in hand.
  • Where a chapter states a position, the steer is that position, in the chapter's words where possible. Where the chapter states none, the steer is the book's reading of its own evidence and is marked [Proposal].
  • When a choice is made: status becomes Decided, with the date and the words used. The chapter text it touches is edited once. Options not chosen are removed.
  • Identifiers are DB-nn (Dashboard book), so they never collide with the Data Brain's D-nn or the register's DD-nnn.
  • Where a probe in 03-tests/PROBES.md already tests the choice, "Comes up when" names it.

Where these came from. The sixteen chapters' "Where the choice is yours" sections, read through the chapter writers' edit notes (08-edit/edit-notes/chNN-NOTES.md, section 3); Chapter 16 §11, the book's own index of open choices in nine groups; the 7 October list in 00-plan/STATE.md; the chapters themselves for a position's wording; and the probe register. Choices that recur across chapters (the floors and the small room; the peer method; the one record; the length of the 60-second version) are merged into one entry each, with every chapter and rule they touch listed. Merged, they made 91 entries. Items the edit itself settled are listed at the end, with the reason each is not a decision, followed by the queries for the register.

A · Before the first screen is designed

The first screen raises these. Each is a choice about what the dashboard is for and whom it speaks to, and every later choice inherits it.

DB-01 · Which job is the dashboard for: monitoring, analysis or communication?

  • Question. Is the Vibe Map built to watch, to explain, or to persuade?
  • What rides on it. The cadence, the depth of each panel, and what counts as the dashboard failing.
  • Options.
    • Monitoring: a heartbeat of figures, refreshed on a cadence.
    • Analysis: figures with their reasons, for a reader who digs.
    • Communication: an authored account, for a reader who decides.
  • Steer. "A public-interest dashboard is realistically a communication and analysis object with a monitoring heartbeat; a position, not a law" (Chapter 1 §10).
  • Touches. Chapter 1 §10; Chapter 11 (the layers).
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-02 · Whose grammar does the first screen speak, and is it one sentence or three?

  • Question. Which reader comes first on the first screen, and does the headline speak once or once per user group?
  • What rides on it. Chapter 2's evidence is that the official reader's grammar will be used to discount the others, and the scene's to judge whether the thing is real. Chapter 2 asked whether one display can be legible to eight graders at all.
  • Options.
    • The official reader's grammar first, the scene's reachable.
    • The scene's grammar first, the official reader's reachable.
    • One sentence for all, or three to choose between (Chapter 11; probe 48).
  • Steer. "Adaptable in the choice, Fixed in declaring it" (Chapter 2 §11, rule 2.25). Chapter 16 §7 closes Chapter 2's doubt: Part 3 found a form that keeps the other grammars reachable one step away rather than on the face, so "the grammar of the first screen is chosen and declared". One sentence or three is tested by probe 48 before any default is fixed.
  • Touches. Rule 2.25; Chapter 2 §11 and 60-second version; Chapter 11 §11; Chapter 16 §7 and §11.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-03 · How much to frame, and is the plain table a first-class route?

  • Question. Does the dashboard author its framing or offer a configurable surface; and for the reader who arrives opposed, is a plain-table view a route of its own?
  • What rides on it. The joy-first register against the sceptic's table is the one of Chapter 16's fifteen tensions that "is a design question". Chapter 2 holds the plain table as a hypothesis, not a rule.
  • Options.
    • Authored framing, honestly labelled (Chapter 1).
    • A configurable surface the reader frames.
    • A plain-table view as a first-class route for the opposed reader (rule 2.10), or the table twin alone (DD-001).
  • Steer. "Authored framing, honestly labelled" (Chapter 1 §10). The plain-table route stays "a hypothesis to test" (Chapter 2 §11, rule 2.10) until probe 7 shows whether opposed readers choose the table; the twin exists either way.
  • Touches. Chapter 1 §10; rules 2.10, 2.25; Chapter 16 §7 (the fifteenth tension); DD-001 (see Register queries).
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-04 · Is the Vibe Map a justified dashboard?

  • Question. Does it have a named reader, a cadence, a combination of figures that must be seen together, and a resource to keep it running?
  • What rides on it. Chapter 11's symmetry test: a dashboard that cannot answer these four is a report with a refresh button.
  • Options.
    • Answer the four in the face sheet before the first screen.
    • Build and see.
  • Steer. Answer the four in the face sheet before the first screen is designed; Chapter 1's reading (DB-01) already supplies the first two. Chapter 11 states no position. [Proposal]
  • Touches. Chapter 11 working record (symmetry test); Chapter 1 §10.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-05 · Which failures to prevent first?

  • Question. In what order does the build guard against the ways a dashboard fails?
  • What rides on it. The first year's tests and the order of the probe programme (DB-88).
  • Steer. "The evidence ranks them: non-use and distrust kill a dashboard outright; aggregation and non-recognition kill its truth; the others degrade it; the order is the studio's" (Chapter 1 §10).
  • Touches. Chapter 1 §10; Chapter 16 §9.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-06 · How much mud to let in?

  • Question. How much uncertainty, gap and uncounted thing does the face admit?
  • What rides on it. A tidier face is read as more certain than the data is; a muddier one is read as less finished.
  • Steer. "Where to set that dial is a judgement about the reader. Adaptable; the floor — never a blank where there is a reason — is Fixed" (Chapter 1 §10).
  • Touches. Chapter 1 §10; Chapter 4 §6 (the six kinds of nothing); Chapter 3 (uncertainty forms, DB-62).
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-07 · Monetise, quantify or describe; which numbers does the investor see?

  • Question. Does the dashboard put a pound sign on value, a count, or words; and for the investor, property value, footfall, business births or something else?
  • What rides on it. The money view is what the official reader discounts by, and what the scene says is not the point. Each investor number tells a different story about the same place, and each is what another reader fears. Whether the money view exists at all is part of DB-67.
  • Options.
    • Monetise; quantify without money; describe; or do both and label which is which.
    • For the investor: any of the three numbers, with the choice shown.
  • Steer. "Do both and label which is which; the labelling is Fixed" (Chapter 2 §11, rule 2.4). The investor's numbers: "Adaptable; showing the choice is Fixed" (rule 2.18).
  • Touches. Rules 2.4, 2.18; Chapter 6 (claims about value); Chapter 12 §12 (the money view and the rising-value panel); probe 45.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-08 · Where does lived experience sit: panel, frame, or route to change?

  • Question. Is the scene's account a panel beside the figures, the frame around them, or the route by which the figures are changed?
  • What rides on it. A supplement panel is what Chapter 2 found the field does and prohibits: testimony shown and nothing changed.
  • Steer. "Adaptable in form; the dialogue that can change the account is Fixed; the supplement panel is prohibited" (Chapter 2 §11, rule 2.22).
  • Touches. Rule 2.22; Chapter 9 §15; Chapter 12 (the recognition record); DB-30.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-09 · Is keeping the problem documented between windows the dashboard's job?

  • Question. When the policy window closes, does the dashboard carry the record of the problem, or does a report?
  • What rides on it. Chapter 2's finding that the problem has to be documented when nobody is asking, so that it is ready when someone is.
  • Options.
    • The dashboard holds the dated record.
    • A report does, cited from the dashboard.
  • Steer. The dashboard holds the dated record, since its snapshots and vintages exist for exactly this (Chapters 8 and 11); the report makes the argument when the window opens. Chapter 2 states no position. [Proposal]
  • Touches. Rule 2.9; Chapter 8 (vintages); Chapter 11 (snapshots).
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-10 · Is a trust question run at all, and in whose waves?

  • Question. Does the studio ask its readers whether they trust the display, and does it ask in its own survey or ride on someone else's?
  • What rides on it. Distrust is one of the two failures that "kill a dashboard outright" (DB-05) and the book has no measure of it without asking. Register DD-033 carries this as its open part.
  • Options.
    • Run it in the studio's own waves.
    • Add a question to a sector wave.
    • Do not run it.
  • Steer. Run it, as probe 73 "Trust in the display itself", in the studio's own waves until a sector wave will carry it; Chapter 16 names "the two measurement rules for trust and use" among the Decision Book candidates. No chapter states a position. [Proposal]
  • Touches. Rule 1.14; Chapter 1 §4; Chapter 15 §9; Chapter 16 §11; DD-033; probe 73.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-11 · Is reach measured by asking, of whom and how often; are the dashboard's own figures published?

  • Question. How does the studio know who the dashboard reached, and does it say?
  • What rides on it. Chapter 15 found that server counts are reported as reach across the sector and are not reach. Chapter 11 notes that publishing the dashboard's own use "would be the first public evidence of its kind".
  • Steer. "Server counts are not reach and are not reported as reach; the asking is the studio's" (Chapter 15 §9; Chapter 16 §7). Publish the result under Chapter 10's analytics rule, since nothing else in the field does and the book's own argument asks for it. [Proposal on publishing]
  • Touches. Chapter 11 §11; Chapter 15 §9; Chapter 16 §7 and §11; probes 4, 72.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

B · The data

What the first table and the first withheld cell raise.

DB-12 · Which grain and which unit does the page land on?

  • Question. Venue, operator, room, event, night or person; and the scene scale or the administrative unit?
  • What rides on it. Everything is counted at the grain shown; the unit decides which reader recognises the place and which can compare it (the MAUP; comparability over time for settlement-shaped units).
  • Steer. "The one shown is named and its row count stated" (Chapter 4 §12, rule 4.1). "The scene scale is the house's declared choice; declared, with the administrative unit beside it and the cost recorded" (Chapter 12 §12).
  • Touches. Rule 4.1; DD-021; Chapter 12 §3 and §12; Chapter 16 §11.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-13 · Which instant or window stands for a day; is 6pm to 6am the display's night?

  • Question. What rule assigns an event that crosses midnight to a date, and is the official night time window the display's?
  • What rides on it. "When an activity has a daily rhythm, the instant or window chosen to stand for the day decides how much of the activity is counted" (Chapter 4 §3).
  • Steer. "Any boundary that suits its subject, provided it is stated and never changed silently" (Chapter 4 §12, rule 4.3). The chapter "takes the window only as an official definition"; the display's rule may be any rule, written down.
  • Touches. Rule 4.3; DD-078; Chapter 4 §3 and §13.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-14 · Which denominator to lead with?

  • Question. Residents, visitors, venues, area, or something else, under each rate?

  • Touches. Rule 4.5; DD-020; DB-40.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-15 · Which concentration instrument, and are distributional figures weighted?

  • Question. How is the spread of a quantity shown, and may it be weighted by another value?
  • Steer. "A median beside the mean is the minimum; showing none is not an option under truth 5" (Chapter 4 §12, rule 4.25). The display "may show the distribution unweighted or weight by another value; may not weight silently" (Chapter 6 §11).
  • Touches. Rule 4.25; DD-089; Chapter 6 §11; probe 19.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-16 · Is "not applicable" a seventh kind of nothing?

  • Question. Every official scheme splits "not collected" into not applicable and not asked; the studio's six kinds do not. Add a kind, split the fifth, or mark a sub-kind?
  • What rides on it. "A decision about the display's vocabulary" (Chapter 4 §12): every status chip, legend and record uses the kinds.
  • Options.
    • A seventh kind.
    • Split the fifth kind (not collected) in two.
    • A labelled sub-kind of the fifth.
  • Steer. Hold the six until probe 15 ("Which nothing reads as which") has been read with readers; until then mark "not applicable" as a labelled sub-kind of not collected, so the vocabulary does not grow before the test. Chapter 4 states no position. [Proposal]
  • Touches. Rule 4.14; DD-083; Chapter 4 §6 and §12; Chapter 16 §11; probe 15 (P-034, P-042).
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-17 · How is a nothing shown, and what can the status chip say?

  • Question. Code, word, pattern or sentence; blank, hatched or annotation; and can one chip carry what six chapters ask of it (the kind of nothing; a robustness mark; the kind of claim; the comparison's terms; "indicator, unvalidated here"; held distinct from withheld)?
  • Steer. "A design decision under Chapter 3's colour and word rules and the design system" (Chapter 4 §12). The holes' form on the place-page "is Decorative provided the kind is named" (Chapter 12 §12). The chip is the first of Chapter 16's fifteen tensions and owes an interim rule (DB-84).
  • Touches. DD-015 (open part); Chapter 4 §12; Chapter 12 §12; Chapter 16 §7; probes 15, 16.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-18 · How much provenance and composition on the face, in what form, and does it fit a phone?

  • Question. What of the record, and of a composed number's recipe card, sits on the face of every panel; how is it set inside the frame (footer strip, margin block, stamp); and is it legible at phone size?
  • What rides on it. The crop test: panels shared as screenshots lose their title, unit, source and date (DL-001). Chapter 12's in-frame rule is a departure from official practice.
  • Steer. "Period, status and the fact that caveats exist at minimum; the rest one tap away" (Chapter 4 §12, rule 4.7). For a composed number, "the fact of composition and the existence of the card, at minimum; the rest is Chapter 11's layout decision" (Chapter 5 §14). "The departure from official practice is the chapter's rule; its form is open within Chapter 13's criteria" (Chapter 12 §12). Chapter 13 finds the criteria met and leaves legibility to the prototype.
  • Touches. Rule 4.7; DD-005; DD-006; Chapter 5 §12 and §14 (DD-112); Chapter 12 §12; Chapter 13 §7 and §11; DL-001; probe 13; DB-89.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-19 · Suppress, round, band or perturb?

  • Question. By which method is a small cell protected, and is it the same across views?
  • Steer. "The Decision Book chooses suppression with secondary suppression; made once and declared" (Chapter 4 §12, rule 4.18). "Once per layer, declared, consistent across views" (Chapter 10 §19, rule 10.7).
  • Touches. Rules 4.18, 10.7; DD-015; Chapter 16 §7 tier table.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-20 · What value does the disclosure floor take, per view?

  • Question. Below what count is a cell withheld, in each view, and who sets it?
  • What rides on it. The floor is what makes the small cells a local reader needs disappear; set too high it empties the map, too low it names people.
  • Options.
    • Three, the static-table convention.
    • Five, the office's suggestion for online tools.
    • Higher, where the scene can name the units.
  • Steer. "The procedure is Fixed; the number is the studio's, per view, and stated" (Chapter 10 §19, rule 10.5). Chapter 6: "the procedure in section 11 is fixed; its number is not". Chapter 16's register carries it as Fixed (sequence), "set per view before it ships; value Adaptable".
  • Touches. Rule 10.5; Chapter 6 §11; Chapter 1 §10; Chapter 16 §7; probes 41, 42, 43.
