DB-21 · The floor of fifty against the small room: unmeasured or held, and who decides?

  • Question. A felt measure for a room with fewer than fifty answers is not published. Is such a room shown as unmeasured or as held, who decides, and what does the house call the held layer?
  • What rides on it. Most of the scene's rooms are small. Shown as absent they vanish; shown as held they look hidden.
  • Steer. "A room under the floor is shown as present and unmeasured, never as absent" (Chapter 9 truth 3). "Who decides which of 'unmeasured' or 'held' is shown is the scene's governance under Chapter 10's record" (Chapter 16 §7); "the house's name for the layer is open" (Chapter 16 §11). The precision floor itself is a requirement with Chapter 9's value as the house default.
  • Touches. Chapter 9 §15 and truth 3; Chapter 10 §5 "Two floors" and §14; Chapter 16 §7 and §11; Chapter 1 §10; Chapter 12 §12; probe 15; DB-34.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-22 · Does a withheld cell state its rule, and is the parameter published as policy?

  • Question. Does the cell say "withheld" or "withheld under five", and does the safeguards record publish the number?
  • Steer. "The cell says the kind, never the parameter; publication is the house's" (Chapter 16 §7). Publish the parameter once, in the safeguards record's public view, since a reader who can find the rule can find the number anyway and the record is where Chapter 10 puts it. Chapter 10 states no position. [Proposal]
  • Touches. Chapter 10 §6, §7 and §19; DD-255; DD-010; Chapter 16 §7 and §8; probe 44.
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-23 · Which outlier rule and threshold?

  • Steer. "Median absolute deviation and 2.5 as the literature's default; rule written before the data arrives" (Chapter 4 §12, rule 4.32).
  • Touches. Rule 4.32; DD-094; rule 1.13 and DD-030 (see Register queries).
  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-24 · Which peer method, and how many peers?

  • Question. CIPFA nearest neighbours, the ONS classification, a bespoke set, or none; twenty by Euclidean distance, ten with closeness labels, or the studio's own?
  • What rides on it. A field of twenty-odd districts; the peer set is the comparison every other panel inherits, and its variables must not include the thing compared.
  • Steer. "The method is published and fixed; which it is, and the variables, are the studio's and the scene's judgement" (Chapter 7 §12). Chapter 4: "open; must be shown; variables must not include the thing compared". Chapter 12 carries it unchanged.

  • Status. Open · 14 Oct 2026.

DB-25 · How is a vague place drawn, and may readers draw their own unit?

  • Question. Core and bands for a scene with no administrative boundary; and can a reader outline an area and get figures for it?

  • Steer. "Core and bands; thresholds (25/50/75 are one precedent) and n are the studio's" (Chapter 12 §12). Reader-drawn units not in the first version: the walk (probe 42) does not yet exist; revisit once the held layer and the intruder walk are built. Chapter 12 states no position on the second beyond the cost. [Proposal on the second]

C · The measure

What the first composite and the first felt panel raise.

DB-26 · Which form: composite, dashboard, profile, user-weighted, longitudinal self-profile, hybrid?

  • Question. Is the vibe one number, a set, a profile, or something the reader weights?
  • What rides on it. A composite is what decision-makers are said to want and what hides a failing part; a profile keeps the parts visible and is harder to quote.
  • Steer. "Whichever is chosen, the components travel with it" (Chapter 5 §14). The chapters after 5 "added no evidence that one form is read better than another" (Chapter 16 §7). Start as a profile, which every form reduces to, and compose only once probes 20 (sensitivity) and 21 (what the weights really do) have been run on real data. [Proposal]

DB-27 · Which construct, which parts, and how is the measure audited?

  • Question. What the measure is of, which parts compose it, and against which independent measure, how often and by whom it is checked.
  • Steer. "The framework is the studio's and the scene's; the rule is only that it is written first and each part carries Chapter 4's provenance" (Chapter 5 §14). The audit is "designed with the measure" (Chapter 5 §7); name the independent measure in the measure record before the first composite is computed, with Chapter 9's descriptor validation as the first candidate. [Proposal on the audit]

DB-28 · Who sets the weights?

DB-29 · Which aggregation, and which tail?

DB-30 · How is recognition gathered, who checks, in what forum, with what power to say no?

  • Question. Member checks of fact, a synthesised late check, a deliberative choice of parts, or all three; who does the member checking and how often; what form the review takes (room, sheet, data walk, online draft) and where the errors channel sits; who the competent are.
  • What rides on it. Recognition is one of the Vibe Map's four tests. "Anything less is a nod" (Chapter 2).

DB-31 · Which register of a vibe is measured first, is the excess register scored, and whose bands?

  • Question. Which of the three registers goes first; whether the third is ever scored; the national cut-points or the scene's own.

DB-36 · What form does "what this changed" take?

F · Safeguards and consent

What the first personal datum and the first contribution raise.

DB-49 · Which lawful basis, and what goes to counsel?

  • Question. Which lawful basis is claimed; whether the research and statistics provisions are claimed at all ("a dashboard is not a research project"; the money view as "measures"); what is owed to a nameable business beyond confidentiality; and whether a public-body partner holding the held layer, the walk's claims or the assessment can be made to release them under information law.
  • Steer. "Record lines 1 and 2 are written first and line 2 dated" (Chapter 10 §19, rules 10.18, 10.20). The research-and-statistics fit is "for counsel" (Chapter 10 §9); defamation and commercial harm are "not researched; for counsel" (§5); the information-law question is "asked before it holds them" (§4). Put the three to counsel in one brief, with DB-74's accessibility questions beside them.

DB-50 · Registration for deeper views, and which views sit behind the door?

  • Steer. None; "a design decision the chapter leaves" (Chapter 10 §19, rule 10.11). No door in the first version: the held layer (DB-34), not a login, is the book's answer to depth, and a door would make the official reader the only one who registers. [Proposal]
  • Touches. Rule 10.11; Chapter 10 §7; DB-34.

CThe deviation log

The nine-line entry every departure from a rule is written to, and the entries so far

One file, in the repository, for every departure from a rule in the register. Chapter 16 §5 derived the entry and §11 states it once; Chapter 0's glossary points here. Three types of entry share the nine-line spine: a departure (the Decision Book's override log), an expressive element (Chapter 14's boundary log) and a borrowed mechanism (Chapter 15's precedent record). An entry is written before the departure ships, in the same change; for a departure from a rule tiered Fixed the build refuses the change without one (Chapter 16 §8). An accepted entry is never edited; it is superseded by a new one and kept. Entries are numbered sequentially and numbers are not reused.

In this appendix

  • The nine-line spine (every type)
  • The expressive type — Chapter 14's lines, added to the spine
  • The borrowed type — Chapter 15's lines, added to the spine
  • Entries

The nine-line spine (every type)

Line What it holds Why
Rule and tier The register's identifier, the rule's wording, and its tier in the register's sense A departure from a requirement, a sequence and a default are three different things
Trigger What made the departure necessary, specific to this case — the data, the reader, the device, the deadline A generic reason is what the regulator found in seventy of seventy-four; "lack of time or knowledge" is not one
Alternative What was done instead, and the alternative that was considered and declined, with why A departure with "a reasonable alternative" available is expedient by the coding standard's rule
Buys and costs What the break buys, from the house's list — attention, retention, comprehension, context, register or fit — and what it costs, named "An unnamed break is a mistake made confidently"; a purchase without a price is a bet
Test and result The form — recomputation, record check, scan, removal, reader test, adversarial walk — and what it showed, as a result and not a tick "it is not the act of ticking off a checklist … but performance of the actions it calls for"
Who decided, who checked Two names; the second not the first, and where the departure changes how a place is shown, someone from the place The regimes that work have a reader; the waivers nobody re-read were granted by those who wanted them
Date When the entry was written, before the departure ships; and, for an entry written after, that it was A record born "accepted" records a conclusion; the quality vocabulary keeps two words for before and after
Review The date by which the entry is re-read, or the condition on which it lapses, and who owns it Near-universal in the regimes read; absent in the house's four lines; the build lists the overdue
Status Proposed; accepted; superseded by; lapsed — with the old entry kept and never edited "If a decision is reversed, we will keep the old one around, but mark it as superseded."

The trigger line's "seventy of seventy-four" is the chapter's reading of the FRC's 2021 finding that four of seventy-four explanations were high quality; the regulator did not say the other seventy were generic.

The expressive type — Chapter 14's lines, added to the spine

An entry of this type is written for every expressive element before it ships; the build's removal check fails where the entry is missing (Chapter 16 §8). The spine's rule and tier line carries the tier claimed for the element; its buys and costs line carries the purchase in Chapter 14's template; its test and result line carries the four removals and the fifth check. The lines below are Chapter 14's own, as printed in its boundary log.

Line What it holds Why
Element What the expressive element is, where it appears, and the version of the display it was added to A register entry outlives the person who made the choice
Tier claimed Decorative; specific sensory experience; or a named Adaptable choice at the encoding level The tier is the argument's first move (Decision Book Ch 18)
Purchase What it buys, in the affective-intent template — "The viewer will [observe / position / strengthen / connect / behave] [noun]" — limited to what expression is measured to buy An unnamed break is a mistake made confidently
Touches Which view, encoding or claim it sits on or near Palette moves feeling more than data; the entry must say what it is next to
Mono What the greyscale render lost or changed Hue is the commonest leak
Silent What muting lost; for sound-as-content, where the text document is WCAG 1.2.1; 1.4.2
Still What disabling motion lost; where the pause control is ONS; WCAG 2.2.2 (Chapter 13)
Undressed What stripping the register lost or changed Mackinlay's second clause
Stripped beside dressed Whether the two versions say the same thing — no added size, order, brightness or cause — and, for a form, its estimated glance cost against a bar The fifth check
Twin and identification Where the precise twin is, how many steps away, and the words that identify the element to a reader who cannot see or hear it Ottley; WCAG's "descriptive identification" for a sensory experience
Tested, and status Whether readers saw the stripped and dressed versions and what each took from the data — figures and trend agreeing is the pass Chapter 14 §11

The borrowed type — Chapter 15's lines, added to the spine

An entry of this type is written for every mechanism the build considers borrowing from another sector — adopted, adapted or declined — before it ships. The lines are Chapter 15's precedent record, as printed.

Line What it holds Why
Mechanism What is borrowed, in one sentence, and the section of the record it feeds A borrowed rule lives in the record it serves, not in this one
Source The project or body, the document, its version and date, and the date it was read Rules change under the same name
Rule as printed The threshold, interval, colour, cadence or wording, quoted, from one named document A paraphrased rule drifts
Reason given The source's own stated reason The reason decides whether the rule transfers
Evidence What was measured about it, by whom, on whom, with n; or "none found" With a reason but no evidence or named cost, the entry is a bet, and says so
Condition or cost What the mechanism needs, and what the display does while the need is unmet A rule adopted without its condition fails silently
What the house changes Any departure from the printed rule, and why The departure is the house's, and is owned
Status Adopted; adapted; declined, with the reason; or awaiting a condition The record is a decision list
Review When the source document is to be re-read for change, and who owns the entry Sources retire

Entries

DL-001 · departure · proposed

Line Entry
Rule and tier The official practice, and the design system's preference, for text outside images (Analysis Function; Style Guide) — the source rule that register rule Every chart carries, inside its frame, title, unit, source, base, address and snapshot date, in addition to page text and never instead (DD-006; Chapters 12 and 13) departs from. Held in the register as Adaptable (house default) for the house, since the practice does not bind it.
Trigger The crop test: panels shared as screenshots from the page lose their title, unit, source and date, and the place-page is the one most likely to be shared as an image (Chapter 12 §8: 55.3 per cent of charts in the one measured corpus were screenshots).
Alternative Every chart carries title, unit, source, base, address and snapshot date inside its frame, in addition to the page text and never instead (Chapter 12 rules 32 and 33; Chapter 13 rule 13 states the condition under WCAG 1.4.5). Declined: page text only with a share control that attaches provenance to the image, because the share control is bypassed by a screenshot.
Buys and costs Buys context — provenance travels with the crop. Costs density on a phone and a second copy of six items on every panel.
Test and result The measured crop test, Chapter 12's form: screenshots of each panel put before readers who have not seen the page, scored for subject, unit, source, date, gate and the other column. Result: pending the first build. (Chapter 16 §11 printed an invented result for method only; it is not this entry's.)
Who decided, who checked Decided: the chapters (12 and 13), as the house's rule. Checker: to be named — the accessibility reviewer, against the 1.4.5 condition Chapter 13 stated.
Date 7 October 2026, written before any panel has shipped.
Review At the first release's crop test, and when the design system's in-frame provenance block exists; owner to be named.
Status Proposed.

Two things Chapter 16 carried to the register are not deviations and have no entry: Chapter 14's re-tiering of the house headline limit (Chapter 11 row 4 superseded by Chapter 14 row 14) and of genre, which are changes of tier made on evidence and logged in the chapters' conflict logs. The register's status column carries them.

DThe probe candidates

Seventy-five small tests the chapters proposed; none has been run

In this appendix

  • How to read this
  • The candidates, grouped
  • Lines not made into probes
  • What the register shows

Compiled 7 October 2026 from every [Validate with users] and [Prototype flag] line in Chapters 1–16 of version 2. Candidates, not a programme: which run first is an open choice with the book's steer in the decision log (00-plan/DECISIONS.md). Method only — nothing here is a finding about any place.

How to read this

A probe is a small, cheap test designed to settle one open question, with real people or with the build's own data. It asks one thing, of someone or something named, in a form that can be repeated, and its answer is set beside what was meant or expected. None of the probes below has been run.

The candidates come from two flags the chapters use. [Validate with users] marks something to test in conversation with the three user groups (policymakers and politicians; advocates and trade bodies; funders and investors) or with the scenes (artists, DJs, promoters, crews, venues). [Prototype flag] marks something the prototype can settle with its own data or its own build, which no literature can. Chapters 1 to 16 carry 189 such lines, numbered P-001 to P-189 in 06-register/work/probe-lines.md with their chapter, line and section.

A probe takes one of five forms. In a reader test, someone named is shown something and asked a fixed question, and the answer is compared with what was meant. A count takes the build's own data or logs over a stated period. A comparison shows two versions with one variable changed and compares the pass rate. In a walk, someone with a stated intent tries to do something. A recomputation works a figure out again with one thing varied. Where a [Prototype flag] is about the build's own data the form is given as a count and what it needs is the build; "count, by recomputation" marks the ones that run a calculation again.

Each row of the table is one probe, and lines that ask the same test of different elements share a row. Rows sit under the part of the book where the question was first raised, in the book's order, which is not an order of importance; a line that names more than one test is listed under each and counted once (P-056, P-097, P-170, P-171, P-175). The sixth column names which of the Vibe Map's four tests the probe serves, in short: useful to all (can something universally useful be co-designed), recognised (does it paint a picture a scene recognises), steers (does it steer decisions and collective action), travels (can it travel to another place and stay useful). The seventh gives the measure and the pass in the chapter's wording where the line gives one; "the plainest one" marks a pass this register suggests because the line gives none, and "names no group" means the flag's own definition applies, the three user groups or the scenes. Cost is small (an afternoon with the data, or a question added to something already happening), a session (one sitting with readers) or a build (something has to be made, or kept running, before the test can be read).

The candidates, grouped

Foundations (Chapters 1 to 3)

Probe What it would settle Lines (P-nnn) and chapters Form Who or what it needs Which of the four tests it serves What is measured, and the pass Cost (small / a session / a build)
1 · The recognition check Whether people from a scene recognise their own place in what is shown about it: the page, the profile, a figure pulled toward its neighbours, the peer set, the area's name and the label it is given. P-012 (Ch 2); P-049 (Ch 5); P-055, P-063, P-064 (Ch 6); P-084 (Ch 7); P-097 (Ch 8); P-143, P-149, P-151 (Ch 12) Reader test People from the scene the page describes, in the room and before release; the three user groups as well for the profile and the composite. The build first computes the direct and shrunk figures and the published peer set. Recognised; useful to all What each person recognises, what each corrects and which form each would act on, recorded by role and count and never by name. It passes only if the check comes before the release and a "no" can change what the next release shows; Chapter 2 calls anything less a nod. A session for each element; the shrunk figure and the peer set need a build first.
2 · The recognition route What has to happen for a scene's "that's not us" to change the next release. P-019 (Ch 2) Walk Someone from a scene with a correction to make; before that, a conversation with the scene about what the route should be. Recognised; useful to all Whether the correction reaches the next release, and by what steps. The line sets no pass mark; the plainest one is that a "no" produces a change, or a recorded reason, before release. A build, after one session to agree the route.
3 · One structure, read three ways Whether each user group sees the same structure in the display and still reads it for its own purpose. P-003, P-007 (Ch 1) Reader test Each of the three user groups, asked separately about the same display. All four, which Chapter 1 reads as one question; chiefly useful to all What each group says the display is made of and what it would use it for. It passes if the groups name the same parts and give their own uses; Chapter 1 adds that this rests on common ground built before the screens. A session with each group.
4 · The use log Who opens the display, what they touch, on what device, and what they take away. P-004, P-005 (Ch 1); P-015 (Ch 2); P-027 (Ch 3); P-126, P-127 (Ch 11) Count The build, logging from day one, in aggregate and under Chapter 10's analytics rule. Steers; useful to all Opens; panels opened by kind of reader and by time in the calendar; time to first interaction; device; the share of sessions that opened a tooltip, by device class; whether anyone uses the plain-table view; what is taken away. No pass mark is set: the dated, aggregate record is the result. A build for the logging; small to read each period.
5 · Positive deviance Which small places do well on the same resources as the rest, so that someone can ask what they do differently. P-002, P-006 (Ch 1) Count The build, on its own data. Asking the places found what they do is a separate conversation. Steers; recognised The places that sit well above others with like resources, by a stated rule. The lines set no pass mark; the plainest one is that the same places stand out on data that did not produce the list. Small.
6 · The reader table Whether Chapter 2's table of readers, which says what each decides and what evidence each accepts, matches the real readers. P-009, P-020 (Ch 2) Reader test The three user groups, with advocates and trade bodies and developers first, since the chapter found no study of either. Useful to all; steers Each reader is shown the row written for them and asked what is wrong with it. The lines set no pass mark; the plainest one is that no row is rejected by its own reader. The chapter expects the three groups to turn out to be at least seven kinds of reader. A session with each group.
7 · Chart against table Whether a reader who arrives opposed believes a plain table more than a handsome chart. P-010, P-014, P-017 (Ch 2) Comparison The three user groups, with readers who arrive opposed among them. Steers The same finding as a chart and as a table; which each reader would take into a room, and which they would believe from an opponent. The reversal counts as seen if opposed readers choose the table; until then the chapter holds it as a hypothesis and not a rule. A session.
8 · A trend panel read as monitoring Whether a panel showing a measure moving over time is read as an account of what happened and not as a claim about what caused it. P-013, P-016 (Ch 2) Reader test Policymakers and their officers. The build supplies a panel with a marked place where a comparison group would sit if an evaluation supplied one. Steers What the reader says the panel claims about cause, and what they say the empty place is for. The lines set no pass mark; the chapter's own words give one, that the panel "never implies a counterfactual it does not have". A build for the panel, then a session.
9 · The big number Whether one large figure with a label is read, remembered and trusted as well as the same fact written as a sentence. P-022, P-026, P-031 (Ch 3) Comparison Readers; the lines name no group. Useful to all; steers The same fact as a big-number tile and as a one-line sentence; which is remembered, which is trusted, and whether the figure is read correctly. No pass mark is set; the chapter found no controlled study of the tile at all. A session.
10 · Legend against direct labels Whether a chart is read more accurately with its labels on the marks or in a legend to one side. P-025 (Ch 3) Comparison Readers; the line names no group. Useful to all Accuracy and time on the same chart in both forms. No pass mark is set; the chapter says no controlled experiment exists and that this one is "cheap to run". Small.
11 · Chart literacy How well the display's own readers read charts and tables, which the chapter says no UK survey measures. P-024, P-028 (Ch 3) Reader test The three user groups. Useful to all A short test modelled on the Visualization Literacy Assessment Test; the share of items answered correctly, by kind of chart and by group, with the base stated. There is no pass mark: it is a baseline. A session.
12 · Forms of uncertainty Which way of showing uncertainty readers read correctly and trust. P-029 (Ch 3); P-085 (Ch 7) Comparison Readers, with those who arrive opposed among them; the lines name no group. Steers; useful to all The same finding as a bare line, an ensemble and a dotplot, and the same projection as two named scenarios and as a shaded band; what each reader says it means, set against what was meant, and which they say they trust. No pass mark is set. A session.

The analytical foundation (Chapters 4 to 8)

Probe What it would settle Lines (P-nnn) and chapters Form Who or what it needs Which of the four tests it serves What is measured, and the pass Cost (small / a session / a build)
13 · Provenance, with and without Whether seeing where a number came from changes what a reader would do with it, or how far they trust it. P-033, P-037 (Ch 4) Comparison The three user groups. Steers The same figure with and without its provenance panel; what each reader would do, and how far they trust it. No pass mark is set: the rule stands as an adopted standard either way, and the result would be what the chapter calls its "missing load-bearing wall". A session.
14 · Which lines get opened Which lines of the provenance panel and of the measure's card readers open, and which they say they needed. P-043 (Ch 4); P-050 (Ch 5) Reader test Readers looking at a figure they distrust; the lines name no group. Steers Of the ten provenance lines and the nine lines of the card, which each reader opens and which they say they needed before trusting the number. No pass mark is set. A session.
15 · Which nothing reads as which Whether readers can tell the kinds of empty cell apart when each is labelled, and what is lost when the cells are left blank. P-034, P-035, P-036, P-042 (Ch 4); P-117 (Ch 10); P-124, P-128 (Ch 11); P-152 (Ch 12) Reader test, with a comparison against blanks The three user groups. The build draws the cells. Useful to all; steers What each reader says each kind means: the six labelled kinds and the same table with blanks; a withheld cell, an unmeasured room and a held room side by side; a named hole in the missed column, read as a finding or as a failing; "could not exist" beside "nobody asked". Their confidence in the neighbouring figure is recorded for each. It passes if readers tell the kinds apart; Chapter 11 expects a shown gap to lower confidence in the panel around it and counts that as the gap doing its work. Whether a seventh kind is added stays Carly's decision. A session, once the cells are drawn.
16 · Count the nothings How much of each source is missing, and in which of the six ways. P-039 (Ch 4) Count The build. Travels; recognised For each source and month, the number of cells in each of the six (or seven) kinds. No pass mark is set: the table is the result. Small.
17 · The feed against a random benchmark How far the ticketing feed can stand as evidence of a whole place and not only of what the feed happens to catch. P-038 (Ch 4) Count, by recomputation The build, wherever a random benchmark exists for something the feed also measures. Recognised; travels Meng's defect correlation for the build's own feed. No pass mark is set; the chapter calls it the one number that "would settle how much the feed is worth". Small.
18 · Alerts that fire on nothing How often an alert or a highlight would fire when nothing has happened. P-040 (Ch 4); P-060, P-062 (Ch 6) Count, by recomputation The build, with the people who will answer the alerts. Steers How often the chosen outlier rule fires on shuffled data; how many views the real filter set lets a reader reach; the alert policy's run-length, limits and average run length. It passes when the false-flag rate is printed with the policy and the highlighting rule's error control is set against the number of views. Small.
19 · The concentration curve How unevenly ticketing revenue is spread across venues, shown as a curve and not as two percentages. P-041 (Ch 4) Count The build. Recognised The Lorenz curve and the Gini coefficient of ticketing revenue by venue. It passes as a statement only with the venue definition and the period stated beside it. Small.
20 · Sensitivity of the measure Whether the order a measure gives survives other defensible ways of building it. P-045 (Ch 5) Count, by recomputation The build. Steers; travels Rank intervals after normalisation, weights and aggregation are varied over the defensible alternatives, by the JRC's public method. It passes when the intervals are published with the measure. Small.
21 · What the weights really do Whether the weights a measure states are the weights it applies, and at what rate it trades one part for another. P-046, P-047 (Ch 5) Count, by recomputation The build. Steers Each part's effective importance, by Paruolo's correlation-ratio method; for any additive form, the exchange rate between each pair of parts in their own units. It passes if the chosen weights are shown to do something and the price list answers the chapter's refusal test. Small.
22 · The measure against platform coverage Whether a measure picks up culture or only how much of a place the ticketing platform covers. P-048 (Ch 5) Count The build. Recognised; travels The correlation of the measure with ticketing-platform coverage, place by place. A high correlation fails: the chapter calls it "the measure's own warning". Small.
23 · The deadweight share What share of visitors with a ticket would have travelled anyway. P-052, P-058 (Ch 6) Count, from one question asked Ticket-holders from outside the area, asked through the prototype. Steers The share who say they would have come anyway, with its base. It passes as a line on the claim ladder only if it is marked as stated preference and not dressed as a measurement. Small, once there is a way to ask.
24 · Measure the lead Whether the scene's series really moves ahead of the official series it is set beside. P-053, P-059 (Ch 6) Count, by recomputation The build. Steers Granger's test, or a turning-point comparison, against a named reference series. It passes either way, provided the "measured lead or its absence" goes on the screen; until then the caption says the lead is the thing being tested. Small.
25 · Written first, checked later Whether what the build noticed, expected or projected, written down with its date beforehand, held when the later data arrived. P-061 (Ch 6); P-073, P-079, P-080 (Ch 7) Count The build. Steers; travels The share of dated patterns that held on later data; for each change being watched, whether its expected shape (level, slope, lag) was logged before the after-data arrived; each projection, with its range and switching value, against outturn a year on. It passes when every entry is dated before its data. A build for the fields, and a year before it can be read.
26 · The funnel, read cold Whether a first-time reader reads a place inside the funnel as "not different", and which ordering of a comparison they read correctly. P-071, P-075, P-076, P-078 (Ch 7) Reader test The three user groups. The build draws a funnel for every rate, with limits set by the data and over-dispersion tested. Steers; useful to all What each reader says a point inside the funnel and a point outside it mean; which of a funnel sorted by size, a distribution with the place marked, a peer set in closeness order and an unsorted small multiple they read correctly. It passes if "inside the funnel" is read as "not different". A session, once the funnels are drawn.
27 · An answer with no rank Whether readers accept "higher / lower / similar" and "these two cannot be ordered" as answers to where a place stands. P-070, P-082, P-083 (Ch 7) Reader test The three user groups. Steers; recognised Whether each reader says the three words, with no rank, meet their need to know where a place stands, and whether they accept "incomparable" as an answer. No pass mark is set; the chapter found no usability research on whether lay readers can read it. A session.
28 · The published peer method How far a peer set made by one published method differs from the peers each place would choose for itself. P-072, P-074, P-077 (Ch 7) Count The build, with the studio and the scene choosing the variables that make two scenes alike. Travels; recognised The published set for each place with its closeness labels, and beside it the peers each place chose, kept as data. It passes when the method is fixed and published before any comparison is drawn, the number of peers fits the size of the field, and chosen peers are labelled as chosen. A build.
29 · The base effect How much of a year-on-year change comes from what happened a year ago. P-081 (Ch 7) Count The build. Steers The base month's contribution to every year-on-year figure the display shows. It passes when no such figure appears without it. Small.
30 · The date on the face Whether readers read the date the data runs to, what they do when it is old, and whether a four-part statement reads as trustworthy or as fussy. P-091, P-096 (Ch 8) Reader test, with a comparison of the single date against the four parts The three user groups. Steers; useful to all Whether the reader notices "data to [date]" at all, and what they do when it is old; which of "last updated" and the four parts (period, published, revised, frequency) they prefer. No pass mark is set; the chapter holds that the four parts read as trustworthy and says it has no user evidence for it. A session.
31 · What a map costs a phone How many bytes one view of the map costs a reader on the baseline phone and network. P-088, P-092 (Ch 8) Count The build, on the baseline device and network. Useful to all; travels Bytes for one view, counting tiles, boundaries, renderer and figures. No pass mark is set; the number goes in line 6 of the service record. Small; the chapter says an afternoon.

P-097 (Ch 8) Walk The slowest quarter of the three user groups' own phones, in their owners' hands. Useful to all Whether each phone draws the vector map and, where it does not, whether the raster version draws. Probe What it would settle Lines (P-nnn) and chapters Form Who or what it needs Which of the four tests it serves What is measured, and the pass Cost (small / a session / a build)

It passes when the floor for each view is set above the highest answer and the answers are kept as the knowability evidence. A session.

The lines ask only that the transfer be recorded; the plainest pass for a view is that nobody is identified. A session; the standard is half a day.

P-113, P-116 (Ch 10) Count, by recomputation The build, with its filters logged. 45 · The money view and the rising-value panel Whether a panel about money or rising property value reads as good news, as a warning or as a listing for buyers, before anyone decides whether it is shown. P-011, P-018 (Ch 2); P-111, P-118 (Ch 10) Reader test The scenes; investors; residents. Each is asked separately. Recognised; steers What each group says the panel means; whether the scenes read the money view as advocacy or as a listing, and whether they want it lit at all. No pass mark is set; Chapter 2 expects the readings to split and says a display that shows the figure "must decide, openly, whose reading it is serving". A session with each group.
46 · Who decides Which people, in what forum, a scene accepts as able to say a pattern is true and to decide what is held back, and what happens when the scene disagrees with itself. P-054, P-057, P-066 (Ch 6); P-114, P-119 (Ch 10) Reader test, as fixed questions in conversation The scenes; the three user groups as well on who counts as competent. Useful to all; steers Whether the scene names its own forum, a studio-convened panel or a public body's list as the body able to decide; who, in its view, "stands at the door"; with what power to say no; and what a procedure for dissent would look like when a venue and the forum want different things. No pass mark is set; Chapter 6 says this cannot be answered from a desk. A session.
47 · Withdrawal, said back Whether contributors understand, at the moment they contribute, what cannot be undone. P-120 (Ch 10) Reader test Contributors, at the point of contribution. Useful to all Each contributor is asked to say back what can and cannot be withdrawn. It passes when what they say matches the withdrawal tiers. Small.

The reading experience (Chapters 11 to 13)

Probe What it would settle Lines (P-nnn) and chapters Form Who or what it needs Which of the four tests it serves What is measured, and the pass Cost (small / a session / a build)
48 · The first screen, said back Whether someone who did not design the first screen can say what it shows. P-023, P-030 (Ch 3); P-131, P-135 (Ch 11) Reader test A reader from each user group, on their own phone; never the person who chose the default. Useful to all The sentence each reader says back, set against the sentence that was meant; how much furniture (stamp, unit, floor, chips) sits above the sentence before they skip; and, with one sentence for all set against three to choose between, which each group says back. It passes when readers say the sentence back, and it is run before any default is fixed. A session.
49 · Two landing patterns Whether a first screen that gives its message before asking for an input works better than one that asks first. P-125 (Ch 11) Comparison The three user groups. The build makes both patterns on the same data. Useful to all Time to the sentence, and whether the input is used. No pass mark is set; the chapter found no head-to-head test of landing patterns for a data tool. A build, then a session.
50 · Generated sentences, labelled Whether readers notice, mind or mark down a sentence when it is labelled as generated. P-132 (Ch 11) Comparison Readers; the line names no group. Steers; useful to all Ratings of the same sentences with the label and without it; whether generated sentences keep to the poster rule. No pass mark is set; the chapter's meta-analysis predicts lower ratings when labelled. A session.
51 · Finding the smallest districts Whether an inset, a tile map or a second view lets a reader find a scene's smallest districts. P-133 (Ch 11) Walk Readers sent to find a named small district; the line names no group. Recognised The share of readers who find the district in each form, set against the 30–40 per cent figure the chapter takes from Schiewe. A build for the three forms, then a session.
52 · The "how this argues" page Who opens the page that explains how the display argues, and whether a sceptical reader finds there what they came for. P-134 (Ch 11) Reader test, with a count of opens Sceptical readers, and the build's log; the line names no group. Steers Who opens the page; whether the sceptical reader finds what they came for; whether its existence changes anything for those who never open it. No pass mark is set. A session.
53 · A citation that survives a year Whether a state of the display cited in a document can still be found after the data has changed. P-129 (Ch 11) Walk The build. Steers A state is cited, the data is changed and the citation followed; then someone tries to make two addresses for one state. It passes if the snapshot and the citation still find what was cited and a second address cannot be made. Small.
54 · Matched legends Whether readers compare two views correctly when the legend's breaks are held the same across them. P-130 (Ch 11) Comparison Readers; the line names no group. The build makes both versions. Useful to all Correct comparisons of two views with the breaks held across periods and peer sets, and again with the breaks re-made for each view. No pass mark is set. A session, with two versions built.
55 · The scene's own area, drawn What area the people who make a scene would draw as its own, set against the units the figures come in. P-138 (Ch 12) Reader test, as a drawing task The people who make the scene, and not only those who live there. Recognised; travels The area each person draws, and how far the drawings agree with one another and with the unit used. No pass mark is set; the chapter says a scene's own unit is unmeasured. A session.
56 · Your own place against somewhere else Whether readers attend to, understand or remember a chart better when it is about their own place. P-139, P-144 (Ch 12) Comparison Readers; the lines name no group. Recognised Attention, understanding and recall for the same chart about the reader's own place and about another. No pass mark is set; the chapter calls it "the experiment the literature has not run". A session.
57 · Equal dignity Whether a column set more roughly than its neighbour is read as mattering less. P-140, P-145 (Ch 12) Comparison The three user groups, reading two mock pages. Recognised What readers make of the missed column on a page with both columns set equally and on one with the missed column rougher. No pass mark is set; the rule stands as the house's stance, and this would be its first test. A build for the two mock pages, then a session.
58 · Different, or better? Whether readers take one place's profile as better than another's when the form is meant only to show that they differ. P-141, P-146 (Ch 12) Reader test Readers; the lines name no group. Recognised Asked what two profiles show, whether the reader says "different" or "better", for each form tried. The lines set no pass mark; the plainest one is that readers say "different". No study the chapter found measured this. A session.
59 · The adjacency row Whether a row of things "close to your taste, new to you" is read as a poor match. P-142, P-147 (Ch 12) Reader test Readers; the lines name no group. Recognised Whether readers call the row a poor match; the chapter's measured caution is that too much that is new reads that way. It passes if they do not; the chapter holds the row as a probe and not a rule. A session.
60 · The crop and its frame Whether a panel cut out of the page still says what it is, and whether the items that travel with it can be read at phone size. P-148 (Ch 12); P-156, P-160 (Ch 13) Reader test Readers who have not seen the page, handed screenshots of built panels cold; the lines name no group. Steers; recognised What the reader can say the cut-out shows and where it came from; whether the frame's eight items are legible at phone size. It passes, in Chapter 0's words for the crop test, when nothing that travels could be read as a league table of places and the cut-out carries its title, unit, source, base, address and date. Small.
61 · A text route for "where" Whether a text route that answers "where" on the map is used, and what it changes for a reader who cannot see the map. P-154, P-159 (Ch 13) Reader test, with a count of use Blind and low-vision readers, and the build's log; the lines name no group. Useful to all Whether the route is used, and whether readers can answer which places border, which cluster and which is nearest. No pass mark is set; whether to build the route at all is a choice the chapter leaves open. A build.
62 · Accessible routes and the sighted reader Whether the accessible routes change what sighted readers take from a view. P-155, P-158 (Ch 13) Comparison, in observed sessions Sighted readers; the lines name no group. Useful to all What readers take from a view with the accessible routes and without them. No pass mark is set; the chapter says a handful of sessions "can begin and not finish" the measurement. A session.
63 · Status messages Whether one status message for each change reads as helpful or as chatty. P-161 (Ch 13) Reader test Readers who use a screen reader; the line names no group. Useful to all Whether readers call the wording "chatty", with one message for each change. The line sets no pass mark; the plainest one is that they do not. Small.
64 · Trend and figures, by which route Whether readers can say what the trend and the figures are, by whichever route they use, and whether screen-reader users find the long description. P-162, P-165 (Ch 13) Reader test Readers from the user groups, screen-reader users among them. Useful to all What each reader says the trend and the figures are, and by which route they got there; whether screen-reader users find the long description in the body text beneath the chart; whether the short description's trend reads as a repeat. The lines set no pass mark; the plainest one is that the trend and the figures are said back correctly. A session.
65 · Sound on the page Whether a sound on the page works as content for a blind reader, and whether its text document gives a deaf reader everything the sound carries. P-157, P-163 (Ch 13); P-168, P-170 (Ch 14) Reader test, with a count of sounds against documents Blind readers and deaf readers; the build for the documents. The lines name no group. Useful to all What a blind reader takes from the sound of a place; whether every sound that is content has a text document equal to it; whether the dressed version adds anything the document lacks. It passes when no sound that is content lacks its document, which Chapter 14 treats as a requirement before it is a test. The claim that one sound serves a blind reader and a curious reader alike stays a design intention until measured. A session; the documents are a build.
66 · The phone-read test Whether a reader on a phone can follow the summary at the lower-secondary level the COGA guidance asks for. P-164 (Ch 13) Reader test Readers on their own phones; the line names no group. Useful to all What the reader says the summary says, set against COGA's lower-secondary summary. The line sets no pass mark. Small.

Expression, precedent and the machinery (Chapters 14 to 16)

Probe What it would settle Lines (P-nnn) and chapters Form Who or what it needs Which of the four tests it serves What is measured, and the pass Cost (small / a session / a build)
67 · The two-audience claim Whether one display serves both of the audiences Chapter 14 says it serves, a claim the book says has no measurement anywhere. P-169, P-170 (Ch 14) Comparison Readers from each of the two audiences, as Chapter 14 names them. Useful to all Not given in the lines; it is to be taken from Chapter 14's statement of the claim when the probe is designed. Whether to build the probe at all is listed as the house's choice. A build.
68 · An expressive form against its plain twin What readers take from the data in an expressive form, set against its plain twin, and what the form costs at a glance. P-171, P-172 (Ch 14) Comparison Readers; the lines name no group. The build makes each twin. Useful to all; steers The glance cost of any form the house invents, "against a bar" in the line's words; what readers take from the data stripped and dressed, for each expressive element. The lines set no pass mark; the plainest one is that the dressed version loses nothing the stripped one gives. The chapter found no reader study that makes this comparison. A build for the twins, then a session.
69 · Dark against light Whether a reader reads the dark register or the light one better. P-171 (Ch 14) Comparison Readers, one by one; the line names no group. Useful to all The same view read in each register, reader by reader. There is no single pass: the chapter says the better polarity is individual. A session.
70 · The lag of late returns How long late figures take to arrive, so that the stretch marked as incomplete is the right length. P-174 (Ch 15) Count The build. Steers The lag distribution of any late-returns series the house will publish. It passes when the window is set from that distribution. Small.
71 · Marks for "not yet" Whether readers read the band over the incomplete tail, and a neutral marker, as "not known yet" and not as "no change". P-175 (Ch 15) Reader test Readers of the house's displays; the line names no group. Steers; useful to all What each reader says the band and the marker mean. It passes if the neutral marker is read as "no arrow yet" and not as "no change", and the tail is read as incomplete. A session.
72 · The one question about use Whether a single question put to readers measures use. P-175 (Ch 15) Count, from one question asked Readers who answer it; the line names no group. Steers The answers to the one question, with its response rate. The line sets no pass mark; the response rate is reported beside the answer. Small.
73 · Trust in the display itself How far readers trust the display, as distinct from the body that publishes it. P-176 (Ch 15) Reader test Readers; the line names no group. Steers A fixed trust question about the display, asked after reading. No pass mark is set; the chapter says trust in a display is not measured anywhere it read. Small, as a question added to another session.
74 · A deviation, disclosed Whether printing a departure from the rules costs the display a reader's trust. P-178, P-183, P-187 (Ch 16) Comparison Readers of the Vibe Map, some shown a published deviation entry and some not; the lines name no group. Steers Trust among readers shown the entry and among readers not shown one. No pass mark is set; the chapter's only evidence is the stated attitude of thirty-four editors, for whom the penalty attached to concealment and not to the deviation. A session.
75 · The first year's own record How often the rules are set aside and what keeping them costs, counted from the build's own first year. P-179, P-182, P-184, P-185, P-188, P-189 (Ch 16) Count The build and its makers' own record of hours. Travels The override rate when a logged reason is required; the first year's overrides set against the Fixed register's estimated about two hundred (the register has 280); hours per record section, per entry and per release. No pass mark is set: the log after a year is itself the measurement. Small to keep, and a year before it can be read.

Lines not made into probes

27 of the 189 lines are left out. None is lost: each is either not a test or is covered by a row above.

Lines Why left out
P-001, P-008, P-021, P-032, P-044, P-051, P-069, P-086, P-099, P-110, P-123, P-137, P-153, P-166, P-173, P-177 Each chapter's "Before you start" note, which defines the two flags and asks no test.
P-087, P-089, P-090, P-093 Whether to call the platforms' interfaces at all: a decision the chapter asks to be made and recorded with the platforms' terms open, and a matter for legal advice where the terms are unclear, not a test.
P-098 A summary row of Chapter 8's gap table, covering tests placed above (P-088, P-091, P-092); its remaining gap, on how stale open data is, names no test.
P-109 A summary row of Chapter 9's gap table, covering tests placed above (P-101, P-102, P-103); its remaining gap, on crowdsourced place scores against residents' own ratings, names no test.
P-136 A summary row of Chapter 11's gap table, covering tests placed above (P-125, P-126, P-127); its remaining gaps, on empty states, map-first landing, dot-density and hex maps and "red = bad", name no test.
P-167 A standard for how any probe is run (logs beside a survey, open materials, what people did set against what they said, and a comparison), not a test of its own.
P-180 A count of the book's 207 gap rows, which says where the flags sit and asks no test.
P-181, P-186 An index of version 1's nine candidates; each one's test, where there is one, sits with the probe for its version 2 home.

Three placed lines also carry items that are notes to the builders and not tests, and those items are not in the table: the boundary log as a working file (P-170); the vintage naming rule, which must exist before the first release, with the retirement plan and the precedent record as a working file (P-174); and the design of where a comparison would sit (P-016), which probe 8 uses and does not test.

What the register shows

The 189 lines make 75 probes: 162 lines are placed and 27 are left out. Eleven probes name people from the scenes and sixteen name the three user groups without them; a further twenty-eight ask for readers, respondents or contributors without naming a group, and one needs ticket-holders. Nineteen the build can settle alone, from its own data, its logs or a test of its own machinery. The probe the most chapters depend on is the recognition check (probe 1), which six chapters ask for (Chapters 2, 5, 6, 7, 8 and 12); the use log and the kinds of nothing come next, with four chapters each. By cost, 27 are small, 36 need a session and 12 need a build first; which of them run, and in what order, is Carly's decision.
